en: Excerpts from the *Yanmi Chao* (Draft Commentary on the Secret Meaning), a Detailed Explanation of the *Mahāvairocana-buddhābhisambodhi-vikurvāṇa-adhiṣṭhāna-sūtra*,
compiled by Shi Changwen, Court Consultant, Acting Record Keeper, Concurrently Serving as Attendant at the Qianwen Pavilion, and Editor of the History Bureau.
Written by Imperial Decree by Your Servant Zhao Xiaoyan, Knight of the Household Cavalry, Recipient of the Purple-Golden Fish Satchel:
How great is the teaching of the Tathāgata! It possesses both the Exoteric and the Esoteric. That which is called Exoteric refers to the five natures and the three vehicles.
That which is called Esoteric refers to the secret treasury of *dhāraṇī*. As for the perfect cultivation of the myriad practices and the complete realization of the ten [stages]...
In a single body one suddenly realizes the Dharma-realm, and with a direct mind one transcends three incalculable eons;

this is the inconceivable power of spiritual transformation and empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Therefore, Vairocana Buddha personally spoke these words of mouth-to-ear transmission for the Vajra Secret Master.
The mind-seal was transmitted in succession, profound beyond the profound and secret beyond the secret. Since the Tang Dynasty, there have been the Tripitaka Masters...
The Venerable Śubhakarasiṃha came from Central India and brought a Sanskrit manuscript to bestow upon the Dhyāna Master Yixing. By imperial decree, they translated it together;
however, as its principles were exceedingly profound and difficult to enter, he requested that Śubhakarasiṃha explain them once more.
Yixing subsequently refined and polished the text, titling it the *Yi-shi* (Exegesis of Meaning). This was truly the pivotal key for opening the gate of illumination. Furthermore—
In our Great Liao State, there was a Tripitaka-maṇi who came from Western India;

personally admiring the sacred transformation and determined to propagate the mantras and scriptures, he had extensively transmitted them but had not yet undertaken their compilation. As many years have passed, it is only now that this endeavor has been initiated.
We humbly reflect upon this:
Heaven has blessed the Emperor with divine wisdom and sagacity;
his strategic planning transcends the mundane,
and he governs the state with supreme impartiality, administering rewards and punishments without partiality.
With great faith he presided over others, his benevolence and majesty providing mutual support.
When examining the Confucian classics, he thoroughly mastered the purport of ritual, music, poetry, and history;

when researching the Buddhist scriptures, he encompassed the schools of Nature and Characteristics (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*) and Expedient Means and Reality (*upāya-tattva*). He had long plumbed the depths of the thirty-two vehicles of the ultimate teaching.
The Sublime Meaning of the *Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: A heroic composition personally authored [by the Buddha],
wherein the practice of contemplation is refined through diligent cultivation.
Having entered the Sudden Vehicle and attained profound awakening,
he had already studied Sanskrit since his residence in the Prince’s quarters.
One born with innate knowledge is by no means merely proficient in nature and habit;
they penetrate the very roots of phonology and script and thoroughly comprehend the source and flow of realization. This is intended so that the profound wind may be simultaneously supported.
During the Prosperous Age, there was the Grand Master of Total Secrecy, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Jueyuan. In his youth, he studied the art of ant-herding; in his maturity, he was called Pengqi.

His learning encompassed the myriad scriptures, and his practice was specialized in the Esoteric Section. Having received the excellent guidance of Maṇi, he exhausted the profound expositions of Yoga, and his reputation stood preeminent among the patriarchal masters.
By imperial decree, a lecture assembly was convened to propagate the ultimate principles of the Most Supreme Vehicle (Agryayāna); it was from this that [the Master] brought them to light.

He subsequently compiled five fascicles of topical outlines (*ko-wen*) for circulation in the world. From then on, during the intervals between his lectures and expositions, he applied himself with refined diligence and contemplation to further compose ten fascicles of commentaries (*chao*).
These works leave no textual passage unexamined and encompass every underlying meaning; they reflect the hidden subtleties of the earlier compositions and illuminate the ignorance of future students.

My intention in harboring these doubts was to repay the national grace in the near term and to propagate the Buddha Way in the distant future. Having already submitted this memorial, I have been urgently commanded to carve [the stele].
In addressing my humble subject, I may recount the aforementioned citation of Dao’an’s words: "The heavens are vast; I fear my narrow vision will merely act as a vain screen. "The moon is high;
I am ashamed that my cataracts prevent me from seeing it clearly. I have forced myself to set forth my vulgar sincerity to offer a slight tribute to these profound words.
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāvairocana Sūtra:
An Elucidation of the Esoteric (Yanmi Chao), Scroll One, with Preface.
By Chong of Yuanfu Temple in Yanjing, Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Acting Grand Preceptor, and Examiner.*
Composed by the Monk Jueyuan, who received the purple robe and the title of Grand Master of the Secretariat for the General Bureau of Salaries.

I reverently hear that the Awakened Sovereign manifested his form, solemnly embodying the ten bodies within the *dharmadhātu*; his subtle words established a model that transcends the five vehicles on divergent paths.
There are sentient beings who attain liberation upon beholding the Buddha’s majestic demeanor, and there are sentient beings who [attain liberation] upon hearing the Buddha’s...
Those who attain liberation through sound and voice truly differ according to their faculties, and thus their responses and influences also vary;

yet, where there is a direction for benefit, the effort is never in vain. As for that which encompasses both nature and characteristics within its principle, penetrates both the shallow and the deep in its meaning, serves as the fountainhead of the Eight Treasuries, acts as the key to the One Vehicle, stands alone as the pinnacle of the Perfect and Esoteric, and transcends all other schools—this is the Mahāyāna.
How magnificent is this *Vairocanābhisambodhi-tathāgatādhiṣṭhāna-vikurvita-nirdeśa-sūtra*!
It is the reservoir of moisture for the *dhāraṇīs* and the spiritual palace of the *dharmadhātu*. Only Vajrapāṇi may explore its mysteries; only the Lotus-Eyed One can peer into its depths.
To transcend the stages and grounds all at once is likened to supernatural powers; to swiftly leave behind the afflictions of entanglement is compared to—
In the practice of mantra-vidyā, one further enters the Vajradhātu, awakens the bodhicitta, ascends the Vajrāsana, and succeeds to the lineage of Bodhi.

Through homa, sacrificial offerings, and the service of the Great Lord (Maheśvara), as well as the rituals of fire-worship and consecration by sprinkling (abhiṣeka), one receives office in the Akaniṣṭha heaven according to its established traces.
Without entering the maṇḍala and without relying upon an ācārya, one shall not gain entry into its hands.

Since the time the Tripitaka Master Wuxie translated [the texts] and the Chan Master Yixing provided their commentaries, many years have passed and the reputation of these works has fallen into decline;
were it not for meeting this auspicious era, who could have brought them to such a culmination?
Now, our Sovereign, Emperor Tianyou, whose sagely writings surpass those of antiquity...
His martial prowess surpasses that of his contemporaries;
he governs the people with the ten wholesome deeds and instructs all creatures with the five constant virtues.

He comprehensively mastered the Confucian classics and produced works of poetry, fu, and epigraphic records; their elegant compositions were as brilliant and radiant as brocade, clearly manifesting the transformative power of education.

He was particularly adept in the Buddhist scriptures, composing hymns, prefaces, commentaries, and chapters; his writings brought splendor to the mountains and grace to the rivers, truly embodying the practice of the profound principles he had long cultivated.
The Imperial Will then charged this humble talent to proclaim the secret mantras. At the beginning of the Xianyong era, [the temple] was placed under the general administration of the Middle Capital.

Although the Great Officer of Qing Temple had been entrusted with its restoration due to the circumstances of the time, he had not yet fully executed it. Thereupon, the Vice Regional Commander and Palace Guard Commandant, Niu Xuan of Longxi;
the Palace Guard Commandant and Great Master Wuxuan Tongyuan, Lord Bi; and the Head Monk, the Purple-Robed Master, [took up the task].
More than one hundred virtuous men sent a joint letter, saying: "We have humbly heard that the purport of the Mahāvairocana teachings is vast and profound;
while the commentaries have already set forth their essential brilliance, the sub-commentaries on the most abstruse points have not yet opened the gateway to their ultimate mysteries.

If you would graciously accept our earnest sincerity, we pray that you may deign to hear us. Although we have long since discarded our writing tablets, we have not yet had the leisure to take up our brushes, and thus we have been unable to travel far beyond the Kang region."

After three years, an imperial decree was suddenly issued ordering the advancement of the *Shenbian jing* (Scripture of Divine Transformations), its commentaries, and its ritual protocols; thus, the time had arrived for the Secret Teaching Bureau (*Mikkyōsho*).

Thereupon, in order to respectfully repay the imperial bounty and simultaneously satisfy the sentiments of the public, I have laboriously gathered various interpretations to compose these fallacious exegeses, entitled the *Yanmi chao* (Commentary on the Elucidation of Esoteric Teachings).
During the previous winter, I was summoned by imperial edict to attend [the assembly].
While traveling, [the Emperor] personally received and presented [the text],
ordering it to be carved and printed; thus, the lost canons were revived.
This is the power of the Benevolent King; yet my awakening garden lacks wisdom, and my past seeds have resulted in a vision that is not innate knowledge.
My efforts are in vain, like the light of a torch—how could they benefit the radiance of the sun? I hope only that those who come after may together tread upon the profound frontier. Thus it is said.

In explaining this commentary, there are two major divisions: first, a preliminary clarification before the text; second, the formal explanation according to the text. The first section is divided into six parts: 1.
The causes and conditions for the teaching’s inception; 2. The inclusion within the scriptural collections (*piṭaka*) and teachings (*śāsana*);
3. The location where the sutra was preached; 4. A discernment of the depth of the teaching; 5. An elucidation of the sūtra’s essential purport; 6. The translation and transmission.

Furthermore, the first section, "The Causes and Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching," is divided into two parts: first, fulfilling past vows; second, conforming to the capacities of present beings.
The first of these is further divided into two: first, clarifying self-realization; second, explaining the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Regarding the initial passage:
"I, the World-Honored One Vairocana, in a past life, at the very first moment of the stage of self-awakening, gave rise to the bodhicitta and relied upon the three secrets."
Through skillful means, they cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the various gates of the perfections such as emptiness, and transcend the three types of false clinging.
Having transcended these three clingings, they immediately realize the body of the Dharma-realm of their own original ground.
Having realized this body, they dwell eternally within the Vajra Palace of the Dharma-realm, surrounded by a host of chief Vajradharas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields.
Taking Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and other bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields as their inner retinue,
and taking the assembly of great bodhisattvas as their vast retinue, the *Prajñāpāramitā* states:

"Those who wish to become the inner retinue of all Buddhas and those who wish to obtain a great retinue shall always enjoy inexhaustibility together with such Vajra Bodhisattvas and their immeasurable followers."
The secret, profound, inconceivable, and vast joy of the Dharma. This is subsequently analyzed in two parts:
first, the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and second, the analysis of its characteristics. Regarding the first, the analysis of its essence:

since it takes compassion and wisdom as its very essence, the World-Honored One Vairocana personally experiences such vast joy of the Dharma; this is due to his original vow to deliver all boundless sentient beings.

Therefore, he was stirred by great compassion and reflected thus: "All sentient beings possess such palaces of the *dharmadhātu* and these two kinds of retinues, as well as various dharma-joys no different from my own; yet, being shrouded by ignorance, they do not realize this for themselves.
Because of this lack of realization, they wander through the three realms of existence, laboring in vain and undergoing every kind of suffering. If...
If I were to abide solely in such an inconceivable and subtle state, sentient beings would not receive benefit;
therefore, I abide in the samādhi empowered by sovereign spiritual power (*vibhutva-adhiṣṭhāna*). Regarding the subsequent analysis of its characteristics:
after the Blessed One had reflected thus, he manifested within that samādhi inconceivable miraculous transformations (*vikurvita*).
The *Dhāraṇī-śambara-sūtra* states: "By the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Vairocana Tathāgata, he manifests with the vigor of the inexhaustible treasury of bodily adornments;
he manifests with the vigor of the inexhaustible treasury of the equality of speech and mind;
and furthermore, he manifests in various forms such as Mañjuśrī, Vajrapāṇi, and Padmapāṇi Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions."

Regarding the explanation of the method of the mantra-words (*mantra-pada*), the preceding section has always fulfilled past vows. The subsequent section, which follows the capacities of the audience, is divided into two parts:

first, the inquiry initiated by Vajrapāṇi; second, the response bestowed by the Bhagavān. The first part is further divided into two: first, the manifestation of the signs of doubt; second, the extension of the questions.
First, Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, beholding the signs of the empowerment manifested by the Buddha, looked upward and inferred as follows:
The wisdom that comes to realize the true nature of reality is like Maitreya beholding the supernatural signs of the Buddha’s light from between his brows and reflecting:
"Now the Buddha emits this light; is he about to preach this Dharma, or will he bestow a prediction of enlightenment?
It is just so now with Vajra, who beholds these signs of adornment—all of which are external traces. When a wise person perceives the branches and tips, they can thereby infer the roots.
It is just as when a great dragon of the world drives forth thunder and lightning, sending down a torrential rain that causes birds and beasts to roar and the hundred rivers to rush forward;
though one does not behold its form, one should know that the majesty and power of this dragon must be immense.

Now, the Buddha manifests auspicious signs, simultaneously responding throughout the entire Dharma-realm and bestowing empowerment; it is likewise so that although one cannot behold the physical marks of the Buddha’s body.
The physical forms and majestic deportment of the Tathāgata may be known by comparison, yet his power of wisdom must be vast;
if such is the case regarding the skillful means that illuminate the mundane, what then can be said of the realm that accords with reality?

When the questioner subsequently raised this doubt, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, having observed the marks of the Tathāgata’s adorned empowerment, further contemplated that these marks of empowerment arose from—
The Tathāgata’s omniscient wisdom arises for the sake of sentient beings; furthermore, upon what does the Tathāgata’s omniscient wisdom rely for its attainment?
Thus, following that [teaching], the assembly, desiring to resolve their own doubts, extended a request for instruction.
The Sūtra says: At that time, the Vajradhara Lord of Mysteries addressed the Buddha amidst the great assembly, saying: "World-Honored One..."
"Venerable One, how does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, attain the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*)?
Furthermore, what is the cause of such wisdom, what is its root, and what is its ultimate intention?
From what is the fruit of the Tathāgata’s unique knowledge of all-knowledge obtained? By what dharma is it caused, and by what..."
Taking the Dharma as its root, by what Dharma is it brought to ultimate fulfillment? Later, the Tathāgata provides the answer:
the Blessed One, having surveyed the entire assembly, responded in accordance with their inquiry. The Sūtra states that Vairocana addressed Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"The bodhicitta is the cause; great compassion is the root; skillful means is the ultimate fulfillment."
This scripture consists of seven fascicles and thirty-one chapters; from beginning to end, it entirely elucidates the meaning of these three phrases.
One should know that this is the collective meaning of the four syllables *ā ā aṃ aḥ*. This constitutes the first cause and condition for the arising of the teaching.
The second section, on the inclusion within the Pitakas and the teachings, is divided into two parts: first, the inclusion within the Pitakas, and second, the inclusion within the teachings.
First, regarding the one great period of teaching spoken by the Tathāgata, it is divided into three Pitakas: (1) the Sūtra-piṭaka, which consists of the *Kṣudraka-āgama* and other discourses;
(2) the Vinaya-piṭaka, which consists of the discipline (*vinaya*); and (3) the Abhidharma-piṭaka, which consists of the *Abhidharma*. Furthermore, within the Sūtra-piṭaka...

From within the middle [division], the *dhāraṇī* gate is separately established as one treasury (*piṭaka*). Furthermore, this is further divided into the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna to form eight treasuries.
The present *Śākyamuni-vikurvaṇa-sūtra* is subsumed under the eighth, the Treasury of Total Retention (*dhāraṇī-piṭaka*). Question:

Since it belongs to the eighth, the Treasury of Total Retention, why is "total retention" not established in the title of the scripture, but rather the word "sūtra" is used? Answer: Regarding the scripture...
This encompasses both the general and the specific; here, as we proceed according to the general, although the general designation is stated, one nevertheless adopts the specific name.

Thus, the ancient sages said that apart from the Three Vehicles there is separately the Vidyādhara [Vehicle], which is precisely this. Regarding the subsequent analysis of the inclusion within the teachings, the classifications of the teachings since antiquity have many branches;
for now, following the categories of the Qīngliáng [Zhìyǐ], there are five types: first, the Hīnayāna teachings, which speak only of the self.
Although the Śūnyatāvādin school taught that phenomena are empty, its teaching was still not fully explicit;

because it established the roots of defilement and purity based solely on the six consciousnesses and the three poisons, it did not exhaust the source of all dharmas, and thus gave rise to much dispute. Second is the Initial Teaching, also called the Partial Teaching (*prādeśika-śāsana*).

Since this has not yet exhausted the principles of the Mahāyāna Dharma, it is established as the first stage where one does not achieve Buddhahood; therefore, it is called "partial. Third is the Final Teaching.

Since it teaches that those of fixed nature among the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), as well as those of no-nature (*icchantika*), shall all attain Buddhahood, it represents the ultimate teaching of the Great Vehicle and is therefore called "Final" (*anta*).
It is also termed the "Jewel Teaching" (*ratna-śāsana*) because it accords with the true principle; thus, the principle is designated as "real.

These first two teachings both rely on stages and positions, achieving realization through gradual cultivation, and are therefore collectively termed "Gradual" (*anupūrva*). The "Sudden" (*tathāgatagarbha*) teaching, however, [is realized] in a single thought-moment.
Non-arising is itself named "Buddha. Because it is taught not by relying on the gradual progression of stages and positions, it is established as "Sudden" (*dun*).

Furthermore, it differs from the aforementioned gradual cultivation and is distinct from the subsequent perfect integration of all virtues; because it suddenly expounds this principle, it is called "Sudden.
Fifth, the Perfect Teaching clarifies that one stage is all stages and all stages are one stage, even within the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
The "Fulfillment of the Mind" (Manxin) subsumes the five stages of attaining perfect enlightenment and so forth;

because it relies on the Puxian Dharma-realm (Samantabhadra-dharmadhātu), with its infinite interpenetration like a celestial net (*jāla*) and its complete assembly of primary and attendant elements, it is called the Complete Teaching (*yuanjiao*). This is explained in detail in that commentary (*shu*).

The present *Shenbian* Sūtra is largely identical to this, differing only in being Esoteric (*mi*) rather than Exoteric (*xian*). Therefore, among the five teachings, this sūtra is subsumed within the Complete Teaching; hence, below—

The Preface states: "This sutra is the secret treasury and the perfect teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), which penetrates deeply into the true nature (*dharmatā*) and serves as the source of all teachings.

Furthermore, the Commentary states: "This sutra universally encompasses all Buddhist teachings. For instance, when it speaks of 'only the aggregates (*skandha*) and no-self,' and that 'the supramundane mind abides within the aggregates,' it subsumes the various schools of the Hīnayāna Tripiṭaka; and when it speaks of the aggregates, the *ālayavijñāna*, and awakening to one's own mind..."

The principle of original non-arising subsumes the meaning of the eight consciousnesses and the three natures as taught in various sūtras such as the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, as well as in treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

As it is said regarding the "mind of ultimate lack of intrinsic nature" and the "ten phrases on dependent origination," the various inconceivable realms described in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* are all contained therein. As it is said, one should know oneself as it truly is.
The mind is named "all-encompassing wisdom" (sarvākārajñatā); thus, the Buddha-nature, the One Vehicle, and the secret treasury are all contained within it.
Furthermore, according to the meaning of the *Akṣara-cakra-pravartana-dhāraṇī*, a single syllable encompasses all syllables, and all syllables are entirely one syllable;
beginning and end mutually encompass one another, pervading horizontally and vertically. All dharma-gates do not depart from this single syllable, which is identical [to the nature of the mind].

In the *Avataṃsaka*, the first of the forty-two syllables, the letter A, encompasses the maṇḍala and so forth; it likewise represents all forty-two positions, such that by citing one, the whole is subsumed.
The commentaries throughout the text judge this to be the vehicle of the perfect, sudden, and inconceivable supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Furthermore, as stated in the *Vajraśekhara-yoga-nirdeśa*, each of the five families possesses thirty-seven [deities].
From one Honored One up to thirty-seven Honored Ones, they mutually encompass one another like the interlacing light of Indra’s net of pearls,
unfolding infinitely and successively; if a practitioner of mantra practice thoroughly understands this principle, they are identical to the Tathāgata Samantaprabhāsa—
identical to each and every limb, each and every pore, each and every mark, and each and every secondary characteristic.

Abiding in the stage of fruition through the accumulations of merit and wisdom, one expounds the uncommon Buddha-dharmas of yoga and is even able to instantaneously benefit and bring happiness to all sentient beings; all that has preceded is subsumed within the second treasury of the teachings.

Regarding the third point, the location where the sutra was preached: according to the *General Catalogue of Dhāraṇīs* translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra, the *Mahāvairocana-abhisaṃbodhi-sūtra* exists in a large version of one hundred thousand verses, comprising approximately three hundred fascicles. The abbreviated version translated in the land of Tang consists of seven fascicles.
Since this scripture has not yet been transmitted in its entirety, the specific location where it was preached is difficult to clarify; for now, I shall cite the *Golden [Sūtra]* of our own school.
The *Gongding yujia bini bianshi yujia zhigui* (The Guide to the Essential Meaning of the Yoga of the Vajraśekhara, Comparing and Manifesting Yoga) states:

"The *Vajraśekhara-yoga* consists of one hundred thousand verses and is taught in eighteen assemblies. The first assembly is named the *Tathāgata-tattvasaṃgraha-rāja* (King of Teachings on the Compendium of the Reality of the Tathāgatas).

It contains four major sections: the first is named *Vajradhātu* (Vajra Realm); the second is named *Trailokyavijaya* (Victory over the Three Worlds); the third is named *Sarvārthasiddhi* (Universal Subjugation); and the fourth is named *Sarva* (All)."
The *Arthasiddhi* (Achievement of Meaning) manifests the four wisdom seals (*jñānamudrā*), each chapter of which describes six maṇḍalas; these cannot be cited in full here.
The second assembly, titled *Sarvatathāgata-guhyapati-yoga*, was taught in the Akaniṣṭha heaven and consists of four major chapters.
It extensively explains the principle of the subtle, ultimate reality (*sūkṣma-tattva-lakṣaṇa*) and describes the subjugation of Māra and the god Maheśvara.
The third assembly, titled *Sarvatantrasamuccayayoga*, was taught in the Palace of the Dharmadhātu;

it describes one hundred and twenty types of homa hearths, each with its own specific object of attainment. The fourth assembly, titled *Trailokyavijayavajrayoga*, was taught on the summit of Mount Sumeru;
it describes the eight great bodhisattvas, such as Vajragarbha, and the teachings spoken by each individual bodhisattva.
The four maṇḍalas— namely, the Great Maṇḍala, the Samaya Maṇḍala, the Dharma Maṇḍala, and the Karma Maṇḍala—

and furthermore, the fifth assembly titled the "Secret Observances and Secret Practices of the Worldly and Transcendent Vajra Yoga," briefly explain the five Buddhas within the realm of space in the city of Vārāṇasī.

The Sixth Assembly, titled "The Great Blissful Amoghasamaya-Truth Yoga," concerning the methods for seeking *siddhi* through the maṇḍalas of the various Bodhisattvas and the outer Vajra families, spoken in the palace of Paranirmita-vaśavartin;
it describes the Maṇḍala of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and so forth, up to the initiation of disciples and the conferral of the principle.
The Seventh Assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā-naya*, titled "The Yoga of Samantabhadra," was spoken within the palace of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
It describes the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of Samantabhadra and others, as well as Vajramuṣṭi and the external Vajra families, and explains that for those who practice,
there is no time or place where they do not rely upon worldly prohibitions, taking instead the bodhicitta as their [foundation].
The eighth assembly, titled "The Supreme First Yoga," which takes the previously established precepts as its basis, was taught in the Palace of Samantabhadra;
it concerns the external Vajra Family of Samantabhadra and is somewhat more extensive than the seventh assembly, though in general outline they are the same.
The ninth assembly, titled "The Yoga of the Net of Precepts of Ḍākinī in the Assembly of All Buddhas," was taught in the Palace of Mantras.
Establishing oneself as the deity, one rebukes one's own body and externally manifests a formal image,
while explaining the yoga method complete with the nine flavors: namely, Splendor (Vajrasattva), Heroism (Vairocana), Great Compassion (Vajradhara),
Joyful Laughter (Avalokiteśvara), Wrath (Vajraprabha), Terror (Trailokyavijaya), Disgust (Śākyamuni), Wonder (Vajrahāsa), and Tranquility (Vairocana within Yoga).
...and so on, up to the tenth assembly within the five sections, titled "The Great Samaya Yoga," which was spoken in the Palace of the Dharmadhātu.

It describes how the sixteen great bodhisattvas, from Samantabhadra Bodhisattva to Vajramuṣṭi, each spoke of four maṇḍalas, ending with the verse: "Foolish children, shrouded by ignorance, do not know this principle."
Seeking the Buddha by going elsewhere, one does not realize that he is right here;
in the worlds of the ten directions, the Buddha cannot be found elsewhere, for one’s own mind is itself the Perfectly Awakened One. Elsewhere, the Buddha is not spoken of.
The eleventh assembly is named the *Mahāyāna-abhisamaya-yogatantra*. It was taught in the Akaniṣṭha heaven, concerning the Buddha Vairocana up to Viśvakarman Bodhisattva.

The twelfth assembly, titled "The Supreme Yoga of Samādhi," which includes the [deities] from Vairocana and the eight great offerings to the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), was spoken at the Bodhimaṇḍa in the realm of space.

It extensively explains the yoga of one's own self as the *iṣṭadevatā* (personal deity), including the eight bodhisattvas of Vairocana and so forth, up to the realization of the gateway of the letter *A*, which penetrates the non-obstruction between defilement and purity. The thirteenth assembly is titled... [name].
In the Vajradhātu Maṇḍala, during the Great Samaya-Truth Yoga, all the Buddhas of the ten directions, with one voice and in unison,
requested Vajrasattva to expound the teachings on the truth of the samayas. Having accepted the request,
he taught the seventeen-syllable mantra of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, which serves to attain all mundane and supramundane siddhis.

The fourteenth assembly, titled "The True Yoga of the Tathāgata’s Samaya" (held at the same location as above), explains within this sutra how the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra and the sixteen great bodhisattvas form a single body through the four means of integration (*saṃgraha-vastu*). It extensively teaches the mutual interpenetration of the five families:
the Tathāgata family is the Vajra family, and so on, up to the Dharmadhātu being *tathatā* and *prajñā* being reality (*bhūtatā*).
The fifteenth assembly, titled the *Guhyasamāja-yoga*, was spoken in a secret location; specifically, it was spoken at the site of the master Upagupta.
It is called the Palace of Prajñāpāramitā, wherein the teachings, maṇḍalas, mudrās, mantras, and observances of the vows are taught.
It is like worldly passion in its correspondence with speech. Within this assembly, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin...
Sāriputra rose from his seat and addressed the World-Honored One, saying, "O Great Being, one should not utter coarse words or speech associated with defilement.
The Buddha said, "What characteristics do you perceive in my speech that is associated with purity?

This speech of mine is a skillful means to guide sentient beings toward the Buddha-way through the empowerment of syllables and the transformation of conditions; it possesses no [defiled] characteristics, yet it brings about great benefit. It should not [be regarded as coarse]."

The sixteenth assembly, titled *Advaya-samatā-yoga*, was spoken in the Palace of the Dharmadhātu regarding the non-duality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, the mundane and the supramundane, and self and other;

it teaches that the movement of the mind, the raising of the eyes, and the sensory objects of sound, smell, taste, and touch—along with all defiled thoughts—are identical to the *tathatā* dharmadhātu, whereby they all become the bodies of all Buddhas. The seventeenth assembly is titled *Tathāgata...* [the title continues].
In the eighteenth assembly, titled the *Vajrābhiṣeka-yoga*, the fourth section, which is spoken from the palace of the *bhūtakoṭi* within the Yoga of Space,
the Vairocana-Samantabhadra Outer Vajra Family is explained one by one. Each of these four-seal maṇḍalas is taught for practitioners who,
through correspondence with each of these deities, become equal in measure to space and identical to the Dharmakāya.
The Bodhisattva Vajrasattva of the Dhyāna-heaven requested the Buddha to explain for Mahābrahmā, the lord of the Sahā world,
the ritual procedures for introducing disciples into the maṇḍalas of the five families, comprising thirty-seven [sections],
up to the point of receiving the training and performing the mental recitation for the disciple; wherein one arranges the mantra syllables in a clockwise sequence upon a moon disc, one by one.
In accordance with the true nature (*dharmatā*), the cycle continues from end to beginning; there is no need for the use of prayer beads or fixed numerical limits.

Rather, the limit is defined by realizing the gateway of principle, maintaining an undistracted mind, and abiding in the yoga of the *iṣṭadevatā*. The above constitutes eighteen assemblies across fourteen locations:
three assemblies in the Palace of the Dharma Realm (*dharmadhātu-kula*), two assemblies in the Palace of Samantabhadra, and [one] in the Vajra [Palace].

The two assemblies at the *dharmadhātu*-maṇḍala both take fourteen locations; the meaning of this sutra corresponds to the sixteenth assembly, spoken at the location of the Palace of the *Dharmadhātu*.
How is this known? Because this sutra states: "Abiding in the vast *vajra*-dharmadhātu-palace sustained by the Tathāgata," and further says:
"Expounding the dharma-gate of the equal phrases of body, speech, and mind"—thus it is identical to that [sixteenth assembly].
This assembly encompasses all within one; the Dharma-gate therein is likewise so. This concludes the third section, which explains the setting of the sutra’s assembly.

Fourth, we shall distinguish the depth and shallowness of the teachings: for the sutra opens up the meanings of sudden and gradual, and these are divided into shallow and deep according to the capacities of sentient beings.

When differences are resolved within the Dharma-realm, there is no duality. This sutra is intended for those of both superior and inferior capacities, and its teaching encompasses both the Exoteric and the Esoteric.

"Exoteric" refers to the teaching on the five natures and the One Vehicle, which subsumes all sutras and śāstras; "Esoteric" refers to the gateways of the *akṣara-cakra* (syllable-wheel), meditative practice, and dhāraṇī.
To briefly cite one or two examples to demonstrate the profundity and excellence of its teachings, and to illustrate its own specific system, we have the *Amoghapāśa* and the *Susiddhi*.
In explaining the construction of maṇḍalas, it is said that one must use gomaya and gomutra;
"gomaya" refers to cow dung, "gomutra" refers to cow urine, and "mūtra" refers to liquid. According to the methods of Western India (Sindh), dairy cows are no longer used at all;
rather, only those raised for breeding are taken, grazing freely on the waters and grasses of mountains and marshes where they eat to their heart's content.

The fragrant grass does not eat grain; its dung is fragrant and pure. In that region, it is collectively accepted as a substance for purification and used for the site of a *śīla-maṇḍala*, where it is easily applied with colorful pigments.
Other oxen are incapable of this. This is a shallow explanation. If explained deeply:
*Gau* has the meaning of "practice" (*caryā*), because by entering the *a*-gate, it signifies that all phenomena are without practice (*acaryā*). *Ma* is the meaning of "I" (*aham*).
What is the meaning of this vehicle (*yāna*)? It is because all phenomena are without movement (*apracāra*), for in all phenomena a self (*ātman*) cannot be apprehended.
Since there is no self, there is neither that which is mounted upon nor a mounter; therefore it is called *gomaya*.
*Gomutra* (a compound of *go* and *mūtra*) is translated as "cow-urine. *Go* is explained as before; *mūtra* means "like" (*tathatā*) and signifies being free from [conceptual proliferation].
The meaning and essence of "dust and defilement" (*rajas*) is the true mark (*dharmatā*) of the mind.
If a practitioner of Mantra cultivates the inner maṇḍala of great compassion, they can purify the ground of the mind with such stainless, *tathatā*-like "fecal liquid," rendering it ultimately pure.
Drawing the circular altar of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-maṇḍala*) therein is precisely the application of the meaning of *gomaya* (cow dung) in this context. Furthermore:

To say that "three months of recitation" refers to the skillful means of the three rotations of *a-a-āṃ* within the pure and perfectly luminous state—how could this possibly be interpreted as a period of ninety days?
If one were to compare it with other teachings, for instance, the Sanskrit term *kalpa* is commonly translated in other systems as "time-period.
If one traverses three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one is said to attain Buddhahood; however, the meaning here is distinct from that of the Sanskrit term.
The term *kapa* is translated as "false attachment" (*mithyā-abhiniveśa*). There are three types of false attachment: coarse, subtle, and extremely subtle.
These three types of false attachment, based on the five root afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*), first branch into ten; secondly, they further branch into twenty;
and so on, up to the fifth stage, where they constitute the number of one hundred and sixty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). If one relies on this sūtra to develop [this understanding]...

Cultivating the Bodhicitta through the secret practices of speech and action, one first contemplates the five types of metaphors—gathering foam, floating bubbles, a mirage, a plantain tree, and a magical illusion—to observe the emptiness of self-nature.
By abandoning the one layer of coarse deluded attachment through these [and] the one hundred and sixty minds, one immediately transcends one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.
Furthermore, one employs the six [metaphors]: illusion, a mirage, a shadow, an echo, a whirling firebrand, and a city of the Gandharvas.
By contemplating the emptiness of the unobtainable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*) through ten similes—

such as a phantom, a mirage, a dream, a shadow, a city of the *gandharvas*, an echo, the moon in water, a bubble, a flower in the sky, and a whirling firebrand— one transcends one hundred and sixty mental states and a layer of subtle deluded attachment, thereby surpassing two *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. Furthermore,
by contemplating the inconceivable emptiness (*acintya-śūnyatā*) through these same ten similes, one transcends another hundred and sixty mental states and a layer [of attachment].

The most subtle deluded attachments transcend the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. If a practitioner can resolve these three deluded attachments within a single lifetime, they will attain Buddhahood in that very life;

what need is there to discuss [longer] timeframes? Furthermore, regarding acts such as sexual misconduct, theft, killing, and lying, all other teachings collectively declare them to be *pārājika* (defeats).
If one commits them, they are strictly defined as grave offenses. In this teaching, however, they are considered *sthūlātyaya* (grave transgressions).
Why is this? Because it does not obstruct the bodhicitta. For a bodhisattva, these four grave offenses are not considered extremely heavy;
rather, they first require that one not abandon the Three Jewels and further require that one not abandon the bodhicitta. This is the true set of four grave offenses for a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva gives rise to such a thought as to forsake the Buddha, it is called a violation of the grave prohibitions. This is why.

The Tathāgata is the source from which all wholesome dharmas arise. Because Bodhisattvas take refuge in the Buddha, they are able to accomplish all the myriad practices, such as the stages (*bhūmi*) and the perfections (*pāramitā*).
Just as one must rely on the seed-syllable *A* to produce the fruit of the syllable *Ā*, if one abandons the natural wisdom of the syllable *A*, then all wholesome dharmas [will not arise].
Because it cannot arise, to abandon the Buddha is to sever the life-force of all Bodhisattvas and cut off the root of their attainment of Buddhahood.
If one commits sexual misconduct, theft, killing, or lying, these merely create obstacles on the path; they do not sever the seed of Buddhahood.

Therefore, they only constitute *stūlātyaya* (grave offenses). *Stūlātyaya* is sometimes called a "great offense" (*mahāpatti*) and sometimes called "coarse evil" (*audārika-akuśala*), because the Buddha cannot be abandoned.
The Dharma and the Saṅgha are likewise, and the bodhicitta is also thus; it is the root of all practices.
If one is separated from this mind, there will be no Dharma of the Bodhisattvas at all. Therefore, to abandon it constitutes a pārājika offense.
Now, within this school, this [offense] is further treated as a preliminary means (*upāya*) for accomplishing the four kinds of samaya precepts, which state that one should not...

Abandoning the True Dharma, forsaking the bodhicitta, being stingy with all dharmas, and acting without benefit for sentient beings—when receiving these precepts, one immediately empowers them with the secret mudrā and seed-syllable.

By this, one receives the empowerment of the water of wisdom (*jñānābhiṣeka*), and seeing one's own body as identical to Mahāvairocana, one turns the wheel of Dharma. Know that this teaching, compared to other exoteric teachings, is...
The preceding sections have collectively constituted the fourth [part], which distinguishes the profundity and shallowness of the teachings.

Fifth, regarding the elucidation of the sūtra’s essential purport (*piṭaka-artha*): that which is the superior point of the discourse is called the "essential" (*piṭaka*), and that to which the essential points converge is called the "purport" (*artha*).
This sūtra takes as its essential the contemplative practice of the secret and inconceivable *dharmadhātu*-dependent origination; if one considers it from the perspective of the secret...
Taking the inconceivable *dharmadhātu* dependent origination as the primary tenet (*śāstra*), one takes contemplative practice as the goal;
or, taking contemplative practice as the primary tenet, one takes the secret, inconceivable *dharmadhātu* dependent origination as the goal.

Thus, the tenet is the goal, or the tenet is itself the goal—this can be understood through reflection. For this reason, throughout the various sections of the commentary, it is sometimes subsumed under the inconceivable *dharmadhātu*.
The dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) or its profound and secret contemplative practice appears in numerous texts; I shall not trouble to cite them all here.
The sixth section, "On Translation and Transmission," is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the translations, and second, examining the transmission. Regarding the first:
during the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty, there was the śramaṇa Śubhakarasiṃha, a native of Central India and a descendant of the Śākya clan, whose character was...

His demeanor was refined, his character noble, and his intelligence transcended the common; he had thoroughly mastered the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) and fully practiced the three trainings (*triśikṣā*).

He attained profound mastery in the sources of *dhāraṇī* and meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*), and there was no artistic skill or specialized talent with which he was not conversant. Setting out from Central India (*Madhyadeśa*), he traveled to the Eastern Land (*Cīna*).
Upon reaching North India, his reputation reached the Imperial Capital. His Majesty dispatched an envoy to welcome him, arriving in the year of Jǐngchén (the 4th year of the Kaiyuan era).
Carrying the Sanskrit originals, he arrived at Chang’an. Initially, they were deposited at Xingfu Temple; later, by imperial decree, he resided at Ximing.
In the fifth year, the Ding-si year, he translated the *Ākāśagarbha-śravaṇadhāraṇī-dharmaparyāya* and other texts at the Bodhi Monastery, and was further ordered to present them to the palace.
Furthermore, in the past, the śramaṇa Wuxing traveled west to India; having completed his studies and prepared to return, he reached Northern India on his way back.
Unfortunately, he passed away; however, the Sanskrit manuscripts he had brought were ordered by imperial decree to be welcomed back to the Western Capital (Chang’an) and stored at Huayan Monastery.
There, Amoghavajra and the śramaṇa Yi Xing selected several Sanskrit scriptures and the sublime gates of dhāraṇī that had previously never been translated.
In the twelfth year [of the Kaiyuan era], they followed the imperial entourage into Luoyang and, at Dafuguang Monastery, translated the *Mahāvairocana-sūtra*.

The *Vairocana Sūtra*, translated orally by the śramaṇa Bao Yue and recorded in writing by the śramaṇa Yi Xing under imperial command, features a refined synthesis of literary elegance and substance that perfectly harmonizes with its profound meaning.
Later, Bianzheng transmitted it, for this sūtra is the deep reservoir of dhāraṇīs and the mysterious gateway to the secret treasury;
through the medium of conditioned phenomena, it extensively reveals the signless. May the Chan Master [Chang] uphold it!
Concerned that students might cling to the literal text while losing the intended meaning, I examined the teachings of both the Great and Small Vehicles to find their corresponding principles.

I synthesized the subtle words of both the Exoteric and Esoteric traditions regarding the nature (*dharmatā*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), compiling them into fourteen fascicles titled *Yishu* (Exegesis on the Meaning).

Before I could propagate this profound doctrine, the Emperor fled to Shu and the Master passed away; thus, this work was nearly lost. It was only upon the accession of our Great Liao’s Emperor Xingzong to the throne that my aspiration was realized.

In order to propagate the treasury of the teachings so that they might reach both near and far, an imperial decree was issued to complete the carving of the woodblocks, requiring individuals to conduct detailed examinations.
Wǒjuéyuànchí received this imperial mandate and, having the honor of participating in the editorial workshop, he collected various commentaries and obtained this manuscript.
It was during the fifth year of the Qīngníng era, when the current Emperor succeeded to the throne.
The imperial decree to carve the woodblocks for circulation has been completed; the preceding six sections, which were briefly selected from the first part of the text, are now finished.

Second, the formal commentary on the text is divided into two major sections: first, an explanation of the preface to the sub-commentary (*śāstra-ṭīkā*), and second, the interpretation of the main body of the sub-commentary. Regarding the preface:
This is divided into three parts: first, the title; second, the author; and third, the main text. Furthermore, within the title, it is again divided into three:
first, the scriptural title; second, the name of the scripture; and third, the word "preface.
Now, regarding the scriptural title, it consists of twelve characters: *Mahāvairocanābhisambodhi-vikurvāṇa-adhiṣṭhāna-sūtra*.
This section is divided into two parts: first, an analysis of individual terms, and second, a synthesis of their combined meaning.
The analysis of individual terms is further divided into two: first, the transliteration of the names, and second, the explanation of their meanings.
Regarding the transliteration of the names: in Sanskrit it is *Mahā-vairocana-siddhi-sambodhi-vajriṇa-tathāgata-sūtra*. *Mahā* means "Great," and *Vairocana* means "Pervasive Illumination."
*Siddhi* means "accomplishment"; *sambodhi* means "perfect awakening"; *vikurvita* means "miraculous transformation"; *adhiṣṭhāna* means "empowerment"; and *sūtra* means "discourse.
Taken together, it is titled *The Great Vairocana’s Perfect Awakening, Miraculous Transformation, and Empowerment Sūtra*.

Regarding the subsequent explanation of its meaning, it is further divided into two parts: first, an explanation based on the three great aspects; second, an explanation based on the three bodies (*trikāya*).

To explain briefly, regarding the three "Greats": the single character for "Great" (大) refers to the Greatness of Essence (體大). This signifies the One True Dharma-realm (一真法界), which extends horizontally throughout the ten directions and vertically through the three periods of time.
It has no beginning to be sought, nor can its center or periphery be seen; it is neither born nor extinguished, neither departing nor arriving.
This is precisely what is called the Greatness of Essence. The four characters "Vairocana" (毗盧遮那) refer to the Greatness of Characteristics (相大), meaning that his radiant light pervades everywhere.

"Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) is another name for "illumination," in the sense that it dispels darkness and is all-pervasive light; because it possesses the constant, blissful, self, and pure qualities of the nature of reality as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it is the "Greatness of Aspect" (*lakṣaṇamahātmya*).
"Buddhahood" (*buddhatva*), which consists of the empowerment of spiritual transformations (*vikurvaṇādhiṣṭhāna*), is the "Greatness of Function" (*karmamahātmya*);

this refers to the fact that by means of the perfectly awakened essence, all obscurations are exhausted, and one gives rise to three kinds of spiritual transformations to empower, sustain, and protect sentient beings.
By means of the empowerment of the supernormal power of miraculous transformations (*ṛddhi-vidhi-prātihārya*), he increases majesty;

by means of the empowerment of the supernormal power of mind-reading (*ādeśanā-prātihārya*), he increases wisdom; and by means of the empowerment of the supernormal power of instruction (*anuśāsanī-prātihārya*), he increases eloquence.

Thus, through these three secret expedients (*triguhyopāya*), he universally encompasses the three types of transformation and the tenfold functions of the retributive body for others, manifesting forms in accordance with sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm to guide the myriad kinds of emotional dispositions.
The roots return to the One Vehicle, and the fire of wisdom is precisely the Great [Vehicle]. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "First is the Greatness of Essence (*tǐ-dà*):
it refers to the fact that the True Suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena is equal, neither increasing nor decreasing. Second is the Greatness of Characteristic (*xiàng-dà*):

it refers to the fact that the Tathāgatagarbha is fully endowed with immeasurable inherent merits. Third is the Greatness of Function (*yòng-dà*): it refers to its ability to produce the wholesome causes and effects of both the mundane and supramundane worlds."

Furthermore, "Great Vairocana" (Mahāvairocana) belongs to the category of the Great Body (*dharmakāya*), while the two characters for "Becoming Buddha" (*abhisambuddha*) represent the Great Marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and the Great Empowerment of Miraculous Transformation (*vikurvita-adhiṣṭhāna-kriyā*).
Alternatively, the single character "Great" is the general term, while "Vairocana," "miraculous transformation," and so forth, are the specific terms;
since the Body, Marks, and Activity are all "Great," these two [aspects] are explained according to the meaning of the Three Bodies (*trikāya*). Thus, "Great Vairocana" is—

The attainment of Buddhahood as the *dharmakāya* (Dharma-body) is itself the manifestation of the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment-body) through its miraculous empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) as the *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation-body).

Alternatively, the attainment of Buddhahood by the Great Vairocana, who belongs to the *dharmakāya*, is likewise the manifestation of the *saṃbhogakāya* through its miraculous empowerment as the *nirmāṇakāya*.
Or, the single character "Great" (*mahā-*) may be understood as encompassing all three bodies: namely, the Great *dharmakāya*, the Great *saṃbhogakāya*, and the Great *nirmāṇakāya*.
Furthermore, if the true and the responsive are unimpeded, then Vairocana is Vairocana; because the entire essence of Vairocana is Śākyamuni, the "Chapter on Names and Titles" states:
"He is called Vairocana, or he is called Śākyamuni. Whether the three great bodies (trikāya) are identical or distinct, contemplate this according to the principle.
As for the "sūtra," it consists of the four elements of sound, name, phrase, and syllable which serve as the means of expression.

The essence [of the *Sūtra*] is the Dharma; according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it also includes the meaning expressed (*vācya*). If one explains the meaning, it takes the five dharmas as its essence.

As for the name, it is derived by encompassing the four meanings of "constant" and "encompassing. Alternatively, according to the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, there are five meanings of a *sūtra*:
a spring, a source, a display, a measuring line, and a garland. A "spring" pours forth without exhaustion; a "source" flows on and on, increasing and flourishing.
Extensive exposition clarifies the principles of phenomena; the carpenter’s line establishes the standard for distinguishing the correct from the deviant.

Just as a garland is formed when a single thread can string together flowers to create a wreath, the subsequent combined explanation is as follows: the term "Great" (*mahā*) refers to the Greatness of Essence (*svabhāva-mahattva*);

Vairocana refers to the Greatness of Characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*); and the miraculous empowerment of attaining Buddhahood refers to the Greatness of Function (*karma-mahattva*). Thus, there are two aspects of attaining Buddhahood.
The term "spiritual transformation" (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*) refers to the wondrous activity of benefiting others through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the perfection of the fruit of self-benefit.

"Spirit" (*ṛddhi*) is its wisdom; "transformation" (*vikurvaṇa*) is its object. Thus, "spiritual transformation" is named after its object. Alternatively, "spirit" is itself the "transformation," and the name is established based on its essential nature.

Because the function of empowerment is present within this spiritual transformation, spiritual transformation is itself empowerment. Furthermore, spiritual transformation is that which can give rise to the three types [of miraculous displays].

The empowerment of miraculous transformations (*ṛddhi-adhiṣṭhāna*) refers to the three types of manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*) that are produced; these are the empowerments of miraculous transformation.

When viewed in relation to the two characters "attaining Buddhahood" (*sambuddha*), they are designated by way of their cause—that is, the name is established based on that which gives rise to them—thus forming "the empowerment of miraculous transformation for attaining Buddhahood.
This constitutes the greatness of function (*vṛtti-mahattva*). Regarding the distinctions between the three kinds of greatness, this is the Great Vairocana, who is "Great" (*mahat*).
Regarding the term "Vairocana’s empowerment of the miraculous transformation of attaining Buddhahood," it is analyzed as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent designation).

If the three greatnesses (*mahat*) are inseparable, then "Great Vairocana" is the empowerment of the miraculous transformation of attaining Buddhahood, analyzed as a *karmadhāraya* (appositional designation).

In this scripture, the single character "empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the designator (*vācaka*), while "Great Vairocana" and so forth are the designated (*vācya*). When the designator and the designated are viewed in relation to one another, the name is established as a *tatpuruṣa*.

Alternatively, "Sūtra" (*jing*) is the general name, while "Great Vairocana," etc., are the specific titles; the latter distinguish the former by means of the specific, and this is also analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
A detailed explanation of the sūtra title is clarified below as set forth in the commentary. Thus concludes the preceding section, which has fully explained the title of the sūtra.

Next, regarding the title "Yixi" (Commentary on the Meaning): this refers to the two characters "yi" (meaning) and "shi" (commentary). "Yi" (meaning) refers to the doctrinal principles, that is, the essential purport of the sutra.

"Shi" (commentary) refers to the explanation, that is, the words of the sub-commentary (*śāstra*). This means that the master of the sub-commentary composed fourteen volumes of magnificent prose to explain the profound meaning contained within the seventeen fascicles of the original text;
thus, it is called a "commentary on the meaning" (*yixi*). Alternatively, both characters "yi" and "shi" may be understood as belonging to the sub-commentary itself.
This work extracts the subtle meanings from various scriptures to explain the profound words of a single sutra;

since the meaning itself constitutes the explanation, it is titled as an "Exegesis" (*vyākhyā*) in relation to the title of the aforementioned sutra. It is named according to the *tatpuruṣa* compound as "An Exegesis of the Meaning of the Mahāvairocana-buddhābhisambodhi-vikurvaṇādhiṣṭhāna-sūtra. Thus, the designation of the commentary is hereby concluded.

Regarding the word "xu" (序) in the title: "xu" refers to that from which the beginning of the commentary (*shu*) arises; alternatively, "xu" means "to explain," for it proclaims the great purport of the entire treatise.
Thus, the *Erya* states: "The walls on the east and west are called *xu*; they are screen-walls. These represent the orderly arrangement (*xiangxu*) of a single residence.
If the term is interpreted through a shift in meaning, "xu" signifies "thread" (*xu*). It is like a cocoon finding its thread; once the thread is exhausted, the cocoon is finished.

The commentary (śū) is like the threads [of a fabric], while the preface (xu) is like the arrangement; since the arrangement fully embodies the intent of the commentary, it is called the "Preface to the Commentary.
Viewing the "commentary" as the object and the "preface" as the subject that arranges it, the name is formed according to the *tatpuruṣa* compound. Thus, it is said:

"Preface to the Exegesis of the Meaning of the Mahāvairocana-buddhābhisambodhi-vikurvāṇādhiṣṭhāna-sūtra. The preceding text has three parts, which together conclude the explanation of the title of the Preface.
Next, the author is explained. "Śramaṇa" is a general title; "Wengu" (溫古) is the specific name of the preface’s author.
"Wen" (溫) means to seek out or review; "gu" (故) means the old or the past. Because the Dharma Master delighted in reviewing the old and establishing new regulations, he was so named.
The *Lunyu* states: "The Master said, 'He who reviews what is old and thereby knows what is new can be a teacher. The commentary notes: "Wen means to seek out."
Furthermore, by tracing the old, one knows that the new can serve as a teacher; thus it is said, "Warming to the Ancient. The compiler describes [the work];
out of particular modesty he establishes the title, hence it says: "Compiled by the Śramaṇa Wengu."
Regarding the subsequent main text: *Preface*. "The Vidyādhara-piṭaka" (Holding the Secret Treasury) is the general designation for the secret treasury;

it refers to the fact that this great root scripture consists of one hundred thousand stanzas, which correctly expound all dhāraṇīs and vidyā-mantras, and thus constitutes a distinct piṭaka, hence it is called the "Vidyādhara-piṭaka."

Regarding the term "holding" (*dhāraṇī*): in the Sanskrit language it is *dhāraṇī*, which is translated here as "total retention. This total retention comprises four types: first, the total retention of phenomena (*dharma-dhāraṇī*), which retains the teachings that express [the meaning];
second, the total retention of meaning (*artha-dhāraṇī*), which retains the meanings expressed; third, the total retention of mantras (*vidyā-dhāraṇī*), which refers to true words (*mantra*);

and fourth, the total retention of patience (*kṣānti-dhāraṇī*), which is the ability to definitively accept the preceding three. What is referred to here as "total retention" refers to these four types of total retention.
This belongs to the third [category]. Although it belongs to the third, because it can encompass the others, while the other three cannot encompass this.

A question is asked: "In various teachings, it is said that all *dhāraṇīs* have mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence; why then is it said that the *dhāraṇī* of mantras refers to *mantra*?
The answer is: "The essence of *dhāraṇī* has both a general and a specific sense. Generally, it refers to mindfulness and wisdom."

Since both the dharmas (teachings) and their meanings, as well as mantras and patience, take mindfulness and wisdom as their essence, they are termed "dhāraṇī" (retention) of dharmas and "dhāraṇī" of meanings respectively;

these names are established based on what is spoken and what is understood. While there are distinctions such as dharmas and meanings, if one discusses their distinct essences, the "mantra-dhāraṇī" refers specifically to the *mantra*. If that is so, since it is already a mantra, how can it encompass the others?

The *Sañcaya-śāstra* explains: This mantra is not merely that which can be expressed by words; rather, it takes as its essence the four dharmas of teaching (*śāsana*), principle (*yukti*), practice (*pratipatti*), and fruit (*phala*).
Because it possesses the teaching, it is able to encompass the *dharmadhāraṇī*; because it possesses the principle, it is able to encompass the *arthadhāraṇī*;
because it possesses the practice, it is able to encompass the *kṣāntidhāraṇī*. The other three types of *dhāraṇī* cannot encompass this, for each of them grasps only a portion of the dharma.

Because its essence consists of the patience of meaning (*arthakṣānti*), there is no contradiction; furthermore, since this third [category] is that which is esteemed by this school, it clarifies the meaning according to the school’s tenets and is thus able to encompass the others.
Therefore, the Preface states: "The immeasurable deeds and all their verbal expressions, when synthesized and traced to their ultimate point, are none other than the Secret Treasury.
Thus, the Sub-commentary below says: "It is like gathering and binding a mass of hair and wearing it upon one's head."
Binding all the hair together at the crown of the head signifies the comprehensive integration of all teachings. Wearing it upon the head symbolizes being above all other vehicles (*yāna*).

Furthermore, because it is like the earth supporting all things, it is called "holding" (*dhṛti*). "Holding" also refers to *adhiṣṭhāna* (Sanskrit), which is translated here as "empowerment" (*jachi*).
This term applies to the three mysteries (*sanmitsu*). Alternatively, it is said to mean "recollection" (*anusmṛti*) alone.

Because it is the secret of the mind, the commentary below states: "The self-realization of the three types of enlightenment (*tri-bodhi*) attained by the Tathāgatas transcends all grounds of the mind;
it is the manifest awakening that all phenomena are primordially unborn. In this state, speech is exhausted and the movements of the mind are stilled.
Apart from the majestic spiritual power (*anubhāva*) of the Tathāgata, even Bodhisattvas of the ten stages do not possess this as their domain, let alone ordinary beings."
"Is this not like being among the dead? Thinking thus, the World-Honored One recalled his compassionate vows from the past and formed this thought:
"If I were to remain only within such a state, sentient beings would be unable to receive benefit therefrom.

Therefore, abiding here through the empowerment of sovereign spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*), I shall manifest all manner of realms for all sentient beings, appearing in whatever way they find pleasing."
The body preaches various teachings appropriate for the inclinations and desires of sentient beings, opening gates of contemplative observation according to their diverse mental activities.

It is like a master illusionist who, through the power of incantations, empowers medicinal herbs to manifest all manner of unprecedented phenomena that delight the hearts of the masses as they encounter them with their five senses.
Furthermore, the sub-commentary states: "Entering the gateway of mantra briefly involves three matters. First:
Regarding these, there are first the gate of body-secrecy, second the gate of speech-secrecy, and third the gate of mind-secrecy.
When the practitioner purifies their own three karmas through these three skillful means, they are empowered by the three secrets of the Tathāgata.
Consequently, they are able to fulfill the *bhūmi* and *pāramitā* in this very life, without having to undergo further kalpas of practice to cultivate various remedial deeds; therefore, it is great.

The *Śāstra* states: "There may be bodhisattvas who, at the very moment they first resolve their minds [for enlightenment], immediately ascend to the stage of a bodhisattva and attain non-retrogression;
or there may be those who, at the very moment they first resolve their minds, immediately attain unsurpassed bodhi and then turn the wheel of Dharma. Nāgārjuna explains this by way of analogy:

it is like two people traveling a long distance—one riding a sheep, who arrives only after a great length of time, while the other on horseback is somewhat faster; yet, compared to one who travels by means of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), both are slow.

In the mere instant of forming the thought, one arrives at the destination; it cannot be said that one arrives in the interval between the thought's arising. How could such a manifestation of supernatural power (abhijñā) be otherwise?
One should not give rise to doubt; this is the profound purport of this sutra.
*Vidyā* is another name for *vidyā-mantra*; in Sanskrit it is *vidyā* (transliterated as *wei-ni*, a compound). This is translated as "illumination," meaning that which destroys darkness.
In Sanskrit, *mantra* is translated as "true word" (*zhēnyán*) or "divine spell. This means that this true word can destroy the dark obstructions of the afflictions of sentient beings;
thus, it is translated as "illumination-spell" (*mingzhòu*), because it is itself illumination. Therefore, the sub-commentary below states:
Failing to comprehend the ultimate truth is called ignorance (*avidyā*). Because of ignorance, various formations (*saṃskāra*) arise, which constitute manifold sufferings.
Although Bodhisattvas have entered the stages (*bhūmi*), they still do not fully comprehend the profound and secret realm of the Tathāgata;
this is subtle ignorance and is likewise suffering. For their sake, the Buddha has taught this ultimate vidyā-mantra.

It causes one to know the realm of the Buddha, to eliminate the suffering of ignorance, and to attain the bliss of nirvāṇa. The *prajñā-citta* (wisdom-mind) is called a "great vidyā-mantra" because it can eliminate all suffering;
it is true and not empty—this is precisely that meaning. Furthermore, it is called "naming" (*nāma*) because it elucidates and manifests the four dharmas;
since sound, name, phrase, and syllable can manifest meaning, it is the "dhāraṇī of teaching," like a golden lamp in the dark night.
Jade is revealed through the light of lamps and torches, and the beauty or ugliness of a person's countenance is distinguished by means of a mirror.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "For example, a treasure in the darkness cannot be seen without a lamp; likewise, if the Buddha-dharma is not explained by someone, even those with wisdom cannot comprehend it.

Furthermore, Qingliang [Zongmi] said: "The Supreme Sage has bestowed his instructions to reflect the profound ultimate of the One Mind. Thus, the dharma and the metaphor are brought into correspondence.
This is easily understood. Furthermore, among the three secrets (*triguhyas*), that which belongs to the general teaching as its essence is primarily the secret of speech (*vākguhya*);

that which is explained specifically as "vidyā" (*vidyā*) is based on the secret of body (*kāyaguhya*). Therefore, the sub-commentary below states: "That which issues from the body and mouth of the Tathāgata is called a mantra (*mantra*);
that which arises spontaneously from the parts of the Tathāgata’s body is called a vidyā. A question is raised: previously, the character *ming* (vidyā) was used...
Regarding the teaching that consists of the four dharmas, such as sound and so forth, the present statement that they "arise from the body" is termed *vidyā* (knowledge/illumination).
How, then, can there be sound? The answer is as stated in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*): "The sounds of roaring and so forth, which issue from the body, are also said to be sound.

Nevertheless, because its essence is the secret of the body (*kāyaguhyaka*), it is established based on the body. This is like the method of arranging characters, wherein names, phrases, and so forth are manifested upon the parts of the body.
The threefold wheel of syllables (*akṣara-cakra*) signifies the turning of the Wheel of Dharma in three ways.

While the preceding [explanation] was based primarily on the establishment of the teaching through sound, it does not preclude its provisional establishment through form, fragrance, taste, and so forth; as the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"Mahāmati, see how these beings in this world—mosquitoes, gadflies, insects, and ants—accomplish their respective tasks without any verbal expression," and so on. However...
Since the arising of understanding through the manifestation of principles constitutes the very essence of the teaching, why must it be restricted solely to vocal sounds?

This is because there are instances such as the transmission of the mind through the lute and flute, or the preservation of the Way through mental impact; thus, it is called "illumination" (*vidyā*). It is both "retention" (*dhāraṇī*) and "illumination" (*vidyā*);
it is either retention itself that is illumination, or it is the illumination of retention. Depending on the context, it is therefore termed "Vidyādhara" (Holder of Knowledge).

"Storehouse" (*pitaka*) signifies that which is capable of encompassing meaning; as Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "Why is it called a 'storehouse' (*pitaka*)? It is because of its capacity to encompass.

That is to say, it encompasses all meanings that ought to be known. The intended meaning of this is that because the teaching that expresses [the meaning] is able to encompass all meanings that ought to be known so that they are not lost, it is established with the name "storehouse.
In Sanskrit, it is called *ālaya*, which refers to a storehouse or a nest-like dwelling.
Because those who dwell within this are not afflicted by the winds and rains of the Vināyakas;
or it is called *kośa*, meaning a sheath or chamber, for all Buddhas abide therein;
or it is called *sambhara*, meaning a womb-treasury (*garbha-kośa*), for all Buddhas are born from it; or it is called *sambara*, meaning a storehouse.

"Treasury" (gter) is here provisionally taken to mean "storehouse," just as in the world a great state treasury can contain and accumulate various kinds of diverse jewels, from which there is an inexhaustible flow of giving and taking for the sake of relief.

The Treasury of Vidyā is likewise so called because it contains and accumulates the secret Dharma and its meanings of all Buddhas, providing inexhaustible benefit and happiness; thus it is designated as the "Vidyā Treasury. It has four distinct [divisions].

Because it is the third of the remaining [categories], it may be interpreted either as "the treasury of the vidyādharas" (*vidyādhara-piṭaka*) or as "the vidyādharas themselves are the treasury"; thus it is called the *Vidyādhara-piṭaka*.

Regarding the statement that "the divisions of its tenets have flowed for a long time," this reveals both its origin and its development. "Tenet" (*zong*) refers to the root, while "divisions" (*fen*) refers to—
"Branches" (*aṅga*) refer to the sub-sections; "streams" (*pravāha*) refers to the lineages.

This means that the Great Root Text of this Vidyā-piṭaka consists of one hundred thousand stanzas, which is so vast and extensive that the Noble One who transmitted the Dharma extracted its essential tenets into three thousand stanzas (this is the core doctrine). It has many branches, namely:
the branch of the Ācārya, the branch of the disciple, the branch of the selection of sites, and the branch of the construction of maṇḍalas.
The constituent parts of the *cakra*, up to and including the branches of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and *homa*—these are its very components.
Furthermore, within those components, the branches and sub-branches proliferate and extend infinitely. Since this Dharma-gate is vast and extensive, it is difficult to fathom its limits;

therefore, for the sake of guiding and transforming beings according to their needs and bestowing conditions upon them as appropriate, [I have] extracted from the great compendium these abbreviated, independent practices, wishing that...

To strip away the branches and leaves to exhaustively reach the root, and to follow the waves and ripples to investigate the source and the cavern—that is what is called tracing the course of a stream.
Now, regarding this current stream of the sutra, since the time of Emperor Ming of the Later Han dynasty, there have been those from generation to generation who propagated and translated it.
The *Mahāvaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra* was translated by the Śramaṇa Fa-zhong of the Northern Liang, and [the *Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*] by the Śramaṇa Buddhabhadra of the Yuan Wei.
The *Vajra-uttama-rasa-dhāraṇī* and other sūtras translated by Dharmakṣema; the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-mantra* and other sūtras translated by the Śramaṇa Jñānayaśas of the Zhou;
the *Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī-dhāraṇī* and other dhāraṇī sūtras translated by the Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda of the Eastern Jin;
the *Ākāśagarbha-dhāraṇī* and other sūtras translated by the Śramaṇa Dhammamitra of the Song; and [sūtras] from the Great Tang... [Śramaṇa]... translated.
The Master Xuanzang translated the *Amoghapāśa* and other sutras, while Bodhiruci translated the *Amoghasiddhi-vikurvaṇa* and other sutras;
furthermore, Vajrabodhi, Amoghavajra, and others extensively propagated these scriptures, as recorded in detail in the *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*.
Therefore, it is said that this school has existed for a very long time.

Preface: Among the scholars of the world who have reached the Middle Way, it is said that although the various streams of scriptures transmitted and translated since antiquity have flourished in the world, those who study and practice within this world do not encounter the great original texts nor meet with enlightened masters.

Consequently, they mostly fix their minds upon the phenomenal characteristics of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*) and rarely succeed in attaining resonance with the unconditioned Middle Way (*asaṃskṛta-madhyamā*). Thus says Qingliang.

It is said that through cultivation involving effort over many kalpas, one ultimately meets with ruin; yet for the essence of the mindless [state], in a single thought-moment, one immediately accords with the Buddha-family.

The sub-commentary below states: "While other bodhisattvas, though they perform difficult and painful practices for the sake of seeking the unsurpassed path, ultimately cannot attain it, a practitioner of Yoga, if endowed with skillful means, may achieve it in a single lifetime. This is because one thereby knows the profound conditions."
Because it gives rise to the dharma-gate of the Middle Way, the mantra is like a *lakṣa*. This is termed "one hundred million" (*koṭi*), which is also a number of one hundred thousand;
it is also termed "seeing. Seeing means that when the practitioner of mantra-rites (*mantrayānika*) brings about accomplishment, the objective realm manifests before them.
To observe this with the mind’s eye, focusing on a single object without distraction, is the meaning of *yoga-lakṣa*. In the present age...
Some practitioners, while holding to scriptures such as the Susiddhi, do not understand the secret instructions and remain merely at the literal level;
if they hope to attain *siddhi* by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, when will it ever be obtained?

Or, regarding those who speak of "having signs" (*sanimitta*), these practitioners fail to understand that for the most part they cling to all phenomena as being existent—thus they are called "having signs"—yet they do not exclude a minor attachment to emptiness, nor do they accord with the Middle Way.

Furthermore, some within the Way cling to emptiness as having the characteristic of finitude; both are termed "having characteristics" (sanimitta) because they do not accord with the Middle Way. Thus it is said:
"The scholars of the world," etc.
Introduction. Regarding the phrase "the Dharma of Yogācāra practice," *yoga* in Sanskrit is translated here as "correspondence" (*xiangying*), which refers to these very characteristics.
One should fully comprehend both the exoteric and esoteric teachings; regarding the exoteric, there are four types, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-vyākhyā*:

"First, concerning the object (*viṣaya*), the *Yogācāra* has both general and specific [aspects]. First, the general: the commentary on the treatise explains that it refers to the nature of all objects being non-erroneous, the nature of being non-contradictory, the nature of being conducive, and the nature of tending toward the ultimate. These four objects correspond, respectively, with..."
Regarding the meaning of the correspondence between principle, teaching, practice, and fruit, there is a further distinction. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"If one contemplates the true meaning, eliminates conceptual discrimination, and remains far removed from defilements, there is neither a grasper nor that which is grasped;
