If I do not practice [the way of the sages], I shall sever the ancestral line of the ṛṣis. Having had this thought, he entrusted the kingdom to his ministers and withdrew into seclusion.
Having entered the mountains to practice the Way, he attained the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) after many years had passed. As his age advanced, his hair turned entirely white.
After his disciples had gone out to gather fruit and fetch firewood, they were long delayed by wild beasts.
When they returned and saw him, they placed him in a basket. Later, while they were again fetching water and hanging it upon a tree, some hunters caught sight of them from afar.
This refers to a white heron that shot an arrow at a *ṛṣi*; struck by the arrow, the *ṛṣi*’s life came to an end.
Two drops of blood fell upon the ground, from which two sugarcane stalks grew. When they were opened by the heat of the sun, one became a young man and one a young woman.
The man was named Sujāta and the woman was named Sujātā. Because people esteemed their lineage, they collectively designated them with the name *Kṣatriya*. From this [the caste originated].
Therefore, his subsequent aspiration lay in the teachings of the *pañcābhijña-ṛṣi* Gautama. [Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "there is nothing that is not the causal condition for the poisoned drum," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in the "Tathāgata-gotra" chapter, states:

"For example, suppose there were a person who smeared a large drum with various poisonous drugs and struck it among a great multitude; although he had no intention [to harm], the sound that issued forth..."
If one wishes to hear [the teachings], hearing them all leads to death, with the sole exception of one person who does not die an untimely death.
"Dying in union with the drum" is a metaphor for the extinction of delusions; "not dying an untimely death" is a metaphor for the *icchantika*.

This illustrates that although the bodies manifested and the vehicles taught within the maṇḍala have fourfold distinctions and are immeasurable, if one enters through whichever gate, there is nothing that cannot be extinguished.
There is no delusion that cannot reach nirvana; therefore, it is used as a metaphor for comparison.
[Commentary] "For example, like the realm of empty space": "realm" here has the meaning of essential nature (*dharmatā*).

To say it is "free from all conceptual discrimination" means that while the essence of empty space is itself devoid of conceptual discrimination, sentient beings nevertheless discriminate empty space, thinking it is blue, yellow, and so forth.
High and low, long and wide, and so forth—these are conceptual distinctions (*vikalpa*), and from them this sickness arises. This constitutes coarse discrimination.

Upon these objects of discrimination, one further increases discrimination, such as by positing "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*) or "lacking resistance" (*apratigha*); this constitutes subtle discrimination.
To speak of "being free from all discrimination" means to eliminate coarse discrimination; to speak of "non-discrimination" (*avikalpa*) means to eliminate... [subtle discrimination].

The subtle discrimination is analyzed as follows: although the two kinds of discrimination—the coarse and the subtle—have been dispelled, the "sickness of emptiness" that performs the dispelling increases further.
It is like a bird walking on sand; its tracks have not yet vanished. Therefore, both are dispelled by saying "there is no non-discrimination.

The "no" above is the agent of negation (*nirākaraṇa*), and the "no" below is the object to be negated. Thus, even the aforementioned emptinesses that serve as the agents of negation for the two kinds of coarse and subtle [discrimination] are all inappropriate.
As for mental states, one must eliminate them again and again until there is nothing left to eliminate;

when the traces of the words themselves are severed, this is the cutting off of the path of language and the cessation of the sphere of mental activity, like a bird traversing the sky. Thus, the "Appearance" Chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"To know that the nature of all phenomena is quiescent is like a bird flying through the sky leaving no trace. Therefore, it speaks of "being like empty space," and so forth.
[Commentary: The reason for repeating the word "equal" (*sama*) is that from "kalpa" onwards, one should read it with an extended force.
It should be stated as: *kalpa kalpa nyāya*. "Kalpa" means differentiation; the term "nyāya" has the sense of "furthermore.
This means that upon the coarse differentiation, a further subtle differentiation arises. This refers to the arising of subtle differentiation upon the coarse differentiation.
For this reason, the Commentary cites examples such as "investigation and analysis" (*vitarka-vicāra*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the "eight worldly winds," these eight winds refer to gain, honor, loss, disrepute, praise, blame, pleasure, and pain.
One who is "unmoved" by them does not rejoice when confronted by gain, honor, praise, and pleasure, nor do they grieve when oppressed by loss, disrepute, blame, and pain. Therefore...
It says: "The eight winds, etc. [Commentary]:

Regarding the phrase "even the bonds of conditions are all exhausted," there are two kinds of bonds of conditions: first, the binding agent (*ālambaka-bandhana*), which refers to the bound object (*ālambana*) acting as the binding agent for the binding mind;
this is like the name *ālayavijñāna*, which is so called because of its capacity for grasping (*upādāna*). Second, the bound object (*ālambya-bandhana*)... [text continues].

The object-condition (ālambana-bandhana) refers to that which is bound by the object of the sovereign subject (ālambaka-rāja); it is called the "object-condition bond" because it is constrained by its objective field.

Furthermore, according to the *Yid-灯* (Yid-kyi mun-sel), the meaning of "bond" (bandhana) is manifold: some say it is the "associated bond" (saṃprayoga-bandhana), because the sovereign subject, together with the afflictions, cannot attain autonomy due to being bound by associated dharmas;
thus, "association is the bond" is a term formed by the identity of the attribute and the substrate (karmadhāraya). Others say it is the "characteristic bond" (lakṣaṇa-bandhana).

When the mind is constrained by characteristics (*nimitta*), it is called "bondage by characteristics" (*nimittabandhana*). All contaminated (*sāsrava*) characteristics are termed bondage by characteristics; this applies to all eight consciousnesses.

Alternatively, some say that "bondage of grossness" (*dauṣṭhulyabandhana*) subsumes all textual accounts. There are four types of grossness: first, active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of all contaminated minds and mental factors;
second, the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*); third, the seeds (*bīja*) of the two obstacles; and fourth, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the two obstacles.

Because those associated with the vital energies (*vāyu*) are collectively termed "coarse and heavy" (*dausthulya*) and are not enumerated in full detail, it says "up to and including the fetters of conditions" (*yāvad-ālambana-bandhana*).

*The Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāvairocanābhisambodhi-vikurvita-adhiṣṭhāna-sūtra: The Unfolding of the Secret*, Fascicle Three.

Composed by the Śramaṇa Jueyuan, a recipient of the purple robe, Grand Master of the Secretariat (Zongmi Dashi), Acting Minister of Rites (Chonglu Qing), Examiner of State Affairs (Jianjiao Taibao), and Grand Master of High Rank (Chonglu Dafu) of Yuanfu Temple in Yanjing.

[The Preface] Regarding the phrase "such as Maitreya Bodhisattva and others," this is the meaning of the Introduction Chapter (*Nidāna-parivarta*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. It says there: "At that time..."
Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to resolve his own doubts and observing the minds of the fourfold assembly—
monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen— as well as the multitude of devas, nāgas, spirits, and others, questioned Mañjuśrī:
"By what causes and conditions has this auspicious sign of supernatural power appeared, emitting a great radiance that illuminates the eastern direction?"
In all eighteen thousand lands, the adornments of those Buddha-fields were fully visible; even as it says in the verse:
"The wondrous Dharma attained by the Buddha while sitting at the site of enlightenment—does he wish to preach this, or will he grant a prediction? At the end, Mañjuśrī replied:
"I see that the Buddha Dīpaṃkara displayed such auspicious signs of his original light; by this I know that the present Buddha wishes to preach the Lotus Sūtra. If one applies this same analogy...
This refers to when the Tathāgata was about to expound this dharma-gate of the verse of equality, he first manifested an auspicious sign;
subsequently, in response to the inquiry of Vajrapāṇi, he expounded it so that the meaning might be easily understood. Regarding the phrase "furious and reluctant":

the Master said, "I do not initiate [the student] unless they are furious, nor do I develop [their understanding] unless they are reluctant. If they do not return with the other three corners after I have shown one, I do not repeat the instruction."

(Zheng says: "When Confucius spoke with others, he would always wait until their minds were accustomed [to the topic] and their mouths were ready to speak—only then would he inspire them and explain it to them. Such was the depth of his insight and reflection. Once they understood, he would present one corner [of the principle] to tell them;

if the person did not contemplate its analogies, he would not teach further. Regarding the phrase "Mañjuśrī’s unfolding": "unfolding" (*fa*) means to reveal and clarify, while "displaying" (*hui*) means to spread and manifest. Thus, "Mañjuśrī’s unfolding" refers to the act of dispelling Maitreya’s doubts.
Regarding the phrase "causing those who hold to attachments to move," "moving" (*dong*) means to follow along.
As for the followers who likewise cling to their attachments: these are the people for whom the Tathāgata preached the Dharma to shatter the attachments of the two vehicles.
As that sūtra states: "I was originally attached to wrong views and served as a teacher to various Brahmins. The World-Honored One, knowing my mind, uprooted my heterodoxy and preached nirvāṇa to me.
I completely eliminated all wrong views and attained realization within the Dharma of emptiness. At that time, he thought to himself that he had attained it.

As for his entry into *nirvāṇa*, it was only now that he realized for himself that this was not a true extinction (*parinirvāṇa*). This extends even to the passage: "His mind is as calm as the ocean; having heard this, my net of doubts is severed. Regarding the statement, "It is like the spring sun," the *Monthly Ordinances* (*Yueling*) of the *Book of Rites* states: "In the first month of spring, the celestial qi descends and the terrestrial qi ascends; heaven and earth harmonize, and the grasses and trees begin to sprout. Spring is the season of growth. It is only when one has attained the Way that one can truly understand this. Therefore, it is said: "The Buddha’s Dharma is profound and subtle; its principles are difficult to fathom. Furthermore, it is said: "The Buddha’s Dharma is vast and great; its essence is difficult to comprehend. Because the Buddha’s Dharma is so profound and subtle, its principles are difficult to fathom; because the Buddha’s Dharma is so vast and great, its essence is difficult to comprehend. It is precisely because it is difficult to fathom that it is called profound and subtle; it is precisely because it is difficult to comprehend that it is called vast and great. Thus, the Buddha’s Dharma is both profound and subtle, and both vast and great. It is for this reason that it is said: "The Buddha’s Dharma is profound and subtle; its principles are difficult to fathom. The Buddha’s Dharma is vast and great; its essence is difficult to comprehend. Moreover, it is said: "The Buddha’s Dharma is profound and subtle; its principles are difficult to fathom. The Buddha’s Dharma is vast and great; its essence is difficult to comprehend. This is because the Buddha’s Dharma is so profound and subtle that its principles are difficult to fathom, and because the Buddha’s Dharma is so vast and great that its essence is difficult to comprehend. In the first month of spring, the vital energy gradually intensifies and the yang qi begins to disperse; those that grow by coiling emerge completely, and those that sprout reach full development (the commentary notes:

"that which grows by curving is called *gou* [hook/sprout], while that which grows straight is called *meng* [bud/sprout]"). Furthermore, the *I Ching* states: "When heaven and earth are unbound (*jie*), thunder and rain arise;
when thunder and rain arise, the fruits and plants all split open their husks. Regarding such expressions as "thunder and wind stirring," "thunder" refers to the yin [element].
The term "sound" refers to that which is produced when the yang forces collide. The *Guliang Zhuan* states: "When yin and yang clash and stimulate one another, thunder and wind arise;
these are the qi. The *Zhuangzi* says: "The Great Mass (the Dao) sighs forth qi, and its name is wind" (the commentary notes:
"When heaven and earth sigh forth their qi, the myriad apertures roar in fury, becoming wind"). Furthermore, thunder is itself wind. Yang Quan’s *Wuli Lun* states: "Accumulated winds form thunder."
Regarding "stirring and so forth," the *Yi Jing* says: "Thunder stirs it, wind moves it, and rain moistens it.

"Obtaining the release from the husk" means that the "husk" (*pi*) refers to the white skin within the pod, and the "shell" (*ke*) refers to the outer casing, which is the same as the "pod" (*jia*). "Oil-like" (*you ran*) describes the manner of growth;
as Mencius said, "Oil-like clouds arise, and pouring rain falls," meaning that [growth occurs] through the stirring of thunder and wind and the moistening of the timely rain.
The sprinkling [of water] causes the sprouts to leave behind their husks and shells, emerging and growing luxuriantly;

all of the above serves as a metaphor for those who cling to movement and attachment attaining liberation from the net of doubt. As for the phrase "if there are those without the capacity," "without capacity" refers to the icchantikas, such as the five thousand [monks];
although they encountered the assembly at Vulture Peak during the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, because they lack the Buddha-lineage (*gotra*), [they cannot attain it].
Therefore, they are unable to give rise to the profound and firm vow for great bodhicitta, which brings about the benefit of the two-fold welfare [of self and others].
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Those of no lineage, because they lack a lineage, will never be able to attain unsurpassed bodhi despite practicing with diligent effort;
it is like seeds that have never had roots in the earth—though they encounter the spring sun and thunderstorms that bring release, they will ultimately not sprout."
Because there is no principle of sprouting or the bursting of buds, it is said that they are like people who lack the "mechanism" (*mēkhā*).
[Commentary]: "You should listen attentively and apply your mind with great care. "Attentively" refers to the profound mind; "listening" refers to lending the ear;
and "applying the mind with care" means examining the principles through the sounds heard.

[Commentary]: Regarding the twenty kinds of merit gained by listening to the Dharma with a focused mind, the *Śūtra* refers to the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra*, though its specific text has not yet been seen.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "If there is someone who hears or receives the teaching of the Seal of the Letter A (*akṣara-mudrā*), they shall obtain twenty kinds of merit.
What are these twenty? First, one obtains powerful mindfulness; this means that the Bodhisattva attains this..."
Because one constantly contemplates the characteristics of all syllables through the practice of recollection, one attains a sense of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*);
this means that by gathering all wholesome dharmas and detesting all unwholesome dharmas, one gives rise to a great mind of shame and remorse.
Because one gathers all merit and wisdom, the mind becomes firm and steadfast like a diamond (*vajra*), such that even matters pertaining to the Avīci Hell [cannot shake it].
One does not regress from unsurpassed bodhi, let alone from other sufferings.
To understand the purport of the sūtras means to know that the Buddha employs five kinds of skillful means in preaching the Dharma: first, knowing that he preaches by employing various gateways;
second, knowing for what purpose he preaches; third, knowing that he preaches by means of skillful methods; fourth, knowing that he preaches to demonstrate the underlying principle; and fifth...
It is known that because of the mind of great compassion, it is said that one attains wisdom;

this means that because a bodhisattva, by means of this dhāraṇī, discerns and deconstructs all letters, speech, names, and meanings such that they are entirely empty, one attains ultimate emptiness, which is precisely the wisdom of the *prajñāpāramitā*. To "attain eloquence" means that having already attained such ultimate purity...
Because one employs unimpeded wisdom and the great compassionate mind of original vows to extensively deliver sentient beings, one attains the *dhāraṇī* of eloquence that is easily acquired.
This means that, for example, when a bamboo stalk is broken, once the first joint is severed, the remaining ones are all easy to break; the Bodhisattva is likewise.
Having attained this *dhāraṇī* of syllables, all other *dhāraṇīs* are naturally acquired, and one attains freedom from doubt and regret.
"Mind" refers to entering into the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;

although one has not yet attained all-encompassing wisdom, because one is without doubt or regret regarding all profound teachings, one neither rejoices upon hearing the good nor becomes angry upon hearing the evil.
This means that by individually discerning each syllable, one neither praises nor disparages. "Abiding mind" refers to dwelling in a state that is neither elevated nor depressed.

Because aversion and attachment have been severed, one attains skillful knowledge of the languages of sentient beings; this means that one has attained the Samādhi of Understanding the Languages of All Sentient Beings.

One attains skillful discernment of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), the twelve links of dependent origination, the four conditions, and the four truths;
as these are quite numerous, I shall not elaborate further here. One attains skillful discernment of the sharpness or dullness of the faculties (*indriya*) of sentient beings; this means that...
There are those whose faculties are all equally dull or all equally sharp; there are those whose faculties are not all the same and not all sharp.
Furthermore, there are those who, desiring bondage, attain liberation, and those who, desiring liberation, attain bondage.

This is like Aṅgulimāla, who desired to kill his mother and harm the Buddha, yet attained liberation; or like a certain bhikṣu who attained the four dhyānas but harbored overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

Therefore, he returns to the hells and knows that this person will certainly fall into the evil realms; he knows whether such a person will find it difficult to emerge, easy to emerge, quickly emerge, or will take a long time to emerge.
He thoroughly and universally knows the characteristics of the superior and inferior faculties of all sentient beings.

His attainment of skill in knowing the minds of others means that he is able to know the distinctions in the mental activities of all sentient beings; thus, he attains skill in discerning days, months, and years.
"Joints" refers to the divisions of days; from dawn to dawn, there are the first, middle, and latter parts, and the night is likewise divided into three parts.

Thus, one day and one night consist of thirty periods (*muhūrta*), which are skillfully distinguished. The supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*) means being able to hear all sounds, whether distant or near, and skillfully distinguishing them.
The supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*) means that there are three types of past lives.

Regarding the types [of knowledge], there are those that possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), those that possess clarity (*vidyā*), and those that possess power. Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) merely attain supernormal powers;

Śrāvakas possess both supernormal powers and clarity; and Buddhas fully possess all three. Why is this so? It is because ordinary persons only know the past lives they have experienced, but do not know the continuity of karmic causes and conditions;
for this reason, they possess supernormal powers but lack clarity. Śrāvakas, however, understand the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) and thus realize it.
Having understood that karmic causes and conditions arise in continuous succession, for this reason even the Śrāvakas possess this clarity (*vidyā*). It is asked:
"If the meaning of 'penetrating clarity' is thus, why is it called a 'power' (*bala*)? The answer is:
"The Buddha, by means of this clarity, knows all the various matters experienced throughout the immeasurable and boundless past lives of his own body and of sentient beings within the world."
To be able to know this thoroughly is called a power (*bala*). Regarding the attainment of skillful discernment of the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*):

it means that when a Buddha uses the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) to see the places where sentient beings undergo birth and death, even an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who possesses this divine eye to a great degree can see the four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*).

A *śrāvaka* who possesses it to a great degree can see horizontally as far as a small thousand-world system (*sāhasracūḍikalokadhātu*), and even a Buddha, when entering other samādhis, [sees further].

Because the divine eye does not perish, one thoroughly knows the destinies of birth and death for all sentient beings and attains skillful exposition regarding what is possible and what is impossible.

That which is called "possible" (*sthāna*) refers to the correspondence between cause and effect: performing wholesome deeds leading to rebirth among humans or devas, and committing unwholesome karma leading to rebirth in the three miserable realms.

Such correspondence of cause and effect is termed "possible. Conversely, that which lacks such correspondence between cause and effect is termed "impossible" (*asthāna*). Furthermore, the wholesome is designated as "possible."
Because unwholesome states and the like are called "improper" (*asthāna*), one attains skillful knowledge of the deportments of coming and going,

sitting and rising; that is to say, whether entering or exiting, going or returning, sitting or lying down, walking or standing, one is constantly mindful with a single mind, lifting and lowering the feet with stability and decorum,
and walking while looking at the ground with a single-minded focus— these are called the twenty kinds of merit obtained from hearing the Dharma.
[Commentary]: "Attaining the power of deep faith" means that the profound mind possesses pure faith; because this faith has power, one is able to leave behind doubt and confusion.
As the subsequent commentary states: "Furthermore, the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the three vehicles is not without reliance upon words and letters;

yet for those of the Mantra vehicle, it is essential to orally recite the Sanskrit text while the mind also contemplates it, or to flex and extend the limbs as if in play, or to cultivate the three [mudrās]."
If one observes the image of a woman, or forms such as those of wrathful deities, or performs the consecration with water, or constructs a fire altar— and yet,
when attempting to deliberate upon them with the conscious mind, the traces of that empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) cannot be seen—
how could anyone who does not possess pure faith avoid falling into doubt? One should immediately contemplate these things as being like illusions, similar to medicinal compounds mixed together.
By combining these, one attains the ability to ascend into the air and dwell there; even for those with sharp faculties and wisdom, this lifespan cannot be conceived by thought.

Yet, for those who can skillfully understand its technique, there is nothing they cannot achieve, because they possess such a profound mind that is free from doubt. Furthermore, if a person hears this sutra, having planted roots of goodness in past lives, their spirit and intellect will be clear and sharp;
they will know with certainty that this principle exists within the minds of sentient beings, even if they do not [yet manifest it].

Because one is able to believe and understand through the process of inference and deliberation, it is called "profound faith" (*adhimukti*). Because this faith possesses power, it is called the "power of faith" (*śraddhā-bala*).
Regarding the phrase "being free from birth through karma," it means that due to ignorance (*avidyā*), one performs various karmas and undergoes birth driven by those karmas;
because one is free from such birth through karma, one attains birth from the nature of true awakening (*bodhi-dhātu*), and thus it is so called.
"Free from karma, sensation, and so forth.

[Commentary] This refers to those with pure, white faith; that is, because they have previously attained deep faith and are free from the defilement of doubt. Therefore, the subsequent commentary states:
"For example, if a tattered garment is heavily stained with grease and filth, it cannot be dyed all at once; first, one must instruct it to be washed."

Only after washing can the work of applying colors and patterns be performed; sentient beings are likewise. If one first cultivates deep defilements, one will not be stained by the colors of the Dharma-realm.
If one uses the water of faith to wash until it is pure white, then one is fit to receive the dye.
Furthermore, although the faculties and powers are fivefold, faith is their beginning; as for the categories of color, white stands at the head. Therefore, it is called "white."
This is pure faith.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "expedient means as the ultimate," there are two kinds of expedient means: first, self-benefit; second, benefiting others.

Self-benefit refers to the perfection of the myriad practices such that they can no longer be increased. Benefiting others refers to the exhaustive mastery of skillful means in responding to sentient beings.
Regarding the statement that "the capacity for activity benefits others" and that "the sublime fruit of *amṛta* (clarified butter) is the source of the three mysteries":
*Amṛta* is a designation for the merit of the fruit, a name derived from a metaphor. Among the five flavors, *amṛta* is the most refined and supreme;
it emerges from within milk, taking milk as its basis. This refers to the fact that within the bodies of all Tathāgatas during their causal stage, there exists fundamentally the Great Pure Mind.

Milk relies upon the ten thousand practices of great compassion; through the expedient means of the three mysteries, it is sequentially churned and stirred, passing through various flavors until it reaches the state of wondrous enlightenment—the *amṛta* (ghee) of an immutable nature, wherein the fruit of self-benefit is fulfilled.

Based upon this, the body of the three mysteries of the empowerment for benefiting others arises; therefore, it is called the "wondrous fruit of *amṛta*, the source of the three mysteries. Thus it is said.
The sub-commentary states: "It is like a fruit produced from a seed that itself becomes a seed again; this is precisely the meaning. [Commentary]:

"Pattern and regulation" (*guīzhì*) refers to the compass and square, or craftsmanship. "Central" (*zhōng*, departing tone) signifies not missing the mark; "expedient" (*quán*) signifies adaptability.
This means that when a skillful art is perfected, whatever one creates is accomplished at will according to the patterns and regulations established.

Regarding the phrases "acting without losing the appropriateness of the occasion" and "the subtlety of attaining the meaning through words": as for "attaining the meaning," Zhuangzi said, "Words are the means by which one reaches the meaning;
once the meaning is attained, the words are forgotten. How can I find such a person who has forgotten words with whom to speak?
Although words are used to benefit others and accord with the expectations of the world, even if one speaks constantly throughout one's entire life...

Because this is the transcendence of words, one knows that the transcendence of words does not mean being mute and remaining silent; it lies rather in attaining the meaning (*yì*), which may be called "sublime.
Now, borrowing these terms: the letter *A* represents Bodhi, similar to pure gold; the letter *Ā* represents Great Compassion, like a practitioner of the arts;
and the letter *Am* represents Expedient Means, like the fruit of skillful artifice. It is, for example, like pure gold that follows various [forms].
The mental aspects of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) are fully realized; all rules and fabrications reach their limit within the profound, secret Middle Way.

Because these transcend the shallow skillfulness of the various vehicles (*yāna*), the wondrous mastery of the mind is attained immediately and not from another—how could it be like the *āmala* fruit held in one's hand that is merely passed on to others? As the ancients said: "The Dharma..."
The meaning that one who has attained [realization] from the Master and can give rise to it within their own mind cannot be transmitted to others is as follows.

[Commentary]: Regarding "the samādhis, the factors of the path, and so forth," this refers to the three samādhis up to the one hundred and eight samādhis; the "path" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path;
and the "factors" refer to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

[Commentary] Therefore, the phrase "as stated above" refers back to the previous point that one must first give rise to faith; here, the essential point is that one must know things as they truly are.
That is to say, this profound and subtle Dharma cannot be understood by anyone who is not an omniscient person (*sarvajña*).

From where, then, is this Dharma obtained? It is none other than from the practitioner’s own mind. Now, the present commentary again points this out to emphasize the necessity of both faith and wisdom.
To be fully endowed with the treasury of jewels so that it may swiftly manifest before one means: because of faith, one does not slander [the Dharma] as being without wisdom;
and because of wisdom, one understands it as it truly is. Furthermore, if one lacks faith, one will loftily defer to the realm [of the Buddhas], claiming it is beyond the scope of one's own wisdom.
If one lacks wisdom, one will give rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*), claiming oneself to be equal to the Buddha. For these reasons, both [faith and wisdom] are established in these two places.
[Commentary] Regarding the Sanskrit term *aṇu* and so forth: the word *aṇu* is sometimes called *aṇḍa*, which is translated here as "extreme atom" (*paramāṇu*).
To say that it is "composed of seven atoms" means that one extreme atom each from the four cardinal directions, the zenith, the nadir, and the center constitute the "seven atoms.
It is said to be "composed" when these seven extreme atoms touch one another and do not separate.
To speak of those phenomena as equal means that they arise from conditions; it refers to the most minute phenomena, namely *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is merely one's own mind. Apart from one's own mind, there exists no other phenomenon—whether composed of seven atoms or otherwise—that is so minute as to be perceivable.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "The causes and conditions are explained therein," "causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya) carries the sense of "the reason why.

This refers to the preceding passage in the Sūtra which states that apart from the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is not a single dharma to be found. Next, the text raises a question to explain this reason, saying:
"For what reason? Space is without marks; this is bodhi," and so forth. This, then, is the illustration within the Sūtra that makes manifest the underlying reason.
[Commentary] "For example, like empty space," etc., is the commentary’s explanation of the analogy. "Pervading all places" means that it has no boundaries and is ultimate.

"Ultimately" means that no material forms whatsoever can defile it. "Free from all marks" means it is free from light and darkness, squareness and roundness, coming and going, identity and difference, and so forth.
"Immovable" means that even if winds such as the *svalana* (whirling) wind were to blow, they could not [move it].
Because it is capable of movement, it is without conceptual discrimination; because it lacks the characteristics of cognitive understanding or clear illumination, it cannot be altered;
because it does not undergo change or transition according to day, night, or the four seasons, it cannot be destroyed;
because it remains even when the world is destroyed, it is like space. By such means as these, it refers to the signless bodhicitta, within which there are immeasurable...
Matters such as the "Secret at the Boundary" cannot be illustrated by the mundane void;
rather, they are used as metaphors only because they share a partial similarity in qualities such as being free from characteristics and being immovable.

[Commentary]: "Only the mind itself realizes the mind" means that the Buddhas' self-realization of *samyak-saṃbodhi* is inherently accomplished within the mental continuums of all sentient beings without any deficiency;
it must be realized through one's own self-awakening rather than being transmitted by another.
If it were something received from the words of another, then Śākyamuni Buddha would have had to receive his prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) from Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
If one were to attain Buddhahood immediately, why must one fully cultivate the ten thousand practices and wait until awakening without a teacher before being called a Buddha?

It is like a person whose eyes witness others being wounded by knives or clubs; although they believe those people are suffering and have no doubt about it, they do not realize or know the nature of that suffering through various descriptions.
Only when they touch and experience the pain themselves do they understand it clearly.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "if one discriminates even a small portion," etc.: if, within the space of the self-realized *sambodhi* of all Buddhas, one discriminates even a slight duality of subject and object, this is precisely the grasping of dharmas and non-dharmas;
how could such a thing be called "Vajra-wisdom"? Vajra-wisdom is none other than *prajñā*. As for the statement "not separated from self, person, etc.," it refers to clinging.

Taking what belongs to one’s own body as "self," one conceives of a self that transmigrates through various realms; conceiving of a self as a "person," one conceives of the continuity of various transformations such as prosperity and decline, suffering and pleasure;
conceiving of a self as a "sentient being," one conceives of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of a single karmic retribution remaining uninterrupted;
and conceiving of a self as a "life-span" (*āyuṣka*). Therefore, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Subhūti, can the Tathāgata be seen by means of physical marks? No.
As it says: "If the mind grasps at signs, or grasps at the signs of dharmas, or grasps at the signs of non-dharmas, one is then attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
You bhikṣus, know that my teaching of the Dharma is like the parable of the raft;
even dharmas should be abandoned, let alone non-dharmas. Therefore, the subsequent explanation clarifies: "Why is this? Because bodhi is signless."

[Commentary]: Although it is said that even when one is free from all [conditions] and has attained accomplishment—meaning that the Tathāgata constantly states that the wisdom of omniscience is free from all causes and conditions—the present statement says:
"If a practitioner of yoga correctly contemplates the three dharmas, such as the mind, space, and bodhi, along with the equality of reality (tathatā), would these not be causes and conditions?
However, what was previously stated regarding being "free from all causes and conditions" refers precisely to being free from the mind of grasping (*upādāna*).

It is because this is the causal condition for external false conceptualization, rather than being the causal condition for the non-discriminative dharmadhātu; therefore it says, "although it is free from [such things]," and so forth.

[Commentary] Regarding "opening and developing the clarity of the mind": "opening" means to reveal and manifest, while "developing" means to give rise to. "Mind" refers to one's own mind, which is luminous.
"The path of light is the place where one traverses. The sub-commentary below states:

"By means of the limit (*koṭi*) wherein the awakened mind is fundamentally unborn, that mind abides in purity and gives rise to the light of great wisdom, which universally illumines immeasurable *dharmatā*. Because one sees the path traversed by all Buddhas, it is said that 'it is developed,' and so forth."

[Commentary]: "To say that the station of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) is itself nirvāṇa" means that a certain class of non-Buddhists, having attained the meditative absorption of the station of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, reckons this most ultimate state of purity to be nirvāṇa.
[Commentary]: Regarding the *Vātsīputrīya-abhidharma*, "Vātsīputrīya" refers to a non-Buddhist who adhered to the Buddha's teachings.
This non-Buddhist, being intelligent, studied the Buddhist scriptures and developed a singular view by aligning himself with the Buddha's Dharma; thus he received this name.
Having studied Śāriputra’s *Abhidharma*, he formulated his own distinct doctrine, stating: "I exist outside the four propositions of the other teachers."

Within the *Saṃyuktāgama*, it is asked: "What are the four propositions of the non-Buddhists? They reckon that form is the self, that there is a self apart from form, that the self is within form, and that form is within the self.
The same applies to the other four aggregates; together these constitute twenty types of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity).
Now, the Vātsīputrīyas reckon that the self is distinct from these six masters [of the views], yet it is neither identical to nor separate from them; furthermore, this self is not the Buddha-dharma."
The treatises all argue that those who do not accept [the Buddha's teachings] are heterodox persons attached to the Buddha-dharma; this master established five dharma-treasuries, namely:
the three time periods, the unconditioned, and the inexpressible treasury.

[Commentary: That which is "neither seeing nor manifesting" refers to the substance of the mind turning outward, which is called the "aspect of being able to see"; its transformation into something resembling external objects is called the "aspect of being able to manifest.
The opposite of this is what is meant by "neither seeing nor manifesting."
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "As Long-nail" (*Dīrghanakha*) to "is a holder of views," the name "Long-nail" was not his original name.
His original name was Mahākoṣṭhila, which means "Great Knee"; he was so called because his kneecaps were large. He was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra;
when Śāriputra was still in his mother’s womb, Koṣṭhila was constantly defeated in philosophical debate by [Śāriputra’s] sister, and consequently departed for South India.
The Brahmin Śrī made a vow not to clip his fingernails nor wash away the grime from his body.
Having mastered the eighteen Vedas, he returned carrying a fire-bowl upon his head and with his belly bound by iron plates, intending to take his nephew as a disciple.
His sister told him, "Your nephew has already become a disciple of the Buddha; you have come here seeking to debate the Buddha’s doctrines. The World-Honored One asked:
"What is your thesis? "I do not accept any dharma as a thesis. The World-Honored One asked in return, "Do you yourself not accept any dharma?
The Brahmin replied to the Buddha, "Gautama, I do not accept any dharma. The Buddha questioned him further, "Long-nail, do you accept this view that 'I do not accept any dharma'?
Having been thus interrogated by the Buddha on the meaning of his own words, you have already swallowed it.
The poison of wrong views has now emerged; this poisonous breath says, "I do not accept any dharma. Do you accept this view?

At that time, like a fine horse that perceives the shadow of a whip and immediately awakens to it, Long-nailed (Dīrghanakha) entered the path of the right upon hearing the whip-shadow of the Buddha’s words.
His mind having been reached, he immediately abandoned his arrogance; filled with shame and remorse, he lowered his head and reflected thus: "The Buddha has placed me between two [extremes]."
Regarding the second ground for defeat (*parājika-sthāna*): if I were to say, "I accept this view," it would be a coarse ground for defeat, as it is commonly known by all people;

how then could I claim that I do not accept any dharma? To now accept this view would be a manifest lie, a coarse ground for defeat known to many. The second ground for defeat is subtle, and I wish to accept it.
Because few people understand this, he formed this thought and replied to the Buddha, saying: "Gautama, I do not accept any dharma. The Buddha said:
"Brahmin, if you do not accept any dharma, then you do not even accept this view. Thus, there would be nothing accepted at all, and you would be no different from the common crowd.
Why then do you exalt yourself and give rise to such arrogance? Long-nailed (Dīrghanakha) was unable to respond.
The answer is: knowing for oneself that one has fallen into a position of defeat, one immediately conceives respectful faith toward the Buddha’s omniscience and reflects to oneself:
"I have fallen into a position of defeat; the World-Honored One does not proclaim my defeat nor speak of right and wrong.
Thus, even those who leave the household life to become śramaṇas and attain arhatship do so. This is excerpted from the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
[Commentary]: "Those who have not yet been able to distance themselves from the mental images" refers to bodhisattvas who employ other methods of distancing;
through various gateways, they contemplate the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and of phenomena—and cultivate the path of remedies to gradually eliminate the defilements of the mind.
Even if they pass through many eons, they may not yet attain the distancing from mental images. Now, this practitioner of *mantra-yoga* directly takes the *mantra* as...
Riding upon the transcendent gateway of the pure bodhicitta, one directly contemplates the true mark of the mind;

because one realizes that it is fundamentally unborn, this is precisely the vision of the reflection of the initial path of the light of Dharma (*prathamadharmāloka-mārga-citta*). Its purity is like empty space. Thus, the sub-commentary below states:
"For example, while ordinary people travel through perilous and evil paths by means of boats or carriages, there is yet another person who rides directly [onward]."

Regarding the passage: "Though there is no difference in the fact that one traverses the space through the air by means of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and reaches the destination one arrives at, the vehicle upon which one rides is indeed distinct. [Commentary]:

"Exerting little effort" means that those who exert little do not require a long period of time or many practices; they do not need numerous remedies (*pratipakṣa*). This refers to the aforementioned.
It is said that other bodhisattvas who employ the means of seclusion gradually cultivate ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom;

yet, even after immeasurable eons, they are unable to distance themselves from the mental images [of subject and object], despite contemplating the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and phenomena—through various gateways.
Furthermore, it is like other bodhisattvas who, aspiring for unsurpassed enlightenment, undergo various hardships and do not spare their own bodies or lives.
Throughout countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas, there have been those who attained success and those who did not.

Now, if a bodhisattva of this mantra-gate can practice through skillful means without violating the dharma-rules, they shall, even within this very life, attain the vision of the realm of inexhaustible adornment and empowerment;
it is not merely a matter of being present before one’s eyes. If they wish to transcend and ascend to the stage of Buddhahood, they shall do so.
The Tathāgata Mahāvairocana can also be realized; therefore, it is said that "little effort is required.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "from the root afflictions up to the eighty thousand [afflictions]": the "roots" refer to greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt.
These five are the roots of all afflictions; as the subsequent commentary states: "Because of the sentient beings' afflicted minds..."
Because one constantly relies on two dharmas and fails to attain the Middle Way, these are given different names according to their respective functions and are immediately divided into two.

Within these two, they are further subdivided through successive refinements—classified by the nine grades of superior, middling, and inferior, and so forth—until they become the eighty thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), which, in their full extent, are immeasurable.
Regarding the specific number of "eighty-four thousand," the *Abhidharmakośa* states that this refers to the actual practices used as antidotes.
The number of specific remedial paths that counteract the eighty thousand types of conduct, such as greed and so forth, is likewise equal.
That is to say, for each of the ten afflictions—greed, hatred, and the rest—there are nine preparatory means, totaling one hundred;
adding another hundred for the subsequent stages makes three hundred. When these are combined with the original hundred, and considering each of the one hundred preparatory stages individually...
Using nine as the expedient means, they combine to form one thousand; the subsequent divisions are likewise, each forming another thousand.

Together with the original hundred, these constitute two thousand one hundred. Both those already arisen and those yet to arise each number two thousand one hundred, totaling four thousand two hundred.
This calculation applies to each of the five types of persons—those with excessive greed, excessive hatred, excessive delusion, attachment to self, and discursive thought.

Four thousand two hundred multiplied by ten equals twenty-one thousand; these serve as the antidotes for the four types of persons—those dominated by greed, hatred, delusion, and those with equal proportions of the three poisons—and as each of these four possesses twenty-one thousand [afflictions], they total eighty-four thousand.

Now, because the practitioner of *mantra* attains the *Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin-samādhi*, they perceive the true nature of these eighty-four thousand afflictions and thereby accomplish the eighty-four thousand meritorious qualities (*guṇa*).
"A treasury of the jewels of virtue. [Commentary:

However, the phrase "not yet ultimate" and so forth all serve to address potential objections. Specifically, there is an objection that says: "Since it is stated that he is 'self-awakened mind,' he is therefore called a Buddha.
A Buddha is one whose awakening is perfected. Now, if his awakening is already perfected, why does he not perform various supernatural transformations?"
Regarding the general explanation of the "Universal Manifestation Adornment" (Puxian Zhuangyan), it is said that this is not the ultimate state of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
It is like the moon from the first day to the fourteenth day: although the moonlight is nearly full and the darkness is nearly exhausted, it cannot yet stir the tides of the great ocean.

Only after turning this one step further into wondrous enlightenment does the light of wisdom become perfectly full; it can no longer increase, just as the moon on the fifteenth day is finally able to stir the great ocean.

The Tide [Commentary] states: "One should not claim what has not been attained as attained, for one clings to the initial mind as the ultimate; therefore it says 'thus,' yet it is not the ultimate," and so forth.

[The *Shu* (Sub-commentary) explains: "To restrain the eight arrivals" means that because the practitioner abides in the unconditioned precepts (*asaṃskṛta-śīla*), they are able to restrain the eight arrivals upon attaining insight into the inconceivable Middle Way and the profound dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). As for the "eight": the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) claim that the world is eternal.

If one considers "permanence, bliss, self, and purity" as the four [inversions] for the two vehicles—whereby they regard eternal quiescence as *nirvāṇa*—then permanence, bliss, self, and purity would themselves constitute four inversions.

If it is argued that the two vehicles lack these four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, this is a case of granting them [the status of having them] while simultaneously depriving them of them;
for they have indiscriminately applied these terms, like a worm eating wood that happens by chance to form characters. Thus, it is not according to reality.
How much more so for one who does not realize that the true nature (*dharmatā*) of birth and death is itself *nirvāṇa*—how could such a person be able to abandon the eight inversions?
[Commentary: Kāśyapa also said, "up to those with false views. This refers to what the Buddha told Kāśyapa in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "Good son, the four inversions are as follows:
to give rise to the perception of suffering within what is not suffering; to give rise to the perception of pleasure within suffering; and [to perceive] the impermanent as permanent..."

To perceive the permanent as impermanent, the selfless as having a self, the self as selfless, the pure as impure, and the impure as pure—these are called inversions. Thereupon, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, from this day forward I have finally attained right view. World-Honored One, prior to this, we were all known as people of false views."

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "Although there are immeasurable heavenly Māras," etc., this is a question concerning how immeasurable heavenly Māras all transform themselves into the bodies of Buddhas and each preach a semblance of the *pāramitās*.
The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (*Zhidu lun*) states: "All Bodhisattvas aspire to attain *sarvajñatā* (omniscience).
When Māras come wishing to destroy them, they say: 'This *sarvajñatā* is empty and non-existent; it is merely a deception by various teachers.'"
Your ear is like space: it is non-existent, colorless, formless, and unknowable. All-knowledge (*sarvajñā*) is likewise;
therefore, it is said to be equal to space. As for all dharmas—such as the six *pāramitās* that lead toward all-knowledge—these dharmas are empty and all-knowledge is also empty.
Being characterized by non-existence, within this there is no attainment of all-knowledge.
"You have endured suffering and toil in vain, even to the point that you now hastily repent and abandon these wrong thoughts.
When the celestial Māra speaks thus, why would he not be able to disturb the net of their doubts? Therefore, it is explained here:
because this bodhisattva illuminates and perceives the clarity of the Path within the mind, all dharmas manifest before them, and they penetrate them all without error.
Therefore, Māra cannot move them; thus it is said, "even though there are immeasurable devas, Māras, and so forth.
[Commentary] The power of faith and understanding means that the practitioner clearly perceives the phenomena and principles herein, remaining free from doubt and anxiety.

It is like looking into a well and seeing the damp mud; although one has not yet reached the water, one knows the water must be near. Therefore, it is said that faith and understanding increase further.
Because it is characterized by diligence, it is called "power" (*bala*).

[Commentary: There are briefly seven meanings for which it is named the Mahāyāna; these may be the same as or different from what is taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, and other texts.
As they are established according to their respective teachings, there is no need to harmonize them.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "initially opening the vajra-treasury" and so forth, this refers to Vajrapāṇi’s question to the Buddha:
"What is the cause of such wisdom? What is its root? What is its ultimate consummation? The World-Honored One replied:
"The bodhicitta is the cause; great compassion is the root; skillful means is the ultimate consummation. Although the World-Honored One thus fulfilled the intent of Vajrapāṇi...
The questions posed by the hand have been briefly answered, yet their characteristics have not yet been revealed. Next, the inquiry and explanation state:
"Lord of Mysteries, what is bodhi? This is the question. "It is knowing one's own mind as it truly is" is the answer.

It is like a poor woman who, though she hears that there is a precious treasure within her own home, has no means to discover or take it out unless it is pointed out to her; therefore, it must first be revealed.
This demonstrates that from this point onward, one is finally able to initiate the sublime application (prayoga) called "the first.

Regarding the phrase "arising apart from causes such as karma," it means that while all sentient beings, due to causes such as ignorance, create various karmas and undergo various births, now, being free from such births, the sprout of the Buddha-tree arises; this is precisely the arising of the Great Emptiness (mahāśūnyatā).
[Commentary] Regarding the "great winds of the eight directions," according to the *Yiwei* (Explanations of the Changes), these are:

the Tiao wind in the northeast, the Ming wind in the east, the Qingming wind in the southeast, the Jing wind in the south, the Liang wind in the southwest, the Sou wind in the west, the Bouzhou wind in the northwest, and the Guangmo wind in the north; these constitute the winds of the eight directions.
[Commentary]: Regarding "Quiescent Light" (*jìguāng*): "quiescence" (*jì*) refers to the true mark of the mind, which is fundamentally unborn, eternally quiescent, and without characteristics.
"Light" (*guāng*) refers to the numinous awareness of this very mental state, which is never obscured. Furthermore, "quiescence" is samādhi, and "light" is great wisdom.

When a practitioner attains the *Sarvāvaraṇaviskambhin-samādhi*, they give rise to the radiance of great wisdom, whereby they are able to universally illumine the immeasurable nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, it is called "Quiescent Light" (*jigō*).
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "All that is said," etc., the following thirteen lines of commentary address a class of practitioners who cling to dhyāna;

they rely on the nature of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), which is without action and without cultivation, a mirror that is inherently luminous, requiring neither wiping nor polishing—this is the merging within the gate of dhyāna.
There is absolutely no basis for establishing doctrines regarding ordinary or holy beings; all such phenomena are like dreams and illusions, utterly non-existent.
They have been empty and quiescent from the very beginning, not becoming non-existent only now. Even this wisdom that realizes their non-existence cannot be apprehended.

In the equal Dharma-realm, there is neither Buddha nor sentient being; even "Dharma-realm" is a mere provisional name. Since the mind itself does not exist, who can speak of a Dharma-realm? Who can speak of cultivation?
Do not cultivate the notion of non-Buddha or Buddha; even if there were a single dharma superior to Nirvana, I would say it is like a dream or an illusion.
There is no dharma that can bind, and no Buddha that can be made. Whatever is done is all delusion. To realize this is to understand that from the beginning there has been nothing to do;
when the mind has nowhere to rest, one is finally free from inversion—this is what is called liberation. Stonehead Ox.
The Master always demonstrated this principle, thereby causing the mind and its activities to correspond with it and not allowing emotions to stagnate upon any single dharma.
When practice reaches its culmination over time, habitual tendencies naturally vanish; thus, one becomes unimpeded toward all things—whether enemies or kin, suffering or joy.
Consequently, there is a class of Daoist practitioners, Confucian scholars, and idle monks who study the principles of Chan meditation who all speak these words.
They have merely reached a superficial extreme, unaware of the ultimate principle; having lost their capacity for awakening, they do nothing but maintain a state of silent, deluded meditation.
The person refuted here is precisely such an individual.

[Commentary] Regarding the meaning of "foolish children" as explained previously: the aforementioned commentary states that this refers to ordinary beings within the six realms who do not understand the Truth of Reality (*bhūtārtha*).

It is so named because one practices the causes of suffering by following wrong paths through mental activities based on cause and effect, and because one is attached to and stubbornly clings to the three realms without relinquishing them.
[Commentary] Regarding "the sixteen views" and so forth: this means that although there are ninety-five types of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika), their general intent is as follows...

Because it transcends the sixteen heterodox views (*vāda*), the *Śāsanodbhāvana-kārikā* states: “Adherence to the existence of the effect within the cause; the manifest existence of the past and future; the self; eternalism; the cause of past actions;
the Lord (*Īśvara*) and so forth as causes; harm to the Dharma; finitude and infinitude; evasive equivocation (*amarā-vikkhepa*); the doctrine of no-cause (*ahetu-vāda*);

nihilism; emptiness; the doctrine of the supreme; purity; and auspiciousness. These sixteen heterodox views are enumerated in sequence as follows: first, the thesis that the effect exists within the cause (*satkāryavāda*)."

1. The Vārṣagaṇya non-Buddhists, who hold the doctrine that [things] are manifested through conditions (*pratyaya-vyakti-vāda*); 2. The Saṃghabhadra masters, who hold the doctrine of the real existence of the past and future (*atītānāgata-dravya-sad-vāda*);

3. The Vaiśeṣikas, who hold the doctrine of the real existence of the self (*ātma-dravya-sad-vāda*); 4. The Īśvarakāpas, who hold the doctrine that all phenomena are eternal (*sarva-dharma-nitya-vāda*); 5.

The followers of Nirgrantha Jñātiputra, who hold the doctrine that all causes are produced by past actions (*pūrva-kṛta-hetu-vāda*); and 6. Those who hold the doctrine of unequal causes (*viṣama-hetu-vāda*), such as those who claim Īśvara and others are the cause.

1. The eight harmful views constitute the core of the dispute over the True Dharma (*saddharma*) at the end of the eon; various Brahmins, desiring to eat meat, falsely give rise to this calculation. 2.

The doctrines of the finite, the infinite, and so forth, which obtain worldly meditative absorption (*dhyāna*); these are the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) of the finite and infinite. 3. The doctrine of the "evasive equivocation regarding immortality" (*amarāvikṣepa*);
these are the evasive equivocal non-Buddhist outsiders. 4. The doctrine that all phenomena have no cause; these are the non-Buddhist outsiders who hold to causelessness. (10)

12. The school of annihilationism which asserts the cessation of the two [types of] seven matters; 13. The school of the emptiness of the thirteen causes and effects belonging to the heterodox who assert annihilationism;
14. The school of false calculation regarding supremacy, which calculates that the Brahmins are the most supreme caste;

15. The school of false calculation regarding purity, which holds that there is nirvana in the present life; 16. The school of false calculation regarding auspiciousness, which consists of the heterodox practitioners of calendrical astrology.
Thus, each of these sixteen types [of teachers] claimed for themselves that their master was a Blessed One, omniscient and all-seeing;
therefore, they are called the "sixteen views of knowledge" and so forth.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "This refers to Nārāyaṇa and others," there are many such explanations.
Specifically, the teachers of the Vedas maintain that the deity Nārāyaṇa can produce the four castes; they maintain that Brahmā can produce all things. Deva says:
"From the navel of the deity Nārāyaṇa, a great lotus flower was produced; upon this lotus flower is Brahmā, the progenitor. It is said that this Brahmā is [the creator]."
The progenitor of all things was born from the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet of Brahmā, giving rise to the four castes and so forth;

it is also said that Nārāyaṇa can produce Brahmā, and Brahmā is the progenitor of all things. Furthermore, there is the teacher Andhaka, who speculates on the primal limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) and other such matters, but there is no need to cite them in full here.
This venerable and noble being is none other than Nārāyaṇa, who is profoundly tranquil and eternal.
He dwells as that sovereign who governs through non-action, while his ministers bring all transformations to completion, like officials receiving and executing orders;
furthermore, there is one even more venerable than these, namely, the god Nārāyaṇa.
[Commentary]: Regarding the loss of the Buddha’s three seals of Dharma, the *Yilin* (Forest of Meanings), fascicle 1, states: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
nirvana is quiescent; all dharmas are without self. If one adds "all contaminated things are suffering," they become the four seals of Dharma.

Now, I say that because the Pāśupatas posit a *puruṣa* (spiritual self) and the dharmas of the three periods of time as eternal, they lose [the truth of] the Tathāgata’s seals that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent" and "all dharmas are without self."
This is the Dharma Seal.

[Commentary: Furthermore, there are those who reckon that the "one capable of seeing" is itself the True Self (*ātman*). This refers to certain non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who reckon that the one capable of seeing constitutes the True Self, which is both unitary and eternal.
Moreover, there are other non-Buddhists who, regarding the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*), [reckon them] to be distinct according to their respective functions.
Since all [these] are designated as "I," the present objection states: "You claim that the one who can see is the 'I,' yet those who can hear and so forth—these five—are also the 'I.
If you do not posit this, what fault would there be? Both positions possess faults. What are these faults?
If you say that each of the other five is individually the 'I,' then there would be six 'selves,' which contradicts the principle of unity; for you maintain that the seer is a single 'I'."

Since this faculty of seeing cannot be heard, felt, or cognized, and since these six faculties do not know one another, your insistence that a single faculty of seeing constitutes the self cannot be maintained as being sixfold.
If you claim that the other five are likewise one with this same self, then although the self would be one, it would nonetheless conflict with the six faculties;
for the eye sees and the ear hears, each functioning separately. Since these six faculties [do not know one another]...

Because they do not know one another, the six sense organs cannot be considered one. If you claim there is something that is "not-self," the commentary raises an objection, stating that this is likewise a point of doubt.

Furthermore, it provides a formal logical argument (*pramāṇa*) by way of analogy: "Since the other five organs and so forth are already established as not-self, that which is able to see the self must also be not-self.
Thus, the syllogism is formulated: "That which you call 'the seer' is the subject (*dharmin*); it must be not-self [the predicate]."
Therefore, my formal argument (prayoga) states: because it is subsumed under one of the six sense faculties, it is like the other five faculties;
since the counter-objection can be understood accordingly, that which they have established is not universally accepted (aprasiddha).

[Commentary: Regarding the scripture’s statement, "If [it refers to] Manuṣya, etc.," one asks: Since there have already been three Tang Tripiṭaka masters who committed translation errors, why is it that nowadays *manuṣya* is not called "human" (*ren*), and *māṇava* is not called "superior to me" (*sheng wo*)?

Furthermore, what difference is there between placing *manasija* (mind-born) and *kumāra* (youth)? Answer: It is to accord with ancient translations and avoid contradicting them. As for the right or wrong within this matter, it follows from...
The commentary merely selects and discards [the details].

[Commentary]: Regarding these six days of fasting (*upoṣadha*), according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is said that on these six fasting days, malevolent spirits harm people and disturb all beings.
If, in any village, hamlet, kingdom, district, or town, there are those who observe the fast, receive the precepts, and practice virtue...
Because of these causes and conditions, evil spirits depart far away and one’s dwelling becomes peaceful and secure.

For this reason, by observing the fast and receiving the precepts on these six days, one gains an increase in merit. Question: For what reason do the various evil spirits afflict and harm people on these six days?
Answer: The *Sūtra on the Original Arising of Heaven and Earth* states that when the kalpa first began to form, there was a certain Brahmā deity.
The prince’s father, a spirit who practiced the path of a brahmacārin, had spent twelve celestial years on the heavens.
During these six days, he cut his own flesh and drew his blood to place it into the fire; for this reason, the various malevolent spirits always possess power during these six days.
He asked: "Why did the father of the spirits cut the flesh and blood from his own body during these six days?"
When asked while amidst the flames, he replied: "Among all the deities, Maheśvara is the greatest and foremost.
All deities have their allotted days; Maheśvara possesses four days in each month—namely the eighth, the eighteenth, the twenty-third, and the twenty-ninth.
Other deities possess two days each in a month—the first and the sixteenth."
The second, seventh, fifteenth, and thirtieth days of the month belong to all the spirits; Maheśvara is the lord of these spirits.
Furthermore, because he possesses many days, these four days are counted as *caitya* (fasting) days.

Moreover, since the fifteenth day is the day of all the various spirits, it is also counted as a *caitya* day. Therefore, on these six *caitya* days, the various ghosts and spirits [are particularly active].
He immediately possessed power. Furthermore, on these six days, the father of the various spirits cut his own flesh and drew blood, placing them into the fire.
After twelve years had passed, the Heavenly King descended and said to his son, "What wish do you seek? He replied, "I seek to have a son.
The Heavenly King said, "The dharma for the sustenance of sages consists of burning incense, sweet fruits, and various pure [offerings]."
"O Purifier, how is it that you cast flesh and blood into the fire like a sinful act? You have destroyed wholesome dharmas and delighted in evil deeds;
therefore, may you give birth to evil offspring who eat flesh and drink blood. At that time, eight great ghosts emerged from within the fire;
their bodies were black as ink, their hair was yellow, and their eyes were red, possessing the radiance of fire. All the spirits and ghosts...
Since these eight ghosts were born from this, on these six days one cuts flesh and draws blood to place them in the fire so as to gain power.
Just as in the Buddha-dharma there is no inherent good or evil in the days themselves, yet because of the worldly conditions associated with these "evil" days,
it is taught that one should observe the fast and receive the precepts.

[Commentary]: Regarding the six types of relatives: first, those related through the father, which refers to one's own paternal kin; second, those related through the mother, which refers to maternal kin; third, those related through oneself, such as brothers and so forth;
fourth, those related through the wife, which refers to the wife’s own family members; fifth, those related through sons, which refers to the brothers of one’s sons;
sixth, those related through the wives of one’s sons, which refers to the internal and external kin of others. Furthermore, according to the Bodhisattva Precepts...
The *Chao* (Excerpts) states: "Brothers, sisters, wives, and children.
[The *Shu* (Commentary) says: Regarding the phrase "reliance on fearlessness," "fearlessness" means the absence of fear. Fear refers to dread;

that is to say, since beginningless time, ordinary beings have experienced rebirth in the evil realms due to the ten unwholesome actions, which are the most terrifying places. Later, they encounter virtuous friends and hear the World-Honored One’s...
Joyfully taking refuge in the Triple Gem and practicing the ten wholesome paths, one gradually approaches *nirvāṇa* and no longer fears the sufferings of the three miserable realms;
this is called "fearlessness. As for the term "reliance" (*niśraya*), "reliance" means to rely upon or take as a support;
that is, the ten wholesome paths are the place where all ordinary beings rely. This reliance of fearlessness is termed the "reliance of fearlessness."

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the wisdom of liberation arises within what has been explained," this is extracted from the section on the basis of fearlessness regarding the eighth birth and death.

That is to say, these ignorant, childish ordinary beings—upon hearing what was previously said by their spiritual friends, namely, "This is the Great Deva who bestows all happiness"—then follow the worldly Three Jewels among the four classes of devas and so forth.
Within which category does one practice in accordance with that, whereby the wisdom that aspires for renunciation and liberation arises?

Because this mind is sublime and superior to what preceded it, and because it remains immovable based upon that [practice], it is said: "In accordance with what has been taught, until the arising of the wisdom of liberation."
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "However, because [they] do not yet know," the meaning of the word "however" (rán) contains both concessive and restrictive senses.

Concessively, it means: although within those teachings they have attained a distinguished state and a wisdom seeking liberation has arisen; restrictively, it means: "However, because they do not yet know," and so forth, up to "they do not yet depart from the views of annihilationism and eternalism.
This is because in the Buddha-dharma, by knowing that things exist through causes and conditions, one departs from the view of non-existence (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
Because one contemplates that the intrinsic nature of causes and conditions is empty, the view of existence does not arise;

yet, because they do not understand whether these causes and conditions exist or not, even though they possess the wisdom that contemplates emptiness, they do not depart from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
Furthermore, this so-called "wisdom" is merely incorrect conceptualization and is not true wisdom. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "What is the dhyāna of the non-Buddhists?"

Question: What is the wisdom of meditative concentration? Answer: Because non-Buddhists pursue dhyāna with a sense of self, because they abound in craving, views, and pride, and because they do not relinquish all phenomena, they possess no true wisdom.
Question: You say that non-Buddhists contemplate emptiness; yet, if they contemplate emptiness, they must relinquish all phenomena.
Why then do you say they do not relinquish all phenomena and thus lack true wisdom?
The answer is: Although non-Buddhists contemplate emptiness, they grasp at the mark of emptiness; although they know that all phenomena are empty, they do not realize their own emptiness.
Because they are attached to the wisdom that contemplates emptiness, they do not transcend permanence.
[Commentary: "Those who cannot know *nirvāṇa* refers to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who do not understand the meaning of emptiness through causes and conditions.

Even if they were to single-mindedly apply themselves with diligence to seek liberation, when examining their realization of the fruit, they reach no further than the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Since they reckon this state to be *nirvāṇa*, they are unable to know the Great *Nirvāṇa* of the Buddha-dharma."
[Commentary]:
As for the phrase "the eightfold right mind and so forth," this means that although the wisdom seeking liberation arises from the initial seed-mind up through the eighth stage,
the infant-like mind, if one does not encounter favorable conditions, one will instead fall back into the views of annihilationism or eternalism.
Even if one temporarily retreats and enters into wrong views, the eight kinds of seeds of the right mind that have been perfumed within the *ālayavijñāna* can never be destroyed or extinguished;
if one hears the Buddha-dharma as a condition, one immediately enters the path of the seeds of the eightfold right mind.
Furthermore, the explanation of the seeds of the eightfold right mind refers to the eight branches of the noble path, namely right view, right thought, and so forth.

While within the ground of the original enlightenment (*prakṛtistha-gotra*) of sentient beings, once the conditions for meeting a virtuous friend have been encountered and [the path] has been initiated, it shall never perish;
because of this firm nature, it is said that its eightfold right mind and so forth are thus.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "those who lack the capacity," this refers to persons who have not yet reached the stage where the seeds of the eight consciousnesses arise and who lack the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).

For such individuals, even when one speaks merely of worldly suffering and pleasure, or explains that time is the cause, or even sets forth the eightfold precepts in their entirety with their minor details and tranquility, they are still unable to believe;
how much less could they believe in the profoundly deep matters of the Buddha-dharma?
[Commentary: Regarding "the perfuming of the true mark of one's own mind": "one's own mind" refers to the True Mind of Original Enlightenment (*mūla-jñāna*).

This true mark of the mind can perfume the defiled mind of ignorance in sentient beings, thereby producing pure function. The *Awakening of Faith* states: "The defiled dharmas of ignorance are in reality devoid of pure karma;
yet, because they are perfumed by True Suchness (*tathatā*), there exists pure function. The aforementioned commentary explains this as "pure perfuming."

The "one who is defiled" refers to the true suchness of original enlightenment within the gate of arising and ceasing; therefore, the principle of permeation exists here. Within the gate of true suchness, however, this principle does not exist.

Because this internal permeation of original enlightenment causes non-enlightenment to give rise to weariness with samsara and the desire for liberation, thereby turning back the flow [of delusion] to accord with truth, it is called "function.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Even those of icchantika nature will, by the power of their future Buddha-nature, eventually [return to the path]."
Regarding the statement that "the power of Buddha-nature" refers to the power of internal perfuming by this very *benjue* (intrinsic awakening), the meaning clarified here is as follows:
because the name of wholesome dharmas has existed within the world from time immemorial, it is precisely this non-empty *benjue* that perfumes sentient beings,
causing them to gradually restrain their eating, admonish themselves, and give rise to the eight minds— beginning with the sprouting of seeds— and other superior states.
Because one definitively develops an impartial mind that loathes the suffering of birth and death and seeks the bliss of nirvāṇa, it is called the "perfuming of the true mark of one's own mind.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the supreme Mahāyāna phrase," etc., this concludes the praise for what Vajrapāṇi asked: "How so, World-Honored One?"
These ten phrases of the Mahāyāna dharma, beginning with "this mind gives rise to bodhicitta," are like the finest essence of clarified butter (*sarpis*) among all teachings;
because their flavor is supreme, they are called the "Supreme Mahāyāna Phrases. Regarding the manner in which the continuum of this mind arises:
although this mind is ultimately pure like space and free from all characteristics, it nevertheless arises from causes and conditions.
Because it arises and possesses the characteristic of origination, it is called "the characteristic of the continuous arising of mind.
Regarding the phrase "the great secret of all Buddhas" and so forth: the secret treasury of all the Tathāgatas has various levels of depth and degrees of magnitude;
since this is the most profound within the secrets, it is called "Great. That "non-Buddhists cannot know it" refers to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
This refers to ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles—these two types of outsiders have not yet recognized the mind of true reality (*tathatā*).
Thus, the *tathāgatagarbha* and the arising-and-ceasing [mind] combine to form the *ālayavijñāna*.

Not only do they fail to recognize the mind that is free from arising and ceasing, but they also fail to recognize the mind of arising and ceasing itself; therefore, they are called outsiders who cannot know the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
