"Just as space is ultimately pure, so no material forms can defile it; the nature of the mind is likewise."

Because all such conceptual discriminations cannot defile it, it is designated by that name. Regarding the aforementioned "Ten Stages" (*daśabhūmi*): "Stage" (*bhūmi*) refers to a dwelling place (*sthiti*), meaning a support (*ādhāra*);

"ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to that which gives rise to [the dwelling], meaning that which supports the arising of the dwelling. Thus, that which supports the arising of the dwelling is called a "stage-ground" (*bhūmi*).

As the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra) states: "The prajñā that enters into principle is called 'dwelling' (*sthiti*); that which gives rise to virtuous conduct is called 'ground' (*bhūmi*). This is from its commentary.

The commentary states: "Entering" (*praveśa*) means realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). "Prajñā" refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); because it realizes the principle of true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), both are termed *prajñā*.
"Abiding" (*vihāra*) means being unmoving; it carries the sense of a support or basis. That which abides gives rise to virtuous qualities and is thus called a "ground" (*bhūmi*):

when wisdom is in profound union with true reality, it can produce and manifest both unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) virtues; all such conditioned merits arise on this basis. There is no [other ground].
Because the meaning of abiding and arising is manifested through these virtues and they mutually illuminate one another, it is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*).

There are ten distinct abidings on these grounds, which are named the Ten Grounds of Abiding (*daśa-vihāra-bhūmayaḥ*); the detailed explanation of their meanings is found in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-ṭīkā*.

Furthermore, these correspond to the ten abidings within the thirteen abidings of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. Regarding the first, it says: "The first is the Abiding of the Spiritual Lineage (*gotra-vihāra*)."
The lineage abiding in its original nature (*prakṛtisthagotra*) refers to those bodhisattvas who have not yet entered the *saṃghāṭī* (the stage of accumulation).

This means that their nature is inherently virtuous and naturally endowed with the qualities of a bodhisattva. Because their nature is inherently virtuous, they are impelled toward the wholesome by skillful means;
it is not through deliberate deliberation that they exercise restraint or protection. Abiding in this state, they maintain the seeds of all the Buddha-dharmas.
The "son" refers here to the foolish, ordinary worldlings who follow the eight worldly concerns.

The second stage, the dwelling of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*), refers to all bodhisattva practices—from the initial generation of the profound and firm mind of great awakening (*mahā-bodhicitta*) until one has not yet entered the first bhūmi—including both the roots of virtue of the provisions (*saṃbhāra*) and the preparatory applications (*prayoga*).
These constitute the essence of this dwelling; it corresponds to the beginning of this sutra.

From the initial arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) until the uprooting of the fundamental afflictions (*kleśa*) of karma, through the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), and even to the dual liberation from the eight mental states of opposition and compliance—the web of karmic and afflictive obscurations regarding the self and the aggregates (*ātma-skandha*)—all these constitute this dwelling.

The third is the Dwelling of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*), also called the Dwelling of Pure Superior Intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-vihāra*), which means that one personally realizes: "I have now directly realized Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*)."

Therefore, because the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) has attained purity, this refers to the first stage of this sutra, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), which is the dwelling in higher morality (*adhiśīla-vihāra*);
for by the purity of intention, one attains the fulfillment of the two types of ethical discipline.

This is the second stage, the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*), which is the dwelling in higher mind (*adhicitta-vihāra*); for by the purity of the internal mind, one is able to radiate the light of boundless sublime wisdom. Thus...
This is the third stage, the Radiant Ground (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*), which is the dwelling in superior wisdom associated with the six factors of enlightenment (*ṣaḍ-bodhyaṅga*).

Because the flames of the light of true knowledge regarding the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharma*) burn the fuel of the afflictions and bring about the illumination of wisdom that establishes the True Dharma, it is identical to the fourth stage, the Blazing Wisdom Ground (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), which is the dwelling in superior wisdom associated with the seven truths. It involves the definitive resolution regarding the various Noble Truths (*āryasatya*).
Because the sublime wisdom of meditative concentration is extremely difficult to surpass, it is the fifth stage, the "Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjayā).

It is the dwelling in superior wisdom associated with the cessation of the forward and reverse progression of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). The phrase "ignorance conditions formations" refers to the branch of the flow of existence;

the term "progression" refers to arising, while "cessation" refers to the contemplation of the reversal [of that process]. Because non-attachment toward the phenomena of dependent origination is manifest, it is—
This sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), consists of the nine dwellings characterized by signlessness with effort;

this is precisely the dwelling in signlessness with application and effort in the seventh stage. The tenth dwelling, characterized by signlessness without effort, occurs in this eighth stage, where one abandons all previous paths involving application and effort, and the mind advances further into a state that is effortless, without application, and spontaneous.

11. The Stage of the Mastery of the Unimpeded Understandings (*pratisaṃvid-vihāra*): Because Bodhisattvas dwelling in the [final] nine stages attain the four unimpeded understandings and are able to preach the True Dharma as great Dharma-preachers;
12. The Stage of the Supreme Perfection of a Bodhisattva (*parama-saṃpūrṇa-bodhisattva-vihāra*):

This is the tenth stage, because all the paths of the Bodhisattvas have attained purity and the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhi-sambhāra*) are most excellently fulfilled; 13. The Stage of the Ultimate... [text fragment].

The "Ultimate Abode of the Tathāgata" refers to the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of the fruit; it is the state of fruition itself, which is the Tathāgata’s ultimate stage of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*) as described in this sutra.
Regarding the phrase "practitioners who possess faith and understanding," "faith" (*śraddhā*) means acceptance and aspiration, while "understanding" (*adhimukti*) means realization and penetration;

each has degrees of depth, with the shallow referring to those prior to the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*) and the deep referring to those on the stages (*bhūmi-stha*). This [refers to] the practice of those on the stages.

Because one proceeds with cultivation, the third sub-commentary below states: "Furthermore, one should contemplate the analogy of illusion, such as how through the combination of medicinal substances one attains the ability to ascend into space and prolong one's life;

this is not something that can be conceived by those of sharp faculties or wisdom alone. It simply requires a profound understanding of its technique, and there is nothing that will not be accomplished.
By means of this deep mind of pure faith and freedom from doubt, one gradually attains the realization of the Dharma."
Furthermore, because the Dharma is now manifest through direct verification, one's faith and understanding increase further and cannot be destroyed. Moreover, the *Vyākhyā* states:
"For example, when digging a well and already seeing moist mud, one increases one's diligence with the expectation that water will surely be found;

likewise, when drilling for fire and already seeing smoke, one redoubles one's efforts with the expectation that fire will surely be obtained. Therefore, it is called "practicing within faith and understanding" (*adhimukti-caryā*).
[Commentary: Regarding the "arising of the ten great vows" and so forth, as stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"When a Bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they are able to accomplish such great vows, such great valor, and such great activities.
That is to say, they give rise to vast, pure, and resolute understanding, and with all manner of offerings, they reverently make offerings to all [Buddhas]."
The Buddhas cause [this] to be without remainder, as vast as the Dharma-realm, ultimate as space, and to continue without rest throughout all kalpas until the end of the future;
furthermore, they make great vows, vowing to receive the wheel of the Dharma of all Buddhas,
to encompass the Bodhi of all Buddhas, to protect the teachings of all Buddhas, and to uphold the Dharma of all Buddhas, and so forth.

Furthermore, he made a great vow, wishing that whenever a Buddha appeared in any world—descending from the Tuṣita heaven, entering the womb, dwelling in the womb, being born, renouncing the world, attaining enlightenment, preaching the Dharma, and manifesting parinirvāṇa—he would go to all those places to attend upon, serve, and make offerings to them;
acting as a leader among the assembly, he would receive and practice the True Dharma, turning the wheel of the Dharma simultaneously in all places. Furthermore, he vowed:
He makes a great vow, vowing that all bodhisattva practices— vast, immeasurable, indestructible, and unadulterated— encompassing all the pāramitās,

the pure maintenance of the stages (*bhūmi*), their general characteristics, specific characteristics, common characteristics, distinct characteristics, the characteristics of formation, and the characteristics of disintegration—

all such bodhisattva practices shall be explained according to reality, teaching and transforming all beings so that they may accept and practice them, and their minds may attain growth. Furthermore...

I make this great vow: may I bring to spiritual maturity all those within the realms of sentient beings—whether with form or formless, with perception or without perception, or neither with nor without perception;
whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; those bound to the three realms and entering the six destinies;
and all who are comprised within name-and-form (nāmarūpa)—and lead them all into the Buddha-dharma.
They eternally sever all worldly destinies and cause beings to dwell securely on the path to the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Furthermore, they make great vows, wishing that in all worlds—vast and immeasurable, whether coarse or subtle, disordered, inverted, or upright;

whether entering, moving, or departing—they may clearly perceive and manifest with wisdom the infinite and manifold differences of the ten directions, such as the distinctions of Indra’s net (*indrājāla*).
With prior knowledge and vision, he further makes a great vow: "May all lands enter into one land, and one land enter into all lands;
may infinite Buddha-lands be universally pure, adorned with arrays of radiant light and various requisites;
may they be free from all afflictions and achieve the path of purity, filled with sentient beings of immeasurable wisdom."
They universally enter the vast realms of all Buddhas and manifest them according to the minds of sentient beings, causing all to rejoice.
Furthermore, they make great vows, wishing to share the same resolve and conduct as all Bodhisattvas, free from enmity or jealousy;
they gather all roots of goodness, and with all Bodhisattvas sharing a single object of focus, they constantly assemble together, never parting, according to their will.
They are able to manifest various Buddha-bodies according to the inclinations of sentient beings' own minds; they are able to know the power, majesty, and wisdom of the realm of all Tathāgatas;
they attain non-regressive, sovereign supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*) and travel through all worlds;
they manifest forms in all assemblies and universally enter all places of birth; they accomplish the inconceivable Mahāyāna and cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva. Furthermore, they resolve:
With great vows, may I ride the non-retrogressive wheel and practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, such that the actions of my body, speech, and mind shall never be in vain.
Should anyone behold me even for a moment, they shall become certain of the Buddha-dharma; should they hear my voice even briefly, they shall attain true wisdom;

and should they give rise to pure faith for even an instant, they shall forever sever their afflictions. May I obtain a body like that of the Great King of Medicinal Trees, and may I obtain a body like that of a wish-fulfilling jewel. May I cultivate...
They practice all bodhisattva deeds and further make great vows,
vowing to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in all worlds without ever departing from even a single hair-tip, manifesting in every hair-tip the birth, renunciation,
proceeding to the site of enlightenment, attaining perfect awakening, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering parinirvāṇa.

Through the power of great wisdom regarding the spheres of experience, in every moment of thought, he manifests the attainment of Buddhahood according to the minds of all sentient beings, causing them to attain quiescence.
By means of a single *samyak-saṃbodhi*, he knows that the entire dharma-realm is the very nature of nirvāṇa;
with a single voice, he preaches the Dharma so that the hearts of all sentient beings are filled with joy, manifesting entry into Great Nirvāṇa while never ceasing his activity.
The Bodhisattva’s practice demonstrates the ground of great wisdom, establishing all phenomena through the supernormal power of dharma-knowledge,
the supernormal power of psychic travel, and the supernormal power of illusion; having attained mastery over transformations that fill the entire dharma-realm,
all these aforementioned vows are likewise vast as the dharma-realm, ultimate as space, and shall continue without ceasing throughout all kalpas until the end of the future.

Regarding the words "Resting, etc.," O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they give rise to such great vows, such great courage, and such great activities.
Taking these ten gates of vows as the foremost, they fulfill a million *asaṃkhyeya* great vows.
O Son of the Buddha, these great vows are accomplished by means of ten points of totality (*paryanta*). What are these ten?

That is to say, should the realm of sentient beings be exhausted, the realm of worlds be exhausted, the realm of empty space be exhausted, the realm of the Dharma be exhausted, the realm of nirvana be exhausted,
the realm of the appearance of Buddhas be exhausted, the realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom be exhausted, the realm of the objects perceived by the mind be exhausted,

the realm of the spheres entered by the Buddha-wisdom be exhausted, and the realms of the revolution of the world, the revolution of the Dharma, and the revolution of wisdom be exhausted— if these were all to come to an end, only then would my vow likewise reach its end.
Only when this world-system, and even the turning of the world, the turning of the Dharma, and the turning of wisdom reach their ultimate end, shall my vow reach its end;
yet because the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible, and because the turning of the world, the turning of the Dharma, and the turning of wisdom are likewise inexhaustible,
these roots of goodness from my great vow shall never come to an end.

[Commentary]: Regarding "generating roots within the ten realms," this means that the compassion and vows cultivated within the aforementioned ten inexhaustible realms are able to give rise to the skillful means of the subsequent stages; thus, they are termed "roots."
[Commentary: "The stages from the eighth ground upward" refers to the fact that the objects of the final three grounds are identical, as they all take the signless (*animitta*) as their object.

Regarding the statement "merely in terms of skillful means (*upāya*) and so forth," this is because there are gradations in the counteracting of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*). As the *Buddhatva-śāstra* states:
"The path of signlessness and effortlessness refers to the signless state from the eighth ground upward; 'signless' here refers to the realm of suchness (*tathatā*)," and so on.
As for what is called "ultimate," it refers to the fact that from the eighth stage upward, the perceived objects are all identical and there are no further distinct objects;
thus it is named "ultimate. However, there remain differences in depth regarding skillful means alone.

[Commentary]: Regarding what is called "faith and so forth," it means that a Bodhisattva on the stage of practice through faith and understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) has already been able to initiate the ten kinds of great vows and has further attained the ten kinds of mind.

Next, they accomplish the ten kinds of dharmas for purifying the stages (*bhūmi-pariśodhana*), which consist of being able to believe in the Tathāgata’s original practices and their entry [into them], up to believing in the accomplishment of the fruit; this is "faith. The Bodhisattva, furthermore...
Seeing that all sentient beings cannot escape various sufferings, one gives rise to great compassion; this is *karuṇā*.
Thinking, "I should protect and rescue these sentient beings and cause them to abide in the bliss of the ultimate Buddha-way," is *maitrī*.
A bodhisattva, in accordance with such laws of great compassion and mercy, has no greed or attachment toward any object and practices the great giving of joyful relinquishment. This is *muditā*.

When a bodhisattva possesses a mind of great compassion, a mind of great generosity, and a mind that rescues all sentient beings without weariness or indolence, they are free from fatigue and exhaustion.
Such a bodhisattva gives rise to the merit of tirelessness and is able to fully understand and resolve all sūtras for themselves;
thus, through these merits, they are well able to deliberate upon what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
The merit of benefiting sentient beings—whether superior, middling, or inferior—in accordance with their needs is precisely the skillful understanding of worldly dharmas.

By virtue of this merit, one knows the proper time and the proper measure, and is adorned with shame and remorse (*hrī* and *apatrāpya*) as one cultivates the path of self-benefit and benefit for others;
such merit is itself shame and remorse. To practice these merits with diligent application and a mind that never slackens or retreats is diligence (*vīrya*).
The merit of withdrawal is the attainment of the power of capability, which is the power of firmness.
Having attained the power of capability, one diligently practices making offerings to all Buddhas; this is the tenth offering to the Buddhas.

Regarding the phrase "furthermore, abiding in these," it means that the Bodhisattva of this stage has already perfected the ten kinds of dharmas for purifying the stages, and furthermore, regarding the Buddhas and their Bodhi...
Because they consult, receive instruction from, and inquire of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) regarding the dharmas that accomplish this stage,
the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "O sons of the Buddha, as for the characteristics of the practice and fruit of a bodhisattva on the first stage,

they consult, receive instruction from, and inquire of the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends regarding the dharmas that accomplish the stages without ever becoming weary, continuing thus even unto the tenth stage."
Thus, one receives instruction without weariness; that is to say, one who well understands the obstacles to the various stages (*bhūmi*).

When entering the first stage, through the power of contemplative understanding, one knows that there are ten obstacles corresponding to the ten stages, and one knows that there are ten wisdoms as the remedies for those ten obstacles.

Thus, the distinctions of the ten stages are established. One who well understands the formation and dissolution of the stages realizes that by gathering practices, a state (*avasthā*) is formed, and by being able to accumulate all practices, it is thereby perfected.

The characteristic of dissolution (*bhanga-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the state of liberation wherein there is no substantiality, because one abides in spontaneous practice; thus it is the characteristic of destruction.

"Skillfully knowing the characteristics and fruits of the stages" means that the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), which involves contemplation accompanied by signs, reaches its conclusion; therefore, it is called the fruit of characteristics.

"Skillfully knowing the cultivation for attaining the stages" means that at the moment of entry [into the stages], the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is manifested; this is cultivation through realization (*sākṣāt-kriyā-bhāvanā*), not cultivation through conditions (*ālambana-bhāvanā*). Therefore, one skillfully knows the purity of the dharmas of the stages.

This refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣa-gati*), which is pure because it is free from the obscurations of the dharmas of faith and so forth on the stages (*bhūmi*).

It is "skillfully knowing the transition from stage to stage" because, by relying on the preceding stage, one gives up the characteristics of that stage when moving to the subsequent one. It is "skillfully knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*) regarding each stage":

dualistic grasping is called "impossible," while the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*) are the "abiding place. This also refers to their correspondence (*samyoga*) and non-correspondence (*asamyoga*).
Furthermore, he is skilled in knowing the excellence of each stage (*bhūmi*). "Wisdom regarding excellence" refers to the skill in increasing what is superior by means of what follows;
"skillfully knowing the non-retrogression of each stage" means being endowed with the non-retrogression of skillful means;
and "skillfully knowing the purification of all bodhisattva stages up to entering the stage of the Tathāgata" means that, having exhausted the remedies for obstacles, one attains liberation.
"Therefore, etc.

[Commentary]: "Furthermore, regarding the ten minds based on the previous three minds" means that the three minds of Bodhi, Great Compassion, and Expedient Means, along with the ten minds of the seed, sprout, bud, and so forth, are explained in sequence within numerous sets of ten dharma-gates.
Thus, they unfold and revolve without end.

[Commentary] "If one understands the generation of the sixteen great bodhisattvas of the Vajraśekhara," refers to the account of the manifestation of the sixteen great bodhisattvas as taught in the *Vajrayoginī-śekhara-sūtra*. If one comprehends those sixteen...
The meaning is that one should understand here the two types of principles for attaining Buddhahood—the superficial and the profound-secrecy. There are two translations:
the first, titled *The Ritual of Recitation within the Vajraśekhara Yoga* in four fascicles, translated by Vajrabodhi;
and the second, titled *A Brief Exposition of the Vajraśekhara Yoga: The Dharma-gate of Distinguishing and Realizing the Holy Stages*, in one fascicle, translated by Amoghavajra.

Although these two translations differ slightly in their literary style, they are no different regarding cultivation and realization (*bhāvanā-sākṣātkriyā*). Now, based on the dharma-gate of cultivation and realization, I shall briefly indicate its general direction.

It says: "At that time, the Buddha Vairocana of the Vajradhātu, residing in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven Palace at the summit of the Form Realm, attained equal and perfect enlightenment as the initial Enjoyment Body (*sambhogakāya*), realizing the four wisdoms of self-enjoyment."

Externally, for the sake of the "other-enjoyment" (*parasaṃbhoga*) of Bodhisattvas who have fulfilled the ten stages, the four Buddhas flow forth from among the four wisdoms and each dwells in its own direction.

Internally, for the sake of the "self-enjoyment" (*svasaṃbhoga*) of Vairocana Buddha’s realization of the samādhi-wisdom of the courageous bodhicitta of Vajrasattva within his own mind, the five peaks flow forth from this samādhi-wisdom.
The radiance of the vajra (the five-wisdom scepter) shines universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
causing all sentient beings to suddenly realize the conduct of Samantabhadra; it then returns and gathers into a single mass so that all bodhisattvas may partake of it,
thereby manifesting as the form of the Bodhisattva Vajrasattva and abiding before the moon disk of Akṣobhya Tathāgata, where he realizes the inner essence of Vairocana.

Because the wisdom of the *vajrāṅkuśa-catuḥsaṃgraha-samādhi* is for one’s own enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*), light rays of the *vajrāṅkuśa* flow forth from this samādhi-wisdom, universally illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.
By means of the four methods of attraction (*catuḥsaṃgrahavastu*), they gather all sentient beings and establish them in unsurpassed enlightenment;
then, returning and withdrawing into a single mass, they serve as the samādhi for the enjoyment of all bodhisattvas.
By virtue of wisdom, he assumes the form of the Bodhisattva Vajrarāja and dwells upon the moon disc to the right of Akṣobhya Buddha.
Within the heart of Vairocana Buddha, he realizes the *samādhi* of Great Compassion known as the "Vajra-Arrow.
From this wisdom, light rays of the vajra-arrow flow forth, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions and piercing all sentient beings who cause harm. In [the state of] non-...
To those who possess the mind of renunciation directed toward supreme enlightenment, [the Blessed One] dwells upon the lunar disc to the left of Akṣobhya Tathāgata;
from within the heart of Vairocana, he realizes the samādhi-wisdom of the "Vajra Well-Done Joyful King" (*vajrasādhu-harṣarāja*).
From this wisdom, the Vajra-Sādhu mudrā flows forth, at which time all sentient beings give rise to a sense of weariness regarding their sorrows and descend into the practice of Samantabhadra.
For those of inferior intent, he causes their bodies and minds to leap with joy, even unto their abiding within the lunar disc behind the Tathāgata Akṣobhya.
Above that, the four bodhisattvas belonging to the east— due to the self-enjoyment of the wisdom of the *samādhi* of attaining the Vajra-Jewel Empowerment within the heart of Vairocana Buddha—
cause the light of the Vajra-Jewel to flow forth from this wisdom.
Illuminating the crowns of all sentient beings with consecration, I attain the rank of non-retrogression and abide before the moon disc of Ratnasaṃbhava Tathāgata.
Within the heart of Vairocana Buddha, I realize the samādhi-wisdom of Vajratejas;
from this wisdom flows forth the vajra-sunlight that destroys the ignorance and delusion of all sentient beings.
Darkness is dispelled as the great light of wisdom arises, and so on, until one dwells within the moon disc to the right of Ratnasaṃbhava;
there, within the heart of Vairocana, one realizes the samādhi-wisdom of the Vajraratnaketu.

From this, the radiance of the Vajraketu flows forth, fulfilling the aspirations of all sentient beings, and so on, until one dwells within the moon disc to the left of Ratnasaṃbhava; there, within the heart of Vairocana, one realizes...
Having attained the samādhi-wisdom of the Vajra-Laughter Seal Prophecy, light radiates from the Vajra-Laughter Seal,
illuminating sentient beings of indeterminate nature and bestowing upon them the prophecy of supreme, equal enlightenment; thus,
even after abiding within the moon disc following Ratnasaṃbhava, these four bodhisattvas belong to the south and realize the Vajra within the heart of Vairocana.
From the samādhi-wisdom of pure and untainted [nature], the light of the Vajra-dharma flows forth,
purifying the five desires of all sentient beings so that their bodies and minds become as pure as a lotus flower, unstained by dust or grime; eventually,
abiding before the moon-disc of the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvararāja, one realizes within the heart of Vairocana the vajra-sharp sword.
If the light of the vajra-sword, which flows forth from the samādhi-wisdom of the pāramitās,
is able to sever all the fetters of sentient beings and free them from all suffering and affliction,

until one dwells upon the moon-disc at the right side of Avalokiteśvara and realizes within the heart of Vairocana the vajra-cause samādhi-wisdom that turns the wheel of Dharma, then the vajra flows forth.
The light of the wheel can eliminate the seeds of all sentient beings' evil karma, even as it abides on the left side of Avalokiteśvara’s moon-disc.
From within the heart of Vairocana, one realizes the samādhi-wisdom of the adamantine secret speech that transcends verbal expression;
from this flows forth the light of the adamantine tongue-mark, which can eliminate all sentient beings' evil karma and cause them to attain [liberation].
The four types of unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna-pratibhāna*), and so forth,
up to the four bodhisattvas residing upon the lunar discs at the rear of Avalokiteśvara— belonging to the western direction of Vairocana’s inner heart—
realize the *vajra-karma-gaganagañja-samādhi-jñāna*. From this, vajra-activity light rays stream forth, causing all sentient beings to [attain] all Tathāgatas...
All Bodhisattvas perform vast offerings and, even dwelling before the moon-disc of the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi,
realize within their hearts the Vairocana Samādhi of the Great Compassionate Ornamented Armor of Vajra Protection;
from this wisdom flows forth the radiance of the vajra armor, which can eliminate the wrath of violent and wicked sentient beings, enabling them to swiftly attain [liberation].
With a mind of loving-kindness, he dwells even unto the moon disc on the right of the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi; within the heart of Vairocana,
he realizes the samādhi-wisdom of the Vajrayakṣa method of "Terror," from which radiate vajra-fang light-rays that subdue stubborn and difficult-to-transform sentient beings,
establishing them upon the path to enlightenment, and so on until he dwells as the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi.
On the left moon disc, Vairocana internally realizes the Samādhi of the Majestic and Responsive Power of the Vajra-Offering Seal;

from this, the light of the Vajra-Offering flows forth, causing all sentient beings to eliminate their karmic obstructions and attain the perfection of both mundane and supramundane siddhis, even abiding in the state of Amoghasiddhi. Above the subsequent moon disc are the four Bodhisattvas.
Regarding these sixteen great bodhisattvas of the northern direction: the first four represent the bodhicitta, while the latter twelve represent great compassion.
Furthermore, among those twelve, the first four represent merit, the next four represent wisdom, and the final four represent diligence.

Although one may possess both types of accumulations—merit and wisdom—if one does not apply diligence, one cannot attain swift transcendence; it is like drilling for fire: if one pauses repeatedly, it will never be achieved.

Because there is no realization of a fruit [in this context], the *Yogacaryābhūmi-vidhi* for ritual confession states: "The Bodhicitta-Vajrasattva Bodhisattva and others are the accumulation of merit;
the Vajraratna Bodhisattva and others are the protection of wisdom; the Vajradharma Bodhisattva and others are great diligence;
the Vajrakarma Bodhisattva and others... When those who practice the path of mantra and conduct ascend to these sixteen positions, they [employ] the ten...
Through the skillful means of the syllable *āḥ* arising from dependent origination, one realizes the Great Emptiness Samādhi;
this is precisely the understanding that the sixteen great Bodhisattvas of the *Vajraśekhara* manifest as Perfectly Awakened Ones.

Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of these sixteen great Bodhisattvas, if one were to explain each one individually according to the Bodhisattva [teachings], there would be sixteen practices; until one transcends these, one has not yet attained Buddhahood.
If one can attain liberation in a single lifetime, this is what is meant by "attaining Buddhahood in one lifetime" (*ekajātipratibaddha*);
since it is collectively termed "one lifetime," there is no distinction of sixteen lifetimes, and thus it is said that these are the "births of the sixteen great bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, because these sixteen bodhisattvas all arise from the mind of Samantabhadra-sattva, the *Dhāraṇī-vidhi* states: "At that time, the Tathāgata Vajradhātu, holding..."
Taking the bodies of all Tathāgatas as one’s own body, born from the samaya of the Universal Worthy (Samantabhadra) Mahābodhisattva of all Tathāgatas,
and having entered the samādhi called "The Vajra Empowerment that Encompasses All Sattvas" (Sarvasattvasaṃgraha-vajrādhiṣṭhāna-samādhi),
this mind of the Great Vehicle Abhisamaya (here translated as "Equal Manifestation") of all Tathāgatas is named "All."
The Tathāgata’s mind emerges from his own mind and then utters the mantra, beginning with *Vajrasattva* and so forth.

The general meaning of the emergence of the fifteen bodhisattvas below is the same as this. The above interpretation should be kept profoundly secret; however, if one were to provide a shallow and abbreviated explanation, it is as a verse says:
The disciple, firm in the bodhicitta, receives the stage of empowerment from the master;
Constantly observing through the sublime cultivation of meditative concentration and wisdom, they enter deeply into the skillful gates of enlightened activity.
(Virtuous Conduct Bodhisattva) Guides all sentient beings toward supreme enlightenment; (Vajrasattva Bodhisattva) Gathers them in by means of the four methods of attraction; (Vajrarāja Bodhisattva).
Never abandoning great compassion without weariness (Vajraprīti Bodhisattva); seeing even a small act of goodness and praising it (Vajrasādhu Bodhisattva);
practicing inexhaustible giving equal to space (Vajraratna Bodhisattva); using the light of wisdom to shatter the darkness of ignorance (Vajraprabha Bodhisattva);
never refusing whatever is sought or desired (Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva); speaking with a smile first to gladden the heart (Vajrahāsa Bodhisattva).
Able to remain unstained within the wondrous Dharma (Vajradharma Bodhisattva), Skillfully employing Prajñā to sever all latent tendencies (Vajratīkṣṇa Bodhisattva),
The unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma never regressing (Vajranetra Bodhisattva), Expounding the four analytical knowledges with fearlessness (Vajravāk Bodhisattva),
Amidst the activities of all Buddhas and sentient beings (Vajrakarman Bodhisattva), Constantly abiding in the armor of firm vows, compassion, and loving-kindness (Vajrarakṣa Bodhisattva).
[Vajradaṃṣṭra Bodhisattva] who crushes the victorious hosts of Māra; [Vajramuṣṭi Bodhisattva] who firmly upholds the secret gates of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, the *Vajraśekhara-yoga-vyūha-vairocana-samādhi-dharma* states:

"If there are sentient beings who encounter this teaching and practice it with diligence during the four periods of day and night, they shall realize the fruit in this very life and abide on the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), after which they will reach liberation within sixteen lifetimes."
This is precisely what constitutes the attainment of Perfect Enlightenment.

[The Commentary states: "Therefore, in other sutras," etc., means that most other sutras extensively praise the King of Śāla Trees (Śāla meaning "firm" or "solid")—its trunk, leaves, flowers, and fruits—which are merely the branches and tips of the Wheel of Dharma; how could they know what the roots and seeds are like? This present sutra, however, is...

It is not so; rather, it is precisely the clarification of the seeds of that king of trees and the causes and conditions for their growth—namely, the eight stages of mind beginning with the seed, sprout, and bud—which constitute the causes and conditions for nourishment, and this is the fundamental Wheel of Dharma.
[Commentary: "Furthermore, transcending one kalpa, one ascends and dwells in this stage" refers to this stage as the Stage of All-Knowledge (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*). As the subsequent commentary states:

"Within the previous three phrases, the Buddha-stage is further distinguished as the 'supreme-supreme' mind of skillful means; upon reaching this mind, one is said to have transcended the Stage of Resolute Understanding (*adhimukti-bhūmi*).
This is because, having already passed through three kalpas in the Stage of Practice through Resolute Understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), one now transcends yet another kalpa to ascend.

Regarding the statement "abiding in the Buddha-ground," this refers to one *kalpa* and not another *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* in terms of duration; rather, it is called one *kalpa* upon transcending the single obstacle to the Buddha-ground.
This is because, according to this school, false attachments constitute one *asaṃkhyeya*. As the previous commentary stated:

"If one can transcend these three false attachments in a single lifetime, then one becomes a Buddha in that same lifetime—what need is there to discuss [vast] timeframes? The preceding passage referred to this.
Regarding the statement that "three kalpas do not mention four": this is because there remains one final obstacle to the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*) while still on the tenth ground (*daśabhūmi*).

Furthermore, another interpretation states that "transcending yet another kalpa" means that by transcending this third single kalpa, one ascends and dwells in the Buddha-ground; thus it is said, "transcending yet another kalpa."

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "when first contemplating emptiness," this means that when one contemplates this ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), one realizes that all phenomena enter the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the mind.
What is called the "limit of reality of the mind" refers to entering the ocean of signlessness (*animitta-samudra*), wherein both body and mind are quiescent and extinguished.

[Commentary]: Regarding the Buddhas of the ten directions appearing simultaneously to exhort and instruct him: all the Buddhas of the ten directions appear before him and extend their sevenfold exhortations.
According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the seven exhortations are as follows: first, the exhortation to proceed toward the merit of the fruition.
The Sūtra says: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! This patience is foremost; it accords with the Dharma of all Buddhas."
"Good son, you have not yet attained all the Buddha-dharmas—the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities—yet you must not abandon this gate of patience;
therefore, I urge you to seek it with diligence. Second, out of compassion for sentient beings, the Sūtra says:
'Furthermore, good son, although you have attained the liberation of nirvāṇa, ordinary worldlings have not.'"
Third, to cause them to remember their original vows, the Sūtra says:

"Furthermore, son of good family, you should recollect your original vow to universally and greatly benefit all sentient beings, causing them all to enter the gate of inconceivable wisdom; thus you should exhort them to fulfill [this vow]."
Regarding the fourth point, "the original vow," it involves rebuking those who equate [the Mahāyāna] with the Two Vehicles. The *Sūtra* states:
"Furthermore, son of good family, whether Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear, the nature of these dharmas remains eternally constant and unchanging.

It is not by attaining this dharma that all Buddhas are called Tathāgatas; all followers of the Two Vehicles are likewise able to attain this non-conceptual dharma. This is said to encourage the dual cultivation [of both wisdom and means].

Fifth, pointing to specific matters to encourage their accomplishment: The Sūtra says, "Furthermore, son of good family, you should observe that our physical marks are immeasurable, our wisdom is immeasurable, our lands are immeasurable, our skillful means are immeasurable, and our radiant, pure voices are likewise immeasurable.
You should now bring these dharmas to fulfillment," because it encourages the practice of accomplishment. Sixth, the encouragement not to give rise to complacency.
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, son of good family, you have now just attained this one illumination of the Dharma.

Son of good family, the Tathāgata’s illumination of the Dharma is immeasurable in its entry, immeasurable in its activity, and immeasurable in its turning; it extends even to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas, such that it cannot be fully known.
You should practice and accomplish this Dharma, and exhort others to cultivate it universally. Thus, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Immeasurable entry" refers to the absence of differentiation among the Dharma-gates; "immeasurable activity" refers to the differentiation of the tasks performed;

and "immeasurable transformation" refers to the differentiation of uninterrupted progression from stage to higher stage. Seventh, one should thoroughly penetrate all these; as the *Sūtra of Exhortation* says:
"Furthermore, son of good family, you should observe the immeasurable lands, the immeasurable sentient beings, and the immeasurable Dharma-gates throughout the ten directions."
One should thoroughly penetrate all such various distinctions as they truly are, for the purpose of exhorting universal knowledge. Having thus set forth the seven exhortations, that sutra concludes:
"If the Buddhas did not grant this gateway to the arising of wisdom, at that time one would enter ultimate *nirvāṇa* and abandon all activities for the benefit of sentient beings.
This refers to the arising of a mind that is utterly devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

In a previous kalpa, he gave rise to the mind of the vehicle of non-objectification (*anālambana-yāna*) and practiced the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*) through six types of analogies.

He realized that all phenomena—such as the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and the defiled factors (*saṃkleśa*)—are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "First is the absence of nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*); next is the absence of nature in terms of self-existence (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*);

and finally, by being far removed from the previously grasped nature of self and dharmas (*parikalpita-ātma-dharma-svabhāva*), [one realizes] the absence of nature. Although he performed this contemplation, he had not yet attained [the realization] called... [the name of the stage].
Now, by means of the ten phrases on dependent origination, one contemplates the ultimate emptiness of one’s own mind.

The self, the aggregates, phenomena, and the objectless—all these share a single nature, which is called "non-nature. The arising of the wisdom of this ultimate non-self-nature is what is meant by the "arising of the mind of ultimate non-self-nature.
Although it is said that one is liberated from all karma and afflictions, this is attained by the practitioner.
At the very moment this mind arises, it is called "illumination," for as light comes, darkness departs;
thus, when ignorance ceases, formations cease, and so on, up to when birth ceases, old age and death cease. These are termed the liberation from karma and afflictions.

Yet, regarding the fact that karma and afflictions still persist, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Without severing ignorance, one possesses the wisdom of illumination and liberation. Furthermore—
It is said that as long as sentient beings have not yet attained Buddhahood, they take bodhi as afflictions (*kleśa*); when Bodhisattvas attain Buddhahood, they take afflictions as bodhi.
Therefore, the *Huayan shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) clarifies that the characteristics of the three poisons universally possess the True Dharma.

Regarding this, there are five meanings: first, their own characteristics are immediately emptiness because they are empty; thus, while these three are the Way, it does not mean that these three are themselves the Buddha-dharma. [As stated in] various sections of the *Prajñāpāramitā*...

First, if its textual expression were not one or two [verses], it would merely be a provisional teaching on the illusory function of gathering and transforming sentient beings; yet it is not identical to suchness. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:

"One practices in what is not the Way, first using desire to entice and lead, and later causing them to enter the Buddha-way. Second, these three [aspects] involve the mind dwelling within delusion, like that of worldly commoners;
this [practice] involves contemplating the mind as the Way, yet it is not identical to the Way itself. Third, retaining delusions to moisten and sustain the growth of great bodhi...

The path of the Bodhisattva is also not identical to the purity of suchness; as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "If one does not enter the great ocean of birth and death, one cannot obtain the jewel of all-knowledge.

These five meanings correspond to the actual characteristics [of the path], and since this fifth meaning differs from the preceding four inconceivable [meanings], it is precisely the same as the present case.
Thus, the *Acaranga Sutra* states: "Lust is itself the path; anger and delusion are likewise [the path]."
However, the meaning is that within these three dharmas, all Buddha-dharmas are fully contained.
Furthermore, just as space transcends all characteristics yet serves as the basis for the manifestation of the myriad forms, the subsequent sutra states:

"Space is stainless and lacks intrinsic nature, yet it can bestow various kinds of skillful wisdom; because its fundamental nature is eternally empty, dependent origination is profoundly deep and difficult to perceive."
Regarding the supreme progress of constant and long-term recollection that bestows the unsurpassed fruit and so forth:

when a practitioner of mantra perceives through the gateway of the letter *A* that all phenomena arising from conditions are the Dharmadhātu-body of Vairocana, identical to space, then the ten directions become unified as a single Buddha-field; this is called ultimate purity and awakening.

Holding the mind with this ultimately pure bodhicitta, one manifests the practice of the bodhisattva path through the physical body simultaneously and universally, in response to the causes and conditions of the inexhaustible dharma-realm and the entire realm of sentient beings without exception.

In every thought-moment, one makes offerings to immeasurable spiritual friends and awakens to and enters immeasurable gates of the perfections (*pāramitā*). Thus, throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* [aeons]...
Throughout the kalpas, he constantly and preeminently advances to adorn and purify all buddha-fields, accomplishing all the buddha-deeds for the sake of sentient beings without ever resting;
this is called the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra. Furthermore, some may doubt, asking:
"How can such inconceivable conditioned activities be performed within the mind of ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*)? Therefore, the sutra below says by way of analogy:
Just as all constructed palaces and dwellings, though relying upon space, proceed without attachment, so too is this pure Dharma.

The complete purification of the three realms of existence and so forth means that all the various destinies of the world, along with their supporting environments and dwelling places, all abide by depending on space; they are established because of space, yet space itself has no dependence whatsoever.
The practice of non-attachment and non-arising is likewise so for this pure Dharma-body:
although it is eternally quiescent and does not manifest the characteristics of any phenomena, it pervades all worlds without exception and performs all deeds.
Because it arises through the causal conditions of the power of roots of goodness born of compassion, and not through the causal conditions of delusion and karma, it is called "pure birth."
[Commentary]: The Buddha again explains this by correlating it with the three preceding kalpas to clarify the gradations.

This means that when the Buddha speaks of these six fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), his intention is to clarify that from the shallow to the deep, and from the ordinary person toward the sage, there are different stages of realization and attainment.

The first, the fearlessness of goodness (*kuśala-vaiśāradya*), corresponds to the stage of the ignorant child and ordinary devas; by practicing the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*), they are constantly reborn among humans and devas, thereby attaining liberation from [lower realms].
The first place of respite from the intense suffering and afflictions of the three miserable realms is precisely the stage prior to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Second is the fearlessness regarding the body, which means contemplating that the body is an accumulation of thirty-six constituent elements and practicing the five kinds of contemplations on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).

Next, by contemplating sensation, mind, and phenomena (*vedanā-citta-dharma*), one attains liberation from the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*) and finds a place of respite from the constriction and bondage of the body. This is...
The third [stage], the fearlessness regarding selflessness, occurs at the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).

It means that when one contemplates the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) as all arising from conditions and being entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one realizes that there is no "self" anywhere; this is the place where one finds relief from the yoke of the self.
This corresponds to the stages of the ten faiths and the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*). The fourth is the fearlessness regarding phenomena (*dharma*), which refers to the practitioner’s mind.
Abiding within the Dharma, by means of the five similes such as illusions and mirages, one realizes that all phenomena are emptiness and attains the realm of tranquility;

thus, being liberated from the yoke of the aggregates, one finds a place of respite—this corresponds to the ten stages of Dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) and the four stages of Application (*catasraḥ prayogabhūmayaḥ*). Fifth is the fearlessness regarding the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*):
it refers to when the practitioner gives rise to the mind of the objectless vehicle (*anālambana-yāna*) and, through contemplating the nature of the selflessness of phenomena, attains [realization].
Mastery over phenomena and attaining a place of rest through non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) corresponds to the stages from the first bhūmi up to the seventh bhūmi.
Sixth, the fearlessness regarding the equality of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena means that when one contemplates the emptiness of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),
one attains a place of rest from the two kinds of fetters— the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) realms— which corresponds to the stages from the eighth bhūmi onwards.

Therefore, it is said that the Buddha again establishes distinctions based on the first three kalpas for the sake of clear elucidation; alternatively, by opening up the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), the initial stage of faith (*śraddhā*) corresponds to "Good Fearlessness" (*kṣema-vaigunya*).

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "seeing this body as consisting of thirty-six substances," etc., it means that when practicing the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), one first contemplates the body.
In the application of mindfulness, one contemplates that this body is a composite of thirty-six substances, fundamentally impure, and never gives rise to craving for it.
Regarding these thirty-six [substances], the "Noble Practices" chapter of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Good son, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the noble path, he observes this body from head to foot; within it there is nothing but hair and body hair."

The nails, teeth, impurities, filth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, liver, gallbladder, stomach, the two internal organs of the raw and the cooked, excrement and urine, mucus, saliva, tears, fat, marrow, brain, membranes, bone-marrow, pus, blood, the brain-base, and all the channels—therefore, the verse says:
"Hair, body hair, nails, teeth, and dust and grime; skin, flesh, tendons, bones, as well as spleen and kidneys."
The heart, lungs, liver, gallbladder, stomach, and intestines; the two organs of the raw and cooked; excrement and urine; mucus and tears;
fat, grease, brain, membranes, marrow, pus, blood, the brain-marrow, and all the channels—these are called the thirty-six things. A practitioner should swiftly seek weary detachment from them.
When a bodhisattva thus contemplates with single-minded attention, who is "I," to whom does "I" belong, and where does it abide?
"In what place does what belong to me? He further reflects: "Is the bone myself, or is it apart from the bone?
At that time, the Bodhisattva removes the skin and flesh and contemplates only the white bones. He further reflects:

"The color and appearance of the bones differ—namely, blue, yellow, white, or pigeon-colored—and these skeletal characteristics are likewise not the self. Why is this? Because the 'self' is also not [the bones]."
When a bodhisattva fixes the mind and contemplates [the body] as being blue, yellow, white, or the color of a pigeon, they immediately succeed in severing all desire for form (*rūpa-rāga*).

Regarding the five kinds of impurity: first is the impurity of the seed (*bīja-aśubhatā*), which refers to the formation of the physical body by taking up the seeds of consciousness (*vijñāna-bīja*) caused by karma, along with the semen and blood of the parents. Second is the impurity of the dwelling place (*sthāna-aśubhatā*), referring to the parents' womb.
Third, it is impure by its own nature because it is situated between the internal organs and the external organs, being composed of thirty-six impure substances;
fourth, it is impure by its own characteristics, which is also called impurity of external appearance, as the nine orifices constantly discharge fluids:

the eyes produce rheum and tears, the ears produce wax, the nose produces mucus, the mouth produces saliva and spittle, and the passages for feces and urine constantly discharge their respective wastes.
Regarding the five types of impurity, they are ultimately impure; after the breath has ceased, the body becomes bloated, putrefied, and foul-smelling—such is this impurity, which is truly loathsome.

This is the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). Next, regarding sensation, mind, and phenomena, these constitute the contemplations of the foundations of mindfulness of sensation, mind, and phenomena (*vedanā-, citta-, and dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
One should contemplate that sensation is suffering, contemplate that the mind is impermanent, and contemplate that phenomena are non-self. When contemplating in this manner:

To be free from the four inversions regarding the nature of self means that by contemplating the body as impure, one becomes free from the inversion of purity, and so on, until by contemplating phenomena as selfless, one becomes free from the inversion of self;
therefore, the conclusion below states: "One finds a place of respite from the yoke and bondage of the body. Furthermore, according to the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*:
"First, the contemplation of impermanence: one who practices this contemplation should contemplate all conditioned things in the world as..."
Contemplate the suffering of impermanence: that all phenomena do not endure for even a moment, but must inevitably change and decay. Contemplate the suffering of pervasive conditioning:

that all contaminated (*sāsrava*) states of mind and mental factors are oppressive and arise and perish from moment to moment; for this reason, they are suffering. Contemplate the suffering of selflessness:

one should contemplate that all phenomena previously thought of were as fleeting as a dream (lacking substance and difficult to pursue); one should contemplate that all phenomena currently being thought of are like flashes of lightning.

(Impermanent in every moment): One should contemplate all dharmas thought of in the future as being like clouds that suddenly arise—originally having no accumulation, yet existing due to the gathering of conditions, and not coming from the ten directions.

Regarding the four contemplations on impurity: one should contemplate all embodied beings in the world as entirely impure, defiled by various foulness, such that not a single one is worth delighting in.
When contemplating in this way, one immediately attains detachment and does not [cling] to a self.
...and through these four kinds of dharmas-nature, one forms inversions and so forth. [Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "that which is accumulated within the appropriated aggregates" (*upādāna-skandha*): "aggregate" (*skandha*) has the sense of a collection as its essence; "appropriation" (*upādāna*) refers to grasping, for ordinary beings grasp at it as a self;
"body" (*kāya*) refers to that which serves as the basis for what belongs to the self (*mama-āśraya*). Thus, it is said that one abandons the self.

Regarding the contemplation of form and appearance: if one considers that form is the aggregate of form and that the aggregate is the self, and then abandons both by relinquishing them, one realizes that even the five aggregates themselves arise from causes and conditions and possess no intrinsic nature;
how much more so, then, is this true for the self? To realize this stillness is called the place of rest.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "all within the segmented [world]," a single part or a single section is termed "segmented" (*fen-duan*).
This refers to dharmas produced from conditions, which, depending upon causes and conditions for their formation, necessarily possess the characteristic of segmented differentiation.

The aforementioned commentary states that this is precisely what is extensively clarified through the analysis of phenomena in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. It is, for example, like analyzing the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) in search of the mind.

One should know that it is unattainable; even when seeking the mind in various ways within the six perfections, the myriad practices, and even all the gates of *dhāraṇī* and *samādhi*, the mind is likewise unattainable.
Because of this contemplation, all forms of self-love, pride, and the like will never arise again;
therefore, it is said that "within all realms of分段 (*bheda*) [existence], etc. means this.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "by means of the five eyes of the Tathāgata" and so forth: the stainless bodhicitta of the Tathāgata is ultimately signless (*animitta*), transcends all sense organs and objects, and surpasses all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Since even the five eyes of the Tathāgata do not perceive its form or appearance, Yuanxiao stated that it is "not something represented by images.
If even these five eyes cannot behold its countenance, how much less can those of ordinary beings subject to birth and death? Now...
Therefore, to clarify the three kalpas and six fearlessnesses, if one does not provide such a comparative analysis,

ordinary people will likely each cling to their prior habits and fail to awaken to their subtle profundity; they would merely speculate on the external traces of phenomena to gauge the depth of cultivation and realization.
[Sūtra] One who practices profound contemplation does so in relation to the first two stages; thus it is called "profound.
That is to say, during the first stage, because the practitioner’s mind sinks into the aggregates (*skandha*), they wish to counteract the grasping at phenomena as having real existence.

Therefore, they contemplate these ten phrases of dependent origination as previously explained—namely, that they are empty and like an illusion—and this is called "shallow. During the second stage, one counteracts the grasping at objective referents (*ālambana*).
Contemplating these ten links of dependent origination as previously explained—wherein the aggregates (*skandha*) and the *ālayavijñāna* are the illusory nature of the mind—is called "shallow.

Now, in this third eon, because one seeks to transcend the realms of both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is called the "profound contemplation" of inconceivable illusion.
Furthermore, regarding "profound cultivation," the lower commentary states: "This refers to the stage from having attained the pure mind (*viśuddhacitta*) onwards..."
It is called "profound" because that which is realized becomes increasingly deep.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the illusion of the discourse on illusion pervades all," the illusion of the Tathāgata’s three vajra-actions is precisely the pervasive maṇḍala of the entire dharma-realm;
this means that within that great maṇḍala of the dharma-realm, each and every deity...
This is the insignia of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*): that which pervades all is called "pervading all places.
Regarding the discourse on pervading all places, it means that the maṇḍala of the Dharma-realm pervading all places is precisely the illusion of the Tathāgata’s three secrets;
since these are fundamentally unborn, they cannot be found when sought through the four propositions, and are thus the inconceivable illusion.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "such as the Four Truths," "such as" (*qie*) is a term indicating that the list is not exhaustive; "as" (*ru*) is a word used for direct reference.

Although the categories of dharmas are truly numerous, the text merely cites the Four Truths and the immeasurable worlds to directly indicate the Sahā world, taking this as but one corner [of the whole].
Thus, the "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths" in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī..."

He addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "O sons of the Buddha, the Noble Truth of Suffering is called 'transgression,' or 'affliction,' or 'transformation,' or 'objectification' and so forth in this Sahā world.
O sons of the Buddha, the Noble Truth of the Accumulation of Suffering is called 'bondage,' or 'destruction,' or 'attachment,' or 'craving' and so forth in this Sahā world."
O sons of the Buddha, what is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering in this Sahā world is, in other places, called "Non-contention," "Freedom from dust," "Quiescence," and so forth.

O sons of the Buddha, what is called the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering in this Sahā world is, in other places, called "The One Vehicle" or "The Way to Quiescence," and so forth. O sons of the Buddha, in this Sahā world...
The Four Noble Truths have four hundred billion ten-thousand such names as these; according to the minds of sentient beings, they bring them all to subdual.

O Sons of the Buddha, what is called the Noble Truth of Suffering in this Sahā world may be called the "Root of Seeking" or "Non-Departure" in the world of Guhyadēśanā, and so on, throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions.
Each has immeasurable names that cannot be fully enumerated, as explained in detail elsewhere; therefore, it says "for instance," and so forth.
[Commentary] Regarding "like an illusion, a mirage, and so on": "illusion" (māyā) means transformation (*nirmāṇa*), referring to that which suddenly appears where there was nothing.

That which previously lacked form or substance, yet acquires a name through the power of causes and conditions, is called an illusory transformation (*māyā-nirmita*). Furthermore, "illusion" can mean deception, or that which deludes others with unreal things.

Because it is the gateway for the human eye, it is called "illusion" (*māyā*). As for what is termed a "dream," it refers to the spirit wandering during sleep. Generally, when people are in deep slumber, their consciousness is unsettled. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that one may have awareness while asleep. According to the *Rituals of Zhou*, there are six kinds of dreams through which one perceives omens of good or ill fortune: first, the "regular dream" (*zhengmeng*), which occurs naturally during peaceful rest; second, the "startled dream" (*emo meng*), occurring upon being suddenly alarmed; third, the "reflective dream" (*simeng*)... [text continues]...

Fourth is the dream resulting from recollecting [experiences] while awake; fifth is the dream resulting from what was spoken while awake; sixth is the joyful dream, which is dreaming while feeling joy;
and seventh is the fearful dream, which is dreaming while feeling fear. Thus it is said that the "city of the gandharvas" is explained in the commentary according to the text.
Furthermore, according to the *Yijing chao*, the Sanskrit term *gandharva* is translated here as "seeker of fragrance."
The gate is named Ghoṣavatī (Scent-Seeker). In the Western Land, musicians seek out scents to beg for alms and construct cities of play;
because they act for the sake of others, it is named the City of Scent-Seekers (Ghoṣavatī), and so forth.
[Commentary] "To seek it through the four propositions and find it utterly unobtainable" means to seek by means of the four propositions of self, other, both, and causelessness.
When one seeks the reality of this dream-event, it can ultimately not be found. As in the four-line verse regarding Zhuang Zhou’s dream of transforming into a butterfly:
when seeking [the truth], does this butterfly within the dream arise from itself? If there were no dreaming person, the butterfly could not arise of its own accord.
If it does not arise from itself, does it arise from another—the dreamer? If there were no butterfly, the dreamer could not give rise to it. If it does not arise from another...
If birth were co-arising, then co-arising itself would not be born. Why? Because there is no such thing as a dharma that sleeps.
If there is no sleeping, then the dream of a butterfly does not exist; thus, the dream of causes and conditions cannot be apprehended at all.

[Commentary]: Regarding the fourteen transformative minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 17, states: "As for all phenomena being like transformations, there are fourteen transformative minds:
[in] the first dhyāna, two; in the desire realm, two; in the second dhyāna, three; in the desire realm, three;
in the third dhyāna, four; in the desire realm, four; in the fourth dhyāna, five; in the desire realm, five; in the first dhyāna, two... [and so on].
The third and fourth dhyānas consist of fourteen transformational minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*) that perform eight kinds of transformations:
first, the ability to become small, even down to the size of a minute atom; second, the ability to become large, even to the point of filling empty space;
third, the ability to become light, even like a goose feather; and fourth, the ability to attain mastery, such as making the large small and the long short.

Thus, these various [powers] are: first, the power of mastery (having great strength because one does not submit to others); second, the power of reaching distant places; third, the power of shaking the earth;
fourth, the power of obtaining everything according to one's wishes; fifth, the power of transforming a single body into many bodies and many bodies into one;

sixth, the power of passing through stone walls as if walking on ice or treading through empty space; and seventh, the power of touching the sun and moon with one's hand and being able to rotate them.
The four great elements may turn earth into water and water into earth; fire into wind and wind into fire; stone into gold and gold into stone, and so forth. [Commentary:

Regarding "city walls" (*chengguo*), the *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states: "City" (*cheng*) means "to contain," for it contains and receives the capital. "Wall" (*guo*) means "expansive," for it is expansive and wide.
Outside the city there was also the *guò*, which refers to the *fú*. The *Zuǒshì chuán* states: "The people of Zhèng entered its *fú*. Dù Yǔ commented: "The *fú* is the *guò*.
Furthermore, according to the *Huáinán zǐ*, Gùn (pronounced xuàn) built the city walls; the *Wúyuè chūnqiū* says:
"Gùn constructed the city to protect his lord (this is the Xiàochéng) and built the mounds to guard the people. This marks the beginning of city walls (*chéng*) and moats (*guò*).
[Commentary: Therefore it is said "unequaled" (*asama*). The first character "equal" (*sama*) refers to that which is equaled, while the second character "equal" refers to that which can equalize.

This means that within all dharmas, there is nothing that can serve as a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s wisdom, nor is there anything superior to it; thus it is called "unequaled. This refers to that which is equaled.
The true nature of the mind and that wisdom are like a box and its lid; they are "unequaled" [in their perfect correspondence].
For these reasons, it is said that they are "unequaled by those who are equal" (*asamasama*).
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "all Māras manifest themselves as Buddhas," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
Furthermore, there are Māras who appear in the guise of bhikṣus and come to say to the Bodhisattva: "Previously, you heard from a minor teacher the method for practicing the six pāramitās."
All these are accumulations of what is false and illusory; even the merit of the mind that rejoices is likewise false and illusory.
All that you have previously heard is but false deception, mere ornamentation, and not true; it was not spoken from the Buddha’s own mouth. Now I shall truly show you the Buddha-dharma.

Even if Māra were to manifest in the body of a Buddha and speak things that differ from the characteristics of the Dharma, you should not believe or accept them—just as, for example, a dog [would not accept] [filth].
When various beasts see one wearing a lion’s skin, they are terrified; yet upon hearing its voice, they realize it is but a dog.
How much less could those who merely transform themselves into other bodies cause a practitioner to alter their mind?
[Commentary: "The spontaneous arising of the wisdom of dependent origination" refers to the arising of the wisdom of the inconceivable, secret dependent origination of the *dharmadhātu*.

This means that by taking the power of the practitioner’s internal contemplative practice as the cause and the power of the Buddha’s external spiritual empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) as the condition, through these two powers, the secret wisdom of the dependent origination of the *dharmadhātu* arises spontaneously.
One who is born [into this state] is able to perceive the inconceivable realm of empowerment; therefore, it is not like that of ordinary beings.
[Sūtra] Chapter Two, Part One: The Chapter on the Mantras and Requisites for Entering the Maṇḍala.
As clarified above, the matter of abiding in the mind while entering the gateway of mantras pertains solely to those practitioners of mantra conduct who enter the maṇḍala.
Regarding this realm, if there are sentient beings who wish to enter this gate, they must first enter the Great Compassion Womb Maṇḍala;
having received the transmission of the mantras from an ācārya, they must generate the bodhicitta and receive the samaya vows. Only after receiving the teacher’s permission may they enter.
If one does not enter the maṇḍala but practices independently at home, even if one were to practice with such diligence, [it would be of no avail].
To proceed [without this] is not merely fruitless; it also incurs the grave offense of transgressing the Dharma. Why is this?
For instance, within the manifest teachings of both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, there are none that do not expound upon the precepts of light and heavy gravity, yet these must be received from a master.

How much more so for the Vajrayāna, the Single Vehicle, where the Buddhas themselves took vows; to practice it abruptly would incur the fault of transgressing the Dharma. Therefore, next, the *Cittasthāpana* (Abiding of the Mind) is explained.
Regarding the title of this chapter, it possesses both shallow and profound meanings. To provide a shallow explanation first: "entry" (*praveśa*) signifies approaching, traversing, or being led in.

This means that when an *ācārya* perceives sentient beings who are capable of serving as vessels for the Dharma and possess great faith and understanding, he skillfully exhorts and guides them into the Great Compassion Maṇḍala. As for "maṇḍala," it is translated here as...
The *bodhimaṇḍa* (place of enlightenment) is the site where disciples generate the aspiration for awakening and attain the Way; thus it is called a *bodhimaṇḍa*, which is to say, the *maṇḍala*.
"Entering" (*praveśa*) refers to the agent of entry, while the *maṇḍala* of entry is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Furthermore, entering this *maṇḍala* requires many conditions, meaning one must possess many constituent factors, namely: the selection of the site and the purification of the site.
Having selected the auspicious time and fixed the date, one constructs the altar, paints the images, and establishes the boundary (*sīmābandha*).

Only then does one lead the initiate in, perform the invocation and offerings, and finally, in due order, confer the Dharma of the generation of the bodhicitta. The general procedure is the same as usual;
even the performance of *homa* and consecration (*abhiṣeka*) belongs to the constituent parts of entering the maṇḍala. To speak of them in brief, they are as extensively explained in the sūtras.
"Entering the maṇḍala" is a *tatpuruṣa* compound (dependent determinative) formed by taking the general [term] as the whole and establishing specific names from it.
Furthermore, each of these individual conditions possesses its own mantra; thus, the "mantra that possesses the conditions" is also a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Regarding the preceding brief and profound explanations: "entering" (*praveśa*) signifies the meaning of realizing, awakening to, and attesting to the essence. "Maṇḍala" refers to the totality.

The original awakening of the self-mind of sentient beings is precisely this maṇḍala of mind, wherein there is always an assembly of immeasurable Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings, along with their infinite retinues.
Yet, because they are shrouded and obstructed by beginningless ignorance, they do not know or see it themselves; it is like a treasure storehouse that constantly exists within a poor man’s house.

Just as one who is unaware of a treasure buried beneath the ground of their own home only becomes conscious of it when informed by a spiritual teacher (*kalyāṇamitra*), so too is the *maṇḍala* treasure-store of one’s own mind:
although it exists, if one remains unconscious of it, it is only through the skillful means of the Buddhas and teachers providing instruction that one comes to know it.
This is called "entering the *maṇḍala*," which is the entry into the essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
The phrase "the wisdom of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) is endowed with conditions" and so forth refers to the characteristics of its merits;
just as one who selects the ground removes all afflictions from the mind-ground, the remaining [explanations] are all esoteric interpretations, which may be understood by analogy with this.

Therefore, it is called "The Mantra Endowed with Conditions for Entering the Maṇḍala. As for "Chapter Two, Part One": the textual flow of this chapter is extensive, and thus it is separated hereafter.
Because it is a fascicle, the word "one" (i.e., *ekottara*) is placed at the beginning, and the sequence of the items follows the usual convention.

[Commentary: It has already been understood that milk and curd possess the nature of clarified butter (*ghṛta*); this serves as a metaphor for the fact that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature within their own minds.
Just as the clarified butter in milk is produced through the power of adventitious conditions, so too is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings; yet, if one were to separate it from the milk...
It is impossible for there to be *amṛta* (the essence of clarified butter) without these stages. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Just as from milk comes curd, from curd comes fresh butter, from fresh butter comes matured butter, and from matured butter comes *amṛta*;
even so, on the Snowy Mountains there is a grass called 'Fatty,' and if a cow eats it, she immediately produces *amṛta*. The Buddha-nature is also like this, O son of good family."
Sentient beings of meager merit do not see this grass; the Buddha-nature is likewise, for it is obscured by afflictions and thus sentient beings do not perceive it.

Now that it has been known, one causes all the necessary vessels to be prepared and, through the skillful means of churning and stirring, the *amṛta* (clarified butter) can be obtained. This correspondence with the Dharma is easy to understand.
[Commentary: "As for 'the compassionate nurturing of worldly people' and so forth: it is just as when people of the world compassionately care for and raise their young children.
Whatever the child may desire, the parents' feelings of affection and love have no sense of stinginess or regret.

Yet, if the child were to demand the Ganjiang or Mohe swords, they would certainly not give them. Why? Because [they know] that if the child does not know the skillful means of using them, they will surely cause injury."
Regarding their substance, the mention of "Ganjiang" and "Moxie" refers to the names of two swords, such as the Da'a, Chunqiu, and Longquan.
According to the *Wuyue Chunqiu*, Ganjiang was a man of Wu (a contemporary of King Helü); he and Ouyezizi studied under the same master.
King Helü commissioned them to forge two swords: the first was named Ganjiang, and the second was named Moxie. Moxie was [the sword of] Ganjiang.
