His wife was named Gan Jiang; she forged a sword from the finest essence of gold and iron, yet the metal refused to melt and flow.
Gan Jiang and his wife then cut off their hair and clipped their fingernails, casting them into the furnace; the gold and iron then softened and yielded, and thus the sword was completed.

The male blade was called Gan Jiang and bore a tortoise-shell pattern (*guiwen*); the female blade was called Mo Xie and possessed a smooth, even grain (*manli*). Gan Jiang concealed the male blade and brought forth the female.
Because he presented his sword to Helü, it is said that the methods of Ganjiang and others are easy to understand when combined.

[Commentary]: "The Tathāgata has already transcended these subtle [delusions]" means that the Tathāgata has attained transcendence beyond the third level of extremely subtle false attachments, reaching the stage of Buddhahood; therefore, it says, "the Tathāgata has already transcended," and so forth.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "in this section on the summary of understanding" (*lingjie*), the Master of the Commentary (*shuzhu*) indicates that although this text of the *Vajra* summary consists of only two lines and is thus concise and abbreviated, it nevertheless captures and highlights the essential tenets of the entire treatise;
its subtle and profound purport is fully and completely encompassed therein.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "as when the father and mother unite until [the consciousness] takes residence in the womb," the "father and mother" mentioned here refer to the Buddhas of the maṇḍala as the father and the vidyā-consorts (vidyārājñī) as the mother;
this is because the seed of the sentient being’s bodhicitta-consciousness takes birth therein. As the subsequent commentary states:
"Just as through the causal conditions of the union of a man and a woman, the seed of consciousness takes residence in the womb, so it is here."
Because the Kings of the Buddhas and their Consorts (vidyārājñī) first give birth within the Dharma-realm maṇḍala of the Great Compassion Womb (mahākaruṇā-garbha),
by harmonizing and uniting the seeds of Vaiśravaṇa, it is said that they are like parents in union.
[Commentary]: Regarding "ignorance is the father and mother," this means that within a single thought-moment of ignorance, there is not a single affliction that does not arise from it;

thus, the twelve links of dependent origination are placed at the head [of the list]. Because Bodhisattvas in the stage of the "Position of Succession" (Bodhisattva-bhūmi) possess only subtle ignorance, when these defilements are removed, all other obstacles are necessarily exhausted;
hence it is called their "father and mother. Furthermore, there is a verse that says: "To kill one's father and mother..."
The King and the two who were highly learned, though afflicted by extreme defilements, attained supreme enlightenment.

Now, taking the first phrase of this [verse], according to the explanation in Ci'en's *Fayuan*: "Taking craving as mother and karma as father," it means that the Bodhisattva in the position of succession has forever severed the seeds of craving, karma, and co-arising ignorance; because there is no further birth in a future existence, it is so stated.
"Ignorance is the most subtle defilement of the parents.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "apart from the dharma-realm there is no separate [sentient-being realm]," one should say: apart from the dharma-realm there is no separate sentient-being realm, because the sentient-being realm is itself the dharma-realm;
apart from the mind-realm there is no separate dharma-realm, because the dharma-realm is itself the mind-realm. Thus says the Commentary.
The middle section is abbreviated as follows.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "at the time of the first fearlessness, by means of sound, syllables, and so forth," this refers to the practitioner of mantras who, relying on the three secrets for worship and practice, contemplates the sound of the mantra and the mantra itself during the first fearlessness.
One should engage in practice as follows. As stated in the *Siddhi-paṭala* (Chapter on Worldly Accomplishment):
"Just as one achieves the fruit through the teachings of mantra, each syllable should correspond [to its meaning], and each phrase should be likewise. The first syllable is the bodhicitta;
the second is called the 'syllabic phrase' (*śabdapada*), which one should visualize as the deity within one's own place. Thus it is said. Second, there is no [duality].

"Fearing the contemplation of signs" refers to the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), for it is the manifestation of the various signs of the samādhi of the practitioner’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) in the context of mantra practice.

"The third fearlessness belongs only to one who possesses the mind that there is no self in the aggregates" refers to the contemplation of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*);
when analyzed and sought, they are found to be utterly unobtainable, which is precisely the practitioner of mantra observing that the mind within the *yoga* object is unobtainable.

Regarding the fourth fearlessness, the mind with objective conditions (*sālambana-citta*), the practitioner contemplates all aggregates (*skandha*) and phenomena as being like illusions, mirages, and so forth;

this is just as the mantra practitioner contemplates the yogic realm as being like reflections in a mirror. Regarding the fifth fearlessness, the mind without objective conditions (*anālambana-citta*), one contemplates the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), seeing that there is nothing at all external to the mind;
this is because the mantra practitioner has attained mastery over the mind within the path of yoga.

Regarding the sixth fearlessness, the mind of equanimity: because one contemplates that the emptiness of the mind, phenomena, and the objectless are all of one single nature, the practitioner of mantra is none other than the stainless bodhicitta of space.

[Commentary]: From the Vimalā-bhūmi (the Ground of Freedom from Defilement) onward, those who cultivate the maṇḍala within their own minds while contemplating the mind observe that the Bodhisattva of the first ground enters into the equality of the three periods of time, which is no different from the fearlessness of equality on the sixth ground.
Therefore, by taking the grounds from the second through the Buddha-ground to supplement the preceding six kinds of fearlessness, the sixteenfold profound meaning is established.

Now, the seventh profound mystery enters through the gate of the ten kinds of profound resolve—such as being upright, supple, and capable—based on the *Vimalā-bhūmi*, and therein practices the maṇḍala rites; others are all modeled after this.
The eighth profound mystery enters through the gate of the ten kinds of profound resolve—such as purity, abiding securely, and renunciation based on weariness—of the *Prabhākārī-bhūmi*. Ninth...

The Double Profundity (Chongxuan) enters through the ten gates of illumination regarding the realm of sentient beings, the dharma-realm, and the world-realm, etc., belonging to the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (Jvalanābhā);
it relies upon the tenth Double Profundity, which takes the ten kinds of pure minds—past, future, and present, etc.—belonging to the Stage Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā) as its gate for practice;
and it relies upon the eleventh Double Profundity, which takes all [phenomena] belonging to the Stage of Presence (Abhimukhī) as its gate.
The twelfth stage of the profound mystery of practice, based on the *Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi* (Far-Reaching Stage), takes as its gateway the single, equal Dharma that is signless, essence-less, and unarisen;
although one cultivates the three emptinesses, one does not abandon sentient beings through compassion—this constitutes the ten kinds of skillful means through which superior paths arise.
The thirteenth stage of the profound mystery of practice, based on the *Acalā-bhūmi* (Immovable Stage), takes non-arising as its gateway.
Taking the patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*) as the gateway, one practices the fourteenth profound mystery;
taking the purification of all *dhāraṇīs* and *samādhis* based on the stage of excellent wisdom (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*) as the gateway, one practices the fifteenth profound mystery;

and taking the *samādhi* of receiving the supreme office of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), beginning from the bodhisattva’s stainless *samādhis* and others numbering one million on the stage of the cloud of dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), as the gateway, one practices.
The practice of the sixteenth profound mystery manifests the sequential characteristics of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) based on the stage of the Tathāgata.

Taking these causal characteristics as its gateway, one cultivates the practices of the maṇḍala until reaching the ultimate goal: the ocean of merit and wisdom that is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The lands of the ten directions could be ground into dust, and one could know their number in a single thought-moment."

One might measure the void by counting its finest hairs, yet even if one were to speak for billions of eons, this could not be exhausted. Question: The sixteen stages and positions are clearly visible;
what are the characteristics of the practice regarding the meaning of the "Twofold Profundity" (Chongxuan)? Answer: There are two gates: first, the cause and fruit within each respective stage;

second, the cause and fruit across different stages. Now, for the first: just as with the first layer of the Twofold Profundity, one cultivates the maṇḍala through the contemplation of sounds and syllables.
Taking the sounds and characters as the gateways corresponds to their causes; the clarity and perfection of contemplative practice corresponds to their roots;

and the continuous growth until entering the Dharma-realm altar corresponds to the ultimate stage. Since this is the case for one stage, it is so for all others; therefore, the subsequent commentary states:
"Each of these stages possesses its own seed of Bodhi, and the mind contains the embryo of great compassion, which grows as the cause."
The fruit of the practice of wisdom and skillful means based on conditions consists of these three phrases in each and every stage; this is the meaning of the three phrases for each position.

As for the cause and effect of the subsequent distinct stages, this refers to the six kinds of fearlessness of the *yogācāra* over three kalpas, the three levels of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*), the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and the initial and fundamental clarity of wisdom, wherein the beginning and end further encompass the mutual identity of the holy and the ordinary—how much more so when the practitioner’s mental application is self-evident and perfected!

The fundamental non-arising spiritual understanding exerts itself and sports within the void; through ten inconceivable phrases of dependent origination, it performs an alchemical fusion of illusions.
By seeing the mind as the attainment of perfect enlightenment and realizing the mind as Great Nirvāṇa, one enters into awakening.
Thus, throughout the sixteen stages of practice, both the objective realm and wisdom are likewise so; is this not the "Twofold Profundity"? Therefore, in the *Vajraśekhara Yoga*, the tenth...
The arising of the six great bodhisattvas is precisely this meaning. Furthermore, there is an interpretation that their gradual realization and entry consists of two types:

first, regarding the six fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), it constitutes a gradual sequence from cause to fruit; second, regarding the ten stages (*bhūmi*), it constitutes a gradual sequence from cause to fruit.
When these two gates are presented together, there are sixteen [categories], which are not sequential practices spanning ten [lifetimes].

"The six stages. [Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "as when a Bodhisattva practices dhyāna within the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*)": this refers to the matter of gradually entering the practice of contemplation previously explained; it is used as an analogy because people might find it difficult to understand. As for the "nine successive attainments": 1. The first dhyāna. 2. The second dhyāna. 3. The third dhyāna. 4. The fourth dhyāna. 5. The sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). 6. The sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). 7. The sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). 8. The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). 9. The attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). These are called the "nine successive attainments" because they are entered one after another in regular order. They are also called the "nine successive abodes" (*navānupūrvavihāra*) because one dwells within them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive concentrations" (*navānupūrvasamādhi*) because one enters these meditative states in sequence. They are also called the "nine successive liberations" (*navānupūrvavimokṣa*) because one attains liberation through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive knowledges" (*navānupūrvajñāna*) because one realizes knowledge through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive paths" (*navānupūrvamārga*) because one traverses the path through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive fruits" (*navānupūrvaphala*) because one realizes the fruit through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive dwellings" (*navānupūrvasvabhāva*) because one establishes oneself in their nature in succession. They are also called the "nine successive vehicles" (*navānupūrvayāna*) because one proceeds by means of them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive powers" (*navānupūrva-bala*) because one exerts power through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive strengths" (*navānupūrva-sthāma*) because one manifests strength through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive dharmas" (*navānupūrvadharma*) because one realizes the Dharma through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive virtues" (*navānupūrvaguṇa*) because one cultivates virtue through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive merits" (*navānupūrvapuṇya*) because one accumulates merit through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive blessings" (*navānupūrvamaṅgala*) because one brings about auspiciousness through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive causes" (*navānupūrvahetu*) because one plants the cause through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive conditions" (*navānupūrvapratyaya*) because one fulfills the conditions through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive roots" (*navānupūrvamūla*) because one establishes the root through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive branches" (*navānupūrvāṅga*) because one develops the branches through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive leaves" (*navānupūrvapatra*) because one spreads the leaves through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive flowers" (*navānupūrvapuṣpa*) because one brings forth the flowers through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive fruits" (*navānupūrvaphala*) because one harvests the fruit through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive harvests" (*navānupūrvavipāka*) because one reaps the ripening through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive transformations" (*navānupūrvavikāra*) because one undergoes transformation through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive manifestations" (*navānupūrvābhāsa*) because one manifests phenomena through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive illuminations" (*navānupūrvāloka*) because one brings illumination through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive radiances" (*navānupūrvaprabhā*) because one emits radiance through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive lights" (*navānupūrvāloka*) because one shines with light through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive splendors" (*navānupūrvatejas*) because one displays splendor through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive majesties" (*navānupūrvamahiman*) because one manifests majesty through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive dignities" (*navānupūrvagaurava*) because one manifests dignity through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive honors" (*navānupūrvapūjā*) because one receives honor through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive respects" (*navānupūrvādarśana*) because one shows respect through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive offerings" (*navānupūrvapūjā*) because one makes offerings through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive gifts" (*navānupūrva-dāna*) because one bestows gifts through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive relinquishments" (*navānupūrvatyāga*) because one practices relinquishment through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive renunciations" (*navānupūrvaparityāga*) because one practices renunciation through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive abandonments" (*navānupūrvaprahāṇa*) because one abandons defilements through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive purifications" (*navānupūrvaviśuddhi*) because one attains purification through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive clarifications" (*navānupūrvaprasāda*) because one attains clarity through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive tranquilities" (*navānupūrvapraśama*) because one attains tranquility through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive cessations" (*navānupūrvanirodha*) because one attains cessation through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive liberations" (*navānupūrvavimukti*) because one attains liberation through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive non-attachments" (*navānupūrvāsakti*) because one is free from attachment through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive non-obstructions" (*navānupūrvānāvaraṇa*) because one is free from obstruction through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive non-hindrances" (*navānupūrvānighāta*) because one is free from hindrance through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive non-bonds" (*navānupūrvabandhana*) because one is free from bondage through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive non-ties" (*navānupūrvanigaḍa*) because one is free from fetters through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive non-fetters" (*navānupūrvasaṃyojana*) because one is free from the fetters through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive non-outflows" (*navānupūrvāsrava*) because one is free from outflows through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive non-leaks" (*navānupūrvāśrava*) because one is free from leaks through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive non-defilements" (*navānupūrvakleśa*) because one is free from defilement through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive non-afflictions" (*navānupūrvakaluṣa*) because one is free from affliction through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive non-corruptions" (*navānupūrvadauṣṭhulya*) because one is free from corruption through them in succession. They are also called the "nine successive non-obscuration" (*navānupūrvā

That is to say, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) constitute the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).

Because they are attained through a sequential cultivation from the lower to the higher levels, distinguished by their relative superiority and inferiority, they are called the nine successive attainments. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"Good son, the bodhisattva mahāsattva enters and emerges from the nine successive attainments with mastery, whether in direct or reverse order, even up to the joy and bliss born of seclusion."
The practitioner further enters the second dhyāna from the stage of joy and bliss born of concentration; then enters the third dhyāna from the stage of sublime bliss free from joy;
then enters the fourth dhyāna from the stage of purity of equanimity and mindfulness; continuing thus until entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
then arising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he again enters the attainment of cessation; and from the attainment of cessation...
Emerging from and re-entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, arising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and entering the sphere of nothingness,
and so on down to arising from the second dhyāna and entering the first dhyāna—
this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s lion-stretching samādhi.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "or contemplating the inexhaustible dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and so forth," this refers to the inexhaustibility of revolving through meditative absorption (*samādhi*), freely engaging with objects and delivering sentient beings.
For the sake of brevity, the phrasing is condensed into sixteen clauses. With respect to the inexhaustible dharma-realm, there are eight clauses:
taking all minds as one mind, taking one mind as all minds, taking one mind as one mind, and taking all minds as [one mind].
All gates of mind likewise possess four [aspects]: the gate of all as one gate, one gate as the gate of all, one gate as one gate, and the gate of all as the gate of all.
With respect to the realm of sentient beings without exception, there are also eight phrases:
taking one mind as all minds, all minds as one mind, one mind as one mind, and one mind as one mind.
The "All-Mind as the Gate of All Minds" also has four aspects: taking one gate as all gates, taking all gates as one gate, taking one gate as one gate, and taking all gates as all gates.

Furthermore, these are formulated as sixteen to accord with the sixteen layers of profound meaning (*ṣoḍaśa-gambhīrārtha*); logically, there should be further combinations of pairs and so forth, which constitute the characteristics of the "All-Mind Gates."
One should contemplate, according to principle, how these [teachings] are infinite in their forward and reverse progression, their transcendence of intervals, and their revolving cycles.
[Commentary: "If by these sixteen," etc., refers to the sixteen aforementioned profound and mysterious principles;

to comprehensively encompass the twelve divisions of the scriptures through both horizontal and vertical arrangements is called "horizontal inclusion" (橫統), while to collect them sequentially and specifically, spanning from top to bottom in their entirety, is called "vertical inclusion" (竪統).
Rong said: "Vertical inclusion" refers to the corresponding dharma-gates; "horizontal unification" refers to the comprehensive gathering of all things.

Regarding the "twelve divisions" (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), they are: first, the *sūtra*; second, the *geya*; third, the *vyākaraṇa*; fourth, the *gāthā*; fifth, the *udāna*; sixth, the *nidāna*; seventh, the *avadāna*;
eighth, the *itivṛttaka*; ninth, the *jātaka*; tenth, the *vaipulya*; eleventh, the *adbhutadharma*; and twelfth, the [upadeśa].

Second, regarding the treatise on discussion (*vāda*), the first is the *Sūtra* (*sūtra*). According to the *Abhidharma*, chapter eleven, this refers to the concise exposition of the meanings that ought to be explained, composed in prose (*gadya*).
Specifically, those teachings that ought to be explained which are briefly set forth in prose within the various sūtras are called *sūtras*.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* do not specify "prose," but state in general terms that the Buddha, in such and such places, for such and such [beings]...

Those sentient beings, relying on various modes of conduct, proclaim immeasurable discourses associated with the aggregates (*skandha*), up to those compiled by the redactors who arrange the true, virtuous, and sublime meanings in sequence through excellent names and so forth; these are called *sūtras*.

Regarding the *geya* (verses), the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* and other treatises agree that these are those passages within the sūtras—either in their middle or at their conclusion—which restate in verse what was previously taught in prose.
Regarding the meaning of "Verses" (*geya*): it is said that those sūtras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) should be further explained through verses.

Although the meaning has been stated in prose (*gadya*), it is not yet exhaustive and must be further versified; thus, they are called "Verses" for two reasons: first, to benefit those of sharp faculties who come later;
second, to clarify and purify the understanding of those listening to the Dharma by revealing the aforementioned provisional meanings. Third, as for "Prophecies" (*vyākaraṇa*):...
This refers to the Blessed One’s prophetic declarations (*vyākaraṇa*) concerning the future births of his disciples, which record cause and effect.
Furthermore, various treatises state that sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) are called "prophetic declarations" because they reveal the profound, hidden intent (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).

As for what is said elsewhere regarding sūtras of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*) being called "prophetic declarations," this means they are termed "non-definitive" because they provide a brief, summary declaration using few words.
Because it explains the profound meaning clearly and explicitly, and because it is generally designated as "vyākaraṇa" (prediction/declaration) based on three meanings:

first, it predicts the causes and effects of birth and death for disciples; second, it clearly and explicitly explains the profound and esoteric meanings of predictions; third, it predicts the future attainment of Buddhahood by bodhisattvas, and so forth.
As the *Geya* (Chanting) and other texts state: "It refers to those passages within various sūtras that are not a repetition of the prose [prose-portion]."

Speaking in two lines, three lines, four, five, or six lines and so forth, as well as the recitation of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, with the exception of the *Sūtras* and the various *Vinayas*, all other spoken verses of four lines—such as "Commit no evil, practice all that is good, purify your own mind;
this is the teaching of all Buddhas"—are called *Geya-sūtra*. Fifth, the *Udāna* (Spontaneous Utterances).

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts state that when a teaching is delivered without a formal request—because it is intended to ensure that the True Dharma will endure for a long time in the future—it is called "Spontaneous Utterance" (*udāna*).
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* explains this as follows: "When the Buddha entered meditative absorption in the afternoon and arose from that absorption at dawn, he spoke without being questioned;
this is called 'Spontaneous Utterance'. These six conditions constitute the basis for the [twelvefold] division of the scriptures.

Regarding the "arising" [of the teachings], there are three causes: first, speaking at the request [of others]; second, establishing precepts due to an offense; and third, teaching the Dharma due to a specific event.
As for the term "causal conditions" (*nidāna*), it refers to speaking at the request [of others] as well as the causal conditions for establishing the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that the fundamental basis upon which the verses of various sūtras depend is as follows: for example, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was a man who used a net to catch [birds].
The bird, having received [the fruit], returned and released it. The World-Honored One, knowing the fundamental causes and conditions of this event, spoke in verse:
"Do not treat a small offense lightly, thinking there will be no calamity; though a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel.
This is called the *Nidāna-sūtra*. Regarding the seven similes, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "The similes as explained within the Vinaya are called *Avadāna* (Parables)."
Regarding the terms "that sutra" and "Abhidharma" and so forth: it means that within the various sutras there are such analogies taught in order to make the primary meaning clear and pure.
As stated in [the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*] 25: "In this context, there are metaphorical explanations;

'Abhidharma' refers exclusively to the sutras, while 'Nirvāṇa' refers only to the Vinaya, and 'Yoga' refers collectively to the metaphors for the Sutra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma. All [of these] are explained together.
The eight *itivṛttaka* (past occurrences) included herein refer to all matters concerning the past that are proclaimed, excluding the *jātaka* (birth stories).
With the exception of the Buddha’s own birth stories, all other accounts of the past are called *itivṛttaka*.
The nine *jātaka* refer to the accounts of the Blessed One’s conduct as a bodhisattva in his various births throughout former ages in various places.
Practicing all that is difficult to practice is called the Jātaka-Abhidharma; as stated in the eighty-first [treatise]:
"That which proclaims the deeds corresponding to the original practices of the Bodhisattvas. The Nirvāṇa-sūtra says:

"Just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, when he was originally a Bodhisattva, took on various bodies—such as a deer, a bear, and even a garuḍa—and these are called the Jātaka-sūtras. Regarding the ten directions: [text fragment].

The *Vaipulya* (Extensive) refers to the teaching of the Bodhisattva path and the principle of the two emptinesses—the uncommon qualities of a Buddha—which encompass the fulfillment of both merit and wisdom;

it is called "Extensive" (*Vaipulya*) because it pertains exclusively to the Mahāyāna and does not extend to the Hīnayāna teachings. The *Vaipeya* (Nirvāṇa) refers to the *Vibhaṅga-sūtra* (Analysis Sutra);
it is also called *Vaipulya* because it extensively refutes [false views] and is the locus for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, and thus it is proclaimed as extensive.

Because it is the most profound Dharma, it is called Vaipulya (Extensive). Eleventh, the Marvelous Teachings (*adbhutadharma*) refers to those sūtras that proclaim the common and uncommon virtues of all Buddhas and their disciples, as well as other supreme, extraordinary, marvelous, and profound dharmas;
these are called the Marvelous Teachings. Regarding Nirvāṇa, it is said that when a Bodhisattva is first born, he immediately takes seven steps and emits [light].

The radiance shines universally throughout the ten directions, even as it was when the Buddha first entered a celestial temple at birth, causing the divine images therein to rise and prostrate in worship; this is called the "Unprecedented" (*adbhuta-dharma*).
The twelfth category, the "Discourses on Analysis" (*avadāna*), refers to those various scriptures that involve repeated investigation and examination, such as the *Mātṛkā* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

To explain according to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, as he taught in various sūtras—analyzing them extensively based on formal treatises (*upadeśa*) to discern their characteristics—is called an *upadeśa-sūtra*.

That is to say, if one takes the principles of the sixteen layers of profound mystery within this [text] to encompass the twelve divisions of the sūtras both horizontally and vertically, they will revolve without end. Furthermore, the Preface states: "As for a sūtra such as this..."

One should know that the intent of all sūtras lies entirely within this; as for the various teachings expounded by the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, one should know that the diverse causes and conditions taught by all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and three periods of time according to what is appropriate are none other than for the sake of these three phrases.
Since these dharma-gates ultimately converge in the same way, with no divergent tracks, it is said: "By means of these sixteen..."
[Commentary: Regarding the "six parts of the body": (1) from the navel downward; (2) from the navel upward; (3) from the heart downward;
(4) from the heart upward; (5) from the throat upward; and (6) the crown of the head—these are the six parts.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "from the navel-circle downward," etc., it refers to the manifestation of the body born in the palace of Śakra from the navel-circle of the Tathāgata downward;

the manifestation of emerging from the womb, infancy, childhood, marriage, departure from home, ascetic practice, and the attainment of enlightenment under the tree—all such manifestations are identical to the dharmas of worldly people.
He manifests such a body as well as the three vehicles and the six [perfections].
They manifest in various forms and types with diverse appearances (blue, yellow, red, white; male, female;

large, small), each with their respective speech and sounds, mandalas and seats (square, circular, triangular, semi-circular, etc.), and retinues that differ in their threefold revolutions as detailed below;
they all abide in sequence within the third court of the Great Compassion Womb Maṇḍala.

[Commentary]: Regarding the four wisdoms and the four samādhis, some say that the four wisdoms are the four pāramitās, while the four samādhis of the bodhisattvas are the bodies of the samādhis of the four directional Tathāgatas.
However, in this context, the four wisdoms are the four Tathāgatas, and the four samādhis are the four bodhisattvas;
this signifies that the four petals in the four directions of the eight-petaled lotus upon which they reside are precisely these.
The four petals at the four corners—namely Ratnaketu, Phullapadma, Amitāyus, and Devadundubhisvara—are the four Tathāgatas.
These correspond respectively to the four Bodhisattvas: Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and Avalokiteśvara, who dwell in order in the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the gateways of one's own *dharmadhātu*," this refers to the various forms and even the respective seats of the Buddha-bodies—the fruits and virtues of the four wisdoms—manifested within the three layers of maṇḍalas mentioned above, including those of the Three Vehicles and the six destinies. Each of these constitutes a gateway of the *dharmadhātu*. In accordance with each such gateway of the *dharmadhātu*, one performs the activities of mantra (*mantrakarma*). As for the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*), it refers to the various mantras and mudrās that are taught in accordance with the specific requirements of each individual practitioner. This is because the *dharmadhātu* is not limited to a single form; rather, it manifests in all manner of forms according to the diverse dispositions and capacities of sentient beings. Therefore, the various mantras and mudrās are established in accordance with the specific requirements of each individual. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the various mantras and mudrās": although there are many types of mantras and mudrās, they are subsumed under the two categories of the *vidyārāja* (wisdom-king) and the *vidyārājñī* (wisdom-queen). Among these, the *vidyārāja* is the principal deity who presides over the entire maṇḍala, while the *vidyārājñī* refers to the female deities who serve as attendants to that principal deity. These are further categorized into male and female types, and each of these is divided into the four classes of *bodhisattva*, *deva*, *yakṣa*, and *asura*. Within each of these four classes, there are again four types: the *vidyārāja*, the *vidyārājñī*, the *vidyāputra* (son of wisdom), and the *vidyāduhitṛ* (daughter of wisdom). Thus, there are sixteen types of mantras and mudrās. Moreover, within each of these sixteen types, there are further divisions into the four classes of *bodhisattva*, *deva*, *yakṣa*, and *asura*. Within each of these four classes, there are again four types: the *vidyārāja*, the *vidyārājñī*, the *vidyāputra*, and the *vidyāduhitṛ*. Consequently, there are sixty-four types of mantras and mudrās. Furthermore, within each of these sixty-four types, there are again four classes: *bodhisattva*, *deva*, *yakṣa*, and *asura*. Within each of these four classes, there are again four types: the *vidyārāja*, the *vidyārājñī*, the *vidyāputra*, and the *vidyāduhitṛ*. Thus, there are two hundred and fifty-six types of mantras and mudrās. Moreover, within each of these two hundred and fifty-six types, there are again four classes: *bodhisattva*, *deva*, *yakṣa*, and *asura*. Within each of these four classes, there are again four types: the *vidyārāja*, the *vidyārājñī*, the *vidyāputra*, and the *vidyāduhitṛ*. Therefore, there are one thousand and twenty-four types of mantras and mudrās. Furthermore, within each of these one thousand and twenty-four types, there are again four classes: *bodhisattva*, *deva*, *yakṣa*, and *asura*. Within each of these four classes, there are again four types: the *vidyārāja*, the *vidyārājñī*, the *vidyāputra*, and the *vidyāduhitṛ*. Consequently, there are four thousand and ninety-six types of mantras and mudrās. Moreover, within each of these four thousand and ninety-six types, there are again four classes: *bodhisattva*, *deva*, *yakṣa*, and *asura*. Within each of these four classes, there are again four types: the *vidyārāja*, the *vidyārājñī*, the *vidyāputra*, and the *vidyāduhitṛ*. Thus, there are sixteen thousand and thirty-eight types of mantras and mudrās. Furthermore, within each of these sixteen thousand and thirty-eight types, there are again four classes: *bodhisattva*, *deva*, *yakṣa*, and *asura*. Within each of these four classes, there are again four types: the *vidyārāja*, the *vidyārājñī*, the *vidyāputra*, and the *vidyāduhitṛ*. Therefore, there are sixty-four thousand and fifty-two types of mantras and mudrās. Moreover, within each of these sixty-four thousand and fifty-two types, there are again four classes: *bodhisattva*, *deva*, *yakṣa*, and *asura*. Within each of these four classes, there are again four types: the *vidyārāja*, the *vidyārājñī*, the *vidyāputra*, and the *vidyāduhitṛ*. Consequently, there are two hundred and fifty-six thousand and eighty-eight types of mantras and mudrās. Furthermore, within each of these two hundred and fifty-six thousand and eighty-eight types, there are again four classes: *bodhisattva*, *deva*, *yakṣa*, and *asura*. Within each of these four classes, there are again four types: the *vidyārāja*, the *vidyārājñī*, the *vidyāputra*, and the *vidyāduhitṛ*. Thus, there are one million and four thousand and three hundred and fifty-two types of mantras and mudrās. Moreover, within each of these one million and four thousand and three hundred and fifty-two types, there are again four classes: *bodhisattva*, *deva*, *yakṣa*, and *asura*. Within each of these four classes, there are again four types: the *vidyārāja*, the *vidyārājñī*, the *vidyāputra*, and the *vidyāduhitṛ*. Therefore, there are four million and sixteen thousand and one hundred and forty types of mantras and mudrās. Furthermore, within each of these four million and sixteen thousand and one hundred and forty types, there are again four classes: *bodhisattva*, *deva*, *yakṣa*, and *asura*. Within each of these four classes, there are again four types: the *vidyārāja*, the *vidyārājñī*, the *vidyāputra*, and the *vidyāduhitṛ*. Consequently, there are sixteen million and sixty-four thousand and five hundred and sixty types of mantras and mudrās. Moreover, within each of these sixteen million and sixty-four thousand and five hundred and sixty types, there are again four classes: *bodhisattva*, *deva*, *yakṣa*, and *asura*. Within each of these four classes, there are again four types: the *vidyārāja*, the *vidyārājñī*, the *vidyāputra*, and the *vidyāduhitṛ*. Thus, there are sixty-four million and twenty-five thousand and two hundred and twenty-four types of mantras and mudrās. Furthermore, within each of these sixty-four million and twenty-five thousand and two hundred and twenty-four types, there are again four classes: *bodhisattva*, *deva*, *yakṣa*, and *asura*. Within each of these four classes, there are again four types: the *vidyārāja*, the *vidyārājñī*, the *vidyāputra*, and the *vidyāduhitṛ*. Therefore, there are two hundred and fifty-six million and one hundred thousand and eight hundred and ninety-six types of mantras and mudrās. Moreover, within each of these two hundred and fifty-six million and one hundred thousand and eight hundred and ninety-six types, there are again four classes: *bodhisattva*, *deva*, *yakṣa*, and *asura*. Within each of these four classes, there are again four types: the *vidyārāja*, the *vidyārājñī*, the *vidyāputra*, and the *vidyāduhitṛ*. Consequently, there are one billion, four hundred and twenty-four million, four hundred and ninety-six thousand and three hundred and seventy-six types of mantras and mudrās. Furthermore, within each of these one billion, four hundred and twenty-four million, four hundred and ninety-six thousand and three hundred and seventy-six types, there are again four classes: *bodhisattva*, *deva*, *yakṣa*, and *asura*. Within each of these four classes, there are again four types: the *vidyārāja*, the *vidyārājñī*, the *vidyāputra*, and the *vid

Because it is the gateway to the *dharmadhātu* of others, it is called "self. When explained deeply, these various gateways to the *dharmadhātu* all flow forth from the *dharmadhātu* of the self-mind of Vairocana; therefore, it is called the "self-*dharmadhātu*.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth" mentioned in the subsequent text, it means that although the following scriptural passages describe the fourfold maṇḍalas, their deities (*bimba*), mantras, and mudrās as being immeasurable...
Although they differ in their distinctions, when one investigates their fundamental source, they are all derived from the mind-king;
they are merely various names, phrases, and characters established to accommodate different capacities for the sake of circulation.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "it does not mean that [the Tathāgata] manifests universally according to the various classes [of beings]," there may be those who harbor doubts, asking:

"The Sūtra states that 'all appear as the bodies of the Tathāgata. Yet, in the Commentary, you instead explain this by means of the six manifestations of the Tathāgata appearing in the forms, postures, and so forth of the three vehicles and the six destinies—various gates of the Dharma-realm.
Does this not contradict the Sūtra? Therefore, the Commentary itself clarifies this by stating: "In the Sūtra..."

It is not that [the Tathāgata] manifests universally according to the various classes of beings, but rather that he speaks of "manifesting the body of the Tathāgata in its entirety" in order to address those doubts and difficulties;

therefore, the subsequent passage states: "The intent of the sutra clarifies that both the fundamental and the provisional are the Dharma-realm, an inconceivable power of empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna) that is ultimately non-dual.
How could one wish to cause the single Dharma-realm body of the Tathāgata to become three?"
Does one ride upon the various forms of the six realms? It is like a skilled goldsmith who fashions many images; does the essence of the gold itself become manifold?
Therefore, the subsequent commentary states: "Vairocana and the spirits, animals, and so forth are equal and non-dual;
thus, by taking 'one' as the gateway, one immediately perceives the Mind-King."

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "therefore performing Buddha-works, etc.": Previously, for the sake of those sentient beings—from the initial generation of the bodhicitta up to the tenth stage—he traveled throughout the ten directions to perform Buddha-works.

Now that he has completed these Buddha-works, he returns and withdraws back to his original position within the Buddha-body (the respective original positions of the three layers). Having settled there, he again enters, and enters once more.

Within all its constituent parts, it expresses that the Dharma-realm is non-dual, that there is nothing that does not flow forth from the Dharma-realm, and that there is nothing that does not return to the Dharma-realm.
[Commentary: "If there were no teacher of ignorance, that which is transmitted would have no locus" means that this sutra is the secret [treasure] of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
In short, one must not keep [this teaching] hidden nor peruse it at will; it must be received from a teacher.
Just as one wishing to cross a treacherous and difficult path must rely on a guide, if there is no guiding teacher, one will reach nowhere. This case is likewise:
those who wish to arouse the bodhicitta and cultivate the secret and essential practices of mantra must rely on a teacher of clear understanding, for what is transmitted has a specific source.

"Entrusting" (ji) means to rely upon or to place one's trust in. If there were no enlightened master, that which is transmitted would have nothing to rely upon or trust; therefore, an enlightened master is required.

[Commentary] Regarding those who receive the transmission of the teachings and the consecration (abhiṣeka), there are two distinct types of consecration: first, the consecration of the transmission of the teachings.

Second, regarding the *kṣepa-grahaṇa-abhiṣeka* (initiation for establishing a karmic connection): as clarified in the commentary below, if a person, upon encountering a ritual site (*maṇḍala*), says, "It is difficult to encounter the conditions for the Dharma;

I beg that you also grant me salvation," one performs the initiation for them. Having received the initiation, they seek to receive the mantras, mudrās, and ritual methods within all the *vidyādhara-pāda* (mantra-gate) practices of their chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) and practice accordingly according to their capacity; therefore, it is called "establishing a connection" (*kṣepa*).

Regarding the second [condition], the empowerment of the transmission of the teaching (*ājñā-abhiṣeka*): from the initial generation of the mind of awakening, one seeks an ācārya with the desire to succeed to the rank of ācārya.
Once the master has granted his permission, he constructs a maṇḍala and, having performed the complete ritual procedures, bestows the empowerment.
Having received the empowerment, one becomes capable of succeeding to the master’s position; therefore, it is called the "empowerment of the transmission of the teaching" and is named *ācārya*.

Liye said: "If one transcends the eight minds of compliance and opposition to realize the realm of tranquility, then that which was described in the first eon—such as seeds, roots, and buds, as well as taking refuge in the Three Jewels—is called the 'eight minds of compliance with the world.

Conversely, from the initial generation of the resolve for the Path in the three vehicles until the uprooting of the fundamental ignorance that is the seed of karma and afflictions, is called the 'eight minds of opposition to the world.'"
By means of five similes, through the gate of non-substantiality, one realizes that all phenomena are emptiness itself;
being unshaken by the aggregates, elements, or sense bases, nor by the grasper or the grasped, one realizes the realm of tranquility—this is what is called the "Teacher's Word.
As for the phrase "if the sovereign mind-king [is attained]," this refers to the six kinds of contemplation, such as the illusory-like, practiced by the practitioner of mantra during the second eon.

This is illustrated by the attainment of mastery over the mind-king, which transcends both the obstacles of persons (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*), as well as the dualities of existence and non-existence.

Because one realizes that the fundamental nature of one's own mind is unborn, the *Commentary* states: "By means of such gates as 'illusion-like,' one illuminates the non-duality of existence and emptiness;

when even the marks of the two-fold emptiness of persons and phenomena no longer occupy the mind, this is called truly entering the emptiness of phenomena and awakening to the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), without lingering in conditioned existence."
The state of a non-conditioned mind free from hindrances and so forth is called the *ācārya*.
If one gives rise to the mind of the ultimate signless intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-nimitta-śūnyatā-svabhāva*), this is the third stage for the practitioner of mantra (*mantra-yogin*).

By observing that one’s own mind is ultimately unborn, such that both the self and the aggregates (*skandha*) are of a single nature, this wisdom of emptiness arises; therefore, it is called the arising of the mind of the ultimate signless intrinsic nature.
The memorial submitted stated: "When the practitioner attains this mind, they observe that among all defiled and pure phenomena, there is not one that does not arise from conditions.
If something arises from conditions, it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If it lacks intrinsic nature, it is the fundamental non-arising of the mind.
That the mind fundamentally does not arise is the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the mind. Furthermore, even this reality-limit of the mind cannot be apprehended."
It is said: "The mind that arises from the ultimate absence of self-nature is called an Ācārya. Thus, in this sequence, from the lower to the upper levels, all may be designated as Ācāryas.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "from here there are again ten stages," the ten stages of profound practice refer to the Ten Bhūmis (Ten Grounds). As for the term "in understanding" (*yú jiě*):

The "Foremost of the Three Mysteries" refers to the *ācārya* who has received the empowerment of the transmitted teachings (*kula-śāsana-abhiṣeka*) and has successively received the secret dharma from his master;
among those who transmit the teachings for the practice of the three mysteries, he is the most preeminent.
Because this person is endowed with all virtues, he is able to propagate the Secret Teaching so that the lineage of the Buddha remains unbroken; such a person is called a true Buddha.
Because he is constantly praised by all the sages, he is called the "Foremost.
Regarding the phrase "like Vajrasattva," this person has generated the bodhicitta within the Great Compassion Womb Maṇḍala and received the samaya;
having been authorized by all the Buddhas, his rank is equal to that of Samantabhadra-Vajrasattva, as he stands at the head of the sixteen bodhisattvas.
Regarding the statement "like Vajrasattva, one says Vairocana," etc.:
when this ācārya performs the duties of an ācārya, whatever he consecrates (*adhiṣṭhita*), he first visualizes himself as Vairocana. Why?

Because it is impossible for another to attain [realization] if one has not attained it oneself. Regarding the phrase "performing the initial [practice] up to being identical with Sattva": as mentioned previously...
Although one should conceive of one's own body as being identical to Vairocana, one merely takes up his empowerment;

then, when the time for the ritual action arrives, one visualizes one's own body once again as Vajrasattva-Vairocana, for one should not perform the rite oneself. Therefore, the sub-commentary below states:
"Next, visualize one's own body as Vairocana. The reason for this is that the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana is this Great Compassion Womb (Mahākaruṇā-garbha).
Therefore, because he is the Ācārya, when the practitioner performs the duties of an Ācārya,
he should regard his own body as the deity; and when performing the various tasks of constructing a maṇḍala, he should regard his own body as Vajrasattva.

[Commentary]: If one’s wisdom and activity are perfected in the same manner as those of Vairocana, then wisdom is the contemplation of oneself as the body of Mahāvairocana, and activity is the contemplation of oneself as identical to the Sattva.
One who acts in this way is called a Master of Profound Practice (Gambhīracaryā-ācārya).

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "comprehensively mastering various arts" and so forth: it refers not only to generating the bodhicitta, sublime wisdom, and compassion, but also to extensively mastering the various worldly arts and crafts.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the science of sound (*śabda-vidyā*) and so forth," "sound" refers to the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), and "reasoning" refers to the science of logic (*hetu-vidyā*).
"The eighteen fields of knowledge (*vidyā-sthāna*) and sixty-four skills" is a general enumeration; "calculation, medicine, physiognomy, and the arts" is a brief indication.
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in its fifth stage (*bhūmi*), states: "For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, the Bodhisattva [masters] worldly crafts..."
There were no arts he did not master, namely: literacy, mathematics, and grammar;
he was thoroughly proficient in the various treatises on calligraphy, seals, and the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, which constitute the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*);

furthermore, he was skilled in medical prescriptions for treating all illnesses—such as epilepsy, insanity, and toxic possession—which he could entirely eliminate, thus mastering the science of medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*); and he excelled in literary composition, eulogy, song, dance, and instrumental music.

He was thoroughly proficient in all such matters: whether it be kingdoms, cities, villages, towns, palaces, residences, gardens, groves, springs, streams, ponds, pools, grasses, trees, flowers, or medicinal herbs—whatever was arranged there, he knew each to be in its proper place.
He knew the locations of all treasuries of gold, silver, *maṇi* jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, coral, and so forth, and would bring them forth to show them to others.
He also knew the movements of the sun, moon, and stars, the cries of birds, earthquakes, and the auspicious or inauspicious nature of dreams at night.
He skillfully observes all physical signs and omens, never erring in his discernment; this is the science of arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthāna-vidyā*).

Upholding the precepts, entering meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), and possessing immeasurable supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)—including the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and all other worldly matters—he reveals them all solely for the purpose of not harming sentient beings and for their benefit, gradually leading them to dwell securely in the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma and other internal teachings.
"Clarifying the requirements for the maṇḍala and so forth" refers to the numerous constituent parts. For instance, as stated in the sixth commentary:
"Regarding the offering of the desired intention—'desire' (rati) means when one offers scented unguents (gandha), there is a 'song of scented unguents';
this applies likewise to flowers, lamps, food, drink, and so on. Each and every chant is a mantra; each and every dance offering is likewise [a mantra]."
Regarding secret mudrās that no one understands, the ācārya should perform them himself;
if he cannot do so, he cannot be called one who has mastered the various arts.
[Commentary]: "Regarding all dhāraṇīs" refers to the dhāraṇī of the Dharma and so forth, as already explained previously.
"Speaking of the gates of samādhi" means that samādhi serves as the gate; these include three, four, or even one hundred and eight samādhis and so forth.

"Speaking of the factors of the path" (mārga-aṅga): "path" refers to entering the noble path, and the "factors" refer to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. "The various perfections" (pāramitās) refers to the six.

Because they transcend the ten perfections and so forth, there are four types of eloquence (*pratibhāna*): first, swift eloquence (*tarkapratibhāna*), which flows like a rushing river; second, quick eloquence (*kṣiprapratibhāna*), which answers questions as they arise;

third, appropriate eloquence (*yuktapratibhāna*), which skillfully teaches in accordance with the faculties [of beings]; and fourth, unimpeded eloquence (*anāvaraṇapratibhāna*), which consists of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

Regarding the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*): through these four dharmas—generosity (*dāna*), kind speech (*priyavāditā*), beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), and cooperation (*samānārthatā*)—the Bodhisattva gathers and sustains the assembly.
The power of birth refers to the ten powers (*daśabala*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

First is the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), by which one discriminates and evaluates whether sentient beings are capable of being delivered or incapable of being delivered.

Second is the power of knowing the retribution of karma (*karmavipāka-jñānabala*), by which one discriminates and evaluates whether a person has karmic obstructions, whether they have [karmic] retribution, or whether they are free from obstructions. Third is the power of knowing meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis (*dhyānavimokṣasamādhi-jñānabala*)...

1. The power of knowing the discrimination and deliberation of the faculties (*indriya-parāpara-jñānabala*): it discriminates and deliberates whether a person is attached to flavors or unattached to flavors. 2.

The power of knowing the discrimination and deliberation of the faculties of sentient beings (*indriya-parāpara-jñānabala*): it discriminates and deliberates the degree of strength or weakness of the faculties of sentient beings. 3. The power of knowing the discrimination and deliberation of various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñānabala*):

it discriminates and deliberates what sentient beings find pleasing. 4. The power of knowing the discrimination and deliberation of various dispositions (*nānā-dhātu-jñānabala*): it discriminates and deliberates the deep-seated intentions of sentient beings.
1. The power of knowing the paths leading to all destinations (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*), which discriminates and evaluates the gateways to liberation for sentient beings; 2.

The power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-bala*), which discriminates and evaluates the origins from which sentient beings have previously come; 3. The power of knowing death and rebirth (*cyutyupapāda-jñāna-bala*), which discriminates the excellence or inferiority of the places where sentient beings are born;
4. The power of knowing the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna-bala*), which discriminates and evaluates the attainment of *nirvāṇa* by sentient beings.
The Buddha employs these ten powers to liberate sentient beings; being precise and unerring, they are all fully perfected.
For this reason, although the Buddha possesses immeasurable power, he speaks specifically of these ten powers. As for "fearlessness," it refers first to the fearlessness of omniscience:
amidst the great assembly, the Buddha proclaims of himself, "I am endowed with omniscience," his mind free from any timidity or dread.

Therefore, regarding the fearlessness of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*), the Buddha himself declared that all afflictions (*kleśa*)—both their seeds and their manifest forms—are exhausted.

Regarding the fearlessness of the obstacles to the path (*antarāyika-dharma-vaiśāradya*), the Buddha himself declared, "I clearly know all things that can obstruct the noble path, such as sensual desire.

Because he is free from timidity, regarding the fearlessness of the path leading to liberation (*nairyāṇika-pratipad-vaiśāradya*), the Buddha said, "I know the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*) that leads to transcendence."

The suffering of birth and death is called the fearless teaching of the path for exiting suffering; because the mind has no timidity regarding these four dharmas, they are called the Four Fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*).
Now, this sutra further contains six fearlessnesses, as previously clarified. The word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) and so forth.
[Commentary]: "That is, to deeply cultivate observation and so forth" specifically clarifies the profound *prajñā*.
How is this known? Because one contemplates the ten conditions of dependent origination during the third eon. Furthermore, it may fully encompass the three types of *prajñā*:

contemplating the phrases of the ten conditions of dependent origination is the *pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā* (contemplative wisdom); seeing the profound Middle Way is the *dharmatā-prajñā* (wisdom of the true nature).

If one explains that all verbal teachings are the *prajñā* of words (*vyañjana-prajñā*), then as for the statement "illuminating the emptiness of non-apprehensibility," it is because the preceding eon is now taken as the object of contemplation.

[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the phrase "wisdom of the first eon" and so forth, this means that during the first eon, this bodhisattva, together with those of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*), [attains realization].
The Śrāvakas practice together for two kalpas and still hear [the Dharma] alongside those of vast wisdom;

yet even Subhūti, within the assembly of the Prajñāpāramitā, was only able to expound the emptiness of both persons and phenomena by relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*), for without the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power he could not do so.
Therefore, these were not [considered] extremely profound. Now, within this kalpa, there is boundless wisdom.
Because those facing it—the followers of the Two Vehicles—do not know it, it is called "profound" (*gambhīra*).
[Commentary: "Capable of being fashioned and perfected": "fashioning" (*jiang*) refers to a master craftsman; "perfected" (*cheng*) means accomplishment.

This is because, by penetrating the Three Vehicles, one is capable of serving as a master for others and accomplishing the three trainings (*śikṣā*) of disciples. Furthermore, "craftsman" (*jiang*) also refers to a manual artisan. As it is said: [text continues].
In the world, a master craftsman can fashion various vessels; likewise, an Ācārya who is a master of the Dharma can fashion those who are vessels for the Three Vehicles and the Three Studies.
Furthermore, he is like a "Master Builder" (jiang). The "Jiangzuo Shaofu" was an official of the Qin dynasty who managed palaces and residences;
the title "Craftsman" (jiang) used here is likely derived from that office.

[Commentary: "That which subsumes the eight consciousnesses and so forth of all sūtras" refers to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and other such texts, as well as the treatises on Consciousness-Only (*Vijñaptimātra*).

Regarding the meaning of "lack of nature" (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), as stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*: "Based on the first [nature], the imagined (*parikalpita*), one establishes the lack of nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*);

because its essential characteristic is ultimately non-existent, like a flower in the sky. Based on the second [nature], the dependent (*paratantra*), one establishes the lack of nature in terms of production (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*)."
This nature is like a magical illusion; because it arises dependent upon various conditions and lacks an inherent nature as it is falsely grasped, it is conventionally described as "natureless.
This does not mean that its nature is entirely non-existent. Based on the subsequent perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the ultimate naturelessness is established.

That is to say, because it is remote from the previously mentioned imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of self and phenomena, it is conventionally described as "natureless," yet this does not mean its nature is entirely non-existent.
Regarding the mention of "Buddha-nature," "One Vehicle," and so forth, these refer to scriptures such as the *Nirvāṇa*, the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda*, and the *Tathāgatagarbha*.

Question: Now, the third meaning already encompasses the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*). As for the fourth, the establishment of "knowing one's own mind as it truly is" (*yathābhūtajñāna*), which separately collects the Secret Treasury (*mizang*):

is the *Avataṃsaka* and *Prajñāpāramitā* inferior to the Tathāgata’s Secret Treasury? Answer: This is because the fruit of the teachings is identical; however, they differ in being Exoteric versus Esoteric.

Since this differs from the previous [classification] which, regarding the characteristics of the teachings, encompasses all definitive meanings (*nītārtha*) through their perfect and ultimate nature, whereas the latter—concerning the efficacy of majestic mantras—belongs to the Esoteric Vehicle (*guhyatantra*), how can there be any further doubt?
[Commentary: To distinguish according to specific phenomena and recognize their respective natures and categories: if within a mantra there are *na na* (meaning "arising") or *u ru*...
One should know that those mantras containing the syllable *va* belong to the category of increasing (*puṣṭi*).
If a mantra contains *māraya*, *pātaya*, and so forth, one should know it belongs to the category of subjugation (*abhicāra*).
If a mantra contains *śānta*, *viśuddha*, and so forth, one should know it belongs to the category of pacifying (*śānti*). Furthermore, if the deity assumes a smiling expression and is yellow...
As for color: that which is of a peaceful (śāntika) nature is yellowish-white; if it manifests as a joyful or wrathful aspect, it belongs to the class of increasing (paustika) nature;
if it manifests as a fierce aspect or colors such as blue-black and the like, one should know that it belongs to the class of subjugating (vaśīkaraṇa) nature.
The colors of the offering substances—whether dull, pale, bitter, or sour—and so forth, should be understood by analogy with these categories.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "The right hand represents samādhi, etc.," Xingshan’s *Yin guan* says: "The left wing [finger] and right wing [finger], the right hand and left hand;

the left stops and the right contemplates, and it is likewise for the others. Regarding the statement "the ten fingers, etc.," Xingshan says: "The right wing [fingers] represent wisdom, skillful means, vows, power, and knowledge;

the left hand represents giving, precepts, patience, diligence, and dhyāna. The little finger of the left hand is the head [of the sequence], ending with the fingers of the right hand—these are the ten pāramitās."
Regarding the meaning of the analogy of the five wheels (*pañcamaṇḍala*) for the term "all-pervading" (*sarvatraga*) as it pertains to the omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) of the Tathāgata:
the omniscience of the Tathāgata is difficult to comprehend, and thus it is illustrated by the analogy of the five wheels. The five wheels are earth, water, fire, wind, and space.
Therefore, Xingshan said: "In the sequence of the five wheels, starting from the left little finger as the head, they are earth, water, fire, wind, and space," which is as stated above.
The Sūtra says: "For example, just as the great earth is the support for all sentient beings, so too is the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) the support for devas, humans, asuras, and others.

Just as the fire element burns all fuel without ever being satiated, so too does the knowledge of all modes burn all fuel of ignorance without ever being satiated. Now, this case is also like that; it is said, "among all conditions..."
"All possess the foremost ultimate reality" means that within all the phenomena of causes and conditions as described above,
when one observes them through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), their ultimate non-arising is what is called "all possessing the foremost ultimate reality."
[Commentary]: Regarding the observation of whether one is a worthy vessel or not within the maṇḍala:

when the ācārya leads the disciple into the maṇḍala and casts the flower, one observes the place where the cast flower lands. According to whether it falls into the superior, middling, or inferior category, one can know if that person is a worthy vessel or not.
For instance, if at the time of casting the flower, it falls upon the head of the Buddha, one should know that [the disciple is a supreme vessel].

A person will easily attain accomplishment through the *uṣṇīṣa* mantras; if one falls into the middle part of the Buddha’s body, it should be known that one will easily attain accomplishment through the *hṛdaya* (heart) mantras;

if one falls into the lower part of the Buddha’s body, one will easily attain accomplishment when seeking *siddhi* through the mantras of the messengers (*dūta*). Accomplishment through other mantras is more difficult. Furthermore—
"Vessel" and "non-vessel" refer to where the flowers reach: those places they reach are designated as "vessels," while places they do not reach are designated as "non-vessels.

Just as worldly vessels receive their names according to their contents—for instance, that which holds incense is called an "incense vessel"—if it does not hold flowers, fruits, or the like, it is not so named;
whereas if it holds flowers, it is called a "flower vessel. Regarding incense, food, and so forth, it is called a "non-vessel. If the flowers reach the crown of the Buddha’s head...

The *Buddhoṣṇīṣa* is called a "vessel" when it is equal to the Buddha-mind; otherwise, it is called a "non-vessel. Alternatively, those who are worthy of the Most Honored One are vessels, while those who do not reach that state at all are non-vessels.

[Commentary: Regarding "those who believe in all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas," this means that the *ācārya* should believe and know that sentient beings possess [the potential] in a single thought-moment.
Within the hearts of all beings reside the bodies of the Buddhas with their immeasurable lifespans, as well as non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas;

yet, being shrouded by ignorance, these have not yet become manifest. One who, regarding this empowerment of the three secrets, maintains profound faith and practices diligently, is called a Master of Profound Practice (Gambhīra-caryā-ācārya).
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the oceanic assembly in the Land of Tranquil Light" (*śāntaprabhāsa-kṣetra*): "Tranquil Light" refers to the land, and "oceanic assembly" refers to the multitude.

These are the sands-of-the-Ganges-like beings within the land of tranquil luminosity; as they encompass both the True and the Responsive [bodies], the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-caryā-dharma-sūtra* states:
"Śākyamuni and Vairocana pervade all places; the dwelling place of that Buddha is named 'Eternal Tranquil Light' (*nitya-śāntaprabhāsa*)."

It is encompassed by the perfection of constancy (*nitya-pāramitā*), established in the station of the perfection of self (*ātma-pāramitā*), purified by the perfection of purity (*śubha-pāramitā*), and characterized by the cessation of the signs of existence through the perfection of bliss (*sukha-pāramitā*). Furthermore, the second commentary states:
"When the practitioner attains this mind, they immediately know that the pure land of Śākyamuni is not subject to destruction, and they perceive the lifespan of the Buddha."

The bodies of those who have long dwelt in their fundamental ground, together with the bodhisattvas such as Ūrdhvaja who have emerged from the earth, assemble in one place to cultivate the path of remedies;
yet, though their rank is adjacent to that of the position of a successor to Buddhahood (Buddha-uttarādhikāra), they do not recognize even a single person [among them].

Such a profound realm is beyond the knowledge of even non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, let alone inferior ordinary beings; therefore, it is difficult to believe when it is said that they are "successors."
Regarding "the one who dwells in the three requests," the "one dwelling in the place of succession" (bhūmyantara-stha) is Maitreya Bodhisattva.

As for the "three requests," the *Nirvāṇa* chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that Maitreya Bodhisattva, having seen the great bodhisattvas emerge from the earth and having heard the World-Honored One’s words, "These are my emanations," then spoke these verses:
"In the past, the Buddha left the Śākya clan to renounce the world and sat near Gayā..."
"It has not been long since the Bodhi tree [attained enlightenment], and so forth... How could you have been taught and inspired to resolve for enlightenment in such a short time?
I pray that the Buddha will expound this for the sake of the future, so that they may gain understanding.
When he had spoken thus, the Buddha then addressed the bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly: "Sons of good family, you should believe and understand the Tathāgata’s truthful words."
After these words had been spoken three times, Maitreya joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we only pray that you will speak it;
we shall faithfully accept the Buddha’s words. Having thus requested three times—this constitutes the triple entreaty—he spoke again:
"We only pray that you will speak it; we shall faithfully accept the Buddha’s words. At that time, the World-Honored One knew that the bodhisattvas had made their triple request.
Regarding the passage "not stopping," since it says "three requests" and yet they do not stop, he next bestows an admonition, saying: "I shall tell you; you all listen attentively.

Because there were three prior expositions, this is called the "fourth admonition. Question: Does this not contradict the *Fahua Xu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), which states, "The Tathāgata gave three commands, and the Regent made four requests"?
Answer: When that text speaks of "three commands," it merely takes the three instances of his speaking as constituting the "three commands."

Regarding Maitreya’s four requests, it refers to what the sutra says: after he had made these three declarations, he spoke again, saying, "I only pray that you will explain it"—this constitutes the fourth request.
Since each is based on a distinct meaning, they do not contradict one another.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "reaching the stage of abiding" (*sthiti-bhūmi*) and so forth: the stage of abiding refers to the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*).

These ten stages of abiding are collectively termed the "stage of practice through faith and understanding" (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*). Alternatively, "transcending faith and understanding" means reaching the Buddha-stage (*buddha-bhūmi*).

That is to say, from within the meanings of the preceding three phrases, the Buddha-stage is extracted as the "supreme expedient mind. When one reaches this fourth mind, it is called the "ultimate" (*niṣṭhā-gata*).
Because it is the stage of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*), the Sūtra states: "One-fourth surpasses the stage of faith and understanding (*adhimukti*).

[Commentary: Even the assembly of worthies and sages offers praise; this is because such a person, having received the empowerment of the transmission of the teaching (*śāsana-abhiṣeka*), has attained the praise of all worthies and sages.
Therefore, the subsequent Sūtra says: "One should know that those good sons and good daughters..."
Born from the mouth of the Tathāgata, these sons of the Buddha’s mind perform the work of a Buddha wherever they travel;
therefore, O Secret Lord, those who wish to make offerings to the Buddha should offer them to these sons and daughters of good family.
And those who wish to see the Buddha should at that time contemplate Vajrapāṇi, Samantabhadra, and other such leaders.
All the bodhisattvas spoke with one voice, saying: "From this day forward, we shall reverently honor and make offerings to these sons and daughters of good family.
Why is this? Because they have seen the Buddha, the World-Honored One, together with us."
[Commentary]: Regarding "creating the mind-maṇḍala and so forth," this means that internal mental yoga is no different from the external maṇḍala.
All such things are gateways to the Dharma of the inner mind; all sentient beings equally possess this nature, yet they cannot believe in it themselves nor realize it for themselves.
The Tathāgata, having clearly realized and personally witnessed it, universally opens [this teaching] for the sake of all sentient beings.
Awakening [the disciple], one also causes them to likewise attain this; the current Master of Profound Practice (Gambhīracaryācārya) has composed this *Cittamaṇḍala-maṇḍalakriyākrama*.

As for the bestowal of the mind-consecration (*cittābhiṣeka*) using the water of compassion and the explicit words as set forth in the "Chapter on Abiding in the Secret Maṇḍala," the commentary on that chapter states:
"The master, abiding in the seat of yoga, should contemplate the letter A and apply..."
Place a drop at the fontanelle (the "cross-seam") on the crown of the disciple's head; one should know that this drop above is the nectar-water of the Dharma used to consecrate the crown of the head.
This is identical to the initial reception of office by the Buddha and constitutes the transmission of the teaching through consecration.
[Commentary: "One should not become the last [of the lineage]" means that the *ācārya* instructs the recipient of the Dharma:
"From this day forward, you should extensively perform altruistic deeds according to what you have received and practice them with diligence;
do not become the one who severs the lineage at the end. This is an instruction to ensure the succession of the work performed by former masters. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
In the treatise, the Buddha entrusts Ānanda, saying: "After my parinirvāṇa, you must skillfully protect the Prajñāpāramitā.
You shall teach your disciples, and your disciples shall in turn teach others, passing it on from one to another like a single lamp lighting other lamps.
Do not become one who severs the lineage at its end. He himself explains this by saying: "It is as when a person has a son, yet the son does not succeed to the family line."
To sever the lineage is considered the most shameful thing; the Buddha used this analogy to instruct Ānanda:
"Do not allow the *prajñā* to be cut off within your own person. Now it is the same: a teacher admonishes a disciple not to allow this Path to fail to proceed within their own person.
Therefore, it is said, "one should not," and so forth.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "all such dharmas are ultimately equal," this should be illustrated by means of the *akṣara-dvāra* (gateways of syllables).
For instance, the gateway of the syllable *sa* (*śa*) explains the meaning of the dull nature of all phenomena.
