That which is dull by its own nature (*svabhāva*) is precisely the non-conceptual mind (*nirvikalpa-citta*), which is neither deluded nor wise, neither false nor awakened, and which cannot be shaken by any phenomena whatsoever. Therefore...
However, just as people in the world, because they do not abandon their preferences for acceptance and rejection,
prize wisdom and discard ignorance, and honor nirvana while despising birth-and-death; now, when one contemplates the gateway of the letter *sa*, the mind is free from discrimination,
and thus the mind has no high or low— therefore, it is called "pliancy."

[Commentary]: "Whatever one performs is all in accord with samādhi" means that if the deity manifests a compassionate countenance or a white body, and one offers white flowers, this is called being "in accord with samādhi.
If one offers yellow or red [flowers], it is called "not in accord. Incense and other such items are to be understood by analogy.
Regarding the phrase "each and every object of focus enters the gate of the Dharma-realm," if one acts in this manner...
One should seek each of the samādhis and so forth through four propositions; since none can be apprehended, this is called "entering the gate of the Dharma-realm.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "in the three families," etc.: the three families are the Buddha family, the Lotus family, and the Vajra family. For instance:

When performing the accomplishment (*sādhana*) of a mantra belonging to the Buddha Family, one takes the substance produced therein—such as *añjana*, realgar, or cinnabar—and places it within the maṇḍala of the tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).
Performing the rite according to the rules, when the *siddhi* is attained, there are three distinct signs of superior, middling, and inferior attainment.
Regarding the superior attainment, there are three signs: first, warmth arises during the early night; during the middle night...
Smoke arises at the fifth watch and flames emerge from within; thus, two signs are formed. This refers to excluding the flames below, whereby one sign is formed, namely the arising of mere warmth.
For the practitioner of mantra (*mantrayānin*), it is necessary to thoroughly penetrate that all such statements correspond to correct principle (*yukti*);
this means that although one performs various accomplishments (*siddhi*), one does not grasp at them, for they are no different from suchness (*tathatā*). Furthermore, regarding the breath...

Regarding the phrase "among the dharmas of calamity," it refers to what is stated below: "If one enters the world of the Universal Gate (Samantamukha), one can, within a single thought-moment, achieve complete and perfect correspondence.
*The Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāvairocana Sūtra: Explication of the Secret (Yanmi Chao), Scroll Four.*
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāvairocana Sūtra: The Explication of the Esoteric (Yanmichao), Scroll Five.* Composed by the Śramaṇa Jueyuan,
Master of the Secret Treasury, Grand Master of Purple Robes, Acting Minister of Rites, Grand Guardian-in-Chief,
and Grand Officer of the Court of Imperial Entertainments at Yuankuasi Temple in Yanjing.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "at that time, settle the mind in immovability," etc.: when this sign appears to the practitioner, they should immediately settle the mind within the *ra* syllable gate.
The *ra* syllable gate signifies that all phenomena are free from the defilement of sensory objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

This means that the aforementioned objective realms are all merely the signs of the six sense-objects, which are simply the domains traversed by deluded perception. Furthermore, one should then turn the contemplation toward the *a* syllable.

Investigate this by means of its own nature: since the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) are fundamentally unarisen, one should know that all objects perceived through seeing, hearing, touching, and cognizing are entirely the *dharmadhātu*.
How could the *dharmadhātu* create obstacles for the *dharmadhātu*? When observing in this way, one is then able to settle the mind in immovability.
As for the statement that one "purifies them by relying on the Dharma teachings," this refers to the aforementioned skillful means.

Furthermore, one may simply contemplate the syllable *ra* to purify it; this means that the syllable *ra* itself signifies the sense of "dust" (*rajas*), which should be understood as the objects appearing as described above.
If a bindu is placed above it, it becomes the syllable *laṃ*; this bindu signifies the Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*).
This means that because space is signless (*animitta*) and difficult to represent, it is indicated by a circular dot.
One then contemplates that the syllable *ra* is identical to the great void (*mahā-śūnyatā*), whereby all obstructions and defilements are naturally purified and removed.
[Commentary] Regarding the "King of the Golden-Winged Birds" and so forth, as stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:

"For example, the King of the Golden-Winged Birds, with his two wings on the left and right, lashes the waters of the ocean until they part in two; he then observes those among the host of nāgas whose lives are about to end."

To seize [the fish] is likewise how the Tathāgata appears in the world: with great tranquility (*śamatha*) and sublime insight (*vipaśyanā*) as his two wings, he stirs the great ocean of the waters of sentient beings' great love, causing it to part on both sides; then, observing those among the masses whose faculties are mature, he delivers and liberates them.
It is by virtue of his courageous and steadfast mind that he is able to do so.
[Commentary: Regarding the causes and conditions for Sadāprarudita’s quest for the Dharma, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata was in the City of Fragrant Flowers (*Gandhavatī*). Sadāprarudita came from afar, not sparing his own body or life, desiring to hear the Dharma.
At that moment, as the sun was setting, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata rose from his preaching and entered his palace. Sadāprarudita...
Sadāprarudita thought to himself: "I have come for the sake of the Dharma; I ought not to sit or lie down.
I shall wait for the Dharma Master to emerge from his palace and preach the Dharma by means of two postures—either walking or standing.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata had for seven years entered one-pointed concentration on immeasurable *samādhis* and practiced the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, while Sadāprarudita likewise remained steadfast.
For seven years, he practiced walking meditation, standing and sitting, neither lying down nor sleeping; free from desire, anger, and affliction, his mind was not attached to flavors.
He thought only of when the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata would arise from samādhi to preach the Dharma.
After these seven years had passed, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita thought to himself: "I shall [serve] the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata..."
"Sadaprarudita, you shall preach the Dharma while seated upon this throne;

I shall sweep and cleanse the ground, scatter various flowers, arrange a couch of the seven precious gems, and seek water to sprinkle upon the earth so that no dust arises. Even Śakra, Lord of the Devas, became aware of his thoughts.
Thus he reflected: "I shall carve my own body to draw blood and sprinkle it upon the ground, so that there may be no dust. Even Śakra came to know this.
In his mind, he immediately took three thousand *śroṇa* of heavenly *māndārava* flowers and gave them to Sadāprarudita. Sadāprarudita accepted the flowers;
he scattered half upon the ground and kept the other half to offer as an act of worship when Dharmodgata sat upon his seat to preach the Dharma.
At that time, Dharmodgata arose from samādhi and expounded the *prajñāpāramitā* for him, which Sadāprarudita beheld.
Dharmodgata’s mind was pure, joyful, and delighted, and upon hearing the Dharma, he attained immeasurable samādhis (and so forth).
Through such various causes and conditions, he never regressed from the bodhicitta. Furthermore, that sutra states:
at that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions comforted the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, saying, "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! We..."
When I was practicing the bodhisattva path, I sought the *prajñāpāramitā* and attained these various samādhis, just as you have now attained them.
You should therefore respect this Buddha-dharma even more and give rise to a pure mind; toward spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), you should conceive the thought that they are Buddhas.
Why is this? Because it is through the protection of spiritual friends that one swiftly attains [enlightenment].
Regarding this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, at that time the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita addressed the Buddhas of the ten directions,
saying, "Who are those who should be approached, served, and honored by me as my spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*)? The Buddhas of the ten directions replied to Sadāprarudita, "Good son,
the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has been teaching and bringing you to maturity throughout successive lifetimes."
"Your *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is your true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
If you were to serve the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata for one eon, two eons, three eons, or even for more than a hundred thousand eons—
bearing him upon your head with reverence and honoring him with all articles of pleasure, including every exquisite form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch found throughout the trichiliocosm— "
Although offerings cannot repay even a moment’s grace, now that the disciple has entered the maṇḍala, they shall also behold the Buddhas of the ten directions,
who will offer consolation and praise, while the ācārya exhorts and inspires their resolve.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) cannot be sought through merit or vows: there are generally two gates for one who wishes to attain the Buddha-way; first, meditative concentration, and second, wisdom.
Now, because one wishes to bring forth the Great Compassion Maṇḍala, one must rely upon meditative concentration.
As for the gate of meditative concentration, it requires the power of great diligence. Why? Because the mind in the desire realm is distracted.
One cannot perceive the true nature of all phenomena (dharmas) just as a lamp burning in the wind cannot provide clear illumination;

however, a lamp in a sealed room will certainly attain stillness and clarity. Therefore, one must possess meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Furthermore, although meditative concentration is required, it is not possible to attain the essential point through coarse observation alone;
one must rely on yoga (*yoga*). Moreover, even if one possesses yoga, if there is no diligence (*vīrya*), realization remains difficult to achieve.
It is like drilling wood for fire: if the smoke does not yet emerge despite repeated efforts, how much less can one obtain fire? One must exert oneself with unceasing vigor to accomplish the task.
Now, if one wishes to attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), one must be diligent;

therefore, the commentary below states that as the Buddha taught, one does not abandon diligence even when blood and flesh are exhausted, and thus it is called "meditative concentration," and so forth.
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "As the Buddha has taught" up to "all are distinguished" (this entire section is from the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*), that treatise further states:

"The Bodhisattva, through various causes and conditions, censures the mind of indolence and causes it to delight in and adhere to diligence. Indolence is like a black cloud that covers all clear wisdom, swallowing and destroying merit while increasing unwholesome states.
Although there is slight pleasure at first, there is great suffering later; it is like poisoned food which, though [seemingly pleasant] at first..."

If fragrant and delicious [substances] are kept for too long, they will kill the person; likewise, practitioners of mantra should cultivate diligence and abandon all laziness, for then *siddhi* will be easily obtained. [Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "because the six sense faculties are purified," it means that this merit applies to both the stages of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and sages (*ārya*); thus, [it is taught in] the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The Treatise states: "Ordinary persons, by the power of the sūtras, attain the superior functioning of their faculties. Furthermore, a sūtra says:
"With the physical eyes born of one's parents, they see the trichiliocosm and so forth. If we discuss the sages, it is because their six faculties are purified that they attain mutual functioning;
that is to say, within a single faculty, they are fully capable of seeing forms, hearing sounds, perceiving fragrances, and discerning tastes.
The realization of touch and so forth also involves the capacity for mutual functioning; this is attained prior to the [first] bhūmi.

Now, regarding those of profound practice, such as the Ācāryas, they are said to have "purified the six sense faculties" either through the power of their own merit or by the power of the majesty of the Dharma.

[Commentary]: Regarding the exclusion of the preceptor’s stinginess toward the Dharma—this lack of stinginess toward the Dharma is precisely the precept maintained by the practitioner of mantra (vidyādhara).

While other sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras define killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying as the four *pārājika* offenses, within the Vidyādhara-piṭaka these are judged to belong to the category of *sthūlātyaya*.
This is because [stinginess] creates an obstacle to the Path and does not sever the life-force of wisdom.
Now, there are four [offenses] by which one incurs the *pārājika* offense: (1) abandoning all the true Dharma; (2) forsaking the bodhicitta; (3) being stingy with all dharmas;

and (4) performing actions that are not beneficial to sentient beings. Since this mind of stinginess regarding the Dharma constitutes an offense against the third heavy prohibition (*gurudharma*), the sub-commentary below states: "There are those who, though they do not abandon the true Dharma nor depart from it..."
If one who possesses the bodhicitta is stingy regarding the True Dharma and refuses to examine the faculties [of others] before bestowing it as a gift, they likewise commit a pārājika offense.
Why is this so? It is because it is only through the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world that the True Dharma exists;

[Commentary]: *Ariṣa-gāthā* is a Sanskrit term; in the Qin language it means "Ancient Sage-King," referring to the supreme merit of benefiting oneself and others, as well as the path of the ancient seers and sages. There is not a single Buddha who does not abide by this.
It is also said that *ariṣa* means "foremost," "supreme," "extremely high," "non-retrogressive," "non-receding," and "non-sinking," being fully endowed with merit.
That virtue does not diminish is called the *ariṣṭa-sthāna-jñāna* (knowledge of the abode of the noble). The fifty-third discourse on wisdom states:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva consists of the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*). What are the four? The Buddha makes this solemn declaration:
'I am one who possesses all-encompassing right knowledge (*sarvajña*). If there be any śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, or Māras...'"

If Brahmā or any other being were to challenge this truth as it really is, saying, "I do not know this Dharma," or even up to, "I do not see even the slightest sign of fear," for that reason I have attained peace and security, I have attained fearlessness, and I abide in the position of the Noble Lord.
Furthermore, in the twenty-eighth discourse, it is asked: For what reason does the Buddha speak with sincerity, establishing the abode of the Ariyas?
It is said: Because he himself is fully endowed with merit and causes sentient beings to attain peace, happiness, and benefit;
and because if a Buddha were to dwell in a state of personal peace and happiness alone without being able to benefit sentient beings, it would not be called the "Ariṣa dwelling";
furthermore, because he is able to eliminate all doubts, regrets, and false views, and because he is able to explain and resolve all profound questions and difficulties, it is so named.
By the power of the merits of such causes and conditions as establishing the dwelling place of the *ariṣṭa*, I speak these words of truth with utmost sincerity:
"I establish the dwelling place of the *ariṣṭa* and roar the lion’s roar amidst the assembly... Now, the practitioner, desiring to construct a maṇḍala on this ground for the sake of disciples, says:
"Just as the dwelling place of the Holy Lord Śākyamuni was established, so do I desire to dwell here."
Therefore, because the earth goddess was awakened and made a truthful declaration to establish the dwelling place of the ancient noble lords,

[Commentary: Regarding the passage from "having first [attained] samādhi" to "making offerings and so forth," it means that when the Master-Ācārya, the translator, instructs a practitioner of mantra (mantrayānin) who wishes to perform this ritual for purifying the ground (*bhūmipariśodhana*), they must first empower their own body with the Samaya-mantra, the Dharmadhātu-mantra, and the Vajrasvabhāva-mantra; it is essential that they act according to the prescribed rules.
Only after distancing oneself from all hindrances can the Great Compassion Maṇḍala be established;
the statement that "all is as explained in the ritual for offerings" refers specifically to the seventh fascicle of this sūtra.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "using the letter-gateway *ra*," etc., the practitioner, having performed the empowerment through visualization as before, then visualizes the letter-gateway *ra*, which signifies the meaning of dust and defilement.
Furthermore, by placing a bindu upon the letter *ra*, it becomes the syllable *raṃ*.

By contemplating the syllable *raṃ*, one purifies the ground of one's own internal mind; thus, realizing Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), one becomes free from all stains and obstructions. This is the ritual for making offerings.

The verse says: "The syllable *ra* is white in color; adorn it with the dot of emptiness (*bindu*). Just as one places a bright jewel in a topknot, so too should one place it upon the crown of the head.

This passage is abbreviated; having performed this, the practitioner further, within the mind of contemplative practice, first generates the form of a wind-wheel shaped like a half-moon, empowered by the *ha*-gate (the character *a* is erroneously written here), and visualizes the syllable *ha* situated thereon.
Within the wind-mandala of the half-month, one first performs the offering by contemplating that wind-mandala as being established upon the syllable *ha*, with black light-flames spreading forth.
Next, one contemplates the water-mandala, empowered by the syllable *ba*; that is, one visualizes the syllable *ba* within a circular wheel.
Then, one contemplates the vajra-earth-mandala, placing the syllable *a* within a square wheel, as described above.

This sequential empowerment is the sign of the initial formation of the world; one must obtain a single condition that is undisturbed, contemplating with careful scrutiny so that the mind and its objects correspond, being clear and unmistakable.
[Commentary: Regarding "the various merits of the pure bodhicitta" and so forth: in the previous shallow explanation, the ācārya performed offerings using fragrant ointments, flowers, and the like;

now, at the time of the profound explanation, the ācārya performs the offering by dedicating the various merits arising from the pure bodhicitta toward the wisdom of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna). This is done through purity.

The practice of reciting the fifteen characters—"the various merits of the bodhicitta are dedicated toward the knowledge of all modes" (*sarvajñajñāna*)—three times should be understood accordingly. [Commentary:
"This refers to the signs of the one and eight being indeterminate" means that this is a dual exhortation regarding all phenomena and their true nature (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, first, phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature; eighth, they arise from various conditions. Since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) lack self-nature, this is precisely the principle of ultimate reality (*tattva*).
Since all phenomena arise from conditions, there are birth and cessation, permanence and annihilation, coming and going, and identity and difference—all of which constitute the conditioned.
"One" is not fixed as one, for it can give rise to the eight; "eight" is not fixed as eight [for they are subsumed within the one].
Since it is precisely one, and because that oneness is indeterminate, one is thereby able to transcend all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "if all," this conversely establishes the contemplation of the "space" category within the ten conditions of dependent origination;
at that time, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are like space, and the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is likewise like space.
Since the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all conditioned phenomena is like empty space, how could one escape from this space to seek that space? [Commentary]:
As for the mention of "three months" and so forth, it refers to the practitioner’s contemplation upon their own mind, wherein they manifest perfect clarity.

Within the perfect clarity, one should visualize three tiers; upon these three tiers, one arranges the thirty-four characters in a circular rotation, which is precisely the meaning of the "three turnings of the Dharma wheel.
How could this possibly be interpreted merely as a ninety-day retreat?

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the violation of the *samaya* by oneself: among the *samaya* precepts of the *ācārya*, the third precept states that one must not be stingy with any of the teachings (*sarva-dharma*).
Although one must not be stingy, one must not bestow the path upon those whose faculties are deficient.

As the sutra says, "bestowing the path upon those of deficient faculties is a source of enmity for humans and devas. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Those of dull faculties and small wisdom are attached to signs (*nimitta*)."

Those who are arrogant cannot believe in this Dharma; when wicked people of future ages hear the Buddha preach the One Vehicle, they will be deluded and fail to accept it, thereby destroying the Dharma and falling into evil realms. Because they thus harm themselves and harm others, they violate the fourth samaya precept.

[Commentary]: Regarding "the expedient means for adorning the body" and so forth, this refers to when the Ācārya constructs the maṇḍala, he is frequently assailed by Piśācas and other obstructive spirits;
consequently, he adorns his own person with the vajra armor and so on, so that Māras dare not approach.
This rite is as explained in the section on offerings, and it should be performed as required at the appropriate time.
[Commentary: Regarding "empowering the five precious substances" and so forth: the five precious substances refer to gold, silver, pearl, conch shell, and red coral.
Some say that the first three are the same as the latter two, while others say they are crystal and jade.
The five grains refer to rice, barley, wheat, small beans, and sesame. The five medicinal herbs refer to *khaṇḍakāri*, *yavani*, *hasti*, *saha*, and *sā*.
The medicinal substances *hādeva* and *yaksata-nirika* are *lingzhi* (Pachyma cocos), cinnabar, realgar, *renshen* (Panax ginseng), and *chijian* (Acorus calamus);
some say they are *bimaba* (Piper longum), *chijian*, *renshen*, *lingzhi*, and *huixiang* (Foeniculum vulgare).
From "Namo Samantabhadra" to "Svaha," this single secret mantra consists of six phrases in total, excluding the phrase of taking refuge. First.
The phrase "unsurpassable" (*asama*) or "unequaled" (*asamasama*) refers to the samādhi-mantra of this King of Maṇḍalas.
Because it transcends all speech and metaphors, and because there is not a single dharma that can serve as its peer, it is called "unequaled.
In Sanskrit, *sama* is translated here as "equal," but with the prefix *a-* (the sound *a*), it becomes "unequaled. Second is the phrase "equality of space" (*ākāśasamatā*).
This refers to the name "Third: The Phrase of Equanimity Appearing in Accordance with Manifestations," because this ground of mind is ultimately pure and identical to empty space.

It refers to the name "Fourth: The Phrase of Innate Purity," because this ground of mind, being equal to empty space, is able to pervade all realms of sentient beings and universally manifest bodies in accordance with their respective types. Now, by means of incense...

Sprinkling water upon the ground is for the purpose of removing defilement; that is to say, by blending the fragrance of naturally pure precepts with the water of naturally pure compassion, one sprinkles it everywhere upon the naturally pure mental ground of sentient beings throughout the *dharmadhātu*. Therefore, this is named the fifth phrase, "The Utterly Pure Phrase of the *Dharmadhātu*.
This means that the *dharmadhātu* is precisely the letter A (*akṣara*), which is fundamentally unborn (*anutpanna*); thus, its nature is free from attachment, just like empty space.
It is called the "Phrase of Ultimate Purity" because it is free from the defilement of dust.

The sixth is the "Phrase of Awakening and Self-Vow," which means that all Tathāgatas, by means of this secret mantra, let out a lion’s roar to awaken all beings so that they may enter therein together; thus it is called "Awakening.
Furthermore, when all Tathāgatas were originally practicing the bodhisattva path, they perceived this meaning and therefore let out a lion’s roar to give rise to [this vow].
This is my sincere word: if there are sentient beings who recite this sincere word of mine without violating the dharma-rules, I shall fulfill all their wishes according to their desires.

Now, since the Ācārya has recited this secret mantra in accordance with the Tathāgata’s samaya teachings, I pray that the Tathāgata will not contradict his original vow and cause my place of practice to be fully endowed and pure; for this reason, it is done.

[Title]. [Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "The mantra says, etc.," "that" refers to the sūtra. Question: Since the sūtra text was translated from Sanskrit into Chinese (Tang), why are the Sanskrit characters retained here?
Answer: The commentary retains the Sanskrit characters in order to capture the meaning of the *mukhadvāra* (gateways of letters).
The meanings of the characters, phrases, syntax, transformations, and numerous auspicious signs—if one were to follow only the Chinese translation, the essential flavor would be lost;
therefore, this commentary sets forth the Sanskrit words to clarify the referents.
[Commentary] "Now, all by means of the universal mind," etc., refers to the mind that takes refuge as being identical to the realm to which one returns.

Furthermore, this meaning of pervasiveness refers to a single Tathāgata who, without division, pervades the entire Dharma-realm, as well as the realms of dust and the places of adventitious defilements;
he also pervades the infinitely layered Indra-net lands contained within those empty spaces, separately taming the inexhaustible realms of sentient beings.
Moreover, there are those who pervade by means of emanated bodies. Thus, it is the same for one Buddha as it is for all Buddhas.

In this manner, having pervaded all of this—so that the object to which one returns is likewise pervaded by the returning self, whether as a single body throughout the field of objects or as many bodies—one universally offers refuge.
Thereafter, one recites this mantra so that these Buddhas shall not transgress their original vow; "not transgressing the original vow" refers to the final phrase of this mantra.

As for the phrase "all other letter-gates," this refers to the thirty-two letter-gates beginning with *ka* and *kha*;

Since these flowers and fruits all belong to the bodhicitta, it is said that they all serve to adorn this word.

The fundamental essence is the letter *sa*; for the deluded, the fundamental essence is the letter *ma*. The letter *sa* signifies that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are entirely free from defilement and attachment.
This meaning of the letter *sa* as being undefiled is precisely what is called the Lotus Samādhi.

Because one abides in this samādhi, the fundamental nature of the lotus is fragrant and pure, such that no dust can stain it; thus, the letter *ma* naturally represents the emptiness of all phenomena.

That even the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) cannot be apprehended is precisely the great wisdom of emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā-jñāna*) of all Buddhas; therefore, the syllable *sa* represents meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the syllable *ma* represents wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because concentration and wisdom are equalized, it is called "the three delusions. This is the explanation according to the gateway of syllables (*akṣaramukha*).

[Commentary: Regarding the statement "these annotations are for the sake of those who have not yet reached certainty," this refers to the fact that the character *sa* has an annotation meaning "leakage" (*āsrava*) and a shallow sense, and another annotation meaning "equality" (*samatā*) or "conformity" (*anuvṛtti*).

If one has already attained certainty regarding the sense of equality or conformity, but has not yet reached a definitive conclusion regarding the sense of leakage and shallowness, then because it is not yet settled, one cannot discard the meanings of leakage and shallowness while retaining only equality and conformity; therefore—
"Preserving both characters" means that "liang" (良) signifies "goodness"; it means that preserving both characters constitutes goodness.
"All are suchness" explains the meaning of the word "many" (*bahu*); it means that "many" expresses the meaning of the suchness of all phenomena.
"Ga" refers to the Great Emptiness Samādhi; this character "ga" is [the seed syllable] within the mantra phrase.

The character *ka* is explained here in a manner distinct from its usage in the sūtras. Furthermore, it is interpreted as the Sanskrit term *samatanugati*, which is translated here as "equal conformity" (*dengsu*).
This means that because the syllable *A*—the vajra-ground—pervades all sentient beings and their sense faculties, it is called "equal.
Moreover, because the body of the *A*-syllable deity responds to all classes of living beings, it is termed "conformity. Based on this, it pervades the ground of the mind.
Because the painted mandala follows the categories of the various classes of beings, it is called "Equal-Following" (*samānubhava*).
Furthermore, the following section specifically clarifies the meaning of the syllables: *sa* signifies "outflows" (*āsrava*) and "shallow"; *ma* signifies "self" (*ātman*) and "meaning.
Since these two syllables each encompass two meanings, they are said to be "indecisive. Because it is difficult to choose between them, both *sa* and *ma* are retained.

Because of the character "ma" (麼), the commentary exclaims that it is "excellent and good. The reason for this praise is that the two characters "sa-ma" (娑麼) are joined with the following character "duo" (多);
thus, both meanings—*tathatā* (suchness) and *samatā* (equality)—are designated as "equal" (*pingdeng*).

[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding "the dharma-realm," etc.: it means that the dharma-realm, the sentient-being realm, and the mind-realm, by entering the gate of the letter *A*, achieve mutual identity (*samasatā*).

Thus, through this successive progression, the mind-realm is itself the fifth phrase of intrinsic purity, and so on, until it becomes the initial letter *A* within the second phrase, which constitutes the essence of the mantra. Therefore, by means of...
All other syllable-gates are strictly formed from the letter *A*, which is the source of the bodhicitta.
[Commentary] Regarding the determination of the Great Vīra of the East and so forth: the name of the Vīra-mudrā is the triangle itself, broad at the top and tapering to a point at the bottom;
this is the Great Vīra-mudrā of all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and three periods of time. It is also called...
The "seal of the mind" (*cittamudrā*) of all Buddhas refers to their place of abiding; that stage is the abode of Great Diligence (*mahāvīrya*).
The term "lower place" (*adhasthāna*) is the same for all [directions]. Regarding the mention of "southeast" and so forth:

*Cintāmaṇi* is also the name of a seal, meaning that the southeastern quadrant of Vairocana is the location where the *Cintāmaṇi* jewel is placed. Regarding "northeast" and so forth: the northeastern quadrant of Vairocana is space (*ākāśa*).

[The Commentary] states that "the practitioner transforms himself into the body of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata. This means that within a piece of white sandalwood, the practitioner first visualizes a precious lotus pedestal and a palace of jewel-kings.
"Jewel-king" refers to the *cintāmaṇi*. Furthermore, within the palace, he arranges a precious throne, and upon that throne—
Having placed it upon a white lotus pedestal, one then visualizes the letter *A* atop that white lotus pedestal;
because this letter *A* is transformed into the body of Vairocana, it is said that "it is transformed," and so forth.
[Commentary: "To observe with the stainless eye" does not mean that one can see by means of the physical eye; rather, it means one should observe with the *dharmacakṣus* (Dharma-eye).
This refers to visualizing the syllable *RA* placed within the two eyes, which is called the "stainless eye. How is this known?
Because the syllable *RA* signifies the meaning of all phenomena being free from dust (*rajas*). As the *Recitation Ritual* states: "The syllable *RA* is named..."

Because one should contemplate the stainless (*vimala*) as being like two suns, it says "by means of the stainless," and so forth. The profound and secret intent herein can be grasped through the mind;
that is to say, while the extremely profound and secret principles of this sūtra are indicated here by way of a mere direction, they are difficult to record in full.
It is easy for scholars to understand them by applying analogies and reasoning according to their own insight. For instance, as in the preliminary purification...

Within the *Bhūmi*, it is taught that among the insentient things such as tiles, pebbles, thorns, and skulls, and the sentient beings such as dung beetles and centipedes found therein, there is a profound and secret significance.
This is established by practitioners whose minds are purified from the sixty-one mental defilements;
when purifying the ground of the mind by constructing the inner Great Compassion Maṇḍala, this must be required.
Because one has attained the power of discernment and removal, it is said that [the teaching] is "profoundly secret," and so forth.
[Commentary: Regarding the transformation of the syllable *A* into *Va* and so on: the practitioner first visualizes the syllable *A* upon the flower pedestal as having the color of a vajra;
within the crown of the head, he places the King of Universal Illumination with a Hundred Rays (namely, Mahāvairocana). Now, he intends to use ointments and flowers...

[Shu] Regarding the transformation and guidance through the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*): because there are three wheels, "transformation" (*hua*) refers to transformative teaching (*jiaohua*), and "guidance" (*dao*) refers to instructional guidance (*shidao*).

This is because the Buddha transforms and instructs all sentient beings by means of the three wheels. First is the wheel of supernormal power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*); its essence is wisdom (*jñāna*) cultivated through practice.

The fruit of its accomplishment and its majestic function are unfathomable; thus it is called "divine" (*śrī*). Because it is capable of manifesting transformations, it is called "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*).

Because it possesses the two functions of subduing and suppressing, it is called a "wheel" (*cakra*). In the first case, "divine" is itself the transformation, and "transformation" is the wheel; this is a *karmadhāraya* (descriptive) compound.

Furthermore, it is said that "divine" is the agent of transformation and "transformation" is the object transformed; because it is the divinity of transformation, this is a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound.
This very essence of the *śāsana* (teaching) possesses the sense of subduing, and is therefore called a "wheel" (*cakra*).

As for "supernatural transformation" (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇā*), the wheel—or rather, the object transformed—is called "supernatural" (*ṛddhi*) because it has the sense of being unfathomable; since it is that which is transformed, it is further termed a "transformation.

Thus, what is transformed is called a "supernatural transformation. As for the term "wheel," it refers to the transformative wisdom (*jñāna*), which is named after its object; this is the "supernatural transformation."
Regarding the "wheel" (*cakra*) and the two types of "recording the mind": the "mind being recorded" refers to the minds of others, which are the objects of the recording;

"recording" means discernment, and this is one's own mind, which is the agent of the recording. Because it is the recording of the mind, the wisdom that performs the recording possesses the sense of subduing, and is thus called a "wheel.
Although the recording of the mind is indeed a wheel, because the primary focus is the mind—whether one's own or that of another—they are both termed [the wheel of recording the mind].

This refers to the "mind-recording" [instruction]. Regarding the three types of instruction, *śāsana* (teaching) means instructing others to cultivate goodness; *avavāda* (admonition) means exhorting them to recognize and abandon evil.
Since these two meanings differ, they are combined under a single name as a *viśeṣaṇa-samāsa* (appositional compound with distinct meanings).

Alternatively, within a single word, both meanings are simultaneously present—both teaching and admonishing—which constitutes a *sāmānādhikaraṇya-samāsa* (co-ordinative compound based on common substratum). The intention of the former interpretation is that it is spoken in reference to two types of persons.

It refers to a person who has neither cultivated various virtues nor committed various evils. Because they have not cultivated virtues, they are instructed to do so; because they have not committed evils, there is no need for admonition.
This is called "instruction" (*anuśāsanī*) rather than "admonition" (*avavāda*). Furthermore, there is another person who practices both good and evil.
Because they have already performed virtuous deeds, they do not require instruction; however, because they have already committed evil deeds, they must certainly be admonished.

This is precisely what is called "admonition" (*avavāda*) rather than "instruction" (*anuśāsana*). Thus it is said that instruction and admonition are two distinct things, yet they are established under a single name.

The subsequent explanation of the meaning is as follows: it is spoken in reference to a single individual. For instance, if there is a person who has not cultivated virtue and furthermore commits various evils, it is therefore necessary to speak of both together.
The wheel has two meanings: first, upon the basis of instruction and admonition, there is the sense of "subduing," which is what it is named.
The wheel of instruction is so called because the wisdom of the two types of vocal expression possesses the power of subduing; thus it is termed the "wheel of the instruction-wheel. Question:

Among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), to which powers do these three wheels correspond? Answer: The wheel of miraculous transformation corresponds to the supernormal power of the basis of psychic power (*ṛddhividhi-abhijñā*);

the wheel of reading minds corresponds to the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna-abhijñā*); and the wheel of instruction corresponds to the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*).
If it is as you say regarding "penetration" (*abhijñā*), then perhaps the previous explanation of the meaning of the "wheels" (*cakra*) refers to the substance of speech;
yet how could that substance of speech be called "penetration"? The commentary explains: because it is produced by penetration and because it is the object of penetration, it is also given that name.

Now, when we speak of the three wheels, they are intended to destroy the lack of faith in those who have not yet believed so as to cause them to give rise to pure faith, to cause those who already believe to engage in practice, and to cause those who have already engaged in practice [to attain realization].
Because it causes them to attain the fruits [of the path], it means that regarding all phenomena there is no obstruction;
like the solar disc, it universally illumines all those with the faculties of the three vehicles, expounding the True Dharma according to what is appropriate for each, without any attachment.

This is called "perfect universal illumination" because, through miraculous transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), it can manifest various spheres of supernatural power so that others may [perceive] him.
They engender supreme respect through their prophetic declarations; they are able to discern the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings through their instructions;

they preach the true Dharma according to how [beings] have entered [the path]; and they provide correct instruction regarding the practices to be cultivated. Furthermore, by means of the three wheels, they purify the skillful means of the three secrets:
they purify the secret of the body through miraculous transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), and they purify [the secret of mind] through the knowledge of others' minds (*ādeśanā-prātihārya*).

The secret of the mind is purified through instruction; the secret of speech is purified [thereby], or alternatively, by means of any one of the wheels, the three secrets and so forth may be purified.
This refers to when the ācārya, at the time of retiring for sleep, first contemplates the lotus pedestal and further contemplates the gateway of the letter *A*;
then, within a dream, he beholds immeasurable Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifesting buddha-activities. Following this—
Those who are to be saved in various ways are taught and guided by means of the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*).

Furthermore, the *Daśacakra-sūtra* states that just as the wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*) belonging to a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) precedes the king when he travels, leading the way, crushing those who are unsubmissive, and pacifying those already subdued;
so too it is with the three wheels: they cause those who have not yet developed faith to give rise to faith, and cause those who have already given rise to faith to [increase it].

[Commentary: Regarding "the Lotus Samādhi," the *Shu* (sub-commentary) states: "It means that when the bodhicitta is entirely free from defilement and attachment toward all phenomena, it is called the Lotus Samādhi."

[Commentary]: "Direct faith" (*ṛju-śraddhā*) and so forth means that one's mind is upright and sincere, possessing faith and inclination without doubt; it is said that there is nothing capable of causing fear.

This is further endowed with wisdom (*jñāna*). Although one possesses direct faith, if one does not give rise to doubt or slander, yet lacks wisdom, then upon hearing the exposition of the three kinds of secret skillful means (*upāya*), one will be unwilling to practice them.
Or, even if one does practice, one may encounter various adverse conditions and...
Only those who feel fear regarding the long duration [of practice], yet do not possess such characteristics of fear, are capable of being received.
[Commentary: Regarding "adorned with profound wisdom," the Dharma of the boundless Buddhas is like space;
it cannot be borne by the shallow and inferior vessels of the Two Vehicles. It requires the profound and superior wisdom of the Mahāyāna to adorn oneself.
Being solemn, one is able to receive and uphold [the teaching]. As the Lotus Sūtra says: "Do not preach this sūtra among those who lack wisdom.
If there are those with keen faculties, clear wisdom, extensive learning, and strong memory who seek the Buddha-way—only for such persons may you preach it."
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Śīlapāramitā*" in the sutra text, the commentary divides this passage into two sections.
The latter section explains non-avarice (*amatsarya*), which maintains the *Dānapāramitā* (Perfection of Giving) and can thus mutually support it.

Now, in the primary explanation of patience (*kṣānti*), why does it instead refer to the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Śīlapāramitā*, wherein these are explained in detail? How could these possibly achieve mutual completion?

Since the attainment of one perfection (pāramitā) inherently includes the others, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, because one possesses the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), one is able to maintain the precept of non-avarice.
Moreover, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "The practice of ethical discipline (śīla) gives rise to patience for the sake of stabilizing the mind;
if one practices ethical discipline without patience, one will fall into the three evil destinies. Thus, patience is a great power that can firmly consolidate ethical discipline.
It is unwavering and its precepts are immeasurable. How does one fully uphold them? One must simply practice patience; through patience, all precepts are naturally attained.
Furthermore, patience serves as the staff of the precepts, supporting people until they reach the Path. (As elaborated at length.

Since the meaning above is drawn from the *Śīla* [Chapter], and it is thus that upholding the precepts gives rise to the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), how could it not give rise to generosity (*dāna*)? The principle of being free from stinginess should likewise be attributed to *śīla*.

Answer: To mutually clarify their meanings and principles, one should refer to that [treatise]. Regarding this patience (*kṣānti*), there are two gates, which should be understood as in that treatise. [Commentary]:

"This essential vow" (*shāoyào*)—the character *yào* here is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*). The meaning of the term "essential" (*yào*) differs from the meaning of the word "vow" (*yuàn*).
That is to say, "this essential vow" (*shāoyào zhī yuàn*) is, in Sanskrit, *sārvabhaumika*; whereas "with-vow" (*zhī yuàn*) is, in Sanskrit, [pranidhāna].
*Vāruya* refers to that which is prayed for by the mind; *dā* means that one is able to fulfill the wishes of others. As the sub-commentary below states:
"The merits realized within the ten worlds, as numerous as the atoms of dust, each and every one become vajra-seals (*vajramudrā*);
this is the fulfillment of the essential vow regarding the fruit-merit of self-benefit. From this body of self-realization, there again arises empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
In this body, the virtues of altruistic practice and the fulfillment of vows shall manifest; therefore, the characteristics of these types of practices differ.
[Commentary: Regarding "thunder and rain" and so forth, the *I Ching* states: "When heaven and earth are unbound (*jie*), thunder and rain arise;
when thunder and rain arise, the fruits and plants all sprout and split open. "Unbound" (*jie*) means to disperse. The second month is the time when the yin energy of heaven and earth disperses.

"The thunder and rain arise; this is the manifestation of bestowal. It is said that regarding the initial sprouting [of things], all phenomena require thunder to be released from their shells and rain to be moistened.
Although thunder and rain are essentially one, there are precedents and sequels among those things that break through their husks and sprout.

One cannot, on account of the distinct natures and categories of herbs, trees, and medicinal plants, claim that a single flavor of rain results in such differentiation. Nor can it be so for sentient beings.

If the natures and categories [of sentient beings] differ, would it not result in the manifestation of the Great Compassion Treasury Maṇḍala also becoming limited? The principle of the Dharma is easy to understand.
[Commentary: Regarding "by means of the three kinds of secret expedient means," this refers to the three types of instruments, namely body, speech, and mind.
One then churns, strikes, presses, and shakes the milk of Buddha-nature within the bodies of sentient beings;
through the five flavors of the stages of accumulation, application, seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning, it becomes the sublime awakening of *amṛta* (clarified butter). To explain this deeply:
by means of the three secrets (*triguhyaprayoga*), one churns and shakes the milk of Bodhi within the bodies of sentient beings, passing through the syllables *a*, *ā*, *aṃ*, *aḥ*, and *o*.
The flavor of these five syllables constitutes the sublime awakening and the *amṛta* (clarified butter) of all Tathāgatas;
therefore, this is called the meaning of the *maṇḍala*.
[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the number of atoms in ten worlds," the number ten signifies perfection, manifesting inexhaustibility through the *dharmadhātu*.
Because it is inconceivable and cannot be fully enumerated, I shall set it aside for now and speak briefly of this present circular mandala, which encompasses all five families.

Regarding its names, characteristics, and general categories, I shall provide a concise description of three aspects: the shapes and colors, the hand gestures (*mudrā*), and the seed-syllables of the various wisdoms.
First, as in the *Karunāgarbha-maṇḍala*, there is the Great Sun Tathāgata at the center, with eight petals and stamens, and the deities of the three families within the three enclosures.
The Worthy One’s penetration encompasses the entire Dharma-realm; the five families are all fully exhausted, so vast that their number is difficult to name.
For the sake of calculation, let us take the atoms of ten worlds and count them one by one.

Suppose a single Bodhisattva acts as the honored leader therein, with the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana presiding in the position above, while the remaining retinue members act as mutual leaders and companions. In this manner, there are ten such worlds.
In this maṇḍala born of subtle compassion, there is an even expanse extending to the realms of the same and different classes of worlds, the paths of dust, and the adventitious dust;
and within those particles, the sages and worthies of the infinitely nested world-systems of dust-particles likewise possess both principal and attendant figures.
Just as it is with the maṇḍala of forms and colors, so too is it with the maṇḍalas of hand gestures (*mudrā*) and the seeds of wisdom (*bīja-jñāna*).
Nevertheless, they are clearly arrayed like stars, mutually unobstructed, sovereignly luminous, and infinitely layered like the realm of Indra’s net;

thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-nirdeśa* states: "The *Vajraśekhara-sūtra* consists of one hundred thousand verses and contains five families (*kula*), four types of maṇḍalas, four seals (*mudrā*), and thirty-seven deities.
Each family contains thirty-seven [deities], down to even a single one."
The Honored One accomplishes the thirty-seven [auxiliaries] and is likewise endowed with the four maṇḍalas;

the four seals interpenetrate one another like the radiance of Indra’s net, reflecting and shining upon one another in infinite succession. Question: This is the maṇḍala of the perfect and wondrous assembly of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).

though various karmas and afflictions cannot cause him harm, even if he were to enter the vehicle of the two vehicles [the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha], [he would not be overwhelmed]."
"In the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), they are likewise not hindered by these [obstacles], and so forth.

[Commentary: Regarding "without remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*) and so on, this refers to the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) regarding the maturation of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). "Remainder" (*avaśeṣa*) signifies that which is not yet exhausted;

when all has been fully stated, it is called "without remainder. This is like the Buddha’s manifest prediction (*sammukhavyākaraṇa*) that at such a time and in such a place, one will realize enlightenment and receive a specific name.
Regarding the name of a certain Tathāgata as "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*): to say it is "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*) means that the Tathāgata has some intention yet to be fully exhausted.
For example, if one says, "In the future, a Buddha will bestow a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) upon you," but does not exhaust that intention, it is called a prediction with remainder.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and so forth," this refers to the prediction concerning the benefits of hearing the sutra. It means that those who hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in this life or future lives shall attain Buddhahood;
because it is spoken exhaustively according to the Buddha’s own intention, it is called an "inexhaustible prediction" (*anavaśeṣa-vyākaraṇa*).

If one were to say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and thus all should be granted the prediction, it would serve to stimulate a certain class of people who have severed their roots of goodness.

However, that which records those whose roots of goodness continue is called "prediction with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa-vyākaraṇa*). Furthermore, the preceding section explains the meaning in terms of the Buddha:

it means that the present Buddha grants the prediction without depending on another Buddha, and thus no further [Buddha] arises; this is called "prediction without remainder. If one says that a future other Buddha will grant you the prediction, it is called "prediction with remainder.
The subsequent section explains the meaning in terms of the Dharma: it refers to hearing the Dharma in both the present life and future lives.

Receiving a prediction (vyākaraṇa) based on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is called a "prediction without remainder" (*anavaśeṣa-vyākaraṇa*), whereas receiving a prediction at a later time by hearing other sūtras is called a "prediction with remainder" (*sāvaśeṣa-vyākaraṇa*). This is the meaning of what is said in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*:
"One shall, within the other profound dharmas of the Tathāgata, provide instruction, benefit, and joy."
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "as for propagating the sutra in an evil age," it might be objected:
"The sutra itself states that the Tathāgata does not attain perfect enlightenment for the sake of a single sentient being, nor for two, nor for many;

rather, out of compassion for all sentient beings—both those with no remainder and those with remainder—the Tathāgata attains equal and perfect enlightenment. Why, then, do you now restrict and establish a fixed number of people?"

Is this not contradictory? Therefore, the general explanation states: "This is merely based on the traces of the phenomenal aspects of one particular path—the shallow practice used as a skillful means to propagate this sutra within a world of turbid evil;
thus it is said that the ritual proceedings for a single period of the Dharma are limited to ten people."

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the immeasurable gates, etc.," the term "regarding" (so-yun) serves both to point to the "immeasurable gates of the path of the Mantra Vehicle" within the sūtra and to further explain the meaning and definition of the name *maṇḍala*.
[Commentary]: Regarding the term "maṇḍala" and so forth: *maṇḍala* refers to the place where the true merits of all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas are gathered and accumulated;
thus it is given this name. As for "the wheel being circular with spokes converging," this is used as a metaphor to clarify the *dharmacakra*.
"Circular" (*yuan*) means complete, because its characteristics—the hub, spokes, rim, and so on—are fully perfected. "Spokes converging" (*fu cong*) means returning and meeting together.
It is also said that the many spokes converge at the hub. Laozi says: "Thirty spokes share one hub;
it is in the emptiness [of the hub] that the utility of the chariot lies. The commentary states: "In antiquity, thirty spokes were used to correspond to the number of days in a month.

'Sharing one hub' means that because there is an empty space within, the many spokes all converge there. This is a metaphor for one who governs the self: by eliminating emotions and discarding desires..."
When the five viscera are empty and void, the spirit returns to them; likewise, a ruler of a state rarely succeeds in governing the multitude, supporting the weak, and maintaining the strong.
Now, let us employ this as a metaphor for this three-layered Maṇḍala, the gateway to the Dharma-realm:

there is nowhere that does not converge upon the Great Sun Mind-King, so that all sentient beings of the three vehicles and five natures may universally advance through the universal gate and all converge within the central womb of the great emptiness.
Because it is the place where all converge like the spokes of a wheel, it is called "wheel-round" (*cakra-vāla*).

[Commentary: As for the phrase "one who aspires to learning" (*śikṣamāṇa*) and so forth, this means that when a practitioner attains even a single dharma within the maṇḍala, they have universally entered all gates of *dhāraṇī*.
Since this is so, does it not contradict the previous passage regarding the introduction into the *dharmadhātu*?
Each of the assemblies of virtuous friends has attained mastery in a single dharma-gate to its boundless limits, yet they do not know one another.

The previous section concerned gradual cultivation, whereas this concerns sudden enlightenment. Furthermore, while the former represents sequential progression (*xingbu*), this text represents perfect realization (*yuanzheng*).
Alternatively, each of the aforementioned treasuries of virtues reaches the ultimate, peerless, and unsurpassed flavor, such that they do not know one another. This means:

Each pervades the entire dharma-realm; now, this text is like seeing a king through a single door—it is precisely the same as entering a thousand doors and ten thousand windows, all equally pervading the dharma-realm.

Furthermore, previously it was based on different gates, and thus they did not know one another; here, it is based on the current gate, whereby they are able to see one another, and therefore there is no contradiction.

[Commentary: Although the Ācārya may not [be permitted to] bestow it upon those with impaired faculties or grant it erroneously—this being a concessive-cum-restrictive explanation establishing the intent of the full-branch initiation that establishes a karmic connection (pratilambha)—if one performs the full-branch initiation, one must not bestow it erroneously upon those with impaired faculties. However, regarding the establishment of a karmic connection, there is no prohibition against directing the mind toward a broad distribution;

therefore, first conceding this point, it says: "Although the Ācārya may not bestow it upon those with impaired faculties or grant it erroneously, for the sake of performing the full-branch initiation..."
The crown jewel is like exquisite food and drink that cannot be placed in a foul vessel; the sublime bliss of a Wheel-Turning King cannot be bestowed upon one of meager merit.
Therefore, the Commentary states: "How could the analogies of the tied jewel and the poisoned drum be exhausted?
'How' (qǐ) means 'it cannot'; 'exhausted' (yǐ) means 'to cease. It cannot be ceased or set aside. Regarding the "tied jewel," this refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
It is said, for example, that there was a man who went to the house of a close friend and lay down after becoming intoxicated by wine;
even though a priceless jewel had been tied inside his garment, while he lay drunk he was entirely unaware of it, yet upon waking he would surely obtain its benefit.
The story of the drum of poison in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* has already been cited as before.
[Commentary: Furthermore, the phrase "in contrast to the two vehicles" (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) serves to manifest the superior efficacy of this precept. Thus, the first commentary states:
"For instance, the pure precepts of a *śrāvaka* must arise only when the conditions of the fourfold formal motion (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) and the assembly are fully satisfied;

moreover, they must be guarded through skillful means as if defending against a sharp blade, such that when the span of one lifetime ends, the precepts also perish along with it. This precept is not like that; it persists from lifetime to lifetime."
"In the place of birth, it is always co-existent and not subject to limitation.
[Commentary] "Partaking of your ambrosia of immortality" refers to the nectar of the heavens; if a person drinks it, they immediately attain the ambrosia of immortality.
In secular classics, it is called "exquisite dew. It is the essence of spiritual numinosity and the moistening grace of benevolent auspiciousness.
It is as solid as fat and as sweet as molasses; it is called "sweet dew" (ganlu) and also "celestial wine" (tianjiu). The *Lidoushewei* states:
"When a sovereign rules by virtue of the Earth element and his governance is in a state of great peace, sweet dew descends. Furthermore, the *He guanzi* says:
"When the virtue of the sage reaches the heavens and the Great Clarity, the earth and the Great Tranquility, and the human spirit and the myriad spirits, then sweet dew descends."

This is a metaphor; the "Dharma-king" mentioned refers to the Dharma-medicine. It means that once one has received the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) of the mantra, one attains the five kinds of wisdom of the Tathāgata and never regresses;
this is called "immortality. Alternatively, it refers to the empowerment by the water of the Vajra-wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Just as when one is sprinkled with ambrosia (*amṛta*)," and so forth.
This is correct. [Commentary:
Regarding "Udumbara" and so forth: *udumbarapāla* is the *hehun* tree; *aśvattha* is the *mulu* tree.
Generally, what is called the *tuo-luo* tree is simply the solitary-growing *mulu*. As for the "silkwood and *gu* trees," these are two types of wood.
As has already been explained above.
[Commentary: The ten kinds of skillful means regarding the training precepts refer to the Bodhisattva’s ten inexhaustible precepts, such as non-killing, non-stealing, and so forth;

these are what are included here under the category of "skillful means training precepts. Regarding the phrase "unimpeded throughout the three periods of time," it means that all Buddhas of the three periods of time have all attained [enlightenment] by means of this.
Because one attains bodhi by means of the Path, it is named as such. It is permitted for all those who have established a karmic connection to hear this;
thus it is said. Regarding the statement "planting the four roots," this phrasing appears inverted; it refers to the four kinds of grave precepts. As that verse says:
"O Son of the Buddha, from this day forward, even at the cost of your body and life, you must never abandon the Dharma (1); you must never abandon the bodhicitta (2)..."
(3) Stinginess regarding all dharmas; (4) conduct that does not benefit sentient beings. Regarding the single verse on speech and the *samaya*, the verse says:
"The Buddha taught the *samaya*: 'O you who dwell well in the precepts, protect the *samaya* just as you would protect your own life.
This verse may only be heard by those who have received the *caturtha-abhiṣeka* (the fourth empowerment); furthermore, it must be whispered to them as an instruction and not [disclosed otherwise].
Bystanders heard this.
[Commentary] Regarding the "Great Self" (mahātman) as referring to the Tathāgatas and others, the twenty-third fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Because Nirvāṇa is the great sovereign (*mahaiśvarya*), it is called the Great Self. What is meant by "great sovereignty"? There are eight [aspects].
Mastery is what is called the "Self. What are its eight aspects? First, being able to manifest a single body as many bodies and so forth is called the Great Self;
second, manifesting a body the size of a single atom to fill the trichiliocosm and so forth is called the Great Self;
third, being able to make a body that fills this trichiliocosm light...
First, because it encompasses the *ākāśagati* (soaring through space) and so forth, it is called the Great Self (*mahātman*). Fourth, because it possesses mastery, it attains sovereignty;
even while abiding eternally in a single land, it causes all other lands to be seen therein, and for such reasons, it is called the Great Self.
Fifth, because its faculties possess mastery, even a single faculty of the Tathāgata can see forms, hear sounds, and so forth; therefore, it is called the Great [Self].
Sixth, because of mastery, one attains the Tathāgata-mind regarding all dharmas; yet, because there is no conceptualization of attainment and so forth, it is called the "Great Self.
Seventh, because of mastery in teaching, when the Tathāgata explains the meaning of a single verse, that meaning remains inexhaustible even after passing through immeasurable kalpas;
thus, it is called the "Great Self. Eighth, the Tathāgata pervades all things...
Abiding like empty space, because the nature of empty space cannot be perceived and so forth, it is called the "Great Self" (Mahātman).
Such a Great Self is named Great Nirvāṇa.
[Commentary] Regarding "accomplishing the great task," etc., this refers to what the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, rely solely upon one Great..."
Regarding the statement that [the Buddha] appears in the world for the sake of a great causal event (*mahā-kṛtya-hetu-pratyaya*):

those who understand the intended meaning of these words will see that the Lotus Sūtra’s "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" into the Buddha's knowledge and vision is what is called the one great causal event; since this sūtra now accords with that intent, it is said to "accomplish the great task."

[Commentary: "Arising apart from conditions, karma, and birth" means that while arising occurs apart from the conditioning of causes and the activity of volitional construction, all sentient beings—with the exception of those of the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas—do not transcend these.

Furthermore, although those of the Two Vehicles contemplate this emptiness, they only realize the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and have not yet attained the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Thus, while they may be said to be "arising apart from conditions, karma, and birth," they are as yet not called "arising through Great Emptiness" (*mahā-śūnyatā*). Bodhisattvas, however, are so named.
Because the Bodhisattva fully realizes the two kinds of emptiness and is thus named "Born from Great Emptiness," it is said that he is "free from conditions, karma, birth, and so forth.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "proclaiming the vajra-words and so forth": this means that after the ācārya has made offerings with various incenses, flowers, lamps, and ointments, he further praises and extols the deities with vajra-verses. As for these "vajra-word verses," they are to be understood according to the following:
The *Saptama-parivarta-sūtra-pūjā-vidhi* states: "Furthermore, by means of the sublime chanting of the Vajradhara, one should make offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
thus one shall swiftly attain accomplishment. It then recites the *Ariṣa-gāthā* of Vajrapāṇi as follows:
"Peerless and immovable, the equal and firm Dharma, out of compassion for those wandering in saṃsāra, it dispels all suffering and affliction."
"Reaching the state of non-defilement in all realms of existence, without reliance upon the triple world"—this praise consists of ten verses known as the *Vajragīti*.
As for the subsequent ritual dismissal according to the Dharma, it says: "Next, one should address the assembly of noble ones and recite these verses:
'All Tathāgatas present before me, Bodhisattvas who save the world, you who do not sever the Mahāyāna teachings and have attained the most excellent station.'"
I only pray that the assembly of noble devas will definitively bear witness to me; each shall follow their own place of rest, and hereafter, may you again deign to come out of compassion.

[Commentary] Regarding "banner" (dhvaja), it refers to flags, streamers, and the like. As for the etymological explanation: "banner" (幢) means "child" (童); "child" (童) means "solitary" (獨). Its appearance is "tong-tong" (dense and upright).
This refers to what is called "emerging alone from within the army. As for the *qi* (banner), it means "an appointment" (*qi*), signifying that one makes an appointment with the multitude below.
Now, regarding the term *kuo-zhi* (canopy-banner), it means that the canopy-banner is added to further adorn and embellish it. Therefore, the fifth section of the sub-commentary states:
"Atop every banner-pole, a crescent moon is placed; beneath the moon, the canopy-banner is positioned. Its form is made by cutting fine silk into a perfect square."

The corners are broken away to form two banners, each attached to the exterior of the flagpole; they are sharp at the top and hang downward, with wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi*) placed upon them, hence they are called "Jewel Banners" (*ratnadhvaja*).
Regarding the phrase "to direct the multitude," "direct" (*hui*) means to beckon, and "guide" (*dao*) means to lead;
it signifies that when the army is beckoned and guided, there are none who do not obey the command.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "or like Ghoṣila," the term "or" indicates that it is not fixed; this refers to what is taught in the *Vajraśekhara Recitation Method* concerning the inverted states experienced by disciples in dreams.
One should take the five kinds of cow products, mix them together, and sprinkle them with purified water.

Then, having empowered them twenty-one times with the Vajra Secret Mantra, one gives them to the disciple to consume. It continues until it says: "This shall cause their [defilements] to be perfected and their calamities pacified."
They may be summoned immediately.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the Great Mind is as previously stated," this refers to what was said in the commentary on the first fascicle: "The mind of this person is capable of performing great deeds...
and will surely be able to preach the Dharma to shatter the great false views, the great craving, and the great ignorance of all sentient beings."
Because my mind is equal to all afflictions, it is called the "Great Mind.

[Commentary] "At that time, all... and so forth means that because one knows, as they truly are, that the aggregates and the ālayavijñāna are fundamentally unarisen, there is no grasping or concealing with regard to any phenomena. At that time, all mental discrimination and volition...

Because such false discriminations as the cognition of measures (*pramāṇa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) no longer function, it is called "pure," which means being free from all false discriminations.

[Commentary]: These two phrases, "long since free" and "concise," are explained as follows: "free" (*jian*) refers to what is to be excluded; "concise" (*lüe*) refers to being brief and abbreviated; "long since" (*jiu*) refers to the duration.
The two characters "li" (離) should be "wen" (文); as the character forms are similar, many old editions contain the cursive script, which I suspect is an error made by the scribe. [Commentary:
This also serves to clarify further the meaning of the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). The preceding verse stated: "You are now able to aspire to become [a Buddha]."
Just as the Tathāgata has already received the prediction of great bodhi, this passage now further states that "this vehicle is supreme" and "you should abide in this path";
thus, it is said to be a reiteration of the meaning of the prediction.

[Commentary]: As for the Buddha’s teaching for the śrāvakas and others, this refers to the brief exposition of the precepts given to the *anavasthāpika-saṃgha* (the community free from formal legal procedures) during the twelve years [following his enlightenment].
The cited text is insufficient; if one were to cite it in full, the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* states: "Guard well your speech, purify your mental intent, and let no evil be done by the body.
When these three paths of action are pure, one is able to attain such practice as this. This is the Great [Vehicle].
From the Path of the Rishis up to the extensive precepts established twelve years later, all were intended to purify the faults and afflictions of the three karmas;
this Brahma-vinaya is likewise so, for even down to the precepts as numerous as dust motes and sands, all these wholesome dharmas serve to purify the three karmas and accomplish the three mysteries.
[Commentary]: "The warp and woof mutually complete one another" means that the vertical is called the warp (*jīng*) and the horizontal is called the woof (*wèi*);
they are mutually possessed. It is like a *śāra* brocade, which is accomplished through the interlacing of warp and woof both horizontally and vertically; the net of views is likewise so.

Because the various views of frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*) are layered and interlaced, weaving them together into a whole, it is said that "the warp and woof mutually complete one another. Furthermore, the character *xiàng* (相) here is pronounced in the departing tone (*qùshēng*).
To read "xiang" (相) as "assistance" is like the way one regulates heaven and earth, assists the state, and helps the people; thus it is called "mutually completing.
This is just as when we commonly speak of "jingxiang" (經相), which refers to this very meaning.
[Commentary: Regarding "such as the precepts of the fifth category," it means that there are five categories of offenses:
first, *pārājika*, which in the Hīnayāna is called "unremitting" and in the Mahāyāna is called "defeat"; second, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, translated here as "residual" (*zhòngcán`);
third, *pāyattika*, translated here as "falling" (*duò`); fourth, *pratideśanīya*, translated here as "to be censured" (*kěhē`); and fifth, *duṣkṛta*, translated here as...

The fifth *duṣkṛta* offense is now to be discussed. The *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*, specifically the *Vinaya-vastu* (Section on Discipline), states that within this *Vinaya-piṭaka*, all rules concerning the methods of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*) are included;

should there be any deficiency in these, the offense is formally adjudicated within this fifth section on *duṣkṛta*. Therefore, all transgressions of the law are subsumed under this section. The application of the law is easy to understand.
[Commentary: What is called the "unequaled bodhicitta" refers to the ācārya visualizing himself as Vajradhara through the practice of Vajrasattva;
thus, his own mind becomes identical to the mind of Vajrasattva.
This mind of Vajrasattva is precisely the unequaled bodhicitta. As for the term "unequaled," it refers to ordinary beings (pṛthagjana).
Because the two vehicles cannot equal it, it is called "unequaled" (*asama*); now, because the mind of the Ācārya is equal to that [Buddhahood], it is called "equal to the unequaled" (*asamasama*).
Furthermore, the Commentary states: "Among all phenomena, there is nothing with which it can be compared, hence it is called 'unequaled';
nor is there anything superior to it, hence it is called 'equal to the unequaled. Therefore, it is said: 'The so-called bodhicitta is equal to the unequaled.'"

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "all should follow the sequence of offerings," this means that the seventh fascicle of this scripture in seven fascicles contains the ritual procedures for performing offerings within the sixth fascicle; therefore, the commentary does not explain it here, as it refers back to that section.
As for the statement "expelling and removing defilements," one should use the mantra of the Vidyārāja Acala (Amoghasiddhi) to remove defilements, and the same applies to expelling them.
That verse says: "Next, one should offer flowers, incense, and so forth; remove impurities by revealing the Lord Acala; perform the ritual of warding off defilements in this manner;
consecrate [the offerings] with the King of Mantras; and declare them pure by means of the syllable of the Dharmadhātu-citta.
Having performed the purification with mantras as described above, if it is still not yet called "truly pure," one should further purify it with the syllable of the Dharmadhātu-citta.
This is called the Vase of Ultimate Purity. That verse says: "The letter *ra* is brilliant white, adorned with the nasal dot (*bindu*);
like a bright jewel in a topknot, it is placed upon the crown. The mantra is: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ raṃ*.
This mantra is identical to the Dharmadhātu; it eliminates immeasurable multitudes of sins and removes all defilements of contact.
"In the respective places, one should add this *dhāraṇī* gate, etc.
[Commentary]: "In this sutra, 'generally used' refers to the *mantras* for empowering all essential matters and accomplishing all tasks;
these are the *Vajrahūṃkāra* (Trailokyavijaya) mantras. Regarding the statement that they are both extensive and abbreviated: the extensive version consists of six phrases."
"Brief" refers to a single phrase.
[The Commentary] states that "the syllable *vaṃ* and so forth" means that this syllable *vaṃ* corresponds to the second water-wheel (*ap-maṇḍala*) among the five wheels;
therefore, it is selected here.
[Commentary: Regarding the "threefold transformation of the pure land": this refers to the time when the *Lotus Sūtra* was preached on Vulture Peak.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions, having been illumined by the light [of Śākyamuni], each addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:

"I shall now go to the Sahā world to the place of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, and together offer worship to the stupa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha. At that moment, the Sahā world was transformed into purity, with lapis lazuli forming its ground.
Furthermore, although Śākyamuni had transformed this land, he feared that it would be difficult for the Buddhas who had come from the ten directions to be accommodated;

therefore, in order to accommodate the various Buddhas who were his emanations, he further transformed two million billion nayutas of lands in each of the eight directions, making them all pure and free from the three evil realms as well as the asuras. At that time, Śākyamuni...
