Because the Muni Buddha intended for all Buddhas to sit there in the future, he further transformed two million billion nayutas of lands in each of the eight directions—just as before—so that they were likewise free from the three evil realms and other such states; therefore, this is called the "Third Transformation."

[Sūtra]: Starting from the east as the beginning and ending at the north, the teacher stands facing southeast, northwest, northeast, or southwest, while the assistant stands facing northeast, southwest, northwest, or southeast.
Holding the cord level with the navel, they measure by circling once to the right.
Having finished, it is said again: "Secondly, establish the boundaries," and they circle again through the cardinal directions; this is the measurement of the exterior.
The sequence for the rotation of the mandala boundaries between preceptor and disciple is as before;

however, regarding the two terms "right" (dakṣiṇa) and "rear" (paścima) in the sūtra, they follow the secular convention of Western India, which faces east when establishing directions: the east is the first direction, the south is the right, the west is the rear, and the north is the superior direction.
The sūtra states that the ācārya turns next because the preceptor was previously in the northwest, and now [the ācārya] performs the binding of the corners.
Because of the measurement, one turns to the right from this point toward the southwest; thus the Sūtra says, "relying on Nairṛti.
Although the disciple was originally in the northeast, he merely turns his face to face the preceptor, which is why it is said that "he receives and maintains the instruction.

Once the maintenance is complete, the disciple returns by turning to the right toward the northwest; therefore it is said that "he shifts his reliance to the direction of Vāyu. As for the preceptor, he was originally... [in the southeast].
Turning clockwise from the southwest to the southeast, one thus dwells in the direction of fire. Next, the *Sūtra on Measuring with the String* states:
"Furthermore, practice this method: the assistant first stands in the south and proceeds clockwise to the southwest;
the master first stands in the southeast and proceeds clockwise to the northeast. Therefore, the sūtra says: "The disciple is in the southwest."

The Master resides in the Īśānī [northeast] corner; his attendants proceed from the southwest, circling clockwise to the southeast, while the Master proceeds from the northeast, circling clockwise to the northwest.
Thus it is said that the disciples rely on the direction of fire, while the Master occupies the direction of wind.
This concludes the delineation of the boundary paths for the four sides and four corners.
[Commentary]: "The place where the mind of the five kinds of jewel-heaps is situated" refers to the center of the maṇḍala.

This means that after the initial preparation of the ground is completed, one determines the spatial divisions; then, having dug a pit at the center of the maṇḍala approximately one cubit deep, one empowers the five jewels with the *karmakara-mantra* (action-attaining mantra) and places them therein.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "from Mahāvairocana Tathāgata," etc., whereas the preceding was the external maṇḍala, this is now the internal mind maṇḍala.
Generally, even when performing external rites, one must contemplate the internal mind; this is the intended meaning of yoga in this scripture. Let students reflect upon this.
[Commentary: Regarding "Ācārya, he transcends it"—the three characters "this transcends it" (*ci yue zhi yue*) should be omitted. [Commentary:

Regarding "The gates all face west, each having its own causal conditions"—this means that this maṇḍala facing west is a great assembly point for the various causal conditions for generating the bodhicitta; the intention is to have the practitioner enter facing east.
The directions are also called "initial directions" because they symbolize the initial arousal of the bodhicitta; thus it is said that the general gate faces west, and so forth.
Alternatively, for the four purposes of pacifying, increasing, magnetizing, and subjugating, one may open gates according to the respective directions as one sees fit.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "these sixteen dharmas" and so forth, it refers to the four wisdoms, the four practices, and the eight kinds of spiritual friends, each holding the seal of adamantine wisdom (*vajrajñānamudrā*);

thus, they constitute the sixteen dharmas. As for the characteristics of these eight kinds of adamantine wisdom seals, they will be explained correctly below in the chapter on the "Eight Secret Seals."
[Commentary: "The filaments and anthers are all... refers to all the filaments and anthers among the petals of the lotus;

these represent all the samādhis and so forth, which signify the merits realized internally by the Tathāgata. These are contained within the three layers of body-seals (kāyamudrā) amidst the lotus petals, for there is nothing that does not flow forth from them. The names and numbers of the samādhi-dhāraṇī gates are immeasurable.
Regarding the eighteen kinds of emptiness: first is internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), which refers to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Because these six sense bases are all produced from conditions, they are not solid and lack a real self or phenomena; therefore, they are called empty.

External emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) refers to form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects (*dharmas*). These arise from various causes and conditions and possess no solidity or substance, as they perish due to causes and conditions.
Therefore, because form and the other aggregates also cease, they are called "empty. Regarding "internal and external emptiness" (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*):

it means that the six internal bases of the sense organs and the six external bases of sense objects all arise from conditions; because their causes and conditions do not exist, internal and external phenomena are empty.

Because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are called "empty. Furthermore, it is said that these various phenomena cause sentient beings to become deluded, inverted, and attached to the six internal sense faculties.

Therefore, when the practitioner destroys these inversions, it is called internal emptiness, external emptiness, and internal-and-external emptiness; it is likewise with the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
First, one uses the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) to destroy internal and external phenomena; then, one uses this [emptiness of] emptiness to destroy the preceding emptiness.
It is just as taking medicine that can eliminate a disease: once the disease has been eliminated, the medicine should also be expelled. If the medicine is not expelled, then it will in turn...

This illness [of conceptualization] is extinguished by means of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Fearing that emptiness itself might again become a source of affliction, one abandons emptiness by means of emptiness; this is called "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).

As for "great emptiness" (*mahā-śūnyatā*), it refers to the fact that the ten directions—namely, east, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, above, and below—are empty of their own characteristics;
this is great emptiness. Question: Why is the emptiness of the ten directions called "great emptiness"? Answer: Because in the eastern direction there is no... [eastern direction].

Because it is at the limit, it is called "great"; and because it pervades all that exists as form, it is called "great," and so forth. Regarding "emptiness of the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*):
within all phenomena, the "ultimate" is precisely *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, the "ultimate truth" is named the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, for it is neither broken nor destroyed;
and since this true reality of all phenomena is also empty, there is the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
The emptiness of the conditioned refers to the three realms, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and so forth; it is empty because there are two reasons:
first, because the self and what belongs to the self, as well as the characteristic of permanence and the characteristic of immutability, are unattainable;
second, because conditioned phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions and thus lack intrinsic nature. The emptiness of the unconditioned refers to that which does not depend on...
Because they arise through causes and conditions, they are unarisen, non-abiding, non-differentiated, and non-ceasing; being like space, they are called "empty.
Ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) refers to the destruction of all phenomena such that not even a single phenomenon remains that is not empty; this is called ultimate emptiness.
For example, an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted is called ultimately pure throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.

Because not a single dharma within it can be found to exist as a fixed reality, it is called "ultimate emptiness" (*atyanta-śūnyatā*); if even the slightest remnant remained, it would not be called ultimate emptiness.
Regarding "emptiness without beginning" (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*), this means that whether it be the world, sentient beings, or phenomena, none have a beginning.
Just as this present life arises from causes and conditions of a previous life, and that previous life in turn arose from what preceded it, so they continue to revolve in succession without end.
The same applies to the beginning of sentient beings and their phenomena. A question is asked: "Since 'beginninglessness' is the reality, it should not be refuted. Why?
If sentient beings and phenomena had a beginning, one would fall into the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) and also fall into the view of causelessness (ahetuvāda).

Now, if one uses emptiness to refute beginninglessness, one falls back into the view of a beginning. The answer is: "Now, by means of the emptiness of beginninglessness (anādibhava-śūnyatā), one refutes the view of beginninglessness."

Furthermore, one should not fall into the view that there is a beginning; just as when rescuing someone from fire, one should not cause them to sink into deep water, so too, having refuted this notion of no beginning, one should not cling to the existence of a beginning—this is practicing the Middle Way. Now, using the absence of a beginning to refute the existence of a beginning, the "absence of a beginning" itself becomes a source of affliction;
thus, one further uses the emptiness of the absence of a beginning to refute that very absence of a beginning. This is called "non-existence."

Regarding initial emptiness and the emptiness of dispersion (*vibhava-śūnyatā*): "dispersion" refers to the characteristic of separation, just as in the world a chariot is formed by the combination of many parts—the spokes, the rim, the shaft, and the hub—and when these are separated and dispersed, it is no longer called a chariot. The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are likewise:
because they are combined through causes and conditions, they are called a "person. If they are separated, the person cannot be found. If this is so, one should only refute the person.

[The opponent] asks: "Is form not destroyed? [The respondent] replies: "Form and the others are likewise destroyed. Why? Because form is a provisional designation based on the aggregation of atoms and dependent upon various causes and conditions;
when these are dispersed, there is no form. Question: "While it may be so for the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), how can the other four aggregates be said to be dispersed?
Answer: "The four aggregates are likewise provisional designations. They are to be observed through [the marks of] birth, aging, duration, and impermanence."

Therefore, when analyzed, they are of the nature of emptiness. "Emptiness of nature" (prakṛti-śūnyatā) means that the nature of all phenomena is eternally empty. There are two types of emptiness of nature:
first, general nature, which refers to [the characteristics of] impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, non-arising, non-ceasing, non-going, and non-coming;
second, specific nature, such as the hot nature of fire, the moist nature of water, and the cognitive nature of the mind. All such natures are...

Because emptiness is unapprehendable, it is called "emptiness of nature" (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Regarding "emptiness of self-characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*): it means that all phenomena have two types of characteristics:

first, general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), such as impermanence and so forth; second, specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), such as solidity being the characteristic of earth, heat being the characteristic of fire, and so forth.

Question: Since "nature" (*svabhāva*) has already been explained, what is now being explained is its "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*). What is the difference between nature and characteristic? Answer: Some say:

In fact, there is no difference; it is said that "nature" (svabhāva) and "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) differ slightly. "Nature" refers to its essence, while "characteristic" refers to what can be perceived.
For example, for a son of the Śākya [a Buddhist], observing the prohibitive precepts is his nature, whereas shaving the head and wearing dyed robes are his characteristics.

If this is so, why not speak only of the emptiness of characteristics rather than the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics? The commentary states: If one speaks of the emptiness of characteristics, one does not speak of the emptiness of the dharma-essence.

If one speaks of emptiness as the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), it means that even the substance of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*) is empty; because this is explained in terms of their characteristics, it is called "emptiness of intrinsic characteristics.

As for the "emptiness of all phenomena" (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), it refers to the inclusion—according to their respective categories—of the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, material and immaterial phenomena, tainted and untainted phenomena, internal and external phenomena, existent and non-existent phenomena, and so forth.

"All dharmas are dharmas; all are empty. Question: Previously, you spoke of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), and so forth, which already exhausted all dharmas.

What is the difference between this current statement that "all dharmas are empty" and what was said before? Answer: There is a distinction based on the intended meaning, and thus it differs from what preceded.
Here, we say that because no fixed characteristic can be apprehended in any dharma, they are called "empty," just as [the term "gold"] is applied to gold, silver, or copper [depending on context].
When [water] meets with the conditions of fire, it immediately abandons its own characteristic and transforms into the characteristic of water;

just as when water encounters cold it becomes ice and transforms into the characteristic of earth, so too does wisdom, which has the characteristic of knowing, enter into the true characteristic (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and thus has nothing to perceive.
It abandons its own characteristic of knowing through such various [transformations] where no fixed characteristic exists; if there were a fixed characteristic, [it would not be so].
It can be said that they are not empty [in the sense of being non-existent], because all phenomena lack fixed characteristics; therefore, it is said that all phenomena are empty.
"The emptiness of the unobtainable" means that all phenomena truly do not exist and cannot be apprehended. As the Buddha himself said:

"From my first generation of the mind of awakening until my attainment of Buddhahood, as well as for the Buddhas of the ten directions, when seeking reality among all phenomena, nothing can be apprehended. This is called the [emptiness of the unobtainable].

Furthermore, because the practitioner attains this emptiness, they find that the three poisons, the five hindrances, the various entanglements, and even the ten unwholesome fetters are all utterly unobtainable;
therefore, it is called the "emptiness of the unobtainable" (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).

By practicing this path, the practitioner attains the dharmas of merit, including the morality, concentration, and wisdom of the four fruits, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and even the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Question: Previously it was stated that all dharmas are unattainable; why then is it now said that they are attained? Answer:
Although these dharmas are attained, they all assist the emptiness of unattainability and are therefore also called "emptiness of the unattainable.
Although the noble ones attain various merits, such as entering nirvāṇa, they do not regard them as attainments; whereas ordinary people regard them as attainments. It is like a lion.

When one performs an action and does not consider it marvelous, while other sentient beings view it as rare and extraordinary—this refers to the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of existence (*bhāva-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of both non-existence and existence (*abhāva-bhāva-śūnyatā*).

Regarding "emptiness of non-existence": that which is called "non-existent" refers to phenomena that have already ceased; because this cessation is a state of non-being, it is called the emptiness of non-existence.
Regarding "emptiness of existence": all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; therefore, although they exist, their inherent nature (*svabhāva*) is empty.

Because they do not exist, there is the emptiness of existing dharmas (*bhāva-śūnyatā*); because the marks of non-existing dharmas and existing dharmas cannot be apprehended, this is the emptiness of non-existing and existing dharmas (*abhāva-bhāva-śūnyatā*).

Furthermore, it is said that past and future dharmas are empty; this is called the emptiness of non-existing dharmas (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), while present and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas are empty;
this is called the emptiness of existing dharmas (*bhāva-śūnyatā*). If [one considers] past and future dharmas and...
Because present unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are empty of both, it is called the "emptiness of non-existence and existence" (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

Furthermore, it is said that because unconditioned phenomena lack arising, abiding, and ceasing, this is called the "emptiness of existence. Such forms of emptiness are termed the "emptiness of non-existence and existence," and so forth. (etc.)

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "The Tathāgata’s Lion-like Display" to "the causal conditions," it means that when the Tathāgata sat at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, he subdued the four Māras with his great majesty and ferocity and attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment. However, this was solely for the purpose of revealing, causing others to awaken to, and leading them into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
This "Buddha’s knowledge and vision" is precisely the seal of universal omniscience; therefore, it is called "The Tathāgata’s Lion... [and so forth].
"Vīryavega and others.
[Commentary] Regarding the meaning of "Mother of Buddhas," as stated in the "Chapter on the Mother of Buddhas" (*Buddhamātṛ-parivarta*) of the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, that chapter says:
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "As the World-Honored One has taught, this Prajñāpāramitā can give birth to all Buddhas and can reveal the characteristics of the world."
“World-Honored One, how is it that the Prajñāpāramitā can give birth to all Buddhas? How can it reveal the characteristics of the world?
How are all Buddhas born from the Prajñāpāramitā? And how do all Buddhas speak of the characteristics of the world?
The Buddha told Subhūti: “Within this profound Prajñāpāramitā are born the ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-buddhadharma).”
Because Subhūti has attained these dharmas—the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) and the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā)—he is called a Buddha, and so forth.
Furthermore, the seventh fascicle of the Treatise states: The Buddha told Subhūti, "The Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas;
they abide by relying upon this Dharma. ... [omission] ... Why is this? It is because this Prajñā gives birth to all Buddhas, and so forth.
[Commentary]: From "the phrase of ultimate purity" to "to serve as clothing," this means that this Honored One uses the phrases of the *mantra* of ultimate purity as an external adornment;
"adornment" (*vyūha*) refers to embellishment. As for the "phrases of the *mantra*," it is the character *yan* (嚴) from the "Universal Treasury of *Mantras*" section below.
"Adornment" (*yan*) refers to the fundamental essence, which is the character *yang* (仰). "Yang" signifies the meaning of Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), which is precisely the Truth (*tattva*).

The gold is the essence of the *tathatā* (suchness) as it truly is; furthermore, by adding a nasal dot (*bindu*) above the character "仰" (*yǎng*), its pronunciation shifts to the character "嚴" (*yán*). This nasal dot is free from all marks and is purely white;
because it serves as an external ornament according to that teaching, it is said to be "white silk" (*gǎosuò*) used as clothing.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "such as the wheel of letters below," this refers to the Wheel of Letters chapter, which describes five types of wheels that encompass all syllables. Specifically, the first wheel is the Wheel of Bodhicitta.
Within this wheel, all consonants—*ka*, *kha*, and so forth—are arranged clockwise, and at the center of the wheel is placed the short vowel *a*. *Asvāh*.

From the three syllables up to the fifth wheel of skillful means (*upāya-cakra*), one arranges all the phonemes—such as the long vowels, the feet (*pāda*), and the voids (*śūnya*)—as previously described.
One places the three syllables *a*, *so*, and *va* with long vowels at the center.
By means of these five sets of three syllables, one governs the five wheels of syllables, making them pure white and distinct so that no confusion occurs; therefore, it is said "as follows."
"Letter-wheel, etc. [Commentary]:
Regarding "garments and insignia," "garments" refers to necklaces and other ornaments that adorn the body; "insignia" refers to the forms of celestial maidens and so forth.
These all symbolize the gestation of various merits. Therefore, they are established as the clarity and sovereignty of Bodhi.
The meaning of the seed-syllable of the Vidyārājñī as containing and giving birth [to all things] is entirely consistent with this.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "from this most pure," it means that this samādhi of the Pure Abode is called the Lotus Family (*padmakula*);
from this, the Universal Eye (*samantacakṣus*) is born. As for the Universal Eye, this refers to all Avalokiteśvaras; that is to say, it refers to the arousal of the bodhicitta by Avalokiteśvara.
Because of this contemplation, it is precisely this [state] that is intended.

[Commentary: "All of them encompass both provisional and real functions" means that, for example, like a diamond (*vajra*), its nature is both firm and sharp. "Firm" means that no object can destroy it; this is the "real.
"Sharp" means that it can crush other objects; this is the "provisional. This refers to the fundamental basis for both self-benefit and benefiting others, which follows [the preceding discussion].
Because its wondrous function is attained, it is said to encompass both the provisional and the real functions.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "this gives birth to the Vajra, etc.": this means that while the Lord of the preceding section is wisdom (*prajñā*), these three samādhis are meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Since wisdom arises based upon them, they are called the "Mother."

[Commentary: As for the passage "even a single body possessing hundreds of thousands of hands," this refers to the Thousand-Armed and Thousand-Eyed [Avalokiteśvara], those with forty-two arms, sixteen arms, down to eight arms, and the Blue-Necked One (*Nīlakaṇṭha*). All such figures are members of the Vajra Family (*Vajrakula*).
[Commentary]: Those who wish to destroy all sentient beings should know that all sentient beings rely solely upon ignorance (*avidyā*).

By destroying only ignorance, the cycle of saṃsāra will naturally cease. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "The ground of abiding ignorance is the root of all defilements and the cause of birth-and-death;

external false objects stir up the waves of consciousness, which are the conditions for birth-and-death. It is by relying on these two meanings [cause and condition] that [the cessation of suffering] is revealed.
Because the various consciousnesses arise and perish through the convergence of causes and conditions, they are called "sentient beings.
Now, this Vidyārāja, receiving the command of the Tathāgata, employs the power of wisdom to sever those causes and conditions; therefore, it is said that he intends to slay all sentient beings.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the lasso is within the bodhicitta," the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) are the dharma-lasso.
This is a metaphor for how Buddhas and Bodhisattvas gather in sentient beings through the four means of attraction without ever failing;

whereas worldly lassos used to capture wild beasts occasionally result in loss, they are thus used as a point of comparison. Furthermore, this lasso is also called "unfailing" (*amogha*) in the world.

When a noose (*pāśa*) is used to capture a beast, it may or may not strike its mark; however, the noose of the four means of attraction (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*) captures sentient beings without fail.
Thus, the preface to the *Amoghapāśa-sūtra* states: "When casting a noose to catch a beast, the rope is sometimes empty;
this teaching is never wavering and never misses its mark, hence it is called the 'Unfailing Noose' (*Amoghapāśa*)."

[Commentary: Therefore, regarding "holding the five-pronged [vajra]" and so forth: this five-pronged vajra mudrā symbolizes the wisdom-jewels of the five Tathāgatas, while the crown symbolizes the adornment of myriad virtues.
Previously, the *pāśa* (lasso) already manifested the non-empty; now this is likewise so. Thus, the commentary states:
"Because these are cleansed and extinguished by the five wisdoms, they all reach the stage of fruition, wherein the myriad virtues are fully adorned."
This solemnity does not merely certify the universal teaching of the Three Vehicles as being simply emptiness; it also expresses the principle of the Buddha-nature and the Middle Way.
[Commentary] Regarding the second point here, "is hidden," etc., it means that the retinue of Śākyamuni constitutes the third enclosure.

That is, it is actually located in the third outer enclosure; the reason it is here called "the second" is that after first establishing the first enclosure—the central matrix (garbha)—one then establishes the Śākyan retinue in the third enclosure from the outside, which is designated as "the second," not because it is the second enclosure.
As for the bodhisattvas who dwell between compassion and wisdom, seeking the higher while transforming those below:

The "Table" (piǎo) refers to that which is situated between the three assemblies, namely the second assembly. When it is now said that Śākyamuni is the second and [Maitreya] is the third bodhisattva, this is explained from the perspective of proceeding from the fruit back to the cause.
If one considers the sequential arrangement according to seeking the higher and transforming those below, he is designated as the second;
therefore, it is called a "cryptic expression" (*saṃdhābhāṣya*). There is a further explanation of this point below.
[Commentary]: Regarding "this white lotus flower" and so forth, the white lotus seat is precisely the womb-treasury of the Dharma-realm lotus within the first enclosure.
As that verse states: "The wondrous white lotus in the inner mind is a womb-treasury, perfectly symmetrical.

This is said to manifest the non-obstruction of the True and the Responsive, and the non-duality of the Expedient and the Real; thus, it is said that this white lotus flower is the pure Dharma of the central womb-treasury.
This is the *Dhātu-kośa* (Treasury of Elements).

[Commentary: Regarding the fact that it is explained at length in such sūtras as the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, those sūtras describe the contemplation of the Buddha’s *ūrṇā-lakṣaṇa* (the hair-treasure between the eyebrows) from the perspective of a newborn infant, his renunciation, his ascetic practices, and his subduing of Māra;
the *ūrṇā-lakṣaṇa* described therein is not the same as the *ūrṇā-lakṣaṇa* of one who has attained Buddhahood, which is what is being analyzed here.
The Sūtra says: The Buddha told his father, the King: "What is meant by 'the Bodhisattva subduing Māra'?

At that time, from the light of the ūrṇā-kośa (white tuft of hair between the eyebrows), Māra Pāpīyas, using his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), observed Jambudvīpa from afar. He saw the Lion of the Śākyas having abandoned his kingdom like spittle;
sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, his body and bones were withered and his frame was emaciated, yet he possessed a golden hue, and his sunken eyes were as black as wells."
The joints of his bones were visible like the stars at the bottom of a well, and the patterns of his skin were lost in their coiling folds. Pāpīyān rejoiced, saying, "Gautama’s body is emaciated;
his remaining life is short. It is fitting that we go to defeat him. With eyes wide with rage, he summoned various kinds of troops, desiring to destroy the Bodhisattva.

The Bodhisattva, however, directed the light from his white tuft of hair [toward them], causing the bodies and minds of Māra’s followers to become peaceful and blissful, just as a bhikṣu enters the third dhyāna.
The Dhyāna-māra then returned to the palace, and the White Tuft followed him all the way up to the Sixth Heaven.
During that interval, countless sons and daughters of the gods saw that the interior of the white pore was entirely empty, perfectly round and lovely like the banner of Brahmā;

within that space were lotus flowers made of various jewels, as numerous as the atoms of dust in hundreds of thousands of millions of Ganges Rivers, and each of these lotus flowers was without [defilement].
It has a pedestal made of boundless, exquisite white light; upon this pedestal is a manifested Bodhisattva who likewise emits white light from his ūrṇā-kośa (white tuft of hair).

Even after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if any member of the fourfold assembly can for even a moment abandon distraction and fix their mind in right contemplation upon the ūrṇā-mark of the Bodhisattva’s subduing of Māra, they shall extinguish the black karma of immeasurable kalpas.

Those with karmic obstacles who are able to see the image of the Buddha in the present life will, at that time, find the ground of the site of enlightenment transformed into what resembles vajra, filling eighty *li* and pure white in color, such that it cannot be fully beheld.

When this sign appears, the light from the white tuft (*ūrṇā-kośa*) between the Bodhisattva’s eyebrows is pure, clean, upright, and straight, pointing directly toward the east; it is one *zhang* and five *chi* in length and possesses ten rays.
Furthermore, the Buddha addressed the King, his father, and commanded Ānanda: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well!

Transmit these words to the disciples of future generations. If, after my parinirvāṇa, any bhikṣus should ask about this matter—namely, what practices the Bodhisattva originally cultivated to obtain this mark of the white tuft between the eyebrows—you should answer them: 'This is the white tuft mark of the Buddha.'"
From the time they cultivated a mind of renunciation free from stinginess throughout immeasurable kalpas, up until their attainment of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment,

the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and all other sublime merits, they have obtained this white tuft of hair between the eyebrows. After my parinirvāṇa, if the disciples of the Buddha abandon all evils,
leave behind the clamor of the world, delight in the dharma of few words, do not busy themselves with many affairs, and are able [to practice] during the six periods of day and night...

Within a single moment, one may divide it into small portions; within those small portions, one can for even a brief instant recollect the Buddha’s white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*), causing the mind to perceive it clearly and without delusive or confused thoughts, maintaining uninterrupted attention.

Those who thus recollect the white tuft—whether they see his physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) or do not see them—shall eliminate ninety-six billion *nayuta* of Ganges-sand particles of dust.
Regarding the sins of birth and death throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, the Commentary Master, in explaining the intent of this sutra,
points out that the Buddha’s ūrṇā-kośa (hair-treasure) is itself the maṇḍala-gate of the Dharma-realm. Therefore, if one enters this gate and beholds the central Womb-store (*garbha-kosa*),
it is equivalent to entering all gates of the Dharma-realm— just as seeing the king through a single door is equivalent to entering everywhere throughout the thousand [palaces].

Furthermore, the ten fascicles of the *Sūtra on the Sequential Contemplation of the Thirty-two Marks and Other Minor Characteristics of the Buddha*, which open up ten thousand gates, contain the secret and essential dhāraṇīs that emerge from the maṇḍala;
these are intended for those who have entered the gateway of the true dharma-realm to hear.
[Commentary: Regarding the "five kinds of Tathāgatas" and so forth, the fact that only four are listed among the five colors is an abbreviation;
furthermore, the red color is included within the three subsequent Buddha-uṣṇīṣas, as stated in the twelfth commentary, and it is fully present among the five Buddha-uṣṇīṣas.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "to investigate and interrogate from birth onwards": *jiǎn hé* (pronounced with the second tone on *hé*) means to pursue and examine a person regarding their offenses.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the Vinaya refers to observing the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) and so forth": this clarifies the robes worn by those residing in the five Pure Abodes.
It means that the three robes and the inner garment currently prescribed for Bhikṣus to wear are identical to those established by the precepts of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Unlike the five categories of precepts, which do not necessarily require uniformity in this regard, all Buddhas of the three periods of time are entirely identical in this matter.
Therefore, in the *Sāpoda-vinaya*, regarding the initial rules of the *saiksa* (training rules) concerning the uneven wearing of the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* by the group of six bhikṣus, it is asked:
"Within the five categories of precepts, why did the Buddha specifically regulate the manner of wearing the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*?"
Question: When a monk puts on the three robes (*tricīvara*), does he observe the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as the Śuddhāvāsa deities? Answer:
When the Buddha established the five categories of precepts (*pañcāpattinikāya*), he intended for them all to observe the Buddhas of the three periods of time and the Śuddhāvāsa deities.

Even in cases where this precept is lighter than others among the various categories, if future disciples were not to give rise to a sense of profound respect, the Tathāgata would have observed with his Buddha-eye [the consequences] regarding the past.
The Buddhas of the future and the Śuddhāvāsa devas have come to establish this seal so that sentient beings of future generations do not give rise to the sin of arrogance.
Because what is cited here is the essential point of the robes worn by those in the Pure Abodes, it is called *vinaya*, and so forth.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "all these great celestial deities and so forth," this serves as a general explanation to resolve potential objections. Specifically, it addresses the following difficulty:

since this second court maṇḍala consists of the retinue of Śākyamuni, and given that at the very beginning of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni’s attainment of enlightenment he subdued all Māras, non-Buddhists, and malevolent spirits and ghosts, why are they now listed as his retinue within the maṇḍala?
The *Yeshu* (Commentary on the Verses) provides its own explanation, which may be understood as follows.

[Commentary: "That which is able to employ the light of eternal quiescence"—"eternal quiescence" refers to the signless (*animitta*). This Bodhisattva holds a blue lotus in his left hand; the blue lotus symbolizes freedom from defilement.
Holding it in the left hand signifies meditative concentration (*samādhi*); therefore, it is called the Samādhi of Non-Attachment to All Dharmas. Furthermore, it says:
Because the mind abides nowhere within this samādhi, a vajra-jñāna-mudrā emerges once more upon the lotus;

therefore, this samādhi is eternally quiescent and the wisdom-seal is eternally illuminating. Because it is quiescent yet eternally illuminating, it is said that one is able to universally illumine the dharma-realm with the light of eternal quiescence.
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage "therefore one contemplates the Buddha’s eldest son," this explains the scriptural phrase concerning the contemplation of the Buddha’s eldest son.
Mañjuśrī, if explained in terms of the fruit, is the Mother of Buddhas; here, however, he is called the Buddha’s eldest son based on his causal status.
This youth Jālinīprabha, adorned with the ornaments of ten thousand virtues, represents merit; he stands to the left of Mañjuśrī, facing toward him.
Because it uniquely manifests the mutual adornment of merit and wisdom, the meaning of "therefore observing the Buddha’s eldest son" lies herein.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "as transmitted by the Ācārya" and so forth: what has been shown above merely indicates the general framework;
fearing that those who encounter actual practice would find it difficult to apply themselves, this diagram of positions has been set forth. This is the first court: the Dharma-realm...

The Honored Ones from the twenty-first line above, with the Tathāgata Mahāvīra as the central figure, are to be arranged only on the left and right, and above and below, according to their respective applications listed previously. Herein, only the names are listed;

their forms, colors, hand gestures (*mudrā*), and so forth are to be found in the subsequent sections on Secret Seals (*guhyamudrā*) and the Maṇḍala of the Revolving Wheel of Syllables (*akṣaracakramaṇḍala*) within the Mantra Treasury (*mantrapiṭaka*).
These chapters mutually reveal one another; why is this? It is because they are indeed of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
Furthermore, in the eleventh line of the second court, Mañjuśrī occupies the central position; in the forty-first line of the third court, Śākyamuni occupies the central position.
Moreover, it is an error to state that the Great Hero (Mahāvīra) Tathāgatas should be depicted in the four corners of the first court.
Draw a downward-pointing triangle as a guide; as described on the twenty-second sheet above, draw the seal of Sarvajñā (All-Pervasive Wisdom) as a triangle with its apex pointing downward.
This is the Great Vīra Seal (Mahāvīra-mudrā) of all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and three times.
Furthermore, regarding the "Tathāgata Eye," the aforementioned commentary states: "To the north of Mahāvīra, reaching toward the northwestern corner, place the syllable *Hūṃ*."
The "Eye of Emptiness" (*śūnyatā-cakṣus*) is none other than the Mother of the Buddha Vairocana. The phrase "those who possess the Tathāgata-eye" at the end of the line must be a scribal error.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the abodes of all the honored ones," etc., the diagram merely indicates the positions of the Bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa;
this is also a general statement that they are all placed as Bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa without specifying their individual names and numbers. Now, following the *Vajraśekhara-yoga*,...
The *Dhāraṇī-vidhi* states that one should apply colored pigments to paint the bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa and so forth, or alternatively, transcribe their sixteen names.
First, paint Maitreya; next, Abhaya-darśin; next, Sarva-pāpa-gati-vinivartana;
next, Sarva-kṛṣṇa-tamo-duḥkha-pramathana; next, Gaja-gandha; next, Śūra; next, Gaganagañja; and so on.
Jñānaketu, then Amitaprabha, then Candraprabha, then Bhadrapāla, then Roca, then Vajragarbha, then Akṣayamati,
then Pratibhānakūṭa, and then Samantabhadra— these are called the sixteen great bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa.
As for why these sixteen are named "Bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa," it is because they belong to the Bhadrakalpa, following Śākyamuni.
Because the female practitioner (*bhikṣuṇī*) continues the lineage until attaining Buddhahood, she is given this name. The various positions and locations are as shown in the diagram.
[Commentary: Regarding the forms and characteristics of the six-faced deity, according to the *Mañjuśrī-yamāntaka-krodha-tantra*, it says:
"One should construct a triangular maṇḍala and, within it, paint the body of the Great Majestic Vidyārāja in the color of a dark cloud."
Flames arise from his entire body as he holds various colored weapons; his body is marked with three syllables:

the syllable *Oṃ* at the crown, the syllable *Aḥ* at the mouth, and the syllable *Hūṃ* at the heart. Once the body of the Accomplished Honored One has been formed, place the *śatru* (enemies) beneath the image and inscribe their names.
Furthermore, paint that image black, with six feet, six heads, and six arms. Thus it is said.
This purifies the six destinies, fulfills the six perfections, and accomplishes the six supernormal powers. Furthermore, another translation reads:
*The Mahāyāna Vaipulya Mañjuśrī Avataṃsaka Root Teaching, Chapter Thirty: The Ritual Manual for the Wrathful Yamāntaka*. Its verse states:
"The image of Yamāntaka has six faces, twelve arms, and a black complexion; his belly is like that of a wolf, and he wears a garland of skulls."
He wears a tiger skin as a lower garment and holds various weapons; his eyes are bloodshot with violent rage, and he has three eyes as his insignia.

His hair stands upright like blazing flames, and his color is like a dark cloud during a summer rain, resembling the conflagration at the end of an aeon (*kalpa*). He should be depicted riding upon a water buffalo and the like.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "if one forms the seal of the covenant (*kṣepa-mudrā*) and so forth," this is called the Tathāgata-ūṣṇīṣa-mudrā.

As stated in the *Guhyamudrā-paṭala*: "With the hands of concentration and wisdom, form fists with the five wheels turned inward; establish the fire-wheel (the thumbs) and place the two wind-wheels (the index fingers) beside them;
bend the two space-wheels (the little fingers) so they are parallel. All subsequent seals are as described in the *Guhyamudrā-paṭala*.
[Commentary]: However, that which is even more profound than this essential principle of mantra refers to when, in a former life, the World-Honored One manifested the Universal Gate Maṇḍala.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi observed each and every part with meticulous attention, yet he could not perceive its fundamental source, nor was there any place of abiding;

it was entirely the body of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the flower pedestal. Thereupon, he felt deep personal joy and gave rise to the thought that such a thing is difficult to encounter, as rare as a precious spirit.
Shuìhuá (Ruishua) further transmitted it from him; thus, the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) cites the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to explain why it is doubly difficult to encounter.
As for the statement, "This is the secret treasury of the Tathāgata, guarded through the long night—how much more so in the final age," it is as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"This sūtra is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas; it must not be distributed or recklessly bestowed."
Even while the Tathāgata is present, there are many who harbor resentment and jealousy—such as the five thousand followers of overweening pride (adhimāna)—let alone after his parinirvāṇa.
[Commentary:

Therefore, those who are not of dull faculties or meager merit refer to the "people of little virtue and scant merit" mentioned in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, who are beset by manifold sufferings.
Those who are oppressed by afflictions, those of dull faculties and small wisdom, those who are attached to signs and full of pride—
people such as these cannot even encounter the Lotus Sūtra, let alone this sūtra.

[Commentary: "As with the Dragon King Sāgara" means, for example, that while the Dragon King Sāgara rises vertically through the six heavens and extends horizontally across the four continents, producing various clouds, thundering various thunders, flashing various lightnings, and raining down various rains, he remains unmoving and unshakable within his own palace;
so it is with the practitioner of the mantra-vehicle (mantrayāna).
It is likewise thus: within the maṇḍala, one forms various secret mudrās, recites various mantras, and contemplates various deities.

Although these are established through the different conditions of the three secrets, when one contemplates them through the four phrases of non-arising, they are no different from the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), being neither born nor extinguished; therefore, it is said that they are "like Sāgara" and so forth.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "Red is the Jewel Banner (*Ratnaketu)*," this means that the color red is the color of the Tathāgata Ratnaketu.

Ratnaketu signifies the adornment of the *bodhicitta*. Why is this? Because once one has generated the *bodhicitta*, one subdues the māras and enemies within the path of the light of the Dharma and eliminates all hindrances (*sarvāvaraṇa*).
Thus, red is the color of subjugation and belongs to the eastern direction.
It is also said that "yellow" refers to the color of the King of *śāla* trees;

this means that when the seed of the bodhicitta nurtures the myriad practices of great compassion and one attains equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), the ten thousand virtues bloom, and thus it is called the Buddha "King of Blooming Flowers.

Regarding the statement that "all have reached the adamantine limit of reality" (*vajra-bhūtakoṭi*): *śāla* is translated here as "firm and solid," and furthermore, because there are no further practices to be added.
It is said: "All arrive at the adamantine limit of reality (*vajrabhūtakoti*); this belongs to the south and is the color of increase.

Regarding the statement that "blue is the color of Amitāyus" and so forth, it means that because all arrive at the adamantine limit of reality and sentient beings are inexhaustible, the Tathāgata’s great compassion and skillful means manifest this maṇḍala, which likewise has no end; therefore, it is called "Amitāyus" (Infinite Life). Furthermore—
This is the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) of all Tathāgatas; once the flower has fully blossomed, the fruit is necessarily attained.
Each Buddha enjoys this fruit, and since this fruit is the inconceivable bliss of the present dharma, it is called the "enjoyment body.
Furthermore, taking this very fruit as its seed, it is transmitted successively so that others may enjoy it immeasurably; thus it is named "Immeasurable Life" (*Amitāyus*).
"Like the pure void" explains the accomplishment of the blue color; "possessing all phenomena within it" refers to the inconceivable joy of the Dharma.
This belongs to the western direction, for blue is the color of reverence and love, as all beings joyfully approach it.

Regarding the statement that "black is the drum-sound and so forth," it means that just as the *maṇi* jewel and the celestial drum have no form and no dwelling place, yet are able to manifest [sound].
It is named because the sound of its preaching awakens sentient beings; furthermore, having attained the great fruit, how could one merely enjoy it for oneself?
Rather, one expounds it for the sake of all beings. It is like the celestial drum, which accomplishes its purpose without thought.
Consequently, after "Immeasurable Life," the sequence is explained in this manner. As for the reason for relying on the "Universal Gate" and so forth:

This explains the reason why [the color] black is abandoned. This [color] belongs to the North; as for its being the "summoning color," there is nothing it does not summon and gather, reaching even unto *nirvāṇa*. [Commentary:

The seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are the seven limbs of awakening. The first is the factor of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*); because of the binding of mindfulness, it causes all wholesome dharmas [to arise].
1. Because there is no false loss [of mindfulness]; 2. because the factor of awakening of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) awakens to its own characteristic;

3. because the factor of awakening of vigor (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) enables one to reach the destination through this power; 4. because the factor of awakening of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) arises from the mind’s courageous gladness and the body’s adaptability; 5.

because the factor of awakening of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) can remove heaviness (*dausthulya*) by means of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); 6. because the factor of awakening of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) relies upon meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Because one attains the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), the seventh factor, equanimity (*upekṣā-sambodhyaṅga*), is able to eliminate greed, sorrow, and so forth by means of the equilibrium of "equanimity of application" (*praśrabdhy-upekṣā*).
Its definition, its essential nature, and so on, are as explained in other passages.

[Commentary] Regarding "skillful wisdom" (*kauśalya-prajñā*) and so forth: it refers to a wisdom possessing skillful means (*upāya*) that is capable of performing pacification (*śānti*), enrichment (*puṣṭi*), and subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).

"From *anurāgaṇa* (loving-kindness) up to being able to employ *anurāgaṇa* as the means for pacifying (*śāntika*), enriching (*pauṣṭika*), subjugating (*vaśīkaraṇa*), and so forth, entering them without obstruction and without exhaustion.
[Commentary] Regarding "the mantra of quiescence (*śamatha*)": "quiescence" refers to the meaning that all phenomena are fundamentally unborn from the beginning.
The meaning of "primordially unborn" (ajāta) is the essence of the syllable A.
Since this syllable A serves as the essence for all mantras universally, and since every point of contact is the syllable A, it is said that [it is] "the mantra of quiescence," and so forth.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the first *ī* and so forth," this refers to the placement of the various inner retinues within the first layer of the triple-layered maṇḍala.
This is because it is formed by the three dots of the letter *ī*: the central dot represents the retinue of the Tathāgata family of Mahāvairocana;
the right-hand dot represents the retinue of the Padma family of Avalokiteśvara; and the left-hand dot [represents the Vajra family of Mañjuśrī].
The dots represent the Vajradhara and the retinue of the Vajra Family; these three dots are all the internal virtues of Vairocana Tathāgata upon the lotus pedestal.
Next, regarding the creation of the second tier of the four Bodhisattvas and so forth:
"four" refers to the four Bodhisattvas—Mañjuśrī, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Kṣitigarbha, and Ākāśagarbha. Because these constitute the great retinue, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
To desire to be the inner retinue of all Buddhas and to desire to be the great retinue of all Buddhas is precisely this.
When it is said that the third level and so forth follow next, this refers to the retinue of Śākyamuni.

[Commentary: The five faculties and powers are faith (*śraddhā*), diligence (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). "Faith" refers to having deep conviction, delight, and aspiration toward reality, virtues, and capabilities;
its intrinsic nature is the purity of mind. The remaining four are: exerting effort based on what has been attained therein; practicing with clear recollection so as not to forget;
focusing single-mindedly on one object; and discerning right from wrong. These five are all capable of producing mundane [attainments].
They are called "faculties" (*indriya*) because they serve as predominant factors for the Dharma;

furthermore, these five dharmas are called "powers" (*bala*) because they increase [in strength], such that Māras, Brahmās, afflictions, and the like cannot subdue them, and because they can diminish obstacles such as lack of faith. As the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:
"That which can destroy the afflictions and attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is called power."
Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāvairocana-sūtra: Explication of the Secret (Yanmi Chao), Scroll Five;
Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāvairocana-sūtra: Explication of the Secret (Yanmi Chao), Scroll Six.
Written by Chonglu Daifu Jianjiao Dabaohang Chong at Yuanfu Temple in Yanjing.
Composed by the Monk Jueyuan, Grand Master of the Secret Treasury, recipient of the purple robe and Minister of State.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "At that time, he enters the Double Profundity," this refers to the second court, which represents exclusively the stages of the various Bodhisattvas who, through their great compassion, seek enlightenment above while transforming beings below.
If one practices the ten thousand practices with a heart of diligent vigor colored red—representing the fire element—until...
In the eighth stage, one abides in attachment to the dharma and craving for cessation;

at that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions exhort one with seven matters to give rise from this state to a mind free from attachment, thereby attaining the difficult-to-traverse Bodhicitta—this is the first gate of profound mystery.
Furthermore, by entering the Tathāgata’s mindfulness through the color yellow, the myriad virtues blossom forth—this is the second gate.
When the Bodhisattvas of the Profound Gate enter this second layer of the maṇḍala, they do so by means of the two colors red and yellow as the gateway;
therefore, it is called "entering the gate of the double profundity. Thus, the *Sutra of the Adornments* states:
"When all Bodhisattvas first attain the seventh stage, they see no Buddhas above to be sought and see no sentient beings below to be saved; this is abiding in the Great [Vehicle]."

Nirvana is the resting of all myriad practices. At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions, through the path of the Samādhi of Avalokiteśvara, inspire their minds so that they may attain liberation from the difficult points of the bodhicitta;

because they advance toward the stage of Buddhahood moment by moment through this gate of samādhi, it is called "entering the gate of profound mystery. To say "dwelling above the *sukhāvatī* (Light of Bliss) realm" refers to the third level.
In this maṇḍala, Śākyamuni is the principal figure; thus it is called the Śākya Maṇḍala. "Śākya" translates as "Able to Pacify.
The boundary color of this maṇḍala is exclusively white, which signifies light. Now, the second tier of the maṇḍala is located in the third enclosure, atop the white light of the Able-to-Pacify;

therefore, it is said to "dwell above the light of pacification. As for the phrase "up to and including": *Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on a Buddhist ritual manual (vidhi) concerning the construction of a maṇḍala.*

Regarding the statement "not knowing a single person": this refers to the fact that those in this second courtyard are all great Bodhisattvas of the highest rank, immeasurable in number, who have already approached the central terrace of the three dots.
Their retinues are like the great Bodhisattvas who emerged from the earth at Vulture Peak;
therefore, even those such as Maitreya, whose traces reside in the position of the successor, still dwell within the realm of causes when compared to them.
"Among them, one does not recognize a single person.

[Commentary] As for the phrase "all sentient beings," although the Tathāgata’s Great Compassion Maṇḍala has three layers and five colors with distinct differences, its ultimate meaning is that of the flower pedestal (*padmāsana*). When practitioners realize and know this, there is [no distinction].
Although there are differences in depth, according to the different ways sentient beings enter [the path], there are those who enter gradually, like one riding a sheep;
those who ascend by leaping over stages, like one riding a horse; and those who enter all at once, as if attaining supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Though the vehicles they ride differ, the destination reached is the same.
[Commentary]: "Flanking the gate with chambers and guards" means to hold or support [the gate]. "Chambers" refers to the curved sections to the east and west; "guards" refers to protection.
This means placing protective stations on the left and right of the gate, just as the gates of a worldly emperor’s palace have guards stationed on both sides to prepare for unforeseen events;
this present case is likewise. All three layers of the maṇḍala have gates opening on all four sides, providing passage through the gates.
On both sides, guards are stationed to prevent demonic interference; all other gates are sealed off with vajra-threads.

At the southern corner of the main entrance, Upasūna is placed as a gatekeeper, and at the northern corner, Sūna is placed as a gatekeeper. In the second enclosure, at the southern corner, Nanda... [text ends]
On the northern cheek is the Nāga King Dharaṇa; on the southern cheek of the central courtyard is the Nāga King Upananda.
The gatekeepers on the northern cheek face those on the southern cheek. As for the names and ranks of the others, they are arranged here according to the commentary;
therefore, they are shown in this diagram.
Regarding the statement "one side has six stakes up to twenty-eight," this refers to the gates being curved like the shape of the character 凸 (tú-mò), while the other gates open straight;
therefore, twenty-eight stakes are placed. Fearing that people might find this difficult to understand, it is illustrated with a diagram:
the stakes are formed as circular rings.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "if one provides a profound and esoteric interpretation" and so forth: if one relies on the superficial interpretation, the square characteristics of the four sides of the maṇḍala must be free from obliquity, curvature, and inequality in order to avoid faults.
However, when providing a profound interpretation, the four directions correspond to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), which can eliminate the four inversions (*viparyāsa*).
Now, when the four [directions] are adjusted and straightened such that concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are balanced and even, one is then able to uphold the subsequent teaching.

Regarding the statement that "the four gates are the four dhyānas," etc.: a "gate" (mukha) is a passage for entering and exiting. When a practitioner enters the first dhyāna, they simultaneously exit from sorrow (*daurmanasya*);
upon entering the second dhyāna, they exit from suffering (*duḥkha*); upon entering the third dhyāna, they exit from joy (*prīti*);

and upon entering the fourth dhyāna, they exit from pleasure (*sukha*). Regarding the statement that these are also the "four means of attraction" (*saṃgrahavastu*), a "gate" signifies the sense of being unobstructed.
Regarding the statement that the "gate insignia" (*dvāra-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the four means of attraction (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*) because they gather sentient beings without obstruction:

the term "insignia" (*lakṣaṇa*) here carries the sense of a sign or marker that reveals [the path]. It enables the practitioner to recognize the categories and the points of entry and exit so that no error occurs.

When explained in depth, the insignia of the four gates are the four divine abodes (*catvāri brahmavihārāḥ*), namely: loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). These are the internal mandalas.

The *caitya* gateways (toraṇas) serve as their insignia: the eastern gate has compassion (*maitrī*) as its insignia, the southern gate has pity (*karuṇā*), the western gate has joy (*muditā*), and the northern gate has equanimity (*upekṣā*).
This is just like the nameplates currently used on city gates—such as those at Andong and Zhuhuai—to mark and identify them;
for one who wishes to proceed to the central terrace, entry must be gained through these gates.
If one does not perceive its gate insignia (*dvāra-lakṣaṇa*), doubt will arise and progress will be impossible.

If a practitioner enters through any one of the gates beneath these insignia for the Brahma-abodes (*brahmavihāra*), they will behold Vairocana at the central terrace within the maṇḍala of their own mind.
Regarding the statement that "the curved corridors are right effort" (*samyag-vyāyāma*): when explained in a superficial sense, vajras are placed at every corner of the curves.
These stakes and five-colored threads serve as a protective barrier; all *vināyakas* and other obstructing spirits dare not approach to create hindrances.
The five colors—white, yellow, red, black, and blue—correspond respectively to the gates of the faculties and powers of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
"Thread" (*sūtra*) carries the meaning of "connecting and sustaining"; it signifies the continuous binding of all virtues so that they are never severed.

When explaining this in depth: regarding the left and right side-walls of the four dhyāna-gates within the maṇḍala of the mind, if one does not guard them with the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*), the mind will become indolent and be harmed by the Piśāca-demons. As for the four right efforts:
they consist of diligently obstructing the two evils and diligently producing the two goods; they sever already arisen unwholesome dharmas, just as one removes weeds.

Severing unwholesome states that have not yet arisen is like preventing a flowing stream from increasing; nurturing wholesome states that have already arisen is like irrigating the roots of sweet fruit trees;

and causing wholesome states that have not yet arisen to arise is like drilling wood to produce fire. Right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*) is fourfold. It is designated as "four" by way of enumeration (*gaṇanā*).

As for the term "four truths," *vī* means a corner or direction. A superficial explanation is as given above; however, a profound explanation is as follows: [The text continues with the detailed analysis of the four truths.]
The four corners of the inner maṇḍala are precisely the places of the darkness of ignorance;

if they are not guarded by the principle of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—then one will be disturbed by the four kinds of Vināyakas of birth, abiding, change, and extinction.
Therefore, it says "the four intermediate directions," and so forth.

[Commentary]: Regarding the traces of the Universal Gate (Pumen), that they are "far-reaching and increasingly vast" means that vertically they reach the limits of the three periods of time, which is called "far," and horizontally they pervade the ten directions, which is called "vast.
The character *yú* (逾) is used twice in the middle; *yú* means to transcend or to surpass.
Because it transcends the three periods of time and surpasses those ten directions, it is said to be "far-reaching and increasingly vast."

[Commentary]: How could it be cumbersome to gradually transcend the four stages? These are the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), and the ten grounds (*bhūmi*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the "voice of Great Diligence and Valor" (*mahāvīrya*): the Tathāgata’s lion-like, vigorous, and great power of diligence is called "Great Diligence and Valor.
Because he utters words of truth from this diligence with fierce and mighty power, it is called the "voice of Great Diligence and Valor."

[Commentary]: This triangular seal (*tri-koṇa-mudrā*) that is thus received and maintained is the seal of universal knowledge (*sarvajña*). It is called the "triangular seal" because it is made in the shape of a triangle;

the triangle signifies the meaning of subjugation (*abhibhava*), and its sharp point directed downward means that whoever receives and maintains it can eliminate the immeasurable terrors and so forth within the Avīci hell.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the mind and the stūpa," if one explains the meaning of *caitya* esoterically, it refers to both the mind and the stūpa.
This means that both the mind and the stūpa possess the function of being a basis for reliance, and thus both may be designated by the name *caitya*.
If the mind is called *caitya*, it is the basis for the *dharmakāya* relics; if the stūpa is called *caitya*, it is the basis for the *nirmāṇakāya* (or *jāti-kāya*) relics.
Regarding the phrase "the mind and the stūpa": the Sanskrit terms *stūpa* or *thūpa* are both corruptions and abbreviations.
The correct term is *sṭūpa*, which translates as "high and manifest. If it is characterized by high, tiered elevations, it is called a *sṭūpa*;
if it is characterized by horizontal breadth and magnificence, it is called a *caitya*. Since both serve as supports, it is said: "the mind and the stūpa."
[Commentary] "Like the great ocean" means that just as the tides of the worldly great ocean must arrive at their appointed time, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states that the ocean possesses ten virtues:
first, it becomes gradually deeper; second, it does not retain corpses; [omitted] up to the ninth, its tides do not exceed their limits;
and tenth, it universally receives great rains—this corresponds to the ninth virtue. Furthermore, as the sūtra says, within the ocean there is...
There is a gem named Moon-Love (*candrakānta*). When the moon is full on the fifteenth night, by the power and merit of this gem, it is able to cause the ocean tides never to exceed their limits.
The Great Ocean of the Tathāgata is likewise; when there is a responsive resonance caused by the conditions of sentient beings’ gem-like moon of faith, [the tide] never exceeds its limit.
[Commentary: Regarding the term "one bound to a single birth" (*ekajātipratibaddha*), the *Shangsheng shu* (Commentary on the Birth Above) states:
"There are three kinds of births for Bodhisattvas: first, those bound to a single birth; second, those in their final body; and third, those seated at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Since this refers to the first, it is called a 'Bodhisattva bound to a single birth. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: 'One bound to a single birth...'"
This means that immediately after this birth, one shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Furthermore, Vimalakīrti said to Maitreya:
"The World-Honored One has granted you the prediction that in one more birth you shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Now, in this school, the term "one birth" refers to the ten successive stages of clarification based on the *dharmatā* of *tathatā*, with the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*) added as the eleventh.

The transformation of both is called "birth from the dharma-nature" (*dharmatā-utpatti*). Now, regarding the tenth stage, the Bodhisattva transforms this birth from the dharma-nature to reach the stage of the Tathāgata;
therefore, the Commentary states: "There is yet another transformation of birth from the dharma-nature, namely, filling the place of the Buddha," and so forth.

Since the dharma-nature itself is without distinction, how can there be eleven differentiations? The answer is: because there are differences in the realization of wisdom, they are distinguished according to their respective hindrances.

The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* also speaks of eleven [stages]. Its commentary cites the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* as scriptural evidence, showing that one realizes ten kinds of equal dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) at each stage, culminating in their perfect accomplishment at the Buddha-stage as the fruit of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Question:
Since the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* and other texts also speak of the dharma-nature, they likewise establish eleven stages; why then do you alone now claim this differs from other schools?

The answer is: because that [previous explanation] refers to the distinction of stages, it is not called "one lifetime"; furthermore, because their functions differ, there is no confusion between them.

Another interpretation is that there is yet another transformation of the *dharmatā*: namely, from the nature of the syllable A of Great Compassion, one transforms and gives rise to the ultimate syllable Āṃ of Great Emptiness, which is the taking of the Buddha’s place.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the Sanskrit term *karma* is stated literally," it refers to what the Sūtra calls "abiding in the stage of karma" (*karmabhūmi*).
The Sanskrit term *karma* (Skt. *karman*) is stated literally here. When explained skillfully, it should be called *kārā-dhāraṇī*, which means "the ground of action.
This "ground of action" refers to training in the Tathāgata’s vajra-activities; therefore, it is said that the Sanskrit term is stated literally.
The statement that it constitutes the "ground" (bhūmi) refers specifically to the tenth ground (*daśamī bhūmi*). Question:

Since this is the Vajra-mind (*vajracitta*), which is the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) situated outside the ten grounds, why is it further called the tenth ground? Answer: Although it transcends the ten grounds, it is still subsumed within the category of the grounds;
furthermore, the *Abhidharma* (Eleventh [Chapter]) states that the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*) are cultivated after the first eon has been completed. Thus, [it is so designated].
If [the marks and signs] are cultivated after the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are completed at the end of the first *kalpa*, what prevents them from being subsumed within those ten stages?
Furthermore, the *Śrīgarbha-sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng) states that although they are cultivated after the three great *kalpas* are completed, they are still subsumed within the *kalpas*.

By the same logic, those cultivated after the ten stages are completed should also be subsumed within the ten stages. Otherwise, if they are neither part of the ten stages nor the fruit of Buddhahood, in what position do they reside? This is the tenth [point].

The *Dì* (Grounds) subsume this principle without contradiction. Regarding the "Gate of the Double Profundity," this refers to the samādhi of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha-samādhi*), which is identical to the samādhi of signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*).
Having already entered the Gate of Profundity within the eighth ground, one now reaches fulfillment in the tenth ground and approaches the stage of Buddhahood;
because one again attains realization through the gate of the samādhi of quiescent extinction, it is called "entering the Gate of the Double Profundity."

[Commentary: "Firmly abiding in the stage of Buddhahood" refers to previously abiding in the stage of karma; that which is "abiding" here refers specifically to abiding in the mind, meaning that one focuses exclusively on the stage of Buddhahood without wavering or distraction.
Thus, it is said that the meaning of the word "abiding" differs from what was stated previously.

Regarding "the path of the samādhi of the position of succession" (*kṣānti*), "position of succession" is that which is to be attained, while "samādhi" is the means by which it is attained. It is called the "position of succession" because it leads to that state.

Furthermore, regarding the samādhi-path of "firmly abiding in the Buddha-ground" (*buddhabhūmi*): it refers to being single-mindedly intent upon the fruit of Buddhahood within the stage of prior karma, without any other distractions;
this is termed "abiding. It is like the focused concentration of one parched with thirst who thinks only of water—this is called the samādhi-path of the "one more birth" (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
Now, this "firm abiding" is the final mind in which all aspiration has completely ceased.
It is called "abiding" (sthiti) just as when a thirsty person has reached a clear stream and, having climbed up to it, seeks rest with a mind that is unmoving;
thus, there is a distinction between these two instances of the term "abiding" when they are compared.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "yet unable to sever the traces of arising activity," one asks:

Since Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage are said to dwell in non-effort (*anābhoga*) and their contemplation is purely signless (*animitta*), why are they still said to have traces of arising activity? The answer is:

They are still designated as having traces of activity in contrast to the higher stages. How is this known? Because the conclusion states: "They are divided into two seals," namely, the eighth stage and [the ninth].
The state of being a successor (the *upapadya-bhūmi*) constitutes the two seals. Furthermore, another interpretation divides these into two seals:

first, when one enters this eighth stage (*bhūmi*), looking upward one sees no Buddhas to be sought, and looking downward one sees no sentient beings to be saved; sinking into emptiness for a long time is called the seal of the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*).
Then, the Buddhas exhort one to arise, and through the illusory-like samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*), one performs various deeds to benefit sentient beings.
Because they are named the Samādhi Seal of Having Characteristics (*sanimitta-samādhi-mudrā*), they constitute two seals.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that one should explain the "Initial Gate of Dharma-Illumination" (*prathama-dharmāloka-mukha*) here, this serves as a general explanation to resolve potential objections.

This means that within these ten stages (*bhūmi*), the first stage attains the initial path of dharma-illumination; therefore, the superior grade [of the text] states: "This Bodhisattva’s gate of the bodhicitta..."

It is called the "Path of the Initial Illumination of Dharmas" because, by awakening to the limit where the mind is fundamentally unborn, one’s mind abides in purity and gives rise to the light of great wisdom, thereby seeing the path traversed by all Buddhas; thus it is so named.
This corresponds to the syllable *A*, the phrase for the bodhicitta. From the second stage through the eighth stage, it is termed "Great Compassion as the Root. That is to say:
The syllable A (ā) refers to the stages from the eighth bhūmi upward to the skillful means of the stage of near-attainment (*sāmantaka*), which is the ultimate;
it is the syllable "Darkness" (*aṃ*), the phrase of the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*). As for the phrase of the bodhicitta, it has already been explained in the first chapter.

[Sūtra]: Regarding the statement that "the assembly of śrāvakas dwells on the ground of having conditions": this means that when śrāvakas contemplate worldly and supramundane phenomena within samādhi, they perceive that all have causes and conditions; this is called "dwelling on the ground of having conditions.
This is distinguished from the mundane because mundane samādhis are dependent upon another master—that is, the *puruṣa* (Self). Ultimately, these are all causes for destruction.
Regarding the statement "the fruit is the consciousness of arising and ceasing," this refers to the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, which possesses four aspects:

first, arising and ceasing; second, non-arising; third, the immeasurable; and fourth, the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Among these four, because people’s minds are shallow regarding the Dharma, they only recognize arising and ceasing and do not yet recognize the others;
therefore, it is said that they "recognize arising and ceasing. Regarding the phrase "removing the two extremes," this means removing the worldly [extreme].

This is because they cling to the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. That is to say, although the non-Buddhist worldlings possess the wisdom that contemplates emptiness, because they do not understand the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), they cannot escape these two extremes.
Within the Buddha-dharma, however, because one knows that things exist through causes and conditions, one is free from the view of non-existence;
and because one contemplates that the self-nature of causes and conditions is empty, one does not give rise to the view of existence. Now, as for the assembly of Śrāvakas...
Because it eliminates the two views of the world, it is said to "eliminate the two extremes.
[Commentary] Regarding "such as the Abhidharma," *Abhidharma* here means "Dharma in Opposition" (or "Counter-Dharma"), referring to the treatises on Dharma-in-opposition.

As for the "nine perceptions," they refer to the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*): first, the perception of bloating; second, the perception of decay; third, the perception of being smeared with blood; fourth, the perception of pus...

The nine perceptions are: (1) the perception of a bloated corpse, (2) the perception of a livid corpse, (3) the perception of a festering corpse, (4) the perception of a discolored corpse, (5) the perception of a mangled corpse, (6) the perception of a gnawed corpse, (7) the perception of a scattered corpse, (8) the perception of a skeleton, and (9) the perception of a burning corpse.

These constitute the contemplation of the body as impure. Such practices are all intended as antidotes to the grasping at a self, and they also serve to initiate the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).

As for the "eight recollections," they are: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of ethical discipline (*śīla*), recollection of renunciation (*tyāga*), recollection of the devas, and recollection of departure [from saṃsāra].
