The mindfulness of inhalation and death is as clearly explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Regarding what is called "the eight liberations" (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*):
"liberation" (*vimokṣa*) refers to turning away from and abandoning; "abandoning" (*śe*) refers to being free from attachment. The *Mahā-zhiguan* states:

"One turns away from the lower stages and the pure, clean five desires of one's own stage, abandoning this mind of attachment; therefore, it is called 'liberation'. First, regarding "having internal form while perceiving external forms," this is not refuted.
Not destroying internal form means internally contemplating the white bones, skin, and flesh; this is called "having internal form while externally contemplating form.

Externally contemplating corpses and so forth, as in the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*) mentioned previously, is called "externally contemplating form. This is termed "having internal form while externally contemplating form.

As explained in detail within the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, there are two types of "internally being without form while contemplating external form" through the liberation (*vimokṣa*). By breaking down the bones into the four subtle elements (*caturmahābhūta*), one knows they arise from the mind.
The mind is like a magically conjured skeleton that vanishes of its own accord; this is called "internally perceiving forms while being without internal form," as previously explained.

This refers to the three pure liberations (*śubha-vimokṣa*) where one realizes them through the body. Specifically, in the first and second dhyānas, there is no bliss pervading the entire body, and in the fourth dhyāna, there is no bliss at all.

It is called "pure" because one contemplates the white bones with such clarity that they are no longer accompanied by sinews or blood, appearing like *kaśa* shells or *śukti* oysters; hence it is so described.

The "pure liberations" (*śubha-vimokṣa*) and the "liberations of the four emptinesses" (*catasraḥ śūnyatā-vimokṣāḥ*) refer to the rejection of form and taking emptiness as the object; there is no separate dharma other than this, but rather the entry into the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).

If ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are largely defiled by attachment to this concentration of emptiness, whereas noble ones (*ārya*) proceed directly with a profound mind without turning back, it is therefore called a "liberation.

Fifth, if one takes emptiness as the object excessively, there is distraction; thus, one abandons emptiness and takes consciousness (*vijñāna*) as the object—this is called the "liberation of that which is turned away from consciousness. Furthermore, regarding consciousness...

Because arising and ceasing are impermanent, deceptive, and devoid of further objects of perception, there remains only the perceiving subject; therefore, it is called the sixth liberation, the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Furthermore, the sphere of consciousness is like an abscess, while the sphere of nothingness is like a wound;

abandoning consciousness and being without consciousness constitutes the seventh liberation, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Moreover, this state of non-perception still possesses subtle afflictions. Now...
Having abandoned the perception that takes non-perception as its object, there is likewise no further perception capable of ceasing it;

because the body is sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-dharma*) such that thought and perception vanish entirely—like a fish in ice or hibernating insects—it is called the eighth liberation, the "cessation of perception and feeling" (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa*).

For a full and detailed account, one should refer to what is explained in the *Zhiguan Xuzheng* (The Essential Proof for the Cultivation and Realization of Calm and Insight). As for the term "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*), these are the eight bases of mastery, meaning that one is able to...
Because the mind is superior to the objects of observation, they are called "Spheres of Mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*); they are also called the "Eight Spheres of Superior Knowledge and Vision.
This means that this mind is superior to form (*rūpa*), not that form binds the mind; because the mind can transform form, it is called "superior knowledge.

Furthermore, because one achieves mastery over the contemplation and understanding of the pure and impure within one's own mind, it is called "superior vision. If these spheres of mastery are accomplished...

At that time, one does not yet spare even one's own body, much less external objects or the bodies of others. The *Commentary on the Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states: "First, perceiving internal forms while observing few external forms;
second, perceiving internal forms while observing many external forms; third, having no perception of internal forms while observing few external forms;
fourth, having no perception of internal forms while observing many external forms; furthermore, having no perception of internal forms while observing external blue or yellow."
The phrase "red, white, and the eight [colors] at the feet" refers to the ten *kṛtsnāyatanas* (totalities).
This means that one thoroughly observes earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, white, as well as the two boundless spheres of space and consciousness;
because one observes these everywhere in all places without any interval, they are called the ten *kṛtsnāyatanas*. Furthermore, by pervading with blue...
At all times, when yellow enters into blue, it also pervades all places; yet the original characteristics of blue and yellow are not lost.
They enter into one another without becoming confused. The same applies to the entry of other colors. This is called the "all-pervading bases" (*kṛtsnāyatana*).

Regarding the phrase "the three samādhis and so forth," the term *samādhi* is used because there are three types of equality. As the *Commentary on the Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states: "To know the true reality of phenomena is called *samādhi*."
Ultimately, emptiness is called the *śūnyatā-samādhi*; knowing the true mark of dharmas as being without marks (*animitta*) and ungraspable is called the *animitta-samādhi*;
and having known that dharmas are empty, not contemplating whether dharmas are empty or not empty, or whether they exist or do not exist, is called the *apraṇihita-samādhi*.
Therefore, the sub-commentary below states: "These three are of one essence; in reality, they have no dual nature. It is for such reasons as these.
It is called *samaya*. As for the term "equal" (*sama*) used below: when referring to the superior level, it means being equal to the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*) up to the three samādhis;
when referring to the inferior level, it means being equal to those three emptinesses (*trividha-śūnyatā*) and the three liberations (*trivimokṣa*).

[Commentary: In the world, that which takes accumulation as its cause and suffering as its fruit consists of these five—ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*)—which, through their conjunction, act as the cause for inviting the fruits of suffering:
consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Therefore, it is said that in the supramundane, "the path" (*mārga*) and so forth [are the cause]; the path is the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to ignorance, old age and death, and the rest.
Skillful means (upāya) is precisely the Noble Path that leads out of suffering. Because this serves as the cause, ignorance through to old age and death are brought to complete cessation;
since this cessation is the fruit, it is said to be "supramundane," and so forth.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "all phenomena arise from conditions" and so forth: "all phenomena" refers to the twelve links of dependent origination—namely, the five links beginning with suffering (consciousness, name-and-form, and so on), and the seven links beginning with birth and old age/death;
"accumulation" refers to the five links beginning with ignorance (ignorance, volitional formations, craving, grasping, and existence);

"path" refers to the skillful means that serve as the counteractive causes and conditions; and "cessation" refers to the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death. Thus it is said.
Regarding the statement "arising from conditions": there are no such phenomena that do not arise from conditions;

that is to say, ignorance is the condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), volitional formations are the condition for consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so on, up to existence being the condition for birth.

Furthermore, "condition" refers to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), which is precisely ignorance, because there are no phenomena that do not arise from it. Moreover, all phenomena take ignorance as their fundamental basis. Therefore...
Regarding the statement that "all phenomena arise from conditions," when it is said that the Tathāgata taught them to have causes, this refers to the designation of "cause" in relation to the effect;

that is, in relation to old age and death and so forth, they are all designated as causes because each one serves as a cause in its respective sequence. Furthermore, since the ultimate credit for their arising is attributed to the root, ignorance is taken as the cause.
When it is said that "the causes and conditions of those phenomena are exhausted," this refers to that which is produced by those causes and conditions.
When the Dharma, through the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), counteracts and exhausts [the afflictions], that is the meaning of cessation (*nirodha*).

To say "this is what the Great Śramaṇa has taught" concludes it as the teaching of the Buddha. Such seals of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*) exist only in the Buddha's teachings; therefore, it is said, "this is what the Great Śramaṇa has taught.

Furthermore, "all phenomena arise from conditions" refers to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*); "the Tathāgata says this is its cause" refers to the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*). That...
The "exhaustion of the causal conditions of dharmas" refers to the latter two truths; because this seal of the Dharma was personally taught by the Tathāgata, it is said that "all dharmas are equal.
Furthermore, the sub-commentary below states that since this verse encompasses the meaning of the Tripiṭaka, it is traditionally known in India as the "Dharmakāya Śarīra."
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "This is the most difficult for all the world to understand," the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"This Dharma cannot be shown; its words and signs are quiescent. Among all other classes of sentient beings, there is none who can understand it.

For this reason, when the World-Honored One first attained the Way, he merely enjoyed the bliss of the Dharma within himself for twenty-one days. Only after that, through the power of skillful means, did he [begin to teach].
Because it is spoken of as arising, it says, "This is all the worlds," and so forth.

[Commentary]: Regarding the five positions in the three-layered maṇḍala, the "five positions" refer to the first layer, which has three parts—namely, the central terrace (*maṇḍala*), the filaments (*keśara*), and the eight petals—along with the second and third enclosures; these together are called the five positions. Alternatively, [the five positions may be defined differently].
The inclusion of the Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, Vajra-holders, and the deities of the Two Vehicles is as indicated within the sections on mantras [in the *Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha*].
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "there are three types of names for Sarvajña," this refers to each of the latter three of the four teachings in the Tiantai system.
There are eight matters: first, teaching; second, principle; third, wisdom; fourth, abandonment; fifth, practice; sixth, stage; seventh, cause; and eighth, fruit.

This *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) corresponds precisely to the third, the character for "wisdom. Furthermore, the wisdom of the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sāmānya*) refers to the skillful attainment of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

The wisdom of the Distinct Teaching (*prativedha-bheda*) is the knowledge of the paths of all beings (*mārgajñatā*). The wisdom of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna*) is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
It is also said that when these three kinds of wisdom reach the meaning of the letter *A*, it establishes their non-duality. [Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "equal to the letters such as those in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*," this means that the sounds and letters of the mantras mentioned above encompass all other letters;
this is the same as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. That treatise states: "Furthermore, regarding the practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva..."
This refers to the gateways of letters, phrases, and all syllables. What are the gateways of letters, phrases, and all syllables? They are:
the letter A-gate, because all phenomena are originally unarisen; the letter Ra-gate, because all phenomena are free from defilement;
the letter Pa-gate, because all phenomena are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); and the letter Cha-gate, because all phenomena are ultimately unobtainable.
The letter-gateway *Na* signifies that all dharmas are devoid of name, nature, and characteristics, because they cannot be attained nor lost;
even the letter-gateway *Ḍa* enters the boundary of all dharmas, because it is unattainable, neither ending nor arising. That treatise explains:
"The letters and so forth, the words and so forth" refers to the *dhāraṇī*; it is equanimity toward all letters, being without hatred or affection. Furthermore, this...
When the conditions for various syllables have not yet met, there is no end, no beginning, and no present;
there is nothing at all, but they abide within my own mind as recollections, conceptions, discriminations, and reflections. What the mind speaks of is the speech of a distracted mind;
it does not see actual reality, just as when wind stirs water, nothing is seen. This is equal to ultimate emptiness and nirvana.
By means of this dhāraṇī, the Bodhisattva attains unimpeded penetration into all phenomena; these are the equality of names and the equality of words.
[Commentary] "Name" refers to that which, by means of such gates of syllables, expresses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); however, there are cases where a single syllable constitutes a name.
Regarding the term "A-sa-mi," the word "A" signifies "non-existence" (wu), while "Sa-mi" consists of multiple syllables forming a single name;
"A-sa-mi" thus means "non-existence and so forth. In the commentary (*shu*), because it seeks to demonstrate that multiple syllables constitute a single name, it states:
"they together form one name."
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "as in the first sentence," it refers to *asaṃmī*, which means "without equal. These three phrases are each complete expressions of the Dharma (*dharmaparyāya*).
For example, although the meaning of phrases such as "neither arising nor ceasing" may not yet be fully realized, they are still called "sentences" because the Dharma is complete within them.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "multiple names collectively forming a single sentence" and so forth, this refers to the four lines such as "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," which constitute a verse;

these are precisely what are called "sentences that fully manifest the meaning. Question: Since the essence of a mantra must necessarily depend upon sound (*śabda*), why does this section speak only of "names" (*nāman*) and "phrases" (*pada*)?
Answer: This explains the general characteristics of mantras in terms of their capacity to express and reveal intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because of these distinctions, they are designated as "names" (*nāman*) and so forth; yet even when referring to their basis, they are not separate from sound.

As the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states, both speaker and listener reach completion through two things: first, excellent sound (*svara*), and second, excellent syllables (*vyañjana*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says:

"Due to this, there is a distinction between the objects of the two types of unimpeded knowledge—dharma and expression (*nirukti*): the former takes names and so forth as its object, while the latter takes expressions as its object."
Is it not the case that there is no sound within sound? Furthermore, this thesis relies on syllables to produce sound;

just as a practitioner contemplates syllables within the perfect luminosity of the mind, it is by producing sound from these syllables that the meaning is revealed. Therefore, one directly takes up the syllables and so forth without explicitly mentioning the sound, so that the reader may fully comprehend it.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "by means of this letter-gateway *kha*," etc., it refers to the meaning taught in the *Vajraśekhara-sūtra* concerning how the Vajra of Touching swallows and destroys various impurities;

this is precisely that meaning. However, the underlying intention (*abhisandhi*) here is that because it swallows and destroys the defilements and stains of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) of all sentient beings, it says "by means of this letter-gateway *kha*," and so forth.
[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the mantra speaks only of the twelve [links of dependent origination]," this mantra refers to the syllable *baddha*.
This syllable *baddha* signifies that the path of verbal expression is severed for all phenomena (*dharmas*). If phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, they are free from all causes and conditions;
therefore, the path of verbal expression is severed. Thus, the subsequent commentary states: "Because the wisdom of the Pratyekabuddhas is profound and sharp."
Because one sees that all phenomena of origination are phenomena of cessation, it is called "Realizing the Tranquil Realm.

When dwelling in this samādhi, one is able to contemplate all phenomena as having the characteristics of nirvāṇa, such that they cannot be expressed in speech; thus it is called the "Samādhi of the Ultimate Cessation of Language.
For this reason, one does not delight in preaching the Dharma; rather, wishing to fulfill the vows of sentient beings, one merely empowers this [samādhi] through spiritual power.

Regarding the phrase "purifying the birth from karma through mantras": this means that one is able to purify the birth produced by the conditioning of causes and conditions, thereby enabling the arising of the wisdom of great emptiness; hence it is called "purifying the birth from karma."
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the Dharma abides in its station" (*dharmasthititā*) and so forth: True Suchness (*tathatā*) abiding within all phenomena is called "the Dharma abides.

Because it manifests the distinct stages (*avasthā*)—wherein phenomena possess both defilement and purity, and where one attains purity by departing from defilement—it is termed "the station of the Dharma" (*dharmapada*). This is explained according to the distinction between principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*).

Alternatively, the Dharma of True Suchness is itself that which abides, and is thus the "station of the Dharma. This is explained solely according to principle; the words "nature and characteristics are eternally abiding" refer to this.
This refers to the fact that the true nature (*tattva*) of mantras and the actual characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of mantras exist eternally, whether a Buddha appears or not.

Furthermore, while their nature (*svabhāva*) is permanent, their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are impermanent. Given this, how can it be said that "nature and characteristics are eternally as they are"?

Answer: Because nature and characteristics are non-dual (*advaya*). Moreover, the permanence of nature is itself permanent, whereas the permanence of characteristics is impermanent; this is not due to [an external] analogy.
Question: Since he has appeared in the world, it may be said that his constant voice is so; but are not the teachings of impermanent sound also spoken by the Tathāgata?
Answer: The Dharma is fundamentally impermanent, yet it is manifested through the Buddha.
[Commentary] "According to each individual mantra" means that the Tathāgata, through universal empowerment (*samantamukha-adhiṣṭhāna*), manifests a universal gate body (*samantamukha-kāya*);
because each and every such body possesses a mantra, they are called "individual mantras.
"Established therein" means that within these individual mantras—whether extensive or abbreviated—the meaning is established by means of a single syllable.
Regarding the establishment of the meanings of all syllables, just as the syllable *ka* establishes all syllables: *ka* has the meaning of "non-action" (*akṛta*).
When all syllables are established by means of this syllable, all syllables become non-action.

As stated in the sub-commentary (*vṛtti*), "All are like the system of Indra" refers to the fact that Śakra, the Lord of Devas, himself composed a treatise on phonology (*śabdavidyā*) within which [this principle is found].
Because there is this meaning, and because, like the nets upon the palace of Śakra-devendra, they interpenetrate one another in infinite layers,
it is said that all are according to the Indra-net system (*indrajāla*).

[Commentary: "The absence of suffering, its origin, and so forth" means that by entering the gate of the letter A, which is primordial non-arising (*an-utpāda*), one realizes that suffering, its origin, cessation, and the path are fundamentally unarisen;
there is only the True Truth (*satya-dharma*). It is like water freezing into ice: the ice is itself the water, and there is no water apart from it.
However, because sentient beings are deluded regarding suffering and its origin, they lose sight of the water of *dharmatā*. If they enter the gate of the letter A...

To thoroughly comprehend that suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are fundamentally non-arising is to realize the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), wherein only the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) exists; therefore, it is said that there is no suffering or origin, and so forth.
[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of the eight inversions (*aṣṭa-viparyāsa*) and so on: all sentient beings, due to delusion and inversion, conceive of all phenomena as...
"Purity is bliss, permanence, and self; now, regarding the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), impurity is suffering, impermanence, and non-self.
Having thus removed the four inversions through these foundations of mindfulness, if one still clings to them and does not relinquish them, they will again become the four inversions.
Now, by entering the gateway of the letter A, one realizes that the foundations of mindfulness are originally unarisen; they are merely the Dharma-realm, constituting true mindfulness.
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, one knows the eight inversions," etc., the "four bases of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*) refer to desire, effort, mind, and investigation.

All supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) arise from these; as the *Renwang jing shu* (Commentary on the Benevolent Kings Sūtra) states: "Desire, effort, mind, and investigation take meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as their essential nature.
Furthermore, the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva relies upon the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*)."
Because of the perfection of concentration (*samādhi*), one attains this basis of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) consisting of the accomplishment of the formative forces of desire (*chanda-saṃskāra*).
Likewise, through the accomplishment of the formative forces of diligence (*vīrya*), mind (*citta*), and investigation (*mīmāṃsā*)-concentration, the bodhisattva mahāsattva—
relying on such factors that assist the arousal of concentration, having thoroughly cultivated and perfectly established them so that they function with mastery— is able to act skillfully.

Having cultivated the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) and accomplished these four bases of psychic power, the bodhisattva mahāsattva—according to his aspirations and desires—is able to manifest before him various and manifold supernormal transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).

Although he manifests immeasurable supernatural powers and transformations, it is all for the sake of liberating all sentient beings. The term "originally unborn" (*an-utpanna*) refers to such as this.

The power of the deity is sufficient to seek through the four lines of the *a*-gate, yet nothing is found; thus one knows that from the beginning there has been no arising, and that it is entirely the *dharmadhātu*.
Therefore, one attains the accomplishment of the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of the *dharmadhātu*.

As for the statement "knowing what is possible and what is impossible" (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna*), knowing what is possible and what is impossible is the first of the Buddha’s ten powers (*daśabala*). When defining its essential nature (*svabhāva*), it is characterized by its specific quality.

If one takes wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essential nature, it consists of that alone; if one takes it together with its associated [mental states], it consists of the four aggregates (*skandha*) beginning with mind (*citta*);

if one takes it together with its retinue, it consists of all five aggregates. This is because the form (*rūpa*) associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the path (*mārga*), such as the untainted (*anāsrava*) matter, assists in the formation of the essence of wisdom.

Thus, knowing that the causes and effects of all phenomena correspond is called "the possible" (*sthāna*); knowing that causes and effects are contradictory is called "the impossible" (*asthāna*). — *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* (Baoji jing).

The Sūtra says: "That which is called 'possible' (sthāna) involves that which is grasped; for example, one who abstains from killing will experience long life, one who abstains from taking what is not given will experience great wealth, and one who abstains from sexual misconduct will obtain a faithful and virtuous wife—such statements as these refer to what is possible.
That which is called 'impossible' (asthāna) involves that which is not grasped; the opposite of the above should be understood accordingly. Regarding the phrase "knowing one's own mind," etc.:
This means that all sentient beings inherently possess the nature of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

because they do not know it as it truly is, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*), whereby they lose the various powers of wisdom of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas. When they come to know it as it truly is through self-awareness, it is then called clarity (*vidyā*).

The phrase "and so forth" includes great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and skillful means (*upāya*). As for the statement "originally unborn," although sentient beings and so forth— (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment. The translation above reflects the available portion.)
To know that the Buddha possesses such power of wisdom is merely to know it through faith; it cannot yet constitute the self-arisen power of wisdom of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
If one realizes that the letter *A* is fundamentally unborn (*anutpāda*), this is knowing reality as it is.

At the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*), one attains perfect awakening; it is not realized through another. Therefore, it is said that the six obscurations are fundamentally unborn, and so forth.

That which deviates from rationality and obscures the true word (*mantra*) consists precisely of the six types of afflictions, such as greed, which are the objects to be remedied by the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
Since these arise solely from delusion, by penetrating them through the syllable *A* and realizing their fundamental non-arising, one departs from that turbulent flow and ascends to the other shore.
To speak of "knowing the eighteen kinds of dharmas" refers to those dharmas unique to this vehicle and not shared with other vehicles; they are the Great Jewel.
The *Jijing* (Sūtra on Accumulation) states: "First, among the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), there is no error or failure in any of his actions;

that is to say, because the Tathāgata’s bodily action (*kāyakarman*) is ultimately free from error. Whether walking, coming, sitting, or reclining, his deportment is dignified and majestic, and his bodily radiance shines most brilliantly.

When he touches sentient beings, it causes them to experience pleasant sensations, and his body is devoid of any faulty marks. Likewise, the Tathāgata’s vocal action (*vākkarman*) is free from error."
Speaking truthful words, words that accord with reality, and so forth—all such speech is free from any fault; the Tathāgata’s mind is without error or omission;
he does not abandon the state of profound meditative concentration; and regarding all phenomena, his unimpeded wisdom and vision function spontaneously.
This is called the second unique Buddha-dharma, "the absence of failure in action. As for the third, "the absence of abruptness in speech," it is as follows:
All the speech and sounds of the Tathāgata are fundamentally free from abruptness or violence. Why? Because he has long since forever abandoned attachment, aversion, strife, litigation, and the like.
Third is the uncommon Buddha-dharma of non-forgetfulness of mindfulness: it means that the Tathāgata’s right mindfulness is without forgetfulness. Why?
Because he dwells in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), and samādhi, never neglecting or forgetting them.
Observing the mental activities of sentient beings, he proclaims the sublime Dharma as appropriate for them;

among the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of meaning, phenomena, definitions, and eloquence, he is without forgetfulness and so forth—this is the fourth unshared Buddha-attribute, the absence of a non-concentrated mind.
That is to say, whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, eating, speaking, or remaining silent, the Tathāgata always dwells in profound meditative concentration.

There is no time when he is not in a state of departure. Why? Because the Tathāgata has realized the profound samādhi and unobstructed dhyāna, and is forever free from a distracted mind. Fifth, there is the uncommon Buddha-quality of being free from all diverse perceptions;
that is to say, the Tathāgata is free from all diverse perceptions, such that even toward those who maintain the precepts, his mind is without attachment, and likewise toward those who violate them.
Because his mind is free from anger and the like, he is called the Tathāgata who possesses no diverse perceptions. Sixth is the unshared Buddha-dharma of equanimity without discrimination:
this means that the Tathāgata has already cultivated the noble path and realized this equanimity; it is not something realized by one who has not cultivated the path.
The equanimity of the Tathāgata enables him to turn the Brahma-wheel, out of compassion for sentient beings, remaining neither haughty nor detached.
The second is the uncommon Buddha-dharma of the non-decline of resolve (*chanda*), which transcends all extremes and surpasses all conceptualization and discrimination.

This refers to the Tathāgata’s non-decline of resolve for the wholesome dharmas, non-decline of resolve for great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), non-decline of resolve for great compassion (*karuṇā*), and non-decline of resolve for teaching the Dharma.
The eighth is the uncommon Buddha-dharma of the non-decline of right effort (*vīrya*).

The ninth unshared Buddha-dharma, which consists of non-retrogression and non-decline in mindfulness, refers to the Tathāgata’s diligent application in not abandoning the sentient beings to be converted, up to and including his continuous preaching of the Dharma without even a moment's interruption—free from conditions such as food or drink—and so forth.

This means that immediately upon attaining enlightenment, the Tathāgata observes the mental continuums of all sentient beings throughout their past and future lives; having known them, the Tathāgata...
Within this, there is the thirteenth *samādhi*, known as "Ultimate and Unfailing Knowledge," which is free from decline and is an unshared Buddha-dharma called the Buddha-samādhi;
it extends even to the point where the limit of saṃsāra is equal to the limit of nirvāṇa. Because the Tathāgata has realized such equality, he abides in samādhi.

Eleventh, the uncommon Buddha-dharma of non-deficiency in wisdom: it refers to the Tathāgata’s possession of inexhaustible knowledge through the realization and entry into a single phrase, which could be explained for hundreds of thousands of great eons, as well as unobstructed knowledge regarding all things.
Twelfth, the uncommon Buddha-dharma of non-deficiency in liberation: it refers to the Bhagavat being utterly free from all [defilements].
Because one is liberated by abandoning attachment to the two extremes, such liberation is unbound in the past and does not proceed toward the future;
because it does not abide in the present, it is equal [to all]. Thirteenth, the uncommon Buddha-dharma of physical action being preceded by wisdom:
that is to say, all the Tathāgata’s physical actions are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom. Fourteenth, verbal action being preceded by wisdom...
The fifteenth unique Buddha-dharma, the guidance of all verbal actions by wisdom: that is to say, all verbal actions of the Tathāgata are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom.
The sixteenth unique Buddha-dharma, the guidance of all mental actions by wisdom:
that is to say, all mental actions of the Tathāgata are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom. The seventeenth unique Buddha-dharma, unimpeded knowledge of the past.
The Dharma refers to the Tathāgata’s unimpeded knowledge that, through his unhindered cognition, knows all the Buddha-fields throughout the immeasurable and boundless past,
whether they are forming or decaying; this is the seventeenth unique Buddha-dharma of unhindered knowledge regarding the future,
which means knowing all the Tathāgatas who will appear or pass away in the future world.
The eighteenth unshared Buddha-dharma, the unhindered knowledge of the present, refers to the Tathāgata’s complete and thorough comprehension of all things equal to those [past and future] aspects.
That is to say, regarding the present world, the Tathāgata knows in full detail all the Buddhas,
the assemblies of Bodhisattvas, the assemblies of Śrāvakas, and the assemblies of Pratyekabuddhas within all the Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions.
To be able to fully comprehend all distinctions and so forth is called the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
Furthermore, because these dharmas enter the letter *A*, which is fundamentally unarisen, the meaning of their uniqueness is even more extraordinary than that of other schools.
[Sūtra] Regarding the phrase "the gateway of the letter A" and so forth: whenever one opens the mouth, the sound *a* invariably arises first.
This sound *a* is the mother of all sounds, for it can give rise to the sounds of all mantras; therefore, it is called the "mother.

Furthermore, this sound *a* gives rise to the fourteen vowels, which constitute the twelve chapters [of the *Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha*]. Since these are not explicitly revealed in the commentary (*vṛtti*), they must be distinguished according to their basis.

These syllables, through their mutual interaction, are able to produce all sounds and words; they are divided into twelve chapters, which encompass and exhaust all speech and sound. That is to say, first, with the short vowel *a*, one flows into the short vowels *ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa; ca, cha, ja, jha, ña; ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa; ta, tha, da, dha, na; pa, pha, ba, bha, ma*. *Ya* follows *ma*. *Ra* follows *ya*. *La* follows *ra*. *Va* follows *la*. *Śa* follows *va*. *Ṣa* follows *śa*. *Sa* follows *ṣa*. *Ha* follows *sa*. *Kṣa* follows *ha*. Thus, these forty-two letters are the source from which all sounds and words arise. Furthermore, by combining these forty-two letters according to the rules of grammar, one can produce all words and phrases. Because they are the source of all sounds and words, they are called the "Source of All Sounds" (*sarva-śabda-ākara*). Because they are the source of all dharmas, they are called the "Source of All Dharmas" (*sarva-dharma-ākara*). Because they are the source of all Buddhas, they are called the "Source of All Buddhas" (*sarva-buddha-ākara*). Because they are the source of all Bodhisattvas, they are called the "Source of All Bodhisattvas" (*sarva-bodhisattva-ākara*). Because they are the source of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, they are called the "Source of All Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas" (*sarva-śrāvaka-pratyekabuddha-ākara*). Because they are the source of all mundane and supramundane dharmas, they are called the "Source of All Mundane and Supramundane Dharmas" (*sarva-laukika-lokottara-dharma-ākara*). Because they are the source of all worldly and transcendental dharmas, they are called the "Source of All Worldly and Transcendental Dharmas" (*sarva-lokottara-dharma-ākara*). Because they are the source of all conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, they are called the "Source of All Conditioned and Unconditioned Dharmas" (*sarva-saṃskṛta-asaṃskṛta-dharma-ākara*). Because they are the source of all dharmas of the three times, they are called the "Source of All Dharmas of the Three Times" (*sarva-trikāla-dharma-ākara*). Because they are the source of all dharmas of the ten directions, they are called the "Source of All Dharmas of the Ten Directions" (*sarva-daśadig-dharma-ākara*). Because they are the source of all dharmas of the three realms, they are called the "Source of All Dharmas of the Three Realms" (*sarva-tridhātu-dharma-ākara*). Because they are the source of all dharmas of the five aggregates, they are called the "Source of All Dharmas of the Five Aggregates" (*sarva-pañca-skandha-dharma-ākara*). Because they are the source of all dharmas of the six sense bases, they are called the "Source of All Dharmas of the Six Sense Bases" (*sarva-ṣaḍāyatana-dharma-ākara*). Because they are the source of all dharmas of the eighteen elements, they are called the "Source of All Dharmas of the Eighteen Elements" (*sarva-aṣṭādaśadhātu-dharma-ākara*). Because they are the source of all dharmas of the twelve links of dependent origination, they are called the "Source of All Dharmas of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination" (*sarva-dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-dharma-ākara*). Because they are the source of all dharmas of the four truths, they are called the "Source of All Dharmas of the Four Truths" (*sarva-catur-ārya-satya-dharma-ākara*). Because they are the source of all dharmas of the two vehicles, they are called the "Source of All Dharmas of the Two Vehicles" (*sarva-dvi-yāna-dharma-ākara*). Because they are the source of all dharmas of the Mahāyāna, they are called the "Source of All Dharmas of the Mahāyāna" (*sarva-mahāyāna-dharma-ākara*). Because they are the source of all dharmas of the Buddha-vehicle, they are called the "Source of All Dharmas of the Buddha-Vehicle" (*sarva-buddha-yāna-dharma-ākara*). Because they are the source of all dharmas of the Tathāgata, they are called the "Source of All Dharmas of the Tathāgata" (*sarva-tathāgata-dharma-ākara*). Because they are the source of all dharmas of the Dharma-body, they are called the "Source of All Dharmas of the Dharma-Body" (*sarva-dharma-kāya-dharma-ākara*). Because they are the source of all dharmas of the Sambhogakāya, they are called the "Source of All Dharmas of the Sambhogakāya" (*sarva-sambhoga-kāya-dharma-ākara*). Because they are the source of all dharmas of the Nirmāṇakāya, they are called the "Source of All Dharmas of the Nirmāṇakāya" (*sarva-nirmāṇa-kāya-dharma-ākara*). Because they are the source of all dharmas of the three bodies, they are called the "Source of All Dharmas of the Three Bodies" (*sarva-tri-kāya-dharma-ākara*).
