The thirty-three characters—zhuó, chuò, náo, zhuó, niè, tuō, tuō, nǎo, dù, nuò, bó, bó, lù, máo (upper tone), bó, mò, yào, luò, luò, fá, zhuó, shuò, suǒ, hào, etc.—are to be applied in sequence as above throughout the entire first chapter;
only then is the structure of the first chapter perfected, which constitutes the exhaustive application of the principles.
Otherwise, the phonology and meaning would be insufficient. Next, the second chapter is explained, following the first chapter.
If one takes the single sounds "a-a" and so forth as the head and proceeds through all the subsequent characters to form a chapter, this constitutes the first.
Now, for the second, one takes the twelve vowels in total and applies them across all the subsequent characters to form the second chapter;

that is, first taking the sounds "a-a-i-e" up to "aṃ-aḥ," one applies them across the thirty-three characters below, each ascending step-by-step until they have been traversed completely. As follows: [The text continues with the phonetic application of the vowels across the consonants.]

Having completed one cycle of *ka*, *kā*, *ki*, *kī*, *ku*, *kū*, *ke*, *kei*, *ko*, *kau*, *kaṃ*, and *kaḥ*, next take the letter *kha* as the head and proceed with another cycle according to the sequence of the wheel above, namely:
*kha*, *khā*, *khi*, *khī*, and so on, up to *khaṃ* and *khaḥ*. Thus, these thirty-three letters are traversed in their entirety;
this constitutes the second chapter. If they are combined, [they begin with] *a*, *ā*, and so forth.
These are *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*; *ca*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha*, *ña*; *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, *ḍha*, *ṇa*; *ta*, *tha*, *da*, *dha*, *na*;
*pa*, *pha*, *ba*, *bha*, *ma*; *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, *ha*, *kṣa*.

This concludes the third chapter, the chapter on repetition (*punarukta*), which explains how the letter *ka* is sequentially applied to the following thirty-three letters, such as *ka-kha* (short and long), *ga-gha*, *ṅa-ca*, *ca-cha*, *ja-jha*, *ña-ṭa*, *ṭa-ṭha*, *ḍa-ḍha*, *ṇa-ta*, *ta-tha*, *da-dha*, *na-pa*, *pa-pha*, *ba-bha*, *ma-ya*, *ya-ra*, *ra-la*, *la-va*, *va-śa*, *śa-ṣa*, *ṣa-sa*, *sa-ha*, and *ha-kṣa*.
*Kai*, *kya*, *khu*, *kyu*, *ki*, *kyi*, *ku*, *kya*, *ke*, *ko*, followed by *tsa* and *ri*; then from *ga* and *gya* up to the letter *ha*—this constitutes the third chapter in its entirety.
Next, following this, one proceeds downward from the letter *ga* and back again from the letter *ka*, assigning them in sequence as follows:
*ga-ka*, *ga-ga*, *ga-gi*, *ga-gye*, up to *ga-gan* and *ga-gyō*. In this manner, these thirty-three characters are assigned and traversed in their entirety to form the [fourth chapter].
The fourth chapter follows with the five sibilant sounds, ending with the letter *ya*. The fifth chapter proceeds from the letter *ka* sequentially until the letter *ha*.

Thus, taking each of the fifth letters of the retroflex (*jihvāmūlīya*), dental (*tālavya*), and labial (*oṣṭhya*) groups as the starting point, one cycles through them in conjunction with the letters from *ka* to *ha* until the cycle is complete; this constitutes the [fifth] chapter.

The sixth, seventh, and eighth chapters likewise take the four syllables *ca*, *u*, *śra*, and *la-va* as their respective heads, arranging them one by one as before to complete the four surrounding sections;
these constitute the ninth through twelfth chapters. Because the Great Parinirvāṇa is established through these twelve chapters, I have now transcribed and explained this chapter.
Although its constituent parts are interlinked like a chain, they are divided into upper and lower sections.
It appears that there may be some incompleteness here. For instance, regarding the twenty-five consonants beginning with *ka*:

first, one takes the letter *ka* and sequentially combines it with each letter from *kha* through *ha*. Furthermore, from within each of the five classes of phonemes, one takes one letter and combines it with *ka*, continuing this until *ha*.
These constitute six chapters; when added to the two preceding chapters consisting of single pronunciations, they together form eight chapters. Next...
Regarding the eight syllables of the *atīta* (transcendent), the syllable *ya* is joined with the syllable *ka*; next, the three syllables *ra-ra-va* are joined as before.
These together constitute twelve. Below these are the four syllables *śa-ṣa-sa-ha*, which are not taken as the head for joining with the various syllables;
if they were all taken, the number of chapters would become sixteen. Therefore, they are not taken. If [they were] not... [the sentence is incomplete].
To employ the term "taking" (qu) would result in the error of failing to exhaust the phonetic range of "taking. We shall now revise this:

by means of the twelve sounds—*a*, *ā*, *i*, *e*, *o*, *u*, *ai*, *ei*, *ou*, *ao*, *an*, and *en*—one should adjust them according to the sequence of the even (*ping*), rising (*shang*), departing (*qu*), and entering (*ru*) tones, ensuring they do not deviate; this is called "name" (*ming*).
The harmonization of sounds and their unified resonance—whereby sounds such as *pi*, *chao*, and others do not become confused—constitutes twelve chapters.
First, the short vowel *a* flows into the short vowels *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*, and so on, up to *sa* and *ha*;
this constitutes the first chapter, beginning with the short vowel *a*. Next, the long vowel *ā* flows through the long vowels *kā*, *khā*, *gā*, [and so forth].
From *ga-aṃ* onwards, proceeding in sequence directly to *saha*, one forms the second chapter of long vowels beginning with the syllable *a*.
Furthermore, from the syllable *i* flowing through to *kī khī gī cī jī* and up to *śī hī*, this constitutes the third chapter of the vowel *i*.
Again, from the syllable *e* flowing into *ke khe ge ce je* and up to *se he*, this constitutes the fourth.

The chapter on the syllable *e* and others further takes the syllable *u* and flows into short vowels; taking *yu*, *ju*, *gu*, *yu*, up to *su* and *hu*, these constitute the fifth chapter on the syllable *u*.

Furthermore, from the syllable *u* up to the syllable *jya*, they follow the flow of sound in sequence as before, thereby forming the twelve chapters from the name of the syllable *u* up to the syllable *jya*. This is established with certainty.

Having first determined the number of chapters in twelve sections, one then combines them two by two, three by three, four by four, five by five, and so forth, taking one sound as the principal and the remaining sounds as its companions.
Thus, there arise infinite chapters of vocal sound, like the net of Indra, without mutual obstruction.
If it is done in this manner, there will be no fault of failing to encompass all characters; may those who read this understand it. Hereafter, the pronunciations are explained.
Regarding the enumeration, it is divided into two parts: first, the general, and second, the specific.
First, as for the *Siddham* syllabary, not only is it opened out into twelve chapters, but it can also generally encompass all categories of phonemes.
That is to say, from *a-a* through to *aṃ-aḥ*, these sixteen sounds of this region are established as the definitive set. Question: Regarding the two characters *a-a* and so forth, up to *aṃ-aḥ*...
Question: Since there are only twelve syllables in the *Vyañjana* (consonants), why does the Sūtra speak of fourteen sounds? Answer:

It is because after these twelve syllables, there are four additional auxiliary phonemes—*ṛ*, *ḷ*, *lṛ*, and *lṝ*. Objection: If that were so, by adding these four further syllables, the total would become sixteen.
Response: These four syllables cannot function as primary vowels (*mātṛkā*); they serve only as auxiliaries, following upon the consonants (*vyañjana*).
Since two [consonants] are taken from each of the "direct" (*ṭhita*) and "intermediate" (*antaḥsthā*) positions of the tongue, fourteen [sounds] are formed.
For example, when the letter *ka* is joined with *ṛ*, *ṝ*, and *ḷ*, the Brāhmī script is exactly this; however, these are merely the characters commonly used by the general populace in the West.
Furthermore, in the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), the Brāhmī script is as follows: for instance, when the letter *ka* is joined with *ṝ*, *ṝ*, and *ḷ*, the Brāhmī script is exactly this.

Regarding "if one assists the skillful," the Brahmī script itself is such that if one knows the locus where the four syllables are subsumed, their essential nature is precisely the two syllables *ra* and *la*; therefore, it is not correct to take both together.
To take the latter two sounds from among the twelve vowels as the "sounds that assist skill" is incorrect. As for the subsequent separate explanation, it refers to this wheel of fourteen phonemes.
In this chapter, only the sounds are listed without their meanings being revealed; thus, the practitioner lacks the complete factors for cultivation.
I shall now explain them individually. First, regarding the short sound *a*, there are three meanings. First, concerning its indestructibility:
it refers to the fact that the essence of the Three Jewels in their single reality is as firm and solid as a vajra; because it is indestructible, it is inexhaustible.
Because it is extinguished, there is no exhaustion; because it is extinguished, it is truly eternal. That which is truly eternal is Great Parinirvāṇa. Second, regarding non-outflow:
the Tathāgata has no leakage from the nine apertures. The nine apertures consist of the two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, the gate of speech, and the two secret orifices.
Thus, the five sense faculties are without loss. Even the names and designations for the five faculties of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body do not exist.
Since even [the conditioned] cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be any outflows? The essence of true permanence is itself nirvāṇa. Third, regarding the reliance on merit:
this does not mean the accumulation of merit through effort, but rather refers to the inherently pure merits that are originally present.
This is precisely the true, permanent nirvāṇa revealed by these three meanings; for this reason, it is called "A" (Ā). Next, the second long vowel is explained.
The letter *A* is the practice of primordial non-arising (*an-utpāda*). In Sanskrit, the letter *A* signifies the meaning of *ācārya*.
There are four meanings of *ācārya*: first, in the sense of relying on instruction, it refers to one who causes the arising of virtue, namely the direct preceptor (*upādhyāya*);
second, in the sense of relying on the system of rules, it refers to the *Abhidharma*, as it reveals the various Mahāyāna precepts and dignified conduct; third... [text continues].
Based on the meaning of "noble one" (*ārya*): in the Sanskrit language this is *ārya*, which means "one who has distanced himself from evil.

It is translated as "noble one" because it serves as a general designation for all noble ones of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Fourth, based on the meaning of "instruction": that is, teaching and guiding others to cease evil and cultivate goodness.
Because of these four meanings, it is called *ā*. Regarding the third, the gate of the letter *i*: this is according to the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*).
The middle is the female voice; that which is manifested by the letter *I* is precisely the Buddha-dharma. There are two aspects of the Buddha-dharma:

first, the Dharma of realization (*adhigama-dharma*), and second, the Dharma of teaching (*deśanā-dharma*). There are two aspects to the Dharma of realization: first, the realized object, which is the truth of *nirvāṇa*;

and second, the realizing subject, which is the wisdom of the true essence (*samyag-jñāna*). The Dharma of teaching also has two aspects: first, the general, which refers collectively to the three vehicles (*triyāna*); and second, the specific, which refers to—
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa* relies upon this teaching to purify the holy life (*brahmacarya*), perfect right wisdom, and realize great *nirvāṇa*.
Since the letter "I" (*i*) elucidates and reveals this dharma, it is said that "I" is itself the Buddha-dharma. Regarding the fourth gate, the letter "E" (*e*):
"E" signifies sovereignty (*vaśitā*). Based on two types of explanations, first sovereignty is explained in general, and subsequently it is explained in detail.
Furthermore, regarding the initial mention of "sovereignty" (*īśvara*) by the Protector of the Dharma:

this is a metaphorical illustration used to clarify that, according to the tenets of non-Buddhist schools, the one capable of producing all things is the deity Īśvara; because he is the father and mother of the world, he is called the "World-Honored One.
As stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha-sūtra*, when the non-Buddhists heard the Buddha’s teaching that all phenomena are unborn and primordially pure, they were startled and bewildered.
He then spoke these words: "This doctrine is not correct. Maheśvara is eternal and is the progenitor of all myriad things;
he can give rise to all dharmas, he can create and fashion, and he establishes the world. Thereupon, the Tathāgata refuted him with various principles, yet his logic remained unconvincing.
Consequently, he attained right view. Now, as for the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas, if one were to confront it...

The number of atoms in the dust of the world during the time of Īśvara is beyond all calculation; how could it serve as a metaphor? Since Īśvara is known by the people of the world, he is cited as a metaphor.
Above, the sovereignty of Īśvara was explained in general; below, the protection of the Dharma (Dharmapāla) is explained in detail:

first, with respect to Mahābrahmā; second, with respect to the World-Protectors (Lokapālas); third, with respect to the speaker; fourth, with respect to the purpose; and fifth, with respect to that which is to be severed. Now, regarding the first point, "self":

That which exists is called Mahābrahmā, who is the Great Brahmā Deva King. Now, while the four dhyānas of the Form Realm are collectively termed the Brahma-world (*Brahmaloka*), the third dhyāna of the first stage is also specifically named Mahābrahmā. The one cited here, however, is the Brahma King of the fourth dhyāna.
This Brahma Deva King takes the syllable *i* as his seed-syllable; the dharmas that flow forth from it are called "sovereign" (*vaśitā*). If one receives [this teaching]...
"To uphold" is what these non-Buddhists claim constitutes "protecting the Dharma.

However, within the Buddha-Dharma, the Great Brahmā is surpassed by the true, eternal Buddha-nature, which is naturally luminous and pure. It is likened to the celestial Lord, sovereign and unimpeded.

If one receives and upholds [this teaching], it is called "protecting the Dharma. There are two ways of protecting the Dharma: first, receiving and upholding it for oneself, relying upon it to cultivate and realize [the truth].

Second, to cause others to accept and uphold [the teaching], to lead them toward the true path, and to sustain and protect it so that it remains uninterrupted—this is the true protection of the Dharma.
Therefore, the syllable *i* is called "sovereignty" (*īśvara*). Furthermore, "sovereignty" refers to the Protectors of the World (*lokapāla*), namely the Four Heavenly Kings.
Because these four kings are able to protect the world, they are called the "Four Kings. Of these, the one in the east is named Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of the gandharvas in the south, known as "Increasing";
Virūpākṣa, or Virūḍhaka, the lord of the kumbhāṇḍas in the west, known as "Ugly-Eyed" or "Broad-Eyed," who is the lord of the nāgas;
and Vaiśravaṇa, known as "Much-Hearing," the lord of the yakṣas in the north—these four Great Kings and their retinues constantly protect the world and are all able to guard the Tathāgata.
The Dharma can also be expounded and proclaimed for others. Furthermore, the four world-protectors (*lokapāla*) represent the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*);
they also represent the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and so forth.

Because one is able to protect oneself and protect others by relying upon these, it is said that they are "based on the world-protectors. Thirdly, regarding the speaker: furthermore, *īśvara* means one who is able to speak with mastery.
That is to say, one realizes Great Nirvana and attains true liberation, which is called "sovereign great liberation. Within this sovereign great liberation, there are eight sovereignties (*vaśitā*).
In order to cause sentient beings to attain these sovereignties, the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is established so that they may diligently practice it;

therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] is able to teach with sovereignty. Fourth, regarding the purpose (*prayojana*): this character *yi* (縊) signifies the purpose, which is the ability to act for oneself...

"Practicing" refers to the cultivation and accumulation of the Vaipulya sūtras. "Vaipulya" is that which is elucidated by these sūtras; one who delights in practicing the Vaipulya constantly studies these sūtras.
By relying on these sūtras, one awakens to the principle of the Vaipulya. What is the fundamental purpose of such cultivation and awakening?
It is because one desires to realize the great parinirvāṇa and attain great mastery; therefore, it is said that this is undertaken for the sake of what is to be accomplished.
Therefore, regarding the five points concerning that which is to be abandoned: this character *i* (縊) signifies that which is to be abandoned because it denotes mastery over what is to be abandoned.
As for the phenomena to be abandoned, they refer to the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-paryavasthāna*), for it is an obstacle to mastery and must therefore be severed.

Furthermore, the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*) is the sublime medicine that sustains [the practitioner]. Since sentient beings have, from time immemorial, possessed deeply heavy defilements of karma, when they see others obtain...

If one feels heat and affliction in the mind because another has gained profit or surpassed oneself, constantly desiring to destroy them so that they do not have their way, one will thereby be bound and long remain submerged within the three realms, unable to attain mastery. All virtuous merits will be defiled by this.
If one wishes to transcend [suffering] and attain mastery, one must sever it; once it is eliminated, all virtues will become perfected.
Because it is full, one is able to proclaim the Dharma of the Great Parinirvāṇa; therefore, it is said that this refers to what is to be severed.

For this reason, "i" (e) is called sovereignty (*vaśitā*). Next, to clarify the fifth gateway, the syllable "u": the syllable "u" signifies that all dharmas are such that no analogy can be found for them.
If there were an analogy, it would not be supreme; thus, the Great Nirvāṇa is unsurpassed among all the Vaipulya sūtras.
Because it further transcends even the most supreme teachings, it is also called "the highest of the high" (*uttarottara*).

Because no analogy can be found for it, the sixth syllable-gateway, *u*, elucidates the meaning of the absence of wisdom and mindfulness. This is because, due to the lack of right mindfulness regarding the meaning [of reality], one falsely imagines a self within all phenomena;
consequently, many sentient beings in the world give rise to slander and revilement toward the secret treasury.
The secret refers to the true self of nirvāṇa; all sentient beings are deluded by it and engage in false conceptualization, just like the analogy of the prince who lost his precious sword.
The prince took the precious sword with him, yet the poor man spoke of it in delusion.
The Bodhisattvas explain the True Vehicle, for which reason they separately open up skillful means to shatter those attachments and reveal that all phenomena are truly non-existent.
The character *wu* (烏) signifies the absence of wisdom and mindfulness; it is said that because one possesses a self, one lacks such wisdom and mindfulness.

The seventh gate, the character *yi* (翳), explains the meaning that all phenomena cannot be found when sought: the Buddha-nature and *nirvāṇa* are remote from both nature and characteristics, beyond the reach of mind and speech, and thus not something to be sought.
As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If one were to see me by means of form, or seek me by means of sound..."
Those who seek a self follow a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata; therefore, it is said that "ā" signifies that all dharmas are sought but cannot be found.
The eighth is the gateway of the letter Ā. "Ā" has two meanings: first, it signifies that the sovereignty of all dharmas cannot be found.
Sovereignty is established in relation to its opposite, and because its opposite is bondage, it is so named.
From now until the present, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have attained true liberation and are truly sovereign.

That which is called "unattainable" refers to the fact that within the principle of true permanence, both the names "bondage" and "liberation" are unattainable; this is precisely the meaning of the character *ai* (藹) as it accords with reality.

Furthermore, the two instances of *ai* signify the excellence of majestic demeanor (*īryāpatha*); every movement and stillness of the Tathāgata’s majestic demeanor is nothing other than benefiting all beings.

Because of sentient beings, it is said that "Āi" (藹) signifies the superior sound of majestic deportment; this is the ninth gateway of the letter *u* (*wu*), which elucidates the meaning of afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Fan" (煩) refers to vexation and agitation, while "nǎo" (惱) refers to distress and harm. By means of these, one may either agitate the practitioner or distress and harm their virtues.

These consist of both the root afflictions and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), as well as the innate (*sahaja*) and the discriminative (*vikalpita*). The discriminative, being coarse and superficial, is eliminated upon entering the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); the innate, being subtle, is eliminated later.
Therefore, the fruit of Buddhahood is only fully realized when this character is uttered. When pronouncing this character, there is grasping at sound;
this grasping is an outflow (*āsrava*), and that which is an outflow is called a "stream. The Tathāgata does not flow; to not flow is to be unmoving; to be unmoving is to be unborn.
The essence of the Buddha is true and eternal, fundamentally free from arising and ceasing. This absence of arising and ceasing is termed Great Nirvāṇa. Thus, the character *wu* (汚) elucidates this.
In all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), afflictions (*kleśa*) are unattainable. The tenth gateway of the letter *Au* elucidates the meaning of the Mahāyāna.

The meaning of the Mahāyāna is precisely the True and Eternal; that which is the True and Eternal is precisely the Ultimate. Now, this ultimate meaning is simply that which is elucidated [by the Mahāyāna]. There are two aspects to the Mahāyāna:
first, the inclusive sense, which encompasses all Mahāyāna within the aforementioned nine divisions [of the scriptures].
"Because it is attained as the ultimate, I say that these ninefold teachings of mine take the Mahāyāna as their foundation.
Second, this clarifies that the perfect and ultimate reality revealed by this *Nirvāṇa* is the final goal.

Furthermore, the scriptures of the non-Buddhists, when compared to the internal teachings (Buddhism), are merely termed "all revealed dharmas" which are generally not ultimate; now, the meaning revealed by the Mahāyāna sūtras is [the ultimate].
Because the principle is exhausted and the nature is fully realized, all are termed "ultimate"; thus it is said that the letter *A* (Ā) signifies the meaning of the Mahāyāna, etc., as the eleventh.
The gate of the letter *Kha* (Khā) signifies the meaning of being able to obstruct impure things; that is to say, gold, silver, and precious objects are precisely what is to be obstructed.

Worldly paupers are called *śramaṇas*; through the practice of mindfulness and contemplation, they employ these means to eliminate greed and attachment, for gold, jewels, and the like are of this world.
Ordinary people cherish these things, and upon seeing them, they all give rise to attachment; because this leads to the production of various tainted (*sāsrava*) karmas, they are called "impure.
All disciples of the Buddhas should abandon them. There are two kinds of abandonment: first, giving what one possesses to the Triple Gem;
second, not giving rise to greedy attachment toward anything belonging to others. If one does not abandon them, one must guard against them throughout the entire day.
Since causing others to doubt or obstruct one’s own practice results in a complete lack of leisure (*akṣaṇa*), those who aspire to the path must renounce such things.
Furthermore, it is not merely that one can renounce all impure objects such as jewels and the like; rather, one must actually renounce all afflictions (*kleśa*).
As the *Siddhi-prakaraṇa* states: "Moreover, in another month, one completely renounces all that is internal and external. This is precisely the meaning [of this passage].
Thus, this character can also manifest the meaning of the fruit of Great Bodhi. Therefore it is said: "The character *aṃ* explains the meaning of being able to exclude impure things.
(12) Regarding the character door of *a* (*akuśala*): it explains the meaning that all dharmas are far removed and unobtainable.

This means that when the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādikṣaya-jñāna*) arises, there is no longer non-enlightenment; at that time, initial enlightenment is itself original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*).

Fundamentally, non-duality is called ultimate awakening; therefore, when one realizes nirvāṇa, ignorance is transformed into clarity, for ignorance is itself clarity and thus there is nothing to be abandoned.
When a bodhisattva enters nirvāṇa, they see that all sentient beings are originally quiescent, because they have realized that all phenomena are without anything to be abandoned.
For this reason, it is called "entering the realization of Mahāparinirvāṇa. Thus it is said: "Evil..."

The syllable signifies the meaning of all phenomena being remote and unapprehendable. Furthermore, the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Syllables," states: the vowel *a* (high tone) is the sound of impermanence;
the vowel *ā* (low tone, with *ā* as a protracted vowel) is the sound of remoteness from self; the vowel *i* (high tone) is the sound of the vastness of the sense faculties;
the vowel *ī* (low tone, with *ī* as a protracted vowel) is the sound of worldly calamities; and the syllable *u* (high tone) is of many kinds.

The sound *ṛ* (with svarabhakti) signifies the voice of the affliction that oppresses many sentient beings in the world; the sound *lṝ* (with svarabhakti) signifies the voice of sentient beings who are direct and gentle in their continuity;
the sound *lṝ* (with svarabhakti and udātta) signifies the voice of severing the play of defilements; the sound *lṝ* signifies the voice of the arising of the characteristics of phenomena;
the sound *lṝ* signifies the voice of the continuity of defilement within the three realms of existence; the sound *e* signifies the voice of initiating what is sought; the sound *ai*...
The syllable *ja* is the sound of superior majestic deportment; *ca* is the sound of grasping; *oṃ* is the sound of miraculous birth;

*aṃ* is the sound of non-possession (*anātman*); and *aḥ* is the sound of sinking. Since the meanings of these twelve syllables have been briefly clarified above, they constitute the essential point here.
Is it not for this reason that the preface to the Commentary states: "Regarding the fact that there are one or two omissions herein, could it be because of this?"

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "as the various non-Buddhists reckon," this refers to how certain non-Buddhist scholars and theorists, apart from causes, reckon that there is a creator and so forth;

because they reckon that effects and retributions exist through such combinations, if a practitioner perceives a creator and so forth within the three mysteries (of body, speech, and mind), they would be identical to the non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, since a creator is a characteristic that arises dependently upon a created object, it lacks any definitive nature. If...

To hold this as definitive is no different from the non-Buddhists; thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* refutes it, saying: "If you claim that an agent exists who performs an action, then there would be no cause;
because there is no cause, it cannot produce an effect," and so forth.
[Commentary: Regarding the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*’s examination of the six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*), these six are earth, water, fire, wind, space (*ākāśa*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Here, we specifically take up space. As a verse in that treatise states: "In the midst of the characterized (*nimitta*) and the uncharacterized (*animitta*), the characteristic has no place to abide.

Apart from the characterized and the uncharacterized, it is likewise in other places. This reveals that both the two characteristics of existence and non-existence have no place to abide; since space is thus...
The same applies to the other five [elements] as well. Furthermore, a verse states: "Therefore, one knows that space is neither existent nor non-existent;
it is neither a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) nor that which possesses characteristics (*lakṣya*); the other five are equal to space.

Now, the gateway of the letter *kha* does not abide in any phenomenon, whether characterized or uncharacterized, because it is like space and so forth. Therefore, it is said in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, in the examination of the six elements, and so on.
[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "if a person does not move from their original location," that treatise asks:

"Although you have refuted 'going' and the 'goer,' as well as 'staying' and the 'stayer' through various methods, one still sees going and staying with the eye. The answer is: "What is seen by the fleshly eye is not to be trusted.
Therefore, the Commentary states: "If a person does not move from their original location, that is precisely the place they have reached."

[Commentary: As for the mention of *vipaśyanā* (insight) and so forth—*vipaśyanā* is translated here as "superior observation" (*shèngguān*)—it is not yet clear which specific superior observation is capable of destroying the afflictions (*kleśa*).
If it belongs to the category of "observation," then observation is wisdom (*prajñā*), wisdom is the agent that conquers, and the afflictions are the objects to be conquered.
This is precisely to distinguish the essence of the combatant in the battle. The general intent of this inquiry is as follows: [Is it the case that] all...
Since, within the Dharma, the definitions of a "self" as refuted by various treatises cannot be established, to whom ultimately do wisdom and afflictions belong?
How can it be said at this time that *vipaśyanā* is able to destroy the afflictions?
[Commentary]: "Light and darkness ultimately do not reach one another" means that phenomena which are mutually exclusive (*pratidvandva*) cannot logically coexist;

how, then, could one destroy the other? This passage specifically challenges the claim that it can be said [the afflictions] are severed. If we discuss the meaning of severance, their essential natures and characteristics are different.

Thus, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "Neither at the beginning, nor in the middle, nor at the end. This refers to their essential nature (*svabhāva*); when sought throughout the three periods of time, they cannot be said [to exist].

"Cutting off is itself non-cutting. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "It is like the flame of a lamp; one grasps it in its beginning, middle, and end. This refers to the characteristics [of the flame].

If one were to grasp all three times simultaneously, one could speak of "cutting off. Thus, while the Sūtra and the Śāstra appear to contradict each other in their phrasing, their underlying intent complements one another.

Why is this? Because by means of the Śāstra’s provisional use of the three times, one comes to know the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), which then accords with the meaning of the Sūtra—since [the flame] is neither the beginning, nor the middle, nor the end.
That which is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is precisely the non-obstruction and non-interruption of the characteristics of nature;

it is the severance that is itself without severance. [Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the passage "all dharmas are fundamentally unarisen," the following establishes the opponent by means of a sudden, absolute, and entirely true discourse on the worldly level, wherein there is no further sense of severance.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the pride that arises" and so forth, this refers to the *ṭa*-gate (*ṭakāra-dvāra*), wherein the pride of all dharmas is unobtainable.

One who enters this gate does not perceive the characteristics of superiority or inferiority between self and other; if one gives rise to views of high and low or inequality, it is called "pride" (*māna*).
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "What is meant by pride? It is the nature of exalting oneself in relation to others based on self-reliance."
Its function is to obstruct the arising of non-arrogance and to produce suffering. That is to say, if there is pride, the mind does not become humble toward those who possess virtue;
because of this, one wanders through birth and death in an endless succession. This pride is divided into seven types:

first, pride (*māna*), which is the mental exaltation that arises toward those who are inferior to oneself, such as friends and the like; second, excessive pride (*atimāna*), which is to consider oneself superior to those who are one's equals.

1. *Māna* (pride): regarding others who are superior, one considers oneself superior. 2. *Atimāna* (excessive pride): regarding others who are superior, one considers oneself even more superior. 3. *Mānātimāna* (pride beyond pride): regarding others who are equal, one considers oneself superior. 4. *Asmimāna* (the pride of "I am"):

within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one clings to them as "self" or "mine. 5. *Abhimāna* (conceit): regarding all excellent qualities that one has not yet attained, one claims to have attained them.
6. *Ūnamāna* (inferiority pride): regarding others who are superior, one considers oneself inferior; yet, toward those who are equal, one acts with pride like a slave toward a master.
The seven types of false pride arise from conceit regarding what has not been attained, or from giving rise to wrong views concerning superior dharmas;
therefore, this syllable-gateway *ṭha* serves as their antidote.
[Commentary]: "Now, observing that all phenomena are unarisen," etc., means that one observes that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen in order to counteract these seven types of pride.

The phrase "and so forth" indicates further observation that all phenomena are fundamentally without fabrication, like the nature of empty space, being far removed from the characteristics of coming and going or of a unified whole;
they are the shifting flow of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and the reflections of the mind. Due to [these causes]...
Since such phenomena as those produced by conditions are all unapprehendable, one knows that *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is equal among all dharmas, with no high or low.
[Commentary] Regarding these five letter-gates and so forth: first, non-arising is the letter *A*; second, it is free from verbal expression.
1. The syllable *va* is the purification of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). 2. The syllable *ra* is the absence of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
3. The syllable *ha* is the absence of causal conditions (*pratyaya*). 4. The syllable *kha* is the characteristic of being like space (*ākāśa-samāna-lakṣaṇa*).

Why is this so? Because these five gateways of syllables nourish that which is ungraspable; for these five gateways of syllables are precisely earth, water, fire, wind, and space. Earth [is able to...]
The water that sustains the seeds moistens them, the fire warms them, and the wind fans them;
unimpeded by space, they grow from the seed through to the flower and fruit—this is called "nurturing. Yet because they are fundamentally unborn, this nurturing is also ultimately unattainable.

[Commentary] Regarding the *Anantamukha-nirhāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (Wuliangyi jing) and others: the present commentary refers to that sūtra to establish that women are enemies of those who practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

That sūtra says: "For example, when a strong man eliminates an enemy for a king, once the enemy has been destroyed, the king is greatly delighted and rewards him by granting half the kingdom as a fief, bestowing it all upon him. It is the same for one who upholds this sūtra; among all [beings]..."
The practitioner is most courageous and robust; the Dharma-treasure of the six perfections arrives of its own accord without being sought.

The enemies of birth and death naturally disintegrate, and one realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). Regarding the "half-Buddha-realm treasure" as a reward of peace and happiness:
this refers to the seven stages (*bhūmi*) belonging to the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, that sutra says: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family generates..."
When the bodhicitta and the great compassionate resolve to deliver all suffering beings arise, even before one has practiced the six pāramitās, the six pāramitās naturally manifest before one;
at that very body, one attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), whereby birth-and-death and afflictions are simultaneously severed and destroyed.
This is the station of the Great Bodhisattva of the seventh bhūmi, which is called "Half-Buddha."
A national treasure. [Commentary:
Regarding the gateway of the letter *na* (*nā-dvāra*), in Sanskrit it is correctly called *nana*, which means "giving" (*dāna*). Furthermore, the *Amoghapāśa Sūtra* states:
"Because all dharmas are understood to be free from the characteristics of names and cannot be apprehended," the Sanskrit for *nama* is *nāma*.
This translation states that the name *nāga* has many meanings, each of which is explained according to its specific sense without contradiction.
[Commentary]: For example, regarding the term "person bound in fetters," the *Analects*, in the commentary by Kong [Qiu], states: "Léi (縲) refers to black ropes; xiè (紲) refers to shackles;
these are used to restrain criminals. This is now used as a metaphorical expression. As for the phrase "when the mind is stilled," etc., it refers to the *asura* being...
When Śakra, Lord of Devas, thought of returning to his palace, he was bound and could not escape; yet when he ceased his combative mind, the bonds were naturally removed.
Thus we know that bondage and liberation depend solely upon one’s own mind and do not arise from another.

As for the phrase "how much more so regarding karma and afflictions," the bondage of karma and afflictions refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), while the unconditioned bondage (*asaṃskṛta-bandhana*) refers to those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). This is the intended meaning.
"Bā" refers to the Bodhisattva. [Commentary:
Regarding the syllable "Bā" and so forth, it means that this gateway of letters (*akṣaramukha*) explains that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are unobtainable.

Furthermore, according to the *Amoghapāśa*, it is because one understands that all things are of a nature of destruction and are unobtainable. In the Sanskrit language, *prajñā* is translated here as...
"Destroying" refers to that which is called "destruction," yet this existence is unobtainable; it is only because of the distinct meaning of the syllable *svabhāva* (nature) that it is so designated.

This means that since this existence is unobtainable, and furthermore, that [unobtainability] itself is unobtainable, it is said that one understands the unobtainable nature of the destruction of all phenomena (*dharma*).
As for the distinction: herein, by means of the gateway of the syllable *a*, all existence is negated, and thus all phenomena are [revealed as] unobtainable.
Because that which is unobtainable therein, along with its negation, does not exist even in conjunction with the letter A,
it is said that the destructible nature of all phenomena is unobtainable.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the three realms of existence" (*trai-dhātu*), it refers to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. The phrase "up to" implies transcending the nine realms of existence;
that is, the six heavens of the desire realm and the human realm constitute one [set], while the four dhyānas and the four spheres of emptiness (*ārūpya*) together form the nine.

As for the "twenty-five realms of existence," these refer to the four continents, the four evil destinies, the Great Brahmā, the six heavens of the desire realm, the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), and the five [pure abodes].
The Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) refer to the four *dhyānas* and the four *ārūpya-samāpattis*.

[Commentary: "That is to say, the King of Samādhis (*samādhirāja*), etc. means that because the gateway of the letter *va* (*vākṣara-mukha*) explains that all phenomena are unobtainable, and because they exist through causes and conditions, it is complete with all gateway letters; thus, it is the samādhi itself.

Because it excels all samādhis, it is called the King of Samādhis; as for its ability to destroy the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*), according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, when a Bodhisattva dwells on the stage of fearlessness, they attain twenty-five samādhis that destroy the twenty-five states of existence. These are:
by attaining the "Stainless" (*vimala*) samādhi, one can destroy existence in the hells; by attaining the "Non-retrogressive" (*anivartana*) samādhi, one can destroy existence among animals.
There are even those who attain my samādhi and are able to destroy existence in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
this is called the Bodhisattva attaining the twenty-five samādhis to sever the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*). Such a samādhi is named the King of All Samādhis.

When entering this King of Samādhis, if one wishes to blow away and destroy Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, one achieves it immediately according to one's will, just as [in the following example].
This samādhi of the letter *va* is further the king of twenty-five samādhis, uniquely capable of destroying the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).

Therefore, the Commentary says: "Now, observing that all existences arise from conditions is precisely the meaning of their being fundamentally unarisen," up to "it is able to destroy the twenty-five states of existence."
[Commentary: For this reason, it is called "the King who Destroys the Existence of Dharmas.
This means that because all dharmas are unattainable as existing entities, and because they are characterized by non-action and non-practice, this is the Samādhirāja-samādhi (King of Samādhis).
Śākyamuni Tathāgata dwells in this samādhi and manifests the traces of supramundane empowerment to destroy the multitudes within the twenty-five states of existence.

To perceive this at birth as the Dharma King who destroys existence (*bhava*) is a misconception; for within the gateway of the letter *A*, the twenty-five states of existence are fundamentally unborn—what, then, is there to destroy?
Furthermore, all phenomena enter the essence of the letter *A*, which is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
If the essence of all phenomena is the Dharma-realm and is fundamentally unborn, then the twenty-five states of existence are likewise the Dharma-realm from the very beginning.
The non-arising of Śākyamuni’s coming is precisely the primordial non-arising of the *dharmadhātu*.
Since all phenomena are the *dharmadhātu* and are primordially unarisen, they are identical to space. How could space destroy space?
How could space be destroyed by space? When one understands in this way, that is the understanding of the letter-gateway *va*.
All phenomena possess the sense of being unobtainable and the sense of the destructible nature of all phenomena being unobtainable, as taught in the *Pāśa-vimocana-sūtra*.
If this is so, are these [phenomena] identical to or different from the *pāśa*? Ultimately, they are not different.
Herein, the syllable *A* is precisely that neutral syllable; that neutral syllable is precisely this syllable *A*. *A*.
This [term] explains the meaning that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen; "fundamentally" refers to their very nature—contemplate this.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* that it employs "various gateways" and so forth, this refers to the more than twenty gateways taught in that treatise, namely:

the examination of causes and conditions, the examination of the six sense faculties, the examination of the five aggregates, and so on, up to the examination of the Four Noble Truths and the examination of the twelve links of dependent origination; these are called "gateways."

Regarding the statement that the four dharmas—consciousness (*vijñāna*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and craving (*tṛṣṇā*)—are all non-existent through various gateways of discourse: when the eye sees a form, consciousness arises immediately; next, there is the arising of awareness-contact (*saṃjñā-sparśa*);
from contact, there is roughness or smoothness, and sensation subsequently experiences the desirable object, giving rise to the defilement of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

Now, because the visible dharma [the object] is non-existent, these four dharmas—consciousness and the others—are all non-existent. Therefore, [the ten... (Note: The final character "十" appears to be a fragment or an abbreviation for a concluding phrase such as "ten [factors]" or "the tenth," but based on the provided text, it remains as a standalone character at the end.)
The two causal factors (*nidāna*) are likewise non-existent. Furthermore, all sentient beings are not like wood or stone, devoid of cognition or sensation;
rather, they give rise to various consciousnesses according to their respective objects, thereby forming the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

When a practitioner of mantra (*mantra-yānika*) attains the inconceivable realm through the skillful means of the three secrets (*triguhyopāya*), although there is that which is cognized and that which is...

Because contact and sensation are purified by means of the syllable *ra*, one does not give rise to craving or attachment; because there is no craving, the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are also absent. [Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "like the three characteristics in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*" and so forth, that treatise states that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) possess three characteristics, namely: arising (*jāti*), abiding (*sthiti*), and... [cessation].
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) characterized by cessation also has three aspects, namely: non-arising, non-abiding, and non-ceasing.

Now, when one contemplates that the essence and intrinsic nature of both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are empty, with what could they have characteristics? Furthermore, the detailed exposition of the three characteristics in the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* need not be cited here at length.
[Commentary]: Regarding "that samādhi," if it refers proximately, the syllable-gateway *va* is called the "Samādhi of the Severance of the Path of Speech";
if it refers distantly, it is the "King of Samādhis," and is therefore inconceivable.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "One might cause the sun to become cold," etc., this refers to the fact that the *satya* (truth) represented by the syllable *sa* cannot be attained. *Satya* means reality;
it is the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*), which is known through wisdom as being free from inversion.

Just as one might cause the sun to become cold or the moon to become hot, the World-Honored One’s truthful teachings never deviate from the truth. Therefore, the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra* says: "The orbs of the sun and moon might fall."

Even Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, could be made to tremble; yet that which all Buddhas have spoken never differs. [Commentary] "Both empty, both provisional, and also the Middle" refers to the gateway of the letter *sa*. Within it, one is far removed from the characteristics of the two truths, the four truths, and so forth; it is primordially equal, being both empty, provisional, and the Middle. Though three, they are one; though one, they are three. They do not obstruct one another. This is called the "Threefold Non-obstruction. It is like a single moon reflected in a thousand rivers: the moon is one, yet its reflections are many; the reflections are many, yet the moon is one. Thus, the three are one, and the one is three. This is called the "Non-obstruction of the Three Truths. Furthermore, the letter *sa* is the gateway to all phenomena. All phenomena are inherently quiescent and originally unborn. Because they are unborn, they are empty; because they are empty, they are provisionally established; because they are provisionally established, they are the Middle Way. Therefore, it is said: "The letter *sa* is the gateway to all phenomena. This is called the "Non-obstruction of the One Truth. Furthermore, the letter *sa* is the gateway to all phenomena.
