[Commentary]: Regarding "victory in battle and success in assault," Emperor Gaozu of Han said: "As for marshaling a host of millions and being certain of victory in battle and success in assault, I am not equal to Han Xin."

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "referring collectively to all Buddhas and so forth," the character "referring" (指) here should actually be "collecting" (攝). This is because *sarva* means "all" and also means "collectively";

it is the collective gathering. The Sanskrit term *sarvathā* translates as "collecting" (*she*) or "collectively gathering all" (*yi-qie-she*). Therefore, [the text] refers collectively to all Buddhas and so forth.
[Commentary: "It is also the power of mastery" means that among the five wheels of this syllable *ha*, it is the wind-wheel;
because it attains supreme mastery in destruction, it is so named.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that the syllable *HA* possesses all [qualities] and so forth, this means that the syllable *HA* signifies the causal nature; it corresponds to the seed-syllable of Bodhi.
When combined with the *bindu* of space-wisdom (*jñāna-bindu*) and the syllable *HAṂ*, it constitutes the seed-syllable entrusted within the womb of the Consort-Mother.
Below this, the syllable *HŪṂ* is added, which represents the compassionate embryonic stage (*karuṇā-garbha*) increasing day by day. Thus, it possesses these three aspects.
Because of this meaning, the sound is uttered and Māra is dispersed.

[Commentary] Regarding "the afflictions within the realms": "realms" refers to the three realms. The delusions of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) within the three realms, which constitute the death and rebirth of limited duration (*paricchinna-vedanīya*), are called "within the realms.
If the delusions of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) pertain to the three realms, they constitute the death and rebirth of transformation (*nirmāṇa-vaipākika*).
This refers to that which is outside the realm (*dhātu*), as is fully detailed in the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra*.

[Commentary: Regarding the six kinds of earthquakes, as stated in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*: "That is to say: shaking, surging, roaring, and striking; first, gradually trembling is 'shaking' (*pra-kaṃpa*); becoming increasingly great is 'moving' (*saṃ-kaṃpa*);
rising and falling is 'surging' (*ut-kaṃpa*); coming and going is 'rolling' (*vi-kaṃpa*); and a loud sound is 'roaring' (*pra-ghoṣa*). These are their characteristics.

Regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it says: "What is meant by 'moving, leaping, shaking, striking, roaring, and bursting'? 'Moving' refers to swaying; 'leaping' refers to emerging and submerging;
'shaking' refers to a deep, resonant vibration; 'striking' refers to knocking; 'roaring' refers to emitting sound; and 'bursting' refers to a startling clamor."
[Commentary]: "Relies upon this passage" means to entrust it to this text. This text refers to the verses on the realization of understanding that follow below.

It means that when Vairocana arose from the Samādhi of Observing the High Peak of the Pure Dharma Banner and spoke these Great Power and Great Protection Vidyārājñīs, at the conclusion of his speech, the entire Buddha-field shook in six ways, and all the bodhisattvas present in the assembly [were moved].
Furthermore, when the bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions beheld such inconceivable miraculous transformations and heard these syllables of the vidyā-queen’s mantra,
there was none whose mind was not opened and whose understanding was not clarified, like a lotus flower blossoming. Expressing their internal realization through external speech,
they all spoke in a single voice, reciting verses that were further able to bring about spiritual realization.
This is due to the power of the Great Protecting Venerable Consort’s majestic spiritual authority.
[Commentary] "Like a golden city" and so forth: there was once a golden city with moats and ramparts in Bingzhou.

Formerly, Emperor Xianzu of the Qi dynasty ascended the Tongzi Temple and gazed upon the city of Bingzhou, saying, "What kind of city is this? Someone replied, "This is a golden city with moats and ramparts."
It is a land of celestial treasures. Furthermore, when Qu Yuan of Chu addressed Duke Huan, he said:
"If you were to rely on military force, the Fang Mountains would serve as its walls and the Han River as its moat; even with all your troops, there would be no use for them.
Now, because the Buddhas of the ten directions collectively protect and sustain [this place] through the power of the mantra, all those who create obstacles will naturally retreat and disperse.

[Sūtra] "The Buddhas, kings, and so forth" refers to the aforementioned three true aspects of the mantras of the Buddhas and sentient beings; their convergence is precisely their mutual empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). "Heavenly beings and humans" refers to the multitudes of ordinary persons who have not yet established the embryo of the noble ones (*āryagarbha*). [Commentary] "The Buddhas, kings, and so forth" refers to the aforementioned three true aspects of the mantras of the Buddhas and sentient beings;

their convergence is precisely their mutual empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). "Heavenly beings and humans" refers to the multitudes of ordinary persons who have not yet established the embryo of the noble ones (*āryagarbha*).
Regarding "birth": now, when the conditions and causes for the resonance between sentient beings and the Buddha coincide, the Buddha manifests his empowerment and speaks this mantra.
When sentient beings enter with faith, this is the initial entrustment of the sacred embryo within the *Mahākaruṇā-garbha* (Womb of Great Compassion).
They co-arise with the seeds of the *Vipula* Dharma-realm; this corresponds precisely to the thirty minds prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*). Therefore, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* says:

The thirty individuals of the Noble Womb of Submissive Patience—the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*)—are further sustained by the Great Compassion Womb Treasury (*mahākaruṇā-garbhakośa*).
Through the cultivation of preparatory applications (*prayoga*), there is no regression or loss. Because of these various causes and conditions, the commentary concludes by stating:
"Therefore, it is called the empowerment of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-adhiṣṭhāna*)."
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the Tathāgata’s manifest realization" and so forth, this refers to the moment of initial attainment, distinguishing it from the time of formal proclamation.

The phrase "seeing all beings" and so forth means that one perceives within the minds of all sentient beings of the three vehicles and five natures the central mandala and its two enclosures of the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*), complete and distinct. Within this Universal Gate mandala...
Because the various activities of body, speech, and mind are themselves the activities of the Tathāgata’s body, speech, and mind, it is said that they are equal to those of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, not only are the three karmas equal to those of the Tathāgata, but the three eyes are also equal. These three eyes are the letter *I*;
the letter *I* is the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, the Dharma-body of liberation; and these correspond respectively to wisdom (*prajñā*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and [the third eye].

It is the body of true reality (*dharmatā-kāya*). Furthermore, because it is equal throughout the three periods of time, the moment of first generating the bodhicitta and the moment of fulfilling the stages (*bhūmi*) and perfections (*pāramitā*) are ultimately identical.
Now, by citing the beginning and the end, the intermediate stages are subsumed; thus it is said, "from the first generation of the mind," and so forth. Why?
Because there is ultimately no duality between the birth [of saṃsāra] and the Buddha; for the essence of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa is without difference. Thus it is said: "emerging."
Because it transcends the three periods [of time] and cuts off all formal expectations, it is therefore equal.

[Commentary: Regarding the term *tathatā*, when considered as a phrase (*pada-artha*), *tathā* refers to the "three"; when considered as a syllable (*vyañjana-artha*), the syllable *ta* signifies "suchness" (*tathatā*).
Therefore, it is said that "the mind is like the true mark. The character *li* (in *tathā*) signifies "dust and defilement," referring to what lies beneath the syllable *ta*.
Because there is the sound "a," it is said that all defilements are fundamentally unborn.

Regarding the phrase "the equality of the three periods of time," this means that the Buddhas of the three periods appearing in the world teach the Dharma through various skillful means according to what is appropriate for sentient beings;
by means of the letter-gate "ra," they reveal, cause others to awaken to, and enter the letter-gate "da," which is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; therefore, this is called the One Great Matter.
Regarding the statement that the term *nidāna* (cause and condition) is equivalent [to *tala*], this syllable *ta-la* carries the meaning of "removing obstructions" within this context.

[Commentary: The wheels of body, speech, and mind refer to the three activities (*karman*) of the World-Honored One being like a chariot wheel: the mind is the hub, speech is the spokes, and the body is the rim.
Because these three dharmas combine to form a single wheel, such a wheel has the capacity to transport [beings].
It is used as a metaphor because of its power to destroy and demolish; furthermore, "wheel" (cakra) means "to turn.
Since the Buddha’s three karmas are each able to turn and enter the minds of sentient beings, this embodies the meaning of the three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement, "One should explain this extensively by means of the *mukha* (gate) of letters," this refers to the six lines and a half [of the text]. Within the commentary, there are four instances of the character *wo* (我, *ahaṃ*).

First, taking the character *hen* (痕) as the basis for explanation: the phrase "I and all others... up to the meaning of equality" refers to the syllable *ha* (*ha*), which signifies the meaning of *bodhicitta*.
Furthermore, the phrase "I shall protect the various... up to the meaning of the original vow" refers to the syllable *hen* (*heṃ*).

The meaning of the syllable *Dā* (大) is "Great Emptiness" (*mahā-śūnyatā*). Furthermore, from "I am the Dharma-realm" up to "the meaning of removing hindrances," this refers to the syllable *Ha*, which signifies *nirvāṇa*.
Moreover, "causing this body of mine to be the master of awakening" refers to the long *Hā*, which signifies *upāya* (skillful means).
Since the practice and realization are unified in the middle, it is said that one should explain [these] by means of the "gateways of syllables" (*akṣara-mukha*).
[Commentary] Therefore, regarding the "different gate": this term "vajra" does not refer to that which is the most hard and sharp among vajras;

rather, it refers to the fact that the self-nature of the dharmadhātu possesses an indestructible meaning and function, which is like a vajra. It is in reference to this doctrinal gate [that the term is used].
It is called "vajra" because the intrinsic nature of phenomena is primordially pure and cannot be defiled by the turbid mud of the two vehicles;
based on this meaning, it is named "lotus. Therefore, it is said that these are alternative designations (*paryāya*).
[Commentary: Regarding "Vajra Armor" (*vajrakaṅkaṭa*): "Armor" (*kaṅkaṭa*) refers to a weapon used to protect the body, like the shell of a tortoise;
"helmet" (*śīrṣaka*) refers to a visor.
[Commentary: Regarding the "one hundred and eight samādhis," these refer to the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the Ratnamudrāhasta Samādhi, and the Siṃhavikrīḍita Samādhi.
The *Lion’s Play Samādhi*, up to the *Samādhi of Non-attachment like Space and Non-defilement*, and so forth—these are called the one hundred and eight samādhis.

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is asked: "As the Buddha has taught that there is but one path to Nirvāṇa—namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—why does Śāriputra further ask about other remaining samādhis that enable a bodhisattva to quickly attain Buddhahood? Answer: [The answer follows in the text].
It is said: when one is not yet close to *nirvāṇa*, there are many other paths; when one is close to *nirvāṇa*, there is only a single path.
All other samādhis—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—enter into these three gates of liberation.
For example, a great city has many gates through which one may enter the city. What are these "other" samādhis? They are the Śūraṅgama-samādhi and others.
In the chapter on the Mahāyāna such as the Samādhis, it shall be explained that if a bodhisattva can practice the hundred and eight samādhis and other such dharanī-doors,
all the Buddhas of the ten directions will bestow upon them the prediction of enlightenment.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the subsequent syllables all explain one another by way of transformation," this refers to the three syllables VAJRA explaining one another in turn.
Why is it that the syllable VA signifies that all phenomena are beyond verbal expression? Because the syllable JA signifies that arising is unobtainable.
Why is it that the syllable JA signifies that arising is unobtainable? Because the syllable RA signifies that intrinsic nature is pure. These three factors are combined as one.
This is the body of the *sattva*. [Commentary:
The phrase "if a dharma is a conditioned production" and so forth explains the meaning of the letter *ka*; that is, the three characters *ka-va-tsa*.
If a dharma is produced by conditioning, this refers to the character *ka*. One should know that it possesses only a provisional name; this refers to the character *va*.
The shifting and changing according to conditions is the character "left" (zuo).

[Sūtra] "The Tathāgata’s eye further contemplates the mantra-practitioner. This single mantra has two names: the first is called the Tathāgata’s Eye, and the second is called the Tathāgata’s Contemplation.

[Commentary: Regarding the addition of the letter *i* and so forth, this means that the stroke representing the sound *i* added as a subscript to the letter *va* is called the "stroke of the letter *i*.

When it is added in this manner, the letter *va* becomes the final vowel (*visarga*). As for the statement that the letter *va* signifies the meaning of "vajra," it is because *vajra* is named "diamond" (*vajra*).
Although it is thus a single phoneme in its meaning, it is said that "samādhi" means "abiding."
"Meaning" refers to samādhi, which is the stroke of the letter *i*; that is, the essence of the letter *va* is wisdom (*prajñā*), while adding the side-stroke constitutes samādhi.
When such concentration and wisdom are joined, it is called "equilibrium," free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
When a practitioner abides in this, they abide in non-proliferation and the unimpeded knowledge of the three times. Regarding the phrase "the fragrance of such precepts": this...

For what reason is morality called "ointment"? It is because the two dharmas of meditative concentration and wisdom are blended in equal measure and placed within the pure water of the *ā* syllable—the nature of the dharma-realm—and are then smeared everywhere upon the Dharma-body, universally perfuming all things;
therefore, this morality is named "ointment."
[Commentary] Regarding the statement that this gateway of letters shall be explained extensively:
it means that the essence of this letter *maṅ* is the pure bodhicitta, for it is like the seed of the king of trees. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Bodhicitta is the cause.
Furthermore, because the letter *maṅ* is accompanied by the stroke of samādhi, it represents the practice of great compassion; it is like a seed within the ground of loving-kindness and compassion.
Regarding the "root," a sutra states: "Great Compassion is the root," and so forth, until it reaches the stage where it gradually grows and blossoms into the flowers of the myriad virtues.
This takes "non-apprehension" as the skillful means (*upāya*). Adding the "dot of emptiness" (*bindu*) above the syllable *maṅ* constitutes this skillful means;
it is the phrase for the ultimate. Furthermore, if two dots are added alongside it, it represents *nirvāṇa*. Another explanation is as follows:

A verse says: "The initial mind knows in a single thought that one becomes a Buddha" (this is sudden enlightenment); "the fruit-virtue must ultimately be the flower of ten thousand practices" (this is gradual cultivation).
If this is so, why is the name of the Tathāgata in the South 'Flower-Blossoming King of Śāla Trees'?
There are two kinds of flowers: first, the flower of ten thousand practices; second, the flower of ten thousand virtues. It is precisely these ten thousand virtues that constitute the Tathāgata.
Flowers and fruits also have two types: first, the fruit of adornment; second, the fruit of seed-essence. The Buddha of the South is the fruit of adornment, which is the syllable *maṃ*.
The Tathāgata Drum-Sound of Heaven is the fruit of seed-essence, which is the syllable *laṃ*.
Therefore, it is said that one should explain this extensively by means of the gates of syllables (*akṣaramukha*).

[Commentary]: "The meaning of 'following wherever one goes' (suìzhì) means that wherever any sentient being gives rise to the initial awakening of the bodhicitta, [the Buddha] follows there without exception;
this is the character *da* (達), signifying that bodhicitta serves as the cause.

Furthermore, 'the meaning of pervading everywhere' (biànzhì) means that the mind of great compassion (mahākaruṇā) pervades the entire realm of sentient beings; this is the character *duò* (馱), signifying that great compassion is [the cause]."
That the "root" (*mūla*) also carries the sense of "departure" (*gati*) is because the practice of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is fulfilled and one wondrously proceeds to the further shore of Bodhi;

thus, it is the syllable *ḍaṃ*, which represents the skillful means (*upāya*) as the ultimate. Regarding the sense of "advancing without abiding," this refers to attaining the fruit while not abandoning the causal gate, thereby initiating transformative activity (*nirmāṇa-vyāpāra*);
this also belongs to the category of skillful means as the ultimate, differing only in that its purpose is solely for the benefit of others. That is to say:
This is the *ta* syllable gateway. [Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "if one proceeds according to the characteristics of the wheel of syllables," this explains the two gateways of *a-ra-ra* and *ka-ra-ra*.

The syllable *a* has two meanings: first, the meaning of the primordial beginning (*ādi*), which refers to the fact that all sentient beings have been in fundamental ignorance since the beginningless past.

Possessing the two obstacles of afflictions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*) and the cognizable (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*), where afflictions act as the dust and the cognizable acts as the grime, it is thereby constituted as the clamor of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
This is the second meaning of "fundamental non-arising" (*mūla-anutpāda*): it is the sudden realization that the two obstacles do not arise, giving birth to the true fundamental reality (*tathatā*).
It is like opening a door and seeing the image [within]; it is nectar never tasted before. Furthermore, there are two meanings for the subsequent syllable *ka*.
First is the meaning of "with effortful activity" (*sābhisaṃskāra*): one diligently cultivates the myriad practices without ceasing, like one parched with thirst seeking nectar;

yet because there is still hope and expectation, the habitual tendencies of obstruction are not absent, and one remains bound by signs. Thus, the *Huayan shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) says: "Cultivation involving effortful activity ultimately results in decay and ruin.

Second is the meaning of "without effortful activity" (*anabhisaṃskāra*): through the previous vigor and strength of practice, one does not cease; however, because there is still something attained...

Before one has yet realized the ultimate truth, this mind is free from both mediation and effort; its function is entirely realized within as suchness (tathatā), so how could it be proclaimed or demonstrated?
Thus, Qingliang said: "When the essence of no-mind reaches its ultimate, one immediately accords with the Buddha-family"—this is precisely that meaning.
[Commentary]: "As for 'having eaten the milk-rice and requiring nothing more': among all foods, the milk-rice possesses a supreme, peerless flavor, a taste beyond compare.
If a person greedily seeks delicious flavors, once they have obtained this milk-rice, what else would they require?
This serves as a metaphor for the practitioner who joyfully seeks the supreme fruit; once Nirvana is attained, what further thing could they aspire to? Furthermore, regarding Śākyamuni..."
When Sakyamuni practiced austerities, his daily consumption of hemp and wheat corresponds to the meaning of *arara* here;

likewise, his bathing in the Nairañjanā River and eating the milk-rice from the cowherd girl correspond to the meaning of *karara* here; therefore, it is said, "as when he ate the milk-rice," and so forth.

[Commentary]: "Neither coming nor going can be apprehended" means that this character *ga* (伽) is actually the character *ga* (誐). The character *ga* encompasses the meanings of both "going" and "coming.
In Sanskrit, *gaccha* is translated here as "going" (*qu*). If one says *āgata*, it is termed "coming" (*lai*); therefore, they are called "coming and going" (*laigù*).

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "observing by means of the characteristics of coming and going," it is as stated in the sūtra: the uṣṇīṣa of the Tathāgata is like empty space and cannot be perceived through the characteristics of coming and going.

It is said that when the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, within a great assembly, desired to know the measure of the Buddha’s body, he commanded Śāriputra to seek it upward as far as the Brahma-heaven; yet even there, he still beheld the Tathāgata.
Regarding the current teaching, the sound of the voice is no different from its original nature; even when proceeding to other Buddha-fields, it is no different from being in the Brahma-palace.

At that time, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin went forth himself to observe throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions, and saw that the Tathāgatas were expounding the Dharma without rising from their seats. Thus did the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin and the others [perceive].
Even when observing it through the aspect of coming and going, one does not perceive its bodily form or boundaries; how much less so, then, can one perceive the uṣṇīṣa of the Tathāgata?

[Commentary] Regarding "the original essence of *na* and so forth": the original essence of this syllable *hūṃ* is the syllable *ha*; upon the body of the syllable *ha*, the vowel *a* (space) is added.
The dot on the syllable *na* (𑖡) is the gateway to the letter *na*; beneath it lies the stroke of the *u* (*ū*) samādhi. This is what is called the "dot of emptiness" (*bindu*) of the syllable *na*.
Beneath the essential body of the syllable *ha*, there are the three letters beginning with *u*, which together form the syllable *hūṃ*.

Now, if you say that the "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) of the essential body of the syllable *na* is the syllable *ha*, you should simply have said that the essential body itself is the syllable *ha*; [your statement] is entirely redundant.
The character *na* (曩) in the middle [of the title] signifies that three characters are omitted; readers should understand this.
[Sūtra] Regarding the "Chapter on Stilling Obstructions" (*Sīzhàng pǐn*): "stilling" (*sī*) means to cease and remove, while "obstructions" (*zhàng*) refers to hindrances.

Because it stills and removes the two kinds of obstructions—internal and external—it is interpreted as a *tatpuruṣa* compound (*yīzhǔ shì*) based on the relationship between the agent and the object. Furthermore, the preliminary branches for entering the maṇḍala have already been explained above.
Regarding the sections on mantras and so forth: when a practitioner establishes this maṇḍala, there may be obstacles created by piśācas and other such beings;
since these must be pacified through the skillful means of mantras, this chapter exists.

[Commentary] The phrase "the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*) and so forth" refers to all the heavy obstacles possessed by ordinary beings prior to the stage of faith (*śraddhā-avasthā*), the number of which is immeasurable.

The phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*) signifies the transcendence of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and the inclusion of all obstacles within the stages of accumulation (*sambhāra-mārga*) and application (*prayoga-mārga*) leading up to the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*). The "subtle obstacles of the bodhisattvas of the ten stages" refers to those [obstacles] that follow...

Because there are ten levels of obstruction across the ten stages (*bhūmi*), [the obstructions are as follows]: first, the obstruction of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*). This refers to the conceptually constructed portion (*parikalpita*) of the two obstructions;

because the nature of an ordinary being is established based on those seeds, and because it obstructs both the karma and the fruits of the miserable realms (*apāya*), it constitutes an obstruction to the first stage through the tenth.
Furthermore, the obstruction regarding the lack of mastery over all phenomena is collectively termed "subtle," as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

Furthermore, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "O son of good family, there is the ignorance that clings to the characteristics of self and dharmas, and the ignorance that fears birth-and-death and the evil realms.
These two types of ignorance obstruct [the attainment of] the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) up until the mastery over great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
There is also the ignorance regarding the manifestation of dharmas and the inability to realize and understand subtle and secret activities."
Regarding "ignorance" and these two types of ignorance that obstruct the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth:

the phrase "arising from conditions and so forth" means that the aforementioned obstacles arise from external conditions such as the objects of the six sense-fields and the teachings of false teachers;

or, because both internal causes and external conditions are termed "conditions," in the Dharma-character school (*lakṣaṇavāda*), seeds within the mind-continuum serve as the cause, whereas in the Nature school (*svabhāvavāda*), the perfuming and activation by ignorance serves as the cause.
Although these phenomena arise from various conditions and are diverse, to state the essential point: there is nothing that does not arise from the mind itself.
Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states that the three realms are illusory and are produced solely by the mind.
[Commentary: "Now, regarding 'contemplating the mind' and so forth, this means contemplating the letter *A* and so on in order to eliminate hindrances.

This gateway of the letter *A* elucidates the meaning that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen (*anutpanna*); that is, because the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the mind being contemplated is fundamentally unarisen, one should know that all hindrances are likewise fundamentally unarisen.
The phrase 'up to and including' (*yāvat*) indicates that one transcends the intermediate letters such as *ka*, *kha*, and so forth."

Since the gateway [of the letter *ha*] is cited here as the final one, it says "up to" (*yāvat*). Regarding the statement "the true reality of the mind, up to its cause being unobtainable," this refers to the gateway of the letter *ha*.
The letter *ha* explains that the cause of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) is unobtainable.
In Sanskrit, this is called *hetu*, which is translated here as "cause. Since there are no phenomena whatsoever that do not belong to a cause, when one now contemplates this very cause itself...
Since the essence [of phenomena] is fundamentally unarisen and thus cannot even be apprehended, how much less could all phenomena belong to causes?
When one contemplates in this manner, all obstacles whatsoever are none other than the Vajra Retinue upon the lotus pedestal within the heart-mind of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata.
How could the Vajra Retinue of Mahāvairocana ever obstruct a practitioner of mantras?
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "one should constantly contemplate in one's mind" and so forth:

whenever an obstacle arises for a practitioner within the maṇḍala, they should reflect and contemplate the Bodhisattva Acala—also known as the Vidyārāja Acala, or alternatively as a messenger (dūta) or a holy being (*ārya*).
Here, only his name is revealed and not his physical form, as it has already been explained above; the original form of that King is as described previously.
The fourth fascicle concludes the section on the maṇḍala, having fully revealed it.

Regarding the instruction to "constantly contemplate according to those signs while binding the secret mudrās," the characteristics of those mudrās are displayed below in the tenth fascicle, within the chapter on Mudrās.
As for the King’s mantra, the commentary below it provides a detailed analysis in the *Sāmānya-mantra-kośa*.
Why is this not explained here? This [section] merely explains the skillful means for pacifying obstacles; as for the mantras and secrets, they are explained according to their respective chapters.
[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the mention of "immovable" and so forth, these skillful means for pacifying obstacles must rely upon three causal conditions.
When these are fully perfected, one is able to universally eliminate all obstacles. Regarding the "three matters," they refer to: the mind visualizing the physical form of the Vidyārāja;
the mouth reciting the mantra of the syllable *HŪṂ*; and the hands forming the mudrā of the Great Wisdom Sword. These are called the three causal conditions.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the characters, etc.," this refers to the clarity of the text in both Chinese and Sanskrit. It means that as the present sutra states, "the letter A is my own essence," one contemplates the letter A as pervading one's own body (one's self).
All parts [of the body] universally become the indestructible color of a vajra (all becoming a pure golden-yellow).
Thus, the essence of the letter A is itself the essence of the letter *Aham* (I); it is nothing other than this.
Regarding the contemplation of the letter-door (the shallow level): if one follows the Sanskrit original, it should be stated as "the letter A," which signifies the essence of non-self (*anātman*).
This refers to the commentary on the sections following the Sanskrit text. If one follows the current Chinese version, the term "letter" (*zi*) represents the shallow level;
however, if one follows the Sanskrit original, the term "non-" (*wu*) represents the profound level. Therefore, it says, "The reason for the [dental] *ya* [radical], etc."

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "Having thus performed the self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*)... and so forth, the commentary at this point provides only a brief indication. The ninth commentary below states:
"In general, the methods for maintaining [the practice], such as the previously mentioned rite of the seven points (*sapta-bindu*), cannot yet be fully exhausted here;
they are explained in their entirety within this section. As the text says, "the direction of wind" refers to the northwest corner.
[Commentary: *Khadira* wood refers to the purple *khadira* tree (*Acacia catechu*).

[Commentary: The *Dharmadhātu-mantra* is the syllable *HŪṂ*. Regarding the phrase "attaining relief," Maheśvara was empowered by Acala Vidyārāja using the *padma-pāda* mantra; immediately thereafter, he fell into a state of unconsciousness.
Having been granted release, one attains respite; the mind becomes tranquil and free from fear, which is called "reaching the state of fearlessness.
Thus, the second commentary states: "In Sanskrit it is *aśvāsa*, translated as 'respite.
It is like a person who, when seized by a powerful man, has their throat constricted and their breath cut off until they are on the verge of death, but suddenly receives release and returns to life."
Birth is likewise so: being entangled by deluded karma and afflictions, one is obstructed and confined;
reaching this point where one recovers is called the "place of recovery," and it is like crossing over dangerous and evil paths, hence it is called the "place of fearlessness."

[Commentary: "The rest are inferred by analogy" means that the afflictions of the four abodes (*catur-vāsabhūmi*), as well as the secondary branches of delusion, karma, and suffering, are all remnants of this fifth, ground of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*); because these are eliminated [by its removal], it is said that "they are inferred by analogy."

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "this is the illusory manifestation (*māyā-nirmāṇa*) of mantras," it refers to those who harbor doubts, asking: "Now that one has heard that the Buddha-dharma is profound and subtle, why does one perform such incantations (*dhāraṇī-mantra*)?
Is this not an involvement in worldly affairs? The answer is: These mantras are the inconceivable, natural state of the dharma of illusion (*māyā-dharmatā*).
They rely upon various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) to manifest the signless (*animitta*); they are not like the coarse and shallow things of the world.
The incantation, if one understands the ten phrases on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), naturally resolves this doubt. [Commentary:
"One must undergo *mingxuan* (dizziness/disorientation) for treatment" means that just as medicine treats illness, it requires the person to experience *mingxuan* before the disease can be cured.
Thus, the *Shangshu* says: "If the medicine does not cause *mingxuan*, the grave illness will not be cured. It is like taking medicine that necessarily causes intense *mingxuan*.

His illness was thereby cured. Desiring to issue urgent words to admonish himself, he did so because, within the ranks of his ministers, there was no one who matched the person he had seen in a dream during the reign of Gaozong of the Yin dynasty—the one named Shuo.
Since no such individual could be found among the officials, he ordered all the officers to search for someone whose physical appearance corresponded to that of the dream figure.
They sought him in the wilds and eventually found him at the crag of Mount Fushi; he was subsequently appointed as Prime Minister. And so it was commanded.
He said: "Morning and evening you shall present your instructions to assist my virtue" (this means that one should present admonitions and direct words to assist my virtue).

"As when using metal, you serve as the whetstone; as when crossing a great river, you serve as the boat and oars; as when there is a great drought in the year, you serve as the rain that falls for days;

as when medicine does not cause dizziness and vertigo, the disease will not be cured. Furthermore, the Correct Meaning says: "If one takes medicine and it does not cause the person to become dizzy..."
When one is dazed, enraged, and disordered, their illness cannot be healed. Now, as for this "interior" method:
it refers to first fashioning the physical form of the obstructing spirit, either out of wood or earth, and coating that body with powdered white mustard seeds mixed with poison.
By doing so, the obstructing spirit will naturally experience mental and physical vertigo and shall immediately retreat and disperse.

[Commentary: "Now, this fundamental maṇḍala is likewise" means that just as when Kṣatriyas and others each abide in their own lineage, the people of the world praise them and their undertakings achieve success, so it is here as well.

When a practitioner of mantra-realization understands the fourfold nature of the maṇḍala and each abides in their original nature according to their primary object of veneration, then those who act as obstacles [cannot prevail].
If one were to manifest that which can obstruct or hinder by means of the *maṇḍala* syllable-gates (*akṣara-mukha*), it is as follows:

first, the square *maṇḍala* of the nature of the vajra-ground, which is the *a*-syllable gate of the originally non-arising nature; second, the circular *maṇḍala* of the nature of great compassion-water, which is the *va*-syllable gate of the nature beyond verbal expression;
third, the triangular altar of the nature of great wisdom-fire, which is the nature free from dust and defilement.
The letter-gateway *ra* is the nature of the wind of the four masteries, the semi-circular maṇḍala; it is the letter-gateway *ha*, which is free from the nature of causes and conditions.
The fifth is the image of signlessness, the maṇḍala of indefinite square or circle; it is the letter-gateway *kha*, the fundamental nature of the great void.
In sequence, these are also the dharma-gateways of increasing, pacifying, subjugating, and magnetizing, corresponding respectively to yellow, white, red, and black. [This is] the void.
The meaning of "variegated colors" is as explained above.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "or in a triangle up to a half-moon," it was previously stated that the triangle is the fire mandala of the syllable *ra* and the half-moon is the wind mandala of the syllable *ha*.
Why, then, is it now said to be "in a triangle or a half-moon"? This refers to space (*ākāśa*).
Because the wheel lacks a fixed characteristic, it is said that it may be triangular and so forth.
Why is it not said to be square or circular, but only said to be triangular and so forth? This is because the natures of fire and wind are empty and porous;
thus, space enters into them. The natures of earth and water are solid and dense; thus, space finds it difficult to enter them. For this reason...

It exists only within the half-moon of the triangle; furthermore, because the half-moon of the triangle is precisely for the purpose of subjugation (*abhicāra*), it is situated within these two wheels. [Commentary:

Regarding "as if a person holds [it] in their hand," it is like how people in the world, though they may obtain an alchemical formula (*rasāyana*), if they have not yet acquired the method for fire, do not [attain the result] through mere proximity.

If one takes the elixir produced through the harmonious refinement of a wise master and yet slanders it as being false and extravagant, how can such a person not know that when the Prince of Huainan succeeded in his alchemy,
his entire household ascended together, and even the chickens and dogs that licked the cauldron were all able to rise into the air?
Thus we know that the secret treasury of the Tathāgata can only be entered by those who are fully endowed with both faith and wisdom.
[Sūtra] Regarding the *Samanta-mantra-garbha*: because the mantras of this chapter universally pervade and encompass all expedient mantras, it is called "Universal" (*samanta*);
furthermore, because it can contain and collect all mantras and so forth, it is called a "Treasury" (*garbha*).
Thus, "Universal" is the Universal Mantra, and the Universal Mantra is the Treasury; hence, it is named the *Samanta-mantra-garbha*. Furthermore, [it refers to] the World-Honored One Vairocana...
In the preceding chapter, the Venerable One has already proclaimed the Great Sword, the Great Protection, and other general mantras through the gateway of the dharmadhātu that pervades all places;

these belong specifically to the Tathāgata Family. Furthermore, there are mantras belonging to the Vajra and Lotus Families, which he intends for the respective Vajra Bodhisattvas who are the leaders of each family to [apply] according to their own respective penetration of the entire dharmadhātu.
Thus, one expounds them through the gates: each individual mantra-dharma phrase is itself a distinct jewel-vehicle of mantra.
For a practitioner of mantra, if they penetrate one gate of the dharma-realm, they universally penetrate all gates of the dharma-realm;
if they penetrate one vehicle, they universally penetrate all jewel-vehicles. Thus it is said:
Generally, the "wisdom of the practitioner" (yogin-jñāna) refers to the Mantra-piṭaka, which universally penetrates all precious vehicles;

thus, "generally" refers to the wisdom of the practitioner, and the "Mantra-piṭaka" is the dharma to be penetrated. When these two—the subject and the object—are considered in relation to one another, the name is established as a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Furthermore, when Vajrapāṇi previously questioned the Buddha on three matters, the first question concerned the construction [of mandalas] by practitioners of mantra.
When establishing the Mahākaruṇā-garbha-maṇḍala, by what skillful means is one not afflicted or harmed by Vināyakas and the like?
This is the second question. How does one maintain the mantras? This is the third question. How does one achieve the fruit of Buddhahood?
Regarding the first question, it has already been answered in the preceding "Chapter on the Cessation of Obstacles. Now, the second and third questions shall be answered.

Regarding the third question: within the various mantras of the Three Mysteries (triguhyamukha) in the extensive version of this sūtra, their number is like that of the sands of the Ganges and cannot be recorded in full.

The holy ones who transmitted the Dharma, wishing to condense the vast for the sake of brevity, selected those mantras of universal application so that practitioners might easily perceive them; thus, this chapter has come forth.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "as when people debate the principles of doctrine" (*lun yi*), this further explains the meaning of "indestructible. As stated in the *Weishi shu* (Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*):

In ancient times, there was a monk in Eastern India who engaged in a doctrinal debate with a student of the Sāṃkhya school. That [Sāṃkhya] master established twenty-five principles (*tattva*), asserting that the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth are eternal.

Now, [the monk] argues that all things arise and perish moment by moment (*kṣaṇika-utpāda-vināśa*). He extensively sets forth the positions of both sides, and the monk challenges them, saying: "Now it must necessarily..."
Because there is cessation after the destruction of the kalpa and so forth, based on that prior cessation, the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) raised an objection, saying:
"The future must not cease, because it is currently not ceasing, just like the mountains and such at this present time. The Saṃgha was ultimately unable to answer him.
Since the King had placed his faith in the Saṃgha, he then humiliated those monks by forcing them to ride donkeys and the like; yet those non-Buddhists...

Because the King, having highly esteemed [the work], composed seventy verses in praise and bestowed one thousand pieces of gold upon it, the *Saptati-śāstra* (The Treatise in Seventy [Verses]) is named for this very reason.
The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu then composed the *Paramārtha-satya-śāstra*, also known as the *Paramārtha-saptati*, to counter that treatise and refute its arguments;
however, that [work] failed to establish the faults of the opponent’s thesis, reason, or example.
My school has no such fault, yet your proposed reason (*hetu*) suffers from at least one logical error. Who says that because there is no cessation now, there will likewise be no cessation later?
My school merely states that for phenomena such as the great earth, there must first be a transformation before cessation occurs, and this [cessation] exists afterward, just like a lamp flame.
It is you who do not understand the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not my school. At that time, the King then took the world...
The Master personally traveled throughout all regions, proclaiming and disseminating the treatise so that no one could oppose it.

Consequently, he took the skeletal remains of former kings, non-Buddhists, and proponents of rival doctrines, or fashioned them into human figures out of straw, and subjected them to flogging as if they were the assemblies of that time.
For this reason, it is said that "nothing can destroy it"; this refers to the treatise’s transcendence.

[Commentary]: "This refers to the fruit of the perfect cause of Mahāvairocana" means that this Bodhisattva, from the initial generation of the mind of awakening through the practice of the perfect cause of Mahāvairocana, has ultimately achieved the perfect fruit of Mahāvairocana; yet, because they do not abandon the gateway of the cause upon attaining the fruit, they are called a "Bodhisattva."

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the syllable *ma* signifies the meaning of Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*)": this syllable *ma* refers to the labial sound *ba*, specifically the fifth letter of that row, which is sometimes pronounced as *ma*.
It has no separate phonetic body; it expresses the meaning of Great Emptiness and is indistinguishable from the *bindu* (dot) of Great Emptiness—it is the Sanskrit letter *ma*.
As for the statement "the syllable *ha* signifies the meaning of cause": this syllable *ha* expresses the nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
The "affiliated cause" (zhushu yin) refers to the syllable *ha* in the Brahmī script; to say it is the "pure bodhicitta" means that bodhicitta serves as the cause.
To say it is "great emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*) is because it forms a complete phrase when joined with this syllable.
This means that since it is not a cause characterized by phenomenal marks, it is the cause of great emptiness; therefore, it is said to be the realm of the Buddha.
The Samādhi of Adornment refers to the Sanskrit letter *Hī* (with the vowel *i*), which is augmented by the stroke of samādhi;

thus, it takes great compassion as its root and is threaded through with the letter *Ma*. This is not a samādhi of adorned characteristics, but rather the Samādhi of the Adornment of the Buddha-realm.
It is also called the Wisdom of Sarvajñā (*sarvajñājñāna*), which corresponds to the long vowel in the Sanskrit script.
Because the syllable *ha* belongs to wisdom (*prajñā*), it is penetrated by the syllable *ma*, thereby accomplishing all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and so forth.

When a practitioner of mantra enters this gateway of the syllable *ha*, they immediately attain equality with Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and are also able to abide in the Buddha-realm of the Samādhi of Adornment.
[Commentary]: When one draws out the sound of the initial letter *a* and calls it rapidly, it is the letter *e*.
This means that when pronouncing the letter *e*, one first begins from the departing tone (*gōngdì*) of the letter *a*; it is simply this rapid pronunciation.

[Commentary]: Regarding the presence of the syllable *laṃ* and others: *laṃ* is the mind of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-citta*). This means that the mind, as its true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), is ultimately pure and can only be indicated by empty space;
therefore, there is the syllable *laṃ*. The primary form of this character is the letter *ra*. *Ra* has the meaning of "that which is" (*ma*).
If one enters the gate of the primordial non-arising (*an-utpāda*) of the letter *a*, it is the "non-arising of that which is" (*ma-anutpāda*).
That which is primordially unborn is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the mind;

because the essence of the mind’s true reality is identical to space, the vowel *am* (the "dot of emptiness") is added to form the syllable *laṃ*. Therefore, this syllable is called the "Dharmadhātu-mind.

As for the statement that it "dispels the traces of the path of teaching," the Sanskrit term *pada* is also translated as "phrase" or "syllabic unit" (*jùdòu*). This refers to the various phrases within the preceding mantra.
The sequential revelation of the meaning of the reality that removes obscurations culminates in the state where saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are equal;
there is nothing that is not thus. While the range of this mind has traces that can be sought, it is not yet called "the Remover of All Obscurations" (Sarvāvaraṇaviṣkambhin).
Now, these two characters truly clarify the point of realization: the first syllable, *laṃ*, is the dharma of space.

The realm (dhātu) is far removed from all marks; this is the trace of the path of instruction. Because it is sent away again and again—sent away after having been sent away—it is expressed with reduplication.
Therefore, because the single, inconceivable Dharma-realm alone is truly free from all veils and hindrances, it is called "laṃ laṃ."
[Commentary: Regarding the statement "because the letter-ra (ra) is fundamentally unborn," this letter-ra should actually be the letter-a (a);
that is to say, because the letter-a is fundamentally unborn, next the letter-ra is free from dust (*rajas*), and finally the letter-ha (ha) is because a cause cannot be found.
Thus, the sequence in the sutra should state "a-ra-ra-ra-ṅa," with the intervening terms omitted by the phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*).
Because the two *ra* syllables between [the words] signify the meaning of being free from dust (*rajas*), the sub-commentary below states:

"In order to counteract the defilements of the three poisons and the defilements of the three paths," and so forth, repeating this three times. If there were not three *ra* syllables, one should not speak of "three repetitions.
This is as explained above regarding the *Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin* mantra, which contains two *talaṃ* syllables; thus, the sub-commentary provides its explanation.
This means that because it abides in the middle way between the two extremes of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, the term is repeated for emphasis;
thus, one should know that the word *ara* is missing from the sūtra.

[Commentary: "The three paths of defilement" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*), karma, and suffering (*duḥkha*). Furthermore, it refers to the three paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).

The obstacles to be remedied are also the three paths of action of body, speech, and mind. As for the "three eyes," they are the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), the dharma eye (*dharma-cakṣus*), and the Buddha eye (*buddha-cakṣus*).
As for the "three knowledges," they are conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), ultimate knowledge (*paramārtha-jñāna*), and middle-way knowledge (*madhyamā-pratipad-jñāna*);

the characteristics of what they remedy can be understood accordingly. Furthermore, according to the *Tiantai Zhiguan*, the meaning of the three eyes and three knowledges is further clarified; although the Tathāgata possesses them...

One should know that the five eyes are fully encompassed by the Buddha-eye, which illuminates all things without omission. Just as when the various rivers flow into the ocean, they lose their original names yet do not lack their four functions:
the Buddha’s wisdom illuminating emptiness, as seen by the two vehicles, is called "all-knowledge" (sarvajñā);

the Buddha’s wisdom illuminating the provisional, as seen by bodhisattvas, is called "knowledge of the paths and categories" (mārgajñatā); and the Buddha’s wisdom illuminating emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, seeing them all as reality, is [the knowledge of all aspects].
It is called "all-aspect omniscience" (*sarvākārajñatā*) because these three knowledges are attained within a single moment of mind;

thus one knows that the three eyes, accomplished through the three types of stillness within a single mind, perceive the inconceivable three truths, for this seeing is obtained from stillness and is therefore designated as "eyes.

Furthermore, the three knowledges, accomplished through the three types of contemplation within a single mind, cognize the inconceivable three objects; since this cognition is obtained from contemplation, it is designated as "knowledge."

The names "object" (*viṣaya*) and "truth" (*satya*), or "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*), are merely different designations for what is essentially the same; they should not be explained as distinct entities.

[Commentary] Regarding "the esoteric terminology of the *Yogācārabhūmi*," this refers to the secret nomenclature corresponding to the *mantras*. This Honored One arises from contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
The one whose eye of mastery arose is Avalokiteśvara as mother; that which is the cause for Avalokiteśvara’s initial resolve is precisely this.
As for the statement regarding the "Amitābha sisters," it means that Amitābha is the elder sister and Tārā is the younger sister—that is, her subordinate.
She who will come to succeed Amitābha, known as the King of the Mountain of Universal Radiance and Merit, is this very person.
Regarding the Venerable Tārā, it is commonly unknown that she possesses a true mantra and secret name; there is no discernment of this distinction.
Although many in the world recite the name of Avalokiteśvara, they do not know the locus of what they are reciting, for they are ignorant of this essential principle.
[Commentary] Regarding the passage beginning with "Just as in the world, all... and so forth, this section consists of three parts.
First, from "Just as in the world" up to "and wishes to extinguish it," is the *sarvabhaya* (all-fear) phrase.
Second, from "Therefore, one regulates them with great compassion" onwards is the *tārasanni* (rescuing from fear) phrase. Third, from [the subsequent text]... is the [fear-removing] phrase.

Furthermore, from "Next, by means of the Tathāgata" onwards is the syllable *haṃ*, which is a phrase of terror. These three kinds of terror correspond respectively to the three meanings of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle;

they serve as the antidotes to the three kalpas and the three types of deluded attachments, and they also represent the meaning of the three syllables A, Ā, and Am, which signify bodhicitta, great compassion, and skillful means.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "this mantra takes the syllable *tad* as its essence," this syllable *tad* signifies the meaning of the ineffability of suchness (*tathatā*).

Because it is suchness within the Middle Way, it is free from increase and decrease. Previously, when the syllable *sat* was used to utterly empty away birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the conceit of self (*asmimāna*), that utter emptiness functioned as an increase [of emptiness] and birth-and-death and the conceit of self functioned as a decrease. Next, by means of...
When the syllable *Taṃ*, the provisional manifestation of great compassion, reaches ultimate emptiness, then the provisional increases while emptiness decreases.

Furthermore, when the syllable *Haṃ*, the majestic power of the Tathāgata, brings the middle way to rest within great compassionate provisionality, then the middle increases while provisionality decreases.
Seeing these differences of increase and decrease, one realizes they are merely skillful means of counteraction and have not yet accorded with suchness (*tathatā*).
The Middle Way of contemplation now enters the Middle Way of Suchness; because one contemplates at the time of the syllable *Taṃ*, there is no distinction of increase or decrease.
This is precisely the attainment of the three wisdoms within a single moment of mind, and it is also the meaning of Nāgārjuna’s "emptiness, provisionality, and the middle" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "if from the gate of the single Dharma-realm," etc., it means that while the number of this Avalokiteśvara’s retinue is immeasurable, one now cites only its essential principles by opening six gates; therefore, it is called "all."

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "this Bodhisattva penetrates," etc., it means that this Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, taking Prajñā as his ultimate desire, intends to bestow Prajñā upon all sentient beings.
Abiding in a body sustained by empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), he manifests the appearance of an infant;
just as a worldly infant lacks discursive discrimination, this represents how this profound wisdom is free from the [duality of] person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma*).
The reason for manifesting the appearance of an infant is due to frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*).
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "this 'ma' refers to the four *māras*," this single character "ma" briefly encompasses three meanings. First, the meaning of the four *māras*:
in Sanskrit, *māra*, which is translated here as "killer" (*śā*) or "destroyer" (*pòhuài*). This is because they are able to kill and destroy the dharmas of merit. Second... [text continues]

Regarding the meaning of *māna* (pride): the Sanskrit term is *mā-ma*, which is translated here as "pride. Regarding the meaning of the three minds: the Sanskrit term is *mana*, which is translated as "mind" (*yi*).

As for the statement that these lack intrinsic nature and depend upon sentient beings, it means that, as with the aforementioned syllable *caṇḍa*, the syllable *ṇa* is free from enmity and opposition, and the syllable *ma* is free from the four māras; all of these lack intrinsic nature and depend [upon conditions].
"Sentient beings" (the character for "beings" is erroneously written as "sorrow") refers to the condition of manifold conditions; this causal condition is the syllable *ha*.
Furthermore, the syllable *ha* has a drawn-out resonance, signifying that they are originally unarisen.

Because they are originally unarisen, they enable the syllable *lu* to be free from dust, while the syllable *ṛṣi* is by nature dull, and the syllable *na* is like the great void. Therefore, it is called *caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa*.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "previously slaying the four abodes," the "four abodes" refer to the abode of abiding in one view, the abode of desire-attachment, the abode of form-attachment, and the abode of existence-attachment;
these are the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "subsequently slaying those who abide in the ground of ignorance," this refers to the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "also slaying all worthies and sages," this means extinguishing [the obstacles] prior to and within the stages.
This refers to all afflictions (*kleśa*).
[Commentary: Thus, regarding the meaning of "ambrosia" (*amṛta*): among the sixteen portions of ambrosia in the heavens, fifteen portions are bestowed upon sentient beings;
because it arises again as it was from the remaining one portion, it is called "immortal," which is to say, "supreme birth."
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "connected with the letter *paṅna*," this refers to the fact that the Sanskrit letter *maṇḍa* has two forms.
When written in a straight manner, it takes this [first] form; when written in a cursive manner, this is *maṇḍa*.
The *ḍha* character immediately following is what is connected with the letter *paṅna*.

[Commentary: Both instances are stated twice because their meaning is the same as the preceding one. Since the former refers to those bound by the four *bhūmi*s of abiding, while the latter refers to those bound by the *bhūmi* of abiding in ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*), it is said that they are the same as before.
[Commentary]: "Combined with the wind-wheel" refers to the half-moon mandala of the wind-wheel.
"Sharing the same essence as the syllable RAḤ" means that the two syllables HA and RA constitute a single entity.
"With dots added to the side up to 'removing all obstacles'" refers to adding two dots to the side of the syllable HA-RA. "'Above' and so forth" means that there is the sound of samādhi above.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the *ba* syllable-gateway establishes the characteristics of equality," this *ba* syllable is correctly rendered in Sanskrit as *sarva*;
the term *ba* here is a corruption. While the *va* syllable-gateway signifies the meaning of being beyond verbal expression, we do not take that syllable-gateway to explain the mantra here;
rather, we take the meaning established within the characteristics of equality. When combined and integrated with the *sa* syllable, it is able to [accomplish its function].
The establishment of the term "all" as the name for "everything" is achieved by combining the two characters *dharma* from the following phrase;
thus, it establishes "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*) as the name. This is what was previously referred to as the establishment of the characteristics of words and names.
[Commentary]: Regarding the term "full moon": this refers to the syllable *haṃ*. When it is the initial *ha* without the dot (*bindu*), it is like the new moon—the bodhicitta.
When the stroke *ū* is added to form the sound *huṃ*, it is like the crescent moon—the root of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
When the dot is added above to form the syllable *haṃ*, it is like the full moon—skillful means (*upāya*).
It is called the "Full Moon" syllable because it represents the ultimate state.
[Commentary] It is said that one gives rise to the two kinds of great emptiness—namely, *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"Because one severs the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) that continue through successive births, one realizes true liberation; because one severs the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that hinder understanding, one attains [great enlightenment]."
Great Bodhi is called "empty" from the perspective of its capacity for emptiness and its ultimate meaning; the arising of the wisdom of this emptiness is termed "the arising of Great Emptiness.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "when one desires to cause it to arise," etc., this refers to a time when the conditions for response and resonance are auspiciously assembled.
It is like sowing in spring and harvesting in autumn, which must be performed promptly according to the seasons; if one does not do so, one will lose the auspicious opportunity.
[Commentary]: Regarding the "Parable of the Phantom City" and other passages in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, when the Tathāgata appears, there are the five vehicles of the Dharma-treasure;

according to the different faculties [of beings], he transforms them differently so that each perceives the reality within the single vehicle path. He provisionally teaches the three [vehicles] as appropriate, yet possessing various jewels, they ultimately all return to the single treasury of jewels.
Thus, that sutra says: "The Tathāgata’s skillful means penetrate deeply into the nature of sentient beings."
Knowing that their aspirations were set upon the Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna) and that they were deeply attached to the five desires as if they were fixed [in concentration], he spoke of nirvāṇa;

even to the point where they first entered the conjured city, giving rise to the thought that they had already crossed over and the thought of security—this refers to the "jewels" of the two vehicles.
Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "You all, go! The place of jewels is near; the great city you previously saw was created by me as a transformation," and so on, up to: "You..."
That which is attained is not extinction; to become a Buddha with all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*), you must arouse great diligence.

When you realize all-encompassing wisdom, the ten powers (*daśabala*) and other Buddha-dharmas, and are endowed with the thirty-two marks (*dvātriṃśan-lakṣaṇa*) and so forth, this is precisely the Jewel of the Mahāyāna. Now, the *ratnasthiti-samādhi* (Jewel-Abiding Samādhi) is likewise:
it contains various kinds of jewels, and according to their respective faculties of faith, each may take and use them. Furthermore, if we speak in terms of the teachings and practice:
Regarding the various jewels, if the principle and the fruit are indeed the single jewel of the One Vehicle, this perfectly accords with the intent of the *Śāstra*.
[The *Śāstra*] states: "Subduing poverty and so forth" refers to the meaning of the Parable of the Poor Son in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. That sūtra says:
"At that time, the poor son, wandering about in search of employment, happened upon his father’s house and stood by the side of the gate... and so on, up to: "...he immediately felt terrified."

Having repented and sought [refuge] until reaching this point, it further says: "At that time, the wealthy elder, seeing his son upon the lion throne, recognized him immediately and spoke to him, saying:
'Ho, good man! You have always worked here; do not go elsewhere again.
The father even came to know that his son’s mind had gradually become open and at ease, and that he had achieved great resolve. This is intended to subdue the inferior minds of those of the Hīnayāna.
This refers to attaining the great fruit.
[Commentary] Regarding the name "Kālarātri": the Sanskrit term *kāla* is translated as "black," and the Sanskrit term *rātri* is translated as "night.
In this context, the name should be written with the letter *ra* placed above the letter *la*, but it has been erroneously transcribed otherwise.
[Commentary: Now, regarding the observation of this "karma" (karman), the syllable *ka* is itself karma.
Since this syllable *ka* is fundamentally unborn, it lacks the characteristic of the syllable *ra*, nor does it possess the defilement of the syllable *ra*.

One who practices such an observation establishes the phenomena of mutual dependence—namely, the presence and absence of characteristics, and the presence and absence of defilement. Therefore, the black night is like that which is not real; it is great.
To clarify "reality as it is" (the syllable *tathatā*) implies the sense of abandoning darkness to seek light;

if one were thus [preoccupied], then that very clarity would become an obstruction (the syllable *varaṇa*). Now, if one abides in this samādhi of the unobstructed dharmadhātu, attaining perfect enlightenment amidst the black night, this is precisely the fundamental equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "māṃtali" and so forth mentioned here: *māṃ* means "mother," *tali* means "seven," and *bhi* means "etcetera" or "many.
Taken together, "the seven mothers etcetera" refers to the general mantra common to the seven mothers.
[Commentary: The phrase "from the ground of the nature-mind" (*śubha-citta-bhūmi*) explains the meaning of these three characters, *śe*, *ke*, and *la*.

That is to say: from the character *śe*, the quiescent mind-ground of one's original nature arises; from the character *ke*, all karmic activities arise; and from the character *la*, the various pure and wondrous six sense-objects arise (meaning:
abandoning impermanent form, one attains permanent form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so). This is precisely the purification of the Buddha-field.

The word "etc. (*ādi*) indicates that within a single syllable, all [qualities] are already complete. Previously, the meaning of *śloka* was explained based on the meaning of the individual syllables;
now it is explained based on the meaning of the phrase. This means that within the single sound *ślo*, there are already present the merits of one hundred syllables.
In the Sanskrit language, the syllable *ślo* is translated here as "hundred" (*śata*), while the Sanskrit *kṛta* is translated here as "merit" (*puṇya*). By means of these one hundred...
Merit is precisely the vehicle of the letter *ya*; therefore, the commentary concludes by stating it is called the "Vehicle of Śakra.

[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding "the half-syllables" and so forth: the fundamental body of these half-syllables is the letter *ba*. This *ba* is the letter of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) upon which a dot (*bindu*) is added;

when it corresponds to the eleventh vowel, it becomes a half-syllable. That is to say, the letter *ba*— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the content available up to that point.)
Because within the single ultimate truth there is no distinction between this shore and the other shore, there is nothing it does not penetrate;
thus it is identical to the "half-character" (the phonetic syllable) of the Great Emptiness. For this reason, it is called the Tathāgata’s Ocean of Great Wisdom.

Therefore, the Dragon King *Bhadra*, the Lord of Mind, constantly dwells therein. Below [this], the character *ye* (曳) appears, which signifies the meaning of "mounting" (*yāna*). Thus, the commentary concludes with the word "Fundamental" (*ben*).
This is the primary vehicle.

[Commentary: Regarding the term *prajā*, translated as "all beings" and so forth: this *prajā* is primarily translated as "all," meaning that all in the world is reckoned to have no existence that does not arise from it. When translating by way of opposition, it may be called...
"Victorious" (*jina*) is also called "other" (*para*); because he is honored as the most venerable and sovereign among all the world, he is named "Victorious.
Furthermore, the non-Buddhist outsiders of the West reckon that Brahmā is able to produce all things; since he is thus their "self" (*ātman*), he is named "the other.

For this reason, he is also called the "Victorious Lord of Beings" (*Jinendra*) or the "Other Lord of Beings" (*Parameṣṭhin*). Below these names, there is the syllable *ye*, which, as mentioned above, serves as a general auxiliary sound.
This refers to the meaning of "riding" (or "mounting").
[Commentary: When the world says that the sun is "constant" (*nitya*), the Sanskrit term is *āditya*. This is translated as "constant.
The character "ye" (耶) at the end belongs to the provisional designation; thus, it means "that which is called the sun, which is constant for the sake of benefiting sentient beings."
[Commentary]: Regarding this "Jewel Buddha" (Ratnabuddha), the character "Jewel" (寶) should be the character "Reality" (實). The *Huainanzi* states: "The sun is 'reality' (實), for it is always full;
the moon is 'deficiency' (闕), for it has its waning and lack. Therefore, the subsequent commentary says:

"Riding upon this mark of suchness (yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa), one gives rise to the station of Vairocana, the Great Sun. As for the phrase "transmitting to all," the fundamental essence of the syllable *ni* is...
The syllable *Na*— the word *na* has the meaning of "giving," and it is pronounced with a feminine vowel—
those who "mount" these [syllables] mount the true nature of this *tadyatha* syllable and are thus born into the station of Mahāvairocana.
[Commentary: Regarding the meaning of "the pure moon of yoga," this refers to the sense of a practitioner of mantra (vidyādhara) cultivating yoga in accordance with its principles.

As explained in the third commentary, in the section on selecting the temporal factors (*kāla-aṅga*), it is said that the "moon" of the practitioner’s concentrated mind is sometimes increasing in clarity, sometimes becoming faint, and even reaches a state of maturation before the actual time and place have arrived.
Or, when ripening occurs beyond these times and places, one must skillfully understand such transformations and adaptations so as not to err;
therefore, it is said that this is the meaning of the "Pure Moon of Yoga" (*yoga-vimala-candra*).

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the Great Emptiness of Emptiness," etc., it means that *na* has the meaning of "giving" (*dāna*), and by adding the dot of emptiness (*bindu*) above it— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
"Emptying the marks of giving"—the repeated mention of the character for "difficulty" here refers to the "Great Emptiness" of emptiness itself.
[Commentary] Regarding the reference to the first chapter of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and so forth:

it means that Vairocana Tathāgata, wishing to ensure that the merit of even a single hair’s breadth of practice by those who have entered the various gates of the dharma-realm mentioned above shall not be in vain, [taught this].
Because there is nothing among all that is undertaken which is not accomplished, this mantra is thus the "Mother" (mātṛ) and so forth of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The term "Mother and so forth" signifies the sense of being able to give birth; it is called "Mother and so forth" because it can give birth to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This is now employed as a metaphor, specifically illustrating how Prajñāpāramitā gives birth to all doors of the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, the first section of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Training in Contemplation," states: "Furthermore, Śāriputra, all bodhisattva mahāsattvas,
dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, should bring to fulfillment the four foundations of mindfulness,
the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path."
Because the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are non-apprehendable, bodhisattva mahāsattvas,
abiding in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, should fulfill the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*),

the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*), and the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*). Because they are non-apprehendable, [this applies] even up to the Tathāgata.

Because the ten powers, the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), compassion, joy, equanimity, and other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*)—all such dharmas being ultimately unattainable—one briefly points out above that there are no phenomena whatsoever that do not arise from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Therefore, *prajñā* is called the "Mother of the Buddhas. Furthermore, it is said that "consort" (*bhāryā*) is another term for "mother."
That which is called its "subordinate" (āya) is like a single lamp that can ignite hundreds of thousands of lamps; thus, it refers to the mother who follows [the primary] as the consort (*vī*).
This means that once one has attained [realization] oneself, one subsequently teaches many sentient beings; because this is the sense of the lamps not being extinguished, she is called the "consort.
Therefore, it is said to be "like the *Prajñāpāramitā*," and so forth.

[Commentary: Regarding "neither practicing nor practicing," as explained above, since all dharmas are fundamentally unarisen and even their causes cannot be apprehended, there is thus absolutely nothing to practice.
If one cannot even apprehend this state of absolute non-practice, that is true practice.
Therefore it is said: in the word *gaga*, the first *ga* signifies "absolutely nothing to practice," and the second *ga* signifies "non-... [omitted].
Because it is that which is practiced, it is said that "not practicing" is itself "practicing.
[Commentary] Therefore, those who call this by its frequent name refer to these words of the mantra: *namo amoghapāśāya*.
Of these six characters, the first five—specifically the first two characters—are the act of taking refuge; the subsequent three characters are "Amogha-pāśa" (the Unfailing Lasso).
The word "many" (*aneka*) signifies a multitude; it is like the common expression *namo buddhāya namo dharmāya namaḥ saṃghāya*, which means "taking refuge in the multitude of the Three Jewels.
Regarding the phrase "like worldly people," the Prajñāpāramitā (Mother of Wisdom) Chapter states:
"For example, when a woman has given birth to many sons and she falls ill, each of her sons diligently seeks [a remedy] for her."
The physician thought to himself: "How may my mother obtain freedom from illness, long life, peace, and happiness;

how may her body be free from manifold suffering and her mind free from sorrow? At that time, each of the sons employed skillful means to seek articles of comfort and protection for their mother's body, so that she would not be afflicted by the touch of mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, scorpions, cold, heat, hunger, thirst, or other such things. Furthermore—
With various kinds of supreme and exquisite articles of enjoyment, they pay respectful homage and offer worship, saying:
"Our mother, out of compassion, gave birth to us and instructed us in the various affairs of the world; how could we fail to repay our mother's kindness?
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is likewise so; he constantly regards and protects us with his Buddha-eye through this profound Prajñāpāramitā."
Why are the pāramitās so profound? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to all the merits of the Buddhas and can reveal the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world.
For these reasons, we Buddhas constantly observe and protect the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with our Buddha-eyes; how could we not repay that kindness?
This can be known through such proofs as "should temporarily relinquish" and so forth.

[Commentary: Regarding "if from various external causes and conditions," external factors refer to instances within the various limbs [of practice] that are not in accordance with the Dharma, which obstruct the arising of realization—such as wind and rain;
internal factors refer to those within the various yogas that do not accord with reality.
Thus, there are obstacles to the arising of attainment, such as the moon of the practitioner’s concentrated mind, which at times becomes increasingly bright and at times becomes faint and obscure;
even things such as the winds of improper recollection are called internal obstacles.

As for the phrase "the two are not in harmony," if a bodhisattva encounters such obstacles, this is the work of Māra, intended to prevent the accomplishment of wholesome deeds and merits; it is not something pertaining to ordinary persons.
That which is realized by the two vehicles is called "subtle. As stated in the *Māra-karma-varga* of the *Prajñāpāramitā*:

"Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose there is a listener who possesses the power of mindfulness and wisdom, and who delights in hearing and listening to, copying, upholding, reading, reciting, practicing, and cultivating the profound *prajñāpāramitā*;
yet the teacher of the Dharma intends to go to another region and is unable to provide instruction. When this occurs, [the obstacle arises].
To know this is to recognize it as a demonic deed of a bodhisattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a teacher of the Dharma delights in speaking and delights in giving,
and through skillful means encourages the transcription, upholding, recitation, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*,
yet the listener desires to go elsewhere and fails to receive and hear it— know that this is a demonic deed of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, there may be a teacher of the Dharma who possesses great evil desires, being deeply attached to fame, profit, robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine,
