This is precisely what appears within. Furthermore, the sixth scripture states: "Buddha-lands as numerous as atoms."
The number of such lands can be made to appear within a single thought-moment, within each and every atom, up to six phrases; that text contains them all in full.

In principle, there should further be the manifestation of the primary and secondary [realms], and the manifestation of the secondary within the primary and the primary within the secondary. If one distinguishes between the partial and the complete:

the pores of the skin represent the partial manifestation of the primary [body], while the entire body represents the complete manifestation of the primary; the atoms serve as the partial manifestation of the secondary [land], while the world-systems represent the complete manifestation of the secondary.
One should reflect upon this according to the Middle Way and the Perfect [Teaching]. Furthermore, the explanation is as follows:

regarding the statement that within a single hair-tip of space there is only the external container-space of one hair-tip, this does not refer to a portion within the Buddha’s own body; rather, it merely demonstrates that the dimensions of the supporting vessel-world (bhājanaloka) are unimpeded, whether vast or narrow.
As the commentary on the subsequent section states: "Yet the Buddha-fields do not decrease by even a speck of dust, nor do they increase."

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "in the Sanskrit original, at the four-line verse, etc.," this refers to the fact that beneath a single four-line verse in the Sanskrit original there is an additional line serving as a concluding particle (*udāttanipāta*).
This is like placing words such as "already" or "finished" at the end of characters in this land [China].
For the sake of textual convenience, it is here included within the four lines; for generally, at the end of a single verse, a concluding particle is frequently placed.
It is an auxiliary sound (*upasaṃhāra*). If it were placed separately, it would be the two syllables *iti*.
As stated in the Fourth Commentary, regarding the final word *iti* in the verse on the "Unobstructed Wisdom of the Three Times," the note says: "This is an auxiliary sentence-sound.
Furthermore, in that same work, at the end of the *Ariṣa* verse used to console the disciples, it says: "*iti*. The commentary states: "Whenever a verse is recited in the Sanskrit original..."
At the end of each [phrase], the auxiliary particle *iti* is added, which signifies "this is. [Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "each within a single Dharma-realm gate," etc., these Bodhisattvas not only personally cultivate the practice of humility and withdrawal, but regarding the Dharma-realm gates attained by the Buddhas, they are as if separated by a thin veil; for example, this is as in the case of the eighth stage itself.
In the samādhi-path of the Bodhisattva, one does not apprehend any phenomena as having arising;
knowing all things to be like illusions, for this reason the world calls him Avalokiteśvara.

Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva in his final birth dwells in the samādhi-path of the Buddha-ground, this is the ultimate generation of the bodhicitta, which is the most firm and powerful among all paths of samādhi.
They have entered the Buddha-way with vigor; they lack only the single rank of the Tathāgata and have not yet attained realized wisdom.

There remains one further turning of the Dharma-nature before they may succeed to the Buddha’s position. Because they know themselves to be like the moon on the fourteenth night—only partially full—they do not dare to proclaim anything before the Tathāgata;
this is their sense of shame. Therefore it is said that each [abides] in a single dharma.
Regarding the "gateways of the realms" and so forth:
[The Commentary] states that these three thousand verses up to the phrase "heard and seen" are all verses of the *siddhi*-outflow.

Now, because these three thousand verses are presented in an abbreviated form, only the four syllables A Ā Am Aḥ are taught as the heart-mind of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi-citta*); furthermore, it is said:
The vajra syllables that subdue the four māras, liberate from the six destinies, and fulfill all-knowledge wisdom (*sarvajñājñāna*) are as follows:
ĀḤ VĪRA HŪṂ KHAṂ. These nine syllables can accomplish various mundane and supramundane *siddhis*.
When a practitioner of mantra-yoga achieves accomplishment and the six sense faculties become purified, [this shall naturally occur].
"Endowed with hearing and seeing. [Commentary:

Regarding the word *hrī* (*xiū*) and others in the Sanskrit original, this refers to the two dharmas of shame (*hrī*) and remorse (*apatrāpya*). Since "shame" (*hrī*) is the general term, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* asks:
"What is shame? It takes as its nature the honoring and revering of the noble and the good, based on the power of oneself and the Dharma. And: "What is remorse?"
Taking the power of the world as its basis, its nature is to slight and reject violence and evil; it continues until it says, "to feel shame for transgressions and offenses.
These two are the common characteristics [of *hrī* and *apatrāpya*], and it is by virtue of this Brahmanical name that they differ from *hrī* and *apatrāpya*.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "because of having a sense of shame, one quickly gives birth [to virtue]," there are two matters here that comprise three layers.
First, one observes for oneself that the lineage of the Tathāgata does not transgress the samaya. Second, one is constantly praised by the holy assemblies of the ten directions.
Furthermore, there are two matters whereby those whose various virtues are not yet complete can be brought to fulfillment.
First is fulfillment; second is the attainment of great compassion and so forth. Furthermore, there are two:
first, abiding in ethical discipline (*śīla*) which leads to rebirth among humans and gods; second, from these two dharmas, the arising of various kinds of merit and so forth.
[Commentary: Regarding "the paths and their elements not yet complete and the Dharma-vessel not yet perfected": "Path" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path;
"elements" (or seeds) refers to the bodhicitta, because the bodhicitta serves as the seed for the Eightfold Noble Path, and thus the bodhicitta is the cause.
As for the "Dharma-vessel," this means that great compassion is the root and skillful means is the culmination. If the vessel of these three mental states has not yet been fully perfected—
Because the *amṛta* (the finest essence) of the three secrets cannot manifest [otherwise], it is called the "Path-Seed" (*mārgajñatā*) and so forth.

[Commentary]: Regarding the *Susiddhi-sarva-mantra-kalpa*, if a practitioner performs the mantra methods for accomplishment (*sādhana*) and the mind and its objects do not correspond, one should perform the "Method of Fulfillment" (*pūrṇa-kalpa*) according to the *Susiddhi-sūtra*. That sūtra states:
Furthermore, if the practitioner of recitation sees in a dream the limbs of the body of the Mantra Lord being added, one should know that the syllables of the mantra have been increased;
if the limbs are diminished, one should know that the syllables are deficient. Having clearly understood these signs, one should perform the rite of fulfillment (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Alternatively, if one sees the mantra as having a different intent from that of the practitioner, doubt will arise; in such a case, one must perform the rite of fulfillment.
First, using paper and *gorocanā*, write out the erroneous mantras in fine script and perform the ritual offerings according to the Dharma.
Next, prostrate to all the Buddhas and make this petition: "I pray that all the Buddhas and the assembly of noble ones will grant their assistance, aid, and protection.
Having made this petition, lie down upon a bed of *kuśa* grass with your head facing east; within that dream, the signs of the *iṣṭadevatā* will appear through the *gorocanā*.
Regarding the additions and subtractions on the paper leaves, the Honored One himself wrote them using ox-gall (gorocanā), providing annotations for their completion;
even the additions and subtractions of strokes were all precisely determined. If there is no error in the mantra, simply state that it is "without error.
Or, if instructions are given in a dream, fulfill them accordingly. When performing this rite, one should perform protective rituals to eliminate obstructing spirits (*māra*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "such as the Susiddhi Vidyādhara precepts," etc.: this tenth clause indicates that one who maintains mantras must receive and uphold the prohibitive precepts (*vidyādhara-śīla*) and the rules of specific discipline (*pṛthag-vinaya*).
These are established separately according to the particular matters [they address]; if one does not rely upon and maintain them, they will become obstacles.
Because it is difficult to achieve even *siddhi* when one encounters obstacles, the *Susiddhikara Sūtra* states that if a wise person upholds various mantras, they must first sever their anger;
they should not give rise to wrath even toward malevolent deities. As a verse says:
"As taught by the World Teacher in the sūtras, nothing can damage great benefit more than anger; in a single thought-moment, it utterly incinerates millions (*koṭi*) of vast [merits]."
Because one has cultivated virtue throughout kalpas, one should therefore abandon anger. Furthermore, one must not give rise to a mind of arrogance toward the ācārya;
one should not speak of various right and wrong, nor see the faults of the teacher.
Moreover, one must not bind other vidyārājas with the mantras one holds oneself, nor cause them harm or inflict punishments upon them. Furthermore...
One should not perform rites for subduing enemies; one should not leap over any sentient beings, whether bipedal or multipedal;
nor should one leap over medicinal roots, stalks, branches, leaves, seeds, or fruits.
One must not sing, engage in frivolous play, adorn the body in various ways, use abusive language, or consume the five pungent vegetables, radishes, sesame oil, rice flour, or bean cakes.
One must not consume the leftovers of offerings or the leftovers of sentient beings; one must not ride upon any vehicle or mounted saddle;
one must not eat from vessels of bronze or copper; one must not sleep on large or small beds or couches; one must not sleep with the face covered;
one must not lie on one's back, but must sleep on the right side like a lion king; one must not eat a second time, nor must one fast.
One must ensure ritual purity during the three periods of the day; the water and earth used for bathing must be consecrated with mantras.
To state the essential points of those mantras: when performing the practice, consult them and adopt them. This is essentially not far removed from the general intent of the Vairocana offerings.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "capable of employing *siddhānta* and skillful means (*upāya*)":

this refers to the various mantra activities wherein one should not lose the fundamental principle when engaging with anything from the worldly level up to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This is termed "knowing the proper time.
One should perform activities using the worldly perspective, while simultaneously employing the individual person (*pudgala*) and so forth, up to the ultimate truth.
As for those who [practice] this, because it is not of its proper time, it is said that they "are able to employ the *siddhānta*s," etc.
[Commentary]: Thus, "being able to perform the diamond dance" is a metaphor for the manifestation of supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*). As stated in the commentary below:
"The dancer is like a worldly performer who, amidst a great assembly, displays various kinds of physical actions (*kāya-karman*), such as bending, stretching, bowing, and looking up."
Furthermore, they produce various kinds of skillful sounds to cause that great assembly to experience joy, give rise to sorrowful reflection, or feel terror;
through these skillful means issued from their body and speech, the benefits conferred upon sentient beings differ.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: manifesting various modes of deportment, all are secret seals (mudrā), and producing various sublime sounds, all are [the same].
Because the mantra perfectly responds without fixed direction, it is called the "Vajra Dance.

Regarding the phrase "unimpeded power throughout the three periods of time": the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom fully comprehends all phenomena of the three periods of time within a single thought-moment without any obstruction;
this very non-obstruction is termed "power" because of its sovereign mastery.
Therefore, it is said that this is the unimpeded power of the three times. Regarding the phrase "relying on the adornments" and so forth:
this samādhi is precisely the basis upon which the mantras are about to be expounded. As stated in the first chapter, one adorns oneself with the pure three karmas of the Tathāgata;
just as a king possesses a great treasury which he may freely open and display whenever he wishes to show it to others.
Because it is thus arrayed and displayed, it is called the "Solemnly Adorned Pure Treasury" (*Vyūha-viśuddhi-garbha*). The samādhi is explained below as follows.

[Commentary: Although all sentient beings fundamentally possess [the Lotus Womb Treasury] and are no different from the Buddha, this is said to resolve potential doubts and difficulties. Specifically, there may be an objection:
"If all sentient beings inherently possess the Lotus Womb Treasury and are no different from the Buddha, for what reason is it that the Tathāgata alone is able to..."

"Can sentient beings not rely on this samādhi? The commentary explains: "Although all sentient beings fundamentally possess the complete original enlightenment (hon-gaku) such as the lotus-womb treasury (*padmagarbha*), it is said that because the power of unimpeded wisdom is not yet perfected, their initial enlightenment (*shiki*) is not yet pure.
Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, although all... and so forth, although sentient beings possess the wisdom of unimpeded phenomena...
Furthermore, although it is inherently thus from the beginning, because it is shrouded by the hindrances of delusion, the lotus-womb treasury (padmagarbha) has not yet been purified;
therefore, its illuminating function does not manifest before one.
[Commentary] Regarding the Sanskrit term *samāpatti* and so forth: *samā* means "equal" and *patti* means "to reach. Master Jing says:

At this point, "attaining" refers to the attainment of the essence itself, which is the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and numerical equilibrium (*samatā*). That which is "attained" is the nature of tranquility and harmony;

this attainment of equilibrium is termed "equilibrium" because it arises from the subduing of mental agitation (*auddhatya*). This equilibrium, moreover, is able to induce birth within the state of concentration.

While in this state of concentration, the meditative concentration and numerical equilibrium derive their names from the preceding preparatory application (*prayoga*); thus, that which induces this equilibrium is called "equilibrium."
Regarding the term "equipoise" (*samāhita*) mentioned here, the verse states:

"In the mirror-maṇḍala, upon the great lotus-king throne, dwelling deeply in samādhi, free from false grasping and conceptualization, one practices equipoise for as long as one month, maintaining it until one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) [recitations] are completed.
This means that the practitioner, as previously described, visualizes themselves as the *samaya*-body of the deity, and furthermore contemplates...
The mind-abode is perfectly clear and pure, like a round mirror. Within the mirror is a great eight-petaled lotus king with a full array of filaments;

upon the flower’s pedestal is the seed-syllable. Furthermore, by transforming the color, sound, and meaning of this seed-syllable, one beholds the true body of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata, adorned with all the marks and signs of excellence. At that time, the practitioner...
Illumined by the light of the Dharma, my mind became increasingly clear and enlightened; I spontaneously realized the ten conditions of dependent origination.
Thus I understood that such wondrous form is not different from emptiness, and although its fundamental nature is eternally empty, it is not different from form.

Since this is the case for form, the same principle applies to the mind. Because both form and mind enter the gateway of the letter *A*, one knows that the nature of the mind is fundamentally [empty].
Quiescence, which is like space, is called the accomplishment of the signless (*animitta*) and is also termed the *samāhita-bhūmi* of the secret contemplation gate.

Question: Regarding this *samāhita-bhūmi*, since all the teachings state that it belongs to the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), how can practitioners of mantras—who currently reside in the desire realm—accomplish it? Answer: This present sutra is precisely the secret [teaching].

In the vehicle of inconceivable empowerment and supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), by relying upon it for practice, one attains perfect enlightenment and turns the wheel of Dharma at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta;
what need is there to mention the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*)? However, while the names of the stages of equipoise are the same, their functional applications differ.

It is like the sound of a single voice which becomes different according to the vessel [into which it is projected]; yet if one blows into a *sheng* or *xiao* flute, the sound does not leave its seat.

When it is turned back and enters the flute, one then hears [the sound] throughout the four distant directions. Now, when entering this contemplation of the *cakra* of the syllables of perfect luminosity (*pariśuddha-prabhāsvara*), it is called "equipoise" (*samāhita*) and is not restricted by the bonds of the realms (*dhātu-bandhana*).
[Commentary: Regarding the characteristics and definitions of the term "equipoise," that treatise states: first, it refers to the four dhyānas; second, it refers to the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*).
"Deliverance" refers to the three *samādhis*; "and so forth" refers to the five *sākṣātkriyā-samāpattis* and others. These are called the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*).

It is not the one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because this [one-pointedness] is induced by freedom from regret, joy, happiness, and bliss, whereas in the desire realm there is no thorough and correct investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) and so forth. If...

Regarding the analysis of characteristics: first, the characteristic of the object of focus refers to the distinct essential natures of the objects of knowledge; second, the characteristic of causal conditions refers to the requisites for meditative concentration;
third, the characteristic of what should be abandoned refers to lethargy, agitation, and so forth; fourth, the characteristic of what should be cultivated refers to the remedies.

It should be understood that, according to their respective applications, these characteristics of what should be abandoned are themselves the characteristics of what should be cultivated (and so forth). This establishes the result.
Regarding the term "equipoise" (*samāpatti*): here, the word "equal" (*sama*) refers to the single factor of meditative concentration within the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).

When one reaches this state—that is, when one abides in the stage of equipoise itself—this single factor of concentration, by virtue of being that which is reached, is called "equipoise" (*samāpatti*) based on the agent of reaching.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "if contrasted with the Abhidharma and so forth," this means that using speech to express what one intends to perform as the ultimate meaning is called vocal informative action (*vāg-vijñapti-karman*).
Such informative action is precisely the constant voice of the Buddha. Regarding the phrase "furthermore, throughout the ten directions," etc., this explains the meaning of vocal informative action:
it signifies that the Buddhas of the ten directions collectively authorize and establish this linguistic expression.
The meaning of "manifestation" (*vijñapti*) is that speech is the manifestor and meaning is the manifested. The manifestors are the four syllables *a* (short), *ā* (long), *am*, and *aḥ*;

the manifested are bodhicaryā, its fruit, and nirvāṇa. Although what is clarified here differs profoundly from the Abhidharma in terms of depth, the linguistic manifestation is the same; therefore, it says, "if [according to] the Abhidharma, etc."
[Commentary]: If one wishes to point to the text and so forth, it is the syllable *piao* at the end of the phrase "I take refuge" that points to the text.
This refers to the discernment of the various skillful means (*upāya*) of the Tathāgatas. That is to say, this syllable *piao* has the same meaning as the syllable *bi*;
*bi* signifies "various" and "skillful."
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the cultivation herein" (*asmin... bhāvanā*), "herein" (*asmin*) refers to within this chapter on *siddhi*, thus it is said "herein.
It now specifically indicates this chapter because it is for the purpose of correctly explaining the two types of *siddhi*;
however, in reality, it generally refers to this entire scripture, which is why it says "herein. As for the phrase "not the stage of *samāhita*," "not" (*na*) means "is not. *Samā*... [text fragment]

The *ṭīkā* explains that "samāhita" (equipoised) refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and "concentration" is the basis, which is termed "ground" (*bhūmi*). Taken collectively in this context, it is called the "non-equipoised ground.
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "There are some that are non-equipoised grounds by virtue of their intrinsic nature, namely the five groups of consciousness;
there are some that are non-equipoised grounds because they lack pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), namely those situated in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)."
Certain mental states and mental factors are called "unstable" (*aniyata-bhūmi*) because they may be distracted;
this refers, for instance, to the beginner, for whom many meanings explain the sense of instability. Here, the intended meaning is as follows:

when a practitioner first perceives the letter *A* and so forth within the lotus of the mind, they abide spontaneously therein, continuing until the time they visualize the deity’s heart-Buddha as their own self.

One perceives oneself within the luminous sphere at the heart of the *iṣṭadevatā*, and upon one’s own heart there is also a subtle, luminous seed-syllable capable of gradually expanding and contracting with sovereign mastery.

Although such a state may manifest before one, because it is still an image within the mind, it is said to be "not the stage of meditative equipoise" (*samāhita-bhūmi*). As for the "stage of meditative equipoise," it refers to the practitioner...
The nature of physical and mental pliancy and equanimity is produced by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Because these [qualities] are designated by the name of their cause—the result of that induction—they are called "equipoise" (*samāhita*). Alternatively, they may be called "equipoise" because they are equally induced;

that is to say, while in the state of meditative absorption, body and mind are equalized through the force of the concentration resulting from the power of the preceding preparatory application (*prayoga*) at the time of entering meditative absorption.
[Commentary]: "Gradually increasing and expanding, with mastery over extension and contraction" means the sense of being unimpeded in mastery over breadth and narrowness.
[Commentary]: "With reference to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and other texts" refers to what that sūtra says:
"For example, in the springtime, there were people bathing in a large pond who, while playing in boats, lost a lapis lazuli gem which sank into the deep water. At that time, all the people..."
Together they entered the water to search for this treasure, competing to seize tiles, stones, grass, wood, sand, and pebbles;
each person individually claimed to have found lapis lazuli, joyfully carrying it out, only to realize it was not the real thing.

At that time, the precious pearl remained still within the water, and by the power of the pearl, the water became entirely clear and transparent. Thereupon, the great assembly saw that the precious pearl was firmly situated beneath the water, just as before.

It is like looking up at the shape of the moon in the sky; at that time, there was a wise person among the crowd who, through the power of skillful means, entered deeply into the water and thereby obtained the jewel.

You bhikṣus should not practice the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity as if they were the ultimate truth, just as those people [in the parable] each took up tiles and pebbles.

And for the sake of the precious jewel, you should skillfully learn expedient means: in every place and at all times, constantly cultivate the perception of self, the perception of permanence, the perception of bliss, and the perception of purity.
Furthermore, you should know that the characteristics of the four dharmas previously cultivated are all inverted.

If you wish to attain the truth and cultivate these various perceptions, you must be like that wise person who skillfully extracts the precious jewel—namely, the perception of self, permanence, bliss, and purity.
The intended meaning of the parable in that sutra regarding "pure perception" is to cause the bhikṣus and others to abandon the four kinds of inverted perceptions;
here, the commentator wishes to have the practicing bodhisattvas take the treasure of their own minds by means of the three secrets,
and thus borrows that parable.
[Commentary] Regarding the passage "as in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* on the dedication [of merit]," it says: "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly offer various kinds of named flowers as alms—
namely, exquisite fragrant flowers, flowers of various colors, and immeasurable wondrous flowers— to make offerings to all Buddhas currently present,
as well as to all stūpas and temples after the Buddhas have passed into extinction, or to those who preach the Dharma."
When giving to the Sangha of bhikṣus, to all bodhisattvas, and even to all others who are poor, destitute, and without refuge, one dedicates these roots of goodness in this way:
namely, may all sentient beings attain the flowers of the samādhis of all Buddhas and be able to cause all dharmas to bloom; may all sentient beings... [all] attain... [and so forth].
May those who perceive [the Buddha] as such attain a joyful mind that is never weary or satiated;
may all sentient beings see what is harmonious and pleasing, their minds free from agitation or confusion; may all sentient beings fully practice vast and pure deeds;
and even may all sentient beings enter the great jewel-island, behold spiritual friends, and fully accomplish all roots of goodness.
This is the dedication of roots of goodness when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives flowers, in order to cause all sentient beings to attain pure and unobstructed wisdom;
the offerings of incense, lamps, and so forth are as extensively explained therein.
[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "another month" and so forth, this appears to be inconsistent with the scriptural text. The Sūtra states:

"Regarding the second stage of perfect awakening, one practices meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for one month within the mirror-maṇḍala; reciting [the mantra] until it reaches one *lakṣa* constitutes the ritual procedure for maintaining the mantra during the first month.
Next, during the second month, one offers fragrant ointments, flowers, and the like, thereby performing the rite of enrichment."
Furthermore, for the benefit of various classes of sentient beings, one again abandons all gains and offerings during the "other month.
According to this scriptural passage, the third month is designated as the "other month"; thus, the first "other" [month] follows this sequence. Now, the present commentary states:
"In this, there are two months of practice, and one immediately reaches the First Ground. As for the further inquiry, it surely possesses a profound intent. There are two...

"Month" refers to another month; a "full moon" is called the "two months. When the practitioner performs the actual accomplishment (*sādhana*) during the third month, within this month he should renounce all gain and honor during the first half of the lunar fortnight. On the fifteenth day, it becomes the full moon;

this month is the time for entering realization. To address this, he addresses "another" so that people may not find it difficult to understand, and thus causes them to ask further. Furthermore, this...

The esoteric explanation is that this serves to cause one to relinquish attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*). This practitioner has cultivated great roots of goodness and should not give rise to grasping or attachment toward them;
if attachment to phenomena arises, it will cause delay and prevent one from swiftly entering the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
One must abandon it in a subsequent month—meaning that the practitioner, having first generated the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*), desires to proceed toward the ten [stages].
Having received the rules for the mantras from one’s teacher, one performs the sequence of recitation according to a three-month period.
Specifically, the first ten stages of the mind (*daśa-cittotpāda*) correspond to the first month; the next ten stages of practice (*daśa-pratipatti*) correspond to the second month;

and the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) constitute the third month. Within these positions, four preparatory practices (*prayoga*) are distinguished; the preceding stages of "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) and "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) belong to another [category].

The "moon-like patience" (*candra-kṣānti*) and the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) belong to the full moon; in the stage of the "summit" (*mūrdhan*), one abandons attachment to dharmas, which is termed the abandonment of gain and honor.
Subsequently, having attained *siddhi* within the full moon, one reaches the first bhūmi; therefore, it is said that there are two "moons" herein.
As for the discussion of three months regarding the stages above the earth, this refers to the first bhūmi as the first month, which is itself bodhi.
Regarding this mind: if this mind lacks great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and skillful means (*upāya*), it cannot increase or develop.
It is like a lotus in a pond that will never bloom unless it receives the light of the sun. Therefore, the Commentary on the *Śāstra* states: "The moon is a metaphor for the bodhicitta.
When a practitioner enters the first stage (*bhūmi*), this mind becomes extremely perfect and pure; thus, it is called the 'first moon. From this point onward, the mind is metaphorized by the moon."

Arising the myriad practices of great compassion to make offerings to the Triple Gem and extensively planting roots of goodness, up until entering the stage of Immovable (*acalā-bhūmi*), is called the "First Month.

From the Immovable stage onward, again using the moon as a metaphor for the mind, one gives rise to immeasurable activities of skillful means and wisdom, correctly aligning with and dedicating [merit] toward the stage of the Tathāgata’s All-Knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); this is called the "Other Months," culminating in the Vajra Path.
The "Full Moon" stage subsequently reaches the stage of the Tathāgata. If one relies on each individual stage, it likewise possesses three months;
as explained in the second commentary, this principle is consistent with the explanation based on the three minds [of the preceding stage], and there is no error in the reasoning.

[Commentary] To explain this according to the text, "abandoning the eight dharmas" and so forth refers to the eight mental states—gain and loss, defamation and praise, fame and insignificance, suffering and pleasure—which involve either opposing or conforming to the world;
these should be abandoned. If one provides a profound interpretation, it means being free from attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).

For if one gives rise to attachment to dharmas, it will detain the practitioner and prevent them from swiftly entering the stage of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*). As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās without skillful means and enters the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they do not fall into the stages of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, yet they do not enter the rank of a Bodhisattva;

this is called the "arising of dharmas" for a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, which is precisely the arising of attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*). This refers to practicing the three triads of the six perfections.
Because of this ignorance, one does not fall into the two vehicles; yet because one lacks skillful means, one does not enter the stage of a bodhisattva.
To say "lacking skillful means" means that if one does not take non-apprehension as skillful means, one will be hindered and obstructed by the six perfections, samādhis, and so forth.
[Commentary] The note states: "Regarding 'external matters' and so forth, 'not seeking' means not giving rise to thoughts of longing.
Most people in the world seek worldly benefits to provide for their fragile bodies; because this hinders the Path, one must abandon them.

'Not receiving' means that even if offerings are presented, one does not accept them. To say 'abandoning these gains and offerings' does not mean that one accepts them first and then gives them away."
Sentient beings say that the merit of relinquishing offerings and gain is dedicated to three categories of beings;
among these three categories, one is called "beings who receive gifts.
[Commentary] This is the heart-mantra of all mantras: it means that when offering flowers, one uses the flower mantra, and for incense, the incense mantra.

Regarding the statement that "the mantra and so forth are now the heart of the three powers, and because they serve as the heart for the mantras of incense, flowers, and the like, they are called the 'Heart of All Mantras'":

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "both ordinary beings and sages alike offer [these]": Question: It can be said that Buddhas and sages "offer" [these things]; why is it that ordinary beings [also do so]?

Now, does this refer to "offering" (*kṣepa*)? Furthermore, in the passage below it says: "Above, one offers to all the assembly of noble ones; below, one bestows upon all sentient beings. Since one gives things to those who are superior, it is called an "offering"; since one gives to those who are inferior, it is called "bestowing. Why, then, is it said here that both ordinary beings and noble ones are "offered to"? Answer: The practitioner uses flowers as an offering. Because the practitioner offers them with flowers, [it is called an offering]. Even though they are offered to both ordinary beings and noble ones, because they are presented as a gift to those who are superior, it is termed an "offering. Therefore, it is said that both ordinary beings and noble ones are "offered to. Furthermore, regarding the statement "above, one offers to all the assembly of noble ones," this means that the practitioner takes these flowers and offers them to all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and so forth. Regarding the statement "below, one bestows upon all sentient beings," this means that the practitioner takes these flowers and bestows them upon all sentient beings, from the highest gods down to the inhabitants of the Avīci hell. Thus, although there are distinctions between "offering" and "bestowing," in this context they are both referred to as "offering. This is because the practitioner’s intention is to offer them to all noble ones and ordinary beings alike. Therefore, it is said that both ordinary beings and noble ones are "offered to. Furthermore, regarding the statement "just as a person gives things to their superiors, it is called an offering": this means that just as when one gives things to one's parents, teachers, or other superiors, it is called an "offering," so too, when one gives to all noble ones and ordinary beings, it is collectively termed an "offering. This is because the practitioner’s mind is focused on making offerings to all sentient beings. Therefore, it is said that both ordinary beings and noble ones are "offered to. Finally, regarding the statement "if one gives to those of lower status, it is called bestowing": this means that when one gives to servants, subordinates, or other inferiors, it is called "bestowing. However, in this case, because the practitioner regards all sentient beings as equal to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, there is no distinction between superior and inferior. Therefore, even though they are given to ordinary beings, it is still termed an "offering. Thus, it is said that both ordinary beings and noble ones are "offered to. This concludes the explanation of the meaning of "offering" and "bestowing. As for the phrase "just as a person gives things to their superiors, it is called an offering," this refers to the fact that when one gives to those who are superior in terms of lineage, virtue, or status, it is called an "offering.
