The timing of this movement arises from the single mind universally pervading the Dharma-realm; this is what is called "pervasive observation.

When one observes all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and does not perceive the marks of an ordinary being, they are identical to the Buddhas. Therefore, there is a specific reason for placing the character for "ordinary" (*fan*) above the character for "sage" (*sheng*).
Furthermore, when speaking of ordinary beings as a whole, there are internal and external distinctions; if we speak specifically of the "internal ordinary," we refer to those at the higher stages.
If one explains this according to the external ordinary person (bāhyapṛthagjana), it is because [the syllable] is bestowed upon them at the moment of hearing the teaching;
thus, there is no contradiction. [Commentary: Regarding "emptiness in all phenomena" and so forth, this refers to the Great Emptiness (mahāśūnyatā).

This means that the syllable *khaṃ* is the principle realized by the All-Knowing One (sarvajña); therefore, saying it "pervades all empty space" means it pervades the ten directions of the *gagaṇa* (the sky).
Because it is empty, it is said to be "equal in all respects.

[Commentary] Regarding "purity is identical to the vajra," this means that the substance of form is called "pure" because there is nothing about it that is not wondrous; thus, its purity is identical to the vajra.
Alternatively, the explanation that "the name is identical to the vajra" concludes the two preceding matters, while the subsequent phrase "purity is identical" refers to the following point.
Since the *vajra* is the third matter, the Commentary concludes below this point by stating: "Because these three matters are identical to the *vajra*, etc.
[Commentary] Alternatively, regarding the *Susiddhi* and so forth, it says that the objects to be accomplished should be perfumed with incense three times every day.
Incense it with fragrant water, sprinkle it with mantras, and further enhance it by gazing upon the object with the eye.
Place a *śrīvatsa* mark upon it, press down on the object with the hand, and sprinkle it with *gorocanā* water or white mustard seeds.
Arrange various offering implements and present them to that object. If it is to be accomplished during the waxing moon, take the fifteenth day.

Regarding those who achieve success during the dark fortnight: on the fourteenth day, one should take [the materials] and perform offerings using the mantra of the Family Mother (*kuleśvarī*), further adding various incenses, flowers, garlands, and other items.
Having anointed the hands with incense and placed a ring of *kuśa* grass upon the object to be accomplished, one should maintain the recitation throughout the night.
Reciting one hundred and eight times during each of the three periods of the night, such radiant manifestation will swiftly bring about accomplishment; thus it is said.

Regarding the method for gathering substances: on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day of either the waxing or waning moon, during an eclipse of the sun or moon, or at a time of earthquake, one should gather the substances before noon.
Alternatively, having attained a meditative state (*viṣaya*) during the recitation of mantras, one should then gather the various substances.
Or else, having bathed for purification, abstaining from food and observing the fast (*upavāsa*), one should seek them with a virtuous mind.
Regarding the objects within one's sphere of activity, whatever items are required as described, one should go to wherever those items are located and purchase them;

however, one may take those items without paying their price. Having taken those items according to their respective natures—whether superior, middling, or inferior—one should select the highest quality ones.
Once they have been obtained in accordance with the Dharma, one should apply diligent effort to perform the rites of accomplishment and so forth.
[Commentary]: "All use the Vajra for self-protection, etc. means that at the beginning of this section, one protects [oneself] with the Vajraprajñā-mudrā.
[Commentary]:
"That Tathāgata is one, etc. refers to the Tathāgatas currently residing throughout all worlds who have attained universal penetration.

Because of the perfection of means (*upāya-pāramitā*), one knows that all phenomena are one, being free from arising and ceasing, permanence and annihilation, identity and difference, and coming and going.
Even if one were to conceptually differentiate arising and ceasing, permanence and annihilation, and so forth, their fundamental nature is emptiness.

However, for the sake of liberating sentient beings, by the power of the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*), one employs the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) upon the unconditioned fruit-nature (*asaṃskṛta-phala-svabhāva*).
"Retinue" (*parivāra*) and "this retinue" (*ayaṃ parivāraḥ*): these characters in the sūtra are indicative terms; while their verbal expressions differ, their meaning is the same. [Commentary]:
Regarding "seeing the Dharma and dwelling in peace and happiness," "seeing" means to realize or attain; "Dharma" refers to the *siddhi*-dharma of the perfectly awakened mind.
Because the practitioner uses this *siddhi*-dharma to amuse themselves, it is called "dwelling in peace and happiness by seeing the Dharma."
To give rise to a joyful mind is precisely the practitioner’s initial realization of the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Because one first attains the nature of the noble ones and gives rise to great joy," and so forth. Furthermore, the sub-commentary below states: "Seeing the Dharma" means realization;
"abiding" means that having seen it for oneself, one then imparts it to all sentient beings. By seeing this matter, both self and others obtain [the fruit].
"Because of the supreme benefit of the Dharma," and so forth.

[Commentary: Regarding the reason for placing Mahāvairocana in the intermediate directions and asking further questions: it is because the objects to be accomplished here pertain to all three families.
If the object to be accomplished belongs to the Buddha Family, Mahāvairocana remains solely in his original position; if it is an object to be accomplished... [text continues].
If an object belongs to the Vajra family or the Padma family, Mahāvairocana Tathāgata is instead placed in a cardinal or intermediate direction.
Why is this? Because the presiding deity of the object is determined by the specific family to which it belongs. The Susiddhi states:

"If one wishes to accomplish substances such as clarified butter (*sarpis*) and the like, one should construct a maṇḍala; its dimensions should be four times [the size of the object], with various mudrās arranged on all four sides."

Proceeding thus, one places the Great Deities of the Eight Directions in the outer enclosure; next, within the central womb (*garbha*), one places the seal (*mudrā*) of the presiding deity of the respective family and the object to be accomplished.
These are placed therein according to what is explained in their respective root texts. The presiding deity of that family is installed above the objects in the central womb.

To the east and west, one places the seal of the deity one personally maintains, as well as the *homa* hearth and other implements. Regarding the statement in the present commentary, "furthermore, it asks":

This means that if, after the maṇḍala has been constructed and Vairocana Tathāgata has already occupied the central womb, the object to be accomplished belongs to another family, it is appropriate to move Vairocana to one of the cardinal or intermediate directions; therefore, he asks again.
[Commentary]: Regarding "those who have obtained *kṣipa*," *kṣipa* refers to footwear. Cui Bao’s *Gujin Zhu* states: "Wooden soles are placed beneath shoes;
because they dry and absorb moisture, one does not fear mud or wetness, hence they are called *kṣipa*. Regarding "the king (*rāja*) and others" in the sutra:
in Sanskrit, *rāja* means "king"; "and others" refers to ministers and commoners.
[Commentary]: "Pervading all internal and external parts of the body" means that "internal" refers to the inside of the body and "external" refers to the outside of the body.

Regarding the "inside of the body," the subsequent scripture states: "Furthermore, for the practitioner of the syllable *va*, relying on the yoga of the ritual procedures for performing activities to benefit sentient beings, the water of the mind becomes profoundly full and pure white like snow or milk, pervading all the pores and flowing forth."
Regarding the statement that "the supreme purity overflows from within and pervades the exterior of the body, such as the great earth," the Sūtra says:

"The syllable *ra* is at the upper body, the syllable *va* is at the navel wheel, and so on down to the syllable *ra* for the lower body, with the syllable *ha* serving as the insignia (*cihna*), and so forth.
Thus, it is said to pervade all parts of the body, both internally and externally.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "when one is accomplished," it means that the seed-syllable of this *iṣṭadevatā* is perfectly luminous;
it is three yet one, and one yet three, without mutual obstruction. Therefore, when one is accomplished, all three are accomplished, and thus it is termed "three lakṣas."
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "this samādhi should... and so forth, "this" refers to the samādhis belonging to [the deities] such as Samantabhadra, which are the samādhis realized by them.

"Should" (ying) refers to those who manifest in response; that is, the provisional manifestations. This means that when a practitioner enters into yoga, these Samantabhadra-Vajras and others—by means of bodies that are the fruits of their meditative concentration—must descend to respond and appear. Although they descend to respond and appear, they may do so either individually or collectively.

One must not definitively judge that accomplishment occurs only when [the deities] manifest in their entirety; rather, one should know that if even a single deity appears at the appropriate time, then accomplishment is attained.
Furthermore, it is explained that the character "ma" (末) should be read as "yi" (亦); thus, when even a single one appears, accomplishment is likewise attained.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the secret teaching can be understood through the mind," when the secret teaching is given, it refers to the words and phrases of the mantra of Samantabhadra and others.
During the practitioner’s yoga, these mantra phrases must appear simultaneously; if there is any deficiency, accomplishment is not attained, from which one knows that obstacles exist.
If they all appear before one clearly and distinctly, one knows that accomplishment has been achieved.

Furthermore, because one knows that there are no obstacles, it is called "esoteric teaching" and so forth. Alternatively, even when a single syllable appears, accomplishment may be attained, such as with the syllables for the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvajñatā*).
[Commentary] "The body born of mind" means that it arises in accordance with the mind; it is not the same as the "body born of mind" of the transformation-rebirth (*pariṇāmi-kāya*).
[The term] "body" (*kāya*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the aforementioned afflictions," it means that various subtle afflictions are called "superior afflictions" (*ūrdhva-kleśa*). Thus, the *Qixinlun chao* (Notes on the Awakening of Faith) states:

"Those of superior grade are called 'superior' because they function constantly; they are called 'superior afflictions' because they transcend [the lower stages], as they exist in those who have attained the ten stages (*bhūmi*)."
Since these are not afflictions according to the Hīnayāna, they are the most difficult points to subdue;
now, by means of the syllable *A-ha*, one is able to subdue them—or rather, the three poisons of affliction mentioned above.
[Commentary]: Regarding "intimately [attaining] all that is equal," the Sūtra says, "intimately realizing all," which refers to the perfection of the fruit of self-benefit.
The Commentary says, "intimately bestowing," which refers to the virtue of the practice of benefiting others. The Sūtra and the Commentary reflect one another across these sections in various places.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "as previously" in the *Aksara-sūtra*, this expression does not appear in that sūtra;

the reason it is included here in the commentary is that it refers to "reciting while maintaining correct mindfulness as before," meaning one should contemplate the letter *A* according to the method described in the preceding text and perform the recitation accordingly.
[Commentary]: "This is the bodhicitta," etc., means that the practitioner transforms this letter *A* into the form of the Honored One (the deity).
This is the Buddha of the true mark (*dharmatā*) perceived within the practitioner’s bodhicitta.

The Buddha of the true mark is precisely the Buddha of the inconceivable dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of the *dharmadhātu*, which is not like other [deities] existing within the mental factors (*caitta*) of deluded conceptualization.
Because it is that which is perceived, it is said: "This is itself the bodhicitta," and so forth. [Commentary]:
Regarding the statement "A is practice, etc.," a note in this *Akṣara-sūtra* states: "The 'A' pronounced with a departing tone (*qùshēng*) and in a rapid manner (*jìhū*).
Before sequentially revealing its meaning, one first manifests its specific form—namely, the syllable 'A' pronounced with a departing tone and rapidly. This refers to what is perceived...
That which is called "the practice of original non-arising" refers to the letter *A* with the departing tone (*ā*).

To say that the two dots on the side signify the meaning of "purifying and removing" means that placing two dots beside the previously mentioned *A* with the departing tone constitutes the *nirvāṇa-bindu*.
To say that "by this meaning it reaches all suffering" means that by means of this *ā*-tone samādhi, one is able to subdue the four māras.
The point beside *nirvāṇa* (the *bindu*) that removes all suffering is the meaning of pronouncing the syllable *A* with a sharp, departing tone.

Furthermore, it has three meanings, up to "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*): *Va* signifies liberation (*vimukti*), *Ra* signifies great wisdom (*mahājñāna*), and *Ha* signifies the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
These three liberations are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither preceding nor following; they immediately return to *Kha*.
The character [for this] is "Great Emptiness" (Mahāśūnyatā).

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage "As when the Buddha first desired to attain enlightenment," according to the *Record of the Western Regions* (*Xiyuji*), the Vajrāsana at the very center of the enclosure of the Bodhi tree was originally formed at the beginning of the Bhadrakalpa and arose simultaneously with the great earth; it rests upon the trichiliocosm.
Situated at the center of the lowest level of the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*), it extends upward from the surface of the earth and is composed of vajra.

Measuring over a hundred paces in circumference, it is the seat upon which the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa sit to enter the Vajrasamādhi; thus it is called the Vajrāsana. It is also termed the *bodhimaṇḍa* because it is the place for realizing the Noble Path.
When the great earth trembled, this alone remained unshaken; therefore, when the Tathāgata was about to realize perfect enlightenment, he passed through this very spot.
The ground in the four corners all shook, but when arriving at this place, it became peaceful and did not shake.
If one does not take the diamond as a seat, there is no ground capable of giving rise to the diamond-like samādhi. Now, wishing to subdue Māra and attain enlightenment, one must dwell here;
therefore, the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa all come to this very spot. Since this [place] is now identical to that, it is said: "As when the Buddha first desired to attain [enlightenment]."
"The Path and so forth.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "emptiness has no fixed form," the four corners produced herein correspond to the syllable *A*, which is the earth wheel;

the circular ring corresponds to the syllable *Va*, which is the water wheel; the triangle corresponds to the syllable *Ra*, which is the fire wheel; and the half-moon corresponds to the syllable *Ha*.
Regarding the syllable *vaṃ*, there is further the fifth, the syllable *khaṃ*, which is the wheel of space (*ākāśa-cakra*).
Because it manifests various and manifold forms without any fixed shape, these four wheels are not uniform; thus they are called "various."
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the reddest among the red," etc., it means that while the flames of worldly fire are extremely red, this [wisdom-fire] surpasses even them;
furthermore, because its meaning is the same as "the burning among burnings," it is called "the reddest among the red," and so forth.

Another explanation is that while worldly fire, once it has burned an object, merely results in ashes, this wisdom-fire of the syllable *ra* (raṃ), having burned away the afflictions (*kleśa*), is then able to... [follow accordingly].
All virtuous merits arise from this; for this reason, it is said to be "the burning among burnings," and so forth.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement that the syllable *ra* must be used as fire:

this means that the syllable *ra* must function as fire, which is to say it serves the purpose of *homa* (fire-offering), specifically the rite of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). Externally, it subjugates evil persons; internally, it...
Because one attains mastery over this matter by subduing the afflictions, it is said that "one must use fire for its purpose.

Regarding the phrase "and when resentment arises," it means that when another person directs resentment toward oneself, at the time of employing this fire, one can cause both self and other to achieve benefit.
"Self-benefit" refers to not being harmed or afflicted by others; "benefit for others" [refers to... [text truncated].
This means that by causing them to be well-disciplined, one establishes the causal conditions for attaining the Buddha-way.
[Commentary] Regarding "empty and yet empty": the first "empty" character is the "emptiness" of the character *ha* (訶), meaning "cause.
Because there is a cause, one is able to create karma and summon its fruit; thus, by entering the gateway of the letter *a*, the cause, karma, and the fruit are all [empty].
The three matters are all quiescent, like empty space. Furthermore, this syllable *ha* transforms into the syllable *kha*;
since the essential nature of *kha* is the meaning of emptiness, or because it merely sweeps away the prior characteristic of emptiness, it is said to be "empty and yet again empty."
[Commentary]: "Furthermore, being able to perform various supernatural transformations" means that by placing the syllable *raṃ* between one's feet, one can travel through the void;

and by placing it within the gates of the eyes, ears, and so forth, performing various beneficial purposes according to their respective meanings, this is called "being able to perform various supernatural transformations."
[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "below, place the letter RA, etc.," it means that as previously described, one first places the letter RA above the navel;
upon the letter RA, one places the banner (dhvaja); and above the banner, one places the letter HA.
Because this is the sequence, it says, "furthermore, below, place the letter RA, etc."
[Commentary]: Regarding the direction of the dragons (*nāga*), the practitioner does not merely face the southwest.
That southwest is properly the domain of the *rākṣasa*, not the domain of the dragons. As for the dragon domain, it belongs to the west; this west comprises two positions:
first, the position of the Earth Deities (*bhūmideva*), and second, the position of the various dragons. Since the Earth Deities are situated precisely...

The West Gate is the position of the Dragon; it is now established to the south of the Earth Deity. When the practitioner faces that direction to perform the ritual, it does not mean pointing directly toward the southwest.
[Commentary] "Various mixed colors" refers to what the Sūtra calls "the various activities of each"; this is within the Wind Mandala.
The various activities performed are not merely the various colors contained within the wheel of the syllable *khaṃ*;
rather, they are called "various mixed colors.
[Sūtra] Regarding the "Chapter on Accomplishing Siddhi": "Accomplishment" (*siddhi*) is a term for obtaining; "siddhi" means to achieve.

The meaning is not yet clear as to whether *siddhi* (accomplishment) and *sādhana* (attainment) are one and the same or different. If they were different, why was *siddhi* previously translated as "attainment" (*sādhana*)?
If they were one and the same, they should not have been placed side by side. However, this single title encompasses both cause and effect;
the upper character "attainment" (*sādhana*) refers to the practitioner's causal capacity for accomplishment, while the lower term "*siddhi*" refers to [the result].
This is because it is the fruit accomplished through mantras. As a verse in the sutra states: "The locus of the mind (*manas*) of the Mahāsattva is called the maṇḍala;
by fully understanding the state of the heart of all mantras, one attains the accomplishment. In this verse, the first two lines explain the two characters *siddhi*.
"Mahāsattva" refers to Vajrapāṇi being addressed; "locus of the mind" (*manas-sthāna*) refers to the locus of the heart (*citta-sthāna*).
Because there is not a single dharma to be found apart from this mind, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas have provisionally explained it through names and terminology for the sake of easy understanding;
thus, what is called the *maṇḍala* is precisely the *maṇḍala* of the sentient beings' own minds.
The following two phrases explain that [the mind] is merely covered by ignorance and is not recognized as such by itself.
The two characters "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) refer to the fruit of the upper mind-sphere maṇḍala. By what means can this be realized?
If a practitioner relies upon mantra as the gateway, they will be able to understand that the stage of the mantra-mind is not different from the mind-sphere of the maṇḍala.

This is the initial awakening (*ādikṣānti-bodhi*) which accords with the original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*); this is called "attaining the fruit. Thus, these aforementioned two characters [refer to this].
The phrase "that which can accomplish" (the cause) and "that which is accomplished" (the result) form a *tatpuruṣa* compound as "the siddhi of accomplishment.

Alternatively, since cause and effect are non-dual, "accomplishment" (*sādhana*) is itself "siddhi," forming a *karmadhāraya* compound. This refers to what was stated in the preceding *Prādurbhāva-paṭala*, where the Tathāgata answered the third question of Vajrapāṇi regarding how one achieves the fruit:
although various mundane and supramundane fruits were mentioned, they all arise from the syllables (*akṣara*).
The "Gate" has already appeared, yet the skillful means for the accomplishment of the Mind itself have not been explained; they are now fully set forth, and thus this chapter follows.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "by means of the four kinds," it means that although the Flower-Pedestal Treasury of one's own mind is already perfectly complete with its stamens, pistils, and petals, because the four kinds of afflictions are constantly co-arising, first—

First, self-delusion (*ātma-moha*) refers to ignorance (*avidyā*); because one is deluded regarding the characteristic of a self and confused about the principle of non-self, it is called self-delusion.
Second, self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) refers to the grasping at a self; because one falsely discriminates a self within phenomena that are not a self, it is called self-view.
Third, self-pride (*ātma-māna*) refers to arrogance; because one maintains the grasped self and causes the mind to become haughty, it is called self-pride. Fourth, self-... [text truncated]
"Attachment" refers to my craving for the grasped self; because one generates deep attachment toward this self, it is called "attachment to self.

These four constantly arise and disturb the inner mind, causing the external evolving consciousnesses to perpetually become defiled. Sentient beings, due to this, circulate through the flow of birth and death and are unable to achieve liberation;
therefore, they are called "afflictions," as is fully explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

[Commentary: Regarding "as when those of the Two Vehicles enter the Path," this means that when practitioners of the Two Vehicles first enter the Path, if the teacher asks about prohibitions and difficulties, one knows that those persons possess a resolute mind for entering the Path. This resolute mind is precisely *samādhi*;
*samādhi* is translated as "vow" (*śamatha*). Because of this vow of equality, one possesses a concentrated mind; this is resoluteness.
The *citta* is the *cit-ta*, meaning the mind that knows and contemplates; the subsequent *han-liduo* (kṣetra) is the mind situated in the center.
If one can realize this "mind within the mind," it is precisely the Tathāgata’s definitive mind (*niyata-citta*). The commentary states: "This refers to *samādhi*. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The definitive mind, when joyful, is called the internal abiding place (*adhyātma-sthāna*). This clarifies that it is merely one.
It is the mind. [Commentary:

As for the statement, "This matter is not so; though one asks, it is of no benefit," etc., it means that this fruit of the unsurpassed One Vehicle must be realized through one's own personal testimony (*pratyātma-vedya*).
If it is not personally realized, then even if one asks, it will ultimately be of no benefit—just as when a person hears a description of the celestial nectar (*amṛta*).
If one does not personally taste a flavor, no matter how many various skillful means one uses to describe it, it will ultimately be of no benefit.

It is like a blind person asking another what the color of milk is like; though others reply that its color is like mother-of-pearl, snow, or a white crane, despite hearing these descriptions, the blind person can never truly understand the actual color of the milk. Each of these blind people forms their own interpretation and competes [with the others].
Holding a conch-shell and powdered snow, he rose up from the four disputes; this was entirely because he had not personally realized [the truth]. Thus, although he questioned, it was of no benefit.
[Commentary] Regarding the principle of the *Aṅgulimāla*’s precept against stealing: as stated above, the fruit of the unsurpassed bodhi of all Buddhas is precisely the self-mind of sentient beings.
Apart from this mind, there is no dharma to be found; one simply requires self-awakening.
In truth, because there is no one who can bestow [the precepts], he cites that sūtra to explain and establish this point.
In the Sanskrit language, Aṅgulimāla means "Finger-Garland," so called because he made a garland from the fingers of many people. As that sūtra says:
"At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Aṅgulimāla: 'You should now receive the precept against taking what is not given. Aṅgulimāla...
Rāhu replied in verse: "I too am currently unable to uphold the precept against stealing.
I constantly practice taking what is not given, plundering the wealth and property of others.
Since there is no giver or recipient in Bodhi, and one takes for oneself what is not given, if one speaks thus, that is truly upholding the precept against taking what is not given."
[Commentary]:
"Nor does one employ other antidotes" means that, as in the first chapter of this very sutra, the World-Honored One,

wishing to cause the practitioner to know their own mind as it truly is, taught the analogy of space to [discern] the various [categories] such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*).
Through various stages of observation, one counteracts the defilements external to the mind until, like space, one gradually attains the path of illumination of the mind-dharma;
now, however, it is not so, for it causes all practitioners to attain it by directly observing the locus of the mind.
Thus it says, "nor does one perform other [practices]," etc. Regarding the phrase "the locus of this mind," "this mind" refers to the physical heart-mass (*māṃsapiṇḍa*).
In Sanskrit, *khaṇḍa* is correctly transliterated as *khaṇḍa* (khri-na); this is translated here as "flesh-mass.
When a practitioner contemplates that their own mind is itself the Buddha, they first visualize the inner mind as a great, luminous orb (*maṇḍala*).
Within this luminous orb, there is a seed-syllable (*bīja*), which transforms into the body of the deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). Upon the heart of the deity, there is again a luminous orb and so forth. If...
When one contemplates through the syllable *A*, the phrase of "original non-arising," there is no distinction between internal and external, or between subject and object.
The mind of the *buddha* (the deity) is precisely one's own mind, and one's own mind is precisely the mind of the *buddha*.
Because they are thus non-dual yet dual, and dual yet non-dual, it is said that "the locus of this mind is precisely the inner mind of the ordinary person," and so forth.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the leaves of the other four corners," etc.: the four corners are the remnants of the four cardinal directions; thus they are called "corners.
These four leaves correspond to the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*). According to what was explained above, the leaf in the southeast corner is the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
This bodhisattva is named the "Worthy Vase" (*bhadraghaṭa*), for he is able to produce various jewels of practice and vows to bestow universally upon sentient beings. This is...

In the southwest corner is Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva; this bodhisattva realizes that all phenomena are fundamentally equal and that Buddhas and sentient beings share one and the same characteristic—this is called "acting in concert" (samānārthatā). In the northeast is Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva;
for all who invoke his name or take refuge in him, he brings about benefit and happiness according to their hearts' desires—this is called...
In the northwest corner of the Beneficial Action (Arthacaryā) is the Bodhisattva Maitreya.

Because this Bodhisattva takes loving-kindness as his fundamental nature and is able to gather and transform sentient beings through gentle speech—which is called "loving speech" (priyavāditā)—it is said that [the others] are in the remaining four corners, and so forth.
Next, regarding the phrase "knowing their fruits" and "further questioning," etc.: it is asked whether the preceding sequence does not all proceed from the letter A, the primordial non-arising.
Because of the bodhicitta, next the practice of the letter *Ā* is clarified; next the great emptiness of the letter *Aṃ* is clarified;
and finally the letter *Aḥ*, which is nirvāṇa, is clarified. In sequence, this means that bodhicitta is the cause, great compassion is the root, and skillful means (*upāya*) is the culmination.
Now, herein, from the letter *A* as primordial non-arising, one proceeds to clarify the letter *Aṃ* as great emptiness and skillful means.
One might ask: "Does this explanation of the long *ā* syllable as the ten thousand practices of great compassion not contradict the preceding text?

Furthermore, does it not lose the sequential order of the causes and effects of generating the bodhicitta, practicing, and realizing the principle? The answer is: The meaning and power of the *akṣara-cakra* (syllable-wheel) manifest in many ways.

That which follows "fundamental non-arising" and precedes "great emptiness" is explained in terms of realization—that is, the sequence of generating the bodhicitta, practicing, and realizing the fruit.

The sequence is as follows: now, with respect to awakening through understanding—namely, the arousal of the mind, the realization of principle, practice, and the attainment of great nirvāṇa—it is for this reason that the stages do not contradict one another.
[Commentary: "Now, wishing to instruct those sentient beings" means that for all sentient beings, the various consciousnesses and mental factors take ignorance (*avidyā*) as their fundamental source.
If ignorance is transformed into clarity (*vidyā*), how could any consciousness or mind be found? Thus, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* says:

"By destroying the characteristics of the synthetic consciousness (*sāṃghāṭika-vijñāna*) and extinguishing the characteristics of the continuous mind (*saṃtati-citta*), the Dharma-body manifests, and wisdom becomes purely immaculate."
Therefore, it says, "Now I wish," and so forth.

[The Commentary] states, "This sūtra is that which was kept secret by the Noble Ones," meaning that this sūtra is a treasury of secret mantras (mantra-garbha), and the noble ones who transmitted the Dharma have passed it down according to the Buddha’s intentional meaning (saṃdhāya-bhāṣita). Thus, the Preface explains: "Now, within the text of the sūtra..."
The hidden and the manifest are elucidated before and after, and phenomena and principle are presented in alternation; this is the Buddha’s skillful means (*upāya*).
Because it is so, how could the holy ones who transmit the Dharma not keep it secret?

[Commentary]: Regarding the instruction that this syllable *Oṃ* should be visualized as being upon the crown of the head: the scriptural passage states that it is marked with the "great empty dot" (*mahābindu*).
Question: Why do you interpret the syllable *aṃ* by explaining it as *oṃ*, which deviates from the literal meaning of the sūtra? Answer:

The intent of the sūtra is to directly reveal that whoever possesses the bodhicitta will necessarily realize the fruit of bodhi; therefore, it bypasses the intermediate stages and simply designates the syllable *aṃ*.

In explaining the scriptural text, the commentary must not add anything gratuitously; that is to say, although one has already resolved upon Bodhicitta, it is necessary to rely upon the skillful means of Great Compassion Samādhi before one can attain the fruit of Bodhi. This is like a lotus flower:

if it does not receive the nourishment of pond water, it will never bloom. The lotus of the mind is likewise. The intent of the scripture is to be concise, and thus merely employs this elliptical expression.
Since the text of the *Śāstra* fully elucidates this, there is no contradiction in marking it with the syllable *Oṃ*.

[Commentary] Question: Regarding the statement "water arises from the letter A" and so forth, why does the preceding *Śāstra* explain the character *An* (暗) in the scriptural text as the syllable *Oṃ*?
Now I ask this again: if one relies on the bodhicitta, great compassion, and skillful means, for what reason is such an explanation provided?
In the end, you have already granted that the water of the *ā* syllable Bodhicitta flows directly to the *aṃ* syllable of skillful means; is this not so?
[The answer is: It is indeed as previously explained. Having generated the Bodhicitta and attained Bodhi, one again gives rise to Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
This question is posed in terms of the distinction between realization through understanding (*parijñā*) and realization through attainment (*sākṣātkriyā*).

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "with the stainless eye" (*vimalanetra*) and so forth: this stainless eye is precisely the eye of the syllable *ra*. This means that by visualizing the syllable *ra* and placing it within the eyes, they are called the "stainless eyes";
they are not physical eyes. Furthermore, because this syllable *ra* is topped with a dot of emptiness (*bindu*), it is named the "Mind of the Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātucitta*);
therefore, it is said that "all are the essence of the Dharma-realm."
[Commentary: "Also seeing the Tathāgata-syllable, etc. refers to the *kṣa*-gate. *Kṣa* signifies emptiness (*ākāśa*);
for all Buddhas take the emptiness of all phenomena as their seat.

[Commentary]: What is called the "nature of the six sovereign kings being pure" means that the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) of sentient beings are like precious jewels whose essential nature is eternally pure, yet they are defiled by the dust of sensory objects. If one polishes them away, they attain clarity and purity.
When the source of the minds of all sentient beings is pure, the six consciousnesses are likewise entirely pure; this is precisely what constitutes the six sovereigns.
The King is like a Tathāgata; therefore, in the *Sūtra on the Names of the Buddhas*, there are six Buddhas, namely:
the Buddha Sovereign Lord of the Eye Dhāraṇī, the Buddha Sovereign Lord of the Ear Dhāraṇī, and so forth, up to the Buddha Sovereign Lord of the Mind Dhāraṇī—it is precisely this meaning.

[Commentary]: This character "luo" (邏) refers to the Sanskrit term *lakṣaṇa* (相). The explanation states that "having a dot above" means placing the great empty dot (*bindu*) upon the character "luo";

this refers to the character "lan" (覽). Regarding the "three emptinesses," these are the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), and the great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*).
This means that the first [emptiness] is the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*), wherein all signs are fundamentally empty; this is the first [emptiness].
It is one emptiness; furthermore, because all characteristics are non-arising in their essential nature, they are the emptiness of emptiness.
Moreover, because all characteristics are fundamentally empty and non-arising in their essential nature, this is the great emptiness; thus it is said, "this letter *la*, etc."

【Sūtra】 Regarding the Chapter on the Practice of the Maṇḍala of the Revolving Wheel of Syllables (*akṣaracakra-maṇḍala-caryā-paṭala*): "Revolving" means to rotate; it refers to the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*.

This means that if a practitioner sees the syllable A (*a-kāra*), they should know that it explains the meaning of the bodhicitta; and so on, up to if they see the long Ā (*ā-kāra*), they should know that it reveals the power of skillful means (*upāya-bala*).
If they see the twenty-eight syllables from Ka (*ka-kāra*) and Kha (*kha-kāra*) through Sa-ha (*sa-ha-kāra*), [they should likewise understand their respective meanings].
One should know that all these are gates of wisdom; if one sees the letter *i* and so forth, one should know they are gates of samādhi.
If one sees the five letters beginning with *aṅ*, one should know they manifest the point (*bindu*) of Great Emptiness, which signifies the meaning of attaining Buddhahood.
If a practitioner thoroughly realizes this meaning, they are able to enter the meaning of all dhāraṇīs; this is called "turning the letters. These are the very letters themselves.

The arrangement and rotation of these letter-gates (akṣaramukha) are unimpeded, like a wheel; thus it is called the "wheel of letters" (akṣaracakra). "Wheel" is its essence (*tattva*), and "rotation" is its function (*vṛtti*).
Since the function is subsumed within the essence, both are held as a *karmadhāraya* compound; therefore, it is named the "Rotation of the Wheel of Letters" (*Akṣaracakravartimaṇḍala*).
The meaning of the term *maṇḍala* has already been explained above. *Maṇḍala* is a general name, which is here distinguished from the specific [term] "Rotation of the Wheel of Letters."
Regarding the maṇḍala, it is formed through the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound; the practitioner’s performance also encompasses multiple meanings.
The practice of the *akṣaracakramaṇḍala* likewise relies on the *tatpuruṣa* compound, and is therefore called the "practice of the *akṣaracakramaṇḍala*.
As above, when Vajrapāṇi first questioned the Buddha, the Buddha answered this question from beginning to end, though his discourse was occasionally interrupted by other speech.
Now the Buddha raises the preceding point and answers it; thus this chapter follows.

[Commentary]: "The bliss of the Tathāgata’s present dharma" refers to the bliss of Great Nirvāṇa, namely the powers, fearlessnesses, unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), and so forth of the Tathāgata.
This corresponds to what was previously stated in the sūtra: "Attaining the vision of the Tathāgata’s phrases," up to "the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom."

[Commentary]: Regarding the terms "vidyā" (wisdom/incantation) and "mantra" (spell), there is a doubt as to why, in some places it is said that this is a mantra, while in other places it is said that this vidyā-queen is the mantra;
are the vidyā and the mantra one and the same, or are they different? Because...
Because of this doubt, it is now said that there is a distinction between *vidyā* and the meaning of *mantra*:
if something issues from the speech of the Tathāgata’s mind and mouth, it is called a *mantra*;
if it arises spontaneously from all the limbs of the Tathāgata, it is called a *vidyā*. If that is so, why does the Sūtra state that these were spoken arising from *samādhi*?
"Is it not the case that the *vidyārājñī* (wisdom-consort) speaks with her mouth? The commentary states: Although she manifests from the body, this is indeed "speaking";
therefore, this is called "bodily speech. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "In some buddha-fields, the Dharma is revealed by gazing;

in others, by raising the eyebrows, or by moving the eyes, and so forth, causing all bodhisattvas to attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This is also bodily speech. Furthermore, one desires...
Because the revealed Dharma is free from words, it is said that its manifestation through the body is called "vidyā" (knowledge).
Because the state of wordlessness does not obstruct words, its expression through the mouth is called "mantra" (true word). Therefore, the essence of vidyā and mantra is no different.

[Commentary]: She is addressed with a feminine noun because of the sense of "increasing. This means that this vidyā (wisdom-consort) can increase and cause the practitioner’s merit and dharmas to grow;
therefore, she is addressed with a feminine noun. In Sanskrit, *vinyate* is the masculine form, while *vinī* is the feminine form;
both are translated as "vidyā" (wisdom). The feminine designation is added because it follows the sense of "increasing."
These are the words of the Consort.
[Commentary] Regarding the inquiry concerning *apratisama*: one is instructed to inquire into the meaning of this mantra’s phrases as well as the meaning of its syllables.
As for the meaning of the phrases, it is explained in the third commentary as having the sense of being "unequaled" and "without counterpart"; that is to say, this clarifies...
The Consort transcends all speech and metaphors; because there is not a single dharma that can serve as her equal, she is called "Peerless" (*asama*).
As for the meaning of the syllables: *A* signifies that all dharmas are fundamentally unarisen;
*Pa* signifies the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); and *Ra* signifies dust (*rajas*). Since all dharmas enter the gateway of the syllable *A*, this is itself the ultimate truth.
That which is fundamentally unarisen within the objects of the truths is the essence of the *maṇḍala* (the many-gated door) accompanied by samādhi;
its invocation is the meaning of "mind" (*citta*) and also the meaning of "suchness" (*tathatā*). That is to say, the true aspect of one's own mind as it is constitutes the bodhicitta.
This mind is without peer and without counterpart, and is thus called "unequaled" (*asama*); it is the *abhyantara-mantra*.
Regarding the phrase "The Vidyārājñī clarifies the non-dual realm of the Tathāgata’s body": the Vidyārājñī refers to the aforementioned mantra-phrase.
As for the "non-dual realm," it means that the Vidyārājñī and the Tathāgata possess non-dual characteristics.
This is because the Tathāgata is identical to the *samādhi* of equality with space, identical to the *samādhi* of supreme victory, and identical to the state of abiding in the ultimate.
This collection of supreme vows consists of many dharmas, which is why it is called a "body" (*kāya*); thus, it is said that the *vidyā-queen* is the body of the Tathāgata and so forth.
Furthermore, this *vidyā-queen* arises spontaneously from the body of the Tathāgata; thus, the Tathāgata’s body is the manifesting subject and the *vidyā-queen* is the manifested object.
This realm is ultimately non-dual. If one does not realize this principle, there is no way to attain Buddhahood. Why?

"As for 'like throwing a vajra,' etc., this indicates that the Vajra-wisdom of the Tathāgata, from within the emptiness of the *dharmadhātu*, performs an empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), causing these secret wisdom-seals (*jñānamudrā*) of all Buddhas to enter into all sentient beings."
Because it gives birth to the ground of the mind, it is said to be "like throwing a vajra," and so forth.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "this very *benu* (original/primordial)": this single character *benu* should be the character *a*.
*A* signifies the meaning of "original" (*benu*). As stated in the fifth commentary above: "In the Sanskrit original, the character *a* possesses the sound of 'original' (*benu*)."
Because it is the root-mother of all these syllables, and because the first [syllable] stands at the head of all syllables, from it all phenomena are produced;
it is also the meaning of "life-span" (*āyus*). Therefore, it is said that the primordial (*ādibhūta*) is itself the life-span.
Thus, he asks again.
[Commentary: Although it says "self-praise" and so forth, this refers to the Sanskrit word for "I. To cite that Sanskrit word: the term for "I" in Sanskrit is *ahaṃ*.
This syllable *ma* (from *ahaṃ*) is pronounced with the vowel *a*, which signifies "I am originally unborn.
Because it is unborn, it is the state of primordial, eternal quiescence; thus, although it says "self-praise," it is actually an exposition [of this truth].
This is the Dharma.

"It was stated above that the Dharma of self-realization is like drinking water, where one knows its coldness or heat for oneself; how then can Vajrapāṇi and others [know it]?"

Within this, there is the manifest realization of the meaning that is firm, immovable, peerless, and incomparable;
although it encompasses all manner of meanings pervading the entire dharma-realm, its essence is the great vow. Thus, the sutra says:
"One is able to see the Buddha’s seat of Bodhi through supreme vows."
[Commentary: "Not departing from such wondrous principle" and so forth refers to this very seat, which is like empty space, free from all conceptualization and discursive proliferation (*prapañca*).
If one proceeds directly to the gateway of letters, it is the letter *A*.

Although the various Bodhisattvas practice through such diverse skillful means (*upāya*), these are nonetheless non-dual and undifferentiated, never departing from this subtle and wondrous state of original non-arising.
The principle of this is precisely the letter A. When understood in this way, it is said that one is "in accord with the principle.

[Commentary] Regarding "all mundane and supramundane merits and so forth": if one is separated from the letter A, the phrase of "original non-arising," then all mundane and supramundane qualities—whether meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*)—cannot be increased. This is discussed by way of the gateway of letters.
In this state, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is precisely the *samādhis* such as *eka*, *ī*, and so forth, while wisdom (*prajñā*) is the long vowel *a*.

If one is separated from the *a* of "original non-arising" (*anutpāda*), then the wisdom of the long *ā*—and the meditative concentrations of *eka*, *ī*, and so forth—cannot be further developed or brought to fulfillment.
[Commentary]: "Each is associated with samādhi and supernatural power (*abhijñā*)" means that *samādhi* is meditative concentration and *abhijñā* is wisdom.
When these three factors accord with one another, they correspond to the principle; if there is any deficiency among them, they do not correspond.
This practice of mantra is called *yogacaryā*. *Yoga* is translated as "correspondence" (*xiangying*), meaning the correspondence between concentration and wisdom, further augmented by...
The secret [teaching] is thus called "inconceivable practice. Therefore, the sub-commentary below states:
"One must first abide in this samādhi and employ the wisdom of correspondence to deploy and measure [the mandala]; hence it is said to be 'in correspondence with the supernormal powers of samādhi.'"
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "next, prostrate to all Buddhas," etc., it means that the essence of the *A* syllable mantra is itself the essence of all Buddhas. Why is this so?
Because this *A* syllable is now capable of performing the deeds of all Buddhas, up to and including the universal manifestation of the form-body (*rūpakāya*).
Thus, when it says "prostrate to all Buddhas," it refers to prostrating to the essence of the *A* syllable.

[Commentary]: "Having finished establishing the corners of the *śikhin* (south-east) and *sūrya* (north-west), he asks again" means that while the Master is in the *sūrya* corner and the disciple arrives at the *śikhin* corner, this establishes the southeast and northwest corners.
Since there should be a corresponding pair for *aiśāna* (northeast) and *nairṛta* (southwest) next, and these are not present here, he causes [the disciple] to ask again;
it does not mean that he intends for later generations to ask. This refers to the period of the Venerable Ācārya Śubhakarasiṃha.

If there were points that the Chan Master had not fully elucidated up to this point, or if he intended for these cases to be judged by analogy, or if there was some other underlying meaning, the Chan Master entrusted the Dharma Master Zhìyán to inquire of the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra; therefore, it says, "ask further."
[Commentary]: This refers to that which is fundamentally without bondage. In Sanskrit it is called *bandha* or *vandha*, translated here as "bondage.
Regarding the statement that "the essence is one while the gates are different": if explained from the perspective of essence (*tattva*), all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen;

since there is neither bondage nor liberation, they are said to be "one in essence. If explained from the perspective of the gates (*mukha*), the letter *a* and bondage are distinct. Furthermore, this *a* and bondage...
Because these two characters are inseparable, their essence is one; because they are unconditioned by birth, their gates are distinct. Thus it is said: "That which is originally so," and so forth.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "as with the cord" cited above: this refers to the three characters of "stretching" (絣), etc.; since the phrasing is incomplete, it should read "as with... [and so on].
Regarding the manner of marking out the lines: although the master and disciple face each other as described above and draw the cord, they have not yet reached the ground of the altar;
rather, they merely assume the posture of marking the ground because the actual marking has not yet been performed. Thus it is said, "as described above," and so forth.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "as above, the non-dual correspondence," etc., this clarifies the matter of entering the mandala of the first enclosure.

It refers to what the aforementioned scripture says: "Fundamentally quiescent, there is nothing superior," and also: "The World-Honored One is like space—without conceptual proliferation, without dualistic practice, and the accomplishment of the marks of yoga and activities.
The commentary on the *Shū* explains that while these words speak of "fundamental quiescence," there is...
The sound "A" (aḥ) reveals the meaning of primordial non-arising (*anutpāda*). Because it is primordially unarisen, it is called "primordial quiescence" (*ādipraśānta*).
This means that primordial non-arising is like space, free from all conceptualization and proliferation (*prapañca*).

Although Bodhisattvas engage in various forms of practice, these are neither dual nor distinct, for they do not depart from such a sublime principle. Furthermore, it is said that "primordial non-arising" is precisely "A."
When the wheel of syllables enters this wheel, it is of one essence with the Buddha and non-dual; thus, it is the very substance of emptiness. Why?
Because the nature of emptiness is itself the Buddha. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The dharma-nature is fundamentally empty and quiescent, without grasping and without seeing.
The nature of emptiness is the Buddha; it cannot be apprehended or conceptualized. This is precisely what that refers to.
[Commentary]: Regarding "one may visualize Mañjuśrī or visualize the syllables," the "syllables" refer to the *pūrṇākṣara* (full syllables), as explained in the *Mantrakośa*. [Commentary]:

Regarding "from the syllable A, which is originally unarisen, to its transformative application": a question is raised as to whether one attains transformative application by means of the syllable A, which is originally unarisen.
Since the syllable A is never separate from the syllable Va, it is likewise permitted for Ka and all other syllables [to function in this way].
The syllable *va* and the syllable *a* are likewise not separate; since they are not separate even in this way, why is it that by taking only the syllable *va*, one may employ it as a substitute?
Answer: In reality, the syllable *a* and all other syllables such as *ka* are also not separate.
However, because the practitioner performs the activity of Vajra, the essence of Vairocana is transformed into the body of a Sattva.
However, because it is associated with the syllable *va*, it can be employed through transformation.

[Commentary] Regarding "entering by means of the meaning of the syllable *a*," this means that while the syllable *va* signifies the meaning of speech, because the syllable *a* enters into it, all speech is fundamentally unarisen.
This fundamental non-arising is what is called the severance of the path of speech.
This is because it is fundamentally quiescent.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "next, one abandons the second court," etc.: this means that first, at the lower level of the first court, one clearly transcends the colors of the second court;
subsequently, at the lower level of the third court, one clearly perceives them, and then, at the lower level of the second court, one [perceives them].
This is because the inner intention has been explained above.
[Commentary] Regarding "the vast dharma-realm" and so forth, a verse in the *Recitation Manual* (*Japa*) states: "The hands of Prajñā and Samaya both form vajra-fists;
the two empties are in their palms, and the wind and banner are both upright. This is called the purity of the Dharma-realm."
This is the secret seal.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "not conjoined with the letter A," etc.: the Sūtra states that one contemplates the luminous clarity of the letter, which is fundamentally non-existent and marked by the great void-point.

Now, when the Commentary says "not conjoined with the letter A," it is because it fears that people might interpret this based on the word "fundamentally non-existent" (*benwu*) found in the Sūtra passage.
Regarding the formation of the syllable *A*: because the syllable *A* is the source of all births, in order to negate that interpretation, it is said that they do not combine.

If that is so, how should one understand the meaning of the scriptural statement "originally non-existent" (*mūla-abhāva*)? "Originally non-existent" means that the *bindu* of primordial emptiness is originally without characteristics;

since the sūtra forms a phrase based on the five syllables, it says "originally non-existent," referring to the great empty *bindu*. It is said that for the purpose of semantic combination, the syllable *Ra* should be used.

The addition of a dot refers to the syllable *raṃ*. If one argues that using the syllable *raṃ* contradicts the sūtra—which states that it is "originally without the great empty dot" (*mahābindu*)—how should this be reconciled?
To provide a reconciliation: "originally without" means that this syllable *ra* is inherently stainless, and thus is called "originally without.
As for the "great empty dot," it refers to the fact that the great empty dot is added [to it] when they are combined.
Because it forms a five-syllable phrase and also possesses esoteric significance, there is no contradiction.

[Commentary: Regarding the subsequent mention of "yellow color" and so forth, this means that when visualizing the yellow color below, one should imagine the syllable *ka* as being the color of pure gold.
Why is this so? It is because this syllable *ka* carries the meaning of "gold. In Sanskrit, *kanaka* is translated as [gold].
The reason for instructing one to visualize the syllable *ka* as being the color of pure gold is that it refers to the Golden Muni Buddha.
In Sanskrit, he is called Kāśyapa-Muni; this translates as "Golden Silence.
He is the fifth of the Seven Buddhas, namely Tathāgata Kanakamuni (the term *Kunāhamuni* is incorrect). Therefore, he is called the Golden Muni.
"Buddha, etc. [Commentary]:
Regarding the instruction "one should contemplate the syllable MA, etc.," this syllable signifies the meaning of crossing over birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

That is to say, sentient beings in the world are agitated by birth and death and are unable to attain tranquility; because Śākyamuni has already been able to transcend them, he is called "The Tranquil One" (*Śānta*). If one wishes to... [the essential point].
To reveal the meaning of this syllable, one transforms this syllable *ma* into the syllable *mu*. In Sanskrit, it is called *muni*, which is translated as "the Silent One" (*寂言*).
This Buddha, who sits upon the Great Seat of Enlightenment (*mahābodhimaṇḍa*), uses this very syllable as his seat of enlightenment.

That is to say, this syllable *ma* signifies the meaning of "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*); because the Buddha takes the emptiness of all phenomena as his seat, it is said that [all] things are [empty].
Regarding the Buddha’s use of these characters and so forth: in the Sanskrit language, *mama* means "I.

Because all sentient beings possess this sense of "I," they are constantly terrified by birth and death. It is like an ignorant painter who, using various colors of the three realms, paints a fearsome yakṣa of birth and death and then becomes terrified of it himself; now it is just the same. This is what it means.
Therefore, because the Tathāgata’s great self of non-self can extinguish them, the aforementioned scripture states:
"In the past, when I sat at the site of enlightenment, I subdued the four Māras; with the voice of great diligence and valor, I removed the fears of sentient beings. The commentary explains:
When the Buddha first sat at the site of enlightenment and subdued the hosts of Māra’s army, he addressed Pāpīyas with truthful words, saying: "I, at..."
"Throughout immeasurable kalpas, for the sake of taming sentient beings, you have relinquished your body and life in incalculable numbers;

now that you have fully accomplished all that is appropriate for entering the Path, and as I am about to realize Bodhi and open the pure eye for those sentient beings, how could your power possibly obstruct me? At the very moment these words were uttered, the entire assembly...
All fears arising were entirely eliminated; the celestial Māras became dazed and fell to the ground, immediately dispersing and retreating.
Within this, the sound of "Great Diligence" (Mahāvīra) is my very name; therefore, it is said that all Buddhas employ this word.

As for what is called the palace of Indra in the west, "Indra" refers to the rainbow (*indrāyudha*), also known as the *chidong* (double rainbow); its form is perfect, with five colors brilliantly displayed.
It is as bright as the palace of Śakra; furthermore, one should apply this term "bow" (cāpa) because the rainbow has the shape of a bow.
Thus, people of the West call it *indrāyudha*, meaning "Śakra’s bow"—this explanation is correct.
[Commentary]: "This is Akṣobhya Tathāgata" means that this syllable *ha*, when joined with the great emptiness of samādhi, becomes the syllable *hūṃ*;
this syllable *hūṃ* is the seed-mantra of Akṣobhya Tathāgata.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "All Buddhas, etc.," these six characters should be construed with the preceding sentence as belonging to that which is taken as refuge prior to the mantra;
this is why it prompts a further question. How is this known? It is because below there is the character *pi* (written as 弊, a conjunct *pi*).
Thus, it says, "I take refuge in all Tathāgatas, etc.," and since it refers to "all gates" and so forth, it belongs to that which is entered into as the object of refuge.
Because the gatekeeper immediately enters the realm of all Buddhas, it is called "All Buddhas as the Foremost.
If a practitioner first enters this gate, they immediately have the expectation of attaining Buddhahood; therefore, it is named as such.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "Svāhā" up to "further questioning": if explained according to the meaning of the individual syllables, *svā* means "self" (or "one's own") and is also its primary sense;

*ha* means "vow. [Note: This is a scribal error in the commentary. If explained according to the meaning of the phrase as a whole, *svāhā* signifies "one's own vow," as well as "awakening" and so forth.

[Commentary: Regarding the "three positions of abandonment" (*tri-parityāga*) of those respective stations: this means that while the southern direction belongs to the realm of Yama, Vajrapāṇi is placed therein;
furthermore, three positions are reserved on either side of Vajrapāṇi, which are the stations of the Vajra-messengers (*vajradūta*).
Because one draws all the retinues of the Vajra family beneath these three positions, they are called the "abandonment of the three positions."

[The text says] "Abandon. [Commentary: Regarding the phrase "within this maṇḍala," it refers to the third enclosure (*prakoṣṭha*). Having completed the painting of Śākyamuni, there is no mention of his retinue.

As for the statement that they "appear mutually above and below": "above" refers to the *Maṇḍalapraveśa-parivarta* (Chapter on Entering the Maṇḍala), while "below" refers to this chapter, or perhaps to that [other section].
Regarding the "omissions in the middle," because these are present within this [section], it is said that they appear interchangeably.
[Commentary] As for "the initial seal for protecting the body, etc.," the initial seal is the Dharma-realm Seal (Dharmadhātu-mudrā).
Regarding the statement that "there is another seal following this," this refers to the Vajrasattva Seal, as described in the *Mudrā-paṭala*.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the binding of that Dharma-wheel, etc.," its general substance is largely the same as the *Maṇḍala-sapratyaya-paṭala*.
That scripture states: "One binds the Dharmadhātusaṃbhava-mudrā and the Dharma-cakra-mudrā, and likewise the Vajrasattva [mudrās], thereby performing the empowerment.
The commentary on that explains: "The Dharmadhātusaṃbhava-mudrā seals the heart; the Dharma-cakra-mudrā seals the navel."
The Vajrasattva mudrā on the wheel seals all the limbs, namely the five places:
the heart, forehead, throat, crown of the head, and both shoulders. Therefore it says, "Furthermore, ask."
[Commentary] "Not empty-handed," etc., means that there are flowers in the hand.

As taught in the fourth fascicle of the *Vajraśekhara-yoga-japa-vidhi*, one instructs the disciple to extend the two fingers, the *anāmikā* (ring finger) and the *kaniṣṭhikā* (pinky), to form a needle, and to hang a white flower garland upon that needle; it must be this [that is being referred to].
[Commentary: Regarding "teaching by whispering in the ear" and so forth, this refers to reciting the *samaya* verses while whispering in the ear.

This may be done if one has received the complete-branch initiation; however, it is not appropriate for those who have only received the initiation for establishing a karmic connection to hear them, and thus they are informed by whispering.

As for the separate location where they are taught, it is precisely at the point after the Dharma-wheel and Dharma-conch have been bestowed in the preceding "Chapter on the Requisites of the Maṇḍala."
The "place of exposition" (shuo chu) may refer to the *Vajraśekhara-japa-vidhi*; there is a separate place where it is expounded. [Commentary:
To further ask what mudrā it is, it refers to the Samaya-mudrā. How is this known? It is because the second scripture states:
"Next, one should personally bind the Samaya-mudrās of all Buddhas; three times, purify the robes and so forth. Furthermore, it is this very same [text].
The Sūtra says: "One should whisper and inform them of the unsurpassed, perfectly equal precepts;
next, one should bind for them the seal of the perfectly equal samādhi, bestow upon them the blossoming flower, and cause them to generate the bodhicitta.
Therefore, this samaya is called the Vajra Oath Precept of All Tathāgatas. This mantra and mudrā are found in the *Guhyamudrā-paṭala*; if one [engages with it] prematurely...
The knower forms the vajra-bind, pinching the middle of the *dāna* (giving) and *prajñā* (wisdom) fingers with the *jñāna-samādhi* (wisdom-concentration) finger,
and supporting them slightly curved against each other with the *vīrya-bala* (power of diligence) finger.
[Commentary] "All and further questioning" refers to the aforementioned master performing the samaya-mudrās and so forth for the disciple.

One casts flowers into the center of the mandala; whichever deity the flower falls upon—whether a deity of the Vajra family, the Lotus family, or any other family—therein reside various mantras, mudrās, and ritual methods.
These are called "all" because they pertain to all families, rather than being the "all" of only a single family.
If one performs the empowerment of the transmission of teachings, these indeed constitute the "all" of all families; therefore, it is said [to be] "furthermore."
Question:
[Commentary] Next, one should perform the mudrā that generates all limbs. Since this mudrā is the Vajrasattva mudrā, the sixth commentary states:
"Having empowered the limbs with Vajrasattva, one causes [the practitioner] to sit according to the auspicious sitting posture."

Among these, it is as follows: furthermore, the "Chapter on the Eight Secret Seals" states that with both hands one forms the unopened lotus mudrā, establishes the two *aṅguṣṭha* (thumb) wheels in *añjali*, and slightly bends them; this is called the "Seal of the Arising of All Limbs of the Tathāgata."

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "on the crown of the disciple's head," one should state here: visualize the syllable *Aṃ* upon the suture of the ten directions, and intensely visualize the syllable *A* within his heart.
Those who have transcribed this erroneously [should correct it] by consulting the sutra. As for the "Chapter on Secret Seals" (*Miyin pin*), "secret" (*mi*) refers to the esoteric;
"seal" (*yin*) refers to a mark or insignia (*biaozhi*). It is called a "seal" because it is established according to worldly convention. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A seal..."
That which is held by secular rulers is their seal of authority; now, this is the seal held by those who uphold the mantras.

Furthermore, just as the worldly kings who possess the precious regalia of successive dynasties are revered and feared by the eight quarters, so too does the Dharma King, the Tathāgata, display the banner of the Dharma-realm, and the eight classes of beings believe in and follow him. Because it simplifies that [secular] manifestation, it is called "manifest" (vyakta).

In the teachings, some speak of the single Dharma-realm seal (*dharmadhātu-mudrā*), while others speak of the three Dharma seals or the four Dharma seals. In the Esoteric Vehicle (*Guhyamantra*), these are specifically hand seals;

that is to say, they are called "emblems" (*cihna*) because they are the seals of the Esoteric. Therefore, they are termed "esoteric seals" (*guhyamudrā*). This sutra takes the three mysteries (*triguhya*) as its central principle:
even if a practitioner recites mantras with their mouth and visualizes the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) with their mind, if they do not maintain the esoteric seals, the three [mysteries]...
The Secret [Teachings] are not complete if they lack even one of the three legs of a tripod as found in the world;
nor can the character *i* (*ī*) be formed if one of its three dots is missing. Furthermore, this mudrā is the emblem of the Dharma-realm maṇḍala;
if it lacks anything, the Dharma-realm will likewise be incomplete. It is for this reason that this chapter has come forth.
[Commentary: Regarding the initial mention of *kāla* and so forth, this refers to the two types of time—*kāla* and *samaya*—clarified in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
As stated in the "Expedient Means" chapter: "At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: 'In this assembly of mine now, there are no longer any branches or leaves;
it consists purely of the firm and the real. Śāriputra, it would be well indeed if such people of overweening pride were to withdraw. You, now...
"Listen well; I shall speak for you. Śāriputra replied, "Yes, World-Honored One; we wish and desire to hear it.
All such expressions refer to the time of *kāla*. This refers to the auspicious occasion of the meeting through responsive resonance (*saṃdarśana*). Furthermore, it says:
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great causal matter," and so forth, until: "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, desire to cause..."

"Because he appears in the world to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and to make them pure," and so forth—this refers to the time of the actual preaching of the sutra. This is the *samaya* (appointed time).
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "Next, the hand seals (*mudrā*) and so forth," the first seven characters serve as a heading indicating the characteristics of the hand seals.
The subsequent nine characters, beginning with "do not exceed the three dharmas," constitute the sūtra’s own concluding explanation of the merits of the samādhi-mantra.
Why, then, is it employed here within the context of these seal characteristics? Is this not a contradiction? Therefore, those who attempt to reconcile this [claim] are mistaken.
However, because the merit of the samaya-mantra does not transcend the three dharmas— the path, the realm, and the perfection of the ground—
and because one desires for the bodily mudrās to all possess such merit while also manifesting that the three secrets are inseparable,
there is no fault of mutual confusion.

[Commentary: Although this practitioner has not yet been able to realize that the essence of all phenomena is the nature of *tathatā* (suchness), even so—whether by way of concession or refutation—one who can merely form this seal of the *dharmadhātu* and recite this mantra of the *dharmadhātu* is already identical in essence to the nature of the *dharmadhātu*. Why is this? Because apart from this...
The mudrās and mantras are no different from the dharmadhātu.
[Commentary: *Ta-ma-ku-gan* (dam-koṣa) means the essence of *dam*, which is the body; *ku-gan* means "to contain," signifying that one's own body is itself the vajra.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "capable of severing the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth," this means that when a practitioner applies the seal of this sword of wisdom, they are able to sever the view of a self-body as well as the defilements of innate views (*sahaja-dṛṣṭi*).
This mention of "innate views" refers specifically to the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), not the latter three views. Why is this?
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Among the ten afflictions, six are common to both innate and conceptually constructed (*vikalpita*) arising."
Since both spontaneous [arising] and investigative [arising] can occur, doubt and the latter three views arise solely through investigation;
they require the influence of evil friends or false teachings, as well as one's own deliberate reflection, to arise.

In this context, although the sutra mentions "all views" and "the view of a self-entity," the mantra designates only the view of a self-entity because once its root is severed, the branches and leaves perish accordingly.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "taking the first Brahmic letter as the heart," the Brahmic letter should be the letter *ma*.

This means that although this mantra is generally divided into seven phrases and individually contains many words, it takes the letter *ma* as its heart (*hṛdaya*), while the others constitute the limbs (*aṅga*).
This letter *ma* signifies the meaning of "self" (*ātman*) and is also a letter with the five void dots (*pañca-bindu*). Furthermore, this letter is also [composed of] *ka* and *cha*.
*Ṭa-ta-pa* refers to the fifth among the five classes of sounds; *yaṅ-raṅ-na-maṅ* refers to the fifth dot among the five dots of emptiness (*pañca-bindu*).
Therefore, it is said to be "also the fifth dot of emptiness."
[Commentary] Regarding the "twenty-three [stages] of descending upon the yoga-seat," when one examines the count, this scripture reaches the twenty-first stage of dwelling upon the yoga-seat.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "it can also cause all sentient beings who are not vessels [for the teaching]," this refers to the second chapter of the scripture which distinguishes the disciples.

The *Sūtra of Virtue* therein states: "If one sees sentient beings who are capable of being vessels for the Dharma—those who are far removed from all defilements, diligent and courageous, possessed of deep faith, and constantly mindful of benefiting others—it is said that those endowed with such characteristics are fit to receive the teachings of the Way of Mantras and are thus called 'vessels.
Those who lack these characteristics are called 'non-vessels. Now, regarding this Seal of the Alms Bowl of Śākyamuni:
One who performs this according to the Dharma is identical to the Tathāgata, upholding the insignia of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
furthermore, because such a person can cause even sentient beings who are not suitable vessels to obtain such merit, it is said that they "can cause all [beings] to be equal," and so forth.

[Commentary]: Holding the two corners of the robe signifies not abandoning ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), but rather causing them to attain deliverance (*niḥsaraṇa*).

Therefore, the subsequent commentary states: "First one leaves behind the afflictions of ordinary beings; next, one leaves behind the afflictions of the two vehicles"—this is precisely what that means.
[Commentary]: Regarding *Jvala*, the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains only the meaning of the individual characters but does not clarify the meaning of the phrase.
These three characters consist of the first two as a *dvandva* (conjunct) compound; it should be read as *jva-la-ra*. This is translated as "flame.
The next phrase is *mālīnī*, which is translated as "garland. This means that the flames of the bodily radiance are continuous and unbroken, resembling the shape of a garland.
The text below says *tathāgata-arcis*, which is translated here as "Light of the Tathāgata.
This is so named because the flames of the Tathāgata’s light are like a garland (*mālā*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the missing mantra, which should be verified against the original text, this mantra appears on the tenth line of the second fascicle of the Sūtra:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ* (1), *vajra-jvala-visphura hūṃ* (2). This text is explained in the forty-third line of the sixth section of the Commentary.
[Commentary]: Regarding the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Tongue, the collated manuscripts lack this section;
it has been omitted from the sūtra, and despite our search, we have not yet recovered it. [Commentary]: *Pratibhāti-citta* may also be translated as "the sense of accomplishment.
The sixth commentary states that because the Tathāgata has constantly cultivated truthful speech throughout immeasurable kalpas, he has attained the accomplishment of this wheel of impartial speech.
Because the truthful words uttered according to the Dharma of the ultimate truth (satya) are certainly without deviation, it is also called "accomplishment" (*siddhi*).
[Commentary: Regarding the term *kharu-pa* and so forth, these three characters at the beginning are an incorrect transcription of the Sanskrit sound.
The correct Sanskrit is *arūpa*, which is translated as "speech. The commentary states that "the division of speech" is mentioned in contrast to what follows, namely *vākya*.
"Vocal expression" (vāk) is called *vāk* in Sanskrit; this is translated as "speech. If *vāk* is taken as speech itself, it belongs to the substance of speech (*rūpa*).
When *rūpa* is called "speech," it refers to the manifesting aspect of speech (*vāgvijñapti*), which is the segmented form of speech; hence it is called "the segmentation of speech.
Furthermore, what is called *rūpa* in Sanskrit is also termed "form" (*śarīra*); this is the marvelous discourse of all Tathāgatas.
[Commentary]: Regarding "the union of the three virtues (*guṇa*)": this character *huǒ* (火) is formed by the combination of bodhicitta, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and skillful means;
therefore, it is called the "three virtues. As for "the *mò* (麼) and *kōng* (空)": this character *mò* is a scribal error and should be the character *cān* (參).
This character *cān* is formed by adding the dot of emptiness (*bindu*); thus, it is the samādhi of Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*). As for the phrase "further questioning," this...
Regarding the three characters *go*, *saṃ*, and *kha*, according to the sūtras they should be placed at the end of various mantra phrases.
Why is it that the Ācārya places them at the beginning of the phrases? Therefore, he was asked again:
"As for *ḍhaḥ śavalan* and so forth," this single mantra phrase consists of five characters; from the character *laṃ* upward, it is called *ḍhaḥ śava*, and *daśa valan*.
The meaning of the single character *yun* (云) corresponds to "body-part" (*aṅga*). If one were to follow the complete Sanskrit term, it should be *āṅga*, which is translated as "body-part.
However, the translators, for the sake of convenience, merely appended a *yin* (引) tone mark beneath the character *lan* (蘭), thereby representing the sound of *āṅ*.
All such instances are treated in this manner.
[Commentary]: Regarding *siddhi*, this character *ti* (底) is, according to the *Qieyun*, included in the rhyme category of *zai* (薺).
