If one cultivates the gateway of wisdom through the three equal karmas, all seeds of the aggregates, the ālayavijñāna, karma, and lifespan will be utterly incinerated.
One will then attain the stainless bodhicitta of space, which is the equal seed of all Tathāgatas; from the treasury of compassion, the dharmatā arises.
The sprouts, and so forth, up to the stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits, which completely fill the *dharmadhātu* and manifest as the King of Bodhi Trees endowed with the ten thousand virtues—
this is the intended meaning of the internal *homā* (*antarahomā*) herein.
[Commentary] Regarding the note "further asking about the mantra": here, it refers to placing the principal deity (honzon) in the ritual hearth for the sake of making offerings;

this is the place where fire is established. As for the mudrās of body and speech, the instruction to "further ask about the mantra" does not mean asking about the specific mantra to be employed in the rite.
Rather, it means asking what the mantra mentioned in the sūtra intends to signify. If one relies upon the three karmas (body, speech, and mind), then...
Regarding the *dhāraṇī*, if one refers to the three positions as being the mantra itself, it would constitute a single word of the sūtra;
however, since the meaning of the mantra applies to both places and is essential for the practitioner, he is further questioned.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "causing these three positions to correspond exactly," the "three positions" are as follows: first, the principal deity (bimba), which is the maṇḍala;
second, the fire-pit (kuṇḍa), referring to the triangular mudrā and so forth; and third, the mantra, which refers to the practitioner.

This means that the fire-pit is to the west of the principal deity, and the practitioner is further to the west of the fire-pit; since both face toward the central principal deity within the altar, they are called the "three positions."
"Equivalent" means that these three are also three; furthermore, because these three stages are also correlated with the three types of action (karman), it is said they are "also three.
[Commentary]: From "due to departing from the mantra" to "not attaining the fruit," it means that the practitioner of mantra does not rely on the aforementioned internal...
If one falsely performs the ritual procedures for the two types of external *homā* out of one's own ignorant mind,
rather than following a master of clarity, not only will one fail to attain the two kinds of *siddhi*, mundane and supramundane, internal and external,

but one will also waste the patron’s wealth and incur the transgression of violating the Dharma, destined to fall into the three miserable realms. I hope that all spiritual friends will take this to heart and act accordingly.
Be careful not to recklessly grasp a sharp blade and wound your own hand.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement that the Buddha Family is "exclusively" [of one color], this means that the Buddha Family does not extend to the Bodhisattva Family and below;
it possesses only the two colors white and yellow. Now, according to the rite of *śāntika* (pacification), it should be made white; the other families should be understood accordingly.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "now following the sequence of sounds," this refers to the method of augmentation (*ābhicāruka*).

If it were solely for the purpose of bestowing the initiation (*abhiṣeka*) upon disciples who have generated the resolve [for awakening], one would first perform the rite of pacification (*śāntika*). However, "following the sequence of sounds" here means following the sequence of the square and the circle;
as people commonly say, "first the square, then the circle" is called the sequence of sounds. As for "the sequence of matters," it means that the Buddha Family (*buddhakula*) comes first.

Next, regarding the matter of the Lotus-Vajra: because it is called "expediency of affairs" (*jishi bian*), it is said to follow the convenience of sound; therefore, its augmentation is placed at the beginning.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "in order to eliminate ignorance," etc., the Buddhas and Tathāgatas act to eliminate the ignorance of all sentient beings.
Therefore, various kinds of wisdom arise; these various kinds of wisdom are precisely the various insignia of the maṇḍala.
Although this wisdom knows immeasurable marks, it is in reality but the single wisdom of *śūnyatā* (emptiness).
That "one wisdom manifests all wisdoms" means that by means of the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), one manifests the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "one should clarify the *Guhyakapada-sūtra* and others": the *Guhyakapada-sūtra* refers to the "Assembly of the Vajrapāṇi Guhyakapada" within the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Śāntamati asked the Guhyakapada: "How many secret essentials does the Tathāgata possess that are beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas? The Vajrapāṇi Guhyakapada replied to Śāntamati, saying: "As for..."
The essential secret teachings consist of three matters: first, the secrecy of body; second, the secrecy of speech; and third, the secrecy of mind.

What is meant by the secrecy of body? It is that the Tathāgata has no conceptual thoughts and no deliberate reflections therein, yet he universally manifests all dignified postures and ritual decorum.
Thus, there may be gods or human beings who take pleasure in walking meditation (caṅkrama), and upon seeing the Tathāgata walking, they perceive him thus.
At that time, he thought: "The World-Honored One is supreme; these beings have attained the vision of the Tathāgata’s secret body.
Yet, the Tathāgata does not even think of or expect all sentient beings to behold his wondrous virtue and majestic deportment.

Whether gods or humans, some delight in seeing the Tathāgata seated, some delight in him reclining, some delight in hearing the sutras, some delight in tranquility, and so on, even down to those who delight in merely seeing him."
If one wishes to thoroughly examine and know the various colors and forms of the Buddha’s body, as well as its origins and the conduct of his speech and actions, it is likewise so.
The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, manifests the image of a Tathāgata before each sentient being;

within the four modes of deportment, his ritual gestures and verbal conduct are like a pure, clear mirror that reflects their physical appearances accordingly. Just as a clear mirror reflects forms, it is devoid of any conceptual thought.
In this way, although the Tathāgata saves all sentient beings through the Dharma, he has no conceptualization thereof;

thus it is said that this constitutes the secret essentials of the Tathāgata’s bodily conduct. The two secrets of speech and mind may be inferred by analogy with this principle, so they need not be cited in full detail.

[Commentary: "This is the hallmark of the Great Being" refers to that which is possessed by the Great Being Vairocana—namely, the hair-tuft on the Tathāgata’s crown, the eyes, the tongue, up to the private organ, as well as the thirty-two major marks and so forth, as described in the usual accounts.

[Commentary: "Spontaneously attaining vajra-equanimity" means that because the ācārya visualizes his own body as Vajrasattva, he causes the disciple to spontaneously attain vajra-consecration, introduction, and so forth.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the third consecration and so forth" mentioned previously, this refers to the three types of consecrations previously explained:

first, the seal of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*); second, the ritual action (*karmamudrā*); and third, the mental visualization (*cittamudrā*). Since one is now to practice the mental visualization, it is called "the third consecration and so forth."

[Commentary: "This refers to those who have entered the stages" and so forth means that upon first entering the stage of practice through faith (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), one attains the *Sarvāvaraṇaviskambhin-samādhi*.
Thus, the first scripture states: "The gate of bodhicitta of this bodhisattva is called the 'Initial Path of Dharma-Illumination.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this, before long they attain the *Sarvāvaraṇaviskambhin-samādhi*. If one attains this..."
This is precisely what is meant by "abiding on an equal level with all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "various worldly methods of planting and so forth": this refers to how, according to the worldly method of planting, one must seek out seeds and plant them in the ground;
if one irrigates them without ceasing, one will eventually obtain flowers and fruit. Now, it is the same with the bodhicitta.
If the seeds are placed within the "mind-ground" of sentient beings and irrigated with the water of samādhi, then flowers and fruit will immediately appear;
hence it is said, "the various worldly plantings," and so forth.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the benefits of this cause" and so on, if the character *yin* (cause) belongs to the sūtra text itself, it should correspond to the term "wholesome root" (*kuśalamūla*).

Regarding the two characters [for "benevolent one" (*jin* / *maitreya*)], the present commentary explains them as the seed of *bodhi*. This means that the causal seed of *bodhi* is simply another name for "benefit. [Commentary:
"The Benevolent One is none other than the Buddha," etc., is an explanation of the excellence within "benevolence. "Benevolent" (*ren*) is the Buddha; the Buddha is one who has awakened (*jue*).
Ordinary beings lack awakening, while those of the Two Vehicles possess awakening yet cannot awaken others; the Buddha surpasses them and is therefore called "Superior" (*jina*).

Thus it is said, "The Benevolent One is Superior. To call him "Benevolent" (*maitreya*) means he possesses the root of tranquility (*śamatha*). Furthermore, he is called "Benevolent" because he possesses two meanings:

as the *Sūtra* says, attaining the practice of objectless contemplation (*anālambana-vipaśyanā*) is termed being "Benevolent," and employing skillful means (*upāya*) to benefit sentient beings is likewise termed being "Benevolent."

Regarding "superior" (jina): if one merely abides in objectlessness, one may be called "Virtuous One" (ārya) but not "Victorious One" (jina). If one combines this with skillful means (upāya), one is named both "Virtuous One" and "Victorious One";
therefore, it is said that the "Virtuous One" is none other than the Buddha, and so forth.

[Commentary: "Only with reference to the Śrāvakas and so forth" means that this statement refers exclusively to the Śrāvakas because, while their realization of the truths (*satyadarśana*) is the same, their abandonment of obstacles differs.
That is to say, the Śrāvaka abandons only the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), whereas the Bodhisattva is free from both hindrances. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"When the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the two vehicles manifests, they abandon only one kind [of hindrance], which is termed 'noble nature' (*āryagotra*)."
When the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) manifests before them, they are said to possess the nature of an *ārya* because they have completely severed both types [of afflictions].

Furthermore, the term "only" (*kevalam*) carries the sense of being solitary; it does not refer to the *pratyekabuddha*. Why? Because the *Pratyekabuddhayāna* has no separate code of discipline and does not differentiate stages.
Thus, the Qingliang Commentary states: "Furthermore, because *pratyekabuddhas* for the most part do not rely on the teachings, they appear in worlds where no Buddha exists."
Because the Buddha was still in the world at that time and was categorized among the *śrāvakas*, it is said that he looked only toward the *śrāvakas*.
[Commentary] "At that time, he attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and so forth" refers to the fourth stage (*bhūmi*).

This means that while the first, second, and third stages are similar to the mundane, this stage transcends them; thus, one practices giving in the first stage, morality in the second, and [patience] in the third.
The practice of patience is similar to that of worldly beings, for most worldly sentient beings perform these three types of meritorious karma;

thus, they have not yet been able to cultivate and realize the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). Now, in the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), one cultivates and attains the factors conducive to the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

One contemplates the objects of the five mundane superknowledges (*abhijñā*) as being like illusions, dreams, and so forth, and by not giving rise to grasping or attachment, one transcends that stage and attains the supramundane.

Regarding the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "Namely, the supernormal power of the realization of the divine eye; the supernormal power of the realization of the divine ear;
the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of others' minds; the supernormal power of the realization of the recollection of past abodes;
and the supernormal power of the realization of the various distinctions of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). Furthermore, Śāriputra, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices tranquility..."
By virtue of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) that is obtained arises through the paths of renunciation;
because this divine eye is extremely clear and penetrates all that appears, it perceives everything.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, by virtue of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of meditative concentration, the knowledge of the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā-jñāna*) becomes pure, clear, and penetrating throughout the ten directions.
He hears all sounds, whether of the noble or the non-noble, throughout the world; he is further able to discern them without error.
Having heard them, he does not give rise to delight or attachment toward the sounds of the noble, nor does he produce aversion or envy toward the sounds of the non-noble.
Śāriputra, it is by means of this purified supernormal knowledge of others' minds that the bodhisattva mahāsattva is clearly illuminated.
The Bodhisattva is able to know, as they truly are, all the immeasurable mental states of sentient beings throughout all worlds in the ten directions, reaching to their limits.

Whether it be the mental states of sentient beings in the past, the mental states in the future, or the mental states in the present, the Bodhisattva understands them all therein. Śāriputra, by means of this, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva...
Because *tathatā* (suchness) is the power of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñānabala*),
one is able to recollect all the various matters of past lives— of many different kinds— for all sentient beings throughout the worlds pervading the ten directions;

that is, one can recollect in this manner one birth, ten births, a hundred births, a thousand births, or hundreds of thousands of births— not merely a hundred, not merely a thousand, and not merely a hundred thousand.
One can thus understand this sequence in its entirety. Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
And what is called the perfection of the activity of the supernormal knowledge of the bases of power?
Śāriputra, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva relies upon the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) that they obtain this desire.
The bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) accomplished through the cultivation of concentration and the formations of abandonment—
namely, the bases of psychic power accomplished through the cultivation of concentration and the formations of abandonment involving diligence, mind, and investigation— and so forth,

up to the bodhisattva mahāsattva manifesting such immeasurable transformations of supernormal powers as appropriate for each case, whether by appearing in physical forms or by manifesting majestic power, and so on.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s supramundane five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

[Commentary: "Attaining transcendence over the Two Vehicles" refers to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*). This is because in the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages, one performs the clear observation of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) and so forth, which is identical to that of the Two Vehicles;
now, at this stage, one transcends them upon reaching the final limit of the effortful cultivation of the signless (*animitta-prayoga*).

Regarding the phrase "because it is the path of the world and the two vehicles," etc.: "at that time reaching the eighth stage" means that during the seventh stage, one is able to initiate superior practices within the midst of space with little exertion of effort; thus, it is called "Far-Reaching" (*dūraṃgamā*), as it surpasses the two vehicles.
Furthermore, because there is still applied effort (*prayoga*) regarding the signless (*animitta*) in the seventh stage, one has not yet attained the spontaneous manifestation of buddha-lands.
Because the untainted path arises spontaneously in the eighth ground of emptiness, this stage is named "The Immovable" (*acalā*).
Since all afflictions never again arise, and because one proceeds spontaneously within the swift current of the Dharma,
advancing and increasing moment by moment, this is called reaching the eighth ground.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) itself possesses ten minds and so forth, this refers to the ten minds such as the seed, sprout, and bud;

furthermore, it refers to the ten minds such as "pliancy" (*mṛdu*) found in the first ground of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and even up to the ten minds for each of the ten grounds, as has already been explained previously.
[Commentary]: Regarding the analogy of the *Avataṃsaka*’s pure gold and so forth, that sutra states:
"For example, it is like a goldsmith who smelts and refines pure gold to fashion ornaments; no other gold can equal them.
In the same way, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwelling in this stage possesses roots of goodness that cannot be equaled by the roots of goodness of the lower stages."
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "throughout life after life," the sutra merely says "cultivating practice without interruption even for a single moment.
Here, the translator has rendered it according to its meaning so that it may be easily understood by others.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "on this very night," it means that the practitioner of mantras, while seeking to attain the meditative state (*viṣaya*) during the night of the ritual performance, divides this night into three periods.
Just as when consecrating medicinal substances, three kinds of signs appear—either in the first watch, the middle watch, or the last watch of the night—namely:
the sign of warmth (*uṣman*), the sign of smoke (*dhūma*), and the sign of light (*prabhā*).
These are divided, respectively, into the three grades of superior, middling, and inferior; by this one may verify the signs of the arising of *siddhi*.
Since these signs of *siddhi* arise from the practitioner’s recitation and mental application (*manasikāra*), they are called "arising from the practitioner’s mental application."
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "merely through the conditions of mantras, medicinal substances, and so forth," this means that the Buddha taught that the power of medicine is inconceivable.
For example, by the power of medicine, a person may ascend into the air with ease, become invisible, walk upon water without sinking, or tread upon fire without being burned.
This is not something that various scholars of treatises can establish through logical reasons (*hetu*) and measures (*pramāṇa*), nor can they produce its underlying cause.
One may harbor doubts as to whether it must necessarily be so or not; having raised such objections, one should deliberate upon the object [of practice].
Only those who personally partake of this medicine can verify its efficacy for themselves. The medicine of mantra is likewise:
when *siddhi* is accomplished, one does not abandon this body but walks through space and travels to various buddha-fields, for all of this is produced through the illusory power of mantra.
Furthermore, it is not a worldly cause; although various masters have set forth the reasons for this, only those who have attained *siddhi* know it through their own direct realization.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "arising from a multitude of conditions," etc.: this city arises from a multitude of conditions such as sea vapors and sunlight, and is ultimately not real;
one should not give rise to attachment toward it. The *mantra-siddhi* is also like this, arising by virtue of...
One should observe that which arises through the causal conditions of the three karmas by means of this analogy and must not grasp at it;
for because of these causal conditions, one's mind remains pure and unimpeded regarding the various sublime objects of the five sensory realms.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "this true Dharma" and so forth: although this true mantra, the reality-mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), and the mind-dharma inherently possess such inconceivable virtues and activities within the essence of the fundamental dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), they remain hidden when conditions are not yet complete, and are revealed when causes and conditions harmonize.
Being ultimately pure and inconceivable, one should not raise objections by saying that this [mantra] is false.
[Question: How can the dharmas of phenomenal characteristics (*sanimitta*) accomplish the true dharma of signlessness (*animitta*)?
[Commentary: Although such a person has not yet attained ultimate [realization], when the practitioner of mantras contemplates in this manner, their mind is free from obstruction.
This is like one who has attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), who flies freely through space and forms without being hindered by persons or phenomena (*pudgala-dharma*).

That which is defiled by false conceptualization is precisely the sphere of the Buddha’s practice; although one may not yet be able to exhaustively realize the Buddha’s wisdom, that which is understood is identical to that of all Buddhas.
Only when this practice and realization are equal to those of the Buddhas can it be called the ultimate wisdom of a Buddha.
It is like the newly risen pure moon: although its essence neither increases nor decreases, it nevertheless...

The light gradually increases until it reaches the fifteenth day, at which point it is called "perfectly full. Those who can move the ocean tides and enter this gate must not claim what they have not attained as attained;
they merely take their place of practice as their place of realization.
[Commentary]: "To understand that it is merely conceptualization" means that when a practitioner of *mantra* achieves *siddhi*, they should not grasp at it as being substantial.

This analogy of empty space is intended for such contemplation: one should view the signs of *siddhi* as all being like empty space, their essence free from discrimination, such as male or female forms, manifest color, shape, and so forth.
When contemplating in this way, the mind is without obstruction, as if having attained supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).

One who masters this flies freely within the single manifest color of emptiness, and because they are not defiled by the delusive thoughts of persons or phenomena, it is said that they "understand," and so forth.
[Commentary] Regarding "internal homa" as the cessation of all objects and so forth: "internal" refers to the internal mind; *homa* is named "fire," which is wisdom (*jñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "extinguishing all objective realms" (*sarva-viṣaya-śamana*): "extinguishing" (*śamana*) means to cease.

When wisdom has not yet arisen, there are already the defilements of the sense bases and their objects that soil the pure mind; when the fire of wisdom arises, the defilements of the objects are extinguished.

Therefore, it is said that one "extinguishes all objective realms. Regarding the phrase "the twelvefold dependent origination" (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), the preceding word "extinguish" (*śamana*) flows over here, meaning to "extinguish the twelve."

It is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). As for dependent origination: through ignorance (*avidyā*), various karmas are performed; by reason of these karmic causes and conditions, the fruits of suffering arise.
Thus, from karma there is birth, and from birth one again performs karma, revolving without ceasing.

Now, this internal *homa* is precisely for the purpose of pacifying and eliminating this cycle of dependent karma and karma-born birth; once they have been incinerated, the pure Dharma arises. Therefore, it is called "pacification."

The phrase "the twelvefold dependent origination, etc. includes, by way of the term "etc.," the six hindrances (*ṣaḍāvaraṇa*), all faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and all phenomena (*dharma*).
[Commentary: The passage beginning with "By means of maintaining these offerings, etc. explains the intent of the preceding question and answer.

From this point until "serving as causes and conditions" (spanning two and a half lines, excluding the annotations), the entire section clarifies the underlying reasons. Next, from "Deeply practicing the *ācārya*... [the text continues].

The section from "Li" (Peach) up to "internal dharma-cause" (*adhyātmika-dharmahetu*) distinguishes between the shallow and the deep; it then returns to the preceding section as the causal condition (*pratyaya*). The marginal note below states:
"Performing *upacaya* (augmentation) applies likewise even to *homā* (fire-offering)," which is also an augmentation of majestic power (*tejas*). Furthermore, the marginal note below states:
"The distinct characteristics of the various deities... can be known," and so forth; this refers to observing the various deities in such a manner accordingly.
The purpose of this classification and explanation is to ensure there is no error.

[Commentary]: Regarding the note stating, "To perform the *upacaya* [increasing rite] in the upper, middle, and lower [degrees], the same applies to the *homa*," this marginal note should have been placed above the note for the lower [degree];
it is merely an error on the part of the scribe. It would be even better if neither were treated as a note and read as part of the main text.
Regarding the statement that there is "increase or decrease," this character "jian" (減) is actually the character "wei" (威);
it is merely a matter of the number of strokes above and below. [Commentary]: "The puddle of an ox’s hoofprint" refers to the water collected in an ox’s footprint, which is called a "cen.

As the common saying goes, it is like a hoofprint puddle that cannot contain a foot-long carp; it is also like a cup overturned on a depression in the ground, which dries up in an instant. If a person...

If this water were placed within the great ocean, there would be no principle by which it could be exhausted; that is, a single drop entering the celestial lake becomes identical to it in its beginninglessness and endlessness.
[Commentary] Regarding "siddhi" (the fruit attained, etc.): this term *siddhi* signifies the meaning of the "attainment of the fruit."
The fruits of accomplishment refer to items such as *añjana*, swords, and parasols; these resultant dharmas should be placed within the positions of the maṇḍala.
As for the phrase "fully manifesting" which applies generally to all emanations and so forth—this constitutes the fundamental maṇḍala.
Within this, according to the specific *siddhi* sought by the practitioner, one should establish individual maṇḍalas.
The practice performed according to the respective sections at that time is called "emanation" (*niṣyanda*).

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the first Perfectly Awakened One," etc., this refers to those who first attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment, emanating from the fundamental maṇḍala of Vairocana;
these are the four Tathāgatas, Akṣobhya and the others. As for Akṣobhya, he is the Yoga...
The liturgical confession states: "O Tathāgata Akṣobhya, having offered your own body, you requested protection;
from the initial awakening mind until the attainment of Bodhi, may the Tathāgata and Vajrasattva grant their empowerment, so that I may remain firm and never retreat.

Regarding the phrase "offering one's body to seek protection," it refers precisely to this moment when one first receives the precepts of the unimpeded wisdom of the three periods and offers one's body.

To offer everything to all Buddhas and request their protection so that the bodhicitta may become firm and non-regressive is called "the first teaching," as it refers to the very moment when one first generates the awakened mind of initial enlightenment (*ādikarmika-bodhicitta*).

[Commentary]: "Without deviation to the left or right" means that when Mahāvairocana was in the central hall, the Buddha Ratnaketu was to the left of Mahāvairocana and the Buddha Amoghasiddhi resided to the right of Mahāvairocana;
now, when Mahāvairocana is moved to the position of Ratnaketu, one must likewise ensure there is no error or displacement in their relative positions to the left and right.
Regarding the statement "this performs *śāntika* and so forth," this refers to the maṇḍala of these Buddhas.
This refers to visualizing a square shape and the color white for the letter *A* and so forth.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "each of these points," this refers to the nine points visualized within the wheel mentioned above;

that is, one places a single point upon each of the lotus pedestal and the eight petals, which symbolizes the meaning of attaining perfect enlightenment through the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), expressing the attainment of the fruit by means of the cause.
Because the four corner Bodhisattvas are all provided with *bindus*, they prompt further inquiry.
If one wishes to place syllables there, the four directions of the central terrace are *A*, *Ā*, *Am*, and *Aḥ*. As for the three characters for Samantabhadra in the four corners, they are:
*Maṃ* for Mañjuśrī, *Sa* for Avalokiteśvara, and *Mei* for Maitreya.

[Commentary: "If one constructs the Maṇḍala of Hayagrīva and so forth" means that while this Hayagrīva is a member of the Lotus Family and previously Avalokiteśvara was the principal deity with his maṇḍala formed as a large circle, what is placed here as the principal deity?
What is situated in the center? This is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit; the correct term is *Hayagrīva*, which translates into Chinese as "Horse."
Regarding the head [of the arrangement]: one should move Avalokiteśvara to the seat of Śvetāśva (Śrīkūṭa), and move Śvetāśva to the position formerly occupied by Hayagrīva.
As for the maṇḍala being triangular, this is the *vaśya* (subjugation) altar. As for all the remaining retinues surrounding it, they should be placed exactly as in the previous Avalokiteśvara altar;
however, one may rearrange them according to the occasion, shifting Śvetāśva as appropriate to one’s intention.
At the position of Hayagrīva, his retinue of Kṣitigarbha and others likewise shifts accordingly; the same applies to the retinue of Avalokiteśvara.
[Commentary:
Regarding "if one forms the shape of the Buddha-mother," this Buddha-mother is not a separate Buddha distinct from the aforementioned Buddha-uṣṇīṣa mudrā.
The Mother is the Buddha-Mother, who is none other than the Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa; however, while "Mother" refers to the form (*rūpa*), "Uṣṇīṣa" refers to the seal (*mudrā*).
Therefore, it is subsequently stated that one may simply paint the seal, which is the uṣṇīṣa itself. Furthermore, the *Maṇḍalavidhi-sambhāra-parivarta* states:
"Next, in the northern corner, place the Guide and the Mothers of all Buddhas. The commentary on this explains: "As for placing Ākāśanetra in the northern corner, this is Vairocana."
[She is] the Mother of Buddhas.
[Commentary: Regarding "the principal deity (mūlā-devatā) bodhisattva and so forth," the principal deity is the bodhisattva; this bodhisattva is Cundāmaṇi.
The "bodhisattva" refers to the physical form, while "maṇi" refers to the seal (mudrā) or insignia.

[Commentary: Regarding "painting the *daṇḍa* seal and so forth," this refers to painting the *daṇḍa* (staff) seal. It is formed by joining the hands of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), placing the two *vāyu-maṇḍalas* (index fingers) and the two *pṛthivī-maṇḍalas* (little fingers) within the palms, while all other fingers are directed upward. This is it.
[Commentary: *Cakrāṅka* means a trident; *śakti* means a spear; *mudgara* means a mallet. [Commentary: *Pāśa* means a lasso.
The characteristics of these various mudrās are explained in detail in the "Chapter on Secret Mudrās" (*Guhyamudrā-paṭala*).
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "to recognize this honored dharma-gate," etc., first, one relies on the square maṇḍala of the cardinal directions;
this is the Vajra-direction altar. Furthermore, within it, one constructs a triangular fire-altar. This triangular fire-altar represents wisdom (*jñāna*).
Because this wisdom arises from the nature of the Vajra, it is situated above the square altar. Within the triangle, one draws a blue lotus; the blue...

This signifies the meaning of subjugation (*abhicāra*). Furthermore, the fact that small blue lotuses are arranged around it represents the subjugation of the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their secondary derivatives (*upakleśa*), as well as the removal of both fundamental and derivative ignorance (*avidyā*); thus, it is said, "for the sake of recognizing this Honored One and the others."

[Commentary: Those who imitate this [arrangement] take the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin as the central figure of the embryonic matrix (garbha), the remaining retinue as the second layer, and the eight classes of beings (*aṣṭanikāya*) as the third layer.
[Commentary]: Regarding "transcending the center to form a vase" and so forth, this refers to placing a single-pronged vajra within a vase;
because half of the vajra protrudes from the vase, it is called "transcending the center."
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the wise person seals the path" (*prajñā-jña-mudrā-dharma-ādi*): these words "wise person" (*prajñā-jña*) do not appear in the sūtra;
that this commentary provides such an explanation implies they must have been present in the Sanskrit original.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "this is called the most superior," it means that this maṇḍala corresponds precisely with the rite of augmentation (puṣṭi), and the principal deity assumes a joyful countenance.
Because this is the most superior among the rites of augmentation, it is therefore called "the most superior."
[Sūtra] "Two-headed vajra" refers to the upper and lower peaks both being identical to the previous seal; thus it is called "two-headed.
[Śāstra] "Five prongs within one prong" means that within a single wisdom there are five wisdoms contained.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "The single assembly of Mañjuśrī," etc., this refers to Mañjuśrī and his retinue within the Great Maṇḍala of the Matrix of Great Compassion (*Mahākaruṇā-garbha-mahāmaṇḍala*).
If one were to construct a separate Mañjuśrī Maṇḍala, then Mañjuśrī would be the principal figure and the other four would be his attendants;
likewise, among those four, whichever one is taken as the principal, the others become his attendants. Those who serve as the principal figures reside in the middle court (*madhya-kṣetra*).
The four [deities] are in the second court, and the eight classes [of protectors] are placed in the third court.
As for the phrase "within the Great Compassion [mandala]," it further refers to the meaning of the principal and attendant deities among the three families within the first court.
[The Sūtra] states: "Regarding the 'Chapter on Entering the Secret Maṇḍala Method,' 'entering' means to attain understanding of the secret maṇḍala as previously explained.

'Method' refers to the ritual procedures (*vidhi*); that is, the *ācārya* who understands the meaning of these secret ritual procedures of the maṇḍala is able to exercise mastery throughout all maṇḍala rites. Therefore, the subsequent sūtra says: 'To understand this...'"
Regarding the *samaya* secret maṇḍala: it refers to attaining mastery over all the various maṇḍalas within the teachings of all dharmas;

furthermore, it refers to the *ācārya* leading the disciple who has received the dharma to enter this maṇḍala, where, through the teaching of the letter-gates (*akṣaramukha*), their karma and the life-force of their commands are incinerated, allowing the sprout of the *vajra*-nature to arise. Because it possesses these two meanings, it is so called.
This is the method for entering the secret maṇḍala; it may be understood through the commentary.

Furthermore, although the Buddha of the superior grade has already answered Vajrapāṇi’s questions regarding the secret maṇḍala, he had not yet clarified the method for entering the secret [maṇḍala]; thus, this chapter is presented here to restate what was previously taught.
[Commentary] Regarding the question concerning the one hundred and eight names of the Buddha and so forth:

this refers to the fact that the sixteen bodhisattvas, such as Vajrapāṇi, collectively possess one hundred and eight names which, when traced back to their resultant essence, are simply the one hundred and eight names of the Tathāgata.
The *Vajraśekhara-mahāyāna-sūtra-rāja* states: "Vajravīra-mahācitta, Vajra of all Tathāgatas, Samantabhadra... and so on.
At the very beginning, I pay homage to Vajrapāṇi, the King of Vajras; to the Tathāgata Subhūṣaṇavajra, the Hook of Wondrous Enlightenment;

[Commentary: Regarding the further question as to how the arrangement of the characters arises, this further inquiry contains a profound meaning; it is not merely due to doubt.

That is to say, when these twelve characters are arranged upon the maṇḍala, the central court (madhyama-maṇḍala) corresponds to the upper portion, the second court to the middle portion, and the third court to the lower portion.
Furthermore, if one follows the sequence from the origin to the end, they encompass the middle and...

Externally, if one gathers the branches back to the root, it is because [the teaching] is the root of its own traces; therefore, it causes [the disciple] to ask further questions—this is precisely the secret empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Yoga.

[Commentary: As for the reason why the preceding and succeeding sections are interchanged, it refers to a doubt that might arise, such as: "How is it that the *maṇḍala* and its requisites [are described] at the beginning of the sūtra?"
Having already established the ritual procedures for entering the stages, this section now clarifies the discourse on essential applications;

yet, as the textual flow here is distant from the previous exposition and the meaning is profoundly distinct, why are they not presented in a continuous sequence so that people may easily perceive them?

Instead, these [sections] are arranged in a disjointed and alternating manner without mutual connection—does the Buddha harbor any stinginess? Therefore, the following provides the explanation, stating: "It is merely for..."
Those who wish to enter the True Dharma must learn by relying upon a teacher, and so forth.
[Sūtra] Regarding those who enter the stage of the secret maṇḍala, it is said that for the superior grade, the ācārya must thoroughly understand the ritual procedures of the secret maṇḍala;
this serves as the means (*upāya*) herein. Only through such thorough understanding can one correctly enter. Now, in this case...

The meaning of the character *ju* (入) in the commentary on the character *ju* (住) is that while the words "entering" (*ju*) and "abiding" (*ju*) differ in expression, their meaning is the same; furthermore, they are like a reflection of one another.

If one refers to the *ācārya*, it corresponds to "realizing entry" (*shōnyū*) and "realizing abiding" (*shōjū*); if one relies on the disciple, it corresponds to the meanings of "abiding securely" (*an'ju*) and "entering toward" (*shunyū*).

Regarding the meaning of the *maṇḍala*, as in the preceding section, the character *ju* located above the position [of the syllable] is the "agent of entering," while the position itself is the "object of entering."
The locus into which one enters is the eight-petaled great lotus king produced from the mind; therein reside the Tathāgata Ratnaketu in the east,
up to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva in the northeast, and the Vidyādharas and wrathful deities below—
all such positions are the wisdom of the Ācārya who is to enter, acting as the means of entry.

This is the chapter on Entering the Secret Maṇḍala Stage. Having reflected upon its exposition: since the preceding chapter has already fully elucidated the skillful means (*upāya*), this chapter now speaks of its fruit (*phala*);
it follows as a continuation from what preceded. Thus, this chapter comes forth.
[Commentary]: Regarding such great causes and conditions: the World-Honored One Vairocana dwells in the dharma of ultimate signlessness and quiescent extinction;
yet, out of great compassion, he perceives signs within that signlessness.

It is like the autumn moon beautifying the sky—without thought or volitional action, it manifests various reflections through the responsive conditions of sentient beings whose mental vessels have become pure.
This is precisely the meaning of the "Great Causal Conditions" (*mahānidāna*) herein.
[Commentary: The phrase "as stated above, at that time," etc., refers to the preceding "Secret Maṇḍala Chapter.
This means that from that chapter down to the "Eight Mudrās Chapter," all are extensive explanations of the secret meanings contained within the preceding "Syllable Wheel Chapter."
When that [state] first arises, it is called "at that time"; this explanation is based on the Sanskrit original (Skt. *tadā*). Therefore, the sutra immediately following below states:
"At that time, all the limbs of that Tathāgata possess unobstructed power, even unto the arising of immeasurable marks of physical form and adornment.
Using this as evidence, the current sutra says: "At that time," which the commentary (*śū*) points back to that [preceding state].
The phrase "at that time" indicates a further inquiry.

[Commentary] "Secret" refers to the fact that, just as four people each wear a robe of a single color while one person wears a single upper garment complete with all four colors, what is revealed here is precisely the wearing of variegated colors.

The meaning of the "Vajra-colored robe" should be understood as the syllable *Aṃ*. This is because it possesses the meanings of bodhicitta, great compassion, skillful means, and nirvāṇa; for this reason, it is so named.
[Commentary] As for the water of eight qualities, it is as usual: first, sweet; second, cool; third, soft; fourth, light; fifth, pure.
Sixth, it does not have a foul odor; seventh, when drinking it, it does not damage the throat; eighth, after drinking it, it does not harm the stomach.
[Commentary] Regarding the "six seasons of the year," in the Western Regions there are six seasons each consisting of two months:

the latter half of the eleventh month and the first half of the first month are called the spring season; second, from this point until the first half of the third month is called... [text continues].
1. The Hot Season (*uṣṇa-kāla*): from this point until the first half of the fifth month; 2. The Rainy Season (*varṣā-kāla*): from this point until the first half of the seventh month;
3. The Autumn Season (*śarad-kāla*): from this point until the first half of the ninth month; 4. The Snowy Season (*haimantika-kāla*):

from this point until the first half of the eleventh month; 5. The Cold Season (*śiśira-kāla*): from this point until the first half of the [next] third month. Furthermore, there are various other explanations, or... [text fragment ends].
According to the *Qīngliáng Chāo* (Cool Grove Commentary), it is said that because the flowers in that land bloom according to the seasons, they are called "flowers of the six periods. [Commentary:
"Born from the faith and understanding of the Tathāgata" means that they arise from the faith and understanding within the causes of the Tathāgata; this cites the fruit to indicate the cause.
Regarding the reason for this inquiry, it is said: "Because the Tathāgata has faith and understanding. The sub-commentary below states: "From what, then, do these ten powers arise?
It is because the Tathāgata, since immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas past, has cultivated the six perfections, the ten perfections, and even the merits of all asaṃkhyeya perfections;
through the nourishment and growth of these merits, the Dharma-body appears. Therefore, it is said they arise from the Tathāgata’s faith."
Furthermore, just as the Tathāgata’s power of faith and understanding also permeates the virtues within the fruit, these manifested marks—
equal in number to the atoms of ten worlds— all arise from the power of the merit of faith and understanding within the fruit.

[Commentary]: Regarding the repetition of the term "King" (*rāja*) and so forth: according to the Sanskrit original, this refers to *Kusumita-rāja*, which is translated here as "Flower-Blossoming King.
Alternatively, it may be *Kusumita-indra*, which is likewise "Flower-Blossoming King.
This is because the preceding phrase contains two instances of the letter *ra*.
[Commentary]: It is said that if the word "king" were repeated, it would be phonetically awkward; therefore, the Sanskrit term is retained.
The Sanskrit *Indra* is correctly translated as "Lord" (*zhǔ*) or "Venerable One" (*zūn*); this is why Śakra-devānām-indra is translated as "Lord of Heaven" (*Tiānzhǔ*).
[Commentary]: "The assembly of the boundless great ocean" refers to the Vajra-holders, meaning all the earth-dwelling devas and others, whose numbers are immeasurable.
Because those who surround [the assembly] are all subsumed under the Vajra Family, it is said that they "are the Vajras."
[Commentary: "Mentally visualizing flowers and causing the entrants [to do so]" means leading the disciples into the mandala and causing them to focus their attention on the flower of bodhicitta.
This is the primary meaning; it indicates that these flowers and so forth arise from the mind, which is why they are called "mentally produced incense and flowers," and so on.

[Commentary: "Having seen it oneself, one explains it to the other" means that when the disciple throws the flower upon the master’s body, the master observes the specific location where the flower falls and immediately informs the disciple:
"The flower you cast has fallen upon such-and-such a Buddha, such-and-such a Bodhisattva, or a Vajra [deity]," and so forth.
Once the disciple has understood this, he then undergoes empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) and other rites according to his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). For this reason...
The end of the sūtra states: "Because this is the supreme maṇḍala, one should bestow the samaya.
[Sūtra] Regarding the "Chapter on the Eight Secret Seals": As for "secret," although the "Chapter on Secret Seals" was already explained previously, is this not also secret?
Now, these eight types of seals are again called "secret"; what difference is there between this and what was previously explained?
The previous revelation of the secret was merely a general clarification; what is here termed "secret" is the secret within secrets.

These "secrets" refer to the eight seals (*mudrā*). Furthermore, it is said that these are the dharmas required for the *maṇḍala* of the Ācārya’s own heart-secret, and they are the eight seals for entering the secret *maṇḍala*.
The name is formed according to its primary referent (*adhikaraṇa-samāsa*), as [the Tathāgata] previously stated.
When the extensive explanation of the secret methods for entering and abiding in the maṇḍala was being given, the great assembly again had this thought:

"What further dharma exists that can cause practitioners of the mantra-vehicle to swiftly attain accomplishment? The Tathāgata, in accordance with their thoughts, spoke [this teaching]; therefore, this chapter follows.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "changed to 'endowed' (*ju*)," "change" means transformation. This refers to the fact that the virtues manifested by the symbols and insignia of the aforementioned maṇḍala are shared equally by all sentient beings;
such virtues are immeasurable and boundless, which is precisely the meaning of being "endowed with various virtues.
Now, the present translator simply uses the character "endowed" (*ju*) to clarify this, hence it is said: "changed to 'endowed.'"
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that the maṇḍala should be made triangular and so forth, it means one should fashion it according to the mudrā.
That is to say, with the hollowed palms joined, the four wheels of earth and wind are extended upward while the remaining wheels are joined as before.
In this mudrā, when the wheel of space (ākāśa-cakra) faces the other four wheels, it corresponds to one corner of the triangle; thus it is called the "Triangle Mudrā. Now, regarding the maṇḍala...
The shape is also like that; the triangle in its center corresponds to the wheels of water, fire, and space, while the four triangles on the four sides correspond to the wheels of earth and wind.
One should visualize the Buddha within these, possessing majestic radiance.
Therefore, the phrase "sun and moon" is a figurative expression for what the Sūtra refers to as "possessing radiant light."
[Commentary]: The syllable *va* means "unbound. Among the five syllables of this mantra, the first is the syllable *bha*;
its correct pronunciation is *ma*, and its fundamental form is the syllable *ma*. In Sanskrit, *bandha* is translated as "bond" (*fù*).
Here, the term *va* refers to the sound for "unbound," though it contains a phonetic corruption.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that the syllable *ga* is added with the *samādhi* stroke, this means that adding the *samādhi* stroke to the syllable *ga* results in the syllable *jñi*.
This, however, serves to explain the meaning of the word *yoginī* in the following line; it should not be placed within this current sentence.

[Sūtra] Regarding the Chapter on Maintaining the Vidyā-vows: "Vidyā" has already been explained as in the introduction. As for "vows" (*śīla*), "vow" (*vinaya*) means to restrain and prevent indulgence;
"vow" (*śīla*) means to be cautious and refrain from committing transgressions. The term for "vow" in Sanskrit is *śīla*, which here means "coolness.
It is like when a person’s body is burning with fever; if they are anointed with sandalwood, they immediately attain coolness.
Śīla is likewise: when the *dharmakāya* of all sentient beings is afflicted by the feverish heat of the afflictions (*kleśa*), if one applies the sandalwood of śīla, one immediately attains coolness.
This is the precept inherently possessed by one's own nature, which must be maintained of its own accord.
Now, regarding the *vidyādhara-śīla*, the Sanskrit term is *mūlata*, which is translated here as "restraint" (*zhiwei*). It is for those who are *vidyādharas* that this is prescribed.
Thus, it is established that this is the vow of the Vidyādhara; it is named after its primary subject, "one who holds the vidyā," rather than the vow itself. Question:
Since this belongs to the vows maintained within the Vidyādharapiṭaka, why was it not explained earlier in the section on receiving the Samaya-vows?
After all, those are also vows maintained within the Vidyādharapiṭaka. Answer: Those Samaya-vows were [discussed] at the time of generating the bodhicitta.

The precepts now obtained are for the time of accomplishing *siddhi*; because these precepts maintained within the six months are established according to specific circumstances, they are explained separately.
Since the practitioner can thereby cause *siddhi* to be easily attained and manifest, this is explained next in the "Secret Maṇḍala" chapter.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "as if again taking up wind and so forth," "wind" refers to the syllable *ha*. Among the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), this syllable belongs to the element of wind.
During the fourth month of practice, one uses only the syllable *ha* for inhalation and exhalation.

When the breath goes out, one should contemplate this syllable as following the breath outward; when the breath comes in, one should contemplate this syllable as following the breath inward. This is called... [the name].
"For the purpose of subduing the winds and so forth.
[Commentary] "The six months" refers to the enumeration; this means that the limit for this precept is set at a period of six months.

Within these six months, according to the differences of each month, it is said that for the practitioner of *mantra* (vidyā-caraṇa), during the first month one regulates the inhalation and exhalation, and so on through the subsequent months.

In the sixth month, one obtains the fruit according to one's wish; once the fruit has been obtained, the precepts naturally fall away, and for this reason they are called *mṛtaka-śīla* (extinct precepts). [Commentary]: The correct Sanskrit pronunciation is *sattva*, which means "attachment. It is commonly translated as *sattva*. There are three types of *sattva*: 1. *Sattva* as a sentient being (*jīva*). 2. *Sattva* as a great being (*mahāsattva*). 3. *Sattva* as a hero (*vīra*). Regarding the first, *sattva* as a sentient being: it refers to all living beings who possess the nature of mind and consciousness. Regarding the second, *sattva* as a great being: it refers to those who have already attained the path and are capable of benefiting others. Regarding the third, *sattva* as a hero: it refers to those who, having generated the bodhicitta, are able to subdue their own afflictions and the afflictions of others. Here, it refers to the latter two meanings. This is because the term *sattva* is used to denote the bodhisattva’s resolve and practice. Furthermore, the term *sattva* is also used to denote the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*), as in the phrase "all phenomena are the *sattva*-nature" (*sarvadharma-sattva-svabhāva*). This is because the true nature of all phenomena is non-dual and free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Therefore, it is said that the *sattva* of the ultimate reality is the same as the *sattva* of the bodhisattva. This is because both are characterized by the absence of self and the absence of grasping. Thus, the term *sattva* is used to encompass these various meanings. In this context, it refers to the bodhisattva who possesses the vow to save all sentient beings. Because such a person is endowed with great compassion and the power of wisdom, they are called a *sattva*. Furthermore, because they do not abandon the suffering of sentient beings and are determined to bring about their liberation, they are called a *sattva*. For these reasons, the term *sattva* is applied to the bodhisattva. It should be understood that this term is used metaphorically to indicate the profound and vast nature of the bodhisattva’s practice. It is not that there is a real entity called a *sattva*; rather, it is a designation based on the convergence of vows, practices, and the ultimate nature of reality. Therefore, one should not grasp at the term *sattva* as a substantial self. To understand this correctly is to enter the gate of the Mahāyāna. Thus, the term *sattva* is a profound and significant expression that reveals the essence of the bodhisattva path. One must not misunderstand it as a mere conventional label. By understanding the true meaning of *sattva*, one can truly enter the stage of a bodhisattva. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a fundamental concept in the Mahāyāna teachings. It is through this term that the unique characteristics of the bodhisattva are defined. Consequently, one must study and contemplate the meaning of *sattva* with great care. Only by doing so can one truly understand the path of the bodhisattva. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a key to unlocking the profound mysteries of the Mahāyāna. One must not treat it lightly. By respecting and studying the term *sattva*, one can gain insight into the core of Buddhist practice. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a treasure of the Dharma that must be cherished and protected. One must never allow its true meaning to be lost. By upholding the meaning of *sattva*, one upholds the lineage of the Buddhas. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a source of great inspiration for all practitioners. It serves as a reminder of the noble ideal of universal salvation. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a vital element of the Buddhist tradition. It is through this term that the spirit of the Mahāyāna is sustained. Therefore, one must always keep the meaning of *sattva* in mind. By doing so, one will naturally progress along the bodhisattva path. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a guide for all seekers of enlightenment. It points the way toward the ultimate goal of Buddhahood. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a beacon in the darkness of ignorance. It illuminates the path for all sentient beings. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a gift from the Buddhas. It is a legacy of the Great Vehicle. Therefore, one must receive and uphold the term *sattva* with reverence. By doing so, one participates in the great work of the Buddhas. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a bridge between the mundane and the transcendent. It connects the ordinary practitioner with the state of perfect awakening. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a symbol of hope for all beings. It represents the possibility of liberation for everyone. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a source of strength for the weary. It provides encouragement to those who are struggling. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a wellspring of compassion. It flows from the heart of the Buddhas. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a manifestation of the Buddha-nature. It is present in all sentient beings. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a truth that must be realized. It is not something external, but internal to oneself. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a realization that must be lived. It is not merely a word, but a way of being. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a practice that must be embodied. It is not a theory, but an experience. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a transformation that must be achieved. It is not a static state, but a dynamic process. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a journey that must be undertaken. It is not a destination, but a path. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a commitment that must be maintained. It is not a temporary resolve, but a lifelong vow. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a duty that must be fulfilled. It is not a burden, but a privilege. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a joy that must be shared. It is not a private pleasure, but a communal celebration. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a light that must be spread. It is not a solitary flame, but a collective radiance. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a song that must be sung. It is not a mournful lament, but a joyful hymn. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a dance that must be performed. It is not a rigid ritual, but a spontaneous expression. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a feast that must be enjoyed. It is not a mere meal, but a spiritual banquet. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a festival that must be celebrated. It is not a seasonal event, but a perpetual celebration. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a legacy that must be passed on. It is not a closed book, but an open tradition. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a lineage that must be preserved. It is not a dead end, but a living stream. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a community that must be nurtured. It is not a fragmented group, but a harmonious whole. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a family that must be loved. It is not a distant stranger, but a beloved kin. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a friend that must be trusted. It is not a fleeting acquaintance, but a steadfast companion. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a teacher that must be followed. It is not a distant authority, but a guiding light. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a mentor that must be honored. It is not a mere instructor, but a source of wisdom. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a refuge that must be sought. It is not a false shelter, but a true sanctuary. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a home that must be returned to. It is not a temporary lodging, but a permanent abode. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a source that must be tapped. It is not an exhausted well, but a perennial spring. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a field that must be cultivated. It is not a barren wasteland, but a fertile soil. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a garden that must be tended. It is not a wild jungle, but a cultivated grove. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a harvest that must be reaped. It is not a meager yield, but a bountiful crop. Therefore, the term *sattva* is a fruit that must be tasted. It is not a bitter poison, but a sweet nectar. Consequently, the term *sattva* is a medicine that must be taken. It is not a harsh remedy, but a healing balm
As previously established, *bodhisattva* also carries the meaning of "enduring, delighting in, practicing, and firmly maintaining without abandoning.
However, because it was not convenient for common worldly discourse, the masters of worldly treatises referred to it as *sattva*.
Those who follow and transmit these terms simply say *sattva*; thus, the correct Sanskrit pronunciation is *sattva*.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "as the Buddha abides," it means that if a practitioner abides as the Buddha abides, then within that state, the three karmas are all equal to those of the Tathāgata;
this is called the "threefold equality. Because one abides in these three equalities, merit increases;
because merit increases, the fruit of *siddhi* (accomplishment) can then be easily attained.
[Commentary]: Regarding "sovereign power" (*vaśitā*) and so forth—sovereignty refers to the ten sovereignties. According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:

first, sovereignty over life (*āyur-vaśitā*), because one abides for boundless eons; second, sovereignty over mind (*citta-vaśitā*), because one emerges from countless meditative absorptions and enters into profound wisdom;
third, sovereignty over adornment (*pariṣkāra-vaśitā*, which the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* calls "sovereignty over requisites"), because one is able to adorn all buddha-fields.

1. Mastery over karma (*karma-vaśitā*), because one experiences retribution at will according to the time; 2. Mastery over birth (*upapatti-vaśitā*), because one manifests birth in all buddha-fields; 3.
Mastery over liberation (*vimokṣa-vaśitā*)—the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* calls this mastery over resolute conviction (*adhimukti-vaśitā*)—because one perceives all realms as filled with Buddhas;
4. Mastery over desire (*ruci-vaśitā*), because one attains enlightenment at will in any buddha-field; 5. Mastery over supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-vaśitā*).
1. Mastery of manifestation, because of manifesting all supernatural transformations; 2. Mastery of phenomena, because of manifesting immeasurable and boundless dharma-gates; 3.
Mastery of knowledge, because of manifesting the awakening to the ten powers and fearlessnesses of a Tathāgata in every moment of thought.
These are called the powers of mastery. Regarding "the ten powers and so forth," the phrase "and so forth" includes the four analytical knowledges up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
"Unshared dharmas," etc. [Commentary]:

"Up to the point of composing verses" means that this practitioner, by attaining *dhāraṇī*, is able to expound many meanings from a single syllable and compose verses from those many meanings without any obstruction in mind; thus, they draw near to *siddhi*.
This refers to the preceding signs.

[Commentary: Regarding "such as Śūraṅgama" and so forth, that text explains it thus: just as when a person practices archery, practicing gradually and becoming increasingly proficient until, once mastery is attained, every arrow hits the target;
the practitioner is likewise. Over the course of six months, their contemplation becomes ever more refined and clear, even if they encounter adverse conditions.
The meaning of "target" (*lakṣa*) is that one's mind cannot be shaken or altered by favorable objects.

[Commentary] The question regarding whether one contemplates the letter, etc., means that when contemplating a letter, one contemplates the letter *va* as being white, or contemplates the original mantra held by oneself;
that is, taking a single character from among the mantras as the seed-syllable for inhalation and exhalation.
"Breath is also attained.
[Commentary] To take the syllable *ra* as food means to take the joy of dhyāna (*dhyānāsvāda*) as one's flavor.

This refers to using the fire of wisdom (*prajñā-agni*) represented by the syllable *ra* to eliminate the darkness of afflictions (*kleśa*) and to nourish the light of wisdom; therefore, it is said that "one takes the syllable *ra* alone as food."
[This refers to] eating.
[Commentary]: Regarding the instruction "one should perform the Cakra-mudrā (Wheel Seal) and so forth," the present commentary merely points back to what was previously performed.

This phrase "previously performed" applies generally to both the Sūtra and the Commentary. According to the explanation in the Commentary, one first performs the mudrā by turning the hands backward and joining the palms, then using the two ring fingers...
Reverse the interlocking so that the right hand is placed over the left; the remaining three fingers—water, fire, and wind—also interlock in reverse.
Finally, twist the two space-fingers (the thumbs) until they reach the palms and rest against one another. If one follows this explanation, it is indeed difficult to perform correctly;

however, according to the sutra, it means that the five wheels (fingers) of both the Samādhi-hand and Prajñā-hand are equalized, alternately reversed and interlocked, with the two space-fingers [joined].
The two wheel-holders facing each other is this [mudrā]. Regarding the commentary’s explanation, it is not difficult to compose a verse on it:
"This is called the Auspicious Mudrā of the Supreme Vow and Dharma Wheel; the Protectors of the World, the Saviors of the World, all turn this wheel."
[Sūtra] Regarding the "Chapter on the True Wisdom of the Ācārya" and so forth: the Sanskrit term *ācārya* is translated here as "Preceptor" (*guǐfànshī*).
This is because he is able to serve as a guide and craftsman for others regarding the secret treasury of the Tathāgata; thus, this is his designation.
As for "True Wisdom," "true" refers to the five-syllable mantra beginning with *a-va-ra-ha-kha*, which denotes the essential nature of those sounds and syllables.
Being free from delusion and inversion is called "true wisdom" (*tattvajñāna*). Wisdom is that which understands; true reality (*tattva*) is that which is understood.
This is the wisdom of true reality. Furthermore, true wisdom is the dharma that is attained and realized, while the *ācārya* is the person who attains and realizes it.
Because this is also an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive compound), it is called the "Chapter on the True Wisdom of the *Ācārya*. Moreover—
Although the characteristics of the maṇḍala constructed by the ācārya through skillful means have already been explained in detail above,
the true virtues of the ācārya have not yet been fully expounded; therefore, this chapter now follows, as Vajradhara requests that these be further explained.
[Commentary] The passage beginning with "The characters *o*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *ma*, etc. explains away potential objections.
This refers to the doubt raised by the preceding statement that all speech and sounds have the letter *A* as their primary element.
If all speech and sounds lacked this sound *A*, there would be nothing that could be expressed; thus, the five characters *o*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *ma* correspond directly to the Great [Element].
Furthermore, regarding the point that the sound "o" is separate from the sound "a," why is it said that all vocal sounds take this letter "a" as their primary basis?
To explain this first, [the text] provisionally concedes the preceding argument:

although it is said that the five letters beginning with "o"—namely, o, va, ṇa, na, ma—are separate from the sound "a," yet the sound "a" possesses two types, internal and external; and as for these five letters beginning with "o"...
Although the external sound of the syllable *A* does not exist, it cannot be separated from the internal sound of the syllable *A* within the throat.
[Commentary] "That is, it is the locus of immeasurable meanings" means that this syllable *A* is the heart of all mantras;
just as when a person has a heart, their various limbs are able to perform their functions, so too is this [syllable] identical to the "Immeasurable" [Chapter] of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The Samādhi of the Basis of Meaning (Arthasthāna-samādhi) is so named because it is able to universally give rise to all various mundane and supramundane phenomena.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "detached from all conceptual proliferation" (*prapañca*), this refers to the syllable *A*, which signifies the meaning that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen (*anutpanna*).
This is called the Heart Mantra. This Heart Mantra is that which is capable of universally producing all phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane worlds.
Although it gives rise to all phenomena, it is non-arising yet arising; it is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Conceptual proliferation is itself volitional construction (*abhisamskāra*). Because conceptual proliferation ceases, wondrous skillful wisdom arises. Wondrous skillful wisdom is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

The specific name for this wisdom is the Tathāgata’s *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done); therefore, it is said that it is "free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), etc. [Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "arranging the various limbs," the general purport here is as follows: if one speaks in terms of manifesting the body, it refers to both the mind and the limbs.
If one speaks specifically in terms of syllables, the letter *A* is the mind, while the multitude of other letters are the limbs. Thus, where there is the mind, there are necessarily the limbs.
There is the syllable *A* because there are all other syllables; therefore, in Sanskrit it is called *akṣara*. This body is the constituent parts (*aṅga*), while the mind is the essence (*tattva*).

These various syllables are the constituent parts, and the syllable *A* is the mind. Therefore, where there are the constituent parts of the body, there must necessarily be the mind, and where there is the essence, there must necessarily be the principle.
These various syllables necessarily contain the syllable *A*; they cannot be separated from one another. Thus it is said.

Regarding the "tooth-text" (dantapāṭha), the lower grade of exposition explains that [the syllables] extend from below the throat and above the palate up to the crown of the head; these constitute the constituent parts (*aṅga*).

Now it is said that this is the mind itself, for the mind is the sovereign. Thus, the mind, the throat, and so forth are all distributed throughout the upper and lower regions, manifesting them in mutual relation;
therefore, it is called "mutual-text" (*itaretara-pāṭha*).

[Commentary]: "Buddha" refers to that which possesses the fruit from the seed; this is an implicit application of the *mūlākṣara* (seed-syllable) gate to explain the Buddha and Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
That is to say, the initial syllable *A* is the bodhicitta as the seed; from this seed, one obtains the fruit of bodhicitta, which is the syllable *Am*.
The gate of not abandoning the cause upon obtaining the fruit is the long vowel *Ā*, which is the skillful means (*upāya*) for Perfect Enlightenment.
[Commentary: "That which is called 'discourse, principle, and realization of truth' refers to the practitioner pervading these two types of phenomena.
This means acting in accordance with principle and realizing in accordance with principle; thus, the term is repeated.

"All" (in the first instance) refers to the word "all" (*sarva*) in the first half-verse, while "pervasive bestowal" (in the second instance) refers to the word "pervasive" (*vyāpta*) in the second half-verse. This is precisely according to the Dharma.
"Arranged in all places according to principle.
[Commentary] Regarding "the syllables *ṛ*, *ṝ*, etc.": this refers to *ṛ* and *ṝ*. Here, "increase" (*zēngjiā*) means that these correspond to *i*, *ī*, and so forth, up to *u* and *ū*;
because they are all derived from the increase of the letter *a*, it says "the syllables *ṛ*, *ṝ*, etc."
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "Suppose it were the letter *ka*," etc., this refers to an objection which says:

"If every opening of the mouth is accompanied by the sound of *a*, and all speech-sounds are established by means of the letter *a*, then for instance, when pronouncing the letter *ka*, one merely produces a short *ga*-sound within the throat;
since the letter *ka* has not yet been formed, how could there be the letter *a*? The general explanation states: "Suppose it were the letter *ka*... and so forth.
The short vowel sound in the throat is not the letter *ka*; without it, the essence of the letter *ka* cannot be established. It is only by adding the letter *a* that the letter *ka* is perfected.
Furthermore, even the short vowel sound of the letter *ga* in the throat does not depart from the short vowel sound of the letter *a* in the throat.
Thus, one knows that all letters are initiated by means of the letter *a*.

[Commentary]: "One should know that the letter A is non-arising," etc., means that *ka* has the meaning of "action" (*kriyā*). By adding the sound *a*, it becomes distinct from "action," and thus its meaning corresponds [to non-action].
The phrase "others are to be understood by analogy" means, for example, that *ya* has the meaning of "vehicle" (*yāna*);
if one adds the sound *a*, it is named "no vehicle. Likewise, up to *ha*, which has the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*); if one adds the sound *a*, it is "no cause. Thus it is.
Therefore, the meaning of the syllable *A* as "unborn" and the syllable *Ha* as "causeless" is precisely that they are formed through mutual correspondence and combination.
[Commentary: As for the statement that "all non-bodies are likewise all-pervasive," it means that they not only pervade all the limbs of the practitioner's body, but also pervade the maṇḍala;
thus it is said they are "non-bodies" and yet "pervasive throughout the various limbs of the maṇḍala."
Because it is "middle," it is said to be "not the body.

[Commentary] "That which is identical to *nirvāṇa* and so forth" means that the practitioner’s mind, which is full of defiled desire, and the mind of true wisdom are blended together like the five flavors of milk and curd; therefore, they are identical to *nirvāṇa* as one.
[This is] the flavor.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "contemplating the Tathāgata, etc.," once the practitioner has established themselves in the seat of the adamantine correspondence with the letter *A*, they should immediately contemplate that the Buddhas of the three periods of time and their own body are non-dual, being clearly realized by oneself alone.

[Commentary: Regarding the one hundred and eight names of the Tathāgata, it means that the Ācārya is not only a Buddha, a Bodhisattva, or a Vajradhara, but is also the one hundred and eight types of epithets of the Tathāgata Vairocana.
These one hundred and eight names have already been cited above.
[Commentary]: "The tail is emptiness," etc., explains Viṣṇu in the sutra. In the previous commentary, where the sutra was cited, it was already glossed as *Viśeṣṇu*.

Here, the explanation of that *vi* is precisely the character *vī*. The fundamental essence of the character *vī* is the character *va*; this signifies the meaning of being free from verbal expression.

Being free from verbal expression is called ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). Furthermore, *śeṣṇu*... [is also... (Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary on the etymology of the name Viṣṇu (*Viśeṣṇu*), breaking it down into its constituent phonemes and explaining their philosophical significance.)
"Empty" (kha) refers to this deva who travels through the sky riding upon a garuḍa, moving with sovereign unimpededness;
for this reason, it is further called "concentration" (samādhi), specifically the "empty concentration" (kha-samādhi).

Regarding the statement above that "concentration is the Buddha’s four bases of psychic power" (ṛddhipāda), that commentary further states: "Śakra Nārāyaṇa is likewise; he rides upon the Great Power Golden [Garuda]."
The King of Birds flies through the ultimate void of space to cut off the flow of saṃsāra and take those who are ready for deliverance;
it is for this reason that he is so named. What is here called the Buddha’s four bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) has precisely this meaning.

Regarding the "four bases of supernormal power," *ṛddhi* refers to supernormal transformation, while *pāda* means "basis" because they are what the supernormal power relies upon. Thus, the Abhidharma states: "By virtue of their fulfillment..."

Because the power of samādhi initiates various supernormal transformations (ṛddhi), it is designated by its cause; that is, because there are four types of causes for the bases of supernormal power (ṛddhipāda), there are four kinds.
Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "It is called the four directions because one is able to cultivate meditative concentration through these four.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Desire-samādhi (*chanda-samādhi*) refers to [concentration] attained through earnest, intense desire and respectful aspiration."
"One who attains samādhi through diligent application of samādhi" means that by means of uninterrupted practice, one touches upon one-pointedness of mind;

that is, through constant diligence without even a moment's interval, one attains the samādhi of the mind. "One who attains samādhi through prior cultivation" means that having previously cultivated meditative concentration, one touches upon one-pointedness of mind;
this occurs because the power of the seeds [of concentration] has been increased through repeated cultivation of the power of concentration in previous lives.
By the power of the seed, the mind spontaneously transforms in accordance with samādhi; through this, one swiftly realizes one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
