This inferior concentration is what is termed "mind. Regarding the contemplation of samādhi: it refers to the contact with one-pointedness of mind through internal discernment based on hearing the teachings of others;
that is, the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī prajñā*). Question: Are the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) exclusively concentration?

Therefore, it is said there are four. The answer is: because the causes are fourfold, they are called "four. This refers to that which is named "divine" (*ṛddhi*) from the perspective of its fruit, "four" from the perspective of its cause, and "bases" (*pāda*) from the perspective of its essential nature;
hence, they are called the "four bases of divine power" (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*).
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the creation of the lords of the world" (*lokapāla*), this explains the three characters "world-lord" (*loka-pati*) found in the sutra.

This means that when the world is formed, it arises from the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) based upon the space-circle (*ākāśa-maṇḍala*). Thus, the fire, water, and earth circles are successively established, each having its own lord;
these are the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) of earth, water, fire, wind, and space. Each of these five, according to its respective...
Because they are lords who have attained mastery, they are called *devas* (gods); the five great [elements] as gods are thus called the Five Great Gods (*pañcamahādeva*).
[Commentary]: Regarding "the *kāla* period," etc., this explains "dark night. The Sanskrit term *kāla* is translated here as "time" (*shí*), referring to the three periods of time and so forth.
The phrase "that which is the self" refers to the conceptualization of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). If one follows the *Sāmānya-mantra-piṭaka* (Ordinary Mantra Treasury):
The commentator within this chapter explains that the complete Sanskrit term is *Kālarātri*. *Kāla* means "black" (*kṛṣṇa*) and *rātri* means "night";
thus, it refers to the Goddess of the Night. This is merely a mutual elucidation of the meaning.
Furthermore, *tṛ* signifies "three," referring to the three periods of the night. It is said to mean *Yama*; this *Yama* is the Sanskrit name for "equality" (*samatā*).
It is also called "the slayer"; now, taking both together, it is the "equal slayer.
Herein, Yama is universally able to slay the afflictions of sentient beings; therefore, he is named the "Equal Slayer."
[Commentary: "To speak of his name" means to speak of the name of that *ācārya*; it means that the *ācārya* is also none other than the Tathāgata.
[Commentary: "That is to say, the bhikṣus and so forth" refers to all those who are present within the maṇḍala.
[Commentary]: "There are also such [beings] among the non-Buddhists" means that these non-Buddhist proponents of omniscience each likewise claim to be omniscient.
"Now, this is indeed so" means it is truly as it is; it is not like the non-Buddhists, who possess nothing more than an empty name.
[Commentary]: "Wealth" refers to Vaiśravaṇa. In the correct Sanskrit, he is called Vaiśravaṇa; *vai* means "much," and *śravaṇa* means "hearing.
Thus, he is the Heavenly King of Abundant Hearing (*Duowenshi Tianwang*). This heavenly king is so named because he possesses abundant wealth and treasures.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the locus is all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*)": "locus" (*sthāna*) here means "pervasive. As the Sūtra says, "pervading all" is a specific name for all-encompassing wisdom.
Because one abides in the samādhi of the *akṣara* (syllable) bodhicitta, the sound "A" emerges from the *akṣara*.
From this sound, wisdom arises and performs its differentiation. It is said that "A" signifies primordial non-arising (*mūlājāti*).
That which is fundamentally unborn pervades all things; therefore, this pervasion of all things is called "omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*).

[Commentary: "To pervade all sentient beings and so forth"—here, "sentient" refers to the various positions within the maṇḍala, while "non-sentient" refers to the gates, boundaries, banners, and insignia.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "there shall be the syllable HA, etc.," the syllable HŪṂ is precisely what is meant here.

This means that since the syllable HA was previously mentioned as being wind, there was a concern that people might harbor doubts; therefore, he causes them to ask again. Furthermore, the phrase "it is precisely this" points directly to the syllable HŪṂ.

[The Sūtra] states: Regarding the "Chapter on the Array of Syllables" (*Akṣaravyavasthāna-parivarta*), "array" (*vyavasthāna*) refers to the arrangement of syllables; these syllables are the "gateways" (*mukha*). This refers to the sequence from *ka*, *kha*, and so forth, up to *aṃ* and *aḥ*;
each one is a gateway for entering the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-mukha*). Because the syllable itself is the gate, it is called a "syllable-gateway.

Furthermore, the syllable is that which is arrayed, and the array is that which arrays; this is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound. When the practitioner takes each individual syllable from the throat...
From the upper surface of the lower jaw up to the crown of the head at the point of the cross, [the syllables] are clearly arranged so that the mind is constantly present before them.

A practitioner who acts in this manner is said to have attained equal and perfect enlightenment, and is even called the "All-Knowing One. Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Arrangement of Syllables" (Buzi-pin).
[Commentary]: Regarding "providing all dharma-wealth as material resources": if one can thus distribute [the teachings] according to the Dharma, this constitutes material resources.
That is to say, by bestowing the Tathāgata’s dharma-wealth upon all sentient beings so that there is no lack, it is given this name.
【Sūtra】 Regarding the Chapter on Receiving the Training in Skillful Means (*upāya-śikṣā-vastu*):

For a practitioner of mantra (*mantra-yogin*), "receiving" refers to receiving from a master the complete training in skillful means, which consists of the ten phrases of practice. Because one receives them from a master, it is called "receiving.
"Skillful means" (*upāya*) refers to expedient artifice; it is so called because one practices by means of such skillful artifice. Thus, it is termed "training in skillful means."
"Abode" (*sthāna*) refers to training; "training" (*śikṣā*) refers to the place of practice, which specifically denotes the ten types of precepts.
These ten precepts are the locus of the practitioner's training, and are therefore called "abodes of training" (*śikṣāpada*). They collectively refer to the skillful means of the precepts.
Through this skillful wisdom, the practitioner receives these abodes of training, thereby achieving that which is unique and not shared with the two vehicles.

Because it is shared with non-Buddhists and others, the "skillful means" (upāya) belongs to the "learner" (śaikṣa). The "precept of skillful wisdom" (*kauśalyajñāna-śikṣāpada*) refers to the training (*śikṣā*) that is the object of study;

since this training in wholesome precepts is established by way of the learner’s skillful wisdom, it is called the "precept of skillful means. Furthermore, "receiving" (*samādāna*) refers to the act of undertaking the precepts;
because it is established by way of what is received and from whom it is received, it is called the "precept of the skillful means of receiving," as taught by the Buddha.
It was previously stated that when one enters the maṇḍala and bestows the precepts upon a disciple, these very precepts ought to be explained;
however, as they had not yet been expounded, this chapter is now presented to bring forth what was previously mentioned.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "Vajrapāṇi has already asked at the beginning of the sūtra," this means that Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi has already inquired about the precepts in which a practitioner of mantra (mantrayāna) abides, within the chapter titled "The Chapter on the Requisites for Entering the Maṇḍala.

The term "beginning of the sūtra" refers to the very first instance of the inquiry concerning the characteristics of abiding in the precepts within the sūtra itself; it does not mean the physical front cover of the sūtra. Therefore, it is so stated.

[Commentary on] the beginning of the Sūtra: "Free from doubt and anxiety," etc., means that just as a person at a forked road hesitates and cannot proceed, so too when a Bodhisattva has not yet abided in this precept, they are hesitant and indecisive regarding all their activities; because they abide in this [precept], [they become certain].
Because the mind that practices what is cultivated attains certainty, it is said to be "free from doubt and anxiety.
[Commentary] Regarding "observing with the Tathāgata’s eye," this means that among the five eyes, one observes by employing the Buddha-eye; therefore, it is called the "Tathāgata’s eye" and so forth.
[Commentary: This present precept is precisely that which is stated in the introduction to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*:

"The original source of the precepts for all sentient beings is the intrinsically pure nature. It is also what the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* refers to as "the nature that is naturally able to uphold the precepts.

Therefore, the *Shibei Shu* (Stone Wall Commentary) on the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "'The original source of the intrinsically pure nature' means that the nature of the precepts is like empty space; it is self-so..."

The subsequent passage explains: "That which has conditions is not without cause; since it belongs to the category of causal conditions, it is the meaning of emptiness. The *Huoshui Chao* (Hushui Commentary) explains:

"The self-nature precept (*svabhāva-śīla*) of all sentient beings is a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); as a characteristic, it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). That which is fundamentally pure refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*);
True Suchness is the nature itself, and thus it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The intended meaning is that this applies to all of these.
The *tathatā* that serves as the basis for the intrinsic morality maintained by sentient beings is primordially pure by nature;
because it has never been associated with defiled phenomena from the very beginning, and because it acts as the support for all phenomena, it is called the "original source" (*mūla*).
According to this explanation, the "intrinsic original source" of all sentient beings is none other than *mūla-awakening* (*mūla-bodhi*).

The essence of the mind is named as such because it is free from all defilements and conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*), and because there are no wholesome merits—whether conditioned or unconditioned—from which it does not arise. If explained esoterically, this is the *A* syllable, the essence of the *dharmadhātu* that is fundamentally unborn.
This syllable can give rise to all phenomena; if one abandons the natural wisdom of the *A* syllable, then...
Because no wholesome dharmas can arise [within it], and because its intrinsic nature is pure like space, being free from all grasping, contention, and conceptual proliferation, it is said:
"This precept is now precisely equality," and so forth.

[Commentary]: Regarding the reference to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, Aṅgulimāla, and so forth, the present citation of Aṅgulimāla is intended to explain and establish the meaning of "skillful means" (*upāya*).
That sūtra states: "At that time, the World-Honored One spoke a verse to Aṅgulimāla, saying:
'Come, Aṅgulimāla! Go forth and receive the Three Refuges. Then Aṅgulimāla replied with a verse, saying: 'This vehicle is the Mahāyāna.'"
It is taught that unimpeded wisdom is the One Vehicle, the One Refuge, and the Buddha is the ultimate reliance.
That the Dharma and the Sangha of bhikṣus are of one meaning refers to the Tathāgata’s wondrous Dharma-body; here, the Tathāgata is the Sangha.
These two—the Dharma and the Sangha of bhikṣus—are the provisional reliance, whereas the Tathāgata is the ultimate reliance. Therefore, today I...

Taking refuge in the Tathāgata among all objects of refuge—the Tathāgata is the true refuge—is like one who desires to eat asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) but instead takes what is false while discarding the real, seeking the counterfeit rather than the genuine; such a person brings no benefit to themselves or others, and even a thousand physicians cannot save such a fool.
Thus, having abandoned the one true refuge, they practice the refuge of expedient means; such are the masses of fools mentioned previously.
"Even a thousand Buddhas cannot save you," the Buddha said, "and so forth, until he told Aṅgulimāla:
'You must receive and uphold the precept against taking life. Aṅgulimāla replied with a verse: 'I can certainly not now receive and uphold the precept against killing.
I shall always receive and uphold the severing of the lives of sentient beings. As for those called "sentient beings," they are the immeasurable afflictions; if one can always [sever them]...'"
"Harming others is what is called 'maintaining the precept against killing,' and so forth.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the Śrāvakas have the four grave prohibitions (*caturmahāpatti*) and so on," this *sthūlātyaya* is translated as "great offense" (*mahāpatti*) or "coarse evil.
It is subsumed under the third of the seven categories of offenses (*saptanikāya*). Its substance encompasses both light and heavy degrees; the same applies here to killing, stealing, and the like.
If, within the samaya precepts, one commits the fourth offense— namely, acting to the detriment of all sentient beings—
it is said to belong to the category of grave offenses; however, if within this context one speaks of a precept involving skillful means, it belongs to the category of light offenses,
being merely a sthūlātyaya and not an extremely grave one.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "if one abandons the letter A," etc.: the letter A is the bodhicitta.
Because of bodhicitta, there exist the letter A, great compassion, the stages (*bhūmi*), the *pāramitās*, and so forth—the very roots for attaining Buddhahood.
If one abandons these, the roots for attaining Buddhahood are severed, and thus all myriad virtues cannot arise; hence it is said, "if one abandons the letter A," etc.
[Commentary: Regarding the sixth point, "one should not [be stingy with the Dharma]," etc.:
Is this identical to or different from the third of the four grave precepts (catvāraḥ pārājikā dharmāḥ) within the three samādhis? Although the names are the same, their scope is vastly different.

While in that [context] one must not be stingy regarding any dharma, one must nevertheless observe that the teaching does not miss the capacity of the recipient; thus, it is broader than the present case.

[Sūtra]: "I now expound the various paths," and so forth. This means that the Buddha, for the sake of Vajrapāṇi, specifically expounds the various paths—ranging from those of the two vehicles up to those of worldly people—as well as the path of the single, unique dharmadhātu-tathatā (suchness) therein;
therefore, it says, "I now expound," and so forth.

[Commentary: "It is like having no seed," etc., refutes the heterodox (tīrthika) view of inequality. This means that heterodox practitioners conceive of a *puruṣa* (ātman) as the producer of all things;
because they do not understand the Buddha’s Dharma of correct causes and conditions, this is a view of inequality.
It is like worldly flowers and fruits existing without seeds—there would be nothing at all, such as the son of a barren woman. This is like a person [who claims such a thing exists].

This means that for a barren woman to give birth to two children, one white and one black—when she originally had no children at all—to further distinguish them as white and black is a contradiction of her own words.
It is also like someone saying, "I can now bind empty flowers into a garland";
this too is false speech. Therefore, apart from a true cause, it is impossible for there to be a fruit.

[Commentary: Furthermore, those who cling to views such as annihilationism (*uccheda*) and eternalism (*śāśvata*)—namely, the two views of annihilationism and eternalism—all do so because they have not yet understood the dharma of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
However, within the Buddha-dharma, because one knows that things exist through causes and conditions, one is free from the view of non-existence;

and because one contemplates the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), the view of existence does not arise. If one thoroughly understands the meaning of existence and non-existence in this way...
If one does not fall into the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism, then the principle of cause and effect is established.
[Commentary] "Like insects eating wood," etc., means that names such as the "ten wholesome paths" used by non-Buddhists and others are confused with those of our own Buddha-dharma.
It is like insects eating wood and accidentally forming characters; those insects have never made any discrimination as to whether it is a character or not. It is the same for those non-Buddhists.

The Way merely involves the successive transmission and observance of this Dharma from remote antiquity; because it does not recognize the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane, it cannot be compared [to the Bodhisattva path].
[Commentary: "Entering into the equality of all things" means that this Bodhisattva enters the letter *A*, which is the fundamental equality of all things.
Because one practices this Dharma-gate of the Single Path within the non-arising *dharmadhātu*, it cannot be equated with the manifest teachings of the permanent [Buddha]. [Commentary:
Regarding the statement that "the Sanskrit term for 'eye' has two names," etc.: first, it is said that *netra* corresponds to the "Eye of Compassion" (*maitrī-netra*); second, it is said...
Because the eyes of those who have been struck down immediately become filled with mutual compassion, it is called "Brahma-voice" (*brahma-svara*) and so forth.
[Commentary] Regarding the prior mention of "non-killing" and so forth: this refers to the relinquishing of all weapons and staves, etc.; the "etc.

includes such things as praising and rejoicing in oneself and others. As for the term "killing-dharma," the *Fanwang-jing shu* (Commentary on the Brahma Net Sutra) states: "Dharma means a rule or standard (*vidhi*), like a ship that has sunk."

The conditions for reducing the number of cooking hearths and so forth refer to external circumstances, which include both general and specific factors. The specific factors consist of poverty, forced labor, customs, entertainment, and the like;

the general factors consist of bows and arrows, swords and halberds, up to falcons and dogs, as well as hands and feet. As for their causes, they pertain to the internal mind and are connected to the three poisons:

greed serves as the cause for killing and harming for the sake of profit; hatred serves as the cause for retaliating against an enemy with enmity; and delusion [serves as the cause]... [text truncated].

Regarding the consciousness of sin and merit, whether through play or preference, delusion (*moha*) serves as the cause; thus, all acts of killing performed apart from greed (*lobha*) and hatred (*dveṣa*) have delusion as their cause.
"Karma" refers to the act of killing itself, which is the actual performance.

Whether this is done for the sake of one's own prosperity or for the benefit of one's family—whether it extends upward or is restricted downward—one can understand this by careful reflection. However, only when the [three factors] are complete does this karma become fully established.

This is because [the precept] would not be fulfilled if it were lacking; the phrase "even those with form" is used because it encompasses all sentient beings, which differs from the Hinayana view where harming animals is considered light while harming humans is grave. Since Buddha-nature is equal and there are none who are not one's parents, it says "those with form.
The phrase "forever having no intent to harm" refers to deeply guarding the mental ground (manas).

[Commentary: "One should also act as a cause and condition for them" means that although this bodhisattva maintains the precepts through skillful means such that—even regarding what is prohibited in the sutras down to the smallest detail, including not taking even a blade of grass or a thread—one nevertheless acts as a cause and condition for all those who are stingy and miserly to experience deprivation.
"Deprivation" (乏) refers to lack; "destitution" (匱) refers to being shut off. If one does not cultivate [these practices]...
The act of giving lacks the seeds for the fruition of future results; fearing that such conditions for deprivation might come to pass,
the Bodhisattva, out of compassion for them, employs skillful means to take [the goods] away, thereby destroying the causes and conditions of their deprivation, as explained in detail below.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "However, there are briefly nine kinds of afflictive and harmful minds," this clarifies the conditions that give rise to killing.
That is to say, with respect to a single individual, nine types of afflictive and harmful minds are described: 1. Concerning oneself:

when another person initiates various conditions of affliction and harm toward one's own self, one gives rise to resentment and subsequently carries out the act of killing. 2. Concerning those who are evil to me, as well as my virtuous friends... [and so forth].
"Malicious" (āghāta) refers to harboring resentment. There are three types: first, toward those who are my virtuous friends, you harbor resentment and give rise to anger and harm;

second, toward those who are my enemies, you instead show a pleasant face while harboring anger and harm; third, [toward those who are neutral]. Because these three conditions apply across the three periods of time, they constitute nine types;
therefore it is said that there are briefly nine kinds of the mind of malice and harm.
[Commentary: However, profound contemplation is identical to being fundamentally endowed with the precepts.

When a Bodhisattva maintains the precepts through skillful means solely for the sake of accomplishing the cause of Bodhi, without grasping at subject or object, this is the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) precept.
If one contemplates the meaning herein through the phrase "A" as the primordial non-arising, it is the non-existence of the secret and inconceivable dependent origination.
This is for the sake of the precepts.
[Commentary: As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* within the section on the *Śīla-pāramitā*, that treatise says:

"If one has a wife of one's own who is pregnant or nursing an infant, and one engages in sexual intercourse by an improper path, such an act is called sexual misconduct. Question: A person guards another person...

If one who guards against the dharma of anger violates the dharma, they should be called a person of sexual misconduct. [Objection: One has one's own wife; why would this constitute misconduct? [Answer:

Since they have already received the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*), they have fallen within the scope of the dharma. Although she was originally their wife, she is no longer under their own control once the time of receiving the precepts has passed;
thus, it is not the guarding of what belongs to oneself. Furthermore, as for a pregnant woman, because her body is heavy, she feels weary of her former habits, and moreover—

When one commits sexual misconduct with a woman who is pregnant or nursing, her milk will dry up; furthermore, because the mind is attached to lustful desire and no longer protects the child, it is an improper act.
Since it is not the female organ and the woman’s heart does not find pleasure in it, yet she is forced by irrational means, it is called sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*) and so forth.

[Commentary]: However, there are also cases where one employs coarse speech as a skillful means (*upāya*). For example, when the Tripiṭaka Master W无畏 (Wuwei) first arrived from India at the Xuanzong era, he said to [the Emperor]:
"The Master has traveled from afar; you must be weary. In which direction do you wish to rest? The Tripiṭaka Master replied:
"When I was in the Western Heaven (India), I often heard that the Vinaya is being proclaimed at the Ximing Monastery in the Great Tang."

The Master, who was foremost in upholding the Vinaya, wished to go and rely upon Xuanzong; Xuanzong consented. He proclaimed the prohibitions and precepts of the Vinaya with such rigorous austerity that his pure and refined practice of *brahmacarya* was unsurpassed.
However, the Tripitaka Master [Daoxuan] drank wine and ate meat, and his conduct and speech were coarse and casual.

He often became intoxicated and engaged in noisy quarrels, defiling the mats and bedding. Xuanzong could not bear this. One night, while Xuanzong was picking lice from his body, he suddenly threw them to the ground.
The Tripitaka Master, half-intoxicated, called out with a loud voice, "Vinaya Master! Vinaya Master! Have you killed a Son of the Buddha?
Only when Xuanlù realized he was an extraordinary man did he straighten his robes, pay homage, and serve him as a disciple; this was his skillful means (41).
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāvairocana Sūtra: An Elucidation of the Secret*, Scroll Nine.
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāvairocana Sūtra: An Elucidation of the Secret*, Scroll Ten.
Written by Chonglu Daifu Jianjiao Taibao Xingchong at Yuanfu Temple in Yanjing.
Composed by the Monk Jueyuan, who received the purple robe and the title of Grand Master for the Secretariat of the State Preceptor.
[Commentary] Regarding the causal narrative of the jackal and the lion, as stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*: The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying, "Listen, monks!
In ancient times there were two evil beasts that were companions; one was named Good-Tusked Lion (*Śubhadanta-siṃha*), and the other was named Good-Pouncing (*Subhañjana*)."
While the tiger was hunting various deer day and night, there was a jackal who followed behind those two beasts to eat their remains in order to sustain its own life.
At that time, the jackal secretly thought to itself: "I cannot continue following these two for long;
by what skillful means can I cause discord between them so that they will no longer stay together? Then the jackal...
He went to the lion Śaṅkha and spoke to him thus: "O Śaṅkha, O well-pouncing tiger, you have such words as these:
'My birthplace is superior, my lineage is superior, my physical form is superior, and your strength and power are inferior to mine. Why is this?
Because day after day I obtain excellent and delicious food, while you, O lion Śaṅkha, pursue me from behind and sustain your own life by eating the remains of my meat."
He spoke in verse: "As for form, color, and the great strength born thereof, even the excellent tusked one cannot match it;
thus has the excellent tusked one been described. Then the excellent tusked one asked the jackal, "By what means did you come to know this?
He replied, "When you two beasts gather in one place and see each other, you will know for yourselves. At that time, having spoken secretly to the excellent tusked one, the jackal departed.
The tiger spoke well, saying, "Do you know what is not good? My fangs are such as these.
He continued, "As for my lineage and place of birth, both are superior to yours, and my strength and power are likewise superior. Why is this?

I always eat choice meat, whereas you, O tiger who strikes well, must sustain your life by eating the remains of my leftovers. At that time, he spoke a verse: "Regarding physical form, birth, and lineage..."
"Though he possesses great strength and is superior, he cannot strike well; such is the description of a 'well-striking' [animal]. Thus it was said. Suṣeṇa asked, "By what means do you know this?
He replied, "When you two beasts gather together in one place and see one another, you will know for yourselves.
Later, when the two beasts gathered together in one place and glared at each other with angry eyes, Suṣeṇa the lion then thought to himself: "I..."
"Without even asking, he has already struck me first. At that time, the lion Sudaṃṣṭra spoke this verse to the tiger Suprahāra:
"In form, color, birth, and great strength, you are indeed superior; Sudaṃṣṭra is not my equal. Is it truly so? Suprahāra thought to himself:
"This must surely be a jackal trying to incite discord among us. Then the tiger Suprahāra spoke this verse:
He replied to the lion Dantika: "O skillful striker, you do not speak of this physical form or the great strength it produces;
yet you are superior to Dantika, who is not skillful. If one accepts harmful words and believes the mutual speech of others, one's own kinship will be destroyed and one will become an enemy.
If one knows the truth, one should eliminate anger and affliction; now, I am speaking with sincerity."
"I have spoken so that you may obtain benefit for your bodies; now you must skillfully subdue and eliminate this evil friend.
You should kill this jackal who incites strife among us! Thereupon, they hunted down and killed the jackal. At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"If these two beasts, having been destroyed by that [jackal], would not find joy upon meeting one another even when gathered in the same place, how much less could humans, being oppressed by others, find peace?"
"Breaking the mind [so that one] can remain untroubled," etc.
[The *Sū* (Commentary) states: "Regarding 'there is no separate word for desire,' the character 'separate' (*bie*) here is a scribal error; it should likely be the character 'benefit' (*li*).
Therefore, the *Sū* below says: 'Although one acts without benefit, by means of this lack of benefit, one eliminates those matters that are without benefit,' and so forth."
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that the maiden Sudarśanā is precisely this [person].

[Commentary: "This is the causal condition for non-greed" concludes the precept of non-greed. Question: In the previous cases of killing, stealing, and so forth, all clarify the preparatory stages (*prayoga*);
why is it not so here? Answer: Because greed is broad in scope, as is the case with the differences found within the category of non-killing.
Regarding skillful means: it is like a great python that wished to harm five hundred merchants;

for the sake of protecting others, the Bodhisattva, through great compassion, killed the snake, thereby saving it from its karmic retribution and causing it to be reborn in heaven, while the merchants were all spared from the serpent's calamity.
Is this not the arising of desire from within great compassion? This is merely a brief illustration of one aspect; the same can be understood to apply to anger as well.

[Commentary]: Regarding the "two lines" mentioned here that do not explain [the meaning], this refers to the two lines in the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* concerning the precept against anger;
because they are redundant, they are not explained.
[Commentary]: "It should pervade all places" means that pervading both sentient and non-sentient locations is what is meant by "all places.

Regarding non-sentient locations, it is as cited above in the section on the precept against killing: the story of the bhikṣu from the time of Kāśyapa Buddha who was felled by a tree stump, gave rise to anger, and was reborn with the body of a python.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "contemplating these as the true nature (dharmatā) and so forth," it means contemplating all phenomena—whether favorable or adverse, defiled or pure, hostile or friendly—as being the true nature.
Here, "contemplating the true nature" refers specifically to contemplating the ten phrases of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Whenever a practitioner encounters any object, they should apply this contemplation of the phrases; for instance, as in the contemplation of space within this context.
Regarding the timing of the phrase: it refers to contemplating that within emptiness there has never been a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span;
yet, because the mind is deluded and confused, various false views such as "self" and "person" arise. Thus, the second commentary states:
"It is like a person whose mind becomes deluded due to various causes and conditions, such as illness or non-human spirits, and falsely perceives various people within the pure, empty sky."

When the forms and characteristics of things may be either terrifying or objects of attachment, if one recovers the fundamental mind, one knows that such events do not defile the void when they arise, nor do they return to purity when they cease; ultimately, from the very beginning, they neither obstruct the void nor are they different from the void.
Now, when this Bodhisattva is subjected to various kinds of harm by others, he simply regards them in this way.

Since observing them all as being nothing but empty space, one does not give rise to a mind of anger toward others; therefore, it is said that "by means of this, one contemplates their true nature (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "these secondary afflictions (*upakleśa)" and so on, these secondary afflictions specifically refer to harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), crookedness (*śaṭhya*), and flattery (*māyā*), which are to say, wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
"Taking this as the cause, one is then able to emerge"—this line is not a scriptural passage but must be a commentarial gloss.
It was inserted by a scribe at his convenience, just as terms such as *siddham* and others that are not scriptural passages are all treated as commentaries.
Furthermore, it says below: "Because there is a repetition within [the text], it is not explained."
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "following the nine precepts above": among the nine types of precepts mentioned above, each contains the expression "maintaining the precepts.

If one were to reverse this, one should instead place the phrase "should abandon" upon [the prohibitions of] killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and so forth, up to malice;
that is to say, "one should abandon killing living beings," and so on, up to "one should..."
Because of abandoning ill-will, it is said "to pursue [virtue]," and so forth. Regarding the statement that one should speak of "upholding" [the precepts] rather than "not killing" and so on:
if one says "upholding the precept of not killing," this is upholding in accordance with the principle; if one says "upholding the precept of killing," this is upholding through skillful means.
[Commentary: "The absence of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya" refers to the non-existence of the four fruits—srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat.
The phrase "and so forth" (等) includes those of the One Vehicle Bodhisattvas.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "transforming those evils and so forth," the character *zhuan* (to transform) here arises in connection with the two preceding instances of *zhuan*.

This means that while the characteristics of wrong view are harmful, crooked, and deceitful, the power of upholding the precepts now transforms that harm, crookedness, and deceit into non-harm, non-crookedness, and non-deceit;
therefore, it is called "transformation."
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "like that skilled physician" and so forth, it is as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
"Good son, suppose there is a king who falls ill and passes away. The crown prince is young and immature, not yet capable of succeeding him.
There is a *caṇḍāla* who possesses abundant wealth and immeasurable riches, and has many kinsmen; relying on his own strength, he waits for the kingdom’s vulnerability and seizes the throne to rule."
Not long after [the king] had transformed the realm, the householders, lay devotees, brahmins, and others perished; they fled far away to seek refuge in other kingdoms.
Even those who remained did not wish to so much as look upon this king with their eyes.
There were some elders and brahmins who did not leave their native lands, like various trees that die where they grow. The Caṇḍāla king knew this.
As many of his subjects as fled and rebelled were soon pursued, and he dispatched various *caṇḍālas* to patrol and guard the roads.
Furthermore, for seven days, he beat drums and issued a proclamation: "To any brāhmaṇa who can serve me as a consecration master (*abhiṣeka-ācārya*), I shall grant half the kingdom as a reward.
When the brāhmaṇas heard these words, not a single one came forward.
Each of them spoke thus: "How could there ever be one of the Brahmin caste who would perform such an act?

The Caṇḍāla king further spoke: "If not even a single person among the Brahmins will act as my teacher, I shall certainly compel all the Brahmins to dwell, eat, and sleep with the Caṇḍālas, and to share their occupations and livelihoods. If there is anyone able to come [to receive the consecration]..."
"The claim that I shall share half the kingdom with you is not false; it was brought about by the power of my incantations.
Furthermore, the exquisite nectar of immortality found in the Heaven of the Thirty-three Gods shall likewise be shared and consumed by us both.
At that time, there was the son of a Brahmin, in the prime of his youth, who practiced pure conduct, wore long hair as his mark, and was well-versed in incantations.
He went to the king's presence and said, "Great King, whatever you command me to do, I am fully capable of performing.
At that time, the great king’s heart was filled with joy, and he accepted this youth as his consecration preceptor (*abhiṣeka-ācārya*).
When the other brahmins heard of this matter, they all became incensed and rebuked the youth, saying, "You who are a brahmin, how can you act as a *caṇḍāla* preceptor?"
At that time, the king immediately divided half of his kingdom with the youth, and they ruled the realm together for a long period.
Then the youth said to the king, "I have renounced the life of a householder to serve as the king's preceptor;
I have taught the Great King secret and profound mantras, yet the Great King still does not show me affection. The king replied, "How could I do so now?"
"Have you not been intimate with me? The youth replied, "The immortal elixir belonging to the former king has not yet been consumed by us together.
The King said, "Excellent, excellent! Great Master, I truly did not know this. If you require it, I pray that you take it with you.
At these words, the youth immediately took it and returned home, where he invited the great ministers to consume it together.
When the ministers had finished eating, they said together to the king, "How wonderful! Our Great Master possesses this nectar of immortality.
Once the king knew this, he spoke to his teacher, saying, "Why does the Great Master alone and the ministers consume the nectar, while no portion is shared with me?
At that time, the youth further gave the king some other medicine mixed with poison and instructed him to take it.
Once the king had taken the medicine, after a short while it took effect; he became dazed and fell to the ground, unconscious, like one who is dead.
At that time, the youth established his former heir apparent as king once more and spoke these words:
"The Lion Throne is, by law, not for a *caṇḍāla* to ascend. From ancient times until now, I have never heard of nor seen a member of the *caṇḍāla* caste [occupying it]."
"To rule as a king like a *caṇḍāla* who governs the realm and the people is impossible. You should now return and succeed to the former king to govern the realm with the True Dharma.
At that time, after the youth had administered the treatment, he gave an antidote to the *caṇḍāla* to cause him to regain consciousness.
Once he had regained consciousness, he drove him out of the kingdom. At that time, the youth—
"Even though he has done this, he still does not lose his status as a Brahmin.

When other householders and Brahmins hear of what he has done, they will exclaim that it is unprecedented and praise him, saying: 'Excellent, excellent! O worthy one, you have skillfully driven away the Caṇḍāla king.
Son of good family, after my parinirvāṇa, the bodhisattvas who protect and uphold the True Dharma shall likewise [do so]."
Furthermore, by means of such skillful power, he associates with those who are monks in name only and have broken the precepts— those who accept and store all manner of impure things—
and shares in their activities. At that time, if a bodhisattva sees someone who, despite having committed many transgressions, is capable of disciplining evil bhikṣus who violate the prohibitions,
he shall go to that person's location, pay respectful homage, and provide the four types of offerings, including scriptures and requisites.
He shall offer all things to the preceptor as if he himself possessed nothing, and for this purpose, he must skillfully seek and obtain from various donors the eight kinds of impure items.
Why is this? It is because this person acts to discipline wicked bhikṣus, just as that boy drove away the caṇḍālas; at that time, although the bodhisattva shows respect, [he does so for this reason].
One who pays homage to such a person incurs no fault whatsoever, even if they accept and keep the eight kinds of impure things.

Why is this? It is because this bodhisattva, desiring to expel and discipline wicked bhikṣus so that the pure Saṃgha may dwell in peace and security, and in order to propagate the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras for the benefit of all devas and humans—good son, it is for these reasons.

It is because, in the sutras, I have spoken these two verses so that all bodhisattvas may together praise those who protect the Dharma, just as that householder and brahmin praised the youth, saying, "Excellent, excellent! A bodhisattva who protects the Dharma should indeed act in this way.
Yet, if someone sees one who protects the Dharma engaging in the same affairs as those who violate the precepts, [they will not understand].

Regarding the statement that those who speak of karma as having faults should know that such persons will themselves receive its calamity, whereas those who protect the Dharma truly have no fault, etc.:
[The Commentary] states that "the ten lines missing herein" refers to the seven lines of scripture found below in this very chapter.

The tenth consists of seven characters, referring to these seven lines of scripture which state that the four grave precepts (*catur-guru-dharma*) are precisely the *samaya* precepts within the *Maṇḍala* chapter.
Regarding the term "omitted" (*k'ien*): in the Sanskrit manuscript, there was [a passage] that should have been translated;
however, because it appeared redundant, it was excised. Thus, it is called "omitted. What has now been added differs slightly from the original text. Among those [precepts], the first precept states:
"One should not abandon the true Dharma. Herein, what is called "slandering all dharmas" refers to this. Furthermore, the following two and a half lines differ from that [preceding] section;
this is precisely their difference.

[Sūtra] Regarding the statement "the chapter on the arising of the hundred syllables," etc.: "to speak" (śās) means to proclaim, which is to say, the one who speaks. "The hundred syllables" refers to the characters (*akṣara*).

Because there are one hundred, it is named by including the number; "arising" (*jāta*) has the meaning of being produced or flowing forth. This means that these one hundred syllables arise from the *dharmadhātu*;
the *dharmadhātu* is the producer (the "dark" syllable), while the one hundred syllables are the produced. Alternatively, the one hundred syllables may be mutually produced.

Furthermore, it is said that the one hundred syllables are the signifiers (*vācaka*), while their arising is the signified (*vācya*). In this case, the compound is analyzed as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) based on its locus.
From this point downward, the intended meaning follows the topical outline (*kośa*); I do not wish to elaborate on the specific references.
[Commentary]: Regarding the further inquiry into the meaning of the "seat" (*āsana*), it means that the meaning of this seat is precisely the *A* syllable mantra.

This *A* syllable is the Vajrāsana; although it is not explicitly stated in the sutra, according to the principles of the meaning, it should be understood as such through the practice of this *A* syllable mantra.
One who contemplates these syllables of samādhi as being originally unarisen and abides therein—therefore, the letter A is called the "seat.
Thus, the *Siddhyabhinirhāra-parivarta* states: "At the time of the great vajra ground-limit, through the empowerment of the lower body, this dharma is taught;
therefore, the most excellent letter A appears as the seat of enlightenment, identical to the great Indra-wheel."
Contemplating all things is termed the "yoga-seat" (*yogāsana*) and so forth; this refers precisely to taking the syllable *A* as the seat.
Alternatively, one may designate the syllable *Āṃ* as the seat, for this syllable *Āṃ* is itself the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
As previously cited from the *Lotus Sūtra*, "all dharmas being empty is the seat. Thus, the meaning of "seat" is further questioned. Furthermore—
These three samādhis are the locus upon which all phenomena rely; therefore, they are termed "the meaning of the seat. [The Commentary] states:
"The perfection of the three dharmas" means that by abiding in this seat, one is able to fully accomplish the three types of dharmas—namely, the principle, the practice, and the fruit.
These are: *ā*, *a*, and *am*. *Ā* is the mind of bodhicitta; *a* is great compassion; and *am* is... [direction/method].
This is indeed the result.

[Commentary]: If one were to translate this as "emitting light" (fangguang) and so forth—regarding this character *āṃ* (*an*), if it is translated according to its meaning as "emitting light," it is as stated in the following commentary:
"The wisdom-light of this mantra is able to destroy all darkness of ignorance, just like the Great Sun."
When [the light] emerges, it spontaneously dispels darkness for all sentient beings, instantly eliminating all the darkness of ignorance;

yet, although this translation captures one aspect of the principle, it is not exhaustive. If it were translated as "pervasive emergence" (biànchū), then both the practice and the fruit would be attained.
As the sub-commentary states: "By means of this gateway of mantras, I manifest forms universally according to their respective types."

The body pervades the entire Dharma-realm; according to the various kinds of sentient beings, this Body of Universal Delightful Appearance can simultaneously manifest its form everywhere, appearing in accordance with their mental inclinations.
For this reason, it is said that "greatly" (dà) signifies the sense of universal manifestation.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "among all types," this expression does not appear in the sutra text; it should instead be taken from the passage below.
Thus, the term "all types" (*sarvākāra*) ought to be annotated as applying to both instances. Let the reader examine this in detail.
[Commentary: Now, regarding that which is the most central within this wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*), this wheel of syllables consists of three parts:
first, one places the syllable *Aṃ*, the king of mantras, within the inner mind;
second, outside the syllable *Aṃ*, one places the four wheels of the hundred syllables, such as *Ka* (with the vowel *ā*) and *Kha*; and third, outside the four wheels, one places *I*.
(Section on the Upper) These twelve syllables constitute the third section; in their general structure, they are largely identical to the "Chapter on the Upper Wheel.
Herein, the statement that "the next outer wheel has twelve syllables" is intended to indicate a hidden meaning (*saṃdhyābhāṣita*):
having first placed the syllable *AṂ* in the first section, one then places the twelve syllables in the third section, which is the next outer [circle], and subsequently [places them] in the second.
The hundred syllables are arranged in sequence as follows: the second section is not indicated; the outer single wheel is divided into three enclosures (*maṇḍala*).
First, place the Principal Deity within the central womb as the first enclosure.
Next, place the assembly of various Bodhisattvas on the outside as the second enclosure. Finally, place the assembly of Śākyamuni on the outermost perimeter as the third enclosure.
If the three maṇḍalas are treated as the five wheels (*pañcacakra*), there are twenty-five syllables within each wheel, totaling one hundred and twenty-five syllables for all five wheels.
Thus, although the title designates "five wheels," it actually reveals four [wheels] to indicate a hidden meaning (*saṃdhāya*).
As for that hidden meaning: although four wheels are enumerated, the significance of the five wheels is complete; this refers to the first short vowel.
The first, the *A* syllable wheel, is named the Bodhicitta Wheel; the second, the long *Ā* syllable wheel, is named the Great Compassion Practice Wheel;

the third, the *Am* syllable wheel, is named the Great Emptiness Wheel; and the fourth, the *Aḥ* syllable wheel, signifies that once Great Emptiness is realized, all manifold practices cease, returning to the origin and source—this is named the Nirvāṇa Wheel.
Furthermore, there is a fifth, the long *Aḥ* syllable wheel, which refers to having already...

The manifestation of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) through skillful means (*upāya*), triggered by the conditions of sentient beings seeking to realize *nirvāṇa*, is called the wheel of skillful means (*upāyacakra*). Thus, among these five wheels:
the second, Great Compassion, is the practice and the cause; the third, Great Emptiness, is the realization and the fruit.

Because cause and fruit are mutually inclusive, although four are mentioned, since the four and five wheels are not lacking, they constitute the hundred syllables, just as with the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*).

This is further clarified within the chapter. Furthermore, according to the commentary (*ṭīkā*), if one follows the interpretation of another master, one takes the twenty syllables—*oṃ āḥ hūṃ haḥ hoḥ haṃ kṣaḥ raḥ laḥ vaḥ yaḥ maḥ bhaḥ baḥ phaḥ paḥ ṭaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭaḥ ḍhaḍaḥ ṇaḥ naḥ maḥ*—as being outside [the central circle], while the twelve syllables *i* and so forth are arranged together within the circle.

If one does not require the mutual inclusion of cause and effect, then the five wheels (*pañcacakra*) are complete. Therefore, it says: "If one constructs the five wheels... up to "further questioning," etc. Now.
The diagram is provided for your reference so that it may be easily understood. Regarding the statement in the *Tri-vihāra-sūtra*: "First, draw the Principal Deity;

second, draw Śākyamuni"—this does not mean that Śākyamuni is to be drawn within the second court (*vihāra*); rather, this is an intentional, esoteric meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*). As for the statement regarding the arrangement of the hundred syllables:
it refers to taking the letters *ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa* from the first wheel.
The twenty-five syllables of these five groups—*ja*, *ṣa*, *ja*, *raṅ*, *ṭha*, *ta*, *na*, *da*, *na*, *ḍa*, *na*, *pa*, *pha*, *ma*, *ba*, *maṅ*—are all short vowels.
"Short vowels" refers to those accompanied by the *udātta* (high) or *udāttatara* (extra-high) accents; therefore, they are called short vowels.

First is the wheel of bodhicitta. Next, take each of the five classes of letters and add a lateral stroke—namely, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, and so forth—to form the long vowels; this is the second wheel, the wheel of great compassion.
"Long" here refers to those vowels bearing the level (*udātta*) or departing (*svarita*) accents. Next, place a bindu (dot) above each of the aforementioned five classes of letters.
*Kam, cham, chan, chan* (level tone) constitutes the third wheel of skillful means; next, *ja, kya, tsa, tra, pa*, etc.,
all pronounced with short vowels and rapid intonation, constitute the fourth wheel of nirvāṇa,
which is the wheel of the hundred-syllable mantra.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "If one constructs five layers of cloth and further asks," etc., the current commentary indicates that the construction of the five-layered explanation is intended as four wheels to prompt further inquiry;
this refers to the hundred characters of the chapter on the Wheel of Characters (*Akṣaracakra*).

【Sūtra】 Regarding the "Chapter on the Correspondence with the Fruit of the Hundred Syllables": "Hundred syllables" is as explained above. "Fruit" refers to the various types of *siddhi* (accomplishments) obtained;
these are designated as "fruits" because they correspond to their respective causes. Since these are the fruits of the hundred syllables, "correspondence" is as explained above:
it takes meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence, meaning that this concentration and wisdom are able to correspond with the fruit of the hundred syllables.
Because these are the corresponding fruits of the hundred syllables, they are explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.
[Commentary] "At that time, Vairocana," etc., refers to the citation of the sūtra. The sūtra contains only four lines, yet the commentary extracts them separately based on the Sanskrit original.
There have been many such instances where the Tripitaka Master passed away before the matter could be fully investigated and refined; this is one of them.

[Commentary]: Regarding the body of Amoghadarśin: since Śākyamuni’s appearance in the world ensures that none among those of the three vehicles or five natures fail to receive benefit, he is identical to a "Great Man who sees [the truth]";
it is for this reason that he is given this name.
[Commentary]: Regarding the term "extraordinary" (*śu yi*), this word does not appear in the scriptural passage;
it is supplied by the commentary where the scripture states that while space pervades all places, the Tathāgata’s two samayas also pervade all places.
Here, we merely take this partial similarity as a metaphor. However, the body of the Tathāgata’s three samayas is immeasurable.
Because this inconceivable matter cannot be illustrated by the mundane void, it is said to be "in a place distinct from the realm of space.
[Commentary] Examining the meaning of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* regarding the mind, a verse by the Bodhisattva Jñānaketu in that scripture states: "If a person wishes to fully understand..."
"One should contemplate that all Buddhas of the three periods of time and the nature of the dharma-realm are entirely created by the mind alone...
It is like a skilled painter who distributes various colors; though the primary elements from which these diverse colors are derived are without distinction, they falsely manifest as different hues.
Furthermore, it says: 'The mind is like a skilled painter, capable of painting all worlds; the five aggregates are all produced from it; there is no phenomenon that it does not create.'"
The mind and the Buddha are likewise, and sentient beings are no different from the Buddha; one should know that the essence and nature of the Buddha and the mind are both immeasurable and equal.

The Master of the Commentary (Sushu) ordered [the inclusion of] the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* because sentient beings do not understand their own minds; if they were to understand them, they would be called Tathāgatas.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "it is not even within the realm of Bodhisattvas" and so forth:

the adornment of the Tathāgata’s speech, if devoid of the power of his sustaining empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), is not even within the scope of Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage, let alone those in the midst of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, the *Tathāgataguhyamudrā-jñānasūtra* states that the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, while in the midst of the Dharma assembly, desired to know the Buddha-body.
Because of this measure, he commanded Mahāmaudgalyāyana to search for him. Maudgalyāyana ascended as far as the Brahma-heaven, yet he still beheld the Tathāgata as if facing him before his eyes;
the Buddha’s physical demeanor and the sound of his preaching were no different from what they had been originally.

Even when he exhausted his supernormal powers and traveled to other buddha-fields, it was no different than being in the Brahma-heaven. At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, by means of [Maudgalyāyana’s] eyes...

Because even this cannot be fathomed, he went himself to observe; throughout the ten directions, across worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he saw the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma without rising from his seat.
Even when extending to the very limits of the ten directions to the full extent of his power, it was likewise so.
Therefore, these marks of adornment arise from the matrix of the Buddha’s mind-mantra, and not otherwise.
Because the multitude can know it, it is said that "it is not even within the realm of Bodhisattvas," and so forth.
[Commentary] Regarding the "various adornments of the sixty kinds" and so on: as for the various adornments, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, Chapter on the Inconceivable, states:
"The Tathāgata is fully endowed with sixty kinds of vocal sounds; each sound has five hundred branches, and each..."

It is divided into immeasurable hundreds of thousands of pure sounds to serve as its adornment. Regarding the sixty kinds of speech, the tenth *Parivarta* (Chapter) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the "Chapter on the Dedication of Merit," states:
"O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva further dedicates the roots of goodness produced by this gift of Dharma in the following way:
namely, to cause all sentient beings to obtain pure and wondrous voices, to obtain gentle [voices], and so forth."
Regarding the phrase "possessing the celestial drum-like voice and so forth," this refers to the sixty-four kinds of vocal qualities.
As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "Furthermore, there are places where it is taught that there are sixty-four sounds. These are based on the eight grammatical cases (*kāraka*), namely:

substance (*svabhāva*), object (*karman*), instrument (*karaṇa*), beneficiary (*sampradāna*), point of departure (*apādāna*), locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and vocative (*saṃbodhana*). Each of these eight cases possesses eight virtues, namely: the harmonious sound, the soft and gentle sound, the clear... [and so forth].
The sounds are fully understood and easy to comprehend; the sounds are free from error, free from feebleness, vast, and profound.
Since there are eight sets of eight, there are sixty-four kinds; therefore, it is said that they are "adorned with various [qualities]," and so forth.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "as in the 'Chapter on the Purification of the Six Senses' (*Ṣaḍindriyaviśuddhiparivarta*) and so forth," although it mentions the six senses, it specifically takes up the excellence of the tongue.
The words "even by means of speech" refer to the verses concerning the faculty of the tongue from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "not merely the two types of bodhi," etc.: the dharma-dhātu consists of immeasurable *bodhi* and so forth that pervade the entire threefold maṇḍala.

From Vairocana in the central womb downward to the outer precincts, including non-human beings and other classes, there are immeasurable retinues of *bodhi* corresponding to each respective category, all of which are omnipresent.
Why is this? Because they are all the dharma-dhātu; therefore, it is said: "not merely."
First. [Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "the eightfold form cultivates the bodhisattva path," the "eightfold form" refers to the eight aspects (*aṣṭākāra*).

This means that those who enter this gate of the empowerment of great wisdom and abide in the lineage of the Buddhas attain the four kinds of immeasurables; because they have attained these four immeasurables, [they cultivate the bodhisattva path].
That is to say, they are able to manifest in accordance with conditions to reach sentient beings according to their faculties; these manifestations are likewise immeasurable, namely:

attaining equal and perfect enlightenment, displaying the ten powers, subduing Māra, uttering the lion’s roar, and so forth; as well as cultivating the bodhisattva path, manifesting the eight phases [of a Buddha's life], and performing the various deeds of a Buddha.
The sub-commentary states: "Or it may indicate his superior practice of the bodhisattva path, the eight phases of attaining Buddhahood, and the events of his previous births (*jātaka*)."
Because they are equal, immeasurable, and boundless, they are called the "eight colors," and so forth.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "knowing that the mind is immeasurable, etc.": the practitioner of the mantra path (mantra-yogin), by relying on the hundred-syllable wheel (*śatākṣara-cakra*) and entering the gate of empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), is born into the family of the Buddha;
that is, they abide within the lineage (*gotra*) of the Bodhisattvas. Therefore, they immediately know that the mind is [immeasurable].
"Equality of measure" means knowing that the syllable *Aṃ* is the heart of all mantras; this is called "knowing the immeasurability of the heart.
Because one knows the heart is immeasurable through the syllable *Aṃ*, one knows that the bodies such as *Akā* are also immeasurable.
Because one knows the bodies such as *Akā* are immeasurable, one knows that the wisdom of the "long *Akā*" (the wisdom of *Ā*) is immeasurable. Because one knows [the long *Ā*]...

Because the wisdom of *a* and so forth is immeasurable, one knows that the syllable *aṃ* (the letter *a* with the bindu of space added) is immeasurable like space; the reason for this will be explained below.
[Commentary: "That is to say, attaining perfect enlightenment" means that when the practitioner attains the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), they have thereby attained [enlightenment].
The Perfectly Awakened One is the transformation of the syllable *Aṃ*; that is, he possesses the long *A* syllable wheel of the ten powers.
He subdues the four Māras through the *E* syllable wheel; thus, he is able to let out the fearless lion’s roar by means of the long *O* syllable wheel of skillful means.
Within this, the implicit and mutual explanations may be fully understood through careful investigation.

[Sūtra] Regarding "the accomplishment of the hundred-syllable position" (*śatākṣara-pada-siddhi*): the "hundred syllables" are as explained above. "Position" (*pada*) refers to the locus, which is the wheel of syllables (*akṣara-cakra*).
This wheel of syllables may consist of three layers or five layers, and all such arrangements are termed "positions.

The "position of the hundred syllables" (*śatākṣara-pada*) can be interpreted in two ways—as the substratum (*ādhāra*) or as the agent (*adhikaraṇa*)—and both are valid. That is to say, the practitioner who achieves accomplishment relies upon this.
When one contemplates the practice and is able to accomplish that stage, one is then able to be designated by the name derived from the stage that has been accomplished;
this is the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound for the "accomplishment of the hundred-syllable stage.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bhagavān, etc.: these thirteen lines of verse answer the questions posed previously in sequence.
The four and a half verses answer the question "Who can know? from the perspective of the capacity for knowing;
these three and a half verses answer the question regarding arising from the eternal and constant, both internally and externally; and the five verses answer the question regarding the locus.
[Commentary: Regarding "this flower pedestal" and so forth: in the practice of yoga, the practitioner contemplates their own mind as being identical to an eight-petaled lotus.
This flower is perfectly complete, radiant, and pure; there is nothing in the world that can serve as its analogue, save for the partial similarity of a round mirror.
Thus, it is taken as a metaphor. For example, just as a clear mirror contains light within it and is capable of producing [reflections] therein...
Although various forms and colors appear [in an ordinary mirror], there are things it does not illuminate, nor can it universally manifest everything; the mirror of the pure mind is not like this.
The mirror that perfectly manifests the *dharmadhātu* and universally illumines the worlds of the ten directions—how could such a thing be adequately compared [to an ordinary mirror]?
It is intended merely to enable the practitioner to grasp the meaning while forgetting the words; hence it says, "this flower pedestal," and so forth.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "as above in the yoga methods," "as above" refers to the preceding categories such as the *yoga-saṃprayukta* (correspondence), which are here further explained.
This passage answers the question concerning the place of origin of the mantra; that place of origin is the state of the mind (*citta-pada*).
To facilitate easy understanding for others, it is illustrated by the metaphor of a round mirror; within this round mirror, one contemplates the King of One-Syllable Mantras.

If one attains correspondence, one immediately beholds the deity; for the deity possesses the forms of many Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, those of the Two Vehicles, and the eight classes of beings, as well as distinct expressions of anger or joy, laughter, various colors such as blue and yellow, male and female forms, and hand gestures (*mudrā*).

Therefore, one should investigate and inquire [into these matters], as the verse in the "Chapter on the Accomplishment of *Siddhi*" states: "The locus of the mind of the Mahāsattva is called the maṇḍala; it is the [source of] all mantras."

When one realizes the state of mind and attains the fruit, all conceptual discriminations arise from the *manas*. To distinguish between white, yellow, red, and so forth—all these arise from the mind.
When a mantra abides in this state, it can bestow vast fruits (that is, the manifestation of the *iṣṭadevatā*).
One should contemplate that lotus location, where eight petals and filaments unfold upon the flower pedestal; the gate of the letter *A* radiates light that pervades everywhere, profound.
Abiding within the circular mirror, one manifests responses in all directions; even by knowing that the nature of the mind is thus, one dwells in the practice of mantra.
The general meaning herein is to cause the practitioner to realize that one’s own mind is itself the locus of mantra;
apart from this locus of mind, there is no other dharma. This mind is the *khaṇḍaroha* mind; by knowing this mind, one immediately—

By attaining the essence of the single-syllable mantra, one realizes that through the attainment of this mantra-essence, one directly perceives the distinct characteristics of oneself as the deity (iṣṭadevatā).
These distinct characteristics do not transcend the essence of the single-syllable mantra;

for just as rivers flow in competition yet their source in Kunlun remains serene, and as Mount Song and Mount Hua vie for height yet the earth upon which they rest remains level, it is said to be "like" this.
Superior. [Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "because it is free from all marks," there are many gateways for this contemplation that is free from marks, according to the differences in the teachings.
Within this present context as well, one must realize its essence; when the meaning is grasped, it is concise and easy to apply, conforming to the mind of the practitioner.
When you see the *iṣṭadevatā* within the perfectly luminous [state], do not give rise to attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*); rather, contemplate it through the analogy of a reflection.

This is the fourth [analogy] among the ten conditions for dependent origination, namely the analogy of a mirror-image and the seventh, the analogy of the moon in water. When contemplating within the gateway of syllables (*akṣaramukha*), one should contemplate the syllable *ca*.
"Ca" signifies that all phenomena are like reflections and are unobtainable; in reality, each and every [phenomenon] is thus.
All letter-gates (*akṣaramukha*) are capable of acting as antidotes; however, because they are manifested through the image and designation of the letter *ca*, this one alone has been cited for now.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the Master’s explanation was not yet clear," this refers to the fact that the explanations provided by the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi were not yet fully lucid.
Now that a Sanskrit manuscript has been obtained, one may proceed to arrange the sequence according to the meanings indicated therein.

Regarding the allocation and arrangement, this refers to a separate explanation. In this context, if one were to follow the sequence of the sutra and cite the passage beginning with "to Guhyapati," that would be appropriate;

however, the reason for instead citing the final two lines of the preceding verse is to ensure the meaning is concise and to create a momentum that leads into the subsequent text, which does not contradict reason. This is why he was asked to inquire further.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "if one were to make this separate statement," it means that the dharmas produced from conditions mentioned above are themselves the primary signlessness (*animitta*) and are not separate from all signs.
Yet, it is not that they are not the primary signlessness nor are they not the dharmas inseparable from signs;
rather, it refers to the act of forcibly using names and words to designate them, asserting that there exists a separate dharma of signlessness. If one were to do this...
To insistently use names and phrases to explain that there exists a distinct characteristic of non-existence is identical to the heretics' calculation of nihilistic emptiness (*uccheda-śūnyatā*).
[Commentary] "Taking the mirror and so forth as the cause" means that the cause is the bodhicitta, which is like a mirror; karma is the practice of great compassion, which is like a body.
The manifestation of an image through the union of these two is the Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), just as in the case of a practitioner and so forth.
This means that the practitioner of mantra-tantra takes the three activities (*trikarma*) of the Tathāgata as a mirror and their own three activities as a face;

because of this union of self and other, the image of *siddhi* appears. Furthermore, taking one’s own activity as a mirror and the Buddha’s activity as a face, through the mutual equality of self and other, the reflection of *siddhi* arises. All of this is accomplished by means of the four non-arisings (*catur-anutpāda*).

Regarding the metaphor of the mirror-image for the contemplation of phrases: it means that [phenomena] do not arise from themselves, do not arise from others, do not arise from both, and yet do not arise without causes and conditions;
this is precisely the metaphor of the mirror used herein.

[Commentary: Regarding "mutually seeing one another," the character *xiāng* (相) may be read with either the level or departing tone, and the character *jiàn* (見) may be read as "manifesting" (*xiǎnxiàn*).

This means that if internal and external factors act as causes for one another and are further distributed among each other—such that "the Buddha is myself" and "I am the Buddha"—and there is no obstruction between them, this is called "mutually seeing. If a practitioner clearly realizes this within samādhi...
To be clear and free from error is what is meant by "the manifestation of signs.
[Sūtra] Regarding the passage "contemplating these dharmas as conditions," etc., this further explains the meaning of the aforementioned mutual dependent origination that is uninterrupted.
"Condition" (pratyaya) means reliance; it refers to how the dharma of reflected images and penetrating wisdom rely upon one another to perform their functions. As it says:
Because the nature of these karmic causes and conditions is empty, it is said: "Contemplate that these dharmas arise from conditions," and so forth.
[Commentary]: Because one contemplates these dharmas such as the mirror-image, one realizes that they exist only through conditions and are both unobtainable and fundamentally and eternally empty.
Since the wisdom that performs this contemplation cannot itself be permanent, all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is cut off.

The treatise states that because it is free from verbal expression, it says "by means of contemplation," etc. If one does not say "etc.," it serves to explain and establish the aforementioned meaning of being uninterrupted:

that after attaining Buddhahood, one preaches the Dharma; by contemplating the Dharma, one becomes a Buddha, and so on until this wisdom arises from conditioned dharmas and returns to perfect the Dharma.
Therefore, it says "if one does not say 'etc.," and so forth.
[Commentary]: "The Dharma is that which is free from all marks" explains the phrase regarding the wisdom of penetrating realization (*pratisaṃvid*) based on the Dharma.

Because this Dharma free from marks gives rise to the wisdom that penetrates the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and because one is able to see the Dharma through that wisdom of penetrating realization, they mutually induce one another.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "Because one knows that dharmas are empty and quiescent," etc., this explains how the wisdom of penetration takes dharmas as its object.

That is to say, it is by means of discriminative wisdom (*vikalpa-prajñā*) that one can penetrate the dharmas of emptiness and quiescence; the dharmas of emptiness and quiescence are manifested through wisdom.

Because these arise in mutual dependence, this is precisely the meaning of the nature-emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) of all dharmas. Therefore, it says, "Because one knows that the nature of dharmas is empty," and so forth.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "as when a person’s eye first sees white," etc., this metaphor explains that the mind is capable of generating thought.

"First seeing" refers to the immediate encounter with an object (*sater-īya*), meaning that one has initially apprehended the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) but is not yet able to discriminate whether it is white or yellow.
Subsequently, the mind gives rise to discrimination, thinking, "This is the color white, distinct from blue and so forth. When one understands it in this way, it causes...

When the mind gives rise to defiled attachment toward what is pure, this is called the arising of the mind. If one understands that this arises solely from conditions, one immediately attains freedom from defilement.
A mind free from defilement arises from the fundamentally pure intention; because the intention is able to produce the mind, it is said, "Just as when a person's eye first sees," and so forth.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "at the time of acting, etc.," the "time of acting" refers to the very moment one is performing the contemplation; this is the third of the four stages of activity (*catur-yoga*). The four stages are:
(1) not yet having acted, (2) desiring to act, (3) the time of acting, and (4) having already acted. This corresponds to the third stage.

One contemplates that the white-colored mind does not come from without, nor does it emerge from within; it exists only through conditions (*pratyaya*), and thus one realizes its nature is empty (*śūnyatā*). It is not the same as [the views of] the Vātsīputrīyas.
Māra sees forms as equal to blindness and knows phenomena as equal to ignorance.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "not using this word 'non-'" (*wu*), the Sūtra says: "Just as when one internally contemplates the maṇḍala within the mind to treat a feverish illness, it is immediately cured and eliminated without any doubt.
The Commentary (*shu*) cites this to explain why the word "non-" is not used here.
The Sanskrit commentary explains that the Sanskrit term *kṣaṇa-deva-vimati* is translated as "immediate absence of doubt.
This means that because the vowel *e* (the "attracted sound," *ākarṣaka-śabda*) follows the syllable *deva*, it corresponds to the character "wu" (無).

Since the *e*-vowel following *deva* already represents the character "wu," there is no need to place the character "wu" separately. If one were to place it separately, it would be redundant. Therefore, the sub-commentary (*shu*) states: "Kṣa..."
That Deva undoubtedly intends for the character "wu" (無) at the end of "Devadatta" to be pronounced with a downward-leading tone; it is not a separate character from this "wu.
[Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "if dharmas are thus," etc., it refers back to the preceding sutra which says: "Contemplating these dharmas, one penetrates through wisdom," and so forth.
The statement that "the emptiness of non-abiding now arises from that intention" should be addressed as follows:

If one contemplates these phenomena through the wisdom of conditions, such that they even function in succession as non-abiding emptiness, how can images arise from the intention within this very emptiness?
Furthermore, regarding the subsequent series of questions concerning how the intention here arises from the mind, who is it that [asks]?
"Is it possible to understand this? [Commentary]:

The Buddha’s statement beginning with "As for the analogies... answers the preceding question. From here until the fifth line, "The body and speech are likewise," answers the question of how images arise from the mind.

Furthermore, from the next... (Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary on a Buddhist sūtra or śāstra, likely concerning the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* or a similar work on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). The bracketed section indicates a structural analysis of the text.)
The analogy leading down to "it is likewise understandable" [is as follows]. These seven lines answer the question, "Who is able to know this?

[The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "For instance, regarding the 'expedient means for removing heat' and so forth: when one wishes to eliminate a feverish illness, one constructs a circular maṇḍala of pure white color, with the syllable *vaṃ* placed in its center.
This means that the circular altar is white in color, and the syllable *vaṃ* is likewise taken to be white.
Regarding water, in order to remove heat, it is said that one may either place the seed-syllable *oṃ* with a bindu (*am*) above it, or use the syllable *va*. The term "or" (*vā*) is indefinite;

the "seed-syllable" refers specifically to the syllable *va*. That is to say, one may either place the syllable *va* or place a bindu (*am*) above it—either is appropriate according to the circumstances.
It should be understood that other similar cases are to be interpreted in this way: for a yellow square mandala, one should place the syllable *a*, or else [place the syllable *va*].
The syllable *Aṃ* belongs to the earth element and is used for the rite of augmentation (*puṣṭi*).
