If a triangular mandala is red in color and the syllable *Raṃ* or *R̥ṃ* is placed within it, it belongs to the fire element and is used for the rite of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).

If the syllable *Haṃ* or *Hr̥ṃ* is placed within a crescent-shaped mandala, it represents the wind element and is used for the rite of coercion (*abhicāra*). Therefore, it is said that they are analogous to these.
[Commentary] As for the phrase "its general meaning," this refers to the method for accomplishing the abiding place of these one hundred syllables. Regarding its general meaning:

one who would perform the accomplishment must first rely on the preceding chapter to realize the corresponding state (*samyoga*), and only then be able to enter this maṇḍala of the reality-mark (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) and the great emptiness altar (*mahāśūnyatā-maṇḍala*). Because this is accomplished, [the altar appears] like a square above, and a triangle below.
There is nothing that is not present within the moon—whether yellow, white, red, black, or otherwise.
Although it is said to be so, if one does not employ this wisdom and skillful means, this stage of the hundred syllables will not be accomplished.

This is because the practitioner of mantra has already previously cultivated the secret yoga practices within the preceding chapters on the wheel of syllables and so forth; thus, they attain this fruit. This fruit is vast and all-encompassing.
Having thus extensively [explained] above, [the author] refutes [this view], saying:

"Even if one uses metaphors such as a mirror image, empty space, or an illusion within this context as a skillful means to contemplate the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of emptiness and wash away the defilements of conceptualization from the mind, if it remains merely a worldly phenomenon, one cannot achieve entry into the maṇḍala of the great emptiness of true reality; therefore, it is said:"
"There is nothing that does not exist," etc.
[Sūtra]: Regarding the "Chapter on the Accomplishment of the Hundred Syllables," the accomplishment of the hundred syllables has already been explained above;
it merely indicated their general characteristics. Now, this section correctly explains how a practitioner of yoga performs the empowerment and recitation within the maṇḍala.

The four characters "of the Dharma" (*dharmasya*) at the beginning refer to the hundred-character dharma that is accomplished; the two characters "of the person" (*pudgalasya*) at the end refer to the practitioner who accomplishes it through recitation.
Because the person derives their name from the dharma, it is called "the accomplishment of the hundred characters through recitation," and so forth.
[Sūtra] "The Mantra World-Saviors" and so forth: this clarifies the characteristics of the practitioner’s correspondence with the formal teaching of the sūtra.
"Mantra" refers to the hundred-syllable [mantra]. Because this mantra is identical to the World-Savior (Tathāgata), it is called "the Mantra World-Saviors.
Regarding the term "body" (*kāya*): the former [instance] refers to the mantra itself; that is, this mantra accumulates many dharmas.

Because it is thus accomplished, it is called "body" (*kāya*). The lower character "body" refers to the practitioner who performs the recitation; these two are one, as they lack any distinct or separate essence.
Furthermore, each of these two bodies has its own upper, middle, and lower parts, and each gives rise to infinite manifestations of body, all of which are of a single substance.

Therefore, it is said that "body and body have no different parts. As for the statement "the mind arises from the mind," and so forth: *Note: The term *kāya* (身) is used here in the sense of both the physical form and the aggregate of the practitioner’s faculties.*
The former refers to the mind with conceptualization (*savikalpa-citta*), and the latter refers to the mind without conceptualization (*nirvikalpa-citta*).

Since the mind with conceptualization arises from the mind without conceptualization, it is said that "mind arises from mind. Regarding "causing it to be well-purified": because the mind is pure, one is able to thoroughly purify all obstructive defilements;
because it is stainless, there is light everywhere. "Everywhere" (*prabhūta*) refers either to the limbs (*aṅga*) or to the eyes (*akṣi*).
Since both the mantras and the practitioners possess constituent parts (*aṅga*), light radiates from such constituent parts to perform the activities of the Buddhas;
therefore, it is said, "to cause them to be thoroughly purified," and so forth.
[Commentary]: Furthermore, the analogy that space is not a sentient being and so forth means that within space there are no sentient beings, no life-span (*jīva*), and no manava (*māṇava*);
it is only because the minds of sentient beings are deluded that such various false perceptions arise. Regarding "not belonging to the category of sentient beings":
space is not a visible phenomenon (*dṛśya-dharma*), just as when a person, due to illness or by non-humans (*amanuṣya*) and other such causes, [perceives things erroneously].
Due to causes and conditions, their minds become deluded and confused, falsely perceiving various forms of persons and things within empty space;
they may give rise to fear or attachment. Yet, empty space is originally pure and free from such characteristics. Nevertheless, it serves as a basis for these perceptions.

Furthermore, regarding that which is called "not a life-sustainer" (*ajīva*), it is like empty space, which is also not a life-sustaining being. This refers to the calculations of certain non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
All phenomena, including the four great elements, grasses, and trees, possess life. Just as grass and trees continue to grow after being cut down, one should know that they have life.

As for those who raise an objection, saying: "If one sees that something regrows after being severed and considers this to be evidence of life, then when a person has a limb severed and it does not grow back again, would they not lack life? One should know that this is merely a statement that space is not a living being.

"Maṇava" is translated here as "Victorious Self" (jina-ātman). Regarding the "Pramāṇa" (Intellectual Measure), it refers to those who calculate that there is a divine self within the body and mind, subtle like a mustard seed and pure;
this is called "pure form. Because it is the very first thing experienced at the moment of receiving a body, it is termed the "Victorious Self.
As for the term "agent," it refers to a class of non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) who calculate that Īśvara is eternal.

Regarding the objection that [the Lord] can produce all things: if sentient beings were the sons of the Sovereign (Īśvara), and if the Sovereign God created sentient beings, who then created this Sovereign? If it is claimed that the Sovereign created himself, that is not so;
for just as an object does not create itself, if there were another creator, he would not be called "Sovereign. This is explained at length in the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*.
Furthermore, the non-Buddhist Sāṃkhya school postulates a self (*ātman*) that is identical to space, capable of creating karma and receiving its retribution.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that there are, in brief, three types of such conceived selves: first, those who maintain that the essence of the self is eternal and all-pervading, equal in extent to space, and that it creates karma and experiences pleasure and pain in every location;
second, those who maintain that while the essence of the self is eternal, its extent is not fixed, but varies [according to the body].

Because the body has expansion and contraction according to its size, [the self] is held to be constant and extremely subtle, like a single atom, yet it shifts within the body to perform various activities;
thus, this agent and experiencer is the first calculation. The term "and so forth" includes the refutation of the first position by means of the following two wheels.
It says: "First, this is irrational. Why? Because you hold the self to be permanent and all-pervading in extent."

If it were identical to space, it should not experience suffering, pleasure, and so forth in accordance with the body; furthermore, because it is eternal and all-pervading, it should be devoid of movement.
How could it follow the body to perform various karmic actions? Therefore, one knows that space is not the agent or the experiencer.
The phrase "all such deluded conceptualizations" summarizes that all aforementioned reckonings are merely false emotional conceptions; such views as these no longer exist now.
The dharma-realm is like space; it cannot be defiled by any conceptual constructions.
Although it is far removed from all discrimination and possesses no coming or going, it is nonetheless not distinct from the realm of sentient beings.

All activities upon which sentient beings rely for their existence are accomplished through this dharma-realm. Because there is nothing that could possibly be accomplished otherwise, it is called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).
Because it is a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), it is said to be "like empty space," and so forth.
[Commentary: That it is not merely empty means that this emptiness of mind is the emptiness of non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*);

it is not a total non-existence, for it actually possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). What is called the intrinsic nature of emptiness is precisely non-emptiness; this is what it refers to.
The profound Middle Way of dependent origination revealed through the ten similes is inconceivable and ultimately unobtainable;
it is emptiness that is not merely empty.

[Commentary: The nature of "emptiness-of-emptiness" is precisely emptiness-and-non-emptiness. The preceding "emptiness" refers to mere emptiness (*prajñapti-śūnyatā*), while the subsequent mention of "emptiness" refers to...
The nature is precisely the nature of non-emptiness, yet it is ungraspable. It is called "empty" because it is ungraspable;
it is not as previously stated that there is absolutely nothing at all. In reality, its own-nature (svabhāva) exists, and this own-nature is precisely non-empty.
[Sūtra]: "A-va" is a designation that indicates the characteristics of various alternative modes (*paryāya*). "A" signifies primordial non-arising (*ādyanutpanna*);
the placement of the syllable "va" below it is intended to demonstrate the meaning of primordial non-arising through the syllable "va.

Since "va" signifies the meaning of speech (*abhilāpa*), by means of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the syllable "A," the speech signified by the syllable "va" is primordially unarisen. Because it is unarisen, it is... [text continues]
The path of language is severed; because the path of language is severed, mental activity is also stilled. This is the virtue of the empowerment of the three secrets.

*A* is the essence of primordial non-arising, which corresponds to the body secret (*kāyaguhyaka*). *Va* is the severance of the path of language, which corresponds to the speech secret (*vāgguhyaka*).
Because mental activity has ceased, this is the mind secret (*manoguhyaka*). Question: By what means of differentiation is the letter *A* realized?

Why is it that, instead of taking the syllables *vi*, *śaṃ*, *ka*, *kha*, and so forth—skipping these twenty-five syllables—one takes this syllable *va* from among the "transcending sounds" (*atīta-śabda*) below?
Answer: This is because the primary principle here is the mantra; since the *va*-syllable gateway (*vākāra-dvāra*) serves as a proof, they are mutually consistent.
Furthermore, regarding the enumeration below, it is intended to demonstrate the departure from prolixity and the transcendence of the intermediate stages; therefore, this [syllable] is indicated.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the designation 'emptiness of emptiness' arises from contemplation," etc., it means that the nature of the emptiness of emptiness exists only as a name;
ultimately, it cannot be found when sought. This is called the "emptiness of emptiness. To say "it arises from the mind" means it is produced from the bodhicitta. Therefore, a sutra says:
"One should give rise to a mind equal to space," which refers to the so-called bodhicitta. Hence, it is called the "emptiness of emptiness," and so forth.

[Commentary]: Regarding this term "division" (*fen*), the character *sheng* (sound) is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*), which refers to speech itself; the character *fen* (division) is also called with the departing tone.
It means that one division is distinct from two, three, and so on up to ten, hundred, or thousand divisions; therefore, it is called "distinct division."

[Commentary]: Regarding "the second refers to these syllables *a* and so forth": these two characters do not refer to the number two; rather, they are the second instance of the preceding sequence being repeated.
One should say "increasing according to the sequence. Regarding "the sequence refers to these syllables *a* and so forth, as well as the visualizations (*saṃjñā*)":
this means that it is solely the meaning of visualization. This is an explanation of what precedes by means of what follows, namely, increasing from one.
Reaching two, increasing from two to three, and so on, successively increasing until reaching one hundred thousand—this is the sequence.

Such a sequence is precisely the contemplation of the letter *A* and so forth. "Contemplation" (*saṃjñā*) means merely conceptualization (*saṃjñāmātra*). That is to say, it is merely the conceptualization of the letter *A*;
because of the letter *A*, there arise the letters *Ka*, *Ca*, *Ṭa*, and so forth, which are differentiated by increasing by one. *Ka*, *Ca*, [and so on].

[The syllables] *ṭa* and so forth arise from *a*, just as the numbers one, two, three, and so on are established based upon space; therefore, it is said that these are precisely the *a*s and so forth.

[Commentary: Regarding the sixteen kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and so forth, they are explained in detail in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* explains that these are: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness,
absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, non-dispersal emptiness, essential-nature emptiness, characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena,
the emptiness of non-existence, and the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "up to those with form and those without form," because the categories of things arranged in the diagrams are so numerous that they cannot be fully enumerated, the term "up to" (*nai zhi*) is employed.
As for "those with form," this refers, for example, to empty space, which originally lacks smoke, clouds, dust, mist, or various colored forms such as blue, white, yellow, and red;
yet, due to the illnesses of sentient beings or the influence of non-human spirits upon their minds...
Delusion arises, and by means of these causes and conditions, one subsequently perceives the various forms and colors described above;
yet when one recovers their original mind, these are ultimately found to be unobtainable. Therefore, they are called "having form" and "lacking form.

As for "having characteristics" and "lacking characteristics," it is like empty space, which is far removed from male and female characteristics and so forth. Due to various illnesses and the like, as previously explained, these are termed "having characteristics."
The signless letter A is likewise so. For instance, when all letters are topped with the stroke of the letter A, they are called "having form";
yet ultimately, they do not depart from the essence of the letter A’s original non-arising, which is called "formlessness.

Furthermore, all letters, according to their specific formations, undergo change, transformation, ego-clinging (*ahaṃkāra*), suchness (*tathatā*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and even dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

The so-called "characterized" (sanimitta) refers to the presence of characteristics; because of the letter *A*, it is also ultimately and primordially unarisen, which is called the "uncharacterized" (animitta).

When explained extensively, the various distinct forms of the three classes of noble beings within the inner and outer maṇḍalas arise from one another and interpenetrate in infinite and boundless ways—all of which proceed from the letter *A*, the primordial non-arising.
Flowing forth from within.

[Commentary] Regarding "the letter A is provisionally established," etc.: this means that upon the essence of the letter A, which is primordially unborn (*an-utpanna*), the union of the causes and conditions of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) arises;
this is termed "provisional establishment. As for "empowerment through words": by means of such causes and conditions, it causes the mantra—
Because those who maintain the recitation at the gate will swiftly attain equality with Vairocana, it is said: "The letter A is provisionally established," and so forth.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "as if a horizontal stroke were placed above the letter Ka," one should say: "as if a horizontal stroke were not placed above the letter Ka."
The horizontal stroke does not constitute the sound *ka*, because within the character *ka* the sound *a* is lacking;

thus, it is difficult to manifest [the sound]. To explain this further using Sanskrit characters: the horizontal stroke above the character *ka* is itself the sound *a*. (This is the sound *a*; this is the character *ka*).
If the horizontal stroke above were not placed upon the lower character, the lower character would not become *ka*. Why?

For this reason, the sound "a" is omitted; thus, in this commentary, there is one missing character "not" (不) beneath the character "if" (若), which is why it says "such as the letter 'ka' and so forth.
[Commentary:

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "all formations (saṃskāra) are unobtainable," the character for "formation" (行) should be read with a level tone (ping sheng); that is, it refers to "coming to a halt" (行止).

"Meaning" (義) is, in Sanskrit, *artha* (pronounced *ga-ti* [with a double *t*]). It refers to "activity" (*caryā*). Alternatively, regarding the phrase "all phenomena are free from combatants" (*yuddha*) and so forth:

these two phenomena, this and that, are mutually defined and thus termed "combatants. For example, between the wholesome and the unwholesome, the wholesome is designated as "this" and the unwholesome as "that.
Furthermore, this applies to flowing against the current of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) versus flowing with it, as well as to generosity (*dāna*) versus stinginess (*mātsarya*), and so on.
Phenomena characterized by mutual opposition, such as wisdom and ignorance, are called "enemies. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because all phenomena are free from *asmimāna*":
in Sanskrit, this is *ṭhakara*, which is translated here as "conceit" (*māna*). This refers to self-exaltation; since there is self-exaltation, there must necessarily be the disparagement of others.
This constitutes an unequal view, such as the various distinctions of superiority and inferiority found within the three realms and the six destinies.
Although there are immeasurable distinctions, even among those who seek the three vehicles, there still exist views of inequality regarding higher and lower stages.
However, if one contemplates the letter *A* and the non-arising of all phenomena, there will be no mutual dependence or opposition;
thus one knows that *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is equal across all phenomena, with neither high nor low. For this reason, the Tathāgata is also called "All Gold."
The Bodhisattva Vajra is also called the noble one of the four fruits, and is also called ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and sentient beings of various evil destinies;

the Great Compassion Maṇḍala precisely symbolizes this meaning. As for the statement that "all dharmas are free from enmity and free from opposition," whether this is identical to or different from the meaning of the gate of the letter *ja* (enemy) as "to fight an adversary," in both cases there is mutual correlation and dependence between them.
Therefore, while the Sanskrit terms are distinct, their meanings also differ accordingly. "Warrior" (*śatru*) in Sanskrit refers to a combatant;

"enemy" (*nāmara*) in this context refers to an adversary. The former refers to warriors who engage one another in battle, whereas the latter refers to enemies who avoid each other out of mutual hostility;
thus, they are not conflated. As stated in the fifth commentary, or as it says regarding all phenomena being free from calamity and transformation:
In the Sanskrit language, *ḍāka* means "calamity" (*vyasana*) or "seizing" (*dhāraṇa*). "Calamity" refers to disasters such as fire, water, insects, or thieves;

"change" (*vikāra*) refers to phenomena such as the aberration of the celestial bodies. In the *Maṇḍalopayika-paṭala*, it is translated as "seizing," meaning being possessed by ghosts and spirits or held by non-human beings.
Regarding the phrase "or all dharmas such as *tathatā* (suchness) and detachment," this means that if one perceives a subject [who sees], [it is not suchness].
That which is observed is a phenomenon of mutual dependence. Now, many characters express the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness).
This means that the suchness of nirvāṇa and the suchness of saṃsāra—these two suchnesses are ultimately non-dual; being without duality, they are without mutual dependence.

If one enters the gateway of the syllable *A*, suchness is primordially unarisen, and is therefore termed "detachment. Hence it is said: "the suchness of all phenomena," or "the state of detachment of all phenomena," and so forth.

The term *sthāna* in Sanskrit is translated here as "place of abiding. This is precisely a "non-place of abiding," for when one perceives the limit of primordial non-arising (*anutpāda*), no place of abiding can be found;
thus it is said that "all phenomena are devoid of place," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "all dharmas, all giving (*dana*), etc.":
*dana* means "giving. To say that something is "not in accord with the Way" means that the Way refers to the "gate of letters" (*akṣaramukha*).

Regarding the statement that it accords with the path of the gateway of the letter *A* as explained in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: because the *Prajñāpāramitā* takes non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) as its skillful means;
or regarding "all dharma-realms" (*dharmadhātu*)—the Sanskrit term is *dhātu*, which is translated here as "realm. This "realm" refers to the essence (*svabhāva*).
Because all things are fundamentally unborn, there is no essence to be apprehended. Furthermore, "realm" carries the meaning of "portion" (*bhāga*), which is to say...
The meaning of "all these images within" is that all the various images within the maṇḍala each maintain their own positions without being confused or disordered.
Alternatively, regarding the phrase "the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena," the character *di* (諦) is redundant;
the Sanskrit term is *paramārtha*, which is translated as "ultimate truth. The Sanskrit term *satya* means "truth" (*di*). This corresponds to...

The syllable *sa* signifies "therefore" or "redundant. Regarding the statement in the *Maṇḍalopāyika-parivarta* that one contemplates all phenomena as being unapprehendable (*anupalabdha*) and so forth:
what is it that is contemplated as unapprehendable? Is it contemplating that giving is unapprehendable, that ethical discipline is unapprehendable, and so on, up to wisdom being unapprehendable?
Since there is no specific referent, the word "existence" (*sat*) should be supplied; that is, one contemplates that existence is unapprehendable.
Therefore, in this context, the Sanskrit term *bala* has been omitted; it is translated here as "existence" (*yu*), referring to the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātu*) and so forth.

As the *Maṇḍala-paṭala* states: "Because all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*) cannot be apprehended as existing. Furthermore, in the sūtras, there is the character "various" (*zhu*) above the character for "contemplation" (*guan*);

because the various contemplations of all phenomena cannot be apprehended. These "various contemplations" are themselves existent phenomena (*yu-fa*). In this [present] text, the character for "various" is missing.

Since the meaning is also insufficient, it says, "In this context, the characters are explained," and so forth. This means that the present explanation of the syllable *ma* signifies "freedom from bondage.
*Ma* has the meaning of "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*). In the Sanskrit language, *bandha* is translated as "bondage.

If one were to explain the meaning of bondage by means of the syllable *ma*, which signifies emptiness, it would be a textual error. This [preceding statement] refers to the manifestation of the character form.
The phrase "and so forth" explains the various characters mentioned above. "Manifesting" (xian) means appearing; that is, for each and every phenomenon (*dharma*), there is a manifesting character.
Thus, the character is the signifier (*vācaka*), while the phenomenon is the signified (*vācya*)—that which is signified and manifested.

[Commentary: "All arise from within this" refers here to the twenty-nine syllables from *a-va* to *ba-ha*, together with the long *ā* within the letter *a* and *am* and *aḥ*, totaling thirty-two syllables. "Regarding all things...
up to 'transform'" means that because the essential forms of the letters *yaṅ*, *raṅ*, *ṇa*, *naṃ*, and *maṃ* are the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), they are able to [transform] all things.
The syllables *ka* and so forth are those that turn all phenomena with mastery over the Dharma. "Mastery" means being unimpeded; "turning" means revolving.
This refers to how the five syllables beginning with *aṃ* revolve without impediment within all phenomena such as *ka* and the rest, just as the worldly void pervades everywhere.
To say that these appear accordingly means that they revolve freely through the empty phrases beginning with *aṃ*.
Wherever [syllables] such as *ka* and so forth manifest, one is able to accomplish the marks and signs of adornment of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Regarding the phrase "and these, etc.," the word "and" (*ca*) carries the sense of inclusion;

it means that not only is the adornment of the Tathāgata’s marks and signs accomplished throughout the thirty-two syllables, but furthermore, each of these individual syllables serves as a gateway, each capable of following [the respective object].

The word "and" (*ca*) is placed because the Mother of the Perfectly Enlightened One who manifests in accordance with forms (*anurūpamātṛ*), and so forth, interpenetrate one another without obstruction.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the aforementioned *ka*, etc.": this means that each of the five classes of sounds—*ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa*—consists of four syllables.

The statement that "the twenty letters beginning with ka, kha, ga, and gha" refers not to the words themselves, but to the letter *ya*—which is the *ya* used in the letter-gates such as *ra* and so forth—is because this [letter *ya*] is excellent.
Regarding "these four," these four characters are the Bodhicitta, Great Compassion, Expedient Means, and Nirvāṇa; "and together" means together with the preceding.

The twenty-eight characters beginning with "Ka" constitute thirty-two; furthermore, within each individual character there is a samādhi, and each of these samādhis is fully endowed with the thirty-two marks.
Thus, the marks are inexhaustible one after another—this is what is called the Tathāgata’s adornment of myriad virtues.

[Commentary]: "These five syllables pervade concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*)" means that among the preceding *a*, *ā*, *aṃ*, and *aḥ*, the first is wisdom and the other three are concentration;
this pattern applies to the subsequent *ka*, *kha*, up to *sa* and *ha*, where concentration and wisdom are likewise arranged.

Since the five syllables beginning with *ya* (the "upward-facing" [syllable] and so forth) all pervade within those, it is said they "pervade concentration and wisdom. To say they "can also accomplish samādhi" means they pervade the remainder as well.

The three syllables can also produce wisdom; this [wisdom] pervades the first syllable. This meaning is difficult to clarify, so it shall be briefly demonstrated by means of the forms of the characters.
Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of the syllable *khaḍga* within the sound of "wisdom," it is illustrated by the syllable *ka*, as in the case of *ka*.
*Ka* has the meaning of "to act. If the syllable *ya* and the nasal dot (*bindu*) are added, it becomes the syllable *khaḍga*, which clearly manifests the sense of "acting."
The meaning is that examples such as *ka* and *kha* are each pervasive within wisdom. Furthermore, the syllable *ci* is the samādhi of the syllable *ka*;

if a nasal bindu (*anusvāra*) is placed above *ci*, it becomes the syllable *ṅci*, and this samādhi likewise belongs to the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), just like the syllable *ci*. This applies equally to *ji*, *ti*, *bi*, and so on, up to *ṃ*.
Each [syllable] is universally explained within the samādhi by means of the "dot of emptiness" (bindu) according to its meaning;
furthermore, when distinguishing the essential nature of the *ā* vowel and so forth, it is like the Sanskrit word *pañca* (five).

If one does not place the dot of emptiness above the syllable *pa*, but instead places the *ra* vowel (*ṛ*) upon the syllable *ca*, this is no different from placing the dot of emptiness above the syllable *pa*. Thus, O Brahmā, it is the same.
Because the Dharma is thus, it is like the Sanskrit word *siṃha*, which means "lion.
If one does not place the *bindu* dot above the syllable *siṃ* but instead places the *ū* vowel-mark (*dīrgha*) above the syllable *ha*, it is no different from placing the dot above *siṃ*.
All other cases follow this same principle; therefore, it is said that these five syllables pervade both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). This is what is meant by "pervasive."

Regarding the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*): it is like adding the vowel *a* (represented by the character "仰") to the four consonants of the *ka*-group, such as *ka*.
Specifically, *ka* (short) and *kā* (long), *ki* and *kī*—the former two represent wisdom (*prajñā*) and the latter two represent meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Furthermore, adding *kha*, *ga*, and *gha*, each having four syllables, results in a total of sixteen phonemes; just as with the *ka*-group, there are likewise sixteen phonemes for the dental sounds (*tālavya*).
There are sixteen sounds of the tongue, sixteen sounds of the throat, and sixteen sounds of the lips; thus, there are eighty in total.

Therefore, they constitute the Tathāgata’s eighty secondary marks (anuvyañjana). In reality, these are also [the sounds of] the eight characters beginning with "bi" (遍) and so forth; here, however, only the first is cited to encompass the subsequent ones.
Hence it is said: "universally accomplishing the Tathāgata," and so on.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the Sanskrit original, etc. in this passage, it refers to one verse in the Sanskrit text which is the scriptural passage from another location;

therefore, it is not preserved here. As for the statement "the broad practices of these Buddhas, etc.," as explained, this is a restatement and commentary on the preceding section of the scripture concerning "entering each of these samādhi-doors, etc."

[Commentary] Question: Regarding the phrase "outside the hundred-syllable wheel" and so forth—previously, in the explanation of the syllable-wheel (*akṣara-cakra*), it was stated that twelve syllables, such as *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *o*, and so on, or alternatively the five syllables *aṃ*, *raṃ*, etc., are all arranged upon the outer wheel.
Now, what further syllables are placed within the four wheels of *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, and *gha* in this intermediate [wheel]?
This is because the question was posed according to the sequence of entry and exit through various aspects of cause and effect.

[Commentary] Regarding the response, "In this case, one must discuss cause and effect," this answers the meaning of the aforementioned sequence of internal and external factors such as *kāya* (body) and so forth;
herein, the distinction between internal and external must be explained by relying on cause and effect, as follows.
[Commentary: "If a practitioner first generates [the mind]" and so forth refers to the aforementioned short *ka*, long *kā*, *kha*, *ja*, and other syllables.

If one considers the practitioner of yoga from the initial generation of the bodhicitta, progressing through the stages of practice until the ultimate consummation of skillful means—this sequential order represents the movement from cause to fruit, according to the principle of the internal and external.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "if explained from the perspective of one's own resultant stage," this means that although one has already attained the ultimate fruit, one does not abandon the gateway of the causal stage.
When explaining in such a sequence, one places the letter *ka* within; next, the seven letters beginning with *ya* are arranged;
and finally, the five letters beginning with *aṅ* are arranged on the outermost layer. The letter *va* is identical in essence to the letter *a*; this refers to the following.
The syllable *va* is the fourth character among the eight transcendent sounds (*aṣṭau vyomavyāpinaḥ*). Why is it taken from there and placed at the center of the wheel of syllables?
It is because one arises from the fruit in order to teach the Dharma for the benefit of others;
furthermore, since *va* signifies speech, it sequentially expresses the long *ka*, the long *ja*, and the long *ga*, which are the means for realizing *nirvāṇa*. Moreover, by means of the wheel...
This is displayed. [Commentary:

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "introducing from the outside," etc., previously this was explained in terms of proceeding from the fruit to the cause, moving from the inside outward; now it is explained in terms of proceeding from the cause to the fruit, moving from the outside inward.
The circular formation is the reverse of the former and may be understood accordingly. As for the words "asked again," they refer to the preceding characters.

The five characters "wheel," "upward," "soil," etc., are contained within the hundred characters; here, they appear on the outermost layer. This is likely due to different explanations according to various gates.

However, if one discusses this from the perspective of ultimate reality, entry and exit are sovereign and free; one may place them as intended for the occasion. Fearing that [readers] might cling to a single fixed location, I have requested you to inquire further.
[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the question concerning "the practitioner’s mind" and so forth: what has been shown above pertains only to the object of observation (*ālambana*).

Now, the question concerns the subject of observation (*ālambaka*), meaning that since the sequence of the objects of observation is thus, the sequence of the contemplative practice (*bhāvanā-caryā*) of the observing subject is likewise so.
Therefore, the answer below states: "In general, the progression of practice possesses a sequential order."
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "contemplating the perfect luminosity" and so forth: what has been explained above concerns only the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*).

Furthermore, because the wheels of seals (*mudrācakra*) and the wheels of the body (*kāyacakra*) each have distinct forms, when these are integrated, they are three yet one, and one yet three; thus, by performing any single activity, all three activities are accomplished.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "arising from my own mind" and so forth: this means that it arises from my *cintā* (contemplative) and *jñāna* (knowing) mind;
one should know that the mind of the middle way is likewise so. This is the meaning of the correspondence between the internal and the external.
[Commentary] Furthermore, the statement that "the Dharma-body possesses sovereignty and so forth" is an exhortation to believe.

This is because, in the common discourse on the Dharma, it is often said that the Dharma-body is quiescent like empty space and devoid of all activity; thus, they fail to realize that it is fully endowed with such virtues.
Consequently, they assume that all manifestations of spiritual transformations are merely the functioning of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). Therefore, [the text] below...
Since this is illustrated by citing four kinds of matters as analogies, how could there be any cause for doubt?
[Commentary] The question regarding the first court of the maṇḍala refers to the Maṇḍala of the Revolving Wheel of Syllables;
it is therein that such a statement is made.
[Commentary] Regarding the response concerning "mantras, mudrās, and so forth," this refers to the *Sāmānya-mantra-kośa* and the *Mudrā-paṭala*.

As for "the Tathāgata’s nails and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes the Tathāgata’s lasso, tongue, teeth, lips, bell, conch, spear, sword, wheel, and other such items—forty matters in total—which are all situated within the positions of the mandala diagrams in the fourth [chapter]. Therefore...
The answer says: "It is like the mantras and so forth.
[Commentary] Regarding the question, "What is the meaning of 'Jewel Banner' (Ratnaketu) Buddha? and so on—there are four questions here, and this is the first.
The answer to these four is likewise as follows: the general intent is that bodhicitta is the cause, great compassion is the root, and skillful means is the culmination.
Ultimately, the sequence represents the meaning of the five syllables *ā ā aṃ aḥ aḥ* (the last being long), and it also represents the meaning of the eight minds:
the "Jewel Banner" (*ratnaketu*) is the seed-syllable mind; the "Blossoming Flower" (*kusumita*) is the five minds of the root, bud, sprout, leaf, and flower;
"Amitābha" is the fruition-mind of self-enjoyment; and "Drum Sound" (*dundubhisvara*) corresponds to the mind of the fruition once again becoming the seed.
[The Sūtra] states:
"Regarding the Chapter on the Dharma of the Hundred-Syllable Mantra: 'Hundred syllables' refers to the aforementioned *a*, *ka*, and so forth.
'Mantra' means that each and every one of these hundred syllables is a mantra; however, because the syllable *a* is now taken as the king of mantras."

It is said: If one takes the hundred syllables as a whole to constitute the essence of the mantra, then since the hundred syllables are themselves the mantra, the name is established based on the identity of the attribute with its substratum (*dharmadharmibhāva*).
If, however, one takes only the letter *A* as the essence of the mantra, then the hundred syllables are the "total" (*samudāya*) and the letter *A* is the "particular" (*vibhāga*);

in this case, the particular derives its name from the total, and it is designated as the "mantra of the hundred syllables" based on the relationship of the substrate and its attribute (*dharmadharmibhāva*). This is the method for the multitude of practitioners.

The meaning of "many" refers to the virtues produced by the hundred syllables, which are designated as "Dharma. Regarding the Dharma of the hundred-syllable mantra, or the method of the hundred syllables:
when the syllable *A* is regarded as the mantra, these hundred syllables constitute the Dharma of that mantra;
therefore, it is called the "Dharma of the Hundred-Syllable Mantra."
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the Honored One is this meaning," etc., "Honored One" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Just as in the world Śakra is foremost among the earth-dwelling devas, Brahmā is foremost among all worldly sages, and the Buddha is foremost among all noble wisdoms—these meanings of being "foremost" arise from the letter A;
that is to say, such primacy is inherently present within the letter itself.

The characteristics of virtue are like the myriad things that depend upon space to come into being; while space itself is fundamentally without characteristics, it manifests various forms within that very absence of characteristics.
Therefore, meaning turns according to characteristics, and the Venerable One is established by means of syllables.

As for the statement that the meaning is the same as in the preceding chapter, the preceding chapter refers to the "Chapter on the Master’s Real Wisdom. That scripture states: "The letter A is called the seed-syllable."
Arranging all the limbs and so forth, performing everything in this manner is precisely for the sake of the Tathāgatas,
Bodhisattvas, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, Asuras, the Sun and Moon, the Water Deities, Śakra Devendra, and the Lords of the World; therefore,
it is said that its meaning is the same as that of the preceding chapter.

[The Sūtra] states, "Sound arises from letters," and so forth. Regarding this, the first verse says that sound arises from letters because when the human mind, taking letters as its object, desires to cause others to hear, sound emerges through the contact of various conditions such as the throat, tongue, and palate.
As for the statement that "letters arise within the true mantra," it refers to the formation of vocal sounds through specific modulations and distinctions upon the aforementioned sound.

The merit of mantras is traced back to their origin, for they arise from the seed-syllables (*bīja*). Thus, the Preface to the *Shijing* states: "Sound forms patterns; these patterns are what manifest.
This is identical to the nature of mantras. Furthermore, based on the syllables, mantras are produced;
and based on the mantras, the fruits of *siddhi* arise. Such mantras that produce the fruits of accomplishment were proclaimed by the Savior as a means of salvation.
The world is itself the Buddha, and the Buddha is the one who protects and delivers the world. As it is said in the *Buddhastotra*:

"The Immovable Wisdom Equal to Space, the World-Savior, the Great Compassionate Honored One. Therefore, it is said that the fruit is established through mantra; this is the teaching of all the World-Saviors.
It should be understood that the nature of sound reaches the practitioner. Regarding the speaker: the aforementioned fruit of mantra is established from sound.
Fearing that they might cling to these [phenomena] and fail to relinquish them, the skillful means of the antidote is taught:

just as non-Buddhists cling to sound as being substantially real and eternally abiding, one is led to contemplate its emptiness. If a practitioner of mantra realizes that both sound and its effects are identical to emptiness, then this is the activity of mantra;
though its manifestations are myriad, when their intrinsic nature is scrutinized, they do not transcend the primordial *ā* syllable.
If one knows that the syllable *jāti* (birth) does not emerge from the syllable *anutpāda* (non-arising), then both sound and emptiness are equally transcended.
Such a characteristic is what the World-Honored One has proclaimed for those practicing the mantra-discipline (*mantra-caryā*): "Entering into sound is liberation;
this is the realization of samādhi. Because the practitioner understands the gateway of the letter *A*, regarding all sounds...
Attaining mastery is precisely the realization of the *Sarvasattvarutakauśalya-samādhi* (the Samādhi of Understanding the Languages of All Sentient Beings).

Regarding the arrangement according to the *dharmas*, when one corresponds with the visualization of the mantra, it correctly explains the fruit of *siddhi* corresponding to the practitioner’s contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).

If, according to the upper wheel of syllables (*akṣara-cakra*), one establishes the arrangement in correspondence with the mind, one is then able to differentiate [the aspects] within a single syllable.
"Separately manifesting immeasurable meanings and immeasurable modes of speech for each and every sentient being.
[Commentary: "Relying upon the letter A, etc. means that by relying on the letter A, there are the letters Ka, Kha, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "each letter is identical to empty space," it is said twice because there is one "letter" which is the letter A, and there are the other "letters" such as Ka and the rest. Thus they are all identical.
The root and the branches, the subject and the object, and the arising of letters: since the root is identical to empty space, the branches follow suit.

Although all are devoid of characteristics, within this state of no-characteristics there still exist such characteristics as coming and going, identity and difference, cause and effect, and so forth; therefore, it is said that they "rely upon A and the other [vowels]."

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "these conditions that can produce [sound]," it means that this sound arises through the mutual dependence and striking together of conditions such as the throat, tongue, palate, and teeth.
Since it arises from conditions, it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Thus, by successively investigating those things that can produce sound—the throat, tongue, lips, palate, and so forth—one finds that they themselves arise from the causal conditions of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Since that which arises also lacks intrinsic nature, one further investigates from what the four great elements arise;
by tracing them back through successive stages until reaching the limit of original non-arising, that limit of original non-arising is precisely the letter A.

[Commentary] Regarding the mutual explanation of the verses: the first two and a half lines consist of one verse that reveals the sequence of cause and effect, which is the meaning of the provisional (*prajñapti*).
The subsequent half-verse clarifies that the aforementioned provisional characteristics, in their entirety, are empty (*śūnya*).

The following half-verse explains that among these provisional and empty phenomena, sentient beings fail to understand the reality and instead falsely cling to them according to words; thus, the final half-verse [reveals] emptiness and the provisional.
The two brushes are swept away and merged back into the Middle Way; furthermore, these three terms are all provisional, all empty, and all middle.
Because they explain one another, it is said that the verses mutually explain each other.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "equal to this samādhi" and so forth, according to the explanation in the commentary below, *dharma* has the meaning of "a multitude of virtues" rather than the meaning of *dharmatā*.
This refers to the arrangement based on the multitude of corresponding virtues associated with the letter A (*akṣara*).

This "multitude of virtues" refers to the various differentiated characteristics of the hundred-syllable wheel (*śatākṣaracakra*), such as the various colors—blue, yellow, black, white—and the various shapes—square, circular, triangular, crescent-shaped, and so forth.
The form relies on this name "Arrangement" (*vyūha*); because it is maintained according to the Dharma or according to the ritual procedure (*vidhi*), it is called "further questioning.
[Commentary: Regarding "both self and other are empty," that which can produce is the "self" and that which is produced is the "other";
since both such subject and object cannot be apprehended, they are termed "empty. From this emptiness of non-apprehension, one perceives that the letter *A* is fundamentally non-arising.
The principle of physiology is termed "establishing principle from emptiness. To understand this principle is itself to abide in samādhi;
therefore, both this emptiness and this principle are the functioning of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "one who realizes this principle," etc., this is an introduction to the preceding text to establish the point.

It refers to the three lines of verse mentioned above, beginning with "one who realizes the samādhi," which state that a person who has realized this *akṣara-cakra-samādhi* (wheel of syllables samādhi) is able to place immeasurable syllables within a single syllable;
and according to the various forms and colors of those immeasurable syllables, they correspond accordingly.
When one contemplates and observes them, by means of a single syllable, all hundred syllables can be known. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Thus, the *ā* syllable and its like are the conceptualizations of immeasurable mantras.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the meaning of these truly manifest syllables," within this gateway of the hundred-syllable mantra, there is the true...

The manifestation of the two kinds of word-meanings—the true word-meaning—is the gateway to the Tathāgata’s spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), which is accomplished through the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
It is not something newly produced, nor was it established by the Tathāgata for the sake of a particular class of sentient beings;
rather, because the path is identical for all Buddhas and the dharma-position (*dharma-sthiti*) is eternally abiding, it is called the "manifestation of the true word-meaning."

As for "meaning" (*artha*), although it has been spontaneously accomplished from the beginning according to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), it is not like that which exists through worldly false conceptualization;
rather, it must be manifested through the causes and conditions of *prajñā* and skillful means (*upāya*). Therefore, it is said that there are these characters and meanings of true manifestation.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "herein it only clarifies a single syllable, etc.": this refers to a challenge posed as follows: "In these preceding five chapters, all speak of 'one hundred syllables.
Furthermore, as stated above in the *Chapter on the Arising of One Hundred Syllables*, therein only the single syllable *am* is used as the mantra;
how, then, can it be called 'explaining one hundred syllables'? To resolve this universally, it says: "Herein it only clarifies a single syllable, etc."
[Sūtra] Regarding the "Exposition on the Nature of Bodhi": This refers to the proclamation and elucidation that arises from what precedes it.

As for the "nature of bodhi," it is the resultant essence of the mantra, free from the characteristics of conditioned activity and conceptual discrimination; because bodhi is itself the nature, it is called the "nature of bodhi.
Since the preceding chapter has already explained that mantras are signless (*animitta*), this is further explained by using space as a metaphor. This is bodhi...
Because it explains the nature of bodhi, it says, "explaining the nature of bodhi," and so forth.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "that is, transmitting the hundred-syllable [mantra]," *teng* (transmit) means "to convey" according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*. Furthermore, "convey" (*zhuan*) means "to circulate.
It refers to explaining [the meaning] by circulating through the hundred-syllable mantra; therefore, it says, "that is, transmitting the hundred-syllable [mantra]," and so forth.

[Sūtra] "For example, like the emptiness of the ten directions" means that the nature of the *mantra*-enlightenment has only a slight resemblance to emptiness, and thus emptiness is taken as a metaphor.
This is because while the characteristic of the emptiness of the ten directions serves as the support for all phenomena (*dharmas*), the essence of emptiness itself has no support;
the *mantra* is likewise the support for all phenomena, yet the *mantra* [itself has no support].
"Essence has no basis" means that the one called the Savior of the World is a transcendent (lokottara) Honored One because of this mantra.
Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, within space, etc.": "Furthermore" (*punaḥ*) means again; it introduces another analogy.
It is like how, within the midst of empty space, many forms and images may appear and be seen, yet they have no place of dependence. That is to say, empty space does not form the thought: "I..."
While they serve as the basis for those forms, those forms themselves do not form the thought, "I depend upon space. Why?
Because their nature is such; therefore, there is nothing upon which they depend.

[Sūtra]: "Abiding solely in names, one proceeds toward the direct perception that transcends verbal expression. Herein, the first verse establishes the essence of space as being merely names and so forth;
because these are conventional designations established in accordance with worldly usage, the essence of space cannot be apprehended.

The subsequent verse explains that conventional names are identical to space, meaning that worldly names— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the content available.*
Names are provisionally established according to circumstances; if one seeks their actual meaning, they are identical to empty space—both are unattainable.

Mantras are likewise so: their essence transcends verbal expression and is ultimately unattainable. Yet, by the power of skillful means, the Buddhas cause all sentient beings to universally enter the Buddha-wisdom.
From emptiness they establish the provisional, and from the provisional they establish emptiness. Sentient beings rely upon this to give rise to reality.
To see such reality—this very seeing is the nature of bodhi; apart from this seeing of reality, it is impossible for there to be a separate bodhi.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "emptiness has only a name" and so forth in the preceding verse, the "preceding verse" refers to the third line of the first verse.
The "subsequent verse" refers to the second line of the following verse.

[Commentary]: Regarding "being free from causes and conditions," etc.: the essence of the *ā* syllable mantra is such that it is without ignorance, without darkness, and without the distinctions of day and night;
this is precisely being free from causes and conditions. Being free from such causes and conditions is the Reality (*tattva*).
The marks are eternally abiding; this eternal abiding of the true mark (*dharmatā*) is the very body of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata.
This body of Mahāvairocana is the nature of bodhi. How could such a nature of bodhi not be free from birth and death?
It is precisely that which can transcend birth and death and so forth, as explained below.
[The Sūtra] states: Regarding the "Chapter on the Three Samayas," "three" is a numerical designation; "samaya" refers to *samādhi*.
Because there are three types of *samādhi*, the title is established by attaching the number; thus it is called the "Chapter on the Three Samayas. This, too, reiterates what was previously explained.

[Commentary]: When the Buddha says that this question concerns the causal conditions for a great matter, it is identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*’s teaching on the opening, revealing, awakening to, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
[Sūtra]: "There are three kinds of dharmas... which arise in succession"—this is the general heading. Such are the three kinds of dharmas.
If there is no continuity, then obstructions arise, and because one cannot attain correspondence, it cannot be called a *samaya-pada*.
If there is continuity, one attains freedom from obstruction; this very continuity without obstruction constitutes correspondence.
Possessing these three factors, one is named a *samaya-pada*. Therefore, it is said that there are three kinds of equality.
[Sūtra] "The initial mind does not contemplate its own nature," etc., refers to the first samaya phrase;
this is merely the arousal of the mind seeking Buddhahood without yet possessing the wisdom of contemplative observation, which is the letter A.
"From this, one gives rise to wisdom until reaching the stage of perfect enlightenment" refers to the second samaya phrase; this is because it relies upon the original bodhicitta.

Thereupon, there arises the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) capable of decisive discernment regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*), and so forth—namely, that the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is possible and the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) are impossible.
Because one is able to definitively comprehend these realms of possibility and impossibility, one can then distance oneself from the net of inexhaustible conceptual proliferation (*vikalpa*).
This is the long vowel *ā*, as previously described; it is the letter *a* with the long vowel mark added to its side.
Therefore, this is the arising of wisdom. Furthermore, "O Lord of Secrets, reaching the mastery of great compassion" refers to the third samaya phrase;
it means that once one has discerned the true from the false, one gives rise to a heart of great compassion toward all sentient beings and reflects:
"All sentient beings possess this same nature; why do they not realize it themselves, suffering in vain?"
"I have now personally awakened to and realized birth and death; I shall universally open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision for all sentient beings, causing them all to be no different from myself.

This refers to the sequential phrases of practice for the samādhis beginning with *i-i*, *i-zhi*, *wu-ao*, and so forth, which correspond respectively to the three minds of the Great Vow, Great Wisdom, and Great Compassion.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because one sees reality, it is not unreal," etc.: In the third samaya, the practitioner realizes the true mark of all phenomena as being free from falsehood;
they understand that these are solely the essence of the letter A, which is fundamentally unborn (*anutpāda*).
Consequently, they give rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward all sentient beings, for all sentient beings share this same nature. And yet...
Having personally realized that the cycle of birth and death is boundless, one desires to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision for those beings so that they may be no different from oneself;
thus, within the state of true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), one gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

If a practitioner at such a time perceives any mark of true reality, it is not true reality; it is only at the moment of self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*) that false views are eliminated and reality is actualized.
The marks manifest spontaneously; they do not come from external phenomena to enter within the body.

The meaning of this samaya is not the same as the previous practice of entering the signless through the contemplation of signs, but is rather the direct observation of the equality of the dharmadhātu and great compassion that is without conditions.
[Commentary]: The phrase "The above statement that this sutra... and so forth is an explanation intended to resolve a doubt.

What has been explained thus far—from the beginning to the end of this sutra—clarifies that it is entirely for the purpose of manifesting the meaning of the three phrases: namely, that the bodhicitta is the cause, great compassion is the root, and skillful means is the culmination.
Why, then, in this [passage], is wisdom instead assigned as the second [element] to serve as the root, while great compassion is placed [elsewhere]?
Regarding the third point: previously, it was explained that the bodhicitta alone serves as the cause, without distinguishing between the two aspects of wisdom (*prajñā*) and mind (*citta*).
Now, this meaning is divided into the three samayas consisting of wisdom and mind;

therefore, one first uses true wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*) to discern right from wrong, and subsequently gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), wherein wisdom constitutes the root and great compassion becomes the third.
Thus, because the sequence of meanings and characteristics is established in accordance with one another, they are not contradictory.
[Commentary] "That is to say, dwelling securely among the sons" is a term that points to a specific teaching;
it refers to the meaning found within the "Secret Treasury for Dwelling Securely Among the Sons" in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "All..."
"O Bhikṣus, just as the great earth produces various medicinal herbs for the use of sentient beings, so too is my Dharma:
it gives rise to the sublime and excellent flavor of the nectar of Dharma, serving as the excellent medicine for the various diseases of the afflictions of sentient beings.
I shall now cause all sentient beings, as well as my own children—the fourfold assembly—to abide entirely within the secret [teachings]."
Regarding the entry into nirvāṇa within the *kośa* (treasury), what is called the "secret treasury"? It is like the three dots of the letter *ī*;

if they are placed side by side, they do not form the letter *ī*, nor do they form it when placed vertically. Only when they are like the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara does one obtain the letter *ī*.
If the three dots were separate, they likewise could not form it. I am also like this: the dharma of liberation is not [attained] in isolation.
The *nirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata’s body is not *nirvāṇa*, nor is the *mahāprajñā* [not *nirvāṇa*]; these three dharmas being distinct is also not *nirvāṇa*.
Because I now abide in these three dharmas for the sake of sentient beings, it is called "entering *nirvāṇa*.
This is like the world's letter *i*; the intent of this sutra is to cause sentient beings to know that the three gates of liberation have a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*).
"Non-different" means it is like the letter *i* (the three dots) abiding within [a circle]; as there is no difference from "me," so it is here as well.
Because the three samādhis are correlated with the three liberations, it says, "it is precisely this wherein the sons abide."
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the previous distinct-time understanding" (this is a marginal note), the current note clarifies the two preceding lines of the commentary.
This means that in the first line, there is the Buddha from whom the Dharma arises, and from the Dharma the Sangha arises; such sequential distinctions of characteristics are *sāmagrī*.

Because their essences (*svabhāva*) are each distinct, they are called the "Three Jewels of Distinct Characteristics. In the second line, these three are of one essence (*ekātmatā*); this is [the meaning of] "one."
The essence of the Three Jewels is *sāma*, which forms a single meaning and is designated simply as "equality" (*samatā*), because there are no two distinct characteristics;
thus it is called "the preceding individual equality.
[Commentary]: Herein, regarding the "three equalities," this refers to the first three *samayas*, from the letter A—the bodhicitta—up to...
The sequential transmission of the syllables *a*, *ā*, *aṃ*, *aḥ*, and *aḥ* without deviation constitutes the meaning of these five syllables.
As for the statement that "a certain class of sentient beings is equal to the Buddhas," this clarifies the meaning of the final expedient means, the long vowel *ā*:
it signifies that while all sentient beings give rise to the bodhicitta, their causes and conditions differ.

The four types are as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: first, one who is able to resolve upon the mind [of enlightenment] upon seeing the inconceivable miraculous transformations and majestic power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
second, one who is able to resolve upon the mind after hearing and developing deep faith in the subtle and sublime True Dharma of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
third, one who, although not seeing or hearing the miraculous transformations of the Buddhas...
Seeing that the subtle and sublime True Dharma—the entire collection of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka—is on the verge of disappearing, and having witnessed this event, he reflects:
"The Bodhisattva-piṭaka is capable of extinguishing the immense suffering of immeasurable sentient beings;

I should uphold the Bodhisattva-piṭaka," and thus he generates the aspiration for enlightenment. Fourth, there are certain classes of sentient beings who, although they do not see or hear the True Dharma...
When the Dharma is about to perish, during the final kalpa, the final age, and the final time, one sees various sentient beings in a state of turbidity and evil,
afflicted by ten secondary afflictions of body and mind: namely, they have much ignorance, much lack of repentance, much stinginess and envy,
much sorrow and suffering, much coarseness and heaviness, much affliction, much evil conduct, and much negligence.
Having seen that this world is now filled with many who are indolent and lack faith, and is being afflicted and disturbed by various secondary afflictions, he thinks:
"In this great, turbid, and evil age that has now arisen, it is already difficult to find anyone who can even give rise to the mind set on the enlightenment of an inferior Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha;
how much more so for one who can give rise to the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? I...
One should resolve to generate the great bodhicitta, thinking: "In this degenerate age, immeasurable sentient beings follow my example and give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment;

seeing the superior power of those who find it difficult to generate such a mind during the final eon, they develop deep faith and understanding in great enlightenment, and thereby initiate the great bodhicitta. And so forth.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "different names for this meaning," it is taught here that abiding in the three samayas means not clinging to any false attachments;
this is the great primary tenet of being free from all obstacles—this is the "tenet" (zong).

If one looks beyond this tenet and finds other distinct names, phrases, or sentences, these are the causes for the arising of obstacles, such as the lack of aspiration and so forth; therefore, it is said [as follows].
Regarding these various names for this meaning,

the *Sūtra Commentary* states: "That which is called 'non-attachment to all deluded attachments' refers to the coarse, subtle, and extremely subtle three types of deluded attachments found within the category of the mind of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*)."
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "not desiring" and so forth: "desire" (chanda) has the nature of longing and aspiration.
Because one possesses this, one is able to apply oneself toward the siddhi of mantras. Now, the failure to give rise to a mind of longing is precisely the cause for the arising of obstacles.
"Lack of desire" (anabhilāṣa) means having no aspiration. "Laziness" (kausīdya) has the nature of indolence; even if [one possesses]...
The mind of desire that does not seek diligently is like drilling for fire that stops as soon as it has not yet grown warm; the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "It is like seeking fire by drilling wood;

if one counts one's breath before the fire emerges, the momentum of the fire is immediately extinguished. The same applies to those who are indolent. Regarding the lack of faith, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Its nature is a defiled state of mind characterized by an inability to endure, delight in, or desire [the truth], virtue, or capability. (The preceding section concludes here.)
If one says they do not wish to believe it now, what are the characteristics [of such a person]? Because of the lack of desire, they do not give rise to aspiration;
because of the lack of faith, they give rise to slander. This is because their practice and understanding are discordant.

[Commentary] "One must not drink alcohol" means that because drinking alcohol serves as a condition for the arising of obstacles, one must not drink it, as it gives rise to various unwholesome states.
As the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Treatise on Wisdom) states, there are thirty-six faults: first, an ugly complexion; second, diminished physical strength; third, manifesting anger;
fourth, ruining one's fields and livelihood; fifth, contracting illness; sixth, failing in study and recitation; seventh, acquiring an evil reputation; eighth... [and so forth].

"Wisdom extinguishes the nine errors; the ten virtuous and good [deeds] prevent falling into the evil realms, up to thirty-six [types of rebirth]. Because there will be much ignorance in future lives, one must not drink.
[Commentary: Regarding the instruction to "spread grass mats and so forth," this passage from the *Cīvaravastu* merely mentions sleeping upon a bed to express a warning.
This is the ultimate expression of caution: since people cannot sleep directly upon a bed, they must rely on auspicious *kuśa* grass;
furthermore, because this is a matter of internal correspondence, the term is added for its symbolic significance.
[Commentary] Regarding the mention of the "Chapter on the Tathāgata" and so forth, this also refers upward to the "Chapter on the Nature of Bodhi.
It states that the nature of bodhi in that chapter exists only as verbal designation; it is free from all marks and is like empty space. It is not earth, water, fire, or wind;
it is not the sun, moon, or the various luminaries; it is not day, night, time periods, years, or kalpas, and so on, up to the statement: "If there were no such things..."
Regarding the various worldly conceptualizations, one should constantly and diligently cultivate the pursuit of the syllables of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Upon hearing the Buddha speak thus, Vajrapāṇi, in order to sever the web of doubt for those who have not yet realized [the truth], addressed the Buddha in verse.
As to what constitutes a Tathāgata, the Buddha again relied upon space to provide a provisional designation (*prajñapti*), and thus it is called the "Chapter on Explaining the Tathāgata."
[Sūtra] Regarding "Awakening has characteristics equal to space," there are four and a half verses that answer the four questions of Vajrapāṇi.
The first verse answers the question: "What is called a bodhisattva? The next one and a half verses answer the question:
"Why is it called a Buddha? The following one verse answers the question: "Who is the Honored One among men? The final verse answers the question: "What is meant by 'suchness' (tathatā)?"
The question that follows and this answer do not follow the proper sequence.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "this meaning is missing from the text of the sūtra" and so forth, this is an answer to Vajrapāṇi’s question concerning why the text of the *Narasūtra* (The Sūtra on the Honored One Among Men) is incomplete.
The commentator has merely cited other sūtras or treatises to provide the answer; hence it is said:
Regarding this meaning, there is a textual omission in the sūtra; now, examining the intent of the commentary (*śāstra*), it appears that the sūtra poses two and a half verses as questions.

The first verse concludes by stating, "Therefore, he is named the Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*)," and the subsequent verse concludes by stating, "Therefore, he is titled Supreme Enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Both of these serve as answers to the question, "What is meant by the Perfectly Awakened One?
However, the response to the further question, "Why is he the Honored One among Men (*puruṣottama*)? is missing. Nevertheless, the wording of the sūtra seems to suggest [this].
It is not lacking because once the Vajra [Holder] has posed the four questions, the Tathāgata must necessarily provide the four answers.

I venture to say that the following verse is precisely the answer to the question, "How is one the Honored One among Men? This refers to the third line of the verse, which states, "Because he has attained the ten powers of a Buddha’s wisdom.
How do we know this line is the answer to the question regarding the Honored One among Men? It is because the hymn praising the Buddha says, "The World-Honored One possesses the ten powers."

It is most rare indeed. Furthermore, it is said that the Honored One of the Ten Powers of Perfect Enlightenment must possess these ten powers upon attaining perfect enlightenment to be designated as the Honored One among Men;
this principle is logically consistent. Moreover, there is no fault of missing textual passages. Please examine this further in detail.
[Commentary]: Although it does not say "ignorance" (*avidyā*) and so forth, the preceding commentary cited the sutra as saying, "Wisdom harms that.
Why, then, is it now said to be "ignorance"? Previously, this followed the Sanskrit original which simply said "that," but here it follows the Tang translation which says "ignorance.
Even though it is not present in the Sanskrit original, its meaning must necessarily exist; since there have been many such precedents above, it says, "although it does not say."
[Commentary]: Regarding "this self-realized realm" and so forth: the realm of self-realization is precisely the *dharmadhātu* (Dharma-realm) and the *bhūtakoṭi* (limit of reality).
Being equal and transcending the path of language, it is termed "Suchness" (*tathatā*). Abiding in such a principle is termed "coming," and likewise [it is termed] "going."
The principle of the Buddha is suchness (*tathatā*); because he has realized it spontaneously and come forth, he is called the Tathāgata.
[Sūtra] Regarding the "Chapter on Worldly and Transcendent Homa Rituals" and so forth:

previously, in the "Chapter on Entering the Maṇḍala," when performing the empowerment for disciples, the methods for the empowerment, offerings, and *homa* were already explained; furthermore, within the Secret Maṇḍala...
Regarding the question-and-answer on the two types of homa rituals—outer and inner, shallow and deep—which are now explained in a separate chapter:
among the many constituent parts of the maṇḍala, this belongs specifically to one particular part.

Furthermore, because the various non-Buddhist practitioners of India all cling to worldly fire rituals as the ultimate goal, my World-Honored One, out of compassion for those who worship fire, [taught this].
The followers of this school further establish a separate chapter on the "Conformity to the Great Root," explaining it extensively based on both principle (*li*) and phenomenon (*shi*).

*Homa* is the general term, while "worldly" and "transcendent" are the specific categories. The name is established by taking the general from the specific; thus, it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound meaning "the *homa* of the worldly and transcendent.

Furthermore, since "dharma" means "method" (*vidhi*) or "upholding" (*dhāraṇa*), one should understand that it is also explained through the distinction between the general and the specific. Therefore, it is called "worldly."
This is the Chapter on the World-transcending Homa Rite.
[Commentary: Regarding "external scriptures such as those on pure conduct," all scriptural teachings outside of the Buddha-dharma are termed "external scriptures.
Here, we specifically take the fire-worship rites from the *Veda* treatises on pure conduct; these are precisely the ritual fire-worship methods of the Brahmins.
In the original language, *Veda* is called *Veda*; here in this land, it is called "Clarification" (*Ming*). Among the non-Buddhist treatises on clarification, there are four types:

namely, the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), the science of logic (*hetu-vidyā*), the science of arts and crafts (*śilpa-karma-sthāna-vidyā*), and the science of medicine and incantations (*cikitsā-mantra-vidyā*).

Within these four *vidyās*, under which category is this fire-sacrifice rite (*agni-hotra*) subsumed? It is subsumed under the science of incantations (*mantra-vidyā*). Why is that? Because those [incantations] also possess mantras.

Because it is the Dharma, those mantras were spoken by whom? They were spoken by Maheśvara and others; therefore, they are called "non-Buddhist scriptures" (*bāhyaka-śāstra*), such as the *Śaucācāra* and so forth.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement that the first is named "Wisdom Fire" (*jñānāgni*) and so on, this explains the sūtra’s phrase: "Wisdom Fire is the foremost; it is named Great."
The three characters for "Indra" (In-tuo-lo) in this context are an explanatory name for Mahendra.

In Sanskrit, Indra is sometimes called "Lord of Honor" (Zun-zhu) and sometimes called "Characterized by Direction" (Zi-fang). Here, we take the character "fang" (direction), which refers to the Vajra Earth-wheel;
therefore, it is called the "Name Characterized by Direction."
[Commentary]: This vajra head with four corners is like that commonly depicted in sculptures and paintings held in the hands of Vajrapāṇi deities;
it is what is called the "Vajra for Subduing Māras."
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "reciting the mantra of the fire of wisdom" and so forth:
this means that one employs the name of the fire of wisdom itself as the mantra, which is *jñānāgnaye*. Here, *jñāna* means "wisdom" and *agni* means "fire."
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "initially generating the bodhicitta," etc., this distinguishes the sequence of the fires.
The former is the bodhicitta, which is the letter *A*; this second [fire] is that which takes great compassion as its root, which is the long *Ā*.
The profound intention of this commentator should further be applied by analogy to establish the ten subsequent fires, namely from *I* (upper) and *Ī* down to *Aṃ* and *Aḥ*, making twelve.

How is it known that this refers to the syllable? It is because the twelfth fire is named "Delusion" (*moha*), which is the place where what was to be done has been accomplished—the site of the tranquil *maṇḍala* (the *dōjō*).

Since it is the syllable *e* (惡), by this principle, when one reaches the point of the ultimate purpose of the *homa* treatise, it is the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*). The wise should reflect upon this.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "its color is blue," etc., this refers to the deity seated upon the wind-maṇḍala holding a white cloth in the hand, shaped like a celestial robe (*devavastra*).
Since it is stated that they "mutually hold white cloths shaped like celestial robes," one should have said "its color is white.
To say it is "blue" is inconsistent with the white cloth; therefore, he asks again. Now, examining this passage, it corresponds to [the section on] Ākāśagarbha.
The *vighāraṇa* rite is the rite of subjugation (*abhicāruka*). In performing any act of subjugation, one should not use white;

rather, it should be said that the hand holds a blue cloth. Furthermore, the commentary explains that its color being blue does not refer to the shape of a garment, but because this Fire Lord assumes the form of wind and dryness, it is said that its color is blue. Thus he asked further.

[Commentary]: These are of the same category as the Vajra-wheel (vajracakra).
