For example, in the third enclosure of the maṇḍala, there are the mudrās of the Vajra-hosts, namely the Vajra-hook (vajrāṅkuśa), the Vajra-noose (vajrapāśa), the Vajra-sword (vajrakhaḍga), the Vajra-wheel (vajracakra), and the Vajra-axe (vajraparaśu).
Because these belong to the category of this wheel, they are so named.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "receiving the fire named, etc.": "Receiving" means to obtain; "food" refers to the *kṣārodaka* (fire-food).
It means at the very time one obtains the fire-food. As for the statement "further questioning," it refers to the forty-second among the previous forty-four types of fires, which says:
"When bestowing the various fires, first use the *vākṣa* fire to bestow it."

Regarding the syllable *la* (領受): if it is understood according to the conventional characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the meaning is distinct; it refers to offering various fire-oblations to the deity Agni using this syllable *la*.
If it is understood according to ultimate reality (*tattva*), it signifies the meaning of the fire of internalized realization (*pratyātma-jñāna*) filling the *dharmakāya*;
thus, the syllable *ra* (受) is used. Because these two [syllables] are mutually related as superior and inferior, let them be further questioned.
Regarding the phrase "having performed the upadhāraṇa," the character *yi* (已) here is redundant; it is originally a character from the Sanskrit script.
This is because the subsequent line states, "by means of the sound of the syllable *oṃ*. In this context, the character *yi* should also be that [Sanskrit] character.
It is because the scribe at the beginning did not recognize the Sanskrit characters and substituted the character *yi* for the syllable *oṃ*.

[Sūtra]: "According to their own forms and colors" means that, as with the fire-gods mentioned above, each has its own distinct form and color—ranging from those with abundant hair and squinting eyes to those whose shape is like the syllable *oṃ*.
Because colors such as yellow, red, black, and white are mutually defined in relation to one another, and are designated as "one's own" only in contrast to others, it is said:
"according to their own [forms and colors]," and so forth.
[Commentary]: "The single nature possessing the three types" means that according to the categories of pacifying (*śāntika*), increasing (*paustika*), and so forth, each possesses three elements:

first, fire; second, the fire deity; and third, the body of the practitioner. Although these three are each distinct in nature, since mentioning one fully encompasses all, it is called "the single nature.
As for the statement that the three locations are combined into one, it refers to the necessity of these three elements being unified.
The first [view] holds that fire is not different from the deity, and the deity is not different from the body;

yet if these do not harmonize as one, they cannot be called "equality," nor can they be called "correspondence. It is impossible for one to attain *siddhi* while losing the meaning of equality and correspondence.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "as above, such as the *yathā-vat* [rites]" and so forth: one must understand the nature and categories of all elements involved in the aforementioned external *homā*, namely, the physical forms and colors of the fire deities, the medicinal substances, the hearths, the fuel, and so on.
This means that one must know that the fire deities have various moods—such as joy or anger—and various colors—such as white or red;

that the medicinal substances have various tastes—such as pungent, bitter, sour, or sweet; that the hearths have various shapes—such as square, round, or triangular; and that the fuel has various qualities—such as fragrance or stench, thorns or smoothness—and so forth, according to their respective characteristics.
If this nature conforms to these activities—pacifying, increasing, or subjugating—and performs the superior, middling, or inferior rites, then they will be accomplished according to one's wishes.
If this fire-method is not obtained, then the fire-method—that is, the *homa* method—cannot achieve the three kinds of accomplishment.
As for the statement that "the internal method is also to be understood by analogy," it means that the present practice of the internal wisdom-fire method is to be compared [to the external].
Even when performing external rites, one attains accomplishment according to one’s will; therefore it says, "the aforementioned [passages], etc.
[Commentary]: "Not like those of the world, etc. means that this fire, named "Wrathful," is the manifestation of the aspect of wrath arising from within a mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);
it is not like the worldly wrath produced by ordinary people, which depends upon an external object.
Its nature is the outburst of anger toward an object that is currently perceived as harmful; thus, it takes a portion of *dveṣa* (hatred) as its essence.
Now, by means of the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*), one illuminates the true nature of this anger, whereby compassion itself becomes its essence.
This is like the Great Compassion Maṇḍala (*mahākaruṇā-maṇḍala*), where from the central womb, the third outer court—the Tathāgata family—is emanated, with Acala as the wrathful *vajra*.
The Lord Candramukha of the Vajra Family acts as the wrathful one for the Lotus Family, and Vighnāntaka acts as the wrathful one for the [Vajra] Family;
by means of the fires of these wrathful deities, they subdue demons such as beginningless ignorance and lead them into the central womb (garbha).
When one understands it thus, because the rite of subduing is performed using the fire of wrath, it is said that this is not like that of the mundane world.
[Commentary]:
Regarding the phrase "on each of the four sides, one [trident] joins with another," this refers to the annotation.

On the four sides of the hearth, one should draw a three-pronged vajra (*triśūla-vajra*) on each side, such that the prongs of these vajras join together like the eight seals (*aṣṭamudrā*). This refers to the "Chapter on the Eight Secret Seals" and...
This is the Maṇḍala Chapter. [Commentary:
Regarding what is said in the *Siddhi* [section], it refers to the twentieth chapter of the *Susiddhikara Sūtra*. [Commentary:
"Mṛttika" (written with the double consonant *mṛ*) means "conjunction"; this refers to the fifth fire-god among the twelve fires.
[This is] merely a name.

[Commentary: Regarding the instruction to "take wind, dryness, and so forth" according to the preceding text, the preceding text refers to the passage on the rite of extinguishing calamities through the wrathful fire.
[Sūtra] Regarding the "Chapter on Explaining the Samādhi of the *iṣṭadevatā*": "Explaining" means to expound upon the *iṣṭadevatā*.

This term generally refers to all the noble ones who follow the maṇḍala, as they are the primary lords and masters of their respective lineages; therefore, they are called *iṣṭadevatās*. There are two types of *iṣṭadevatās*:
first, those of pure form, which means being free from marks (*nimitta*); second, those of impure form, which means possessing marks. There are likewise two kinds of samādhi: the first...

There are two types of siddhi: first, that which can be accomplished through conceptualization (saṃjñā) as the siddhi with signs (sanimitta); second, that which can be accomplished through non-conceptualization (asaṃjñā) as the signless siddhi (animitta).
Now, Vairocana expounds upon what Vajrapāṇi has previously inquired about; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Samādhi of the Honored Deity" and so forth.
[Commentary: "Furthermore, it is like a square jewel facing the moon," and so forth. Here, the square jewel and the round mirror represent the practitioner’s faith;
the sun and moon represent the vows of the Buddhas. If the practitioner’s faith is free from doubt, the vows of the Tathāgatas will necessarily respond.

One must employ this analogy because it is essential to inspire faith while simultaneously clarifying that the principle of resonance and response (*saṃgati-pratibhāsa*) is inconceivable. [Question: What is meant by "square" in the mundane world?
It is an indubitable fact that we currently witness the production of fire from water and the manifestation of light from the sun and moon through the power of the *maṇi* and the mirror.

Yet, among those who follow the stream of mantras, it is rare for those who practice with faith to obtain spiritual realization. Why is this so? The answer is: The fundamental vows of all Buddhas never fail to bear fruit;

however, while many may have faith in the practice itself, few truly believe in the efficacy of the mantras. It is because they rely upon the mantras [merely out of habit] rather than with genuine conviction.

Although there are such skillful means, if one possesses faith yet the mind remains defiled—just as when a mirror or a *maṇi* jewel is obscured by dust and grime—the reflection of the sun or moon cannot enter, and the response of fire or water can never be achieved.

The Buddha taught that causes and conditions are like an echo arising from sound; if the causes and conditions are discordant, how could *siddhi* exist? Furthermore, the Buddha taught that mantras possess [efficacy].
There are two kinds of accomplishment: first, the mundane; second, the supramundane. Both types of accomplishment possess ritual procedures (*dharmavidhi*).
If one seeks mundane accomplishment, it is based on what is taught in the seventh fascicle of this scripture; briefly, it requires five conditions:
First, one must first fully maintain the *samaya* precepts—namely, the three of body, the four of speech, and the three of mind, totaling ten [precepts] in their exoteric and esoteric aspects.

Regarding the two types of precepts, next one should increase and protect the practice of purity; that is, constantly practicing the five repentances three times every day according to the Yoga method:

paying homage to all Buddhas, confessing all transgressions, offering up one’s body as a gift, generating the bodhicitta, rejoicing in merit, requesting [the turning of the wheel of Dharma], and even dedicating the merit while cultivating the three samayas. Gold.
Regarding the third [section], the Method for Purifying Demonic Obstacles through the Great Protection of the Tathāgata Vimalamaṇivicitrasiṃhavikrama-vajra-kavaca-viśuddha-dharmadhātu-citta:

First, perform the ritual for making offerings; visualize the syllable *ra* to purify one’s own mind-ground and the defilements of the maṇḍala site, then generate the five wheels (*pañcacakra*) by means of the five syllables, and subsequently summon the deities and establish the boundary (*sīmābandha*). (etc. Fourth, the arising of inexhaustible benefit for all beings.
One whose mind has been generated [in bodhicitta] should dwell in the yoga-seat and practice the method of recitation:
transforming the seed-syllable into the body of the deity, and so forth, until one is well-established in the fifth stage of the maṇḍala, such as the *lakṣa* [recitation].

At that time, there are further numerous ritual practices, namely: the dismissal of the deities, the dissolution of the boundary, and other various virtuous acts for disciplining the mind during each session.

Not failing in the rules is as explained at length above; if one does not fail in each of the five types of ritual procedures mentioned above, one will attain mundane accomplishments (*laukika-siddhi*).

If there is even a single deficiency, one cannot obtain even minor mundane accomplishments, let alone the supramundane fruit of Buddhahood, the great *siddhi*. Question: There are those who currently practice and employ mantras.
If one can dispel malevolent influences and eliminate illness by reciting and dispatching [the mantra], and if those who are mute can speak, is this not the power of the *mantra*?
Answer: The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states: "This *Mahākaruṇā-hṛdaya-mantra* can even cause flowers and fruit to grow upon withered trees, let alone such matters as these.
It is simply because the path of the Sages has long been distant and the hearts of men have become turbid and deceitful that, when first hearing of the merits of the *mantra*, [doubts] truly arise.

If one admires, recites, and contemplates [this teaching] for a long time with joy, yet the mind gives rise to deviance—whether seeking worldly profit, demanding that others submit, giving rise to various thoughts, desiring to know the affairs of others, or wishing to cause others' illnesses to be cured—if the mind is thus not upright, the spirits will find an opportunity.
Since the person gains profit, the spirits gain many adversaries; therefore, the *Mohe zhiguan* states that the spirits cannot... [intervene].
When a person is possessed by a malevolent spirit, the spirit gains an opportunity to ride upon that person's mind;
it then provides them with its own power, enabling them to know the affairs of one or many people and to cure the illnesses of one or many people.
Those who lack understanding call such a person a "sage. Is this knowledge the knowledge of a sage, or is it the knowledge of spirits and the like? It is certainly not the knowledge of a sage.

This is not knowledge through mantras, but rather knowledge of a ghost; the person themselves does not realize this and is either personally in doubt or free from doubt, yet gives rise to a resolute conviction.
Furthermore, they claim that others cannot produce such views or attachments, harboring overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
If this arises due to the continuous flow of scriptural teachings or the words of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), one should quickly abandon it as something improper. If not...
Quickly abandon [this], for it will long cause harm and lead one into the evil realms. Furthermore, from beginning to end, this sutra does not transcend the three minds:

namely, the bodhicitta, the mind of great compassion, and the mind of skillful means. These three minds are fulfilled by means of the three secrets—namely, the secret of body, the secret of speech, and the secret of mind.
These three secrets are themselves the mudrās, mantras, and *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deities). Such are the mudrās.

One must not exclusively recite mantras, nor should one hastily chant the dharani of one’s tutelary deity (honzon). One must not arbitrarily observe [the ritual] without entering the mandala and receiving instruction from a master.
If one seeks the wish-fulfilling jewel at the spring-pool, one must possess the necessary skillful means (*upāya*) to grasp the true gem;
do not compete for pebbles and rubble, mistaking them for genuine lapis lazuli. Furthermore, do not rashly wield a sharp blade that will instead wound your own body—know this.
Because one must be cautious in this regard, it is necessary to rely externally on the five dharmas and dwell internally in samādhi;
if it were not so, then the conditions of the square bead and the round mirror would not interact with one another.

[Commentary] My private opinion is that the phrase "perhaps first attaining [the image]" and so forth refers to the previous discussion of relying on the observation of painted images, which is termed "having form. From...
The manifestation of the mind is called "formless" (*amūrti*). Now, the Master of the Commentary specifically states that what manifests from the mind is called "having form" (*mūrta*);
furthermore, when one contemplates this form as being like a reflection in a mirror, such that the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) do not arise, this is called "signlessness" (*animitta*).
This is precisely what constitutes the profound contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); hence the words, "I personally maintain," and so forth.
[Commentary] I, the author of this commentary, maintain that these three are not equal; thus, the Master further explains them according to the sequence of practice.
In this sequence, each has two types of meditative aspects: pure and impure. That is to say, first one contemplates the letters and sounds of the scripture, which have two aspects;

next, one contemplates the form of the Honored One, which likewise has two aspects—namely, the gradual refinement and the further refinement. Next, [the contemplation] does not rely on external objects.

Furthermore, to speak more precisely, there are those that are mixed with impurity; observing these three matters separately is called "mixed observation," while observing them collectively is called "unmixed.

As for what is called "pure": if one is led into purity by means of what is not pure, it is not "pure" in the absolute sense; rather, that which is inherently free from defilement from the very beginning is called "pure.
Therefore, it is said: "It is called 'equal' (sama), etc."
[Commentary: As for the phrase "there must be a source," this refers to the letter A.

Regarding the sequence of practice as clarified above, one first relies on the contemplation of individual dependent origination to fully perceive the realm of the maṇḍala, ensuring that each detail is without error.
Thereafter, relying upon Prajñā and taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, one washes away and purifies [all obscurations], whereby the dharmas of accomplishment are attained.
Regarding the phrase "the inconceivable great function of the causal origination of the realms":

if one does not know the sequence of practice—that is, if one does not first recognize the order of the stages of practice—one will merely contemplate the text of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and for the most part misunderstand the intent of the sūtra.

To enter directly into emptiness without relying on the fundamental source is called "direct entry. The "fundamental source" refers to the letter *A*; *A* is the source. It is not [that which is] not.
The place of birth for the arising of bodhicitta and great compassion through skillful means is followed by the sequence beginning with *ā* and so forth;

it is precisely through these sequences of *ā* and so forth that one enters the great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) by taking non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) as the skillful means, namely, the bindu of the syllable *aṃ*.
If one were to proceed directly toward the syllable *aṃ* from the bodhicitta of the syllable *a* alone, without relying on the sequential order of *ā* and so forth, [the goal would not be realized].
The principle of Great Emptiness (mahāśūnyatā) is precisely the sudden-sudden loss of the principles of the Perfectly Sudden (yuanton).

My intention in composing this commentary on this doctrine—to propagate and expound the secret treasury—is to harmonize the two schools of the North and South so that they may equally enter the gateway of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), thereby setting aside the distinction between defilement and non-defilement and transcending the difference between erasing and not erasing; this is recorded here following the Tripitaka.
Because this is explained with particular care and refinement beyond [the standard], it is called "my personal interpretation" (*sīwèi*).
[Sūtra] Regarding the chapter on the Teaching of the Signless Samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*): this also transmits the aforementioned teaching.

Although a practitioner of the mantra path (*mantrayāna*) may, by relying on the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) of the aforementioned samādhi, presently attain the wondrous, signless realm of body, speech, and mind, they have not yet departed from the [limitations of] the mind.
This concludes the summary of frivolous conceptualization (prapañca), leading one into this Middle Way;

by entering the true reality of the mantras of body, speech, and mind, one enters the initial Path of Dharma-Illumination, which is precisely the Samādhi of Ultimate Signlessness. Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Explaining the Samādhi of Signlessness."

[Commentary: "However, 'samādhi' and so forth" refers to the Sanskrit term *samādhi*, which is translated here as "equipoise" (*dengchi*). Its essence is characterized by being free from dullness and agitation;

it is called "equipoise" because it maintains focus on a single object. It encompasses both cause and fruit; in the causal stage, it includes both meditative concentration (*samāhita*) and non-concentrated states, whereas in the resultant stage, it is exclusively concentration.
It consists solely of mind. In Sanskrit, it is called *samāpatti*, which means "attainment" or "realization."
The passage through both the mindless and non-mindless states is precisely this present entry into the three equalities.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the mind is the pure mind," etc.: this mind is free from all marks;

it cannot be apprehended even when sought within samādhi, and because it is like empty space, free from all obstructions and defilements, it is called the "pure mind. Ordinary beings rely upon the portion of the self...

The arising of inversions and the production of various conceptual discriminations is precisely the *manas* (intellect). Now, does this signless samādhi arise from the *citta* (mind) or from the *manas*?
It does not arise from the *citta*, nor does it emerge from the *manas*, nor does it arise from both together; seeking it in these three locations, it cannot be found in any of them.
It arises through the causal conditions of the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm) of true mantras. Although it arises from the *dharmadhātu*, [it is ultimately ungraspable].
Because it arises through causes and conditions, like a phantom or a dream, it is truly unobtainable; therefore, it is said that "the mind is pure," and so forth.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "clinging to these empty dharmas gives rise to many divergent views" and so on: as mentioned above, when observing in this manner, one first proceeds from the perspective of existence.
To enter the signless through the signs—if one were to enter emptiness directly without following the signs, one would lose great compassion and the myriad practices;
by what skillful means could one then enter emptiness? If one becomes attached to such dharmas of emptiness, various heterodox views will arise.

Have you not seen that among the monastics and laity today, many fail to extensively open the scriptural treasuries and, upon hearing the teachings of the Sudden School, immediately dismiss the gradual approach?
Not relying on the gateways of formal practice, yet following a mind that is indolent, self-indulgent, and stained by anger, they learn from one another like dogs barking at a wooden barrier;

therefore, I, Emperor Tianyou, whose sagely wisdom resides within me and whose enlightened model transcends the mundane, have exhausted the two teachings of Nature and Characteristics and mastered the two schools of the North and South.
To exhort this current of practitioners, I must present these fine verses, saying: "If you wish to study the Chan school, first proceed toward..."

The Perfect [Nature] is also not characterized by attachment to the extreme of emptiness through the negation of marks; otherwise, if one were to now destroy these marks and abandon practice, the three miserable realms would soon be before one's eyes.
Those who delight in the Way should inscribe this upon their sashes. Therefore, it is said: "Attachment to this emptiness," and so forth.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that this chapter follows the sixty mental states, all faults and afflictions do not transcend the two characteristics of body and mind.

If one wishes to be free from these two views, one must deeply cultivate the observation of the ten phrases of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) to be introduced into the Middle Way of equality, because all things lack inherent nature (*svabhāva*). As stated in the preceding commentary: "Each and every one is conditioned."
[The text] explains them by removing [the repetitions] according to the sequence of arising.

[Commentary: Since it says, "each and every one is explained according to the sequence of arising," why were they not explained in sequence as sixty mental states and ten phrases of dependent origination?
To resolve this objection, the subsequent passage provides the explanation: "the sequence of the meaning of the explanation," and so forth.

[The Sūtra] states: "The Chapter on Mundane and Supramundane Recitation" also reiterates what was previously taught. That is to say, the methods for reciting mantras and attaining *siddhi* explained in the preceding chapters do not exceed two types:
namely, those with signs (*sanimitta*) and those without signs (*animitta*). Those with signs are called mundane, while those without signs are supramundane.
However, these were merely brief explanations and were not yet complete; it is now, in this chapter, that they are fully resolved.
Because these are selected and categorized into a separate chapter, they are called "the mundane, supramundane, and so forth.

[Commentary]: If any of the constituent branches are lacking—if one performs the mental recitation with a different mode of attention (*manasikāra*) than this, or performs the recitation while attending to the inhalation and exhalation of breath—then there is the fault of deficiency in the branches of the mantra, just as a person’s body has four limbs, and it is deficient if one is missing.
First, that which cannot be recited is likewise so; if it were otherwise, it would lack its constituent parts (*aṅga*) and thus be unfit for accomplishment.
Furthermore, "lacking constituent parts" refers to the essence of the mantra (*mantra-tattva*), which is established based on syllables (*akṣara*) and sounds (*svara*). These include:

syllables with their phonetic components, the causal basis of syllables, the boundaries of syllables, long vowels, short vowels, and syllables possessing vowel-marks (*mātrā*). It is not [the case] that... while the syllables possess vowel-marks... [they are not recited].

If one takes up the sounds with incorrect tones (level or oblique) without relying on the [proper] rules, or takes them up without relying on the pauses (*pada*), all such instances are called "recitation deficient in its constituent parts. [Commentary:
When divided according to the correspondence between the internal and external, there are four types: the supramundane is internal, while the mundane is external; each has its own [distinctions].
Each corresponding division is further differentiated into four types, namely two for the external and two for the internal, making four kinds in total. Regarding the two external types:

the practitioner contemplates this consciousness; knowing that its fundamental nature is such that the seal (*mudrā*) is the syllable (*akṣara*), the syllable is the body, and the mind is serene—when these are all unified as one, this is recitation (*japa*). Furthermore, this syllable is itself the mantra.

Contemplating the body as the inhalation and exhalation, and using this to sustain the body, is called mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*). Reciting this constitutes the two external recitations;
the internal [recitations] should be understood by analogy. Therefore, it is said: "by means of the correspondence between the internal and external," and so forth.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "this internal and external correspondence," etc.: "this" (you) refers to the right side in contrast to the left;

it points to the preceding cited scriptural passage located to the right of the explanation. As for the statement "it is precisely the four kinds of form" (*rūpa*): "form" (*rūpa*) refers to the category of form, and since there are four categories of form, it is said to be "precisely the four kinds of form."
[Commentary: Regarding the recitation of three *lakṣas* and so forth, the meaning of these "three *lakṣas*" is as previously explained in terms of numerical count;
that is to say, *lakṣa* refers to the total number of recitations, where three hundred million is called "three *lakṣas*.
Furthermore, *lakṣa* refers to periods of time—namely, morning, midday, and evening—or divisions of the seasons such as cold, heat, and rain; these are also called "three *lakṣas*. Moreover, *la*...

*Chā* refers to the manifestation of signs, which is the appearance of the three types of signs: heat (*ūṣman*), smoke (*dhūma*), and light (*arci*). Furthermore, *locha* refers to the rites of augmentation (*puṣṭi*) and so forth;

that is to say, when the sign of heat appears, one performs the rite of pacification (*śāntika*); when the sign of smoke appears, one performs the rite of subjugation (*abhicāruka*); and when the sign of light appears, one performs the rite of augmentation.
These are collectively termed the "three worldly *loca*s. Therefore, it is said: "recite the three *loca*s," and so on.
[Commentary: "I, regarding the various sūtras and teachings," etc., means that "I" refers to the Buddha himself.

"Regarding the various sūtras and teachings" refers to the One Great Period Teaching (*ekamahākāla-dharma*), which is termed "various. Generally, when one speaks of *lakṣa* (hundreds of thousands) or more, it is called a "number.
However, this sense of "number" is a term that is incomplete and not exhaustive; it is a statement whose principles are not yet fully exhausted.

[Commentary]: Regarding "the three virtues arise," etc.: when the practitioner perceives the three true marks (*trisvabhāva*), they eliminate the three defilements of body, speech, and mind, thereby attaining the three virtues of the Buddha’s body, speech, and mind; this constitutes a partial realization of the Tathāgata’s merits.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "as in the Mañjuśrī-sūtra," etc., this now cites the method of practicing archery from these two sūtras to explain the meaning of the "target" (daṭa) and to clarify the gradual stages of mantra contemplation practice.
Just as one who practices archery initially focuses their attention on the target;
because they are not yet proficient, they must first shoot at a distant target, then gradually move closer until they can hit the mark. It is the same in sequence here.
The true nature of this body, the true nature of speech, and the true nature of mind—these three are the *lao-yi* (the essential meaning).
Regarding the statement "as it says in the Mañjuśrī Sūtra," that sūtra states: The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī, "Have you entered the inconceivable samādhi?
Mañjuśrī replied to the Buddha, "No, World-Honored One. If I were to enter the inconceivable samādhi, I would then become..."
“World-Honored One, since the mind of the Bhagavat is no-mind, how could I enter the inconceivable samādhi?
Furthermore, World-Honored One, when I first resolved upon the bodhicitta, I said, ‘I shall enter the inconceivable samādhi.
World-Honored One, today I have no such intention to enter the inconceivable samādhi. World-Honored One, it is like a beginner at archery who first...”
He forms this thought: "I shall shoot the leaf. Having succeeded in shooting the leaf, he again forms this thought: "I shall shoot the bark.
Having succeeded in shooting the bark, he again forms this thought: "I shall shoot the wood. Having succeeded in shooting the wood, he again forms this thought: "I shall shoot the iron.
Having succeeded in shooting the iron, he no longer has the previous intention; rather, according to where he previously struck, he is able to pass right through it.
It is also like this: at first, one resolves to seek entry into the inconceivable samādhi; now, that intention is no longer present, thinking, "I shall enter the inconceivable samādhi.
Why? Because this samādhi is inconceivable. When it is said that the Śūraṅgama Samādhi is also like this, that sutra states:
the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, if a bodhisattva desires..."
"How should one train in the Śūraṅgama-samādhi? The Buddha told Resolute Mind: "It is like this:

for example, when training in archery, one first shoots at a large target; having mastered shooting at the large target, one trains in shooting at a small target; having mastered shooting at the small target, one next trains in shooting at a bullseye;

having mastered shooting at the bullseye, one next trains in shooting at a branch; having mastered shooting at the branch, one trains in shooting at a hundred hairs; and having mastered shooting at a hundred hairs, one trains in shooting [at a single hair]."
Having learned to shoot ten hairs with ten hairs, and having learned to shoot one hair with one hair, he is able to shoot a hundredth part of a single hair;
once he has mastered this, he is called a skilled archer who never misses his mark at will.

If such a person, in the darkness of night, wishes to shoot at any sound he hears—whether from a human or a non-human—he does so without exerting mental effort, and every arrow hits its mark. Thus it is.
Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati, if you wish to study the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, you should first study the mind of loving joy (*anurāga-citta*).
Having studied the mind of loving joy, you should study the mind of attachment (*rakta-citta*). Having studied the mind of attachment, you should study great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).

Having studied great loving-kindness, you should study great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Having studied great compassion, you should study the four noble brahma-vihāras, namely: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. You should study these four.
Having trained in the noble holy life, one should cultivate the five supreme supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) as a repayment of virtue;
by constantly training in these powers, one is then able to accomplish the six *pāramitās* and so forth.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "although they have resolved their minds and practice," etc., this refers to those who are like the *icchantikas* mentioned in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

The Sanskrit term *icchantika* carries the meaning of "desire" or "longing. Those who long for saṃsāra and sever their roots of goodness—meaning those who enter the maṇḍala but do not receive the *samaya* vows—are persons of no lineage (*agotra*). Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Those of no lineage have no lineage."
Therefore, even if one generates the resolve for awakening and exerts oneself with fierce diligence, one will ultimately never attain unsurpassed bodhi; it is exactly like this.

[Sūtra] The "Chapter on Entrustment" (Parindanā-parivarta) refers to the standard practice of entrusting the teaching to those who shall preserve it as the sūtra is about to conclude. "Entrustment" (zhù) means to hand over.
It is like a worldly elder who possesses vast wealth and, wishing to entrust it to his son, gives instructions with great care and diligence so that it shall not be lost;
the Tathāgata, the Elder, is likewise possessed of abundant Dharma-wealth which he must entrust to his disciples, giving instructions with great care and diligence so that it shall not be lost.
Therefore, it is called "entrustment" (*parindanā*), which signifies the sense of repeated and continuous succession without interruption.

The terms "successive generations" (累世) and "successive kalpas" (累劫) refer to the entrustment (*parindanā*); thus, they have been transmitted from generation to generation so that the lamp remains unextinguished.

In this regard, "entrustment" (*zhù*) refers to the present, while "succession" (*lèi*) extends through the future; though these terms differ in their specific connotations, they are established as distinct names.

Furthermore, "entrustment" (*fùshǔ*) refers to the intention directed toward the faculties of the recipient, meaning the transmission of the lamp; "succession" (*lèi*) is itself the act of entrustment. Moreover, "succession" (*lèi*) implies repetition—indicating that the Buddha did not grant this teaching lightly. Although...

Because there may be those who are negligent or lax regarding the entrusted resources, it is necessary to repeat the instruction twice or thrice. By doing so, the secret treasury of the One Vehicle will abide long in the world;

thus, there will be no faults such as acting according to one's own whims, yielding to self-indulgence, bestowing the Way upon those of inferior faculties, or transgressing the Dharma through negligence—hence it is called "entrustment" (*zhùlèi*).
[Sūtra] *Namaḥ samantabhadrebhyaḥ svāhā*. This dhāraṇī is called the "Mantra of Empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhāna-pada*).
With Vajrapāṇi as their chief among the various Vajradharas, and Samantabhadra and Maitreya as their chiefs among the various Bodhisattvas, they have received the entrustment of Vairocana Tathāgata;
they are not insignificant, but are the messengers of the Tathāgata who carry out the Tathāgata’s work and shoulder his great responsibility.
Although we harbor joy and uphold this with single-minded devotion, this sutra is the secret within secrets among secrets;
even during the Tathāgata’s own lifetime, there were many who felt resentment and jealousy, let alone in this final age.

Fearing that it may not be sustained by our own power without the empowerment and support of the Tathāgata’s divine mantras, we respectfully join our palms and address the Buddha, entreating him to speak.
The phrases for the empowerment of the Savior cause the Eye of Dharma and the Path to abide long in the world;
at that time, the World-Honored One, in response to the requests of Vajrapāṇi and others, immediately spoke this mantra.

[Commentary]: Regarding "one who transgresses the dharma-ordinance": "transgressing" means to violate. If one fails to accord with propriety in the transmission [of the teachings] and instead acts according to one's own arbitrary whims, this is precisely heedlessness—a violation of the secret dharma-ordinances of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. Such a person incurs the offense of transgressing the dharma-ordinance (*dharmavyatikrama*).
The offense of transgressing the dharma-ordinance refers here to the violation of the *samaya* and the third of the four *pārājika* precepts; namely, the transmission...

A person of the Dharma must skillfully discern the faculties and conditions of others, as well as understand the specific measures of the various Dharma-gates, so that they may administer medicine according to the illness without mistaking the faculties.
If one preaches the profound meaning of emptiness to those who are attached to signs, it will increase their lack of faith;
if one suddenly bestows shallow and superficial gates upon those with sharp faculties, deep roots, and wisdom, it will give rise to contempt in them. Since this brings no benefit to others...
Because it further leads to the commission of transgressions against the precepts, it is said that one "transgresses the dharma rules.
[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the three phrases mentioned above:

as explained previously, the meanings of these three phrases—taking bodhicitta as the cause, great compassion as the root, and skillful means as the culmination—are precisely the two benefits of the mantra.
The Buddha exhorted his disciples: "You should abide in the meaning of the letter *A*, that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen;

this is precisely because of the bodhicitta of the letter *A*. Following this, there is the practice of the fundamental non-arising of the long *Ā* and so forth, which subsequently realizes the principle of the letter *Aṃ*, the fundamental non-arising.
Abiding within these three phrases of the secret teaching, one performs all acts for one's own benefit."
If one does not accord with these various activities for the benefit of others and enters directly into emptiness, this is to abide in the state of negligence (*pramāda*).

Negligence means being dissolute and unrestrained. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Its nature is to be dissolute and unrestrained, such that one is unable to guard against or cultivate the defiled and pure categories;
its function is to obstruct non-negligence, increasing evil and diminishing the good. If one abides in this...
This constitutes a *pārājika* offense within the Secret Teachings; hence it is said, "Furthermore, regarding the superior [level]," etc. [Commentary]:

To be an enemy of humans and devas means that if a bodhisattva does not deeply contemplate the causes and conditions of sentient beings' origins and ends, nor teaches the Dharma according to their differing faculties, they become an enemy of humans and devas.
Furthermore, if an ācārya dwells in negligence and transmits the teachings inappropriately, he likewise becomes an enemy of humans and devas.
Both teacher and disciple shall fall into the three evil realms; since evil itself becomes their kin, they can never again be born among humans or devas in the wholesome realms.
Because humans and devas are thus their enemies, it is said that they are "enemies of humans and devas."
[Commentary: "Excluding my disciples" refers to those who abide in the True Word (mantra) Esoteric Teaching by means of stabilizing the mind;
furthermore, only those whose minds have long since realized its essence and who possess deep faith without doubt are fit to receive it.

Excluding these, others—such as worldly non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who have not yet entered this [teaching]—are all termed "non-Buddhists," as they have not yet entered the True Dharma of the True Word.

For those such as these whose faith is not yet perfected and who are unable to endure hearing the secret treasury, one should first provide instruction, benefit, and joy within the profound teachings of other manifest doctrines (*vyakta-dharma*) as a skillful means.
One may only explain the Dharma of the three phrases once they have given rise to faith and delight; if faith and delight have not arisen, one must not hastily teach it.
This is the profound intent of this entrustment; therefore it says, "except for my disciples and others.

[Commentary] Regarding the further clarification of external traces and so forth: although what has been discussed above regarding the characteristics of the distinctions in the transmission of the Dharma pertains only to the internal mind, we now further distinguish them by means of external manifestations.
This is also to prevent those with inferior faculties from erroneously receiving the transmission.

Dwelling in heedlessness, one also speaks of external traces; for example, by observing the tracks of sentient beings such as birds and beasts, one immediately knows their differences regarding whether they fly or walk, their size, and their qualities of good or evil, ease or distress, and so forth.

Now, by observing the traces of the birth-times, the *nakṣatras*, days, and hours encountered by disciples, as well as their manifest physical forms and colors, one immediately knows whether that person is good or evil, tranquil or agitated, broad or fierce, and foolish or wise.
Only after discerning such various distinctions of characteristics can one appropriately bestow the dhāraṇī-mantra practices.
If one does not understand this and bestows them haphazardly, one often errs; the fault regarding the roots and bonds is the same as mentioned before.
Therefore, it is said that the mantra-ācārya must thoroughly understand the treatises on yin-yang and divination; if one does not practice these, one cannot be so named.

Question: Since one who masters various arts may not act as an *ācārya* for others, and since other sutras state that a bodhisattva must not study divination, calendrical calculations, or the prognostication of good and ill fortune, does this not contradict the teachings established by the Tathāgata?
Answer: When other sutras say "must not," they refer to practicing such things without cause or for the sake of profit.
Therefore, because it would obstruct the Path, it is said that one must not [practice it]. This does not mean that one should not study it at all;

rather, practicing it does not obstruct the Path provided it is not for the sake of seeking profit. Since the primary aim is to benefit sentient beings, one may integrate these practices without contradiction.
[Commentary: This refers to Rāhula; "Rāhula" is the son of the Buddha, and it is phonetically close to the Sanskrit term.
The analysis of characteristics herein is for the most part no different from that in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

[Commentary]: The "Path of the Dharma-Eye" (*dharmacakṣus*) is the path of great wisdom that opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*). If one realizes the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), this corresponds to the first fruit;
if one realizes the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), it corresponds to the first stage (*bhūmi*). Furthermore, "eye" refers to the five eyes:

the flesh eye, the divine eye, the dharma eye, the wisdom eye, and the Buddha eye. The Buddha possesses all of these; here, however, we clarify this dharma eye specifically to distinguish it from the other four. Thus, it is as follows:

The sphere traversed by all Buddhas is called the "Path" (*mārga*); since the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) is itself the Path, it is referred to as the "Dharma-eye Path" according to the appropriate application of the two grammatical interpretations:
the *adhikaraṇa-sādhana* (locative/substratum) and the *karmasādhana* (objective/action).

[Commentary: As for those who ask further questions regarding the meaning of the phrases not yet explained, it is likely because this mantra possesses eleven functions that are so vast they cannot easily be set down in writing;
thus, they are urged to inquire further. Now, relying on the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment, I shall briefly point out the corresponding meanings of the preceding and following phrases.
Should there be anything that is not appropriate, I pray you will delete it.
Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāvairocana-abhisambodhi-vikurvaṇa-adhiṣṭhāna Sūtra: The Explication of the Secret (Yanmi Chao), Scroll Ten (End)
